practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the succession crisis in England in 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Four rival claimants pursued the throne after Edward’s death — Harold Godwinson, William of Normandy, Harald Hardrada of Norway and Edgar Atheling — with overlapping claims based on promise, oath, treaty and royal blood.
• Edward the Confessor was childless, so the Witan had to choose a successor; this council of leading earls and bishops elected Harold on 6 January 1066.
• Edward’s deathbed gesture to Harold and an earlier 1051 promise to William created competing ‘promises’ that each side used to justify its claim.
• Harold had reportedly sworn an oath to support William while in Normandy around 1064, which Norman writers used to portray his coronation as oath-breaking.
• Why it mattered: with four claims in play and no rule to settle them, the throne could only be decided by force, which brought two invasions in a single autumn.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the events that led to Harold Godwinson’s coronation as king in January 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Edward the Confessor’s long childless reign meant the question of succession was open well before his death; he had made gestures to William in 1051 and to Harold by 1066.
• On his deathbed Edward extended his hand to Harold and commended his kingdom to him; this gave Harold a public claim that the Witan could endorse.
• The Witan met immediately at Westminster on 6 January 1066, the day of Edward’s funeral, and elected Harold king because England needed an adult ruler to face the threats forming abroad.
• Harold was crowned the same day at Westminster Abbey, the first king to be consecrated in Edward’s new church — tying his rule symbolically to the dead king’s legacy.
• The result of these linked steps was that within 24 hours of Edward’s death, England had a new, anointed king — setting up the confrontations with William and Hardrada that would define the rest of the year.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Witan’s decision to choose Harold Godwinson as king in January 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Witan’s decision gave Harold immediate legitimacy under Anglo-Saxon custom — he was the formally chosen king of a unified, anointed realm.
• The choice meant Edgar Atheling, the only male of the old West Saxon line, was passed over — demonstrating that the Witan prioritised an adult, militarily capable ruler over royal blood.
• In the longer term it gave Norman writers their central propaganda point: from October 1066 onwards William’s side described Harold as an oath-breaker, an interpretation we now know was post-conquest framing.
• It shows the Anglo-Saxon system of elective kingship in action one final time before the Normans replaced it with hereditary, primogeniture-leaning succession.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the way William of Normandy built his claim to the English throne between 1051 and 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William claimed that Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne during a visit in 1051, when relations between Edward and the Godwin family had collapsed.
• Norman sources insisted Harold Godwinson had sworn a sacred oath to support William’s claim while a guest in Normandy in around 1064, an oath taken over holy relics.
• William secured Pope Alexander II’s blessing in 1066, including the gift of a papal banner, which framed the invasion as righteous Christian reform.
• William was already a battle-tested ruler in Normandy, with a reputation for ruthless effectiveness that strengthened the credibility of his claim abroad.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Edgar Atheling in the succession crisis of 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Edgar represented the strongest blood claim to the throne — grandson of Edmund Ironside and direct male heir of the West Saxon royal line.
• His age (around 14) and lack of military following meant the Witan passed him over for Harold; this shows that Anglo-Saxon kingship in 1066 valued capability above pure descent.
• Importance later: Edgar was briefly elected king after Hastings in October 1066 before submitting to William at Berkhamsted, which made him a rallying point for later revolts.
• The fact that the Witan chose an adult earl over a royal teenager helps disprove the Norman framing of Harold as an obvious usurper — the choice reflected the political reality of facing two foreign invasions.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of why the succession was disputed.

‘What drove 1066 was ambition, not law. Each of the four men wanted the richest crown in northern Europe, and the promises, oaths and treaties they talked about were cover for that.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the causes of the succession crisis of 1066? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: personal ambition, not law or custom, drove the crisis of 1066.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• Each claimant pressed his case because the prize was uniquely valuable: England’s geld revenue, mints and royal demesne made the throne worth fighting for.
• William chose to invade despite the risks of a sea crossing because his political position in Normandy depended on big victories abroad.
• Harald Hardrada’s claim through the old Cnut-Magnus treaty was thin; he pursued it because he was the most ambitious warrior in northern Europe and Tostig Godwinson’s exile gave him a pretext.
• Tostig’s personal grievance against his brother Harold turned a Norse expedition into a serious northern threat that forced Harold to fight at Stamford Bridge.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• Anglo-Saxon custom — the role of the Witan, the importance of a deathbed gesture, the king’s right to nominate — framed every claim and made the Witan’s choice of Harold immediately legitimate inside England.
• Religious law gave William’s side decisive weight: the papal banner from Alexander II turned the invasion into a sanctioned crusade, which custom and ambition alone could not have produced.
• Edgar Atheling’s blood claim, rooted in inheritance custom, would resurface in revolts after 1066, showing that custom continued to matter.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the creation of the Danelaw for the development of Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed points of significance, addressing both significance at the time and significance over time, with precise factual support (Edington 878, Guthrum’s baptism, place-name evidence, Norse loanwords).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with relevant detail; some sense of long-term legacy.
Developing: Significance described rather than explained; mostly short-term consequences.
Emerging: Generalised statements about Vikings without focused significance.

Indicative content:
• At the time: the Danelaw stabilised a frontier after years of raids, allowing Wessex and the Danish-settled north to coexist and trade.
• At the time: it formalised a legal and cultural divide (wapentakes, carucates) that shaped land law for centuries.
• Over time: place names ending in -by, -thorpe and -toft mark the area to this day; everyday English words such as sky, egg, law, them are Norse in origin.
• Over time: the Christianisation of the Danes after Guthrum’s baptism set a pattern of integration rather than expulsion that recurs across the unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Alfred the Great’s defence of Wessex.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed points of significance, addressing both immediate impact and longer-term legacy, with precise detail (Athelney, Edington 878, burhs, fleet, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with detail.
Developing: Description of Alfred’s actions without explaining significance.
Emerging: Generalised praise of Alfred.

Indicative content:
• At the time: Edington (878) prevented a complete Viking conquest of England and preserved an Anglo-Saxon kingdom.
• At the time: the burh network changed how the kingdom defended itself, enabling rapid response to future raids.
• Over time: Alfred’s administrative and military reforms underpinned his successors’ reconquest of the Danelaw, leading to a single English kingdom under Athelstan.
• Over time: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle shaped how the period was remembered and the very name ‘the Great’, unique among English kings.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Lindisfarne raid of 793.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing the raid’s short-term shock and its longer-term place in shaping Britain’s relationship with Scandinavia, with precise detail (Alcuin, monastic wealth, opening of three centuries of Viking activity).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with detail.
Developing: Recounts the raid without explaining wider significance.
Emerging: General statements about Viking violence.

Indicative content:
• At the time: a wealthy, undefended Christian monastery was attacked, exposing the vulnerability of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms’ coastlines.
• At the time: Alcuin’s letters and chronicles preserved the event, shaping the way contemporaries saw the Norse threat.
• Over time: the raid is the conventional opening of nearly three centuries of Norse arrivals that produced the Danelaw, the North Sea Empire and ultimately the Norman Conquest.
• Over time: it warns against treating 1948 (Windrush) as the start of migration to Britain — large-scale arrivals were already shaping the country a thousand years earlier.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Christianisation of the Danes for British identity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed significance points addressing both immediate religious change and the longer pattern of integration, with precise detail (Guthrum’s baptism 878, Norse-built churches, hybrid place names).
Secure: Two clear points of significance with detail.
Developing: Describes conversion without explaining significance.
Emerging: General statement about religion.

Indicative content:
• At the time: Guthrum’s baptism in 878 turned the Danelaw boundary from a religious as well as political frontier into a shared Christian world.
• At the time: shared Christianity made intermarriage and shared law enforcement easier, easing the integration of Norse settlers.
• Over time: it set a pattern for Britain in which incoming groups (Normans, Huguenots, later Irish Catholics) integrated rather than being expelled.
• Over time: it complicates the modern claim that British identity is ‘Christian’ in some pure Anglo-Saxon sense — the Christianity that prevailed was already shared with the Norse newcomers.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Viking arrivals in Britain in the ninth century were similar to or different from later migrations to Britain (such as the Huguenots in the seventeenth century).
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct similarities or differences, each supported with precise detail from across the period.
Secure: Two valid points with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; second weak or repetitive.
Emerging: Vague comparison without specific detail.

Indicative content:
• Difference: Vikings arrived as armed raiders and conquerors (Great Heathen Army 865); Huguenots arrived as Protestant refugees (after 1685) seeking asylum, not conquest.
• Similarity: both groups settled and integrated economically — Norse settlers farmed and traded across the Danelaw; Huguenots brought silk-weaving and finance to London.
• Similarity: both left a lasting linguistic footprint — Norse vocabulary in everyday English; French-derived terms in textiles and finance.
• Difference: the Vikings imposed their own legal system in part of the country (Danelaw); Huguenots adapted to existing English law and church structures.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for our understanding of this period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed significance points addressing both contemporary purpose and long-term influence on the historical record, with precise detail (begun in Wessex in the 890s, multiple copies, continued to 1154).
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Describes the Chronicle without explaining significance.
Emerging: Vague statement about written history.

Indicative content:
• At the time: the Chronicle gave Alfred’s court a written record of West Saxon achievement, useful for political legitimacy.
• At the time: it spread to monastic centres outside Wessex, creating the first sustained narrative of an English-speaking people.
• Over time: it remains the chief contemporary source for the Viking Age in Britain — without it, our knowledge of Edington, the Danelaw and the Norse rulers would be much thinner.
• Over time: its preservation shapes the questions historians can ask — the Norse perspective survives mainly through the eyes of the people they fought.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a memorandum by French foreign minister Théophile Delcassé to the French Chamber of Deputies, March 1895.
‘For two decades since the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, France has stood alone. The new accord with Russia changes this. Our eastern partner doubles every soldier France can put in the field, and the German general staff in Berlin must now reckon with a war on two fronts whenever it considers war on one.’

Source A suggests that the Franco-Russian Alliance ended France's isolation and created a new problem for Germany. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Delcassé says France has ‘stood alone’ for two decades since the loss of Alsace-Lorraine.
• Russia ‘doubles every soldier France can put in the field’.
• Berlin must now reckon with ‘a war on two fronts whenever it considers war on one’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The alliance was ratified in January 1894, ending Bismarck's twenty-year effort to keep France without allies.
• The two-front problem it created was the puzzle the Schlieffen Plan was later designed to solve.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Bismarck’s diplomatic system unravelled between 1888 and 1894.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Wilhelm II accession, Bismarck dismissal, lapse of Reinsurance Treaty, French loans to Russia, Franco-Russian Alliance); reaches the 1894 alliance through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1888: Wilhelm II inherited the German throne, determined to be his own chancellor.
• March 1890: Wilhelm dismissed Bismarck (‘Dropping the Pilot’).
• 1890: Wilhelm allowed the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia to lapse, leaving Russia diplomatically exposed.
• 1891 onwards: French banks financed Russian railway and industrial projects, building economic ties.
• August 1892: secret Franco-Russian military convention drafted.
• January 1894: the Franco-Russian Alliance was formally ratified, ending French isolation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from the diary of Prince Bernhard von Bülow, German diplomat and later chancellor, recorded in 1893 and published in his memoirs.
‘We have allowed the wire to Russia to be cut. The Tsar will not forget. France, with her wealth and her hatred of us, will buy what Berlin would not give. The result must be an entente of opposites — republic and autocracy — against us.’

Source C: An extract from a leading article in The Times of London, 5 January 1894, on the announcement of closer Franco-Russian ties.
‘British policy must reckon with a new fact. The European balance has shifted. While London has held to splendid isolation, Paris and St Petersburg have built a partnership of mutual defence. The continent is no longer arranged as Bismarck left it.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of the Franco-Russian Alliance on European diplomacy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Bülow blames Wilhelm for letting the Reinsurance Treaty lapse and predicts a Franco-Russian alignment despite ideological differences. Provenance: a contemporary diary by a senior German diplomat, but published later as memoirs which can be self-serving. Own knowledge: the Reinsurance Treaty did lapse in 1890; French loans to Russia began in 1891; the alliance was ratified in January 1894 — confirming Bülow’s prediction.
Source C — Content: argues British isolation looks weaker because the European balance has shifted. Provenance: leading article in a major British newspaper at the moment of the alliance’s announcement — informed contemporary commentary, but reflecting a particular British liberal viewpoint. Own knowledge: by the late 1890s Britain was reconsidering Splendid Isolation, leading eventually to the 1904 Entente Cordiale.
Judgement: B is highly useful as insider commentary on German strategic error but limited by its memoir provenance; C is useful as informed contemporary reaction but speaks only to British perceptions.

practice_questions.text:
‘The decisions of Wilhelm II were the main reason European diplomacy shifted between 1890 and 1894.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Wilhelm forced Bismarck out in March 1890 and then let the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse, leaving Russia without a German guarantee.
• His impulsive style made Germany look an unreliable partner in St Petersburg.
• Without that gap in German policy, France would have had no opening to fill.

Disagree:
• France had wanted Alsace-Lorraine back since 1871, and that motive had nothing to do with Wilhelm.
• Russia needed French money for railways and industry whatever Berlin did; French loans began in 1891.
• Bismarck's system was already strained - the Three Emperors' Alliance had lapsed in 1887 over Balkan rivalry.
• The naval visit to Kronstadt in July 1891 showed the two states drawing together before the treaty lapsed.

Judgement: Wilhelm's decisions speeded the shift up, but French and Russian interests were pushing the two states together anyway.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British Foreign Office briefing paper to Lord Salisbury, dated February 1894.
‘Information from St Petersburg confirms that the military convention between France and Russia is now ratified by the Tsar and the President of the Republic. The instrument is defensive in form but its effect is plain: the Continent is divided into two armed groups. Britain may continue to stand apart, but the cost of doing so will rise year by year.’

Source F suggests that British officials already saw the Franco-Russian Alliance as dividing Europe into two armed camps. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The convention is ‘defensive in form but its effect is plain’.
• The Continent is now ‘divided into two armed groups’.
• Britain may stand apart, but ‘the cost of doing so will rise year by year’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The alliance was ratified in January 1894 and ended two decades of French isolation.
• Britain kept to Splendid Isolation for another decade, then signed the Entente Cordiale in 1904 and the Anglo-Russian Convention in 1907.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how France escaped diplomatic isolation between 1890 and 1894.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the 1894 alliance through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 1890: Wilhelm II allowed the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia to lapse, leaving Russia without a German guarantee.
• 1891: French banks began funding Russian state loans, deepening economic ties.
• July 1891: a French naval squadron paid a high-profile visit to the Russian port of Kronstadt, signalling closer relations.
• August 1892: French and Russian general staffs drafted a secret military convention.
• December 1893: Tsar Alexander III and the French president confirmed the convention.
• January 1894: the Franco-Russian Alliance was formally ratified, ending two decades of French isolation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Galen for the development of medicine in medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Importance at the time: Galen’s Theory of the Four Humours gave medieval physicians a complete framework for diagnosis and treatment, structuring how illness was understood from c1000 onwards.
• Importance at the time: his anatomical writings became the textbook used in medical training at universities such as Salerno, Bologna and Oxford for over 1,000 years.
• Importance over time: Galen’s authority became the very thing the Renaissance had to overturn — Vesalius’s 1543 corrections and Harvey’s circulation theory in 1628 only mattered because Galen had been so dominant.
• Importance over time: his fusion of natural philosophy with a divinely-ordered body made his ideas attractive to the Christian Church, which helped preserve them through monastic copying.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement about why Galen mattered.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with relevant examples covering both at the time and over time.
Developing: Some explanation of significance, mostly focused on at the time, with limited reach into later periods.
Emerging: Simple description of who Galen was; little explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: a ‘zodiac man’ diagram from a fifteenth-century English physician’s folding almanac. The drawing links each part of the body to the star sign thought to govern it, and beside it a table tells the physician when it is safe to bleed a patient.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying how medieval doctors decided on treatment?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: the diagram ties each body part to a star sign and sets out safe days for bleeding, so astrology was built into ordinary diagnosis.
• Content: it is a working tool rather than a theory book, so it shows what a physician actually did at the bedside.
• Provenance: folding almanacs were carried and used by practising physicians, so this reflects real practice rather than what a scholar thought should happen.
• Contextual knowledge: physicians also used uroscopy and the pulse, and treated by the theory of opposites; the diagram fits that wider Galenic system.
• Limitations: it covers one part of diagnosis, shows nothing about whether patients recovered, and says nothing about the barber-surgeons and wise women most people actually saw.
• Judgement: very useful for the beliefs behind medieval treatment, much less useful for the care of ordinary sick people.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which medieval physicians and barber-surgeons were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: physicians trained at universities such as Oxford by reading Galen in Latin; barber-surgeons learned through apprenticeship and practical work.
• Difference: physicians diagnosed using uroscopy, pulse and astrology; barber-surgeons did practical tasks such as bleeding, tooth-pulling and bonesetting.
• Similarity: both worked within the framework of the four humours — bleeding by a barber-surgeon was prescribed using Galen’s system.
• Similarity: both were paid services available mainly to those who could afford them; the rural poor relied on wise women.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Has communication been the main factor in why Galen’s ideas dominated medicine in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to communication and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh communication against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of communication as the main factor:
• Latin manuscripts copied in monasteries (St Albans, Canterbury, Salisbury) preserved Galen’s writings when most other classical texts were lost.
• Universities such as Salerno and Bologna taught directly from Galen’s books, locking his ideas into formal medical training.
• Translation routes through Toledo and Salerno carried Islamic commentaries on Galen back into Britain.

Weighed against religion:
• The Church controlled education and approved Galen because his hierarchical body fit Christian theology — without religious endorsement, communication alone could not have spread him.
• The Church also restricted dissection, protecting Galen’s anatomy from challenge.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Galen himself wrote with such confidence and completeness that no rival framework existed; later figures like Hippocrates also shaped the system.
• Without an individual capable of producing such a comprehensive system, communication would have had nothing to spread.

Judgement: Communication was the means but religion provided the protection and the role of the individual provided the content. The strongest answers identify communication as a multiplier rather than the cause itself.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others, with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples comparing the named factor to others; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them; judgement is asserted rather than substantiated.
Emerging: Lists factors without comparison or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Hippocrates for medieval medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Hippocrates established clinical observation and ethical practice as the foundation of medicine, shaping the medieval doctor’s training.
• At the time: the Hippocratic Corpus was used as a teaching text in medieval universities alongside Galen’s writings.
• Over time: his approach (observe, record, predict) outlived the four humours — modern clinical practice is still rooted in observational diagnosis.
• Over time: the Hippocratic Oath shaped the ethical framework that physicians from Sydenham in the 17th century onwards explicitly invoked.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with relevant examples.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Simple identification of who Hippocrates was.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of university training for medieval physicians in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: training meant reading Galen in Latin, debating texts and memorising authority rather than examining patients.
• At the time: it produced doctors who diagnosed by urine chart, pulse and the zodiac man and treated by the theory of opposites.
• At the time: dissection was rare and closely controlled, so bodies were used to confirm Galen rather than to test him.
• Over time: the same training kept Galen in place for centuries, which is why the challenge had to come from anatomists such as Vesalius in 1543.
• Over time: the gap between the university physician and the practical barber-surgeon shaped the low status of surgery until the 1745 split from the barbers.
• Limitation: most people never saw a university-trained physician, so this mattered more for medical ideas than for everyday care.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the idea of Manifest Destiny on US policy in the 1840s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked back to Manifest Destiny through an explicit causal chain; precise factual support (Polk’s 1844 election, Texas annexation 1845, Mexican-American War 1846–48, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo 1848).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail and some causal linking.
Developing: Effects identified but partly described rather than explained; thin causal links.
Emerging: Generalised statements about expansion without clear effects or links.

Indicative content:
• Polk’s presidential platform (1844) made acquiring Texas, Oregon and California explicit policy.
• Annexation of Texas (1845) and the Mexican-American War (1846–48) were justified as carrying out a manifest duty.
• The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) added all of present-day California, Nevada and Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming.
• The doctrine hardened attitudes to the Plains nations: their land was treated as already destined to be American.

practice_questions.text:
Has the idea of Manifest Destiny been the most important reason for westward expansion in the 1840s?

• Manifest Destiny
• Push and pull factors

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs Manifest Destiny against other factors and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support across both bullets and other relevant material; examiner-style judgement (e.g. ‘the doctrine was decisive because it converted material push factors into a sense of moral duty’).
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement made.
Developing: Both bullets covered but treated as a list rather than weighed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet covered or general narrative without judgement.

Indicative content:
• Manifest Destiny: O’Sullivan 1845, Anglo-Saxonism, Providence, Polk’s 1844 election platform, justification for Mexican-American War.
• Push and pull factors: 1837 Panic, soil exhaustion, urban overcrowding, Oregon valleys, gold strikes, religious freedom for Mormons.
• Other relevant material: improved transport (steamboats, early railroads), missionary reports, treaty acquisitions (Louisiana 1803, Texas 1845, Oregon 1846).
• Judgement: top answers argue that material factors created the demand, but Manifest Destiny supplied the moral cover that turned migration into national policy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of geography on American attitudes to the West before 1845.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects of the physical geography on attitudes, with precise detail (Long 1820, ‘Great American Desert’ label, school maps, the role of the 100th meridian, scarce timber and water); explicit causal links.
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail and some causal links.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about geography without explaining attitudes.

Indicative content:
• Stephen Long’s 1820 expedition stamped ‘Great American Desert’ on official maps, shaping policy and schoolbook geography for two decades.
• Lack of timber, water and reliable rainfall west of the Mississippi made eastern farming methods look impossible.
• The Rockies and the Sierras were treated as barriers to be crossed quickly, encouraging a focus on the Pacific coast as the real prize.
• These attitudes only began to shift in the 1840s when push and pull factors and missionary reports recast the Plains as a route, not a destination.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of Manifest Destiny.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a school textbook published in 1893.
“The frontier was the gift of America to the world. Each new acre opened in the West renewed the energies of the Republic and offered a fresh chance to honest, hardworking men.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a university history textbook published in 1990.
“Manifest Destiny dressed up dispossession in the language of duty. Beneath the rhetoric of God and Providence lay a simple fact: someone already lived on the land that was being claimed.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, precisely-supported differences drawn from both interpretations.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support from each interpretation.
Developing: One clear difference; second weak or repetitive.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone without specific differences.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 presents Manifest Destiny as a positive force (‘gift to the world’) while Interpretation 2 presents it as a justification for harm (‘dispossession’).
• Interpretation 1 focuses on the white male settler experience; Interpretation 2 foregrounds the people already living on the land.
• Interpretation 1 frames expansion in moral and patriotic terms; Interpretation 2 strips away the moral language to describe a transfer of land.
• Interpretation 1 stresses opportunity and renewal; Interpretation 2 stresses cost and concealment.

practice_questions.text:
Why might the two interpretations of Manifest Destiny in the previous question give different views?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise contextual knowledge of historiographical change.
Secure: At least one clear reason rooted in provenance or context, briefly supported.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’ rather than ‘why’.
Emerging: Restates what each interpretation says.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: Interpretation 1 is from 1893, the Frontier Thesis era when expansion was celebrated; Interpretation 2 is from 1990, after revisionist scholarship that foregrounded conquest and Native experience.
• Audience and purpose: a 19th-century school textbook was meant to build patriotism; a late-20th-century university text was meant to challenge inherited stories.
• Evidence: writers in 1893 had little access to Native voices; writers in 1990 could draw on tribal histories and 20th-century scholarship.
• Top answers explain WHY the two writers reach different verdicts, not what each verdict is.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the geography of North America that shaped attitudes to westward expansion before 1845.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with at least one precise factual point.
Secure: Two valid features with brief support.
Developing: Two features identified but one undeveloped.
Emerging: One feature only or generalised description.

Indicative content:
• The Great Plains: a vast treeless grassland west of the Mississippi, labelled the ‘Great American Desert’ on the 1820 Long map and seen as too dry for eastern-style farming.
• The Rocky Mountains: a high north-south barrier with few passes, making the journey slow and dangerous and reinforcing the idea that the West Coast, not the interior, was the real destination.
• Rivers and rainfall: scarce reliable water west of the 100th meridian made established eastern farming methods look impossible.
• The Pacific coast: fertile valleys (e.g. the Willamette in Oregon) and natural harbours pulled settlers across the continent rather than tempting them to settle the Plains.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Declaration of Breda helped bring Charles II back to the throne in 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Declaration won over moderate opinion by promising a pardon for most Parliamentarians, which made it safer for former Roundheads to accept the king's return rather than fight to keep him out.
• By offering 'liberty to tender consciences', it reassured Dissenters that they would not face immediate persecution — though Parliament later overturned this with the Clarendon Code.
• The promise to pay the army's arrears removed the most dangerous obstacle: a hostile army of around 40,000 men. General Monck was able to disband most of the New Model Army peacefully.
• By referring every difficult issue (religion, land, indemnity) back to Parliament, it established that Charles returned by parliamentary invitation, not by conquest — strengthening Parliament's long-term position.
• The carefully limited promises also meant that the new king kept his options open on patronage and ministers, allowing him to reward supporters such as Monck and Hyde.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Convention Parliament of 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was not summoned by a king. The Long Parliament had been dissolved and the Convention met in April 1660 on General Monck's authority — making it technically illegal until Charles II later confirmed its acts.
• It was elected with a clear royalist majority. Many MPs had previously sat under Charles I and the new House of Commons accepted the Declaration of Breda within days of meeting.
• It passed the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion in August 1660, pardoning most Civil War actions but excluding the regicides.
• It voted Charles II a fixed yearly income of around £1.2 million from customs and excise — an amount that proved far too small in practice.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about General Monck’s march south in 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Monck's disciplined army was the only force capable of imposing order on the rival army factions in London. Without him, England might have collapsed into a third Civil War.
• He insisted on free elections rather than a continuation of the purged Long Parliament — this was the decisive step that allowed a royalist majority to be returned.
• He provided cover for Charles II's negotiations with Edward Hyde at Breda, signalling to royalists that the army would not block a Restoration.
• Over time, his actions established the principle that a peaceful return of the monarchy was possible — a precedent later echoed in 1688 when William of Orange's army backed another constitutional settlement.
• His personal reward (Duke of Albemarle, Master of the Horse) showed how Charles II used patronage to bind former Parliamentarian generals into the new regime.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the problems the Restoration settlement left unsolved.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Parliament continued to control taxation. Under both the Commonwealth and the Restoration settlement, the Crown could not raise major new taxes without parliamentary consent — customs duties and the hearth tax were voted by Parliament.
• Religious tension remained unresolved. Both before and after 1660, England contained large numbers of Dissenters (Presbyterians, Independents, Quakers, Baptists) who could not accept the official church.
• The army was still a key political question. Cromwell's New Model Army had been politically powerful; after 1660 the question of who controlled the small standing army would remain a flashpoint.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion settled scores after the Civil War.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It allowed most former Parliamentarians and New Model Army soldiers to return to civilian life without fear of arrest — important for stability, since this group included thousands of men with military experience.
• By excluding the regicides, it satisfied royalist demands for revenge without provoking a wider purge. Ten were executed; others fled to the Netherlands or New England.
• The exhumation and hanging of Cromwell, Ireton and Bradshaw was a public statement that the Republic had been a crime — the displayed skull on Westminster Hall acted as a permanent visual warning.
• Over time the Act made it harder for old Civil War grievances to be raised in court, helping to bury the conflict at a legal level even though religious and political tensions persisted.
• It also created a class of dispossessed regicide families and exiled radicals, some of whom would surface again in plots such as the Rye House Plot of 1683.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Restoration of 1660 changed the relationship between Crown and Parliament far more than it preserved it. The king came back on Parliament’s terms.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the Restoration settlement of 1660? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The Crown lost its prerogative courts (Star Chamber abolished 1641, not restored) and feudal income, meaning the king depended on parliamentary grants for the first time.
• Charles II returned by parliamentary invitation, not by conquest — establishing the principle that Parliament could create as well as serve a monarch.
• Parliament increasingly used finance as leverage: the chronic gap between the king's income and his needs forced repeated negotiations.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The monarchy, House of Lords and Church of England were all restored, with bishops and the Book of Common Prayer back in place.
• The king kept the right to choose ministers, direct foreign policy and command the (small) army.
• In law, all acts of the Republic were declared void — the legal fiction was that the reign of Charles II began in 1649, denying any constitutional break.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the relationship between citizen and state in Britain in c1170 was different from the relationship today.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In c1170 most people were unfree serfs tied to a lord's land, with no political voice; today every adult citizen has the legal right to vote, protest and stand for office.
• In c1170 the king ruled by divine right with no Parliament; today Parliament is sovereign and the monarchy is ceremonial.
• In c1170 the only formal challenge to royal power came from the barons and the Church; today challenge is institutionalised through elections, the courts and a free press.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two clearly distinct ways, each fully developed with specific evidence.
Secure: Two ways with some supporting detail.
Developing: Two simple points or one developed point.
Emerging: One simple point or vague comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the seven factors framework in studying the changing relationship between citizen and state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: each factor (war, religion, chance, government, communication, economy, ideas) names a real driver of change in different periods, helping historians explain why protest happened when it did.
• Significance over time: tracking factors across all four parts of the course shows how the same forces (e.g. ideas of representation) reappear and evolve from 1265 to 1965.
• It enables comparative judgement: by comparing how war drove change in 1646 and 1918, students reach the level of analysis the question asks for.
• It guards against single-cause explanations, which are the commonest weakness in factor essays.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time, with specific examples from at least two parts of the course]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both then and over time, with specific evidence from multiple periods.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence; may favour one period.
Developing: Some explanation of significance; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Description of factors with little analysis of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the widening of citizen rights in Britain between c1170 and the present day.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, each step was narrow: Magna Carta (1215) gave due process to free men only, and the 1265 Parliament summoned property-owning knights and burgesses, not ordinary people.
• At the time, each step still bound the ruler: 1215 tied new taxes to the common counsel of the realm; 1649 showed that a king could be tried and removed by his own subjects.
• Over time the franchise widened by Act of Parliament — 1832, 1867, 1884, 1918 and 1928.
• Over time citizenship grew beyond the vote: the Race Relations Acts of 1965, 1968 and 1976, and the Human Rights Act 1998.
• Over time the pattern matters as much as the dates: change came in waves driven by organised pressure, not by smooth evolution.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: 'Ideas have been the main factor in changing the relationship between citizen and state in Britain.' Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arguments for ideas as main factor: Lockean natural rights driving 1689 Bill of Rights and 1776 American Revolution; Leveller demand for manhood suffrage at Putney 1647; suffragette slogan 'Deeds not words' built on belief in equality.
• Arguments for the role of the individual: Simon de Montfort, Wilberforce, Pankhurst, Doreen Lawrence — but none of them acted alone.
• Arguments for war: English Civil War; First World War accelerating 1918 franchise; Second World War shaping the welfare state.
• Arguments for the economy: 1381 poll tax; 1815 Corn Laws; 1926 mining wages; 1981 unemployment driving Brixton.
• Judgement: ideas may be primary because they outlive their carriers, but they only translate into reform when economic and political conditions allow.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Top band rewards a sustained argument addressing the named factor and weighing it against at least two others, with examples from at least two parts of the course]

Mastering: Sustained, substantiated argument addressing the named factor and weighing against at least two others, drawing on multiple periods.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant comparison; may underweight one factor.
Developing: Some argument with basic comparison; explanation limited.
Emerging: Single-factor or single-period response.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the role of individuals and the role of ideas have been similar in driving change in Britain.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both have produced lasting reform only when conditions allowed: Wilberforce's parliamentary campaigns succeeded because Quaker networks and abolitionist petitions had built public pressure; Lockean ideas reshaped politics because the Civil War had already broken royal absolutism.
• Both can be misread as sole causes: crediting one individual or one idea ignores the war, religion or economic context that made change possible.
• Both reappear across the course: individuals (Montfort, Cromwell, Pankhurst, Lawrence) and ideas (representation, equality, rights) recur in every period, allowing comparative judgement.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, fully developed.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of judgement, rather than listing, in answering the 16-mark factors essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time of writing: the essay asks for a substantiated overall judgement, not coverage of every factor.
• Significance over time in students' performance: inventory-style answers are the commonest reason able candidates miss the top band.
• It models historical thinking: real historians weigh causes against each other, they do not just list them — students who do this are practising a transferable skill.
• Without judgement, comparison is impossible: a student cannot say a factor is 'more important' without first taking a position.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both for individual answers and for the discipline more broadly]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of why judgement matters, with specific evidence.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the wartime alliance moved from agreement at Yalta in February 1945 to open disagreement at Potsdam in July–August 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Yalta agreements, Roosevelt’s death, German surrender, Trinity test, Potsdam disputes); reaches Potsdam through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• February 1945: Yalta produced agreement on four-zone occupation, free elections in liberated Europe and Soviet entry into the war against Japan within three months of German surrender.
• April 1945: Roosevelt died and was replaced by Truman, who was more suspicious of Stalin’s intentions, narrowing the diplomatic warmth that had carried Yalta.
• May–July 1945: Germany surrendered on 8 May; Soviet troops occupied most of Eastern Europe and the promised elections did not materialise.
• 16 July 1945: the USA tested the first atomic bomb at Trinity, giving Truman a weapon that altered the balance of negotiation before Potsdam opened.
• 17 July–2 August 1945: Potsdam confirmed the ‘Four Ds’ for Germany and the Oder-Neisse border, but exposed deep splits over Eastern European elections and reparations.
• 26 July 1945: Attlee replaced Churchill mid-conference, signalling to Stalin the political instability of his western partners.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the disputes at Yalta and Potsdam shaped the future of Germany between February 1945 and August 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the post-Potsdam shape of Germany through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• Yalta agreed Germany would be divided into four zones of occupation, with Berlin similarly divided though deep inside the Soviet zone.
• Yalta postponed reparations totals, leaving the issue to be resolved later.
• Germany’s surrender on 8 May 1945 brought Soviet, American, British and French troops into their respective zones, putting the Yalta plan into practice.
• Potsdam confirmed the four zones and added the ‘Four Ds’: denazification, demilitarisation, democratisation and decentralisation.
• Potsdam set the German-Polish border at the Oder-Neisse line, transferring large areas to Polish control.
• Reparations would now be taken zone-by-zone, with limited cross-zone exchange — a compromise that allowed each occupier to run its zone differently and prepared the ground for two German economies.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a memorandum by Charles ‘Chip’ Bohlen, the State Department’s Russian expert and Roosevelt’s interpreter at Yalta, written for internal US use shortly after the conference in February 1945.
‘The Marshal speaks of friendly governments along his frontier in the same breath that he signs a declaration promising free elections. We must accept that these two ideas, in his mind, are not in conflict; in ours, they cannot both be honoured. The Polish question is therefore the test of whether the alliance can survive the peace.’

Source A suggests that the Polish settlement agreed at Yalta was unlikely to last. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Stalin treats ‘friendly governments’ as compatible with free elections, while the Americans see the two as contradictory.
• Stalin signed the Declaration on Liberated Europe but is already attaching a security condition to it.
• Bohlen argues the two ideas cannot both be honoured at the same time.
• The Polish question is described as the ‘test’ of the alliance, implying its failure would unravel cooperation.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Stalin had already installed the communist Lublin government in Poland before Yalta met.
• The Declaration on Liberated Europe promised free elections, but no free election was held in Poland in 1945.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from Stalin’s remarks at Yalta on 6 February 1945, recorded in the official British minute of the plenary sessions.
‘For Russia, the question of Poland is not only one of honour, but one of security. Twice in thirty years, Germany has invaded Russia through the Polish corridor. We need governments to our west which are loyal, not hostile. The Soviet Union cannot accept any other solution.’

Source C: An extract from Truman’s diary entry of 17 July 1945, the first day of the Potsdam Conference.
‘Stalin came in to see me before the meeting. He is a hard-headed bargainer; one must give to get. He wants Eastern Europe; we want Japan and a stable Germany. The atomic test in New Mexico has changed the picture in ways he cannot yet see.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the breakdown of cooperation between the wartime allies in 1945. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Stalin frames Poland as a Soviet security issue, citing twice-invaded territory. Provenance: an official British minute of Stalin’s own words at Yalta — close to a primary record of his stated position, though shaped for an Allied audience. Own knowledge: the German invasion of 1941 began a war that cost perhaps 27 million Soviet lives; the Soviet demand for ‘friendly’ governments was rooted in this trauma.
Source C — Content: Truman casts Stalin as transactional and the atom bomb as a quiet game-changer. Provenance: a private diary on the day of a major meeting — useful for capturing immediate impressions but coloured by Truman’s own self-image. Own knowledge: the Trinity test had occurred the day before; Truman would mention the bomb to Stalin on 24 July, though Stalin already knew through Soviet intelligence.
Judgement: Both are useful but partial — B reveals Soviet logic in Stalin’s own words, C reveals American instincts at the moment Potsdam began — together they show why the alliance frayed before either side took an obviously hostile step.

practice_questions.text:
‘The change of leaders between Yalta and Potsdam was the main reason the wartime alliance broke down by August 1945.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945 and Truman, who replaced him, was far more suspicious of Stalin.
• Churchill lost the general election and Attlee took his place at Potsdam on 28 July, mid-conference.
• Truman pressed hard for free elections in Eastern Europe in a way Roosevelt had not at Yalta.
• Stalin argued that constant changes of leader showed the democracies were unreliable partners.
Disagree:
• Churchill wrote of an iron curtain in his telegram of 12 May 1945, before either leader changed.
• Stalin ignored the Declaration on Liberated Europe in Poland whoever sat in the White House.
• The Trinity test of 16 July 1945 would have reached Potsdam under any American president.
• Reparations and the meaning of friendly governments were structural disputes that pre-dated the change.
Judgement: the change of leaders speeded up a breakdown that the disagreements over Poland, Germany and reparations had already begun.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Potsdam Conference exposed the disagreements between the Allies between 17 July and 2 August 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; reaches the end point through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 16 July 1945: the USA tested the first atomic bomb at Trinity, the day before the conference opened.
• 17 July 1945: Potsdam opened with Soviet troops already in control of most of Eastern Europe.
• 24 July 1945: Truman told Stalin of a powerful new weapon; Stalin, told by his own spies, showed little reaction.
• Late July 1945: Truman pressed for free elections under the Yalta declaration; Stalin answered that Soviet security needed friendly governments.
• 26 July 1945: Attlee replaced Churchill after the British election result, changing the Western side mid-conference.
• 2 August 1945: the conference closed having agreed the Four Ds and zone-by-zone reparations, but with no agreement on Eastern Europe.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the royal court in the government of Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The court was a travelling household of around 1,500 people that moved between palaces such as Whitehall and Hampton Court and made summer progresses through nobles’ estates.
• Access to the queen was tightly controlled through the Privy Chamber, where only senior ministers and favourites such as Robert Dudley could meet her in private.
• Patronage — appointments, monopolies, lands and titles — was distributed at court, binding ambitious nobles and gentry to the Crown.
• Court ritual and image-making, including portraits and processions, performed Elizabeth’s authority in public.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how patronage bound the nobility to Elizabeth between 1568 and 1603.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Patronage allowed Elizabeth to reward loyal nobles with lands, monopolies and offices, binding them to the Crown without the expense of a standing army.
• It set rivals against each other — Cecil against Leicester, then Robert Cecil against Essex — so ambitious men competed for the queen’s favour rather than combining against her.
• It extended royal authority into the counties, since Lord-Lieutenancies and Justice-of-the-Peace appointments were used to manage local militia and the law.
• When patronage broke down — Essex losing his sweet wine monopoly in 1600 — it directly contributed to rebellion, showing the system’s limits.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Elizabeth’s upbringing and education for the way she ruled after 1568.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Her humanist education in Latin, Greek and theology gave her the confidence to argue directly with ministers and bishops — visible in later disputes with Parliament over the succession.
• Her imprisonment in the Tower under Mary I taught caution and secrecy, which shaped her habit of delaying decisions on marriage and war.
• Her popular touch — cultivated during her uncertain youth — helped her play the role of ‘Gloriana’ on progresses and in speeches.
• Significance over time: these qualities supported a 45-year reign in which a Protestant female ruler survived plots, excommunication and the Armada.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about monopolies and offices as rewards at Elizabeth’s court.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Monopolies on traded goods such as sweet wines were granted to favourites, allowing them to charge a fee on imports.
• Appointments such as Lord-Lieutenancies and Justices of the Peace gave nobles authority over county militia and law in return for loyalty.
• Court favourites such as Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, gained access to the Privy Chamber, the most valuable form of patronage.
• Lesser gentry and clients reached the Crown through chains of intermediaries — for example, through Burghley’s household.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Elizabeth’s character shaped the way she governed.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Caution and delay — on marriage and on intervention abroad — meant the regime avoided rash commitments but frustrated ministers and Parliament.
• Public image-making (the Rainbow and Armada portraits, progresses) projected authority that compensated for the absence of an heir or husband.
• Her temper inside court (slapping courtiers, throwing a shoe at Walsingham) reminded ministers that final authority lay with her.
• Her humanist learning allowed her to dominate council debate and theology arguments, reinforcing her personal control.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Elizabeth ruled England through her own personality. Her ministers and Parliament followed where she led.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the way England was governed between 1568 and 1603? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Patronage flowed from the queen personally; lands, monopolies and offices were her gift, which bound nobles to the Crown.
• Elizabeth’s caution, image-making and personal authority over the court controlled the speed and direction of policy — for example, refusing to name an heir for 45 years.
• Even her ministers’ power depended on her favour: Burghley remained influential because she trusted him, and Essex fell when she withdrew patronage.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• William Cecil and Walsingham ran day-to-day government and intelligence; without their administration the regime would not have functioned.
• Parliament granted taxation and passed laws (e.g. the religious settlement and Poor Laws) that the Crown depended on.
• Local government — Justices of the Peace, county gentry — enforced law without direct royal supervision.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (an SPD pamphlet from 1912 arguing that the Kaiser still controls all real power) and Interpretation B (a 1900 article in a liberal magazine arguing that the Reichstag's growing influence is steadily democratising Germany) on the nature of political power in Imperial Germany. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A claims that genuine power remained with Kaiser Wilhelm II despite the elected Reichstag — the Chancellor was appointed by the Kaiser, the army answered to him, and SPD voters had no representation in cabinet.
• Interpretation B claims that the Reichstag's growing role and the wide male franchise show Germany moving towards democracy — bills had to pass parliament and parties were becoming more organised.
• Main difference: A focuses on who appointed the executive (the Kaiser), while B focuses on the elected lower house and the franchise.
[Mastering (4): identifies the key difference and supports it with specific points from each interpretation. Secure (3): identifies the difference with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each interpretation with weak comparison. Emerging (1): summarises one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1912 SPD pamphlet stressing the Kaiser's continued autocratic power) and Interpretation B (a 1900 liberal article stressing the rise of parliamentary government) give different views about political power in Wilhelm II's Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written at different times and react to different events — the 1900 article was written before the 1908 Daily Telegraph affair, while the 1912 pamphlet followed the SPD's election victory and showed how that vote had not changed who governed.
• They were written for different purposes and audiences — the SPD pamphlet wanted to mobilise workers against the system; the liberal article wanted to reassure middle-class readers that reform was happening peacefully.
• They use different evidence — the SPD writer focused on cabinet appointments and the army; the liberal writer focused on the franchise and Reichstag debates.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason fully explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again rather than explaining why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Wilhelm II's dismissal of Bismarck in 1890 on the political system of Imperial Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Power drifted from the experienced Chancellor to the Kaiser himself — Wilhelm II appointed weaker successors (Caprivi, then Bülow from 1900) so that big decisions on foreign and naval policy were taken by the throne.
• The careful balance between Junkers, Catholics and socialists that Bismarck had managed broke down, leaving the SPD growing unopposed in the Reichstag while no socialist was ever admitted to government.
• Prussian conservative dominance in the Bundesrat continued, blocking reforms wanted by southern states and by the rising urban middle class.
• Wilhelm's personal interventions, such as the 1908 Daily Telegraph affair, shook even conservative confidence in his judgement and contributed to Bülow's resignation in 1909.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects supported by precise dates/names; clear causal reasoning. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed effect or two underdeveloped effects. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how power was shared in Imperial Germany between 1890 and 1914.
You may consider:
• the role of the Kaiser and the Chancellor
• the powers of the Reichstag and the Bundesrat.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Kaiser kept the most important powers under the 1871 constitution — commanding the army, directing foreign policy and appointing the Chancellor; Wilhelm II used these powers more personally than Bismarck had done.
• The Chancellor was responsible to the Kaiser, not the Reichstag, so weaker Chancellors after 1890 (Caprivi, Bülow, Bethmann-Hollweg) struggled to manage parliament when the Kaiser interfered.
