• The Reichstag, elected by all men over 25, could approve laws and budgets but could not choose or remove the government; the SPD's 1912 victory had no impact on cabinet membership.
• The Bundesrat, dominated by Prussia's seventeen seats out of fifty-eight, could veto constitutional change — meaning Junker conservative interests were entrenched.
• Conclusion: power was shared in name but concentrated in practice; the system kept democratic forms while preventing democratic outcomes.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and a substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both bullets covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet covered well or both covered superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised description without judgement.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a modern textbook claiming Imperial Germany was already a 'paralysed' political system before 1914) and Interpretation B (a 1980s academic study arguing that gradual democratisation was visible by 1912) on whether the Kaiserreich was politically reformable. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A argues the system could not adapt — competing interests (SPD voters, Junkers, the Kaiser, southern states) cancelled each other out, so no major reform passed in the years before 1914.
• Interpretation B argues genuine democratic change was happening — the SPD had become the largest party, the franchise was wider than in many neighbours, and parliamentary practice was strengthening.
• Main difference: A focuses on outcomes (no reform passed); B focuses on processes (parties and voters becoming more powerful even if cabinet stayed the same).
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): difference identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one side only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the rapid growth of the SPD between 1890 and 1914 on Imperial German politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The SPD grew from a marginal party to the largest in the Reichstag by 1912, polling more than 4.25 million votes — this exposed the gap between the elected parliament and the unelected cabinet that excluded all socialists.
• Bismarck's earlier attempts to crush the party with the Anti-Socialist Laws (1878-90) had failed; SPD strength after 1890 forced even conservative Chancellors to consider welfare reforms to keep workers loyal.
• The Junker elite and the Kaiser became increasingly alarmed by socialism, encouraging policies of distraction such as Weltpolitik and the Navy Laws aimed at uniting voters around imperial prestige.
• The presence of a large socialist vote that could never enter government created long-term frustration with the constitution — a tension still unresolved when war broke out in 1914.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with precise figures/dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed effect or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Korea moved from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 to the outbreak of war in June 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (38th parallel division, the two 1948 republics, the 1949 Chinese communist victory, the Acheson speech, Soviet rearmament of the North); reaches the June 1950 invasion through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• August 1945: Japan surrendered; Korea was divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and US occupation zones.
• 1948: two rival republics emerged — Kim Il Sung’s DPRK in the north, Syngman Rhee’s ROK in the south — each claiming to rule all of Korea.
• October 1949: Mao’s communists won the Chinese Civil War, transforming the strategic balance in Asia.
• January 1950: US Secretary of State Dean Acheson placed Korea outside the US ‘defence perimeter’, which Stalin read as a signal that Washington would not fight for the south.
• Spring 1950: Stalin and Mao agreed to back a North Korean invasion; Soviet T-34 tanks and combat-experienced soldiers strengthened Kim’s army.
• 25 June 1950: North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the steps by which the Cold War spread from Europe to Asia between 1947 and 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Berlin blockade, NATO, communist victory in China, Acheson speech); arrives at the 1950 Korean situation through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• March 1947: the Truman Doctrine pledged US support to any ‘free people’ threatened by communism — making containment global.
• 1948–49: the Berlin blockade hardened East-West divisions and showed superpower confrontation could be local.
• April 1949: NATO formed, formalising US commitment to defend non-communist allies.
• October 1949: Mao’s communist victory in China shifted the Cold War centre eastward.
• February 1950: Sino-Soviet Treaty allied Beijing and Moscow, alarming Washington.
• January–June 1950: Acheson’s speech, accusations Truman had ‘lost China’, and Soviet authorisation for Kim’s plan combined to make Korea the next flashpoint.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how rival regimes developed in Korea between 1945 and 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained narrative with three or more linked events, precise factual detail on Kim, Rhee, the two republics and border clashes; reaches the 1950 stand-off through a clear chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events present but loosely linked.
Emerging: Thin or muddled.

Indicative content:
• 1945: Soviet occupation of the north placed Kim Il Sung in power; American occupation of the south backed Syngman Rhee.
• 1946–47: Joint US-Soviet talks on reunification collapsed; trade and movement across the 38th parallel ended.
• August 1948: the Republic of Korea was proclaimed in the south with Rhee as president.
• September 1948: the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea was proclaimed in the north with Kim as leader.
• 1948–49: communist guerrilla activity in the south was crushed by Rhee; Soviet weapons flowed to Kim’s army.
• 1949–50: thousands died in border clashes along the 38th parallel; both leaders publicly demanded reunification on their own terms.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the 1949 communist victory in China changed the situation in Korea.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain showing how Mao’s victory shifted the strategic balance; precise detail (PRC declared October 1949, Sino-Soviet Treaty 1950, McCarthyism, Acheson speech, Stalin’s green light); arrives at the June 1950 invasion through linked events.
Secure: Three or more linked events with some causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• October 1949: Mao’s communists declared the People’s Republic of China; Nationalists fled to Taiwan.
• Late 1949: Republicans in the US Congress accused Truman of ‘losing China’, narrowing his political room to retreat further in Asia.
• February 1950: the Sino-Soviet Treaty bound Beijing to Moscow, raising fears of a coordinated communist push in Asia.
• Spring 1950: Mao agreed to release Korean troops who had fought in his army to return to North Korea, strengthening Kim’s forces.
• Stalin’s thinking shifted: with China communist, the cost of backing Kim looked low and the gains looked high.
• June 1950: Kim invaded the south, expecting US inaction and Chinese protection if it went wrong.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Kim Il Sung came to lead a Soviet-armed state in northern Korea between 1945 and 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Linked analytical narrative with precise detail on Kim’s background, Soviet sponsorship, the 1948 DPRK and Soviet rearmament; arrives at 1950 capability through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events present but loosely linked.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Pre-1945: Kim was a Korean communist who had fought as a guerrilla against Japan in Manchuria; Soviet contacts dated from this period.
• August 1945: Soviet forces entered northern Korea; Kim returned with them as a trusted communist organiser.
• 1946–48: Soviet authorities suppressed rivals and confirmed Kim as the dominant political figure in the north.
• September 1948: the DPRK was declared with Kim as Premier.
• 1948–49: Soviet advisers built a North Korean People’s Army equipped with T-34 tanks, artillery and air support.
• 1949–50: Korean veterans returning from Mao’s armies further strengthened the force; by spring 1950 it numbered around 135,000.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Syngman Rhee’s southern regime became established and unstable between 1945 and 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events; precise detail on Rhee’s background, US occupation, the 1948 ROK, suppression of left-wing uprisings, weak army and border clashes; reaches the 1950 stand-off through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1945: Rhee returned from US exile with American backing as the leading anti-communist Korean figure.
• 1946–47: US military government in the south struggled with strikes, food shortages and political violence.
• August 1948: the ROK was proclaimed with Rhee as president, after UN-supervised elections held only in the south.
• 1948–49: Rhee crushed left-wing uprisings on Jeju Island and elsewhere with thousands of civilian deaths.
• 1949–50: Washington deliberately denied Rhee tanks and heavy artillery, fearing he would invade the north.
• Spring 1950: thousands died in border clashes along the 38th parallel; Rhee publicly threatened to march north to reunify Korea.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of mass production in the American motor industry in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A moving assembly line at Ford’s Highland Park plant carried each car past stationary workers, each doing one repeated task — the time to build a Model T fell from over twelve hours to ninety minutes.
• Standardised parts were used across every Model T, so cars could be built quickly and repaired anywhere — Ford famously offered the Model T ‘in any colour, so long as it’s black’.
• Workers were paid $5 a day, double the going rate, so that they could afford to buy the cars they were making.
• Mass production was rolled out beyond cars to consumer goods such as refrigerators and radios, which dropped sharply in price across the decade.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature with detail]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did hire purchase and advertising drive the growth of the consumer society in 1920s America?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hire purchase let ordinary Americans buy expensive goods on credit — by 1929 about 75% of cars and 50% of household appliances were bought this way, multiplying demand far beyond what cash purchases could have produced.
• ‘A dollar down and a dollar a week’ schemes made middle-class consumption normal rather than shameful, removing the cultural brake on borrowing.
• Advertising spend tripled across the decade to nearly $3 billion a year; firms used psychology, film-star endorsements and bright colour magazine ads to sell feelings (modernity, glamour) rather than just products.
• Radio — from 1920’s KDKA Pittsburgh to 618 stations and ten million sets by 1929 — carried adverts into the home every evening, reaching audiences no print campaign could match.
• The two effects reinforced each other: advertising created the desire for the latest washing machine, hire purchase removed the obstacle to owning one, and the result was a self-sustaining consumer cycle.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation tracking how hire purchase and advertising fed the consumer society, with precise figures and a chain of effects.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail on both factors.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one factor or to description rather than effects.
Emerging: Identifies hire purchase or advertising without explaining their effect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two Republican government policies of the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Fordney–McCumber Tariff (1922) raised the average duty on taxed imports to around 38%, protecting US factories from European competition.
• Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon cut the top rate of income tax from 73% in 1921 to 25% by 1925, leaving wealthy Americans with more money to invest.
• Laissez-faire: presidents Harding, Coolidge and Hoover deliberately kept federal regulation of business to a minimum, summed up by Coolidge’s line that ‘the chief business of the American people is business’.
• Hostility to trade unions: courts banned strikes and union membership fell across the decade, keeping wages flexible for employers.

[4 marks — 2 marks per policy: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did Henry Ford change the American economy in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ford’s moving assembly line at Highland Park cut Model T production time from over twelve hours to ninety minutes, dropping the price from $850 in 1908 to under $300 by 1925.
• By 1929 there were over 26 million cars on American roads — about one car for every five Americans — transforming travel and stimulating the demand for petrol, road-building and suburbs.
• The car industry pulled forward demand for steel, rubber, glass, leather and paint, making it the keystone industry of the decade.
• Ford’s $5-a-day wage policy raised expectations of working-class living standards and meant his own workers could buy his cars — demonstrating the link between high wages and high consumption.
• Mass production methods spread from Ford to other manufacturers (electrical goods, household appliances), turning the assembly line into the model of American industry.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of effects across multiple sectors with precise detail and a clear sense of how Ford’s methods reshaped the economy.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail on Ford’s impact.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description of the assembly line.
Emerging: Identifies Ford as important without explaining how he changed the economy.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on the Boom of the 1920s: mass production, or Republican government policies? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of mass production:
• Ford’s assembly line cut the cost of a Model T from $850 to under $300, making car ownership realistic for working families and pulling steel, rubber and glass with it.
• Mass production methods spread to refrigerators, radios and washing machines, creating the goods that the consumer society then bought.
• Without affordable goods, hire purchase and advertising would have had nothing to sell.

In support of Republican policies:
• The 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff shielded US factories from European competition, allowing prices and profits to rise.
• Mellon’s tax cuts (top rate from 73% to 25%) freed wealthy Americans’ money to invest in new factories and stocks.
• Laissez-faire allowed mass production techniques to be rolled out without regulation, child-labour disputes or worker protection.

Judgement: The strongest answers note that the two factors worked together — Republican policies created the protected, low-tax environment in which mass production techniques could be most profitable. A defensible verdict is that mass production was the engine but Republican policies were the fuel.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument weighing both factors, with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both factors but weighs them unevenly; judgement is asserted rather than substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each factor without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Fordney–McCumber Tariff and Mellon's tax cuts on the American economy in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff raised the average duty on taxed imports to around 38%, making foreign products expensive and encouraging Americans to buy from US factories.
• This protection meant domestic firms could maintain higher prices and profits, fuelling investment in new plant and machinery.
• Mellon cut the top rate of income tax from 73% in 1921 to 25% by 1925, leaving wealthy investors with billions more to channel into shares and corporate bonds.
• These freed funds drove the Wall Street boom; share prices rose steeply across the decade as the demand for stocks outpaced new issues.
• A side effect was inequality: high tariffs and low income tax rewarded shareholders far more than wage earners or farmers, who faced higher prices for everyday goods and shrinking export markets — a problem covered in Lesson 2.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects linking tariff and tax policy to investment, the stock market and inequality.
Secure: Clear explanation of effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one policy or to description.
Emerging: Identifies the policies without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Henry III’s reign shaped the kingdom Edward I inherited in 1272.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Civil war between the king and his barons (1264–65) left England exhausted, with armed bands of ‘disinherited’ rebels still active when Edward came home; this meant Edward needed to restore order and secure the loyalty of the magnates from his very first days as king.
• The Provisions of Oxford (1258) and Simon de Montfort’s parliament (1265) had set a precedent that the great barons could supervise or even capture the king; Edward inherited a tradition of baronial assertion that pushed him to clarify and defend royal rights through inquiries and statutes.
• Henry III’s reliance on foreign favourites and expensive foreign schemes (the ‘Sicilian Business’) drained the treasury; this caused Edward to launch the Hundred Rolls inquiry in 1274–75 to find out what crown lands and revenues had been lost.
• Local government had become corrupt, with sheriffs and bailiffs taking bribes and private liberties expanding; this caused Edward to challenge baronial franchises through the Quo Warranto inquiries and to begin the long programme of legal reform.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking at least three effects of Henry III’s reign directly to Edward’s situation in 1272–74, using precise terminology.
Secure: Two clear effects developed with relevant detail and explicit links to Edward’s inheritance.
Developing: Some effects identified but explanation is partial or descriptive rather than causal.
Emerging: Simple statements about Henry III with no clear link to what Edward inherited.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the political settlement Edward I inherited in 1272.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A royal council ruled in Edward’s name while he completed his crusade and travelled home through France and Gascony — recognition of the king before coronation was a new precedent.
• The Provisions of Oxford (1258), although effectively dead, had established that great barons might claim a right to limit royal power through a council and regular parliaments.
• The crown lands and revenues had shrunk, leaving Edward with weak finances and a need to pursue inquiries such as the Hundred Rolls.
• Disputes with the Welsh prince Llywelyn ap Gruffudd were unresolved — he refused to attend the coronation or pay homage.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Battle of Evesham (1265) for the reign of Edward I.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The battle restored royal authority decisively: Simon de Montfort was killed and his army destroyed, ending the threat of baronial rule and allowing Henry III — and later Edward — to govern as king again.
• Evesham gave the young Lord Edward a military reputation just as he was about to inherit the throne; he had escaped captivity and led the royalist counter-attack, which made him a credible warrior-king at home and on crusade.
• The defeat of Montfort’s reform movement meant Edward came to the throne in 1272 free of the Provisions of Oxford, but he never forgot how close the magnates had come to running the kingdom — this shaped his determination to recover royal rights through the Hundred Rolls and Quo Warranto.
• Although the war was over, Evesham left behind ‘disinherited’ rebels whose lands had been confiscated; the Statute of Marlborough (1267) and Edward’s later legal reforms can both be traced back to the unresolved damage of 1265.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance assessed both at the time and over time, with sustained explanation and precise detail.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with relevant detail and at least two reasons for impact.
Developing: Some significance offered but limited to events at the time, with partial detail.
Emerging: Simple description of the battle with no real discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: ‘The biggest problem facing Edward I when he became king was the weakness of royal authority left behind by Henry III.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• Henry III’s reign had produced civil war, the Provisions of Oxford and Simon de Montfort’s parliament — all of which set precedents for the magnates to limit royal power.
• Local government had decayed: sheriffs and bailiffs were corrupt, private liberties had expanded, and royal courts had lost business.
• Henry’s reliance on foreign favourites and the Sicilian Business had drained the treasury, leaving Edward financially weak.

Arguments for other problems:
• In Wales, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd refused to attend the coronation or pay homage; this challenge to English overlordship became the immediate crisis of the reign.
• Royal finances were dangerously thin, forcing Edward to rely on Italian bankers and parliamentary taxation from his earliest years.
• The unresolved status of magnate liberties and franchises, dating back to before Henry III, was as serious as Henry’s personal failures — many privileges had been claimed since the Norman Conquest.

Judgement should weigh weakness of royal authority against the Welsh challenge and financial strain, reaching a substantiated conclusion that recognises the inheritance was a connected system of problems rather than separate boxes.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument with precise detail, weighed factors and a justified overall judgement that recognises connections between problems.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail on more than one factor and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Single factor described with little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Edward I’s absence on crusade between 1270 and 1274 affected his kingdom.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The realm was governed in his name by a council of trusted men — the first time an English king had been recognised as ruler before coronation, which strengthened the constitutional principle that kingship was continuous.
• The crusade gave Edward a Europe-wide reputation as a warrior, especially after surviving an assassination attempt at Acre in 1272; this reputation deterred rebellion when he finally returned.
• His absence delayed urgent reforms: corrupt local officers, decayed royal finances and unresolved baronial liberties were all left to fester until 1274, which is why Edward acted so quickly with the Hundred Rolls inquiry that year.
• The journey home through France and Gascony allowed Edward to pay homage to the king of France for his French lands — a smooth handover that contrasted with Henry III’s troubled relations with the French crown.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal explanation linking the crusade absence to multiple later developments, using precise terminology.
Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about the crusade with no clear effect on the reign.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Edward I’s character as a king.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Tall, physically imposing and famously a skilled warrior — nicknamed ‘Longshanks’ because of his unusual height and long arms; chroniclers stressed his energy and military leadership.
• Disciplined and hard-working in matters of government, with a strong personal interest in law and statute-making, supported by able ministers such as Robert Burnell.
• Devoutly religious: he had taken the cross and gone on crusade, and saw kingship as a sacred duty to deliver justice.
• Quick-tempered and merciless to anyone he believed had betrayed him; this would later be seen in his treatment of Dafydd ap Gruffudd and the brutal sack of Berwick in 1296.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Orlando Figes (A People’s Tragedy, 1996), arguing that Witte’s industrialisation papered over deep peasant misery. Interpretation B is from the Soviet-era textbook A Short History of the USSR (1965), arguing that Witte’s reforms created the modern proletariat that would carry through the revolution.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of Russia’s economy in 1894 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Figes presents industrialisation as a top-down imposition that left the peasantry impoverished, while the Soviet text presents it as the necessary precondition for working-class revolution.
• Figes emphasises the human cost (famines, factory conditions, debt), while the Soviet text emphasises the achievement of building a modern proletariat.
• Figes is critical of the regime that drove the change; the Soviet text frames the same change as historically progressive.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with exact reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences identified, each rooted in the interpretations.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments about the interpretations without identifying specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Orlando Figes (1996). Interpretation B is from the Soviet-era textbook A Short History of the USSR (1965).
Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of Witte’s industrialisation differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The interpretations differ in purpose: Figes is writing a critical history for a Western readership, while the Soviet textbook is teaching a generation of Soviet schoolchildren to see industrialisation as the prelude to socialism.
• They differ in time of writing: Figes wrote after the collapse of the USSR with full archival access, while the Soviet text was produced under censorship that demanded a Marxist framework.
• They use different evidence: Figes draws on peasant memoirs and famine statistics; the Soviet text foregrounds factory output figures and union membership.
• They reflect different traditions of historiography — the liberal/Western and the Soviet/orthodox schools.

Mastering: A clearly explained reason linked to purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective, with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason explained with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment about disagreement without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Russia in 1894 was a backward society where industrial growth only deepened the misery of the peasantry.’
How convincing is this interpretation about Russia in 1894? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Redemption payments kept peasants in debt for decades after the 1861 Emancipation; the 1891 famine killed up to 500,000.
• Witte’s reliance on indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches fell hardest on the peasants.
• The mir’s strip-farming system blocked productivity gains and shrank with every generation.

Arguments against:
• By 1914 Russia was the world’s fourth largest industrial economy — the change was real and rapid.
• New urban opportunities, however brutal, drew millions off subsistence farms by choice.
• Some peasant regions, especially the Black Earth zone, exported grain successfully.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation that uses precise contextual knowledge to test the interpretation and reaches a clear judgement.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Sergei Witte’s industrial policies on Russia between 1892 and 1903.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Industrial output grew at roughly 8% a year in the 1890s, making Russia the fourth largest industrial economy by 1914.
• The Trans-Siberian Railway opened Siberia to settlement and trade, and tied the empire together militarily.
• The gold standard (1897) and high tariffs attracted French and Belgian investment but increased foreign ownership of heavy industry.
• Indirect taxes on peasants funded the loans, deepening rural poverty and discontent.
• The growth of the urban proletariat created the social base for the revolutionary parties that emerged after 1898.

Mastering: A chain of consequences explained, linking economic, social and political effects.
Secure: Two or more developed effects supported by specific evidence.
Developing: One developed effect plus simple identification of others.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about Russian industry.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Russia in 1894 was held back more by its rural society than by its political system.’
How far do you accept this view of Russia in 1894? In your answer you should:
• consider the rural society of 1894
• consider the political system of 1894
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for rural society holding Russia back:
• Redemption payments and the mir blocked agricultural reform.
• 80% of the population were peasants, most illiterate and resistant to change.
• Famines (1891) showed the fragility of the rural economy.

Arguments for the political system holding Russia back:
• Autocracy excluded talent — the small middle class had no political voice.
• No legal trade unions, no parliament, no free press limited the safety valves available to other industrialising states.
• Witte’s programme could not be sustained politically because the Tsar resented modernising ministers.

Judgement should weigh both factors against each other rather than describing them in turn.

Mastering: A substantiated judgement weighing both factors with precise evidence.
Secure: A clear argument addressing both factors with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description of both factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of life in the cities of St Petersburg and Moscow on Russian factory workers by 1900.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Long hours (typically 11 hours, six days a week) and low wages produced widespread exhaustion and poor health.
• Overcrowded artel dormitories spread disease and broke up family life as men migrated alone from the village.
• Bans on trade unions and strikes pushed worker grievances underground and into illegal political organisations.
• The Okhrana’s surveillance and the army’s readiness to fire on protesters made revolutionary parties the only safe outlet for protest.
• Concentration in factories like the Putilov works in St Petersburg made coordinated mass action possible — this would matter in 1905 and 1917.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking working conditions to political radicalisation.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned only briefly.
Emerging: General description of factory life without explanation of effects.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a speech by David Lloyd George to the British House of Commons, March 1919, during the Paris Peace Conference.
‘We must take care that the peace we make is not so harsh that it will breed another war within a generation. Germany must be punished, but a Germany driven to despair will be a Germany of revolution and rearmament. The dragon’s teeth, once sown, will spring up again.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Lloyd George gives for moderating the peace terms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• A harsh peace risks another war within a generation (‘breed another war’).
• A Germany driven to despair will turn to revolution.
• A despairing Germany will rearm.
• The metaphor of ‘dragon’s teeth’ implies that vengeful terms produce future enemies.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Germany moved from military strength in spring 1918 to signing the armistice in November 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Spring Offensive, Hundred Days, blockade, naval mutiny, abdication, Compiègne); reaches the armistice through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• March 1918: Ludendorff Spring Offensive made huge initial gains but exhausted German troops.
• August 1918: Allied counter-attack (the Hundred Days) drove Germany back beyond the Hindenburg Line.
• The naval blockade caused civilian starvation, undermining home-front morale.
• October 1918: German High Seas Fleet mutiny at Kiel sparked wider revolution.
• 9 November 1918: Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated; new republican government sought peace.
• 11 November 1918: Armistice signed at Compiègne, ending the fighting at 11am.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter sent by Georges Clemenceau to a French general in February 1919.
‘Twice in my lifetime I have seen our cities burned and our farms ruined by German armies. I will not sign a treaty that does not place Germany under restraint for a generation. The Americans speak of fairness; the British of trade. I speak of survival.’

Source C: An extract from an article by Wickham Steed, editor of The Times newspaper in London, published in May 1919.
‘President Wilson came to Paris with the goodwill of all Europe. He has, however, allowed his Fourteen Points to be filed down one by one to satisfy French anxieties and British electoral promises. The treaty that emerges is a compromise that fully reflects no single vision.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the aims of the peacemakers in 1919. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Clemenceau frames French aims as survival, dismissing American idealism and British trade focus. Provenance: a private letter from the leading French negotiator to a general; likely to express genuine views without diplomatic varnish. Own knowledge: France had lost roughly 1.4 million soldiers; Alsace-Lorraine and the Rhineland buffer were direct expressions of this thinking.
Source C — Content: argues Wilson’s Fourteen Points were diluted to suit French and British concerns. Provenance: a major British newspaper editor in May 1919, well-informed but writing for a public audience and reflecting British liberal opinion. Own knowledge: only four of the Fourteen Points were accepted in full; the Senate would reject the treaty in 1920.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding French priorities but partial; C is useful as informed contemporary commentary but reflects one British viewpoint.

practice_questions.text:
‘The disagreements between the Big Three were the main reason the Treaty of Versailles failed to satisfy any of them.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Wilson wanted a lenient peace, Clemenceau wanted Germany crippled and Lloyd George wanted a workable trading partner — three aims that could not all be met.
• Only four of the Fourteen Points were accepted in full; Clemenceau did not get the permanent French hold on the Rhine he wanted; Lloyd George feared the terms would bring another war within twenty years.
Challenging the statement:
• Domestic politics narrowed what each leader could accept: the British ‘Khaki Election’ of December 1918 and Senate hostility to foreign entanglement in the USA.
• Germany and Russia were absent from the conference, so the settlement was made without two of the states it most affected.
• Self-determination could not be applied cleanly to the mixed populations of central Europe.
• Some compromises were negotiation working as intended rather than failure.
Judgement: the clash of aims was a major factor, but it was compounded by domestic constraints and by the practical limits of redrawing Europe.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British civil servant Maurice Hankey, secretary to the British Cabinet, recording a conversation with Lloyd George on 30 March 1919.
‘The PM said the French were impossible — they wanted to destroy Germany altogether and would not listen to reason. Wilson, he said, was clever but tired and increasingly stubborn. The PM’s own task, he believed, was to hold the centre and prevent the peace from being either too soft or too vengeful.’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about Lloyd George’s role at the Paris Peace Conference.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• Lloyd George saw his own role as ‘holding the centre’ between Wilson and Clemenceau.
• The entry is a contemporaneous diary note by his Cabinet secretary, recording a private conversation.
• Own knowledge: Lloyd George did press Clemenceau to moderate territorial demands and Wilson to accept reparations.
• Worth noting: Hankey was a sympathetic insider, so the diary may flatter Lloyd George’s self-image.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the diplomatic steps from Wilson’s Fourteen Points speech in January 1918 to the opening of the Paris Peace Conference in January 1919.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the conference opening through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1918: Wilson set out the Fourteen Points to US Congress, providing a framework for peace.
• Spring/summer 1918: the Fourteen Points circulated widely, raising expectations across Europe.
• October 1918: Germany approached Wilson seeking armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points.
• November 1918: armistice signed; the Allied powers agreed in principle to use the Fourteen Points as a basis but with reservations on freedom of the seas and reparations.
• December 1918: Lloyd George won the ‘Khaki Election’ on harsh-peace slogans, narrowing his negotiating room.
• January 1919: the Paris Peace Conference opened, bringing Wilson’s ideals into direct collision with French and British priorities.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the consequences of the Iran-Iraq war created tension in the Gulf between 1988 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Iraq emerged from the 1980–88 war with around $80 billion of debt, including roughly $14–15 billion owed to Kuwait, creating direct financial pressure on Saddam Hussein's regime.
• Saddam expected Gulf states to write off loans as reparations for defending the Arab world from Iran's revolution; their refusal — particularly Kuwait's — sharpened his grievance.
• A million-man army could not be demobilised without political risk, so Iraq remained on a war footing in peacetime, encouraging external solutions to internal problems.
• Saddam's 1989–90 demand that OPEC raise oil prices to ease his debt clashed with Kuwait's overproduction, turning a debt dispute into an oil-price dispute.
• Use of chemical weapons at Halabja in 1988 had drawn only muted Western criticism, so Saddam believed brutal action carried little international cost.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Saddam Hussein's regime changed in the two years after the Iran-Iraq war ended in August 1988.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The August 1988 ceasefire left Saddam with a million-strong army he could not afford to pay, so Iraq stayed on a war footing in peacetime.
• Repression deepened: the security services that had hunted deserters turned on dissenters, and Saddam's clan from Tikrit tightened its grip on military and intelligence posts.
• State media rebuilt him as the indispensable defender of the Arab world, using the war dead to justify continued sacrifice.
• From 1989 the regime turned outwards, demanding that Kuwait and the other Gulf states write off war loans and that OPEC raise oil prices.
• Muted Western criticism of the Halabja attack of March 1988 convinced Saddam that brutal action carried little international cost.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'The Tanker War of 1984–88 was the most important reason for outside involvement in the Gulf by 1990.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: the Tanker War showed how easily Gulf shipping could be closed, drew US and Western navies into escort duties, and rehearsed the intervention seen in 1990–91.
• Agree: it crushed Iraqi oil revenue and frightened insurance markets, deepening the debt crisis that pushed Saddam towards Kuwait.
• Disagree: the Gulf held around two-thirds of the world's proven oil reserves, so outside powers had a permanent interest whatever happened to shipping.
• Disagree: Cold War alignments mattered more — Soviet arms ties to Iraq, US ties to Saudi Arabia and the smaller Gulf states — and outlasted the Tanker War.
• Disagree: the 1979 Iranian Revolution reset the region and made the Gulf a standing Western security problem.
• Judgement: the Tanker War sharpened an involvement that already existed; oil reserves and the 1979 revolution are the deeper causes.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: 'Iraq was in a weaker position in 1989 than it had been in 1980.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: in 1980 Iraq went to war with a healthy oil-funded economy; by 1989 it carried roughly $80 billion of war debt, $35 billion of it owed abroad.
• Agree: the civilian economy was wrecked, so a million men could not be sent home into mass unemployment without political risk.
• Agree: oil revenue had been crushed by the Tanker War and by Kuwaiti and Emirati overproduction.
• Disagree: Iraq now had the fourth-largest army in the world, battle-hardened and equipped with the chemical weapons it had used at Halabja.
• Disagree: the Ba'athist regime held Iraq more tightly in 1989 than in 1980, with the security services dominant and dissent crushed.
• Judgement: stronger militarily, far weaker financially — and it was the financial weakness that drove the decision to invade Kuwait.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Iraqi policy towards Kuwait changed between the ceasefire of August 1988 and July 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• After the August 1988 ceasefire Iraq asked the Gulf states, Kuwait included, to write off war loans it said were owed for defending the Arab world.
• When Kuwait insisted the loans were commercial debts, Saddam began pressing OPEC to raise oil prices so that Iraq could pay.
• Through 1989–90 Kuwaiti and Emirati production above quota kept prices down, and Iraq recast a debt dispute as an oil-price dispute.
• By spring 1990 Iraq was accusing Kuwait of slant-drilling at the Rumaila field and reviving its claim to the islands of Bubiyan and Warbah.
• In a speech of 17 July 1990 Saddam called overproduction a kind of war against Iraq, moving from private request to public threat.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'The Iran-Iraq war paused the quarrels of the Gulf rather than settling them.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: UN Resolution 598 stopped the fighting in August 1988 but left the Shatt al-Arab dispute legally unresolved.
• Agree: around $80 billion of war debt was unpaid, and hundreds of thousands of unemployed veterans still needed wages.
• Agree: Halabja and the Kurdish question simmered on, and the Tanker War had shown Saddam how easily Gulf shipping could be choked.
• Disagree: the war did settle some things — it ended the Iranian threat to Iraq for a decade and left the border roughly where it had been in 1980.
• Disagree: the 1990 crisis had causes of its own, above all Kuwaiti overproduction and Saddam's choice to solve a cash problem by force.
• Judgement: every loose end of 1988 fed the crisis of 1990, so the 'pause' reading is the stronger one, but Saddam's own decision still made the war.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Cnut’s rule of England was similar to or different from earlier Viking arrivals (such as the Great Heathen Army of 865).
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct ways, each precisely supported with detail from across the periods.
Secure: Two valid ways with brief support.
Developing: One clear way; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comparison.

Indicative content:
• Difference: the Great Heathen Army (865) sought conquest by force and divided the country into Danelaw and Wessex; Cnut governed the whole country through existing English institutions and confirmed Edgar’s laws.
• Similarity: both arrivals brought Scandinavian rulers and warriors into Britain who then settled rather than left.
• Difference: Cnut presented himself publicly as a Christian English king (pilgrimage to Rome 1027); the Great Heathen Army arrived as a pagan force, with Christianisation following only after Edington 878.
• Similarity: both episodes left a lasting linguistic and political footprint and reshaped England’s relationship with the wider Scandinavian world.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the position of Emma of Normandy was similar to or different from the position of other royal women in this period.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct ways, precisely supported.
Secure: Two valid ways with brief support.
Developing: One clear way.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

Indicative content:
• Difference: Emma was queen consort to two kings of rival dynasties (Aethelred and Cnut), unusual for the period.
• Similarity: like other queens she was used to seal a foreign alliance — the 1002 marriage was an Anglo-Norman pact against the Vikings.
• Difference: Emma actively shaped her own historical reputation by commissioning the Encomium Emmae Reginae, where most royal women left no first-person record.
• Similarity: her power, like other medieval queens’, depended on producing royal sons (Edward the Confessor and Harthacnut both became king).

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Cnut’s North Sea Empire for England’s relationship with the wider world.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed points addressing significance at the time and over time, with precise detail.
Secure: Two clear points of significance with detail.
Developing: Description of Cnut’s rule without explaining significance.
Emerging: Vague claim about importance.

Indicative content:
• At the time: under Cnut’s personal union England was tied into Danish and Norwegian trade and military networks (1018-1035).
• At the time: Anglo-Saxon government, law and church carried on largely unchanged, showing that foreign rule did not always mean institutional overthrow.
• Over time: the empire collapsed within seven years of Cnut’s death, ending a Scandinavian orientation and clearing the way for the Norman kings to look south.
• Over time: it complicates the ‘raid then resist’ story of the Vikings — by the eleventh century England’s rulers were themselves Norse.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1066 succession crisis for the long-term development of the English crown.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing both the immediate crisis and its long-term consequences.
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Description of 1066 events.
Emerging: General narrative.

Indicative content:
• At the time: four rival claimants — Harold Godwinson, Edgar Aetheling, Harald Hardrada and William of Normandy — produced three battles in a single year.
• At the time: each claim grew out of cross-Channel marriage networks built up under Cnut and Emma, showing how migration shaped politics at the highest level.
• Over time: William’s victory bound England to Normandy for centuries (covered in Lesson 3) and made cross-Channel rule the new normal.
• Over time: the succession crisis ended the Scandinavian orientation begun by Cnut and reoriented England towards France.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Danegeld and the St Brice’s Day massacre were similar or different responses to Viking raids.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct ways, precisely supported.
Secure: Two valid ways with brief support.
Developing: One clear way.
Emerging: Vague comparison.

Indicative content:
• Similarity: both were attempts by Aethelred to deal with Viking pressure rather than fight a sustained military campaign.
• Difference: the Danegeld was a financial response (payment to make raiders go home); the massacre was a violent attack on Danes already living in England.
• Difference: the Danegeld bought short-term peace at the cost of inviting more raids; the massacre directly provoked Sweyn Forkbeard’s invasion.
• Similarity: both ultimately failed and contributed to Cnut’s accession in 1016.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Emma of Normandy as a link between three royal houses.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed significance points addressing immediate political role and long-term dynastic consequences.
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Description of Emma without significance.
Emerging: Vague comment about queens.

Indicative content:
• At the time: her marriages (1002 to Aethelred, 1017 to Cnut) sealed alliances first with Normandy and then with the new Danish ruling house.
• At the time: she actively shaped her image through the Encomium Emmae Reginae, a rare written voice for a medieval woman.
• Over time: her sons Edward the Confessor and Harthacnut both became king of England.
• Over time: her Norman ties gave William of Normandy a basis for his 1066 claim — her family network helped produce the most consequential succession crisis in English history.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Brigham Young’s leadership on the Mormon migration of 1846–47.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects of Young’s leadership, each linked back through an explicit causal chain; precise factual support (companies of fifty, ten captains, planted crops at staging posts, low death rate, Salt Lake arrival 24 July 1847).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail and some causal linking.
Developing: Effects identified but partly described rather than explained.
Emerging: Generalised statements about the trek without clear effects.

Indicative content:
• Tight organisation: companies of fifty and ten with named captains gave the trek a chain of command, which meant orders were obeyed even in crisis.
• Shared supplies and crops planted at staging posts meant later companies could eat, lowering the death rate compared with the secular Oregon Trail.
• Choosing the Salt Lake Valley meant settling somewhere no one else wanted, removing competition for land in the early years.
• Religious authority gave Young the power to enforce decisions that purely civil leaders could not, holding the community together when more than 350 died at Winter Quarters.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of the Mormon settlement of Utah.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a popular American history written in 1925.
“The Mormons in Utah are the supreme example of pioneer self-help. Driven out of the East, they crossed a continent and turned a desert into a garden through faith and hard work.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a 2008 academic essay on the American West.
“The Mormon project succeeded because Brigham Young built a tightly disciplined community in which land, water and even marriage were controlled by the church. It was less an example of frontier individualism than of organised theocracy.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, supported differences drawn from both interpretations.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support.
Developing: One clear difference; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 stresses self-help and individualism; Interpretation 2 stresses central control and theocracy.
• Interpretation 1 emphasises faith and hard work; Interpretation 2 emphasises institutional power over land, water and marriage.
• Interpretation 1 frames the achievement as American pioneer typical; Interpretation 2 frames it as unusual and organised, even un-American by frontier standards.
• Interpretation 1 is celebratory; Interpretation 2 is analytical.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of polygamy on relations between the Mormons and other Americans by 1857.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (1852 public announcement, federal officials, hostile press, build-up to Mountain Meadows in 1857).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements without explaining the consequences.

Indicative content:
• The 1852 public announcement of polygamy by Brigham Young intensified hostility from churches and newspapers in the East, painting Mormons as un-American.
• Federal officials sent to Utah resigned or were driven out, prompting Washington to send troops in 1857 (Utah War).
• Polygamy provided political ammunition against statehood: Utah would not be admitted to the Union until 1896, after polygamy was officially renounced.
• The hostility created a siege mentality that helps explain the violent overreaction at Mountain Meadows in September 1857.

practice_questions.text:
Has Brigham Young’s leadership been the main reason the Mormons succeeded in Utah?

• Brigham Young’s leadership
• Geographic isolation of the Salt Lake Valley

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs Young’s leadership against geography (and other factors), reaching a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support across both bullets and additional material.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached.
Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative.

Indicative content:
• Young’s leadership: company-of-fifty system; planted crops at staging posts; grid plan of Salt Lake City; church-controlled land and water; theocratic governance from 1850.
• Geographic isolation: high desert valley nobody else wanted; protected from settler competition for over a decade; bitter winters made independent survival a community task.
• Other relevant material: shared faith and persecution; collective ownership of resources; the ‘miracle of the gulls’ in 1848; Mormon willingness to follow orders.
• Judgement: top answers argue that isolation gave Young the chance to build a society, but his leadership turned that chance into success. Without either factor the project would have failed.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Mormon settlement of the Salt Lake Valley.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features with precise factual detail.
Secure: Two valid features with brief support.
Developing: One feature developed; one undeveloped.
Emerging: Generalised description.

Indicative content:
• Irrigation: pioneers diverted mountain streams onto the valley floor within hours of arrival, making farming possible in a high desert.
• City planning: Salt Lake City was laid out on a strict grid with ten-acre blocks and a central temple square.
• Church control of land: families were allocated plots based on what they could work, not what they could pay, with water rights held communally.
• Satellite settlements: new arrivals were directed to towns like Ogden, Provo and Manti, allowing the colony to spread without fragmenting.

practice_questions.text:
Why might historians give different views of the Mormon migration?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 (above) and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: Reason rooted in provenance or context with brief support.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’.
Emerging: Restates content of each interpretation.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: a 1925 popular history reflects an inter-war Frontier-Thesis culture that celebrated pioneer individualism; a 2008 academic essay reflects modern scholarship interested in institutions and power.
• Audience: a popular history wanted patriotic stories; an academic essay wanted to explain causes precisely.
• Evidence: by 2008 historians had access to detailed records of the church’s economic role; in 1925 the available materials emphasised the dramatic trek.
• Purpose: one celebrates; the other analyses.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the membership and routine of the Privy Council.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It had around 19–20 members chosen by the queen, including senior nobles, ministers and officials such as the Lord Treasurer.
• It met two or three times a week to debate foreign policy, religion, the harvest, law and order and the granting of monopolies.
• Its decisions were recorded by the Clerk of the Council and sent out as letters carrying the queen’s authority.
• Elizabeth herself often did not attend; ministers presented options and she ruled on them privately.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Walsingham’s intelligence network.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Walsingham recruited and paid agents personally, often from his own pocket, posing as Catholic exiles in Paris, Rome and the English seminaries abroad.
• His agents intercepted, copied and decrypted letters; codebreakers such as Thomas Phelippes worked in his service.
• The network unmasked the 1586 Babington Plot by intercepting ciphered messages between Anthony Babington and Mary, Queen of Scots.
• The service ran through Walsingham’s personal household, not as a formal Crown department, leaving him in debt by his death.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how William Cecil served Elizabeth between 1558 and 1598.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• His 40 years in office (Principal Secretary 1558–1572, Lord Treasurer 1572–1598) provided continuity in administration through religious threats, plots and war.
• His careful drafting of options and resistance to expensive wars kept Crown finances stable, so Elizabeth could choose when to fight.
• He trained his son Robert to succeed him, allowing an almost seamless transition in 1598 and protecting policy from disruption.
• His backing for the eventual execution of Mary in 1587 — built on years of legal preparation — removed the Catholic claimant without leaving Elizabeth politically exposed.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Walsingham uncovered the Babington Plot of 1586.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It produced the documentary evidence that convicted Mary, Queen of Scots, leading to her execution at Fotheringhay in February 1587.
• It removed the Catholic figurehead around whom plots could form, weakening domestic Catholic conspiracies.
• It hardened Spanish hostility — Philip II saw Mary’s execution as the final justification for invasion, contributing to the launching of the Armada in 1588.
• It demonstrated the value of state intelligence, embedding Walsingham’s methods (interception, code-breaking, agents abroad) as part of how the regime defended itself.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Privy Council for the way decisions were made.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Council channelled expert advice on foreign policy, religion and finance to the queen, allowing decisions based on weighed evidence rather than personal whim.
• It turned royal decisions into administration: instructions to Justices of the Peace, county sheriffs and ambassadors carried Council authority.
• Significance over time: the Council shaped major events including the religious settlement, the response to the 1569 Northern Rebellion and the build-up to war with Spain.
• Elizabeth used Council debate strategically — absent from many meetings, she preserved ultimate authority while letting ministers refine the options.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Elizabethan England survived because of its ministers. The queen took the credit for work that Cecil and Walsingham did.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the running of Elizabeth’s government? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Cecil’s 40-year administration kept finances stable and policy continuous through religious threat, plots and war.
• Walsingham’s intelligence network produced the evidence that condemned Mary in 1587, removing the Catholic claimant.
• The Privy Council co-ordinated the response to the Northern Rebellion, the Armada and Essex’s rebellion, channelling local administration to the centre.
• Robert Cecil’s back-channel negotiations secured a peaceful Stuart succession in 1603.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Patronage flowed from the queen personally; ministers depended on her favour for their offices.
• Elizabeth made the final decisions on marriage, religion and the execution of Mary, often delaying ministers’ preferred options.
• Her image-making and personal authority compensated for the absence of an heir or husband.
• Parliament, county gentry and Justices of the Peace also enforced the regime far from the Council.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Battle of Stamford Bridge in September 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was fought on 25 September 1066, seven miles east of York, between Harold Godwinson’s English army and Harald Hardrada’s Norse force supported by Tostig Godwinson.
• Harold surprised the Norse by marching about 185 miles in four to five days from London, catching Hardrada’s men without their mail at the bridge.
• Both Harald Hardrada and Tostig were killed, and only about 24 of the original 300 Norse ships returned to Norway.
• A famous Norse warrior held the bridge against the English advance until he was speared from beneath through the timbers.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Harold’s victory at Stamford Bridge for the Battle of Hastings three weeks later.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stamford Bridge wore down Harold’s elite housecarls and southern fyrd, so the army that fought at Hastings was depleted in numbers and physically tired.
• Casualties at Stamford Bridge meant Harold could not call on the same numbers of trained warriors at Hastings — the shield wall had fewer men in its rear ranks.
• The need to march back south at speed (250+ miles) prevented Harold from waiting for further reinforcements from the Midlands and the North, particularly Edwin and Morcar.
• On the other hand, the Stamford Bridge victory removed the second front entirely — without it, Harold would have faced two invasions simultaneously, which would almost certainly have destroyed his rule before October.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Anglo-Saxon shield wall at the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Housecarls formed the front rank, equipped with mail, helmets and two-handed Dane axes capable of cutting through Norman mail.
• The fyrd, the general levy of able-bodied freemen, stood in the ranks behind, supplying numbers and replacing fallen housecarls.
• Shields were locked edge-to-edge in a continuous wall, with spears braced over the top, on the crest of Senlac ridge to negate Norman cavalry advantage.
• The formation held repeated archer volleys, infantry assaults and the first major cavalry charge; it was only thinned by feigned retreats and Norman repeat attacks late in the day.
• Why it mattered: on the crest of the ridge the wall cancelled out Norman cavalry and archery for most of the day, which is why the battle was still open at dusk.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the way the Battle of Hastings changed the political situation in England in late 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Harold and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine were killed, eliminating the entire Godwinson leadership and removing the only adult military rivals to William inside England.
• The destruction of the housecarls meant no professional army was left to fight William in the field; later resistance in 1067–71 had to rely on revolts and sieges, not pitched battle.
• Edgar Atheling was briefly proposed as king by the Witan but had no troops to back him; with the southern earls dead and Edwin and Morcar still recovering from Fulford, no plausible alternative could be assembled in time.
• William’s subsequent march via Dover, Canterbury and Berkhamsted forced submissions one after another, leading to his coronation at Westminster on 25 December 1066.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Norman military innovations — cavalry, archers and combined arms — for the outcome of the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the combination of archers, infantry and mailed knights gave William flexibility on the day — when one arm failed, he could feed in another and resume the assault.
• Archers were significant in that they kept pressure on the shield wall throughout the day; later traditions claimed an arrow finally struck Harold, though contemporary sources are unclear.
• Cavalry on its own did not win the battle — the first major charge stalled against the ridge; significance lay in cavalry working with feigned retreats to peel off sections of the English line.
• Importance later: combined arms and the prefabricated castle at Hastings became templates for William’s next 20 years of conquest, marking a permanent shift in how war was waged in England.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of why William won.

‘William won at Hastings because he was lucky. The wind, Hardrada’s invasion and an arrow in the right place handed him a victory that his generalship had not earned.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for William’s victory at Hastings? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: luck and circumstance, not tactical skill, won the battle for William.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The wind turned in William’s favour just as Harold’s southern army had stood down on 8 September after running out of provisions, so William landed unopposed at Pevensey.
• Harold was forced to fight Stamford Bridge first; without that distraction his army would have been fresh and full strength at Hastings.
• The shield wall held until late afternoon; Harold’s death — whether from an arrow, a knight, or both — was the accident that broke a battle that had otherwise gone to the English.
• William’s personal escape from a panic on the left flank, riding bare-headed to rally his men, depended on luck as much as leadership.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
