• Combined-arms tactics — archers, infantry and cavalry working together — were a genuine Norman tactical innovation that the English shield wall was not designed to face.
• Feigned retreats, even if some were genuine, required disciplined cavalry able to regroup under fire — a real tactical achievement.
• William’s decision to fortify Hastings within days of landing showed strategic foresight; he could fall back on the castle if defeated.
• Pope Alexander II’s blessing and the papal banner gave the Norman army a moral and recruiting advantage that was political planning, not luck.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which medieval Christian and Islamic approaches to medicine were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: the medieval Christian Church restricted routine dissection (Council of Tours 1163); Islamic teaching did not generally place such restrictions, allowing earlier anatomical study.
• Difference: Islamic Bimaristans were large state-funded hospitals that treated all faiths and trained doctors at the bedside; Christian hospitals were typically attached to monasteries and focused on care for the dying, elderly and lepers.
• Similarity: both built on Galen and Hippocrates and preserved their writings — Islamic scholars in Baghdad, Christian monks in Britain.
• Similarity: both saw caring for the sick as a religious duty — the Christian gospel and the Prophet’s teaching ‘For every disease, Allah has given a cure’ both endorsed medical work.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Ibn Sina (Avicenna) for medicine in medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: his Canon of Medicine systematised Galenic and Hippocratic medicine into a single million-word teaching encyclopaedia.
• At the time: it was translated from Arabic into Latin via Toledo and Salerno, then reached Oxford and Bologna where it was taught alongside Galen.
• Over time: the Canon remained the standard European medical textbook for over 600 years — meaning every British physician trained between c1200 and the 1600s used him.
• Over time: his classification of diseases shaped Sydenham’s 17th-century clinical observation tradition; his name still labels modern medicine in Iran and beyond.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument across both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, focused mainly on at the time.
Emerging: Identification only; little explanation of why he mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Christian Church for medical progress in medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the Church founded and ran the hospitals — over 700 in England by 1500, including St Bartholomew’s (1123) and St Thomas’s (1173).
• At the time: monastic scribes copied Galen and Hippocrates, so the Church decided which medical knowledge survived and who could read it.
• At the time: it taught that disease could be divine punishment, which shaped responses such as the flagellant processions of 1349.
• Over time: the 1163 Council of Tours barred clergy from cutting open bodies, and Church control of learning helped shield Galen from challenge until the Renaissance.
• Over time: when Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries in 1536-40 England lost its hospital network, a gap the 18th-century voluntary hospitals had to fill.
• Judgement worth making: the Church was engine and brake at once — the same institution preserved medicine and slowed its testing.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Has religion been the main factor in shaping medicine in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to religion and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh religion against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of religion as the main factor:
• Religion controlled hospitals (St Bartholomew’s 1123) and care for the sick.
• Religion controlled education and the texts taught at universities, locking in Galen.
• Religion shaped explanations of disease (sin, divine punishment) that drove patient behaviour, including flagellant processions in 1348-9.
• Both Christianity and Islam endorsed care of the sick as a religious duty — without that endorsement, Bimaristans and monastic infirmaries would not have existed.

Weighed against communication:
• Latin manuscript copying carried Galen forward but the medium of transmission — books and translations — was a separate factor.
• Toledo and Salerno translation routes carried Islamic medicine to Britain; without these routes, Ibn Sina and Al-Razi could not have shaped British practice.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Galen, Hippocrates, Al-Razi, Ibn Sina, John of Arderne all produced specific advances that religion did not cause.
• Without the original individuals, religion would have had nothing to preserve.

Judgement: The strongest answers identify religion as the dominant institutional setting in this period, while noting that communication and individuals worked inside that setting. A clear comparative judgement (e.g. ‘religion shaped what was preserved, but individuals shaped what was discovered’) earns the top band.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing religion against at least two other factors with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes religion only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Al-Razi for the development of medieval medicine.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: ran the first medical hospital in Baghdad and trained physicians at the bedside.
• At the time: was the first to clearly distinguish smallpox from measles, sharpening diagnosis.
• Over time: his Comprehensive Book of Medicine was translated into Latin and used in European universities including Salerno.
• Over time: his clinical case notes and emphasis on observation influenced later figures including Sydenham.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification of who he was.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: the surgical treatise of John of Arderne, an English surgeon writing in the 1370s. It sets out his method for treating anal fistula, records the cases he treated and what happened to them, and is illustrated with drawings of his instruments.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying surgery in medieval England?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: a worked-out operation with instruments and results shows that medieval surgery could be skilled and planned, not only cautery and prayer.
• Content: the case records show a surgeon judging his work by what happened to patients rather than by classical authority.
• Provenance: written by a practising surgeon for other surgeons, so it reflects real practice; but Arderne was also advertising himself to wealthy patrons, so his success rate is likely to be flattered.
• Contextual knowledge: most surgery was done by barber-surgeons trained by apprenticeship, using cautery, trepanning, bonesetting and dwale for pain.
• Limitations: Arderne was exceptional, so the treatise tells us little about the ordinary barber-surgeon or about the poor who could not pay.
• Judgement: strong on the best medieval surgery and on how surgeons learned, weak on the typical patient’s experience.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street stock market boom in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Share prices rose steeply — the Dow Jones industrial average climbed from 100 points in 1924 to 381 points in September 1929.
• Buying on the margin allowed investors to put down 10% of the price and borrow the rest from a broker; by 1929 margin loans totalled over $9 billion.
• Around three million Americans owned shares by 1929 — many for the first time — encouraged by newspaper tips and stories of overnight fortunes.
• Speculators bought shares not for long-term investment but to sell quickly at a higher price; companies like RCA saw share prices rise 500% in two years despite paying no dividend.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did buying on the margin and speculation reshape the American stock market in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Buying on the margin let ordinary Americans put down 10% of a share price and borrow the rest from a broker, opening the stock market to clerks and small savers who could never have paid in full.
• Margin loans rose to over $9 billion by 1929; the loans were repayable in full whatever happened to share prices, building large hidden risk into the system.
• Speculation — buying to resell quickly — meant prices rose because of demand from buyers, not because of company performance; RCA shares rose 500% in two years without paying any dividend.
• Banks invested customers’ deposits in the rising market, so a fall in share prices would directly hit the savings of millions of ordinary Americans who had never bought a share themselves.
• The combined effect was a self-feeding bubble: rising prices attracted buyers, whose buying lifted prices further — the structure that would collapse in October 1929 (Lesson 6).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from margin buying through speculation to systemic risk, with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description rather than effects.
Emerging: Identifies margin or speculation without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the position of farmers in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Wheat prices collapsed from $2.50 a bushel in 1920 to under $1 by 1929 as European agriculture recovered after the First World War.
• Around six million Americans were forced off their farms across the decade, often into debt.
• Mechanisation through tractors and combine harvesters meant farms needed fewer labourers, so rural employment fell sharply.
• Sharecroppers, particularly African-Americans in the South, rented land for half their crop and fell deeper into debt to landlords as cotton prices fell.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the 1920s Boom create inequality between different groups in American society?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The richest 5% of Americans took home a third of national income in 1929 while the poorest 40% received less than a sixth — the gap widened across the decade.
• Farm prices collapsed from 1921 onwards, while urban industrial profits grew; rural Americans fell further behind their city counterparts.
• Sharecroppers, often African-American, were locked into debt by falling cotton prices and could end seasons owing the landlord more than they earned.
• Jim Crow segregation in the South limited African-Americans’ access to skilled work and education; even in northern cities like Chicago and Detroit they faced housing discrimination and were sacked first when work slowed.
• Native Americans on reservations lived in extreme poverty — the 1928 Meriam Report described conditions as a national disgrace.
• Recent immigrants from southern and eastern Europe were funnelled into the lowest-paid factory jobs and faced the immigration restrictions of 1921 and 1924 (Lesson 5).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking specific groups to specific causes of exclusion, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples covering several groups.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one or two groups.
Emerging: Lists groups left out without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on American inequality in the 1920s: the collapse of farm prices, or the position of African-Americans? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the collapse of farm prices:
• Wheat fell from $2.50 to under $1 a bushel; cotton prices fell sharply too, hitting the largest single occupational group in 1920s America.
• Six million Americans were forced off their land — an enormous displacement that affected the entire countryside.
• Falling farm incomes pulled down rural communities of all races, making this a nationwide problem.

In support of the position of African-Americans:
• Jim Crow laws across the South locked African-Americans out of skilled work, decent schooling and voting, regardless of the national economy.
• Even northern industrial cities offered only segregated housing and the lowest-paid jobs.
• The double burden — sharecropping in the South and discrimination in the North — meant African-Americans faced inequality the wider country did not.

Judgement: The strongest answers note that the two intersected — African-American sharecroppers were hit twice over, by falling prices and by racial discrimination. A defensible verdict is that the collapse of farm prices was wider in scale, but the position of African-Americans was more fundamental because it would persist whether crops sold or not.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument weighing both factors, with precise detail and a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both factors but unevenly; judgement is asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Wall Street boom on different groups of Americans by 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• For wealthy investors and Wall Street brokers, rising share prices created enormous paper fortunes — speculators making 500%+ on companies like RCA.
• For middle-class clerks and small savers, buying on the margin made the market accessible — but their borrowed-up positions made them dangerously exposed.
• For ordinary depositors, banks investing their savings in the market meant they were exposed to a crash without ever buying a share.
• For farmers and sharecroppers, rising stock prices were irrelevant — their crop incomes fell across the decade and 6 million were forced off the land.
• For African-Americans and Native Americans, the boom was largely invisible: Jim Crow laws and reservation poverty kept them out of both the consumer society and the share-buying class.
• The effect overall was uneven prosperity at the top, hidden debt in the middle, and stagnation or decline at the bottom — setting up the unequal pain of the Crash in 1929 (Lesson 6).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation distinguishing effects across multiple named groups with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one or two groups.
Emerging: Identifies the boom without explaining its uneven effects.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Robert Service (Lenin: A Biography, 2000), arguing that Lenin’s 1903 demand for a small disciplined party showed his authoritarian instincts from the start. Interpretation B is from the American revisionist historian Lars Lih (Lenin Rediscovered, 2006), arguing that Lenin’s 1903 position was a normal Marxist response to operating under Tsarist police repression.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Service presents Lenin as authoritarian by temperament; Lih presents him as a pragmatic Marxist responding to Russian conditions.
• Service emphasises continuity with the later one-party state; Lih emphasises the influence of German Social Democracy on Lenin’s thought.
• Service blames Lenin personally; Lih blames the Tsarist police state for forcing underground organisation.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences identified, each rooted in the interpretations.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of the 1903 split differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different evidence: Service emphasises Lenin’s polemics; Lih draws on Lenin’s own footnotes citing German socialists.
• Different traditions of historiography: Service draws on a liberal-Western reading; Lih is part of a revisionist re-reading of Lenin.
• Different time of writing: Lih’s book responds to thirty years of revisionist scholarship since the opening of Soviet archives.
• Different purposes: Service is writing for a general readership and giving a clear moral judgement; Lih is writing a specialist re-evaluation.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with reference to purpose, evidence or time of writing, with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason explained with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Tsarist Russia in the early 1900s was effectively a police state, with all opposition either driven underground or assassinated.’
How convincing is this interpretation about Tsarist Russia before 1905? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• The Okhrana ran extensive networks of informants and infiltrated the Bolsheviks (e.g. Malinovsky).
• Trade unions and political parties were illegal; meetings of more than three required police permission.
• Socialist Revolutionary assassinations — Sipyagin (1902), Plehve (1904), Grand Duke Sergei (1905) — show how violent the politics had become.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Liberal zemstva, professional associations and a critical press operated at the limits of legality.
• Exile, not execution, was the standard punishment for political crime; Lenin spent three years writing in Shushenskoe.
• A small but real middle class debated reform openly, especially after the 1891 famine relief campaign.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the 1903 split in the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party between Bolsheviks and Mensheviks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The split divided the Marxist opposition for fifteen years, weakening it during the 1905 Revolution and again in early 1917.
• It produced two competing models of revolutionary organisation — Lenin’s small disciplined cadre and Martov’s mass party.
• It explains why the Bolsheviks were able to act decisively in October 1917 when other socialist groups hesitated.
• It set the precedent for one-party rule, since Lenin had spent fourteen years arguing that purity mattered more than unity.
• It pushed the Mensheviks into permanent opposition after 1917 — many were arrested or exiled in the 1920s.

Mastering: A chain of consequences explained, linking 1903 to 1917 and beyond.
Secure: Two or more developed effects supported by specific evidence.
Developing: One developed effect plus simple identification of others.
Emerging: General comments about disunity.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The greatest threat to Tsarist autocracy before 1905 came from liberal opposition rather than revolutionary parties.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the strength of liberal opposition before 1905
• consider the strength of revolutionary opposition before 1905
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for liberal opposition being the greater threat:
• The zemstva and Kadets enjoyed respectable middle-class support that the regime could not easily smear.
• Liberal demands for a Duma and constitution would, if conceded, end pure autocracy.
• Many in the army officer corps and even the imperial family sympathised with moderate reform.

Arguments for revolutionary parties being the greater threat:
• Socialist Revolutionary assassinations directly killed senior officials.
• The Marxist parties built networks inside the new factory cities.
• The 1903 split made the Bolsheviks more disciplined, not weaker.

Judgement should weigh the immediate physical threat against the long-term political threat.

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing both factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both factors with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Russification on the non-Russian peoples of the Tsarist empire by 1905.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Polish, Finnish and Ukrainian languages were restricted in schools and public life, alienating educated minorities.
• Jewish communities were confined to the Pale of Settlement and faced pogroms tolerated by local police, fuelling emigration and radicalisation.
• Finland lost much of its previous autonomy under Nicholas II, turning a previously loyal grand duchy hostile.
• Educated minority elites supplied a disproportionate share of revolutionary activists, including many leading Bolsheviks.
• National movements grew alongside the imperial centre, weakening unity in 1905 and 1917.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking Russification policies to political destabilisation.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned only briefly.
Emerging: General description of Russification without explanation of effects.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a speech by French foreign minister Théophile Delcassé to the French Chamber of Deputies, May 1904.
‘The agreement signed in April with His Britannic Majesty’s government is not an alliance — it engages neither army nor navy. It is, however, the end of a century of mistrust. From this day forward the rivalries that consumed our two peoples in Egypt, Morocco and Newfoundland are at an end.’

Source A suggests that the Entente Cordiale settled old quarrels rather than creating a military alliance. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Delcassé says the agreement ‘engages neither army nor navy’.
• It ends ‘a century of mistrust’ between Britain and France.
• It closes the rivalries in Egypt, Morocco and Newfoundland.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Entente Cordiale was signed in April 1904 and settled colonial disputes, not defence commitments.
• Britain and France had come close to war over the Sudan at Fashoda in 1898.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Britain shifted from Splendid Isolation to the Triple Entente between 1900 and 1907.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Boer War unpopularity, Anglo-Japanese Alliance, Entente Cordiale, First Moroccan Crisis, Anglo-Russian Convention); reaches the Triple Entente through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1899-1902: The Boer War left Britain diplomatically isolated and exposed the costs of going it alone.
• 1902: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance secured British interests in the Far East — the first formal break with Splendid Isolation.
• 1903: King Edward VII’s Paris visit warmed Anglo-French public opinion.
• April 1904: The Entente Cordiale settled colonial disputes with France.
• 1905-06: The First Moroccan Crisis pushed Britain and France closer through joint military staff talks.
• August 1907: The Anglo-Russian Convention completed the Triple Entente by settling disputes in Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Sir Eyre Crowe, senior Foreign Office adviser, on the state of relations with Germany, dated 1 January 1907.
‘The German menace is not the policy of any single statesman but the structural ambition of a state that has outgrown its earlier role. Britain has slowly responded — through Tokyo, Paris, and now St Petersburg. The result is not yet an alliance, but the lines of cooperation are unmistakable.’

Source C: An extract from a 1908 article in the Vienna newspaper Neue Freie Presse, on Anglo-Russian relations.
‘London and St Petersburg, divided for half a century by the Great Game, have signed an agreement carving up Persia between them. Berlin must understand the meaning of what has happened: the encirclement is complete.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying European reactions to the formation of the Triple Entente. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Crowe argues the German threat is structural, and Britain has responded through agreements with Japan, France and Russia. Provenance: a confidential Foreign Office memorandum by a senior official, intended for cabinet readers — likely to express genuine analysis. Own knowledge: the so-called ‘Crowe Memorandum’ was an influential statement of British anti-German thinking in 1907.
Source C — Content: argues the Anglo-Russian Convention completes Germany’s ‘encirclement’. Provenance: a leading Austro-Hungarian newspaper — sympathetic to the German viewpoint, useful for showing how the Triple Alliance side perceived the Entente. Own knowledge: German leaders did speak of Einkreisung (encirclement) from this period; the perception, accurate or not, shaped German strategy.
Judgement: B is highly useful as insider British analysis but reflects one current of Foreign Office opinion; C is useful as Central European reaction but rhetorical and one-sided.

practice_questions.text:
‘The completion of the Triple Entente in 1907 was the main reason Europe drifted towards war.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The Entente turned three separate agreements into one bloc facing the Triple Alliance.
• German leaders read it as Einkreisung, or encirclement, and grew readier to take risks.
• Once both blocs were fixed, a quarrel between any two powers risked pulling in their partners.

Disagree:
• The Entente was not a military alliance; it settled colonial disputes and committed nobody to fight.
• Anglo-German naval rivalry, Slav nationalism and Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans each ran on their own.
• Crises at Fashoda in 1898 and Tangier in 1905 were settled without war, so blocs did not make war automatic.
• Italy's secret deal with France in 1902 shows the Triple Alliance was already weaker than it looked.

Judgement: The Triple Entente narrowed the room for compromise, but it worked alongside naval rivalry and Balkan instability rather than causing the drift on its own.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter by Italian foreign minister Giulio Prinetti to Italy’s ambassador in Paris, dated November 1902.
‘The Triple Alliance protects us from invasion, but binds us only to a defensive war. There is therefore no contradiction in promising France that, should Berlin take up arms unprovoked, Italy will not stand against her. Our partners in Vienna and Berlin need not be told what they cannot demand.’

Source F suggests that Italy did not intend to honour the Triple Alliance if Germany attacked France. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Prinetti says the Triple Alliance binds Italy ‘only to a defensive war’.
• Italy will promise France that it ‘will not stand against her’ if Berlin attacks first.
• Vienna and Berlin ‘need not be told’ - the promise is to be kept from Italy's own allies.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Italy did sign a secret neutrality agreement with France in 1902.
• Italy stayed neutral in 1914 and joined the Entente in 1915 under the Treaty of London.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Triple Entente was assembled between 1894 and 1907.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the Triple Entente through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1894: The Franco-Russian Alliance was ratified, ending French isolation and creating a two-front problem for Germany.
• 1898: The Fashoda Incident nearly brought Britain and France to war over Sudan, but its peaceful resolution paved the way for later cooperation.
• 1902: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance freed Britain to focus diplomacy on Europe.
• April 1904: The Entente Cordiale settled Anglo-French colonial disputes.
• 1905-06: The First Moroccan Crisis pushed Britain and France into joint military planning.
• August 1907: The Anglo-Russian Convention completed the Triple Entente by settling disputes in Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Clarendon Code for religious life in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every clergyman to use the Book of Common Prayer and accept Anglican ordination, with a deadline of St Bartholomew’s Day, 24 August 1662.
• The Conventicle Act of 1664 made it illegal for more than five people outside one household to meet for non-Anglican worship, targeting Dissenter congregations.
• The Corporation Act of 1661 required officers of borough corporations to take Anglican communion and reject the Solemn League and Covenant.
• The Five Mile Act of 1665 banned ejected ministers from approaching within five miles of any town or any place where they had previously preached.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Great Ejection of 1662.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 2,000 Puritan and Presbyterian ministers were expelled from the Church of England for refusing to use the Book of Common Prayer.
• It took effect on 24 August 1662, St Bartholomew’s Day, the deadline set by the Act of Uniformity for clergy to conform.
• It created a permanent body of Protestant Dissenters — preachers without legal pulpits — who continued to gather in private houses and barns.
• Several ejected ministers, such as Richard Baxter, became leading writers of Nonconformist theology, while others (including John Bunyan) were imprisoned for unlicensed preaching.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Act of Uniformity changed religious life in England after 1662.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It produced the Great Ejection of around 2,000 ministers in August 1662, removing experienced preachers from parish life and leaving many congregations without their familiar clergy.
• It created a permanent class of Dissenters — Presbyterians, Independents, Baptists, Quakers — who continued to meet illegally and were targeted by the Conventicle and Five Mile Acts.
• It re-established the Book of Common Prayer as the only legal liturgy, locking Anglican worship into the parish system across the country.
• Over time it pushed Nonconformist groups into private worship, family-based education and emigration to the American colonies, shaping religious patterns long after the reign.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence for relations between Crown and Parliament.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Declaration suspended the penal laws against Dissenters and Catholics by royal prerogative, attempting to bypass the Cavalier Parliament’s religious settlement.
• It triggered a confrontation in 1672–73: Parliament refused to vote war taxes for the Third Dutch War unless Charles withdrew the Declaration, which he did in March 1673.
• Parliament then forced through the First Test Act, requiring all officeholders to take Anglican communion — this drove James, Duke of York and Lord Treasurer Clifford from office.
• Significance over time: it set a pattern in which Parliament used finance to control religious policy, a precedent that would shape the Exclusion Crisis and the Glorious Revolution settlement of 1689.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Conventicle and Five Mile Acts drove Dissenters out of public worship.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Conventicle Act 1664 made it illegal for more than five people outside one household to meet for non-Anglican worship, criminalising the ordinary gatherings of Quakers, Baptists and Independents.
• The Five Mile Act 1665 banned ejected ministers from coming within five miles of any town or place where they had previously preached, cutting them off from their old congregations.
• Together the Acts pushed Dissenter worship into private houses, woods and clandestine meetings, while filling local gaols with Quakers in particular.
• John Bunyan was held in Bedford gaol from 1660 to 1672 for unlicensed preaching, and began ‘The Pilgrim’s Progress’ there — a long-term cultural effect of the persecution.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Parliament, not the king, decided what English people were allowed to believe after 1660.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about religious policy in Restoration England? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The Cavalier Parliament drove the Clarendon Code through despite Edward Hyde’s and Charles II’s preference for wider toleration, showing MPs set the boundaries of permitted worship.
• Parliament forced Charles to withdraw the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence in March 1673 by withholding war taxes, then passed the First Test Act of 1673.
• Royal finance gave Parliament permanent leverage: the £1.2 million annual grant was always too small, so Charles needed parliamentary supply for any war or major project.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Charles II retained the formal right to issue royal proclamations and could attempt to suspend penal laws — the 1672 Indulgence shows he could act, even if he had to retreat.
• In day-to-day enforcement, magistrates and bishops applied the Code unevenly: persecution of Dissenters varied locally as much as nationally.
• The king’s personal preference shaped the climate — Charles disliked persecuting his own brother for Catholicism and used patronage to protect favoured Dissenters.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1908 Navy League pamphlet praising Weltpolitik for uniting Germans behind the Kaiser) and Interpretation B (a 1912 SPD newspaper editorial arguing the Navy Laws benefited industrialists at the expense of working families) on the domestic effects of the Navy Laws. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Navy Laws as a unifying national project — jobs, prestige and a million-strong Navy League membership show ordinary Germans backing the Kaiser.
• Interpretation B presents the Navy Laws as a class issue — profits flowed to Krupp and Thyssen while workers paid through indirect taxes and got little say.
• Main difference: A frames the laws as positive national integration; B frames them as economic redistribution from poor to rich.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support from each interpretation. Secure (3): difference identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each interpretation. Emerging (1): summarises one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1908 Navy League pamphlet) and Interpretation B (a 1912 SPD newspaper editorial) give different views about the impact of the Navy Laws on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the Navy League pamphlet was recruitment propaganda for middle-class patriots; the SPD editorial was campaign material for the 1912 election.
• They use different evidence — the pamphlet cites enrolment numbers and shipyard employment; the editorial cites tax burdens and the absence of socialists from cabinet.
• They were produced at different points in the cycle — 1908 came before the Daily Telegraph affair when the Navy League was at peak influence; 1912 came after the SPD election victory.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again rather than explaining why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Navy Laws on the domestic politics of Imperial Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Created jobs and contracts — shipyards at Kiel, Hamburg and Wilhelmshaven employed tens of thousands and Ruhr firms like Krupp won huge steel orders, binding industrial workers and capitalists to the regime.
• Forced political bargaining — Tirpitz had to assemble Reichstag majorities of Conservatives, National Liberals and the Centre Party for each law, exposing how dependent the Kaiser was on parliament.
• Strained the budget — the navy cost roughly half the imperial budget by 1912 and forced new taxes including the 1913 inheritance tax, which split the conservative bloc.
• Damaged Junker farmers — cheaper grain tariffs were traded away to win urban votes, eroding the political base of the Kaiser's traditional supporters.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with precise figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped effects. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Kaiserreich kept the appearance of democracy while denying its reality — the SPD's 1912 victory changed nothing about who governed Germany.' How convincing is Interpretation A about political power in Germany before 1914?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A is convincing because cabinet appointments stayed with the Kaiser — despite winning 110 seats and 4.25 million votes in 1912, no SPD member ever became a minister.
• Convincing because the Bundesrat, dominated by Prussia's seventeen seats, could veto reform regardless of how the Reichstag voted.
• Less convincing because the Reichstag did exercise real power over budgets — Tirpitz had to bargain for every Navy Law, and the SPD's votes mattered for the 1913 inheritance tax.
• Less convincing because welfare reform continued (the 1911 insurance code) and trade-union strikes affected real outcomes — democratisation was uneven, not nonexistent.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on cabinet appointments but overstated on legislation and policy.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases the interpretation or adds context but does not evaluate. Emerging (1-2): describes the topic without engaging with the interpretation.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a Navy League pamphlet stressing the unifying power of Weltpolitik) and Interpretation B (a 1914 SPD historian's analysis arguing Weltpolitik widened class divisions) on whether Weltpolitik united or divided German society. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A claims Weltpolitik successfully united Germans — the Navy League had over a million members; jobs and patriotism cut across class lines.
• Interpretation B claims Weltpolitik deepened divisions — the costs fell on working-class taxpayers while profits enriched a narrow industrial elite, and SPD opposition grew with each Navy Law.
• Main difference: A focuses on patriotic mobilisation; B focuses on economic and class outcomes.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each interpretation. Emerging (1): summarises one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the rise of the SPD between 1890 and 1914 on Wilhelm II's domestic policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Drove the regime towards Weltpolitik and the Navy Laws as a way of distracting workers from socialism and uniting them behind imperial prestige.
• Forced the extension of welfare reform — building on Bismarck's earlier insurance laws, the 1911 imperial insurance code expanded sickness, accident and old-age cover to undercut SPD appeal.
• Hardened the Kaiser's hostility to constitutional reform — he refused all suggestions of admitting socialists to cabinet, calling them ‘traitors’, despite their 1912 election win.
• Forced bargains in the Reichstag — Tirpitz needed to manage Centre Party and National Liberal votes carefully because SPD members consistently voted against military spending.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates/figures. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from Winston Churchill’s ‘Sinews of Peace’ speech at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, 5 March 1946.
‘From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent. Behind that line lie all the capitals of the ancient states of Central and Eastern Europe… all are subject, in one form or another, not only to Soviet influence but to a very high and increasing measure of control from Moscow.’

Source A suggests that Churchill was alarmed by how far Soviet control had spread across Europe. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• An ‘iron curtain’ has descended — Europe is now divided.
• Capitals of Central and Eastern Europe lie behind that line — the divide includes major historical cities.
• Those countries are subject to Soviet influence and growing Moscow control.
• The ‘increasing measure of control’ phrase implies that Soviet domination is deepening, not stable.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Churchill spoke at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri on 5 March 1946, with Truman on the platform.
• Between 1945 and 1948 rigged elections put communist governments into power across Eastern Europe.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a State Department telegram from George Kennan, US chargé d’affaires in Moscow, sent on 22 February 1946 and known later as the ‘Long Telegram’.
‘The Soviet view is that there can be no permanent peaceful coexistence with capitalism. The USSR will press at every weak point until it meets resistance. We must build economic strength in our partners abroad and self-confidence at home, for force is the only language they respect.’

Source B suggests that Kennan believed the USA could not cooperate with the Soviet Union. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Build economic strength in partners abroad.
• Build self-confidence at home.
• Recognise that the USSR sees no permanent peaceful coexistence with capitalism.
• Use force as the ‘only language they respect’ — meet pressure with resistance.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Kennan sent the Long Telegram from the US embassy in Moscow on 22 February 1946.
• His argument became the policy of containment, announced as the Truman Doctrine in March 1947.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C and Source D.

Source C: An extract from a Soviet government statement on the Iron Curtain Speech, broadcast by Moscow Radio in March 1946.
‘Mr Churchill calls for a war of nerves against the peace-loving peoples of Eastern Europe. He forgets that the USSR lost millions of dead defending those same peoples from fascism. Our friendship with our western neighbours is not control; it is the natural product of shared sacrifice.’

Source D: An extract from a private letter from US Secretary of State James Byrnes to a Senator, written in April 1946.
‘The Russian elections in Poland and Romania have been a humiliating spectacle. Our protests through diplomatic channels have produced nothing. The patient policy of the past twelve months is at an end; we shall now speak more plainly.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources C and D to a historian studying the breakdown of cooperation between the USA and USSR in 1946. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source C — Content: rejects Churchill’s argument and frames Soviet influence as ‘natural friendship’. Provenance: an official Soviet broadcast in 1946, designed to shape domestic and international opinion — useful for revealing the public Soviet line, less useful for revealing private Soviet calculation. Own knowledge: Soviet wartime losses were genuine and shaped the demand for friendly western neighbours, but the rigged elections in Poland and Hungary contradict the ‘natural friendship’ framing.
Source D — Content: announces a tougher US line after twelve months of patience. Provenance: a private letter from the Secretary of State to a Senator in 1946 — close to the inner US discussion, candid in tone, useful for capturing the moment policy shifted. Own knowledge: the Truman Doctrine was less than a year away; Byrnes’s frustration matches Kennan’s ‘Long Telegram’ arguments from February 1946.
Judgement: Both are useful but partial — together they show how each side framed the breakdown for a domestic audience while privately recognising the structural problem.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Eastern Europe came under Soviet control between 1945 and 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the consolidation of Soviet control through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1945: the Red Army occupied Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and eastern Germany at the end of the war.
• 1945–46: provisional governments were formed in which local communists held key ministries (interior, security, agriculture).
• 1946: rigged elections in Bulgaria and Romania confirmed communist-led governments.
• 1947: a fraudulent election in Poland produced a communist majority despite the popularity of non-communist parties.
• 1947: in Hungary, ‘salami tactics’ sliced off the smallholder and social-democratic rivals one at a time.
• February 1948: a non-violent coup in Czechoslovakia, the most genuinely democratic of the bloc, completed the pattern.

practice_questions.text:
‘The atom bomb was the main reason relations between the USA and the USSR broke down between 1945 and 1946.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Hiroshima and Nagasaki gave the USA a monopoly that made Soviet help against Japan unnecessary.
• Stalin ordered a crash Soviet bomb programme at once, so an arms race began immediately.
• Truman knew the Trinity test had worked before Potsdam opened, which hardened his negotiating line.
• The USA kept the bomb secret from its ally, which confirmed Soviet suspicion of Western intentions.
Disagree:
• Rigged elections put communist governments into Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria whatever the bomb did.
• The gap between capitalism and communism was older than 1945 and neither side trusted the other.
• Churchill's Fulton speech of March 1946 blamed Soviet expansion in Europe, not the bomb.
• Kennan's Long Telegram of February 1946 blamed Soviet ideology and insecurity, not American weapons.
Judgement: the bomb sharpened and speeded a breakdown whose main causes were ideology and Soviet control of Eastern Europe.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the use of the atom bomb in 1945 affected superpower relations through to early 1946.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the deteriorated relationship through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 16 July 1945: the Trinity test in New Mexico gave Truman a working atomic weapon on the eve of Potsdam.
• 24 July 1945: Truman told Stalin of a ‘new weapon’; Stalin’s muted reaction reflected prior knowledge through Soviet espionage.
• 6 and 9 August 1945: Hiroshima and Nagasaki destroyed; Japan surrendered on 15 August, ending the Pacific war and reducing US dependence on Soviet entry.
• Late 1945: Stalin ordered the acceleration of the Soviet atomic project, including using captured German scientists.
• February 1946: Kennan’s Long Telegram warned that the USSR understood only firmness, partly because the bomb had not produced cooperation.
• March 1946: Churchill’s Fulton speech publicly named the rivalry the bomb had hardened — setting the stage for an open Cold War.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a radio address by US President Harry S. Truman to the American people, broadcast on the evening of 27 June 1950, two days after the North Korean invasion of South Korea.
‘The attack upon Korea makes it plain beyond all doubt that communism has passed beyond the use of subversion to conquer independent nations and will now use armed invasion and war. I have therefore ordered United States air and sea forces to give the Korean government troops cover and support.’

Source A suggests that Truman saw the invasion of South Korea as a threat far beyond Korea itself. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Truman says communism has ‘passed beyond the use of subversion’ to armed invasion and war.
• He treats the attack as evidence about communism as a whole, not only about Korea.
• He has already ordered US air and sea forces to give South Korean troops ‘cover and support’.
Contextual knowledge: Truman had been accused of ‘losing China’ in 1949, so containment made Korea a test of whether the United States would fight.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a confidential report by the British Foreign Office, dated late June 1950, on the United Nations Security Council vote to authorise force in Korea.
‘The vote could not have been carried had the Soviet representative been present to exercise his veto. He has been absent since January, in protest at the seating of Nationalist China rather than the People’s Republic. The Americans seized the opportunity at speed.’

Source B suggests that the UN vote to authorise force was only possible because of a Soviet mistake. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The vote ‘could not have been carried had the Soviet representative been present’ to veto it.
• The USSR had been absent since January in protest at the seating of Nationalist China.
• The Americans ‘seized the opportunity at speed’ while the Soviet seat was empty.
Contextual knowledge: Resolutions 82 and 83 passed on 25 and 27 June 1950; the Soviet boycott had begun in January 1950 and lasted until August.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C.

Source C: An extract from an article in a British newspaper, the Manchester Guardian, published on 26 June 1950, the day after the invasion.
‘The North Korean attack appears to have been carefully prepared. Soviet-built tanks led the advance, and the South Korean troops, lightly armed and lacking armour, fell back in disorder. Seoul itself is now reported under threat. The democracies must decide quickly whether this aggression will be met or accepted.’

Source C suggests that the South Korean army was in no position to stop the invasion. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source C and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The attack had been ‘carefully prepared’ and was led by Soviet-built tanks.
• South Korean troops were ‘lightly armed’ and lacked armour of their own.
• They ‘fell back in disorder’, which points to weak command and morale.
Contextual knowledge: Washington had deliberately denied Rhee tanks and heavy artillery, while about 90,000 North Korean troops attacked with 150 T-34 tanks; Seoul fell within three days.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from an internal US State Department briefing, written on 26 June 1950 and later declassified, summarising why immediate intervention was felt necessary.
‘The fall of Korea would expose Japan, demoralise our allies in the Pacific, and confirm the perception that the United States retreats whenever communist powers attack a small ally. The strategic value of Korea is small. The strategic value of resisting is great.’

Source D suggests that American officials valued resisting in Korea more than they valued Korea itself. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Losing Korea would ‘expose Japan’ and demoralise allies across the Pacific.
• It would confirm that the United States retreats whenever a small ally is attacked.
• The briefing says plainly that Korea’s own strategic value is small but the value of resisting is great.
Contextual knowledge: Korea had little industry or strategic weight of its own; after the communist victory in China in 1949 Truman could not afford to look weak in Asia.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a private memorandum written by the Soviet ambassador to the UN, Yakov Malik, justifying the Soviet boycott in June 1950.
‘The Council’s recognition of the Nationalist faction on Taiwan as the lawful representative of China is an offence we cannot accept. Our absence is a protest. Until that injustice is corrected we will not return to the Council chamber.’

Source E suggests that the Soviet boycott of the Security Council was a deliberate political protest. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source E and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Malik names the seating of the Nationalists on Taiwan as ‘an offence we cannot accept’.
• He calls the absence a protest rather than an accident.
• The USSR will not return to the chamber until the China seat is changed.
Contextual knowledge: The boycott ran from January to August 1950, so no Soviet veto was cast against Resolutions 82 and 83 in June.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a wartime British army intelligence report on the Pusan Perimeter, August 1950.
‘Despite catastrophic losses on the retreat south, the defensive line is being stabilised by US air superiority and the steady flow of fresh divisions from Japan. North Korean supply lines are now stretched and vulnerable. The enemy may have peaked.’

Source F suggests that the balance of the fighting was starting to turn against North Korea. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The defensive line is being ‘stabilised by US air superiority’.
• Fresh divisions are arriving steadily from Japan.
• North Korean supply lines are ‘stretched and vulnerable’ and the enemy ‘may have peaked’.
Contextual knowledge: By August 1950 UN forces held the Pusan Perimeter, a 230km line in the south-east, while North Korean supply lines ran the length of the peninsula.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Hundred Rolls inquiry of 1274–75.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Royal commissioners were sent into every hundred of every county and questioned local juries on oath about royal rights, corrupt officials and private liberties.
• The inquiry recorded its findings on long parchment rolls, which gave Edward I a written record of where royal authority had been lost or abused.
• The questions were standardised across the country, drafted in the chancery under Robert Burnell, so that answers could be compared between counties.
• The data fed directly into later legislation, including the First Statute of Westminster (1275) and the Quo Warranto inquiries that began in 1278.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the Quo Warranto inquiries changed relations between Edward I and the nobility.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Many barons resented being challenged to prove their right to liberties their families had held for generations — this caused tension between Edward and the older nobility, captured in stories like Earl Warenne’s ‘rusty sword’.
• The inquiries forced barons to look for old charters and royal grants in their muniments rooms; this made the relationship between king and noble more legalistic and document-based, and reduced reliance on custom alone.
• The Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) was a compromise: continuous use since 1189 was accepted as warrant, which calmed baronial anger but still asserted that all jurisdiction came from the crown.
• Edward avoided open rebellion by working with leading magnates such as the earls of Gloucester and Norfolk, but he stored up resentment that would surface later in the reign over taxation and the Welsh and Scottish wars.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of effects on king-noble relations, with explicit causal links and precise vocabulary.
Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but explanation is descriptive rather than causal.
Emerging: Simple statements about Quo Warranto with little reference to relations with nobles.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Robert Burnell for Edward I’s government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Burnell was Lord Chancellor from 1274 until his death in 1292, providing eighteen years of administrative continuity at the heart of royal government.
• He designed the Hundred Rolls inquiry and shaped the great Edwardian statutes, including Westminster I (1275), Gloucester (1278), Mortmain (1279) and Westminster II (1285); without his organising mind, the legislative programme would have been impossible.
• His mastery of the chancery and the great seal turned royal government into a paper machine that could reach every county; the writs that summoned juries, opened pleas and demanded warrants all flowed through his office.
• Over time, the Burnell era set a template for English government: a learned chancellor, a permanent chancery, and a king who governed by statute and writ rather than by personal command alone.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise terminology.
Secure: Clear discussion of why Burnell mattered, with relevant detail and at least two reasons.
Developing: Some significance discussed but largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about Burnell’s role with no real discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: ‘The Hundred Rolls inquiry was the most important reform of Edward I’s early reign.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The inquiry produced the data that drove every other reform: the Statutes of Westminster, Gloucester and Mortmain all responded to evidence gathered in 1274–75.
• It established a new style of government — rule by paper, evidence and standardised questions — which would become a permanent feature of English administration.
• It restored confidence in royal justice by exposing corrupt sheriffs and bailiffs, giving ordinary people reason to trust royal courts again.

Arguments for other reforms:
• The Statute of Westminster I (1275) translated complaints into actual law, banning corruption in juries and protecting widows and tenants.
• The Quo Warranto inquiries challenged baronial liberties directly, which the Hundred Rolls only described.
• The First Statute of Westminster fixed the rules for elections to parliament and is sometimes seen as the foundation of later parliamentary practice.

Judgement should weigh the data-gathering of the Hundred Rolls against the legal change produced by the early statutes, recognising that the inquiry made the reforms possible but that the reforms themselves changed lives.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument with weighed factors and a justified overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail on more than one factor and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Quo Warranto inquiries between 1278 and 1290.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• From 1278, royal justices on circuit demanded that barons prove the warrant for their private liberties — courts, markets, fairs and hundred jurisdictions.
• The inquiries assumed that all jurisdiction belonged to the crown unless a lord could produce a royal charter or grant.
• The famous response of Earl Warenne — brandishing an old sword as his ‘warrant’ — captured baronial resistance to written-charter standards of proof.
• The Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) accepted continuous use since the coronation of Richard I (1189) as valid warrant.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of Quo Warranto (1290) for the relationship between the crown and the nobility.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The statute was a compromise: it accepted continuous use since 1189 as proof of warrant, which calmed baronial anger that the king was trying to strip away ancient privileges.
• It still asserted the principle that all jurisdiction flowed from the crown, even where the crown could not actually take it back, which mattered in later disputes between kings and over-mighty subjects.
• The compromise allowed Edward to keep working with leading magnates through the 1290s while he turned to the Welsh and Scottish wars; this is why historians speak of Edward as a constitutional pragmatist rather than a tyrant.
• Over time, the principle of warrant from royal grant shaped how franchises were granted and policed under later medieval kings.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance discussed at the time and over time with sustained causal explanation.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance described but largely tied to immediate effects.
Emerging: Simple statement of what the statute did with no real significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Magna Carta in the changing relationship between citizen and state in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time (limited): a peace treaty between King John and rebel barons; protected the elite, not ordinary subjects; annulled by Pope Innocent III within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
• Significance at the time (real but small): clause 12 required common counsel for taxation; clause 39 promised due process for 'free men'; established that the king could be made to negotiate.
• Significance over time: reissued under Henry III in 1216, 1217, 1225 — survived as a constitutional document.
• Significance over time: 17th-century lawyers like Sir Edward Coke reinterpreted clause 39 against Charles I; foundation for the 1628 Petition of Right and parliamentary supremacy.
• Long-term legacy: clause 39 still in UK law today; basis of due process and habeas corpus; echoed in the US Bill of Rights and in modern human rights debates.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both then and over time, with specific evidence.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence; may favour one timeframe.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the crisis of King John's reign between 1199 and 1215 for the limits on royal power.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: John lost Normandy and Anjou to Philip II by 1204 and was beaten at Bouvines in July 1214, stripping him of the prestige that held the barons in line.
• At the time: eleven scutages in seventeen years and the papal interdict of 1208-1214 turned grievance into armed revolt; the rebels took London in May 1215.
• At the time: Stephen Langton used Henry I's coronation charter of 1100 as a template, so the demands looked like old rights restored rather than new ones invented.
• Over time: the charter sealed at Runnymede on 15 June 1215 put in writing that the king was under the law, even though the Pope annulled it within ten weeks.
• Over time: reissues in 1216, 1217, 1225 and 1297 kept the text alive for lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke to use against Charles I.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the limits placed on King John in 1215 were similar to the limits later placed on Charles I in the 1640s.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both limits emerged from armed revolt, not voluntary concession: barons forced John to seal Magna Carta; Parliament fought a Civil War against Charles I.
• Both centred on taxation: clause 12 of Magna Carta required common counsel for scutage; the Civil War was triggered partly by Charles's ship money and personal rule.
