• Both used the language of established law against the king: Langton invoked Henry I's charter; Coke and parliamentarians invoked Magna Carta itself.
• Both produced documents claiming to bind future kings: Magna Carta (reissued repeatedly); the Petition of Right 1628 and 1689 Bill of Rights.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, fully developed.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: 'The role of individuals was the main factor in producing Magna Carta.' Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arguments for individuals: Stephen Langton drafted the terms using Henry I's charter as a template; King John's personal failures (Bouvines, the interdict) created the crisis; rebel barons led by Robert Fitzwalter organised the revolt.
• Arguments against — war: defeat at Bouvines 1214 stripped John of military prestige and made revolt possible.
• Arguments against — the economy: eleven scutages in seventeen years and arbitrary fines drove baronial anger.
• Arguments against — religion: papal interdict 1208–1213 weakened John; Langton's mediation flowed from his church position.
• Arguments against — government overreach: arbitrary justice, abuse of forest law, exploitation of feudal incidents.
• Cross-period weighing: ideas (rule of law) shaped 1689 and 1832 too — but only because individuals like Coke later reinterpreted Magna Carta.
• Judgement: individuals mattered, but only because military defeat, taxation crisis and church conflict had already created the conditions.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Top band rewards a sustained argument addressing the named factor and weighing it against at least two others]

Mastering: Substantiated argument addressing individuals and weighing against at least two other factors, with examples from at least two periods.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant comparison.
Developing: Some argument with basic comparison.
Emerging: Single-factor or single-period response.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the impact of Magna Carta in 1215 was different from its impact in 1628.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In 1215 the charter was annulled by the Pope within ten weeks and civil war resumed; in 1628 it was used by Sir Edward Coke and Parliament as binding constitutional law against Charles I.
• In 1215 'free man' covered only the elite; by 1628 lawyers were arguing clause 39 protected every Englishman.
• In 1215 it was a peace treaty between king and barons; in 1628 it was treated as a statement of universal liberties underlying the Petition of Right.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, fully developed.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of clause 39 of Magna Carta.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: protected free men from arbitrary imprisonment without lawful judgement of their peers — but free men were a minority of the population.
• Significance at the time: the first time a king conceded in writing that he was bound by the law, not above it.
• Significance over time: cited by Sir Edward Coke against Charles I in the 1620s; foundation of habeas corpus.
• Significance over time: text echoed in the 1628 Petition of Right, the US Fifth Amendment, the European Convention on Human Rights.
• Significance over time: the clause is still in force in UK statute today, renumbered 29 in the 1297 reissue and among the oldest law still on the statute book.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance with specific evidence.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the official text of the Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, signed 28 June 1919.
‘The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons why this clause was so resented in Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief supporting quotations.
Secure: Two clear reasons, briefly supported.
Developing: One clear point; second weak or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• It forced Germany alone to accept responsibility for the war (‘the responsibility of Germany’).
• It blamed the war on Germany’s ‘aggression’, which most Germans rejected.
• It implied Germany must pay for ‘all the loss and damage’ — opening the door to vast reparations.
• The clause spoke for ‘nationals’ as well as governments, suggesting Germany owed compensation to private citizens too.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the steps by which the Treaty of Versailles was finalised, from the opening of the Paris Peace Conference in January 1919 to its signing on 28 June 1919.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1919: Paris Peace Conference opened; the Council of Ten and later Council of Four met in private.
• March–April 1919: the Big Three argued bitterly over reparations and the Rhineland; Wilson briefly fell ill.
• 7 May 1919: terms presented to the German delegation at Versailles; Germany given 15 days to respond, later extended.
• Late May 1919: German counter-proposals were almost entirely rejected.
• 16 June 1919: an ultimatum demanded German signature within seven days or fighting would resume.
• 28 June 1919: the Treaty of Versailles signed in the Hall of Mirrors, five years to the day after the Sarajevo assassination.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a German government memorandum to the Allied powers, drafted by Foreign Minister Count Brockdorff-Rantzau in May 1919.
‘Such a peace would condemn the German people to perpetual slavery. The army restrictions leave us defenceless before any neighbour. The reparations cannot be met without ruining our economy. The territorial losses sever millions of Germans from the Reich. We cannot accept that one nation alone be branded as the cause of the war.’

Source C: An extract from a private letter by Marshal Ferdinand Foch, French commander-in-chief of Allied forces, to a colleague in June 1919.
‘This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years. The Rhine is not the frontier; therefore Germany will rise again, and we shall be invaded a third time.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying reactions to the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Lists the four pillars of German objection: military, financial, territorial, war guilt. Provenance: official German government document by the leading negotiator; designed to put the German case to the Allies and to a domestic audience. Own knowledge: Germans called the treaty a Diktat; Article 231 became the most hated clause; reparations were eventually set at £6.6 billion.
Source C — Content: A French general dismisses the treaty as merely a 20-year armistice because the Rhine is not the western frontier. Provenance: a private letter by France’s most senior soldier; expresses unguarded views to a peer. Own knowledge: Foch had wanted the Rhine as the French frontier; Clemenceau accepted demilitarisation instead. Foch’s prediction proved accurate when Germany invaded France in 1940.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the German political reaction but partial as it omits the harsher Brest-Litovsk precedent; C is useful as informed French military opinion but reflects a particular hawkish position.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Treaty of Versailles was an economic disaster waiting to happen.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Keynes, who had been at Paris for the Treasury, argued the treaty did nothing for Europe’s economic recovery.
• Reparations of £6.6 billion (set in 1921) outran Germany’s capacity to pay; the 1923 hyperinflation followed German default and the French occupation of the Ruhr.
• Loss of the Saar coalfield, the merchant fleet and all the colonies stripped Germany of significant wealth.
Challenging the statement:
• French opinion saw the treaty as security, not economic ruin, and France had real reconstruction costs to meet.
• Germany paid only a fraction of the bill; the terms were renegotiated by the Dawes Plan (1924) and the Young Plan (1929).
• The 1929 Wall Street Crash and the Depression were the decisive blow, not Versailles itself.
Judgement: the economic terms were severe and short-sighted, but ‘inevitable disaster’ underestimates the role of later shocks.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British civil servant Sir Eric Phipps, who was attached to the British Embassy in Paris in 1919. Diary entry for 7 May 1919.
‘Today the German delegation was handed the treaty. They were not permitted to debate it. Brockdorff-Rantzau read his reply seated, which was taken as an insult. The whole proceeding had the air of a sentencing rather than a negotiation.’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about how the Treaty of Versailles was presented to Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• The German delegation was excluded from negotiation — direct support for the Diktat charge.
• The proceedings had ‘the air of a sentencing rather than a negotiation’.
• Own knowledge: Brockdorff-Rantzau’s seated reply did cause offence; Germany was given 15 days to comment and most counter-proposals were rejected.
• Worth noting: as a British observer, Phipps may underplay Allied reasons for the format.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the territorial losses Germany suffered under the Treaty of Versailles, identifying which lands changed hands in which direction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more territorial settlements with reasons and consequences; precise place-names.
Secure: Three or more territorial changes covered with some causal explanation.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin coverage.

Indicative content:
• Western frontier: Alsace-Lorraine returned to France after 48 years; Eupen-Malmédy ceded to Belgium; the Saar placed under League administration for 15 years with French use of its coal.
• Northern frontier: North Schleswig given to Denmark following a 1920 plebiscite.
• Eastern frontier: Posen and West Prussia ceded to recreated Poland, forming the Polish Corridor; Danzig made a Free City under League supervision; East Prussia separated from the rest of Germany.
• Overseas: all German colonies in Africa, the Pacific and China stripped away and redistributed as League of Nations mandates to Britain, France, Belgium, Japan and South Africa.
• Specific bans: union with Austria (Anschluss) forbidden; the Rhineland demilitarised.

practice_questions.text: Source A is a briefing on Gulf oil security written inside the US State Department in 1990. Source B is an article looking back on Western interests in the Gulf in 1990, published in a UK foreign-affairs journal in 2016. Study Sources A and B. How useful are Sources A and B to an historian studying why outside powers were drawn into the Gulf in 1990? Explain your answer using Sources A and B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Source A is contemporary, written by officials with direct access to oil-supply intelligence — useful for showing official Western priorities at the time, especially the Strait of Hormuz and OPEC dynamics. Limited because it cannot reflect on outcomes and is shaped by realpolitik framing.
• Source B has the benefit of hindsight, drawing on declassified material and post-Chilcot reflection — useful for weighing whether 1990 priorities were proportionate, but coloured by later political controversies.
• Own knowledge: Gulf held two-thirds of proven oil reserves; Strait of Hormuz carried roughly a fifth of seaborne oil; OPEC quota disputes and the First Intifada reinforced perceptions of US bias.
• A judgement should weigh the two sources rather than dismissing one as biased — both have value if their provenance is read carefully.
[12 marks — Mastering: Integrated content, provenance and own knowledge with substantiated overall judgement on usefulness. Secure: Clear use of all three with some judgement. Developing: Two of the three integrated. Emerging: Surface-level reference to who wrote each source.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the United States responded to the Iran-Iraq war between 1982 and 1988.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In 1982 Washington removed Iraq from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, opening the way to a working relationship during the war.
• Through the mid-1980s the United States tilted towards Iraq as a counterweight to revolutionary Iran, sharing satellite intelligence.
• During the Tanker War the US navy re-flagged Kuwaiti tankers and escorted them, keeping Gulf oil moving under American protection.
• Basing and arms agreements with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain deepened, protecting the route through the Strait of Hormuz.
• Washington's response to the Halabja chemical attack of March 1988 was muted, because breaking with Baghdad would have helped Tehran.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'Oil was the main reason outside powers involved themselves in the Gulf by 1990.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: the Gulf held roughly two-thirds of the world's proven oil reserves, and around a fifth of the world's seaborne oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz, only 39 kilometres wide at its narrowest.
• Agree: the Tanker War of 1984–88 showed how easily that shipping could be disrupted, drawing Western navies into escort duties.
• Agree: OPEC quota disputes gave outside powers a direct interest in who controlled Gulf production.
• Disagree: Cold War alignments mattered too — Soviet arms ties to Iraq, American basing and arms deals with Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain.
• Disagree: the Israeli-Palestinian conflict pulled outside powers in, fed perceptions of US bias and gave Saddam pan-Arab cover.
• Judgement: oil was why the region could never be ignored, but Cold War clients and the Israeli-Palestinian quarrel shaped how each power acted.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how superpower involvement in the Gulf changed between the Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the summer of 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 1979 revolution destroyed the American position in Iran; US embassy staff were taken hostage in Tehran and Washington lost its Gulf anchor.
• Within months the USSR invaded Afghanistan, so both superpowers were suddenly without a comfortable client in the region.
• Through the 1980s the United States tilted towards Iraq while the Soviet Union kept selling it weapons and opened cautious channels to Iran.
• American basing and arms links with Saudi Arabia and the smaller Gulf states deepened, especially during the Tanker War.
• By 1989–90, with the Berlin Wall down and Gorbachev seeking better relations with Washington, Moscow was ready to work with the United States at the UN.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Israeli-Palestinian conflict added to tension in the Gulf between 1987 and August 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The First Intifada from December 1987 dominated Arab media, intensifying public anger at perceived US backing of Israel just as the Iran-Iraq war was ending.
• Saddam Hussein began linking Iraqi grievances to the Palestinian cause, casting himself as the leader of an Arab nation betrayed by the West.
• Returning Arab veterans from the Soviet-Afghan war absorbed Intifada imagery, helping to shape the jihadist narrative that the United States was the patron of every Arab grievance.
• In August 1990 Saddam tried to make an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait conditional on Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank, an explicit attempt to link the two conflicts.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'The United States helped to create the conditions for the 1990 Gulf crisis.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: the 1982 removal of Iraq from the terrorism list and the intelligence-sharing tilt of the mid-1980s helped Saddam survive the war with Iran.
• Agree: muted criticism of Halabja taught the regime that brutality carried little cost.
• Agree: mixed American signals in July 1990, including the Glaspie meeting, left Saddam believing the United States would not fight for Kuwait.
• Disagree: the decisive pressures were Iraqi — $80 billion of debt, an army that could not be demobilised, and a leader who needed a victory.
• Disagree: Kuwait's overproduction and refusal to write off loans supplied the immediate trigger.
• Judgement: American policy shaped the setting, but the decision to invade was Saddam's and rested on Iraq's own problems.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text:
Has the discovery of gold been the main reason settlers went west in the 1840s?

• The 1848 California Gold Rush
• Pioneer farming and the trails

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Gold Rush against pioneer farming (and other factors) and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support across both bullets and additional material.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached.
Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative.

Indicative content:
• 1848 Gold Rush: Sutter’s Mill discovery, 80,000 forty-niners in 1849, California population from 14,000 in 1848 to 220,000 by 1852, statehood 1850, boom towns, vigilance committees.
• Pioneer farming: Oregon Trail from 1841, California Trail, wagon trains from Independence, fertile Willamette Valley, 1846 Oregon settlement with Britain.
• Other relevant material: 1837 Panic, soil exhaustion, urban overcrowding, religious freedom (Mormons), missionary reports, transport.
• Judgement: top answers might argue gold caused a faster but shallower transformation, while farming changed the West more permanently, OR that gold was decisive because it triggered the railroad, statehood and Chinese immigration. Either view, substantiated, can reach the top band.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the 1848 California Gold Rush on the American West.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (forty-niners, San Francisco growth, Chinese immigration, Native population fall, vigilance committees, 1850 statehood).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about the rush.

Indicative content:
• Demographic change: California’s population grew from around 14,000 in 1848 to over 220,000 by 1852; California was admitted to the Union in 1850.
• Boom towns and lawlessness: rapid growth of San Francisco, vigilance committees in the absence of courts, soaring food and tool prices.
• Chinese immigration: roughly 25,000 Chinese arrived 1849–54, creating a new ethnic community that would face discrimination and violence.
• Native displacement: California’s Native population collapsed from around 150,000 in 1845 to under 30,000 by 1870.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the journey west on the Oregon or California Trail.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features with precise detail.
Secure: Two valid features with brief support.
Developing: One developed; one undeveloped.
Emerging: Generalised description.

Indicative content:
• Wagon trains: columns of fifteen to fifty covered wagons gathering at Independence, Missouri, with elected captains setting the pace.
• Use of oxen: oxen rather than horses pulled the wagons because they ate prairie grass and could pull heavier loads.
• Length and timing: roughly 2,000 miles, four to six months, requiring a spring start to clear the Rockies before autumn snow.
• Hardships: cholera and dysentery from contaminated water, river-crossing drownings, accidental shootings, hail and blizzards.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of the 1849 Gold Rush.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a popular history of California, 1948.
“The forty-niners were the first true Californians — men of energy and grit who turned a sleepy backwater into a great state in twelve months.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a 2010 study of the American West.
“The Gold Rush was an environmental and human catastrophe. Rivers were ripped up, forests felled, and the Native population of California reduced by more than three quarters in a generation.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, supported differences drawn from both interpretations.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support.
Developing: One difference; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 celebrates the forty-niners; Interpretation 2 focuses on the harm caused by the rush.
• Interpretation 1 frames California’s growth as positive; Interpretation 2 frames it as catastrophe.
• Interpretation 1 centres white male migrants; Interpretation 2 centres Native peoples and the environment.
• Interpretation 1 talks about ‘energy and grit’; Interpretation 2 talks about ‘reduction by three quarters’.

practice_questions.text:
Why might the two interpretations of the Gold Rush above give different views?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise context.
Secure: Reason rooted in provenance or context with brief support.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’.
Emerging: Restates content of each interpretation.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: 1948 was a high-water mark for celebratory state histories; by 2010 environmental and Native voices had reshaped the field.
• Purpose: 1948 popular history meant to entertain and build California identity; 2010 study meant to question received accounts.
• Evidence: a popular history relied on memoirs of successful miners; a 2010 study used demographic data, environmental records, and indigenous oral history.
• Audience: a general California reading public versus academic readers and policymakers.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the dangers of the trail on pioneer migration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (cholera, river crossings, Donner Party, wagon-train captains, oxen, spring start).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about danger.

Indicative content:
• Need for organisation: the danger of cholera, accidents and weather meant migrants could not travel alone, encouraging the wagon-train system with elected captains.
• Timing: pioneers had to leave Independence early in spring to cross the Rockies before snow, as the Donner Party of 1846–47 showed.
• Equipment: oxen, large wagons, communal supplies and shared tools became standard because individual families could not survive the trail alone.
• Public reaction: stories of disaster like the Donner Party reached the East and shaped how migrants prepared for the journey rather than stopping it altogether.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the succession problem developed in the 1590s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It increased anxiety among ministers and gentry that Elizabeth’s death might trigger civil war between rival claimants.
• It encouraged Catholic writers abroad — for example Robert Persons in 1595 — to argue for foreign claims, including the Spanish royal family.
• It pushed Robert Cecil to open secret correspondence with James VI of Scotland from the late 1590s, ensuring a peaceful succession in 1603.
• It preserved Elizabeth’s personal authority by stopping ambitious nobles ‘setting their eyes on the rising sun’.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Parliament for Elizabeth’s government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Parliament was the only body that could grant taxation, so the Crown depended on it for the funds to defend the kingdom — for example, the wars in the Netherlands and against Spain.
• Parliament passed the Acts that underpinned the Religious Settlement, the Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598, and the laws against Catholic recusants.
• Significance over time: clashes with Wentworth and others (1566, 1576) set early limits on royal control of debate that later parliaments would push back against.
• Elizabeth restricted these powers by calling Parliament only ten times and ruling marriage and succession out of bounds.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Elizabeth used marriage negotiations in her dealings with France and Spain between 1568 and 1581.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Negotiations with the Habsburg Archduke Charles in the late 1560s helped balance France against Spain without committing England to either.
• Talks with Francis, Duke of Anjou, in 1581 cooled tensions with France and delayed open war with Spain.
• Continued Spanish hopes that Philip II might secure influence over the English throne discouraged earlier invasion plans.
• At home, the unresolved question fed Parliamentary anxiety and pressure on Elizabeth to commit, which she resisted.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Elizabeth’s claim that marriage and the succession were matters of royal prerogative.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It limited Parliament’s freedom of speech: when Paul Wentworth raised these issues in 1566 and Peter Wentworth followed in 1576, both were silenced and Peter was imprisoned.
• It preserved Elizabeth’s personal authority during her reign by keeping the most sensitive decisions in her own hands.
• It deepened uncertainty about the future, leaving the regime exposed if she died unexpectedly.
• It set a precedent that the Stuart kings would later try to extend, contributing to longer-term constitutional tensions.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Robert Cecil’s secret correspondence with James VI of Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it filled the gap left by Elizabeth’s refusal to name an heir, ensuring the political class knew where the succession was heading.
• It marginalised rival claims, including those Robert Persons advanced for the Spanish royal family in 1595.
• Significance in the moment of crisis: when Elizabeth died on 24 March 1603, James was proclaimed within hours, avoiding civil war.
• Significance over time: it began the Stuart era and shaped a peaceful union of the crowns of England and Scotland.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Being a woman was Elizabeth’s greatest political weakness. It gave her Parliament, her suitors and her enemies a hold over her.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about Elizabeth’s position as a female ruler? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Pressure from Parliament in 1566 and 1576 over marriage and succession showed many MPs believed only a male heir or a husband would secure the kingdom.
• Foreign suitors created diplomatic complications, and the failure to marry meant no direct heir; Cecil had to manage the succession in secret.
• Catholic writers used Elizabeth’s sex to argue she could not be a legitimate ruler, fuelling plots and Spanish hostility.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Elizabeth turned the marriage question into a diplomatic tool that delayed open war with Spain for two decades.
• Her cultivated image — Gloriana, the Virgin Queen, the Armada Portrait — built a form of authority that did not depend on a husband.
• Ministers (Burghley, Walsingham, Robert Cecil) compensated for any structural weakness by running effective government and intelligence.
• The peaceful 1603 succession suggests the system, however awkward, ultimately worked.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from Lenin’s 1906 article Lessons of the Moscow Uprising, arguing that 1905 proved the workers could only win through armed revolution. Interpretation B is from the British historian Dominic Lieven (Nicholas II, 1993), arguing that 1905 was a missed chance to put Russia on a constitutional path that the Tsar deliberately squandered.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of 1905 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Lenin presents 1905 as a defeat that taught the workers they needed armed revolution; Lieven presents it as a missed opportunity for liberal reform.
• Lenin focuses on the workers and soviets as the decisive force; Lieven focuses on Nicholas’s political choices.
• Lenin treats the October Manifesto as a deception; Lieven treats it as a real concession that could have led somewhere.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences with grounding in both.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of 1905 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: Lenin is writing a political essay to recruit followers; Lieven is writing an academic biography of the Tsar.
• Different perspectives: Lenin writes from inside a revolutionary movement that wants to seize power; Lieven writes as a Cold-War-era British academic.
• Different time of writing: Lenin’s article (1906) was written without knowing how 1917 would unfold; Lieven knows the eventual collapse and judges accordingly.
• Different evidence: Lenin draws on the experience of the soviets and strikes; Lieven draws on archival material from the court.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason explained with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Bloody Sunday destroyed the bond between the Russian people and the Tsar that the autocracy had relied on for three centuries.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• The marchers had carried icons and portraits of Nicholas; their faith in the ‘Little Father’ was directly broken when troops fired.
• Eyewitness accounts, including Gapon’s own, describe workers swearing they would never again petition the Tsar.
• Membership of revolutionary parties surged in the months after Bloody Sunday.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Many peasants in 1917 still spoke of the Tsar in religious terms, suggesting the bond was not universally broken in 1905.
• The October Manifesto re-stabilised relations with the moderate middle class.
• Loyal regiments crushed the Moscow Uprising in December, suggesting the army’s bond with the regime held.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the October Manifesto of 1905 on Russian politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• It legalised political parties for the first time, allowing the Kadets and Octobrists to organise openly.
• It split the opposition: liberals welcomed the concessions; revolutionaries rejected them, isolating the Bolsheviks.
• It created the Duma, an elected parliament that Nicholas regarded as a temporary nuisance and would shortly try to neutralise (see next lesson).
• It allowed the regime to redeploy troops from the Manchurian front to crush the Moscow Uprising in December.
• It produced the constitutional tension that would dominate 1906–1917, with the Fundamental Laws of 1906 stripping the Manifesto of much of its substance.

Mastering: A chain of consequences explained, linking political, constitutional and military effects.
Secure: Two or more developed effects supported by specific evidence.
Developing: One developed effect plus simple identification of others.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about the Manifesto.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The most important reason the Tsarist regime survived the 1905 Revolution was the loyalty of the army.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the role of the army
• consider other reasons the regime survived (such as the October Manifesto and the end of the war)
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for the army being the most important factor:
• Guards troops sent from St Petersburg crushed the Moscow Uprising in December 1905 with artillery.
• Despite mutinies on the Potemkin and elsewhere, the bulk of the army remained loyal to officers.
• Without loyal troops, the October Manifesto would have been a worthless piece of paper.

Arguments for other factors:
• The October Manifesto split moderate liberals from revolutionaries, draining mass support from the uprising.
• The Treaty of Portsmouth ended the war and freed troops for domestic use.
• Witte’s tactical advice convinced Nicholas to concede before the situation became unrecoverable.

Judgement should weigh the immediate effectiveness of the army against the political conditions that allowed it to be deployed.

Mastering: A substantiated judgement weighing all factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the factors with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description of factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Russia’s defeat in the Russo-Japanese War on the political situation at home in 1905.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The destruction of the Pacific and Baltic fleets at Port Arthur and Tsushima discredited the regime as militarily incompetent.
• Plehve’s ‘small victorious war’ gamble backfired — the war that was supposed to distract from domestic discontent intensified it.
• Military defeat made Bloody Sunday possible: the marchers’ petition explicitly cited the war as evidence of misrule.
• Mutinies in the armed forces, including the Potemkin in June, were partly fuelled by anger at the war.
• The Treaty of Portsmouth (Sept 1905) ended the war and freed loyal troops for use inside Russia.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking military defeat to political crisis and back to military deployment.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned only briefly.
Emerging: General description of the war without explanation of its political effects.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the cinema industry in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hollywood was the centre of the global film industry by 1920, with major studios such as MGM, Paramount and Warner Brothers building star systems around actors like Charlie Chaplin and Clara Bow.
• Cinema-going was cheap and mass: tickets cost as little as ten cents and there were over 23,000 cinemas across the USA by 1929.
• The 1927 release of The Jazz Singer introduced synchronised dialogue (talkies) and ended the silent era within five years.
• The 1922 Hays Office introduced a moral code limiting on-screen alcohol, crime and nudity, in response to Hollywood scandals such as the Fatty Arbuckle trial.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the spread of cinema and radio change American life in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• By 1929 about 100 million cinema tickets were sold every week in a country of 120 million — cinema-going became the standard weekend leisure activity.
• Hollywood’s star system created national celebrities (Chaplin, Pickford, Bow), and films set fashion and consumer aspirations across the country.
• The 1927 talkie revolution made acting careers depend on voice as much as appearance and gave audiences in small towns access to the same stars as New York.
• Radio reached 10 million homes by 1929 and the formation of NBC in 1926 created the first national broadcasting network — allowing a Texas farmer and a New York clerk to hear the same baseball commentary or political speech.
• Advertising on prime-time radio reinforced the consumer economy from Lesson 1 by reaching millions of households every night.
• Both industries deepened the urban/rural split: city Americans embraced them; many rural communities saw them as immoral.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking cinema and radio to specific changes in everyday life with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one industry or to description.
Emerging: Identifies cinema or radio without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of jazz music in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jazz grew out of African-American communities in New Orleans and spread north to Chicago and to Harlem in New York via the Great Migration.
• Louis Armstrong (trumpet), Bessie Smith (blues) and Duke Ellington (Cotton Club bandleader from 1927) became national stars and helped jazz reach white audiences.
• Dance crazes such as the Charleston, the Black Bottom and the Lindy Hop spread from speakeasies to college campuses across the country.
• F. Scott Fitzgerald nicknamed the decade the Jazz Age, reflecting how jazz became a defining cultural symbol — both celebrated in cities and condemned in many rural towns.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the rise of spectator sport reflect the wider 1920s Boom?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Shorter working hours and higher wages gave Americans both the time and the disposable income to attend matches — Yankee Stadium opened in 1923 with capacity for 60,000.
• The motor industry (Lesson 1) carried fans to stadiums and tracks, while radio (this lesson) carried play-by-play to those who stayed at home.
• Babe Ruth’s 60-home-run season in 1927 made him a national hero on the same scale as Hollywood stars — sport produced celebrities of equal cultural weight.
• Boxing draws like the 1927 Dempsey vs Tunney rematch produced boxing's first $2 million gate, showing how sport had become a major commercial industry.
• Aviator Charles Lindbergh’s 1927 New York to Paris flight was treated like a sporting victory; ticker-tape parades celebrated him in every major city.
• These effects all rested on the same combination as the wider Boom: a consumer audience, mass media advertising and rising urban prosperity.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects linking sport to the wider Boom with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies sports stars without explaining how they reflected the Boom.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on American life in the 1920s: the rise of Hollywood, or the rise of radio? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of Hollywood:
• Cinema-going reached around 100 million tickets a week by 1929 — a near-universal weekly habit.
• The Hollywood star system shaped fashion, consumer aspirations and gender roles (the flapper image owes much to Clara Bow).
• The 1927 arrival of talkies showed how quickly Hollywood could reshape entertainment culture.
• Hollywood’s reach was global; American films exported the consumer society to Europe and Latin America.

In support of radio:
• Radio entered the home directly, reaching 10 million households by 1929 every evening of the week.
• NBC’s 1926 launch created the first national audience — political speeches and baseball games could now reach the whole country live.
• Radio carried adverts that drove the consumer economy described in Lesson 1.
• Radio was cheaper and more frequent than cinema, so its cumulative impact on daily routines may have been greater.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that radio had the deeper impact on day-to-day life because it was domestic and frequent, while Hollywood had the bigger weekly cultural impact because of its star system and global reach. The strongest answers note that the two reinforced each other — Hollywood films were promoted on radio, and stars appeared on radio shows.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of jazz and Hollywood on the divide between urban and rural America in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jazz clubs, cinemas and stadiums clustered in cities like New York, Chicago and Los Angeles, where they became central to weekend leisure.
• Many rural Americans, especially in the South and Midwest, saw jazz as immoral and primitive — church groups campaigned against it.
• The Charleston, with its short skirts and energetic dancing, was condemned by older Americans as obscene; some small towns banned public performances.
• The 1922 Hays Office was created to police Hollywood’s on-screen alcohol, crime and nudity in response to small-town anger at the studios’ perceived immorality.
• These cultural anxieties fed into the political backlash described in Lesson 5 — Prohibition, the revived KKK and immigration restriction were partly attempts by older rural America to push back against the new urban culture.
• The result was a deepening cultural and political divide that would persist long after the Boom itself ended.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking 1920s popular culture to a deepening urban/rural divide with specific examples.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies urban culture without explaining the rural reaction.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a public speech by US Senator Henry Cabot Lodge to the United States Senate in November 1919, opposing ratification of the Treaty of Versailles.
‘I will never consent to bind the United States by treaty to send our soldiers to fight in every quarrel that may arise in Europe. The League of Nations, as drafted, would oblige us to enforce decisions taken in Geneva by men who do not answer to American voters.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons the United States Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn from the source with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One clear point; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• It would oblige the USA to send soldiers to European quarrels (‘send our soldiers to fight’).
• It would bind the USA to decisions taken by foreigners in Geneva (‘men who do not answer to American voters’).
• It would compromise US sovereignty.
• Lodge frames it as opposition to permanent foreign entanglement.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the wider 1919-1920 peace settlement was completed, naming each treaty in turn.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more treaties as a chain of consequences for Europe; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more treaties covered with causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Treaties listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• June 1919: Treaty of Versailles signed with Germany — set the template for the wider settlement.
• September 1919: Treaty of Saint-Germain dissolved Austria-Hungary, recognised Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, banned Anschluss.
• November 1919: Treaty of Neuilly placed limits on Bulgaria and stripped it of territory to Greece, Yugoslavia and Romania.
• June 1920: Treaty of Trianon stripped Hungary of two-thirds of its pre-war territory, leaving large Hungarian minorities outside its new borders.
• August 1920: Treaty of Sèvres dismembered the Ottoman Empire — later overturned by Turkish nationalists and replaced by Lausanne (1923).
• Together these treaties redrew central and eastern Europe but left widespread minority resentment that fed the revisionist diplomacy of the 1930s.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a German newspaper editorial in the Berliner Tageblatt, published 29 June 1919, the day after the signing of the Treaty of Versailles.
‘Today we have signed under duress what we will never accept in our hearts. The treaty leaves Germany neither a great power nor a free nation. The war guilt clause is a public lie. The reparations are slavery. We did not lose this war on the battlefield; we were betrayed at home.’

Source C: An extract from a private memorandum by British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, September 1919.
‘The settlement is imperfect, but it is a settlement. The Germans complain because they cannot do otherwise. Our task now is to bind them by gradual concessions into the new order. The League will be the chief instrument of this work.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying reactions to the wider peace settlement. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a public German rejection of all four pillars of the treaty, including the stab-in-the-back claim. Provenance: a German newspaper the day after signing, reflecting public mood and shaping it. Own knowledge: this matches the wider German rhetoric of ‘November Criminals’ and Diktat; the stab-in-the-back myth was a powerful but historically false narrative.
Source C — Content: a measured British view that gradual concessions will integrate Germany. Provenance: a private memorandum by the British Foreign Secretary, written for an internal audience and so likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: matches Lloyd George’s view that Germany must be a partner; foreshadows the Dawes Plan, Locarno and Germany’s 1926 League entry.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German public reaction but partial — it amplifies the stab-in-the-back myth; C is useful for moderate British policy thinking but reflects only one strand of British opinion.

practice_questions.text:
‘The wider peace settlement of 1919-1920 created more problems than it solved.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• The successor states were fragile: Czechoslovakia held about three million Germans, and Poland faced disputes with Germany, Russia, Lithuania and Ukraine.
• Trianon left Hungary the most revisionist state in Europe, having lost two-thirds of its pre-war territory.
• The settlement excluded the USA, isolated Russia and alienated Germany, leaving small states to defend themselves.
Challenging the statement:
• Self-determination was applied to Poland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Finland for the first time in generations.
• The great powers of Europe stayed out of war with one another for over a decade; Locarno and German League entry suggested the system could evolve.
• Some problems were inherited from the war and the collapse of four empires, not created by the treaties.
Judgement: the settlement contained genuine reforms, but its structural exclusions and unresolved minority questions outweighed them in the long run.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a memorandum by Italian Prime Minister Vittorio Orlando to King Victor Emmanuel III, June 1919, after Italy partially withdrew from the Paris Peace Conference.
‘We were promised much in 1915 to bring us into the war. We have received little. Fiume is denied us. The Dalmatian coast is denied us. Our soldiers died for victories that have made others great. The Italian people will not forgive a peace that calls itself just but treats us as a junior partner.’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about Italian reactions to the peace settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• Italy felt it had been promised much in 1915 and received little.
• Fiume and the Dalmatian coast were denied, producing the ‘mutilated victory’ complaint.
• Own knowledge: the secret 1915 Treaty of London promised Adriatic territory; D’Annunzio seized Fiume in 1919; Italian disillusion fed Mussolini’s rise.
• Worth noting: this is one official view, and Italian opinion was divided between nationalists and socialists.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the ‘stab-in-the-back myth’ emerged in Germany after 1918 and why it shaped public reaction to the Treaty of Versailles.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a causal chain; precise factual detail; arrives at the impact on Versailles reaction through substantiated steps. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives; mostly accurate. Developing: Events listed; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage. Indicative content: • Autumn 1918: German army in retreat after the failed Spring Offensive and Allied Hundred Days, but no Allied soldier had crossed onto German soil. • November 1918: naval mutiny at Kiel, revolution across Germany, abdication of the Kaiser; civilian politicians took office at the moment of military collapse. • 11 November 1918: civilian government signed the armistice; right-wing generals like Hindenburg and Ludendorff later distanced themselves from this decision. • 1919 onwards: nationalist and far-right politicians spread the ‘stab-in-the-back’ (Dolchstosslegende) narrative, blaming socialists, communists and Jews for betraying an unbeaten army. • The civilian signatories of the treaty were branded the ‘November Criminals’. • Result: the new Weimar Republic was associated with national betrayal, making rational debate of Versailles almost impossible and feeding the rise of extremists including the Nazis.

practice_questions.text: Source A is an extract from a televised speech by Saddam Hussein on 17 July 1990, addressing the Iraqi people on Kuwaiti oil overproduction. Study Source A. Source A suggests that Saddam had economic reasons for threatening Kuwait. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The source frames Kuwaiti overproduction as deliberate harm to the Iraqi economy and uses the language of war to justify a response.
• It also carries a pan-Arab framing, presenting Iraq as the injured defender of the Arab nation rather than a state seeking territory.
• Contextual knowledge: Iraq owed Kuwait $14–15 billion, and Saddam reckoned every $1 fall in the oil price cost Iraq about $1 billion a year.
• Contextual knowledge: at Jeddah in late July Iraq demanded $2.4 billion in compensation for Rumaila, showing the same economic case in private.
[4 marks — 2 marks for each of two points that use a detail from the source together with contextual knowledge.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Iraqi forces took control of Kuwait between 2 and 8 August 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Iraqi forces crossed the border at around 2am on 2 August, spearheaded by the Republican Guard.
• Helicopter-borne special forces seized Kuwait City's government buildings, the airport and the Dasman Palace before sunrise.
• Kuwait's roughly 16,000-strong military was outnumbered about six to one and was not on full alert; organised resistance collapsed within a day.
• The al-Sabah family fled to Saudi Arabia, and Iraqi troops looted gold reserves, art collections and shops.
• Within days Iraq installed an interim government under an Iraqi-appointed officer, and on 8 August announced a permanent merger with Kuwait.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Kuwait crisis developed between the breakdown of the Jeddah talks and the annexation of Kuwait.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Jeddah talks broke down on 1 August 1990 when Kuwait refused Iraq's territorial and financial demands.
• Iraqi forces crossed the border at around 2am on 2 August, with the Republican Guard taking Kuwait City within hours; the al-Sabah dynasty fled to Saudi Arabia.
• The UN Security Council passed Resolution 660 within hours, condemning the invasion and demanding withdrawal.
• On 8 August Iraq announced a permanent merger with Kuwait; on 28 August it declared Kuwait its '19th province'.
• The annexation hardened international opinion, made a negotiated reversal almost impossible, and brought US and UK forces to Saudi Arabia.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'Kuwaiti oil policy was the main reason Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: Kuwaiti production above its OPEC quota pushed prices down, and Saddam reckoned every $1 fall cost Iraq about $1 billion a year.
• Agree: the slant-drilling accusation at Rumaila turned an oil dispute into a charge of theft and produced the $2.4 billion demand at Jeddah.
• Disagree: the deeper pressure was Iraq's $80 billion war debt and an army of a million men it could not afford to demobilise.
• Disagree: Iraq had a long-standing territorial claim to Bubiyan and Warbah islands, which had nothing to do with oil prices.
• Disagree: Saddam also wanted the prestige of a pan-Arab victory and believed the world would not stop him.
• Judgement: oil policy supplied the public case and the timing, but the debt crisis and Saddam's own ambition supplied the motive.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: 'Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait because he believed the world would not stop him.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: Saddam left the Glaspie meeting of 25 July believing that Washington would not fight over an Arab border dispute.
• Agree: the muted Western response to Halabja in 1988 had taught him that brutal action carried little cost.
• Agree: he expected a fait accompli to be accepted, and expected the Soviet Union to shield its old client at the UN.
• Disagree: the financial trap was the driver — $80 billion of debt, collapsed oil revenue and an army he could not pay.
• Disagree: the specific grievances against Kuwait (Rumaila, Bubiyan and Warbah, overproduction) gave him targets he would have pursued anyway.
• Judgement: his misreading of the world made him bold, but the debt crisis explains why he needed Kuwait in the first place.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the international community responded to the invasion of Kuwait during the first week of August 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• On 2 August the UN Security Council passed Resolution 660, condemning the invasion and demanding immediate withdrawal.
• Bush and Thatcher met in Aspen on the same day and agreed that the annexation could not be allowed to stand.
• On 6 August Resolution 661 imposed comprehensive economic sanctions on Iraq.
• King Fahd accepted American forces in Saudi Arabia, and the first deployments of Operation Desert Shield began on 7 August.
• The Soviet Union declined to shield its old client at the UN, while Jordan, Yemen and the PLO equivocated, exposing Arab divisions.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Cabal ministry of 1668–1674.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was made up of five ministers — Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley and Lauderdale — whose initials happened to spell the nickname ‘Cabal’.
• Its members did not act as a unified cabinet; Charles II deliberately kept them divided so that no one minister could dominate as Clarendon had done.
• Two of its members — Clifford and Arlington — knew the full secret Treaty of Dover with Louis XIV in 1670, including the clause about Charles’s eventual conversion to Catholicism.
• It collapsed after the First Test Act of 1673 forced Catholics out of office: Clifford resigned, Shaftesbury was dismissed and Buckingham impeached.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Charles II governed through the Cabal after the fall of Clarendon.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It allowed Charles to govern through a small inner circle without a single dominant chief minister, giving him personal control of patronage and policy after the fall of Clarendon.
• It produced the secret Treaty of Dover in 1670, binding English foreign policy to France in return for a subsidy and committing Charles to a war on the Dutch.
• Its collapse after the 1673 Test Act revealed how reliant the regime was on Catholic ministers and exposed James, Duke of York’s Catholicism in public.
• Its break-up created the political space for the Earl of Danby to build a Court party in Parliament after 1674, and for Shaftesbury to begin organising the Country opposition.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the secret Treaty of Dover of 1670.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Louis XIV promised Charles a subsidy worth around £225,000 a year and England was committed to the Third Dutch War on the French side.
• It tied English foreign policy to France for the rest of the reign, leaving Charles dependent on Louis’s subsidies whenever he could not get parliamentary supply.
• Significance over time: when its existence leaked through pamphlets and rumour after 1678, it fed the fears that powered the Popish Plot panic and the Exclusion Crisis.
• It also made later Anglo-French alliances politically toxic, contributing to the Glorious Revolution settlement of 1688 in which Parliament insisted on a Protestant monarchy aligned against France.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Charles II ruled without Parliament between 1681 and 1685.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It ran from the dissolution of the Oxford Parliament on 28 March 1681 to Charles II’s death in February 1685, with no Parliament summoned in between.
• It was financed by a French subsidy of around £385,000 from Louis XIV in return for English neutrality, alongside booming customs and excise revenue.
• Charles used the Rye House Plot of 1683 to justify a purge of Whigs from corporations through quo warranto writs, remodelling more than fifty borough charters.
• It left James II a strong inheritance in 1685: a Tory-dominated political landscape and a Treasury running a small surplus.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the First Test Act of 1673.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It forced Sir Thomas Clifford, an open Catholic, to resign as Lord Treasurer; he died within months of leaving office.
• It compelled James, Duke of York to give up the Lord High Admiralship, publicly confirming his Catholicism for the first time and creating the succession question that would dominate the rest of the reign.
• It broke the Cabal as a working ministry, with Shaftesbury dismissed in November 1673 and Buckingham impeached in 1674.
• It established a precedent that Catholics could not hold civil or military office, which was extended by the Second Test Act of 1678 to Parliament itself.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Charles II only managed without Parliament because Louis XIV was paying his bills.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about how Charles II governed between 1681 and 1685? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The 1670 Treaty of Dover promised a subsidy worth around £225,000 a year, filling the gap when Parliament withheld supply during the Third Dutch War.
• A renewed subsidy of around £385,000 between 1681 and 1685 made the personal rule financially viable when Charles refused to summon another Parliament.
• Without French cash, Charles would have had to recall Parliament to vote taxes, which would have meant accepting Exclusion or some other limitation.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The Cabal’s flexible style of government — running policy through a divided inner circle — let Charles act faster than under a single chief minister and exploit each crisis personally.
• Customs and excise revenue boomed in the 1680s as English trade grew under the Navigation Acts, providing a domestic income that did not depend on Louis XIV.
• The Tory reaction after 1681, including the corporations purge, gave the Crown political stability that no amount of money could buy.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from President Harry Truman’s speech to a joint session of Congress, 12 March 1947, asking for aid to Greece and Turkey.
‘At the present moment in world history nearly every nation must choose between alternative ways of life… One way of life is based upon the will of the majority and is distinguished by free institutions, representative government, free elections… The second way of life is based upon the will of a minority forcibly imposed upon the majority. It relies upon terror and oppression, a controlled press and radio, fixed elections, and the suppression of personal freedoms.’

Source A suggests that Truman saw the world as divided between two opposed ways of life. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Free institutions and representative government depend on majority will and need protection.
• The alternative is rule by a minority based on terror, oppression and fixed elections.
• A controlled press and radio show how the second way of life suppresses personal freedoms.
• ‘Nearly every nation must choose’ implies a global stake, not just a Greek-Turkish problem.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Truman spoke to Congress on 12 March 1947 and asked for $400 million for Greece and Turkey.
• Britain had told Washington in February 1947 that it could no longer fund either country.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from George Marshall’s speech at Harvard University, 5 June 1947, announcing what became the Marshall Plan.
‘Our policy is directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. Its purpose should be the revival of a working economy in the world so as to permit the emergence of political and social conditions in which free institutions can exist.’

Source C: An extract from Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov’s statement to the Paris Conference, 2 July 1947, walking out of talks on the Marshall Plan.
‘The American proposal is not aid — it is a programme of conditions. We are asked to disclose our economic plans, accept American supervision and bind ourselves to a Western bloc. The Soviet government will have nothing to do with such a scheme.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why the Marshall Plan divided Europe in 1947. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: presents Marshall’s offer as humanitarian, aimed at hunger and poverty rather than at the USSR. Provenance: a public Harvard speech by the US Secretary of State; useful for the official US framing, less useful as a guide to the political calculation behind the offer. Own knowledge: in private the State Department understood that economic aid would also strengthen pro-Western governments in France and Italy; the offer was crafted to be unacceptable to Stalin without being publicly directed at him.
Source C — Content: rejects the plan as an instrument of American supervision. Provenance: an official Soviet statement at the Paris Conference, designed for the public record — useful for the Soviet line, partial because it does not reveal the internal Soviet decision to forbid Czechoslovakia and Poland from accepting.
Own knowledge: by July 1947 Stalin had blocked both Czechoslovakian and Polish negotiation with the plan; sixteen Western European states received aid from 1948 to 1952; Cominform followed in September 1947.
Judgement: Both sources are useful but partial — B reveals the public US framing, C reveals the public Soviet line; together they show how the plan’s conditions, not just its money, made acceptance impossible for Stalin and so divided Europe.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the USA moved from announcing the Truman Doctrine in March 1947 to launching the Marshall Plan a year later.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the launch of the Marshall Plan through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 21 February 1947: Britain told Washington it could no longer fund Greece and Turkey, forcing the US to act.
• 12 March 1947: Truman addressed Congress, set out the doctrine and asked for $400 million for Greece and Turkey.
• Spring 1947: State Department officials, including Kennan and Marshall, concluded that economic recovery in Europe was the second pillar of containment.
