• 5 June 1947: Marshall’s Harvard speech offered economic aid to any European country, including the USSR, on condition that they cooperate with each other.
• July 1947: Molotov walked out of the Paris Conference; Stalin forbade Czechoslovakia and Poland from accepting.
• April 1948: Congress passed the Foreign Assistance Act; Marshall aid began flowing to sixteen Western European countries.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a private memorandum by Will Clayton, US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, written for Marshall in May 1947 after a tour of Western Europe.
‘Without further prompt and substantial aid from the United States, economic, social and political disintegration will overwhelm Europe. The communists, organised and disciplined, will fill the vacuum created by hunger. We have only weeks, not months, to act.’

Source D suggests that Clayton thought American aid to Europe could not wait. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Without aid, ‘economic, social and political disintegration’ will overwhelm Europe.
• The communists are ‘organised and disciplined’ and will fill any vacuum.
• Hunger creates the political opening for communist parties.
• ‘Weeks, not months’ emphasises the time pressure on US decision-makers.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Clayton toured Western Europe in spring 1947 and reported to Marshall on what he had seen.
• Marshall announced the plan at Harvard on 5 June 1947 and aid began to flow in 1948.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Marshall Plan did more than the Truman Doctrine to divide Europe by 1949.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Every European country had to choose a side by accepting or refusing American dollars.
• Stalin forbade Czechoslovakia and Poland to negotiate, which drew a hard economic line across Europe.
• Moscow answered the plan with Cominform in September 1947 and Comecon in January 1949.
• Around $13 billion went to sixteen Western countries, so the two halves of Europe grew visibly apart.
Disagree:
• The Truman Doctrine came first, in March 1947, and set the principle of containment the plan then funded.
• The division of Germany into occupation zones had begun at Yalta and Potsdam in 1945.
• Rigged elections had already put communist governments across Eastern Europe by early 1948.
• The Berlin Blockade of 1948-49 did more than any aid programme to fix the split in place.
Judgement: the doctrine set the aim and the plan supplied the money, so the plan made the division visible but did not begin it.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how American aid to Greece and Turkey turned into a worldwide policy of containment between February and June 1947.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the Harvard speech through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 21 February 1947: the British note to Washington created an immediate gap that needed to be filled.
• Late February 1947: State Department drafts framed aid to Greece and Turkey as a wider commitment, not a one-off rescue.
• 12 March 1947: Truman’s speech to Congress turned the immediate crisis into a doctrine of supporting ‘free peoples’.
• April–May 1947: Will Clayton’s tour of Western Europe convinced Marshall that the doctrine needed an economic engine.
• 5 June 1947: Marshall at Harvard offered aid to any European country, on a cooperative basis — broadening the doctrine to the entire continent.
• July 1947: Soviet rejection at the Paris Conference confirmed that what had begun as Greek-Turkish aid had become the framework of two opposing camps in Europe.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Parliament of 1265 in the development of representation in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: first parliament to include knights of the shire and burgesses alongside barons and bishops; expanded who counted as 'the realm'.
• Significance at the time: the move was politically motivated — de Montfort needed broader support against royalists, not democratic in intent.
• Significance over time: Edward I's 1295 Model Parliament copied the format, embedding it as custom.
• Significance over time: laid the structural foundation for the two-chamber Parliament with Lords and Commons.
• Significance over time: cited by 17th- and 19th-century reformers (Levellers, Chartists) as evidence that ordinary representation had medieval English precedent.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both then and over time, with specific evidence.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the growth of Parliament between 1215 and 1265.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Magna Carta's clause 12 required the common counsel of the realm for new taxes — the first written commitment to consultation.
• At the time: the Provisions of Oxford in 1258 made consultation institutional, with a 15-member council supervising the king and three parliaments a year.
• At the time: de Montfort summoned knights and burgesses in January 1265 because he needed political support after Lewes, not from democratic principle.
• Over time: Edward I's Model Parliament of 1295 copied the format, and by the fourteenth century it had hardened into custom.
• Over time: the two-chamber Parliament of Lords and Commons grew directly out of these summonses.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the role of Simon de Montfort in 1264–65 was similar to the role of the rebel barons in 1215.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both used armed revolt to force constitutional concessions on a king: the 1215 barons captured London; de Montfort captured the king at Lewes.
• Both produced lasting precedents while pursuing immediate political goals: the 1215 barons wanted feudal grievances addressed but produced clause 39; de Montfort wanted political support but produced the precedent of summoning commoners.
• Both were elite movements: free men in 1215 and knights/burgesses in 1265 were property-owners, not ordinary subjects.
• Both faced royal counter-action: the 1215 charter was annulled by the Pope; de Montfort was killed at Evesham within months.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, fully developed.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: 'The role of the individual was the main factor in the development of Parliament between 1215 and 1295.' Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arguments for the role of the individual: Stephen Langton drafting Magna Carta; Simon de Montfort summoning knights and burgesses in 1265; Edward I institutionalising the format in 1295.
• Arguments against — government overreach: King John's scutage and Henry III's Sicilian Business were the trigger for revolt in both cases.
• Arguments against — war: Bouvines (1214) and Lewes (1264) created the political conditions for reform.
• Arguments against — the economy: tax demands without consent provoked baronial revolt at every stage.
• Arguments against — religion: Stephen Langton acted partly as a churchman, the 1258 Provisions began with religious complaints.
• Cross-period weighing: in later parts of the course, the role of individuals (Pankhurst, Wilberforce, Lawrence) followed the same pattern — they succeeded only when economic, ideological and political conditions allowed.
• Judgement: individuals matter, but only in conjunction with structural pressures; the strongest case for individuals is that they shape WHEN and HOW change happens, not WHETHER it happens.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Top band rewards a sustained argument addressing the named factor and weighing it against at least two others, with examples from at least two parts of the course]

Mastering: Substantiated argument addressing individuals and weighing against at least two other factors.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant comparison.
Developing: Some argument with basic comparison.
Emerging: Single-factor or single-period response.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the Provisions of Oxford in 1258 were different from Magna Carta in 1215.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Magna Carta primarily protected baronial property rights and required consultation on tax; the Provisions of Oxford created a permanent 15-member supervisory council with three parliaments a year.
• Magna Carta was a one-off concession that John repudiated; the Provisions established ongoing institutional restraint that lasted years.
• Magna Carta said almost nothing about local justice; the Provisions reformed sheriffs to answer to local communities.
• Magna Carta is a single document; the Provisions are a programme of reform implemented through several parliaments and royal decrees.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, fully developed.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Edward I's Model Parliament of 1295.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: included two knights from every shire and two burgesses from every major borough — formalising de Montfort's 1265 precedent.
• Significance at the time: established that Parliament represented 'the community of the realm' beyond the baronage.
• Significance over time: hardened into custom by the 14th century; created the structural distinction that became Lords and Commons.
• Significance over time: cited by later reformers as the medieval root of English representative government.
• Significance over time: the format remained essentially unchanged in structure until the 1832 Reform Act.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

Mastering: Sustained analysis with specific evidence.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1909 election leaflet of the British Navy League, distributed in industrial constituencies during the dreadnought controversy.
‘Germany has laid down four great ships this year. We have laid down two. Within five years the German fleet will be a match for our own. We want eight, and we won’t wait! Vote only for candidates who pledge to maintain the two-Power standard.’

Source A suggests that the Navy League believed Britain was falling behind Germany in warship building. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Germany has laid down four ships this year to Britain's two.
• ‘Within five years the German fleet will be a match for our own.’
• Voters are told to back candidates who will keep the two-Power standard.
• The slogan ‘We want eight, and we won’t wait!’ frames the demand as urgent.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The 1909 scare followed the German naval amendment of 1908, which speeded up dreadnought building.
• The two-Power standard meant a Royal Navy larger than the next two fleets combined.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Anglo-German naval race developed between 1898 and 1909.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Tirpitz appointment, First Naval Law, Second Naval Law, HMS Dreadnought, ‘we want eight’ campaign); reaches the 1909 dreadnought crisis through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1897: Tirpitz appointed German Naval Secretary, committed to a battle fleet to challenge Britain.
• 1898: First Naval Law authorised nineteen battleships.
• 1900: Second Naval Law doubled the programme, signalling sustained competition.
• 1906: Britain launched HMS Dreadnought, making all earlier battleships obsolete and resetting the race.
• 1908: Germany passed an amendment accelerating dreadnought construction.
• 1909: British public alarm produced the ‘we want eight, and we won’t wait’ campaign and a record naval estimate.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a public speech by Bernhard von Bülow, German foreign minister, to the Reichstag in December 1897.
‘We do not want to put anyone in the shade, but we too demand a place in the sun. We must have a fleet sufficient to defend our trade, our colonies and our growing population. The era when our fathers were content to leave the seas to others has come to an end.’

Source C: An extract from a 1908 article in The Times of London, on the Daily Telegraph affair following Wilhelm II’s controversial interview.
‘The German emperor’s well-meaning words have given universal offence. He has reassured no British reader of his goodwill, while alarming his own ministers and infuriating his French and Russian neighbours. Germany is not made stronger by such interventions; she is made more dangerous.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying Anglo-German rivalry. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Bülow articulates Weltpolitik — colonies, fleet, global presence. Provenance: a public Reichstag speech — useful for the official line, but rhetorical. Own knowledge: the speech preceded the Second Naval Law (1900) which doubled the German fleet plan, putting Bülow’s words into action.
Source C — Content: Argues Wilhelm’s personal interventions damage Germany’s standing. Provenance: a leading British newspaper — informed but reflecting British liberal anti-Wilhelm opinion. Own knowledge: the Daily Telegraph interview of October 1908 did damage Wilhelm’s reputation; subsequent German policy was more cautious for a time.
Judgement: B is highly useful as the official articulation of Weltpolitik; C is useful as British contemporary reaction but partial. Used together they capture both the structural and personal dimensions of the rivalry.

practice_questions.text:
‘The personality of Wilhelm II was the main reason for the breakdown of Anglo-German relations before 1914.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Wilhelm's own interventions did the damage: the Kruger Telegram of 1896 and the Daily Telegraph interview of 1908.
• He backed Tirpitz and the Naval Laws personally and made the fleet a matter of imperial prestige.
• His speeches told Britain that Germany wanted a global role, which raised alarm in London.

Disagree:
• The Naval Laws had wide support in the Reichstag and from the Navy League, so the programme did not depend on him.
• German industry and trade had outgrown Bismarck's Europe; pressure for colonies came from merchants and pressure groups.
• Britain's own difficulty in defending a global empire pushed it towards France and Russia whoever ruled Germany.
• Sir Eyre Crowe's memorandum of January 1907 argued the rivalry was structural, not personal.

Judgement: Wilhelm gave the rivalry its provocative tone, but the clash between a rising industrial Germany and a global Britain was structural and would have caused friction anyway.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British Foreign Office memorandum prepared by Sir Eyre Crowe in January 1907.
‘The German Empire’s policy is governed less by the personal will of its sovereign than by the strategic and economic interests of a state grown great in a generation. The fleet she now builds is the fleet she would have built without the present emperor; the colonies she demands are demanded by her merchants, scholars and admirals alike.’

Source F suggests that British officials traced the rivalry to Germany's position as a state rather than to the Kaiser himself. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• German policy is ‘governed less by the personal will of its sovereign’ than by strategic and economic interests.
• The fleet is ‘the fleet she would have built without the present emperor’.
• Colonies are ‘demanded by her merchants, scholars and admirals alike’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Naval Laws of 1898 and 1900 passed with broad political support in Germany.
• Eyre Crowe's memorandum of 1 January 1907 shaped British thinking about German intentions.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Weltpolitik developed in the decade after Bismarck’s dismissal in 1890.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the 1900 Second Naval Law through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 1890: Wilhelm II forced Bismarck’s resignation, opening the door to a more ambitious foreign policy.
• 1896: The Kruger Telegram angered Britain by publicly congratulating the Boer leader, signalling German willingness to challenge British interests.
• 1897: Tirpitz appointed Naval Secretary; Bülow appointed Foreign Minister.
• December 1897: Bülow’s ‘place in the sun’ Reichstag speech publicly articulated Weltpolitik.
• 1898: First Naval Law authorised nineteen battleships.
• 1900: Second Naval Law doubled the programme — making clear the policy was a long-term commitment to global power.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how UN forces moved from the Pusan Perimeter in August 1950 to the recapture of Seoul on 28 September 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Pusan defence, Operation Chromite, Wolmido, X Corps landing, Pusan breakout, recapture of Seoul); reaches Seoul through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• August 1950: UN forces held the Pusan Perimeter while planning a counter-stroke.
• MacArthur ordered the planning of Operation Chromite, an amphibious landing at Inchon despite Joint Chiefs’ objections.
• 15 September 1950: morning landings seized Wolmido at high tide, then evening landings put X Corps ashore at Inchon.
• North Korean supply lines were cut, forcing forces around Pusan to retreat.
• Mid-September: the Eighth Army broke out of the Pusan Perimeter (the Pusan breakout).
• 28 September 1950: Seoul was recaptured after heavy urban fighting; the South Korean flag flew again over the capital.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how UN forces advanced from the recapture of Seoul to the Yalu River between September and late November 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details (28 Sept Seoul, 1 Oct ROK at parallel, 7 Oct UN authorisation, 9 Oct US crossing, 19 Oct Pyongyang, late Nov forward units at Yalu); arrives at the Yalu position through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 28 September 1950: Seoul recaptured; UN forces stood near the 38th parallel.
• 1 October 1950: ROK forces crossed the 38th parallel, raising the question of UN war aims.
• 7 October 1950: the UN General Assembly authorised UN forces to take ‘all appropriate steps’ for a unified Korea.
• 9 October 1950: US troops crossed the 38th parallel, formally moving from containment to rollback.
• 15 October 1950: at Wake Island, MacArthur assured Truman that Chinese intervention was unlikely.
• 19 October 1950: Pyongyang fell.
• Late November 1950: UN forward units were in sight of the Yalu River and the Chinese border.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of why the Inchon landings on 15 September 1950 succeeded.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain of three or more linked reasons with precise factual detail (extreme tides, lack of North Korean defence, Wolmido bombardment, naval gunfire support, Pusan breakout coordination); arrives at success through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked reasons with causal connectives.
Developing: Reasons listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin reasoning.

Indicative content:
• MacArthur identified Inchon precisely because its 9-metre tides made an attack appear impossible — so the North Koreans had not strongly defended it.
• Operation Chromite was carefully timed to the narrow tidal windows; this enabled landings only at limited hours.
• Naval bombardment of Wolmido Island on 13–15 September neutralised North Korean guns covering the approach.
• Marines seized Wolmido at the morning high tide, securing the channel for the main evening landing.
• X Corps was ashore within 24 hours, far behind enemy lines, cutting supply lines.
• Coordination with the Pusan breakout meant North Korean forces could not redeploy to defend Inchon.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the UN advance into North Korea between October and November 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Linked analytical narrative with precise detail; arrives at the late-November forward position through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events present but loosely linked.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1 October 1950: ROK forces crossed the 38th parallel, the political question of war aims unresolved.
• 7 October 1950: UN General Assembly authorisation for advance into the north.
• 9 October: US forces crossed the parallel and pushed northwards.
• MacArthur split his forces into two columns — X Corps east, Eighth Army west — separated by mountainous interior.
• 19 October: Pyongyang fell to Eighth Army.
• Late October–November: rapid northward advance through cold and mountainous terrain.
• Beijing issued repeated warnings through Indian diplomats; MacArthur dismissed them as bluff at the Wake Island meeting on 15 October.
• Late November: forward units sighted the Yalu River, with MacArthur publicly promising soldiers would be home by Christmas.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how UN war aims shifted from containment to rollback between September and October 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain showing how military success drove a political shift; precise detail; arrives at the new aim of unified Korea through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Original UN war aim: restore the 38th parallel under Resolutions 82 and 83.
• 15 September 1950: Inchon landings transformed the strategic position.
• Late September: North Korean army shattered; UN forces stood at the parallel by 1 October.
• Truman administration debated whether to cross; arguments included permanently ending the threat and reunifying Korea under Rhee.
• 7 October: UN General Assembly resolution authorised ‘all appropriate steps’ for a unified, independent, democratic Korea — effectively endorsing rollback.
• 9 October: US forces crossed the parallel; rollback was now policy in practice.
• MacArthur publicly framed the war as one to end North Korea altogether, ignoring rising Chinese warnings.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how MacArthur ignored warnings of Chinese intervention between October and late November 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise detail (October warnings via Indian diplomats, Wake Island 15 October, MacArthur’s ‘greatest slaughter’ remark, divided columns, late November position); reaches the eve of Chinese counter-attack through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Early October: Beijing began warning through Indian ambassador K.M. Panikkar that China would not accept hostile forces on its border.
• 15 October 1950: Wake Island meeting — MacArthur reassured Truman that Chinese intervention was unlikely and would be defeated.
• Mid-October to early November: limited Chinese probing attacks signalled the People’s Volunteer Army was already across the Yalu.
• MacArthur dismissed the contacts as Korean reinforcements, not Chinese regulars.
• Late November: UN forces split into two widely separated columns advancing northwards.
• Forward units reached within sight of the Yalu River as MacArthur announced the war was almost won.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1919 right-wing pamphlet arguing the German army was undefeated and was ‘stabbed in the back’ by socialist politicians) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook arguing Germany was militarily exhausted and starving by November 1918) on why Germany lost the First World War. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A claims military defeat was caused by political betrayal — civilian leaders signed an armistice while the army was still on French soil.
• Interpretation B claims defeat was caused by exhaustion — the spring 1918 offensive failed, troops were retreating, and the home front had collapsed under blockade and food shortages.
• Main difference: A blames civilians and revolutionaries; B blames structural collapse on both fronts.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): difference identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one side only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1919 right-wing pamphlet promoting the ‘stab in the back’ theory) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook on the home-front collapse) give different views about Germany's defeat in 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the 1919 pamphlet aimed to discredit the new Weimar government; the modern textbook aims for balanced explanation.
• They use different evidence — the pamphlet relies on the fact that German troops were still in France; the textbook uses casualty figures, food statistics and the Kiel mutiny.
• They were produced at different times — the 1919 pamphlet had political motives in the immediate post-war crisis; the textbook has access to archives, including private generals' memoirs.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Germany's defeat in 1918 was decided not at the front but in the queues for bread, the soup kitchens and the strike halls of the home front.' How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for Germany's defeat in the First World War?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Allied blockade triggered the 1916–17 turnip winter and roughly 750,000 civilian deaths from hunger-linked illness, breaking civilian morale.
• Convincing because the January 1918 strikes, with over a million workers, foreshadowed the Kiel mutiny that ultimately ended the monarchy.
• Less convincing because the spring 1918 Ludendorff offensive failed for military reasons — American troop arrivals, supply shortages and Allied counter-attacks — not just home-front pressure.
• Less convincing because Ludendorff himself accepted defeat in late September 1918 because of military collapse, not bread queues; the home front then collapsed afterwards.
• Overall judgement: home front and front-line collapse were tightly linked — the interpretation is partly convincing but underplays the army's exhaustion.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Allied blockade on Germany between 1914 and 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cut imports of food and fertiliser, reducing rations to roughly 1,000 calories a day for civilians by 1916 and contributing to the turnip winter of 1916–17 in which the potato crop failed.
• Caused approximately 750,000 civilian deaths from hunger-linked disease and a sharp fall in birth rates, especially in working-class urban districts.
• Drove industrial unrest — the April 1917 Berlin strike and the January 1918 strike of over a million workers across major cities directly cited food and peace as demands.
• Helped break the Burgfrieden by exposing the gap between the elite (still well-fed) and the working class, paving the way for the SPD split and the rise of the USPD.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how the First World War destroyed the German monarchy by November 1918.
You may consider:
• the impact of military defeat in 1918
• the impact of the home-front collapse and the Kiel mutiny.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Military exhaustion: the spring 1918 Ludendorff offensive failed and Allied counter-attacks from August 1918 forced the German army back; Ludendorff told the Kaiser the war was lost.
• Civilian leadership replaced military leadership: a new government under Prince Max of Baden took office in October 1918 to negotiate peace.
• Home-front collapse: the blockade, turnip winter, 750,000 civilian deaths and January 1918 strikes destroyed loyalty to the regime.
• Kiel mutiny (3 November 1918): sailors refused a final death-or-glory mission; revolt spread to Hamburg, Munich and Berlin within days; workers' and soldiers' councils replaced state authority.
• Abdication: with the army no longer reliable and the SPD demanding a republic, Hindenburg and Groener told the Kaiser the troops would not fight for him; Wilhelm crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November 1918.
• Conclusion: military defeat made peace inevitable, but it was the home-front collapse and Kiel mutiny that turned defeat into republican revolution — the two reinforced each other.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and a substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1925 SPD memoir crediting the November 1918 revolution to the working class and the Kiel mutineers) and Interpretation B (a 1923 conservative writer arguing the abdication was forced on the Kaiser by his own generals) on the cause of Wilhelm II's abdication. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A locates the cause in popular revolution from below — sailors refused to fight, councils sprang up, workers' strikes finished the regime.
• Interpretation B locates the cause at the top — Hindenburg and the army told the Kaiser the troops would not stay loyal, removing his last protection.
• Main difference: A emphasises bottom-up popular agency; B emphasises top-down elite calculation.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which public health in medieval towns and medieval monasteries were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: monasteries had piped water and flushable latrines (reredorters); medieval towns relied on cesspits and shared wells, which often contaminated each other.
• Difference: monasteries had organised infirmaries with herb gardens; towns relied on rakers, royal proclamations and ad hoc rules.
• Similarity: both relied on rules and routine rather than germ theory; the underlying medical knowledge was the same.
• Similarity: both were responses to a shared belief that filth and bad air caused disease (miasma) — the difference was in resources and enforcement.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of government action during the Black Death for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Edward III’s 1348 proclamation ordered London’s streets cleaned and the Lord Mayor pushed burials outside the walls.
• At the time: some towns tried isolating the sick, which cut transmission even though nobody knew why it worked.
• At the time: none of it stopped the plague, which killed roughly a third of the population in 1348-50.
• Over time: the Statute of Labourers (1351) showed government legislating on the social effects of an epidemic.
• Over time: it set the precedent that the state could act on public health, taken up on a far larger scale in 1848, 1875 and 1948.
• Limitation: action was occasional and local; Britain had no permanent public health machinery until the 19th century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Black Death for medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: killed roughly one-third of England’s population in 1348-50; depopulated villages and disrupted the economy.
• At the time: drove the Statute of Labourers 1351 as Parliament tried to freeze wages; survivors won bargaining power.
• Over time: contributed to the Peasants’ Revolt 1381 and to the long-term decline of feudalism in England.
• Over time: prompted tighter urban public health rules in the late 14th century — a precedent that government action could (and should) intervene in disease.
• Over time: established quarantine as a tool that returned in the 1665 Great Plague and beyond.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Description of the disease without significance argument.

practice_questions.text: Has religion been the main factor in how people in Britain responded to disease? Explain your answer with reference to religion and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh religion against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of religion as the main factor:
• The dominant explanation of the plague was that it was God’s punishment for sin, preached from pulpits.
• Religious responses (prayer, processions, flagellants) were the largest public response in scale and visibility.
• Compare with later periods: religious explanations of disease persisted into Jenner’s vaccination opposition (clergy condemning ‘beast matter’) and Simpson’s chloroform debate (clerical claims that pain in childbirth was God’s will).

Weighed against government:
• Edward III’s 1348 proclamation and the Lord Mayor’s burial rules show government acting independently of the Church.
• Across the sweep, government action grew in importance — Public Health Acts 1848 and 1875, NHS 1948 — while religion as a factor declined.

Weighed against communication:
• News of the plague spread by ship and word of mouth; explanations from the Paris medical faculty (planetary alignment) reached London via written reports.
• Communication shaped which beliefs spread — without preaching, religious explanations would not have dominated.

Judgement: In 1348 religion was the dominant explanatory framework, but government and communication both played supporting roles that grew across the period. Top answers compare directly — e.g. ‘in 1348 religion was the main factor, but in 1848 government had taken over’.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing religion against at least two other factors with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes religion only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: the report of the medical faculty of the University of Paris, written in 1348 at the request of the king of France. It blamed the plague on a conjunction of the planets in 1345, which it said had corrupted the air.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying beliefs about the causes of the Black Death?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: it names an astrological cause working through corrupted air, so it shows how astrology and miasma fitted together in educated medicine.
• Content: it offers an explanation rather than a cure, which shows that the best-trained doctors in Europe had no idea of infection.
• Provenance: written by the leading medical faculty in Europe for a king, so it is the official expert view of 1348 — the view that shaped royal and Church responses.
• Contextual knowledge: other explanations in Britain included God’s punishment for sin, miasma from filth and earthquakes releasing bad air; responses ran from prayer and flagellants to street cleaning.
• Limitations: a university document tells us what scholars believed, not what a Norfolk villager believed, and it is French, so it needs care when applied to Britain.
• Judgement: very useful for elite medical belief, much less useful for popular belief or for what people actually did.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of monastic public health for medieval Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: monasteries provided the cleanest large-scale living conditions in Britain — piped water, flushed latrines, herb gardens, organised waste removal.
• At the time: monastic infirmaries (St Bartholomew’s, St Thomas’s) provided structured care that towns could not match.
• Over time: when Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries in 1536-40, England lost its main hospital network — a gap that voluntary 18th-century hospitals had to fill.
• Over time: monastic plans (e.g. Christchurch, Canterbury) provided engineering models that 19th-century reformers studied when designing modern sanitation.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Description without significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Henry II’s expedition to Ireland in 1171.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Anglo-Norman barons such as Strongbow had entered Ireland on private invitation in 1169-70 and were becoming an independent power; Henry’s expedition brought them under royal control.
• At the time: most Irish kings and lords submitted to Henry as overlord, though the high king Ruaidri Ua Conchobair held out until the Treaty of Windsor in 1175.
• At the time: the Irish church accepted reform along Roman lines, giving the expedition religious cover through the bull Laudabiliter.
• Over time: Anglo-Norman settlement spread along the eastern coast, the area later called the Pale, creating a permanent English foothold.
• Over time: English involvement in Ireland ran on through the Ulster plantations, famine migration and partition, so 1171 begins one of the longest strands in this study.
• Limitation: royal control was thin outside the Pale; the significance is in starting a claim rather than in governing Ireland.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘War was the main factor in changing the relationship between England and France between 1066 and 1204.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to war and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• War (in support): William’s conquest in 1066 tied England to Normandy by force and replaced the English aristocracy.
• War (in support): Philip Augustus’s campaigns of 1202-04 took Normandy, ending the cross-Channel realm.
• Government: the same king ruled both sides of the Channel, and Henry II built an exchequer and travelling judges that could work in his absence.
• Role of individuals: Henry II’s inheritance and his 1152 marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine created the Angevin Empire; King John’s failures lost it.
• Economic resources: cross-Channel landholding tied the aristocracy to both kingdoms until 1204 forced them to choose.
• Judgement: war opened and closed the cross-Channel realm, but marriage, inheritance and government decided how it was held together in between.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Henry II’s changes to royal justice in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: ruling lands from northern England to the Pyrenees forced Henry to build institutions that worked while he was abroad.
• At the time: the royal exchequer at Westminster handled finance year-round and record-keeping became more systematic.
• At the time: justices in eyre rode regular circuits, taking royal justice into the localities and drawing cases away from local lords.
• Over time: the regular use of juries and the consistent application of royal law produced the common law, still the basis of English law today.
• Over time: a strong royal administration survived the loss of Normandy in 1204 and gave the crown a machine for governing an island kingdom.
• Limitation: the reforms served royal income and control as much as justice for ordinary people.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Angevin Empire of Henry II was similar to or different from Cnut’s North Sea Empire.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both were personal unions. Each territory kept its own laws, language and government, and only the king was shared.
• Similarity: both depended on one life and broke up quickly once that king died or failed — Cnut’s empire by 1042, the Angevin lands by 1204.
• Difference: Cnut’s empire faced north and east into Scandinavia; Henry II’s faced south into France, from the Cheviots to the Pyrenees.
• Difference: Cnut ruled England through existing Anglo-Saxon earls and law, while the Normans replaced the English aristocracy almost completely after 1066.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named examples.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Norman Conquest for the English language.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: after 1066 Norman French replaced English at court and in royal business, and Latin stayed the language of church and record.
• At the time: English remained the language of the great majority, so a three-language stack settled in for about two centuries.
• Over time: the layering left parallel words still in use, such as pig and pork or house and mansion, with the French term carrying higher status.
• Over time: English returned to court and law from the fourteenth century, but as a language reshaped by French vocabulary.
• Over time: the language that later travelled with British traders and migrants was itself the product of conquest and migration.
• Limitation: English never died out; the change was to its vocabulary and status, not to the language spoken in most homes.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the loss of Normandy in 1204 for England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Normandy was followed by Anjou, Maine and most of Poitou, leaving only Gascony in the south-west.
• At the time: the Anglo-Norman aristocracy had to choose between English and continental estates, breaking the cross-Channel landholding of the previous 150 years.
• At the time: John’s heavy taxation to fund a reconquest provoked the baronial revolt of 1215 and Magna Carta.
• Over time: English politics turned inward and the king became clearly a king of England rather than of a cross-Channel realm.
• Over time: England and France became rival kingdoms, setting up the Hundred Years’ War and the sharper English identity it produced.
• Limitation: the crown kept Gascony and a claim to France, so 1204 was a turning point rather than a clean break.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of Mortmain (1279) for relations between the crown and the church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the statute stopped wealthy nobles giving large estates to the church without royal permission, protecting the king’s feudal incidents (reliefs, wardships, marriages) which were a major source of revenue.
• It established the principle that the crown had a say in how land moved between lay and religious owners; this asserted royal authority over the church in a sphere where canon law had previously dominated.
• Over time, the licensing system became a steady source of crown income and a model for later regulation of charitable land — the same idea would still be operating under the Tudors.
• The statute fits the wider pattern of Edward’s reform programme: law made in parliament, designed by Robert Burnell, and aimed at recovering rights the crown had lost during Henry III’s reign.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance discussed both at the time and over time with sustained explanation and precise terms.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with at least two reasons and relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance offered but largely tied to immediate effects.
Emerging: Simple statement of what the statute did with little discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which English law was changed by the First Statute of Westminster (1275).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was issued at Edward’s first parliament in April 1275 and contained fifty-one chapters of reform.
• It targeted abuses uncovered by the Hundred Rolls inquiry, including corrupt sheriffs, exploitation of widows and bullying of jurors.
• It set rules for free parliamentary elections and regulated the costs of legal proceedings.
• It confirmed Magna Carta and was written in French so that more royal officers could read it directly.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which landholding in England was changed by the Second Statute of Westminster (1285).
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Its opening chapter De Donis Conditionalibus created the entail, allowing land to be tied to a particular line of heirs and protected from sale; this caused great families to lock down estates that could not be broken up by an heir. • It expanded the writ system, providing new remedies for trespass and wrongful occupation; this caused more disputes to be channelled into the king’s courts and away from local lords. • Together with the Statute of Winchester (1285) it strengthened policing through the watch and the hue and cry, which caused a more visible royal presence in towns and on highways. • Over time, the entail shaped the structure of English aristocratic estates for centuries, and the wider statute remained a foundation document for the common law. [8 marks] Mastering: Sustained causal explanation with multiple linked effects and precise vocabulary. Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail. Developing: Effects identified but explanation is largely descriptive. Emerging: Simple statements about the statute with little explanation of effects.

practice_questions.text: ‘Edward I deserves the title “English Justinian” because of his great statutes.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: • The statutes between 1275 and 1290 are the largest body of royal legislation any English king had produced; many provisions of Westminster I and Westminster II were still cited in English courts in the nineteenth century. • The statutes turned the findings of the Hundred Rolls into permanent law, addressing corruption, land disputes, mortmain and policing in a single legislative programme. • The doctrine of the entail (De Donis Conditionalibus) and Quia Emptores reshaped land tenure for centuries, fitting the ‘lawgiver’ comparison. Arguments against / for other achievements: • Edward also reformed parliament — the ‘Model Parliament’ of 1295 broadened representation, even if not for democratic reasons. • His military achievements in Wales (Statute of Rhuddlan 1284) were as transformative for British politics as any law of land tenure. • Critics like Marc Morris note that ‘justice’ under Edward had hard limits — the 1290 expulsion of the Jews and the brutal punishment of Dafydd ap Gruffudd suggest a darker side that the ‘English Justinian’ nickname can obscure. Judgement should weigh the legislative achievement against military and constitutional change, recognising that the statutes were genuinely transformative but were one part of a broader reign. [16 marks] Mastering: Sustained argument with weighed factors and a justified overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail on multiple factors and a supported judgement. Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing. Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of Winchester (1285) for law and order in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the statute organised the watch in towns and on highways, requiring every adult man to keep arms suitable to his rank; this gave local communities a structured role in catching criminals.
• It re-stated the duty of the hue and cry: anyone who witnessed a crime was bound to shout an alarm and join the chase, with collective responsibility on the whole hundred for unsolved offences.
• Over time, the statute’s framework for community policing remained the basis of English local law enforcement until the creation of professional police forces in the nineteenth century.
• It is significant alongside the Hundred Rolls and Westminster II as one part of a coordinated programme of legal reform: gathering data, then writing law, then enforcing law in the localities.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance discussed both at the time and over time, with sustained explanation.
Secure: Clear discussion of significance with relevant detail and at least two reasons.
Developing: Some significance described but largely tied to immediate effects.
Emerging: Simple statement of what the statute did with no discussion of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the way the Statute of Mortmain (1279) protected the king’s income.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It banned the transfer of land to the church without a royal licence, blocking the ‘dead hand’ absorbing more estates into permanent religious holding.
• It protected the king’s feudal incidents — the reliefs, wardships and marriages collected when lay tenants died — which the church never owed.
• Royal licences could be granted for a fee, turning the rule into a source of crown revenue.
• It applied to all churches, abbeys and friaries, including the new Franciscan and Dominican houses.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of William’s march from Hastings to London in late 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William moved east along the coast first, taking Romney and Dover, before turning inland to Canterbury — using submissions rather than pitched battle to extend his control.
• Rather than assault London directly, William circled the city via Wallingford and Berkhamsted, ravaging Surrey and Hampshire to force the leaders inside to come out and submit.
• Norman troops fortified key points along the route, including Dover Castle within eight days of arrival, projecting Norman power into the local landscape.
• The march ended at Berkhamsted where Edgar Atheling, Edwin, Morcar and the leading bishops submitted and offered William the crown.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It gave William legal title to the throne under Anglo-Saxon ritual: he was anointed by Archbishop Ealdred of York and presented as Edward the Confessor’s lawful successor, not a foreign conqueror.
• It bound the surviving English bishops and nobles to him through their participation in the ceremony, making future resistance look like rebellion against a crowned king rather than national defence.
• The riot outside the abbey, when Norman guards burned the surrounding houses after mistaking the congregation’s shout for an attack, showed the fragility of consent and prefigured the harder Norman line later.
• Coronation released William to leave for Normandy in March 1067, since he could now appoint regents and govern at a distance — a freedom uncrowned conquest would not have given him.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the first Norman motte-and-bailey castles in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A motte was an artificial earth mound, often 5 to 10 metres high, topped by a wooden tower (the keep) where the Norman lord and his small garrison lived.
• A bailey was the fenced courtyard at the base of the motte, holding stables, storerooms, a hall and quarters for soldiers, surrounded by a ditch and palisade.
• Castles could be thrown up in weeks using forced English labour and prefabricated timber sections William had brought from Normandy.
• They were placed in occupied towns and at river crossings — for example in London (the future Tower), Dover, Canterbury and Winchester — to project Norman power into civilian life, not just to defend borders.
• Why it mattered: a castle could be raised in weeks and held by a few dozen men, so a small army could dominate towns it could never have held in open battle.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of William’s policy of conciliation between October 1066 and spring 1067.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Confirming Anglo-Saxon law and the rights of London in a charter written in English allowed William to claim continuity with Edward the Confessor’s rule and reduced the case for revolt.
• Keeping English bishops, including Archbishop Stigand for the time being, helped the regime function: the Church administered baptisms, courts and charitable provision that an alien clergy could not have run alone.
• Letting Edwin and Morcar retain their earldoms (on renewed oaths) bought time while William imported Norman lords gradually rather than triggering a unified national revolt.
• The policy was a tool, not a settlement: when revolts began in 1067–68, William increasingly removed English nobles and replaced them with Normans — the harsher policy of the next phase only worked because conciliation had bought him 18 months of stability first.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Edgar Atheling’s submission at Berkhamsted in December 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Edgar’s submission removed the only blood-line claimant capable of rallying the Witan against William; without him, no rival coronation was possible.
• It was performed alongside Edwin, Morcar and the leading bishops, which gave William’s coronation broad Anglo-Saxon endorsement — significance lay in who submitted, not just that someone did.
• Importance later: Edgar became a recurring figurehead for revolts — the 1068 northern revolt, the 1069 Danish-backed revolt — showing that submission did not equal loyalty.
• Edgar’s long life (he survived into the 1120s) meant the Anglo-Saxon claim never died; this shaped Norman policy on hostages, Church appointments and northern garrisons for decades.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of the ten weeks after Hastings.

‘Hastings was won with cavalry, but England was won with politics. The ring drawn round London, the Anglo-Saxon coronation and the charter to the citizens mattered more than anything William’s knights did after 14 October.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the way William turned victory at Hastings into control of England? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: political skill, rather than military force alone, turned Hastings into a conquest.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The decision to circle London via Wallingford and Berkhamsted rather than assault it traded slow encirclement for negotiated submission, sparing the army a costly siege.
• Using Anglo-Saxon coronation ritual at Westminster Abbey, performed by Archbishop Ealdred of York, framed the new regime as a continuation of Edward’s kingship rather than a foreign takeover.
• Confirming Anglo-Saxon law and the rights of London in a charter to the citizens reassured the city’s elite that conquest did not mean dispossession — in the short term.
• Allowing Edwin and Morcar to keep their earldoms and Stigand to keep his see bought 18 months of stability that pure force would not have produced.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• Hastings itself was a military victory; without it no political settlement was possible.
• Ravaging Surrey and Hampshire and the threat of further violence at Berkhamsted were forms of military pressure that compelled the political submission.
• Motte-and-bailey castles in London, Dover and Canterbury were a military investment from the start, not a political gesture — their purpose was projection of armed power into towns.
• The riot at the coronation showed how thin consent really was, suggesting force was always the underlying guarantor.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1923 Nationalist Party leaflet arguing the Treaty of Versailles caused all of Germany's problems) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook arguing Germany could have managed reparations if its governments had raised taxes and stabilised the currency earlier) on the role of the Treaty of Versailles in the 1923 crisis. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents Versailles as the single cause — the diktat, war-guilt clause and 132 billion gold marks made German recovery impossible.
• Interpretation B presents Versailles as one factor — German governments worsened the crisis by printing money to fund passive resistance rather than raising taxes.
• Main difference: A externalises blame onto the Allies; B emphasises internal policy failures.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1923 Nationalist Party leaflet on Versailles) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook) give different views about the cause of the 1923 hyperinflation crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the 1923 leaflet was designed to mobilise nationalist voters; the modern textbook seeks balanced analysis.
• They use different evidence — the leaflet focuses on Versailles clauses and the diktat; the textbook uses tax records, monetary statistics and policy decisions.
• They were produced at different times — the 1923 source had political motives during the crisis; the modern textbook benefits from later archival evidence.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The 1923 hyperinflation destroyed the German middle class and laid the foundation for the rise of the Nazis a decade later.' How convincing is Interpretation A about the long-term consequences of hyperinflation?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because middle-class savers, pensioners and civil servants lost their savings; trust in Weimar democracy among this group never fully recovered.
• Convincing because middle-class voters disproportionately turned to nationalist and later Nazi parties when the Depression returned in 1929–33.
• Less convincing because hyperinflation was actually contained within a year — the Rentenmark of November 1923 stabilised the currency and recovery followed under Stresemann.
• Less convincing because the Nazi vote rose mainly because of the post-1929 Depression, not 1923 trauma alone — the Nazis polled only 2.6% in 1928 when 1923 was still recent.
• Overall judgement: 1923 created the grievance reservoir; 1929 turned the tap on. Convincing for long-term resentment but overstated as a single cause.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923 on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Triggered passive resistance — Berlin paid striking workers from central funds, removing roughly 80% of Germany's coal and steel output from production and government tax revenue.
• Accelerated hyperinflation — the Reichsbank printed billions of marks to fund strike pay, peaking with a loaf of bread costing 200 billion marks by November 1923.
• Strengthened nationalist anger — the occupation became a rallying cry for the right; 132 Germans were killed in clashes with French troops, providing martyrs.
• Indirectly enabled Stresemann's recovery — the cost of the occupation forced Germany and the Allies into the 1924 Dawes Plan, restructuring reparations and bringing US loans.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1924 SPD pamphlet arguing hyperinflation hurt all Germans equally) and Interpretation B (a modern academic article arguing hyperinflation had clear winners and losers across class lines) on the social impact of hyperinflation. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A frames hyperinflation as a national disaster — bread queues, panic, chaos affecting every citizen.
• Interpretation B frames hyperinflation as an unequal redistribution — pensioners and middle-class savers lost everything; debtors and large industrialists often gained.
• Main difference: A emphasises shared suffering for political solidarity; B emphasises class-based outcomes for analytical accuracy.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Treaty of Versailles on the political stability of the Weimar Republic between 1919 and 1923.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Created the ‘November Criminals’ smear — politicians who signed Versailles were branded traitors; right-wing assassins murdered Matthias Erzberger (1921) and Walter Rathenau (1922).
• Provided ammunition for the ‘stab in the back’ myth — the war-guilt clause was used to argue the Republic itself was treasonous, fuelling far-right movements including the early Nazi Party.
• Imposed reparations of 132 billion gold marks (fixed 1921) which combined with German governments' fiscal weakness to trigger the 1923 hyperinflation.
• Encouraged French enforcement — the 1923 Ruhr occupation, justified by reparations default, deepened nationalist anger and weakened parliamentary moderates.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific names and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1906 British Foreign Office despatch from Sir Charles Hardinge to the Foreign Secretary, written during the Algeciras Conference.
‘Germany came to this conference expecting allies; she has found only Vienna at her side. The other powers — including the United States — have closed ranks behind France. Berlin will leave the conference with less than she had before, and with a clear lesson taught about the strength of the Entente.’

Source A suggests that Germany came out of the Algeciras Conference weaker than it went in. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Germany ‘came to this conference expecting allies; she has found only Vienna at her side’.
• The other powers, including the United States, ‘have closed ranks behind France’.
• Berlin ‘will leave the conference with less than she had before’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Algeciras Conference of 1906 recognised French and Spanish predominance in Morocco.
• The crisis led straight into secret Anglo-French military staff talks.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Bosnian Annexation Crisis from October 1908 to March 1909.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Young Turk Revolution, Aehrenthal’s diplomacy, Russian outrage, German ultimatum, Russian climbdown); reaches the March 1909 outcome through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• Summer 1908: The Young Turk Revolution weakened Ottoman authority, opening an opportunity in the Balkans.
• October 1908: Austria-Hungary unilaterally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina.
• Late 1908: Russia and Serbia protested furiously; Russia had been told by Aehrenthal compensation would be offered.
• Winter 1908-09: Russia mobilised diplomatically but was militarily unready after the 1905 Russo-Japanese defeat.
• March 1909: Germany issued an effective ultimatum demanding Russia accept the annexation.
• March 1909: Russia backed down — humiliated but vowing not to retreat again over Slav interests.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a speech by David Lloyd George at the Mansion House, City of London, 21 July 1911, drawn from contemporary press reports of the Agadir Crisis.
‘If a situation were to be forced upon us in which peace could only be preserved by the surrender of the great and beneficent position Britain has won, then I say emphatically that peace at that price would be a humiliation intolerable for a great country like ours to endure.’

Source C: An extract from a 1911 Berlin newspaper editorial in the Berliner Tageblatt, on Lloyd George’s Mansion House speech.
‘The British minister speaks as if our gunboat at Agadir threatened London itself. We sought a colonial compensation, not a war. Yet British ministers have chosen to wave the flag and rattle the sword. The lesson Germany must draw is plain: the Entente is closer than its founders pretended.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of the Agadir Crisis on European diplomacy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
