Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Lloyd George signals Britain will not be ‘treated as of no account’ — a clear public warning to Germany. Provenance: a major Cabinet minister giving a high-profile speech in the City — designed for European ears. Own knowledge: the speech was widely understood across Europe as Britain backing France in the crisis; it shocked Berlin.
Source C — Content: argues Britain has overreacted to a colonial gesture, but acknowledges the Entente is stronger than it appears. Provenance: a leading liberal Berlin newspaper — useful for German public reaction, though shaped by domestic outrage. Own knowledge: the German climbdown that summer and the Anglo-French naval agreement that followed bear out the source’s implicit conclusion.
Judgement: B is highly useful as the public British warning; C is useful as German public reaction. Used together they capture the moment alliance lines hardened in public view.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Bosnian Annexation Crisis was the most damaging of the three pre-war crises for European peace.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Russia was humiliated in March 1909 and swore never to back down over Slav interests again - the promise that shaped July 1914.
• Serbian anger at losing Bosnia fed the nationalist secret societies, including the Black Hand founded in 1911.
• Unlike the two Moroccan crises, Bosnia touched Austria-Hungary's survival as a multi-ethnic empire.

Disagree:
• The First Moroccan Crisis produced the Anglo-French military staff talks that turned the Entente into a partnership.
• Agadir in 1911 brought Britain publicly behind France and led to the Anglo-French naval arrangement.
• The Balkan Wars of 1912-13 nearly doubled Serbia's size and left south-eastern Europe more dangerous than 1908 had.
• None of the three crises actually caused a war, so all were survivable at the time.

Judgement: Bosnia did the deepest damage to trust between Russia, Austria-Hungary and Germany, but the Moroccan crises built the western coalition that made a general war possible.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British First Sea Lord Sir Arthur Wilson, dated August 1911.
‘The Admiralty is now planning for cooperation with the French navy in the Mediterranean. Should war come, the French fleet will hold the Mediterranean and we shall hold the Channel and the North Sea. The arrangement is informal but unmistakable. After Agadir, no minister can pretend the Entente is a thing of words alone.’

Source F suggests that the Agadir Crisis pushed Britain and France into a military partnership. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Planning is under way for the French fleet to hold the Mediterranean and the Royal Navy the Channel and North Sea.
• The arrangement is ‘informal but unmistakable’.
• ‘After Agadir, no minister can pretend the Entente is a thing of words alone.’

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Anglo-French naval arrangement was settled in 1912, the year after the Agadir Crisis.
• The Entente Cordiale of 1904 had carried no military commitment at all.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the three pre-war crises reshaped European alliances between 1905 and 1911.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the 1911 outcome through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• March 1905: Wilhelm II’s Tangier landing opened the First Moroccan Crisis.
• 1906: Algeciras Conference produced a German diplomatic defeat and Anglo-French military staff talks.
• October 1908: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia, infuriating Russia and Serbia.
• March 1909: German ultimatum forced Russian climbdown — Russia vowed not to back down again.
• July 1911: German gunboat Panther arrived at Agadir, sparking the Second Moroccan Crisis.
• Late 1911 - 1912: Lloyd George’s Mansion House speech and the Anglo-French Naval Convention completed the British shift towards France.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Charles II’s court at Whitehall.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It occupied a sprawling palace of around 2,000 rooms beside the Thames, mixing government offices, royal apartments, kitchens, chapels and staff lodgings.
• It was organised by graded access — from public chambers open to any well-dressed gentleman to the king’s private bedchamber, which only a handful of trusted courtiers entered.
• It supported around 1,000 permanent staff and dependants, paid through the royal household budget.
• It was the engine of royal patronage, distributing offices, pensions, peerages and military commissions.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how royal mistresses came to hold political influence at Charles II’s court.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were given titles, lodgings at court and access to the king — Barbara Villiers became Countess of Castlemaine and dominated court life 1660–70.
• They acted as channels of patronage, with courtiers and ambassadors approaching them to lobby for offices and contracts.
• Some had open political agendas: Louise de Kéroualle, sent from France in 1670, was widely seen as a French diplomatic asset.
• Nell Gwyn, an actress from Drury Lane, was popular with the public for her low-born wit and was politically harmless — the ‘Protestant whore’ of London ballads.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Charles II’s marriage to Catherine of Braganza shaped the politics of his reign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It brought a huge cash dowry of around £300,000 plus the cities of Bombay and Tangier and trading rights in Brazil and the East Indies, strengthening English overseas reach.
• It allied England with Portugal against Spain, supporting Portuguese independence and English Atlantic trade.
• It produced no living heir despite at least three miscarriages, leaving Charles’s Catholic brother James as heir presumptive.
• Over the longer reign this lack of a Protestant heir created the political problem that erupted into the Popish Plot panic and Exclusion Crisis from 1678 onwards.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about court life under Charles II for the politics and culture of Restoration England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the court was the engine of patronage: offices, pensions, peerages and military commissions were distributed through household and bedchamber appointments.
• Court mistresses were political actors, not private companions: Louise de Kéroualle’s influence supported Charles’s pro-French policy and the secret Treaty of Dover settlement.
• Significance over time: French and Spanish fashions like the long wig and the vest shaped English elite style for a generation; the king’s introduction of the vest in 1666 is the origin of the modern waistcoat.
• Court Catholicism — the king’s sympathy, his brother’s open Catholicism after 1673, his queen’s Catholic chapels — fed the fears that powered the Popish Plot panic and the Exclusion Crisis.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about court patronage for the management of Parliament under Charles II.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It allowed the Earl of Danby, Lord Treasurer 1673–79, to build a Court party majority by distributing pensions and offices to selected MPs.
• It made attendance at court an essential part of political life for ambitious gentry, who hoped that proximity to the king would yield favours for themselves and their counties.
• It tied royal mistresses and Bedchamber officers into political negotiation, since they could relay petitions and requests directly to the king.
• It also produced backlash: opponents accused the Court of corruption and bribery, helping to define the Country opposition that would become the Whigs.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Charles II’s court was a serious political machine. The parties and the mistresses were how power actually worked.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about Charles II’s court? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Patronage at court was systematic: Bedchamber and household offices, pensions and peerages were the currency of political management, and Danby used them to assemble a Court party in Parliament.
• Royal mistresses were political actors: Barbara Villiers shaped early appointments, Louise de Kéroualle worked as a French diplomatic asset, and Nell Gwyn served as a popular Protestant counter-image.
• Religion ran underneath the wit: court Catholicism was real, theatre and print were censored under the Licensing Act of 1662, and the king’s sympathy for Dissenters and Catholics produced the 1672 Indulgence crisis.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The court did stage genuine entertainment — theatre, opera, racing, dancing — and Charles enjoyed it personally; the ‘merry monarch’ image is not entirely invented.
• Some mistresses, especially Nell Gwyn, had no real political agenda and represented court life as enjoyment rather than power.
• Daily court life involved a great deal of leisure and ceremony alongside the politics.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Dominic Lieven (Nicholas II, 1993), arguing that the Fundamental Laws of 1906 deliberately destroyed the October Manifesto’s constitutional promise. Interpretation B is from the conservative Russian historian Sergei Pushkarev (The Emergence of Modern Russia, 1963), arguing that the Tsar acted reasonably to protect Russia from extremist Duma majorities.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of the Fundamental Laws differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Lieven presents the Fundamental Laws as a deliberate betrayal of the October Manifesto; Pushkarev presents them as a reasonable defence against extremism.
• Lieven blames Nicholas; Pushkarev partly blames the radical Duma majorities.
• Lieven sees the laws as the cause of long-term political decay; Pushkarev sees them as a stabilising measure.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences identified, each rooted in the interpretations.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of Tsarist constitutional reform differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different perspectives: Lieven writes from a British liberal-democratic tradition; Pushkarev writes as a conservative émigré sympathetic to the Romanovs.
• Different evidence: Lieven uses court archives showing Nicholas’s contempt for the Manifesto; Pushkarev emphasises Duma speeches that he found extreme.
• Different time of writing: Pushkarev writes in 1963 in the émigré tradition that idealised pre-1917 Russia; Lieven writes after the Soviet collapse with full archival access.
• Different purposes: Lieven is producing a critical biography; Pushkarev is producing a sympathetic survey.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Stolypin’s assassination in 1911 was the moment the Tsarist regime lost its last serious chance of reform.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• No senior minister of comparable energy was appointed after Stolypin; Nicholas preferred mediocrities he could control.
• Land reform stalled after 1911 even though peasants had only partially left the mir.
• The Lena Goldfields massacre in 1912 and renewed strikes by 1914 suggest the regime was drifting again.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Stolypin was already losing the Tsar’s trust before his death; the reforms might have been blocked even if he had lived.
• Even his admirers admitted he needed twenty years of peace, which the First World War would have denied him in 1914 regardless.
• Land reform reached only a quarter of peasant families — the underlying structural problems were too deep for a single minister.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Stolypin’s land reforms on Russian society between 1906 and 1914.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• About a quarter of European peasant families had left the mir by 1916, creating a small but genuine class of independent peasant farmers.
• The abolition of redemption payments in 1907 lifted a major financial burden from the rural poor.
• Grain output and exports rose, helping fund continued industrialisation.
• The poorest peasants often sold their consolidated plots and migrated to the cities, swelling the urban proletariat.
• In northern, infertile provinces the mir survived almost untouched, leaving the underlying land hunger that fuelled the 1917 peasant seizures.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking reform to both stabilisation and continued tension.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about Stolypin.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The Dumas of 1906–1917 made no real difference to how Russia was governed.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the powers and limitations of the Dumas
• consider any genuine effects they had on Russian politics
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the Dumas made no real difference:
• The State Council could veto Duma legislation; the army, navy and court budgets were outside Duma control.
• Nicholas dissolved the first two Dumas after refusing to accept their composition; the changed franchise of 1907 made the Third Duma compliant.
• Ministers answered only to the Tsar, not to parliament; the regime ruled by decree under Article 87 when the Duma was inconvenient.

Arguments that they did matter:
• They legalised political parties for the first time, giving liberal opposition a public platform.
• The Third Duma worked with Stolypin on land reform that genuinely changed rural life.
• The Fourth Duma’s Progressive Bloc helped delegitimise the regime during the war and supplied the personnel of the 1917 Provisional Government.

Judgement should weigh formal weakness against political influence.

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing both sides with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one side only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Stolypin’s use of repression on Russian politics between 1906 and 1911.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Field court martials authorised in 1906 produced around 3,000 hangings (‘Stolypin’s necktie’), reducing political violence in the short term.
• Strikes and political crime fell sharply between 1907 and 1911, contributing to the apparent stabilisation of the regime.
• Repression alienated liberal opinion that had hoped for cooperation with the Crown after the October Manifesto.
• Socialist Revolutionary terrorism continued, ultimately killing Stolypin himself at the Kiev Opera in September 1911.
• The use of military justice against civilians set a precedent that would feed into the police-state habits the regime would deepen during the First World War.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking repression to short-term order and longer-term political costs.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General comments about Stolypin’s harshness.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about patronage and royal image in holding Elizabeth’s authority together in the 1590s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Continued use of patronage — lands, monopolies and offices — to bind nobles to the Crown despite the deaths of Walsingham and Burghley.
• Active cultivation of the Gloriana image through portraits, court ceremony and progresses, even as the queen aged.
• Robert Cecil’s administration after 1598 maintained finance, foreign policy and intelligence without disruption.
• The legacy of the 1588 Armada victory, used in speeches and portraiture as a continuing symbol of God’s favour.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the loss of the sweet wines monopoly led Essex towards rebellion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It removed his main source of income, threatening his lavish household and ability to reward followers.
• It left dependents — soldiers, servants, gentry clients — without patronage and willing to back desperate action.
• It signalled to the political class that Essex had lost the queen’s favour, isolating him at court.
• Combined with his Irish disgrace, it pushed him toward the February 1601 rising as his last political option.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Essex’s rebellion of February 1601.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the speed of its collapse (within hours) proved the effectiveness of Robert Cecil’s intelligence network and the Privy Council’s control of London.
• It demonstrated that patronage, not military force, anchored Elizabethan authority — without the queen’s favour, even a charismatic noble could not raise the city.
• Significance over time: it cleared the way for Robert Cecil’s unrivalled position from 1601, allowing him to manage the 1603 succession in secret.
• It signalled the limits of charismatic court favouritism in late Elizabethan politics; no later favourite would attempt the same.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Essex’s Irish campaign of 1599 and what followed it.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• His failure to defeat Tyrone undermined his reputation as a war-leader, on which his political identity depended.
• His unauthorised truce with Tyrone breached his commission and angered the queen and Council.
• His abandonment of Ireland and unannounced return to Nonsuch Palace was treated as defiance of royal authority and led to house arrest.
• It triggered the chain of events — loss of court access, then of the sweet wines monopoly — that drove him to rebellion in 1601.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Robert Cecil for the late Elizabethan regime.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, his succession to his father Burghley in 1598 ensured continuity of administration through war and harvest crises.
• His intelligence work uncovered Essex’s plans before the 1601 rising, allowing the Council to act before Essex could rally London.
• Significance over time: from 1601 onwards he secured the back-channel correspondence with James VI that produced the peaceful 1603 succession.
• He demonstrated that effective ministers could compensate for an aging queen and a system without an heir, preserving stability into the next reign.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘By 1601 the queen’s authority rested on her ministers and her patronage, not on her own popularity.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about Elizabeth’s authority at the end of her reign? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Robert Cecil’s administration after 1598 absorbed the deaths of Walsingham and Burghley without disruption.
• Essex’s rebellion failed because Cecil’s intelligence and the Privy Council’s grip on London denied Essex any military or political base.
• The withdrawal of the sweet wines monopoly — a patronage decision — was decisive in turning Essex against the regime.
• The succession itself was settled by Cecil’s back-channel correspondence with James VI, not by any public statement from the queen.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The Gloriana image and the cult around the queen continued to inspire loyalty in the army, courts and London crowds.
• Elizabeth’s personal speeches — including her so-called ‘Golden Speech’ of 1601 to Parliament — rallied MPs at moments of crisis.
• Final authority on patronage, marriage and succession remained hers; Essex fell precisely because she withdrew her favour.
• The 1588 Armada victory still gave her personal credit through the 1590s.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the international community responded to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait between August and November 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• On 2 August UN Security Council Resolution 660 condemned the invasion and demanded immediate withdrawal; Resolution 661 followed with comprehensive sanctions on 6 August.
• Bush and Thatcher aligned at Aspen on 2 August, with Thatcher's 'don't go wobbly' insistence shaping the firm allied response.
• King Fahd invited US forces to Saudi Arabia on 7 August, beginning Operation Desert Shield and the largest American overseas deployment since Vietnam.
• A 35-nation coalition was assembled through autumn 1990, with Egyptian, Syrian and Saudi divisions providing crucial Arab cover; Germany and Japan contributed funding.
• On 29 November Resolution 678 authorised 'all necessary means' if Iraq had not withdrawn by 15 January 1991, supplying the legal basis for war.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how coalition forces were assembled in Saudi Arabia between August and December 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Defense Secretary Dick Cheney flew to Riyadh to brief the Saudi cabinet, and King Fahd invited American forces into the kingdom on 7 August 1990.
• Operation Desert Shield began as a defensive deployment to protect the Saudi eastern oil fields from a further Iraqi advance.
• By autumn around 250,000 US troops were in the Gulf; by December the coalition force exceeded 500,000.
• Bush and Secretary of State James Baker worked to make the coalition visibly Arab: Egypt sent two divisions, Syria one, and Saudi Arabia provided forces and bases.
• Britain's Operation Granby eventually contributed some 53,000 personnel, including the 1st Armoured Division, and allied governments met most of the cost.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'United Nations authorisation was the most important reason the coalition against Iraq held together in 1990–91.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: Resolution 678 of 29 November 1990 supplied the legal authority for force, without which Arab support would probably have collapsed.
• Agree: running the campaign through a stream of resolutions, from 660 to 678, kept the Soviet Union alongside Washington rather than against it.
• Disagree: Arab participation depended on diplomacy rather than law — Egyptian and Syrian divisions, and the deliberate exclusion of Israel.
• Disagree: money held the coalition together too, with Saudi Arabia and Kuwait-in-exile each contributing around $16 billion.
• Disagree: Saddam's own conduct, above all the annexation and the use of foreign hostages as human shields, united opinion against him.
• Judgement: UN authorisation was necessary but not sufficient; Arab cover and allied funding were what made it work in practice.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Source A is the text of United Nations Security Council Resolution 678, adopted on 29 November 1990. Source B is President Bush's televised address to the American people on the deployment of US forces to Saudi Arabia, 8 August 1990. Study Sources A and B. How useful are Sources A and B to an historian studying how the coalition against Iraq was built in 1990? Explain your answer using Sources A and B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content of Source A: the resolution sets a deadline of 15 January 1991 and authorises member states to use 'all necessary means', showing exactly what the coalition was legally permitted to do.
• Provenance of Source A: it is the agreed text of the Security Council, so it records what fifteen governments could all sign up to, but it hides the bargaining behind it.
• Content of Source B: Bush explains the deployment to a domestic audience, so it shows how the case was sold to American voters as defence of Saudi Arabia rather than liberation of Kuwait.
• Provenance of Source B: a president speaking in August 1990 is making a case, not describing one; useful for aims and language, less useful for the military reality.
• Own knowledge: King Fahd's invitation of 7 August, Egyptian and Syrian divisions, the exclusion of Israel, and $16 billion each from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait-in-exile.
• Judgement: together the two sources cover both the legal framework and the political selling of the coalition, but neither shows the Arab diplomacy that made it possible.
[12 marks — Mastering: Content, provenance and own knowledge integrated for both sources, with a substantiated judgement on usefulness. Secure: Clear use of all three with some judgement. Developing: Two of the three integrated. Emerging: Surface-level reference to who wrote each source.]

practice_questions.text: 'Reversing the invasion of Kuwait depended on Arab support for the coalition.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: without Saudi bases the operation had nowhere to deploy, and King Fahd's invitation of 7 August made Desert Shield possible.
• Agree: Egyptian and Syrian divisions denied Saddam the claim that this was a Christian war on an Arab country.
• Agree: Israel was deliberately kept out precisely because Arab governments would have walked away.
• Disagree: Western air and armoured power did the fighting, and the United States supplied the great majority of the troops.
• Disagree: UN authorisation and Soviet acquiescence were what made the operation legal and unopposed at the Security Council.
• Judgement: Arab support was the political condition of the war rather than its military engine, but without it the coalition would not have held.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Britain committed itself to the coalition against Iraq between August 1990 and January 1991.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Margaret Thatcher was in Aspen, Colorado when the invasion began and met Bush there on 2 August, pressing for the annexation to be reversed by force if necessary.
• Britain treated the annexation as an unambiguous breach of international law and backed the UN route from the start.
• British forces deployed to the Gulf under Operation Granby, eventually some 53,000 personnel including the 1st Armoured Division.
• Britain supported Resolutions 660, 661 and 678, including the deadline of 15 January 1991.
• John Major replaced Thatcher as Prime Minister in November 1990, but British policy did not change, and British forces went to war in January 1991.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Hundred Years’ War for the development of English identity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed points addressing significance at the time and over time, with precise detail (Crécy 1346, Statute of Pleading 1362, Chaucer, Henry V’s English letters, fall of Bordeaux 1453).
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Narrative without significance.
Emerging: Vague claim about identity.

Indicative content:
• At the time: war with France made it politically uncomfortable to keep speaking French at the English court.
• At the time: the 1362 Statute of Pleading required cases in English courts to be argued in English.
• Over time: Henry V’s use of English in official letters set the language of government for the next six centuries.
• Over time: an ‘us-against-them’ sense of Englishness emerged, sharpening national identity in a way that influenced later periods covered in this unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the rise of Parliament during the Hundred Years’ War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing immediate impact and long-term constitutional legacy, with precise detail (Good Parliament 1376, Wonderful Parliament 1386, redress before supply).
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Description without significance.
Emerging: Vague claim.

Indicative content:
• At the time: only Parliament could authorise the taxes needed to sustain campaigns in France, giving the Commons leverage over royal government.
• At the time: the principle of redress of grievances before supply allowed Parliament to demand reform in exchange for grants.
• Over time: Parliament became a permanent feature of English government, not a privilege.
• Over time: the same institution provided the framework for seventeenth-century constitutional struggles and modern democracy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the loss of England’s French territories by 1453.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing immediate political consequences and long-term shifts in outlook.
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Narrative without significance.
Emerging: Vague claim.

Indicative content:
• At the time: the English crown lost almost all its continental possessions, retaining only Calais — the cross-Channel realm built since 1066 was over.
• At the time: returning soldiers and unemployed nobles fed into the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between York and Lancaster (1455-1487).
• Over time: with no continental option, English elites looked outward across the Atlantic, paving the way for sixteenth-century colonisation in North America and the Caribbean.
• Over time: the smaller kingdom became more clearly ‘England’, governed in English from Westminster — an institutional precondition for the British Empire.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1362 Statute of Pleading for the long-term development of English.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing immediate change and long-term linguistic and political legacy.
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Description without significance.
Emerging: Vague claim.

Indicative content:
• At the time: legal pleadings switched from Norman French to English, reflecting and accelerating the shift away from French at court.
• At the time: it gave English subjects the right to be tried in their own language, a direct change in everyday legal experience.
• Over time: combined with Chaucer’s vernacular literature (c1387) and Henry V’s use of English in royal correspondence, the Statute helped establish English as the language of state.
• Over time: it laid the groundwork for the English Bible (Wycliffe in the late fourteenth century, the King James in 1611) and for the English-language identity that travelled with British migrants and traders in later centuries.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the use of the longbow at battles such as Crécy and Agincourt.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing immediate military impact and longer-term influence on social structure and identity.
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Description without significance.
Emerging: Vague claim about weaponry.

Indicative content:
• At the time: longbow archers allowed smaller English forces to defeat numerically superior French armies, producing famous victories at Crécy 1346 and Agincourt 1415.
• At the time: it gave the English crown a sense of military reach disproportionate to its population.
• Over time: longbow training drew yeoman archers into national service, contributing to the ‘every-man-a-soldier’ image that fed later patriotic mythology.
• Over time: the eventual obsolescence of the longbow against gunpowder armies foreshadowed the changes that ended the war and ushered in the gunpowder age covered in later parts of the unit.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Hundred Years’ War as a cause of the Wars of the Roses.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed points addressing immediate causal links and longer-term political consequences, with precise detail (military families, end of continental conflict, Lancaster vs York).
Secure: Two clear points with detail.
Developing: Description without explanation.
Emerging: Vague claim.

Indicative content:
• At the time: the loss of France in 1453 left great noble families without a foreign enemy on which to focus their military followings.
• At the time: returning veterans, unpaid soldiers and disappointed commanders provided manpower for civil war.
• Over time: the Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) ended with the Tudors, who set the political and religious framework for the early modern empire-building covered later in the unit.
• Over time: the link between war abroad and stability at home became a recurring theme — one the spec invites comparison with for later wars (1914-18, 1939-45).

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of the Plains nations.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a US schoolbook published in 1895.
“The wandering tribes of the Plains had no settled homes, no cities and no fixed laws. They lived as nature lived — following the herds and waging endless war upon one another.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a 2014 study of Native America.
“The Plains nations built sophisticated political councils, networks of trade, and an economic system based on the horse and the buffalo. To call this ‘wandering’ is to miss the careful seasonal rhythm that organised every camp.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, supported differences drawn from both interpretations.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support.
Developing: One difference; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 dismisses the Plains nations as ‘wandering’; Interpretation 2 stresses careful seasonal organisation.
• Interpretation 1 says they had ‘no fixed laws’; Interpretation 2 describes ‘sophisticated political councils’.
• Interpretation 1 emphasises endless internal war; Interpretation 2 emphasises trade networks.
• Interpretation 1 is hostile and primitivising; Interpretation 2 is analytical and respectful.

practice_questions.text:
Why might the two interpretations of the Plains nations above give different views?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: Reason rooted in provenance or context with brief support.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’.
Emerging: Restates content of each interpretation.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: Interpretation 1 is from 1895, the Frontier-Thesis era when the closing of the frontier was celebrated and Native peoples were treated as obstacles passed; Interpretation 2 is from 2014, when scholarship had foregrounded Native agency.
• Purpose: a 1895 schoolbook aimed to build patriotic identity; a 2014 study aimed to explain Native life on its own terms.
• Evidence: 1895 writers had little access to Native voices; 2014 writers used oral history and tribal records.
• Audience: white American children versus a modern academic and general readership.

practice_questions.text:
Read this short interpretation and use it to answer the question that follows.

Interpretation: An extract from a popular history of the West, 1932.
“The Plains Indians were a doomed people. Their nomadic life could not survive contact with the modern industrial American Republic, and the long sad story that followed was the price of progress.”

How convincing is this interpretation about the Plains nations? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, weighing what is convincing and what is not, with precise contextual knowledge of Plains life and US–Native relations; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation drawing on context with at least one developed convincing/unconvincing point each side; judgement reached.
Developing: Some evaluation but reliance on retelling the interpretation; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without using context.

Indicative content:
Convincing:
• Plains nomadism did struggle to coexist with railroads, ploughs and the buffalo trade.
• By 1890 the buffalo were almost extinct and most Plains people were on reservations.
Unconvincing:
• ‘Doomed’ treats outcomes as inevitable; in reality, US policy choices (treaty-breaking, the 1887 Dawes Act, deliberate buffalo destruction) shaped what happened.
• ‘Long sad story’ erases Native agency — Red Cloud’s War, Little Bighorn, the Ghost Dance all show resistance, not passivity.
• Plains nations were not monolithic; some allied with the US.
Judgement: the interpretation captures part of the cultural collision but underplays both Native action and the role of specific US policies.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Plains nations’ way of life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features with precise factual detail. Secure: Two valid features with brief support. Developing: One developed; one undeveloped. Emerging: Generalised description. Indicative content: • Buffalo hunting: nations like the Lakota and Comanche followed the bison herds and used every part of the carcass — meat, hide, sinew, bone, dung. • Tipi life: portable buffalo-hide tents could be packed onto a travois in fifteen minutes, allowing the camp to move with the herds. • Council government: chiefs were chosen for wisdom and bravery, decisions made collectively rather than by a single ruler. • Spiritual life: belief in Wakan Tanka, sacred places like the Black Hills, vision quests for young men.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the horse and the buffalo on the Plains nations’ way of life.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (Spanish horse, 30–60 million buffalo, tipi, travois, Comanche horse empire).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about the buffalo or horse.

Indicative content:
• The horse (introduced by the Spanish) transformed nations from foot hunters into mounted hunters and raiders; the Comanche built a horse-trading empire on the southern Plains.
• The buffalo provided every essential resource — food, shelter, clothing, tools and fuel — making nomadic Plains life possible.
• Together they shaped settlement: the tipi, the travois and seasonal movement followed the herds.
• They also explain vulnerability: when the buffalo herds were destroyed and treaties cut access to horses, the way of life collapsed within a generation.

practice_questions.text:
Has the buffalo been the most important factor in shaping the Plains nations’ way of life?

• The buffalo
• Spiritual beliefs and council government

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the buffalo against beliefs/government (and other factors); precise factual support across both bullets and additional material; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached.
Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative.

Indicative content:
• Buffalo: 30–60 million herds, food/clothes/tipis/tools/fuel, seasonal movement.
• Beliefs and government: Wakan Tanka, vision quests, sacred Black Hills, council decision-making, warrior societies.
• Other factors: the horse (Spanish-introduced, mounted hunting and warfare), tipi technology, inter-tribal politics, smallpox-driven demographic change.
• Judgement: top answers might argue the buffalo was decisive because it determined where camps could be, OR that beliefs and councils held the camps together once they were there. Either view, substantiated, can reach the top band.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the flapper image in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Flappers wore short bobbed hair, knee-length dresses and visible make-up — a deliberate break with the long hair and ankle-length skirts of pre-war fashion.
• They drove cars, went out unchaperoned, smoked and drank in public, often in speakeasies, signalling new social freedoms.
• They danced the Charleston, the Black Bottom and the Lindy Hop — energetic dances that scandalised older Americans.
• They appeared in Hollywood films (Clara Bow, the ‘It Girl’) and in cosmetics and fashion adverts that helped spread the image across the country.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the position of women in American society change during the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 19th Amendment (1920) stopped any state denying women the vote, the political symbol of a long-running suffrage campaign.
• The flapper image normalised new public behaviours — cars, cigarettes, dancing, going out unchaperoned — for young urban middle-class women.
• About 10.5 million women worked outside the home by 1929 (~25% of adult women), with the white-collar economy creating hundreds of thousands of typing and switchboard jobs marketed to young single women.
• Domestic appliances bought on hire purchase — refrigerators, washing machines, vacuum cleaners — reduced the hours of unpaid housework, especially in cities with electricity.
• Birth rates fell as more women used contraception; family size in cities dropped from around four to closer to three children.
• In 1923 the Equal Rights Amendment was first proposed in Congress, though it did not pass.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation across political, economic and cultural changes with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to flappers or one area only.
Emerging: Identifies the 19th Amendment without explaining other changes.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of women's work in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• About 10.5 million women worked outside the home by 1929, roughly a quarter of the adult female population.
• Women earned approximately half a male wage for similar work, so the gender pay gap remained large despite higher employment.
• They were concentrated in ‘women’s work’ — secretarial work, teaching, nursing, telephone operating, shop work — rather than in higher-paid industries.
• Many employers, especially in teaching and clerical work, operated ‘marriage bars’ that forced women to resign once they married.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the lives of rural women in the 1920s differ from the lives of urban flappers?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Fewer than one in ten American farms had electricity by 1929, compared with 70% of urban households — so rural women still washed by heating water on a stove and stored food by canning.
• A 1929 Department of Agriculture survey found the average farm wife worked over 60 hours a week, with little of the consumer-society relief that domestic appliances brought to cities.
• Rural birth rates remained higher because farms relied on family labour, so rural women had less reproductive freedom even though contraception was beginning to spread in cities.
• Religious and small-town moral codes condemned flapper fashions and the Charleston as immoral; few rural women could have appeared in public with bobbed hair and a knee-length dress without serious social cost.
• Cinema, jazz and radio (Lesson 3) reached cities first, so rural women had less access to the cultural mass-market that helped define the flapper image.
• The result was a near-invisible flapper presence in rural America, where most women’s lives looked closer to pre-war patterns than to the Manhattan nightclub image.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained contrast across multiple aspects of daily life with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one aspect.
Emerging: Identifies a difference without explaining its scale.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on the position of women in 1920s America: the 19th Amendment, or new patterns of work and consumer life? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the 19th Amendment:
• It removed a fundamental civic exclusion: women could now vote in every state and stand for office.
• It produced symbolic political change — the 1923 Equal Rights Amendment proposal was unthinkable a generation earlier.
• The political principle, once established, made later legal gains (e.g. 1972 ERA push, Lesson 13) possible.

In support of work and consumer life:
• 10.5 million women working outside the home by 1929 reshaped daily life and household income on a scale far broader than the political vote.
• Electric appliances bought on hire purchase cut housework hours and gave urban women genuine leisure time.
• The fashion, cosmetics and Hollywood industries built a public female cultural identity that mattered as much in practice as the right to vote.
• Falling birth rates and growing access to contraception in cities transformed family life.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that the 19th Amendment was politically more important in the long run, but in the daily lives of 1920s women, the changes in work and consumer life had more immediate impact — especially because the vote did not always lead to higher female political participation in the South. The strongest answers also note that for rural and African-American women, neither factor produced very much change.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both factors unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of marriage bars and the wage gap on the lives of working women in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Marriage bars across teaching and clerical work forced women to resign on marriage, so the white-collar boom benefited mainly unmarried women in their twenties.
• Once married, women lost access to professional jobs and depended on a husband’s wage; this entrenched the male-breadwinner family.
• The wage gap — women earned about half a male wage for similar work — meant working women contributed important household income but were rarely able to support themselves alone.
• During downturns, employers tended to dismiss married women first, treating their wages as supplementary, deepening insecurity for working-class families.
• Top professions remained over 95% male: women were under 5% of doctors and lawyers in 1929, despite the rising number of women in higher education.
• The cumulative effect was that 1920s women had more access to work than ever before but were locked out of the most secure and best-paid roles — a contradiction the women’s movement of the 1960s and 70s would target (Lesson 13).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects linking marriage bars and the wage gap to women’s economic position with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies the wage gap without explaining its effects.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1919 report by Lord Robert Cecil, British negotiator on the League of Nations Commission at Paris.
‘The League will rest on the principle that no nation may go to war against another without first submitting its dispute to discussion. Members are bound to apply economic sanctions against any state that resorts to war in defiance of the Covenant. The League will not have an army of its own; it will rely on the goodwill and self-interest of its members.’

Using Source A, identify two ways in which the League of Nations was supposed to prevent war.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One point clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Members must submit disputes to discussion before going to war (‘submitting its dispute to discussion’).
• The League could impose economic sanctions on aggressors (‘apply economic sanctions’).
• It would rely on members’ self-interest in collective security.
• It explicitly would NOT have its own army — useful contextual detail.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the League of Nations was created and opened, from Wilson’s January 1918 Fourteen Points to its first Council session in 1920.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1918: Wilson’s Fourteenth Point called for a ‘general association of nations’.
• November 1918: armistice signed; planning for a peace conference began with the League at the centre of Wilson’s agenda.
• January-April 1919: League of Nations Commission at Paris drafted the Covenant under Wilson and Cecil.
• June 1919: Covenant included as the first 26 articles of the Treaty of Versailles.
• 10 January 1920: Treaty of Versailles came into force; the League opened.
• 16 January 1920: first session of the League Council met in Paris.
• November 1920: first Assembly meeting in Geneva, with 42 founding members.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter by Eric Drummond, first Secretary-General of the League of Nations, to a colleague in 1923.
‘Our task is harder for the absence of the United States. Without American power and prestige, the League acts in Europe as a body of friends rather than a body of judges. The British and French are willing partners, but neither can bear the chief burden alone.’

Source C: An extract from a 1922 article in the New York Times by an American journalist reporting from Geneva.
‘The League’s headquarters at Geneva is busy and serious — but it is a European body. Without American membership, decisions taken here have no weight in Washington and little weight in the wider world. The League may yet prove its worth, but the absence of the largest economy on earth is a permanent shadow.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the early difficulties faced by the League of Nations. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: identifies US absence as the chief difficulty; describes the League acting as ‘a body of friends rather than a body of judges’. Provenance: a private letter from the Secretary-General to a peer; likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: matches the wider record — the US Senate’s 1919-20 rejection deprived the League of its strongest power.
Source C — Content: stresses the absence of American economic power. Provenance: an American newspaper, reporting back to a US audience; reflects American liberal pro-League opinion. Own knowledge: confirms US economic dominance — by the 1920s the USA was the world’s largest economy; without it sanctions had limited bite.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the official insider view but partial; C is useful as informed contemporary commentary but reflects pro-League American opinion.

practice_questions.text:
‘The League of Nations was an effective international organisation in the 1920s.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• The agencies achieved real results — ILO conventions on hours and child labour, Nansen passports, public-health work in eastern Europe.
• Political successes in the 1920s: the Aaland Islands, Upper Silesia and Bulgaria.
• German entry in 1926 suggested the League was integrating former enemies.
Challenging the statement:
• The unanimity rule and the absence of a League army meant a great power could block or ignore any decision.
• Vilna and Corfu showed exactly that: Poland kept Vilna and Mussolini got his terms outside the League.
• The USA never joined and the USSR was excluded, so the League covered Europe better than the wider world.
Judgement: effective in humanitarian work and in disputes between small states; ineffective whenever a great power was the aggressor.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a 1926 speech by Gustav Stresemann, German Foreign Minister, to the League Assembly on Germany’s admission to the League.
‘Today Germany takes her seat as an equal member of this Assembly. We come not as petitioners but as partners. We bring with us no demand for revenge, but the resolve to work, with the other powers, for a peace that endures because it is just.’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about the changing membership of the League of Nations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• Germany takes its seat as an ‘equal member’, marking the League’s expansion in 1926.
• Germany comes ‘not as petitioners but as partners’, presenting itself as rehabilitated.
• Own knowledge: Germany joined in 1926 after Locarno and resigned in October 1933 after Hitler came to power.
• Worth noting: a public diplomatic statement presents an idealised picture; German policy still sought treaty revision.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of changes in League of Nations membership between 1920 and 1939, focusing on the great powers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more membership changes with reasons and consequences; precise dates.
Secure: Three or more changes covered with causal connectives.
Developing: Changes listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin coverage.

Indicative content:
• 1920: League opens; the USA refuses to ratify and never joins, weakening the League from the start.
• 1923-1925: Locarno reconciliation creates conditions for German admission.
• September 1926: Germany joins as a permanent Council member — high-water mark of internationalism.
• 1933: Hitler comes to power in Germany; both Germany and Japan resign within months over rearmament and Manchuria.
• 1934: the USSR joins, partly to balance against Nazi Germany.
• 1937: Italy resigns after Abyssinia.
• 1939: the USSR is expelled for invading Finland; by 1939 the only great-power members are Britain and France — the League has effectively collapsed as a great-power forum on the eve of the Second World War.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in the changing relationship between citizen and state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: rebels reached London, killed the Archbishop of Canterbury and Treasurer, forced a face-to-face meeting with the king — unprecedented for ordinary subjects.
• Significance at the time (limited): the revolt was crushed; ringleaders executed; charters revoked.
• Significance over time: the poll tax was abandoned and not revived for centuries.
• Significance over time: serfdom declined steadily across the 15th century, partly because lords feared another rising.
• Significance over time: established the precedent that ordinary people could organise national protest — cited by 19th-century radicals and Chartists.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both then and over time.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the widening of resistance to royal authority between 1215 and 1381.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: in 1215 resistance was confined to the barons, who forced written limits on King John and then went back to war.
• At the time: the Provisions of Oxford in 1258 and the Parliament of 1265 drew knights and burgesses into the argument about how England should be governed.
• At the time: in 1381 peasants, artisans and lower clergy marched on London, killed the Archbishop of Canterbury and forced Richard II to negotiate face to face.
• Over time: the social base of protest had broadened from barons to commoners in under two centuries.
• Over time: after 1381 no English government could ignore the political existence of ordinary people, even though every rising in this period was crushed.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was different from the baronial revolt of 1215.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1215 was led by elite barons demanding feudal property protections; 1381 was led by commoners (peasants, artisans, lower clergy) demanding an end to serfdom and the poll tax.
• 1215 produced a written charter (Magna Carta); 1381 produced verbal royal promises that were quickly revoked.
• 1215 ended in renewed civil war and a French invasion; 1381 ended in the execution of about 150 ringleaders.
• 1215 was a property-rights dispute within the feudal elite; 1381 challenged the legitimacy of the social order itself, drawing on John Ball's egalitarian preaching.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, fully developed.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: 'The economy was the main factor in causing the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.' Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arguments for the economy: the 1381 poll tax of 12d per adult was the trigger; the 1351 Statute of Labourers had built long-term grievance; Hundred Years War costs forced repeated taxation.
• Arguments for chance: the Black Death (1348–49) created the labour shortage that empowered peasants — without it, wage demands and the Statute of Labourers would not have produced the same anger.
• Arguments for the role of the individual: Wat Tyler organised the Kentish march; John Ball provided the religious slogan; their charisma turned grievance into action.
• Arguments for communication: travelling preachers and market-cross sermons spread ideas across Essex and Kent.
• Arguments for government: a boy king and the unpopular John of Gaunt left the regime weak.
• Cross-period weighing: similar economic triggers (Corn Laws 1815, mining wages 1926, unemployment 1981) recur — but each only produced revolt where leaders and ideas existed.
• Judgement: the economy provided the trigger and the long-term grievance, but chance (plague), communication (preaching) and individuals (Tyler, Ball) gave the revolt its scale and shape.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Top band rewards a sustained argument addressing the named factor and weighing it against at least two others, with examples from at least two parts of the course]

Mastering: Substantiated argument addressing the economy and weighing against at least two other factors.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant comparison.
Developing: Some argument with basic comparison.
Emerging: Single-factor or single-period response.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the actions of the rebels in London were similar to the actions of John Ball in the months before the revolt.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both targeted symbols of corrupt authority: Ball preached against landlordism and a corrupt clergy; the rebels burned the Savoy Palace and beheaded the Archbishop of Canterbury.
• Both drew on religious legitimacy: Ball cited Genesis ('When Adam delved and Eve span'); the rebels saw themselves as restoring divine justice, not overturning it.
• Both used public spaces to spread ideas: Ball preached at market crosses; the rebels paraded the heads of Sudbury and Hales on London Bridge.
[8 marks — 4 marks per way: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, fully developed.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of John Ball in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: provided the revolt with religious and ideological framing — 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?' challenged the divine justification for serfdom.
• Significance at the time: travelling preacher whose sermons in Essex and Kent built networks of supporters before the rising.
• Significance at the time (and as warning): hanged, drawn and quartered at St Albans 15 July 1381 — the regime treated him as a primary threat.
• Significance over time: cited by later radicals (Levellers, Chartists) as proof that calls for equality have deep English roots.
• Significance over time: the line about Adam and Eve became a touchstone of English egalitarian political language.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both then and over time.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Vesalius and Paré were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: Vesalius worked at Padua university through dissection of corpses; Paré worked on the battlefield through experience with gunshot and amputation wounds.
• Difference: Vesalius corrected anatomical knowledge (the structure of the body); Paré changed surgical practice (treatment of wounds and amputations).
• Similarity: both used direct observation of the body to challenge older teachings, rather than relying solely on classical authority.
• Similarity: both faced opposition (Vesalius from Sylvius and the medical faculty; Paré from the Paris faculty who scorned his lack of Latin).

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Andreas Vesalius for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: corrected over 200 of Galen’s anatomical errors in Fabrica (1543), including the structure of the jaw, breastbone and heart.
• At the time: established dissection of human bodies as the basis of anatomical study, undermining the old text-and-barber model.
• Over time: laid the foundation for William Harvey’s 1628 work on circulation — without Vesalius’s corrections to the heart, Harvey’s breakthrough is unthinkable.
• Over time: showed that classical authority could be challenged by observation, opening the door to the scientific revolution and 18th-century scientific surgery.
• Limitation: impact on day-to-day treatment in Britain was slow — humour-based therapy continued for over a century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with explicit acknowledgement of the gap between discovery and uptake.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven, often missing the slow-uptake point.
Emerging: Brief identification of who Vesalius was.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Renaissance for medical knowledge in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: humanist scholars returned to the Greek originals and exposed centuries of translation errors in the texts physicians were taught from.
• At the time: dissection became routine in Italian universities, so Vesalius could correct over 200 of Galen’s errors in 1543.
• At the time: the printing press (c1450) carried illustrated anatomy across Europe within a few years rather than a few generations.
• Over time: it established that classical authority could be tested by observation — the principle Harvey used in 1628 and Hunter in the 18th century.
• Over time: British uptake was slow; universities still taught Galen and treatment stayed humoural for over a century.
• Judgement worth making: the Renaissance changed what could be questioned long before it changed what doctors did.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Has science and technology been the main factor in challenging old ideas in medicine? Explain your answer with reference to science and technology and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh science and technology against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of science and technology as the main factor:
• Dissection technique and anatomical accuracy were direct technological/methodological advances.
• The printing press (c1450) was a key technological development that multiplied the reach of new ideas.
• Paré’s ligature technique was an advance in surgical method.
• Across the period this factor accelerates: 1543 Vesalius, 1628 Harvey, 1796 Jenner, 1860s Pasteur, 1928 Fleming.

Weighed against communication:
• Without printing, Vesalius’s findings would have stayed in Padua; communication is what carried them.
• Vernacular translations and the Royal Society (founded 1660) later made science a public conversation in Britain.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Vesalius personally challenged his own teacher Sylvius and risked his career to publish.
• Paré’s observation in 1537 depended on individual willingness to record an unexpected result.
• Without the right individuals, science could have stalled at any point.

Weighed against religion:
• The Reformation (1517) weakened Catholic control of learning, opening space for heterodox ideas.
• Religion remained a brake — opposition to dissection was still strong in Catholic countries through the 17th century.

Judgement: In the Renaissance science and technology was a necessary but not sufficient factor — it required communication and individuals to translate discovery into change. The strongest answers compare directly across periods: science was bigger by the 19th century (Pasteur, Lister) and biggest by the 20th (penicillin, DNA), so its weight grew over the sweep.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing science and technology against at least two other factors with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes science only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Ambroise Paré’s own account of the siege of Turin in 1537, published in his collected works later in his life. He describes running out of boiling oil for gunshot wounds, dressing the rest with a salve of egg yolks, rose oil and turpentine, and finding those men resting quietly the next morning while the men treated with oil were feverish.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying change in Renaissance surgery?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: it describes an accidental test and its result, so it shows observation overturning a standard treatment.
• Content: comparing the two groups of patients is why the story is used as an early example of scientific method.
• Provenance: Paré’s own published account, written years afterwards to defend and promote his methods, so it is first-hand but not neutral.
