• Contextual knowledge: standard practice was to cauterise gunshot wounds with boiling oil because gunpowder was thought poisonous; Paré also replaced cauterisation with ligatures.
• Limitations: one surgeon, one night and no figures; and it says nothing about how slowly British surgeons took the method up.
• Judgement: strong on how a change was made and argued for, weak as proof of how far practice actually changed.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Paré for surgery in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: replaced boiling oil for gunshot wounds with a soothing salve, reducing pain and inflammation.
• At the time: introduced ligatures (threads around blood vessels) to replace cauterisation in amputations.
• Over time: laid the foundation for later surgical reform — though without antiseptics, infection rates remained high until the 19th century (Lister).
• Over time: his published surgical writings were translated and used in British surgical training, demonstrating that battlefield observation could overturn classical authority.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Description without significance argument.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a letter sent by General Douglas MacArthur to Republican Congressman Joseph Martin in March 1951, later read aloud on the floor of the US House of Representatives.
‘There is no substitute for victory. To meet the Asiatic communist with limited weapons and limited geography is to invite future slaughter. We must take the war to the source of aggression in China itself.’

Source B: An extract from a press conference given by President Truman on 11 April 1951, the day he relieved MacArthur of command.
‘General MacArthur has, by repeated public statements, made it impossible for the United States Government to control its policy of limited war. The military authority must serve the civilian, not lead it. I have therefore relieved him of his commands.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources A and B to a historian studying the conflict between Truman and MacArthur over the conduct of the Korean War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source A — Content: MacArthur explicitly rejects limited war and argues for taking the war to China. Provenance: a private letter to a Republican congressman, but read aloud in Congress — MacArthur knew it would become public, so his words served a political purpose as well as expressing genuine belief. Own knowledge: MacArthur had also publicly issued his own ultimatum to China in March 1951, sabotaging Truman’s peace initiative.
Source B — Content: Truman frames the issue as civil-military authority and the necessity of limited war. Provenance: a public press conference on the day of dismissal — clearly serving Truman’s justification of an unpopular decision (his approval fell to 22 percent), so likely framed for political defence. Own knowledge: the Senate ‘MacArthur Hearings’ later supported Truman’s position, with Bradley calling MacArthur’s preferred war ‘the wrong war’.
Judgement: A is highly useful for understanding MacArthur’s strategic philosophy but partial; B is useful for Truman’s public justification but inevitably one-sided. Together they capture the Cold War’s defining debate over limited war.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C.

Source C: An extract from a confidential telegram from Mao Zedong to Stalin, dated 13 October 1950, declassified after the Cold War.
‘We have decided to send our volunteers across the Yalu. Allowing American forces to reach our border would gravely threaten the security of north-east China and the future of our revolution. We expect Soviet aviation cover.’

Source D: An extract from a public statement by US Secretary of State Dean Acheson, made in November 1950 after intelligence confirmed Chinese intervention.
‘The Chinese intervention is an act of aggression. The United States and the United Nations had no aggressive intent towards the People’s Republic, and the entry of the Chinese into Korea is unjustified.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources C and D to a historian studying the reasons for Chinese intervention in Korea. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge for both; reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or bias-only.

Indicative content:
Source C — Content: gives Mao’s own reasons (border security, revolution, expectation of Soviet air cover). Provenance: a confidential telegram to Stalin, declassified after the Cold War — private communication between allies, less filtered than public statements. Own knowledge: the decision was finalised on 18 October 1950; the Chinese leadership debated intervention; Stalin’s air cover was largely not delivered.
Source D — Content: Acheson denies any aggressive intent and condemns Chinese intervention as unjustified. Provenance: a public statement during the war by the US Secretary of State — serving political and propaganda purposes; needs care. Own knowledge: UN forces had crossed the 38th parallel and approached the Yalu, ignoring repeated Chinese warnings; Acheson’s framing therefore omits crucial context.
Judgement: C is highly useful as direct evidence of Chinese motives; D is useful as evidence of US public framing but unreliable on the question of whether intervention was justified.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from the diary of British war correspondent Reginald Thompson, written near Hungnam in December 1950 during the UN evacuation.
‘Marines staggering down the road in the snow, faces blackened, weapons frozen, asking only to be told where the next defensive line is. They have walked from the Chosin Reservoir, fighting all the way. The army of victory has become the army of escape.’

Source F: An extract from a statement to the press by General Douglas MacArthur, December 1950.
‘We face an entirely new war. Hostile communist Chinese have engaged our forces in such strength that the situation requires the gravest reconsideration of our entire approach. The men are conducting an orderly withdrawal under enormous pressure.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources E and F to a historian studying the impact of Chinese intervention on UN forces in late 1950. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge for both; reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or bias-only.

Indicative content:
Source E — Content: vivid eye-witness picture of UN soldiers retreating from Chosin in extreme conditions. Provenance: a contemporary diary by a British war correspondent — unfiltered, immediate, but one observer’s view. Own knowledge: Chosin saw 30,000 UN troops surrounded by 120,000 Chinese in -30°C; UN forces fought a 17-day breakout to Hungnam.
Source F — Content: MacArthur frames intervention as ‘an entirely new war’ and presents the retreat as ‘orderly’. Provenance: a public press statement by the UN commander — political function in shaping public perception, defensive of his own command. Own knowledge: the retreat was not orderly in many sectors; Eighth Army was driven into headlong retreat; Seoul fell for the second time in January 1951.
Judgement: E is highly useful for the experience on the ground; F is useful for understanding MacArthur’s public framing but partial — the ‘orderly withdrawal’ description is shaped for political effect.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source G.

Source G: An extract from a private letter by President Truman to his wife Bess in April 1951, kept in his personal papers.
‘The MacArthur business is a hard one. He will not accept that policy must come from the elected government. I cannot have a general who undermines the United Nations effort while serving as its commander. The decision is mine and I have made it.’

Source H: An extract from a modern history of MacArthur’s dismissal, published in 1996.
‘MacArthur in 1951 was no longer the cool strategist of Inchon. The retreat from the Yalu had wounded his pride, and he sought public vindication of his position by undermining a President he despised. The dismissal was not only justified but overdue.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources G and H to a historian studying Truman’s decision to dismiss MacArthur. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge for both; reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or bias-only.

Indicative content:
Source G — Content: Truman frames the issue as civilian control of policy. Provenance: a private letter to his wife — less performative than a press statement; likely captures genuine thinking. Own knowledge: Truman dismissed MacArthur on 11 April 1951 after the Martin letter and the unauthorised ultimatum to China.
Source H — Content: a historian’s judgement that dismissal was justified and overdue. Provenance: a modern history written with hindsight and with access to declassified material, but taking one interpretive stance. Own knowledge: the Senate hearings supported Truman, and Bradley described MacArthur’s preferred war as ‘the wrong war, at the wrong place, at the wrong time’.
Judgement: G is highly useful for understanding Truman’s thinking; H is useful as a historian’s synthesis but reflects one interpretive position. Together they capture decision-maker reasoning and historical judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source I.

Source I: An extract from a confidential US Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum to MacArthur, dated 9 January 1951.
‘The position of the United States must remain that of limited war. The defeat of communism in China is not within current capabilities. The aim must be the restoration of South Korean territorial integrity, not the destruction of Chinese power.’

Source J: An extract from a letter to a Republican congressman by General MacArthur, dated 20 March 1951.
‘Limited war in Asia means defeat in Asia. To accept restraint where the enemy accepts none is to accept slow strangulation. The American people did not send their sons to Korea to lose half a country and call it victory.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources I and J to a historian studying the disagreement between Washington and MacArthur over the conduct of the Korean War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or bias-only.

Indicative content:
Source I — Content: official position framing the war as limited and explicitly excluding the destruction of Chinese power. Provenance: confidential JCS memorandum — an internal directive, not propaganda; high reliability for official policy. Own knowledge: Truman feared escalation to Soviet involvement and possibly nuclear war; restoration of the 38th parallel had become the working aim by 1951.
Source J — Content: MacArthur publicly framing limited war as defeat. Provenance: a letter to a Republican congressman — written for political effect, expecting publication; the same kind of communication that triggered his sacking. Own knowledge: the Martin letter was read in Congress on 5 April 1951; Truman dismissed MacArthur six days later.
Judgement: I is highly useful as official policy; J is useful as evidence of MacArthur’s political stance but performative. Together they capture both sides of the central strategic disagreement of the war.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source K.

Source K: An extract from testimony by General Omar Bradley, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, given to the US Senate in May 1951 during the MacArthur Hearings.
‘Frankly, in the opinion of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, this strategy would involve us in the wrong war, at the wrong place, at the wrong time, and with the wrong enemy.’

Source L: An extract from a memoir by Marshal Peng Dehuai, Commander of the Chinese People’s Volunteer Army, recalling the autumn of 1950.
‘Our soldiers had no air cover and no tanks. We had to compensate with surprise, night-fighting and infantry willing to die in great numbers. Without these methods we could not have driven UN forces back from the Yalu.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources K and L to a historian studying the strategic conduct of the Korean War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Two of three elements handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or bias-only.

Indicative content:
Source K — Content: official US strategic verdict against MacArthur’s preferred wider war. Provenance: Senate hearing testimony by the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs — high-status official, public setting, intended to settle a political controversy. Own knowledge: testimony came in May 1951, supporting Truman’s decision and breaking MacArthur’s political momentum.
Source L — Content: Chinese commander explaining how mass infantry and night-fighting compensated for lack of equipment. Provenance: a memoir, written years later, by a senior Chinese figure — likely shaped by hindsight and political context (Peng later fell out with Mao). Own knowledge: the Chosin Reservoir battle in late November 1950 illustrates these tactics; UN technical superiority did not translate into battlefield dominance.
Judgement: K is highly useful for US strategic thinking; L is useful for Chinese tactics but mediated by memory and politics. Together they capture both sides of why the war became a stalemate.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the northern revolt of 1069.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A Danish fleet of around 240 ships, sent by Sweyn II and commanded by his sons, sailed up the Humber in September 1069 to support the Anglo-Saxon claim of Edgar Atheling.
• Northern English earls and Yorkshire nobles joined the Danes, storming York in late September and wiping out the Norman garrison and castles.
• In January 1069 the new Norman earl of Northumbria, Robert de Comines, had already been killed in Durham along with around 700 men — setting up the autumn rising.
• William responded by paying the Danish fleet to leave and then by launching the winter Harrying campaign across Yorkshire and beyond.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the revolts of 1067 to 1071 for William’s policy of conciliation.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Repeated revolts — Kent in 1067, Exeter in 1068, the North in 1068 and 1069, Ely in 1070–71 — broke the assumption that Anglo-Saxon nobles could be left in place under renewed oaths.
• William increasingly removed English earls and replaced them with Normans: by the end of 1071 Edwin was dead, Morcar imprisoned for life, and the great earldoms had passed to Robert of Mortain, William FitzOsbern and others.
• Land was concentrated in the hands of a small group of tenants-in-chief, accelerating the dispossession of Anglo-Saxon thegns — by 1086 fewer than 10% of pre-conquest landholders still held land.
• Castle-building became the standard response: Rougemont after Exeter, the Roman-road chain (Warwick, Nottingham, York, Lincoln) after the 1068 revolt, double castles at York after 1069. The shift from conciliation to occupation was direct and rapid.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the revolt at the Isle of Ely in 1070–71.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was based on the Isle of Ely, a patch of dry ground in the Cambridgeshire Fens, where the marshes made conventional siege impossible until William built causeways.
• It was led by Hereward, a Lincolnshire thegn whose lands had been confiscated, and joined by Earl Morcar after his second revolt.
• A Danish fleet briefly supported the rebels in 1070 before being bought off, leaving Hereward and his English supporters isolated.
• William’s causeway across the marshes collapsed under the weight of his army, killing many men, before the rebels were betrayed by the monks of Ely; Morcar was captured and imprisoned for life.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the revolt at Exeter in 1068.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 18-day siege showed that the largest towns of the south-west could not be taken by show of force alone; this prompted William to invest in permanent castles inside walled towns — Rougemont was begun before he left.
• William used English troops in his army for the first time at Exeter, demonstrating that conquest depended on co-opting some English fighters as well as crushing others — a model he kept using.
• The flight of Gytha, Harold’s mother, removed the last Godwin figurehead in southern England; this freed William to focus on the northern revolts later in 1068 without a southern second front.
• The relatively measured terms at Exeter (no massacre, walls left intact) showed that conciliation was still the policy in early 1068; the harsher line came only after the northern revolts.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about castle-building as William’s response to revolt between 1067 and 1071.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, each revolt produced a new wave of castles — Rougemont after Exeter, the Roman-road chain after the 1068 revolt, rebuilt double castles at York after 1069 — turning temporary fortifications into permanent military infrastructure.
• The castles concentrated power in the hands of trusted tenants-in-chief such as Robert of Mortain, William FitzOsbern and Odo of Bayeux, who garrisoned the new strongpoints; significance lay in changing who held local power, not just where it was held.
• Importance later: by 1100 around 500 castles dotted England, an unprecedented density that made any future Anglo-Saxon revival impossible — the shape of post-conquest England was set in this period.
• It corrects the misconception that castles were primarily defensive: Norman castles were instruments of conquest, planted in towns and at road junctions to dominate civilian populations, not just to repel raids.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of English resistance.

‘For a few weeks in the autumn of 1069 the conquest was close to collapse. English resistance came far nearer to driving William out of England than his reputation suggests.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about English resistance to Norman rule between 1067 and 1071? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: resistance came close to forcing William out of England.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• Eustace of Boulogne’s 1067 attack on Dover, even if it failed, showed that foreign allies were already willing to back English rebels in the year after Hastings.
• At Exeter in 1068 the largest town of the south-west withstood an 18-day siege, demonstrating that conquest by submission alone was running out.
• The Danish fleet of 240 ships at the Humber in September 1069, combined with the storming of York and the death of Robert de Comines at Durham, threatened William with simultaneous foreign invasion and northern revolt.
• The Ely revolt of 1070–71 used terrain to neutralise Norman cavalry; William’s causeway collapsed and many men drowned before betrayal by the monks ended the rising.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• William successfully bought off the Danish fleet in 1069 with a payment, showing the resilience of Norman finances and diplomacy.
• The Roman-road castle chain (Warwick, Nottingham, York, Lincoln) shows that William used revolt as an opportunity to extend permanent control rather than simply reacting to crisis.
• Anglo-Saxon resistance was uncoordinated — risings in Kent, Exeter, the North and Ely never combined into a single national movement.
• The lack of a single adult royal claimant once Edgar Atheling fled to Scotland meant rebels had no rallying figure capable of replacing William as king.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Stalin built parallel institutions to the West between September 1947 and 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the consolidation of the Soviet bloc through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• September 1947: Cominform was founded at Szklarska Poreba, coordinating communist parties and announcing the ‘two camps’ doctrine.
• Autumn 1947: French and Italian communists, out of government since May, followed the Cominform line and led waves of strikes.
• June 1948: Cominform expelled Yugoslavia after Tito refused to accept Soviet direction; the headquarters moved from Belgrade to Bucharest.
• 1949–1952: show trials in Hungary, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia removed leaders accused of ‘Titoism’, tightening Soviet control.
• January 1949: Comecon was founded, integrating Eastern European economies into a Soviet planning system as a counter to the Marshall Plan.
• 1950: East Germany joined Comecon, completing the political and economic structure of the Soviet bloc.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Yugoslavia’s relationship with the USSR broke down between 1947 and 1949.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the post-1948 Yugoslav position through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 1944–45: Tito’s Partisans liberated Yugoslavia from Nazi occupation largely without Soviet help, leaving Tito with independent legitimacy.
• September 1947: Yugoslavia hosted the founding Cominform meeting and the new headquarters in Belgrade, suggesting close cooperation.
• Spring 1948: Stalin objected to Tito’s independent foreign policy in the Balkans and to plans for a Balkan federation.
• April–May 1948: a series of letters between Stalin and Tito escalated into a public quarrel.
• 28 June 1948: Cominform expelled Yugoslavia; the headquarters moved to Bucharest.
• 1949: the USA began quietly providing food and credits to Yugoslavia, despite its communist government — a sign that the split had become permanent.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from Andrei Zhdanov’s speech to the founding meeting of Cominform, Szklarska Poreba, September 1947.
‘The world is divided into two camps. On the one hand stands the imperialist camp led by the United States, dedicated to the enslavement of nations and the suppression of democracy. On the other stands the anti-imperialist camp led by the Soviet Union, dedicated to the cause of peace, sovereignty and democracy. Between them there is no neutral ground.’

Source A suggests that the Soviet Union believed no country could stay neutral in the Cold War. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• An imperialist camp led by the USA is dedicated to the ‘enslavement of nations’.
• An anti-imperialist camp led by the USSR is dedicated to peace, sovereignty and democracy.
• Each camp has fundamentally opposed aims, with no shared ground.
• Between the two camps there is no ‘neutral ground’, ruling out a third path.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Zhdanov spoke at the founding meeting of Cominform at Szklarska Poreba in September 1947.
• Cominform was set up to make communist parties across Europe attack the Marshall Plan in the same terms.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a Cominform resolution expelling Yugoslavia, Bucharest, 28 June 1948.
‘The Yugoslav leaders have departed from the path of socialism, conducted a policy of slander against the Soviet Union, and refused to acknowledge the leading role of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Their party has placed itself outside the family of fraternal parties.’

Source C: An extract from Tito’s reply to the Cominform resolution, broadcast on Yugoslav radio in early July 1948.
‘We have not departed from the cause of socialism. We have refused only to be told by foreign comrades how to run our own country. The Yugoslav road is independent, but it is not anti-socialist. The accusation that we are agents of imperialism is an insult to the Yugoslav people who freed themselves with their own hands.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Tito-Stalin split in 1948. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: frames Yugoslavia as having abandoned socialism and rejected Soviet leadership. Provenance: an official Cominform document, designed to justify the expulsion to other parties — useful for the public Soviet line, less useful for the private grievances Stalin held. Own knowledge: the real disputes were over Tito’s independent foreign policy in the Balkans, not over socialist principle.
Source C — Content: rejects the accusation of departing from socialism, frames the dispute as one of independence rather than ideology. Provenance: Tito’s public broadcast, addressed to a Yugoslav audience that needed reassurance — useful for the line Tito wanted heard, partial because it cannot show the internal Yugoslav debate.
Own knowledge: the Yugoslav army and party stood with Tito; the USA began supplying food and credits in 1949; show trials in Hungary, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia followed in 1949–52, removing leaders accused of Titoism.
Judgement: Both are useful but partial — B reveals how Cominform justified the expulsion to the bloc, C reveals how Tito framed it for his own people; together they show why neither side could back down.

practice_questions.text:
‘Stalin's response to the Marshall Plan was driven by fear rather than ambition.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The USSR had lost perhaps 27 million people and wanted friendly states along its western border.
• Marshall aid would have opened Soviet economies to American inspection and supervision.
• Zhdanov's two camps speech described a hostile imperialist camp closing in on the socialist one.
• Expelling Yugoslavia in June 1948 and the show trials of 1949-52 are the acts of a leader afraid of losing control.
Disagree:
• Cominform told communist parties in France and Italy how to behave, which reaches well beyond the bloc.
• Comecon set prices and production targets in Moscow and ran Eastern trade on Soviet terms.
• Rigged elections from 1945 had already extended Soviet power over countries the Red Army occupied.
• Stalin blocked Czechoslovakia and Poland from aid they wanted, which is control rather than defence.
Judgement: fear of losing the buffer and ambition to control it were the same policy, but the defensive motive came first.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a 1950 article in the Yugoslav newspaper Borba, defending the new Yugoslav line of independent socialism.
‘Comecon offers eastern Europe planning without choice, prices set in Moscow, and a single road to socialism. Yugoslavia has chosen another road. Workers in our factories make decisions through workers’ councils, our trade is open to East and West alike, and our diplomacy serves Yugoslav interests, not foreign ones.’

Source E suggests that Yugoslavia claimed to be following a different road to socialism from the rest of the bloc. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source E and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Yugoslavia uses workers’ councils to make factory decisions, rather than central planning from above.
• Yugoslav trade is open to East and West, not restricted to the Soviet bloc.
• Yugoslav diplomacy serves Yugoslav interests, not foreign ones.
• Yugoslavia rejects the ‘single road to socialism’ that the source attributes to Comecon.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Cominform expelled Yugoslavia on 28 June 1948 after Tito refused to accept Soviet direction.
• Comecon, founded in January 1949, set prices and production targets for its members in Moscow.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the wool customs introduced by Edward I in 1275.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The duty was set at half a mark (six shillings and eightpence) per sack of wool exported, with a smaller duty on hides.
• It was paid by exporters at the dockside in London, Boston, Hull and other ports as the wool left for Flanders.
• It brought in around £10,000 a year, a transformative new source of royal income.
• It was granted by parliament with the consent of merchants, making it the ‘Ancient Custom’ on which later wool taxation was built.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Edward I’s government was affected by the collapse of the Riccardi of Lucca in 1294.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Crown lost its main source of credit just as war with France and the Madog rising in Wales required heavy military spending.
• Edward demanded the maltolt of 1294 — forty shillings a sack, six times the ordinary rate — on wool exporters, which produced an outcry from English merchants.
• The Florentine Frescobaldi were drafted in to replace the Riccardi, transferring royal credit from one Italian house to another but on tighter terms.
• The combined pressure of the maltolt, French war and Welsh rising fed into the political crisis of 1297, when Edward had to confirm Magna Carta and accept limits on tax-raising.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple causal links developed with precise figures and named bankers.
Secure: Two or more effects clearly explained with supporting detail.
Developing: Effects identified but explanation is largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about the collapse with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Great Re-Coinage of 1279–80 for trade in Edward I’s England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the re-coinage replaced clipped and worn pennies with heavier coins whose larger inscription made clipping obvious, restoring confidence in royal money.
• The introduction of the groat (4d) and farthing (quarter-penny) gave merchants more flexible denominations for everyday trade.
• The seigniorage profit collected by the mint paid for the operation, so it strengthened the Crown without an unpopular new tax.
• Significance over time: a trustworthy currency was essential for the wool trade and for the credit deals with Italian bankers; the new coin standards lasted into the fourteenth century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the Statute of Merchants (1285) changed trade and credit.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It allowed merchants to register debts before the mayor of a chartered town, creating an enforceable record of credit.
• If the debt was unpaid by the agreed date, the creditor could seize the debtor’s movable goods immediately.
• After three months of non-payment, the creditor could also seize the debtor’s lands.
• It extended an earlier 1283 Statute of Acton Burnell, building a national network of registered debts.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the wool trade for Edward I’s ability to wage war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Customs duties on wool gave Edward a steady cash income that he could pledge to Italian bankers for far larger loans.
• The Riccardi of Lucca advanced around £400,000 between 1272 and 1294, repaid through wool customs at the ports — this paid for the first Welsh war and the early castle programme.
• When wartime needs spiked in 1294, the maltolt squeezed the trade six times harder, funding the Madog rising response and the early Scottish campaigns.
• Heavy reliance on wool also created political risk: the merchant outcry of 1297 forced Edward to confirm Magna Carta and limit future taxation without consent.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple effects developed with precise figures and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: ‘The wool trade was the most important factor in shaping Edward I’s government.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The 1275 wool customs of half a mark per sack created the steady income that secured loans from the Riccardi of Lucca, financing the Welsh wars.
• The Riccardi collapse in 1294 and the maltolt that replaced it triggered the constitutional crisis of 1297, forcing the confirmation of Magna Carta.
• The 1279–80 re-coinage and the Statute of Merchants (1285) were both designed to keep the trade flowing safely through English ports.
• Wool revenue paid for both the Iron Ring castle programme in Wales and the Scottish campaigns, making it the financial backbone of the reign.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Parliamentary grants of taxation also funded military campaigns, including the £116,000 grant linked to the 1290 expulsion of the Jews.
• The Hundred Rolls, Quo Warranto and the great statutes (Westminster I, II, Mortmain, Winchester) shaped government in ways unrelated to wool.
• Edward’s personal authority and his use of Robert Burnell as Lord Chancellor mattered as much as any single revenue source.
• The conquest of Wales had political and dynastic motives beyond money — Llywelyn’s defiance and the desire to settle the British Isles.

A strong response weighs the wool-trade factor against the legal, parliamentary and personal aspects of Edward’s government and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on multiple factors and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1919 SPD government statement crediting the Freikorps with saving the Republic from Bolshevism) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook arguing Ebert's reliance on the Freikorps was a long-term mistake) on the use of the Freikorps in 1919. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Freikorps as saviours — without them the Spartacist uprising would have brought soviet government and a second Russian Revolution.
• Interpretation B presents the Freikorps as a long-term threat — they were unaccountable right-wing militias whose later involvement in the Kapp Putsch and political assassinations damaged the Republic they had helped save.
• Main difference: A frames the Freikorps as an emergency necessity; B frames them as a strategic blunder.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1919 SPD government statement on the Freikorps) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook) give different views about the use of the Freikorps in early 1919.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the 1919 SPD statement was justification at a moment of crisis when Bolshevism appeared to threaten Germany; the textbook offers reflective historical analysis.
• They use different evidence — the SPD statement focuses on the immediate Spartacist threat; the textbook integrates later events including Freikorps involvement in the Kapp Putsch and political murders.
• They were produced at different times — the 1919 source had no knowledge of what would follow; the modern source benefits from the full sweep of Weimar history.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the failed Kapp Putsch of March 1920 on Weimar Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Demonstrated army unreliability — General von Seeckt's refusal to fire on the rebels showed the Reichswehr could not be relied on to defend the Republic against the right.
• Showed the power of organised workers — the SPD-led general strike paralysed Berlin within days and forced Kapp to flee, proving working-class solidarity could save the Republic.
• Exposed judicial bias — few conspirators were properly punished; Kapp himself died awaiting trial; this leniency contrasted sharply with the murder of the Spartacist leaders by Freikorps the year before.
• Encouraged further right-wing violence — surviving Freikorps members carried out political assassinations of Erzberger (1921) and Rathenau (1922), normalising violence as a political tool.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific names and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of the political unrest faced by the Weimar Republic between 1919 and 1923.
You may consider:
• threats from the far left and far right
• how the Republic survived these threats.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Far-left threat: Spartacist uprising in Berlin January 1919 — Liebknecht and Luxemburg called for soviet government and were crushed by Freikorps; communist short-lived republics in Bavaria followed.
• Far-right threat: Kapp Putsch March 1920 — Wolfgang Kapp and Lüttwitz used the Ehrhardt Brigade to seize Berlin; the army refused to defend the elected government.
• Munich Putsch November 1923 — Hitler and Ludendorff attempted to march on Munich; sixteen Nazis and four police were killed before the Bavarian state arrested Hitler.
• Survival mechanisms: Ebert allied with army and Freikorps in 1919; SPD called a general strike against Kapp in 1920; Bavarian state police defeated the Munich Putsch.
• Political assassinations: Erzberger 1921, Rathenau 1922 — persistent right-wing violence even between coups.
• Conclusion: the Republic survived each threat, but at the cost of compromises (using Freikorps, lenient courts) that weakened it for later crises — the threats reflected the constitutional and judicial weaknesses set up in 1919.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1924 Bavarian newspaper editorial calling the Munich Putsch a near-miss that almost overthrew the Republic) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook describing the Munich Putsch as a fiasco crushed by police fire within minutes) on the seriousness of the November 1923 Munich Putsch. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Putsch as a serious threat — 2,000 marchers, Ludendorff's prestige, and the chaos of hyperinflation made revolution genuinely possible.
• Interpretation B presents the Putsch as a failure — Bavarian police shot the marchers within minutes and Hitler was arrested two days later.
• Main difference: A emphasises the moment's potential; B emphasises the actual outcome.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Munich Putsch of November 1923 on the future of the Nazi Party.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Provided national publicity — the February 1924 trial was reported across Germany and let Hitler give long propaganda speeches in court that introduced him to a national audience. • Lenient sentencing rewarded extremism — Hitler was given the minimum five-year sentence and served only nine months at Landsberg; Ludendorff was acquitted entirely. • Allowed the writing of Mein Kampf — Hitler dictated his political programme during his comfortable Landsberg imprisonment, fixing Nazi ideology in print. • Forced strategic rethink — Hitler abandoned violent putsches in favour of building a mass electoral party, a strategy that would carry the Nazis to the Reichstag from 1928 onwards. [Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific names and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Christopher Read (From Tsar to Soviets, 1996), arguing that the February Revolution was caused by long-term structural strains the Tsarist system could never have survived. Interpretation B is from the conservative Russian historian Sergei Pushkarev (1963), arguing that the dynasty was destroyed mainly by the personal failings of Nicholas, Alexandra and Rasputin.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of the fall of the Tsar differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Read locates the cause in long-term structural strain (war, economy, peasant question); Pushkarev locates it in the personal failings of the imperial family.
• Read presents collapse as inevitable; Pushkarev presents it as avoidable with better leadership.
• Read emphasises mass forces (workers, soldiers); Pushkarev emphasises individual decisions (taking command, listening to Rasputin).

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences with grounding in both.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of the fall of the Tsar differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different perspectives: Read writes from a left-leaning structural tradition; Pushkarev writes from a sympathetic émigré conservatism.
• Different evidence: Read uses statistics on conscription, inflation, casualties; Pushkarev uses court memoirs about Rasputin and Alexandra.
• Different time of writing: Pushkarev writes in 1963 in the Cold War émigré tradition; Read writes after the Soviet collapse with full archives.
• Different purposes: Read is producing a structural survey; Pushkarev is mounting a defence of the dynasty.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason with reference to both.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Rasputin’s real influence was modest, but the perception of his hold over the imperial family destroyed public trust in the dynasty.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Most ministers were appointed and dismissed by Alexandra rather than Rasputin himself; archival evidence shows his actual political reach was limited.
• The damage was reputational: even Romanov relatives publicly condemned Alexandra’s reliance on him.
• Milyukov’s November 1916 ‘stupidity or treason’ speech listed Rasputin’s alleged influence as a key grievance, suggesting perception mattered more than reality.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Rasputin did secure some ministerial appointments, including Protopopov’s as Interior Minister in 1916.
• Yusupov’s decision to murder him suggests aristocrats took his influence seriously enough to act.
• Even if ‘modest’, his role was symptomatic of a court detached from political reality — arguably itself a real problem.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of military defeat between 1914 and 1916 on the political position of Nicholas II.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Tannenberg, the Masurian Lakes and the ‘Great Retreat’ of 1915 destroyed faith in the regime’s competence.
• Nicholas’s September 1915 decision to take personal command made every defeat his, removing scapegoats.
• Government during his absence fell to Alexandra, who was widely suspected of pro-German sympathies.
• The army officer corps was decimated and replaced with peasant conscripts, who would later mutiny in February 1917.
• Industry’s failure to keep up with German output produced shortages of rifles, shells and food, fuelling the strikes that brought down the regime.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking defeats to political collapse.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about the war.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Nicholas II’s decision to take personal command of the army in September 1915 was the single most important reason for his fall.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the consequences of taking personal command
• consider other reasons for his fall (such as economic strain, Rasputin and the February Revolution)
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for taking command being the most important factor:
• Made every defeat after September 1915 personally his.
• Left government to Alexandra and Rasputin in Petrograd, fatally discrediting the dynasty.
• Removed Nicholas from contact with the Duma at the moment political negotiation was most needed.

Arguments for other factors:
• Economic strain (inflation, transport collapse, bread shortages) would have toppled even an effective leader.
• Alexandra and Rasputin damaged the dynasty regardless of whether Nicholas was at headquarters or in the capital.
• The actual trigger was the spontaneous February Revolution and the Petrograd garrison’s mutiny.

Judgement should weigh the personal decision against structural pressures.

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one side only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the First World War on the home front in Petrograd between 1914 and February 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Mass conscription stripped factories and farms of labour, contributing to grain shortages.
• Transport collapse meant grain rotted in sidings while Petrograd starved; daily bread rations fell below subsistence.
• Inflation reached around 400% by 1917, devastating real wages.
• Coal shortages closed factories and froze homes during winter 1916–17.
• These conditions produced the bread strike of 23 February 1917 that triggered the February Revolution.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking wartime economy to revolutionary outbreak.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about wartime hardship.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a telegram by German chancellor Theobald von Bethmann-Hollweg to the German ambassador in Vienna, dated 6 July 1914.
‘His Majesty has assured Vienna of Germany’s steadfast support in any action she may consider necessary against Serbia. The chancellor concurs. Whatever Vienna decides, Berlin will stand behind her.’

Source A suggests that Germany gave Austria-Hungary unconditional backing against Serbia. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Wilhelm assured Vienna of ‘steadfast support in any action she may consider necessary against Serbia’.
• The chancellor agrees, so this is government policy and not the Kaiser's private opinion.
• ‘Whatever Vienna decides, Berlin will stand behind her’ - no limits are set.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The promise of 5-6 July 1914 is known as the blank cheque.
• With Berlin behind it, Vienna sent Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July that it expected to be rejected.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Europe moved from the assassination at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 to a general European war by 4 August.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (assassination, blank cheque, ultimatum, Serbian reply, Russian mobilisation, German declarations, Belgian invasion); reaches the British declaration through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 28 June 1914: Princip shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo.
• 5 July 1914: Germany gave Austria-Hungary the blank cheque.
• 23 July 1914: Austria-Hungary delivered an ultimatum to Serbia, designed to be rejected.
• 28 July 1914: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
• 30 July 1914: Russia ordered full mobilisation.
• 1 August 1914: Germany declared war on Russia.
• 3 August 1914: Germany declared war on France.
• 4 August 1914: Germany invaded Belgium; Britain declared war on Germany.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from the personal diary of Russian foreign minister Sergei Sazonov, dated 30 July 1914.
‘The Tsar has signed the order for general mobilisation. He hesitated through the morning, weighed by what he called the responsibility of millions of lives. Yet partial mobilisation, our generals confirm, is technically impossible. Berlin will use this against us. We have no choice — to retreat now would be to repeat 1909.’

Source C: An extract from a 1925 memoir by British Foreign Secretary Sir Edward Grey, recalling the events of late July 1914 and published as Twenty-Five Years.
‘In all the years since, I have come back to those last days of July and asked whether anything could have stopped what came. The fault lay not with one man, but with the system: alliances that bound, timetables that tightened, ministers that telegraphed past one another. We were all of us prisoners of arrangements made years before.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why diplomacy failed in July 1914. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Sazonov captures Russian decision-making — Tsar’s hesitation, technical impossibility of partial mobilisation, fear of repeating the 1909 humiliation. Provenance: a contemporaneous private diary by the foreign minister at the heart of the crisis — likely to record genuine thinking. Own knowledge: Russia did mobilise on 30 July; the 1909 reference points to the Bosnian humiliation that Russia had vowed never to repeat.
Source C — Content: Grey argues the system, not individuals, made war inevitable. Provenance: a memoir written eleven years later — useful for considered reflection but shaped by hindsight and self-justification (Grey faced criticism for failing to deter Germany).
Judgement: B is highly useful for the immediate Russian decision; C is useful for considered later analysis but should not be taken as objective. Used together they capture both the granular pressures and the structural picture.

practice_questions.text:
‘The decisions of Germany’s leaders were the main reason a Balkan crisis became a European war in 1914.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The blank cheque of 5 July encouraged Austria-Hungary to write an ultimatum designed to be rejected.
• Germany rejected Grey's four-power conference on 27 July, closing the last diplomatic route.
• The Schlieffen Plan meant that once Germany mobilised it had to attack France and invade Belgium, so a Balkan quarrel became a war in the west.
• Fritz Fischer argued in 1961 that German leaders deliberately sought war.

Disagree:
• Austria-Hungary chose the terms of the ultimatum and declared war on Serbia on 28 July.
• Russia ordered full mobilisation on 30 July, having sworn after 1909 never to back down over Slav interests again.
• When he read Serbia's reply Wilhelm thought every reason for war had gone, which suggests confusion rather than a plan.
• Christopher Clark argues responsibility was shared across all the powers.

Judgement: German leaders carried more responsibility than any other single government, but the war came from choices made in Vienna, St Petersburg and Berlin together.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from an exchange of telegrams between Kaiser Wilhelm II and Tsar Nicholas II, the so-called ‘Willy-Nicky’ correspondence, dated 28-29 July 1914 and published in the post-war diplomatic dossiers.
‘[Nicholas to Wilhelm] I beg you in the name of our old friendship to do what you can to stop your allies from going too far. Yours always, Nicky. [Wilhelm to Nicholas] I am exerting my utmost influence to induce the Austrians to deal straightly to arrive at a satisfactory understanding with you.’

Source F suggests that the two emperors could not control the crisis their own governments had created. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Nicholas begs Wilhelm ‘in the name of our old friendship’ to restrain Austria-Hungary.
• Wilhelm answers that he is ‘exerting my utmost influence’ on Vienna.
• Both write as private friends rather than as heads of government giving orders.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The telegrams were exchanged between 28 and 31 July 1914 and changed nothing.
• Russia ordered full mobilisation on 30 July and Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the events of the July Crisis between the Sarajevo assassination and the Austrian declaration of war on Serbia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the 28 July declaration through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 28 June 1914: Princip assassinated Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo.
• 5 July 1914: Germany gave Austria-Hungary the blank cheque.
• Mid-July 1914: Austrian leaders drafted an ultimatum designed to be rejected.
• 23 July 1914: Ultimatum delivered to Serbia, with a 48-hour deadline.
• 25 July 1914: Serbia accepted most demands but rejected Austrian officials operating on its soil; Austria broke off relations.
• 28 July 1914: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, opening the path to general war.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the royal courts under Edward I.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Court of King’s Bench handled major criminal cases and offences against the king and sat at Westminster.
• The Court of Common Pleas dealt with civil disputes between subjects, especially disputes over land.
• The Exchequer of Pleas handled cases concerning royal revenue and the king’s debtors.
• Each court had its own chief justice and clerks who built up the case law cited for centuries afterwards.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of Winchester (1285).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Every man aged fifteen to sixty had to keep arms suitable to his rank, from a knight’s sword to a peasant’s bow.
• A formal watch was set in each town, with gates closed at sunset and strangers arrested if they entered after dark.
• Anyone hearing a crime reported had to raise the hue and cry and join the chase.
• Hedges and undergrowth within 200 feet of major roads had to be cleared so that highwaymen had nowhere to hide.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the eyre changed the relationship between the Crown and the counties.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The eyre pulled every Crown plea, coroner’s roll and claim of liberty into a single royal court — this caused the king’s justice to reach into local communities that might otherwise have been dominated by their lord.
• Counties dreaded the eyre because it could fine whole hundreds for unsolved crimes, which caused them to keep careful records of offences and pursue criminals more energetically.
• Because the eyre was so heavy, Edward’s reign saw it supplemented by faster assize commissions; this caused royal justice to reach the counties more often, even if in smaller doses.
• Travelling judges built case law shared across the country, which caused local custom to be steadily replaced by a single common law administered from Westminster.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal explanation with multiple linked effects and precise vocabulary.
Secure: Two effects clearly explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but explanation is largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about the eyre with little explanation of effects.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the change from trial by ordeal to trial by jury.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • At the time, the change replaced a religious test (whether a priest’s blessing made an iron heal cleanly) with the sworn judgement of twelve neighbours, making outcomes more predictable. • The two-stage system — a presenting jury naming suspects and a trial jury deciding guilt — channelled local knowledge into the king’s courts and gave villagers a stake in the justice system. • Refusal to plead was punished by peine forte et dure; this was harsh but kept cases moving through the courts at a steady rate. • Significance over time: trial by jury became the central feature of English criminal procedure and was carried across the British Empire and into the United States, lasting in modified form into the twenty-first century. [8 marks] Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples. Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail. Developing: Some significance with limited examples. Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about public punishment in medieval English society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, punishments such as the pillory, the stocks and public hanging were designed to humiliate and deter; market-day executions guaranteed the largest possible audience.
• The hanging-drawing-and-quartering of Dafydd ap Gruffudd in 1283 was a deliberate new spectacle for treason, designed to mark the crime as qualitatively different from any other.
• Bodies were sometimes left in chains at crossroads as a warning to travellers, embedding the king’s power into the everyday landscape.
• Significance over time: the visual language of medieval punishment, including the gallows and the pillory, persisted into the eighteenth century before being slowly replaced by imprisonment.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘Royal justice under Edward I depended on local communities as much as on the king’s courts.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The frankpledge system made groups of ten men collectively responsible for each other’s good behaviour, putting policing into community hands.
• The hue and cry required every adult to drop work and join a chase — if no one was caught, the whole hundred was fined.
• Trial juries depended on local knowledge of suspects and reputations; jurors were expected to know what their neighbours had done.
• The Statute of Winchester (1285) organised the watch and the keeping of arms locally, not through royal officers.

Arguments to weigh against:
• The royal courts at Westminster (King’s Bench, Common Pleas, Exchequer of Pleas) issued binding judgements that overrode local custom.
• The eyre and the assize judges enforced central law on counties that had no choice in the matter.
• Statutes such as Westminster I (1275), Gloucester (1278) and Winchester (1285) defined the limits of local action by royal command.
• Punishments such as hanging, drawing and quartering were imposed by the Crown, not the community.

A strong response weighs the role of local responsibility against centralised royal courts and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the legal system with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: 'Operation Desert Storm achieved its aims.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: the UN mandate was to expel Iraq from Kuwait, and Kuwait was liberated in 100 hours of ground fighting.
• Agree: air supremacy was won within days, the 38-day air campaign wrecked Iraqi command and air defences, and coalition military deaths were around 392.
• Agree: the coalition held together, Israel stayed out, and Arab partners remained inside the operation to the end.
• Disagree: Saddam stayed in power for another twelve years, and the Republican Guard survived largely intact.
• Disagree: the Shia and Kurdish uprisings of spring 1991 were crushed while coalition forces watched from the border.
• Disagree: chemical-weapons stocks were unaccounted for, and no-fly zones and sanctions became a twelve-year holding pattern.
• Judgement: measured against its stated UN aim the operation succeeded; measured against a lasting settlement for the region it did not.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the coalition air campaign against Iraq developed between 17 January and 24 February 1991.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The air phase opened at about 2.30am Baghdad time on 17 January 1991, two days after the UN deadline expired.
• F-117 stealth fighters, Tomahawk cruise missiles and B-52 bombers struck command bunkers, air defences and the electricity grid.
• Air supremacy was achieved within days; many Iraqi pilots flew their aircraft to Iran rather than fight.
• Iraq answered with Scud missiles against Tel Aviv, Haifa and Riyadh, and the United States sent Patriot batteries to keep Israel out of the war.
• Over 38 days the coalition flew around 100,000 sorties; the Amiriyah shelter strike of 13 February, which killed several hundred civilians, damaged the image of a clean war.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'The most important consequence of the 1991 Gulf War was that Saddam Hussein stayed in power.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: the UN mandate covered Kuwait, not regime change, so Bush stopped at the border and Saddam survived for another twelve years.
• Agree: because the regime survived, containment through no-fly zones, sanctions and weapons inspections replaced a settlement.
• Agree: the survival of the Republican Guard allowed the crushing of the Shia and Kurdish uprisings within weeks.
• Disagree: US forces stayed on Saudi soil, and that presence became the central grievance behind al-Qaeda's campaign.
• Disagree: Kuwait was restored and the principle that borders cannot be changed by force was upheld.
• Disagree: the war split Arab opinion between the Gulf monarchies and poorer republics, a fault line that outlasted Saddam.
• Judgement: Saddam's survival shaped the next twelve years, but the arrival of American troops in Saudi Arabia had the longer reach.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Arab states reacted to the invasion of Kuwait and the war that followed, between August 1990 and March 1991.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Saudi Arabia, fearing for its eastern oil fields, invited American forces into the kingdom in August 1990.
• Egypt and Syria joined the coalition with ground forces, giving the operation Arab cover that Washington judged essential.
• Jordan, Yemen and the Palestine Liberation Organisation sided with Iraq, partly persuaded by Saddam's linking of Kuwait to the Palestinian cause.
• Popular opinion in several Arab states was more sympathetic to Saddam than governments were, exposing a gap between rulers and ruled.
• After the liberation of Kuwait in February 1991, the Gulf monarchies celebrated while poorer Arab republics were left with restive populations.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the coalition tried to contain Iraq in the eighteen months after the Safwan ceasefire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At Safwan on 3 March 1991 Iraq accepted the UN resolutions, agreed to stop firing and pulled back, but the regime was left intact.
• From April 1991 Operation Provide Comfort protected the Kurds in northern Iraq and kept Iraqi aircraft out of the north.
• UN Resolution 687 established UNSCOM, beginning the long process of locating and dismantling Iraqi weapons programmes.
• Sanctions were tightened, and oil-for-food arrangements were proposed to ease the effect on civilians.
• In August 1992 Operation Southern Watch extended a no-fly zone over southern Iraq, completing a containment policy that lasted twelve years.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained chain of cause and consequence with explicit links between events. Secure: Clear chronological account with some causal links. Developing: Some relevant content but mostly descriptive. Emerging: Limited or chronologically muddled material.]

practice_questions.text: 'The Highway of Death was the main reason Bush ordered a ceasefire on 28 February 1991.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Agree: photographs of the burnt-out column on the road to Basra raised concerns inside the Bush administration that liberation was tipping into slaughter.
• Agree: the coalition's legitimacy rested on limited aims, and images of a rout threatened that.
• Disagree: the UN mandate had already been met — Kuwait was liberated and Iraqi forces were in retreat.
• Disagree: advancing further risked shattering Arab support and leaving coalition troops responsible for an occupation nobody had planned.
• Disagree: Schwarzkopf's plan had always been a short ground campaign, and 100 hours was close to what had been intended.
