• Judgement: the imagery hardened a decision already shaped by the mandate and by coalition politics.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument with limited evidence. Emerging: Description with little judgement. The 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the experience of medieval Jews in England was similar to or different from the experience of Hanseatic merchants at the London Steelyard.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Jews were invited in by William the Conqueror around 1070 specifically to provide credit; Hanseatic merchants were not invited but tolerated for their Baltic trade.
• Difference: the Jewish community was expelled in 1290 by royal edict and was officially absent for 366 years; the Hanseatic Steelyard was tolerated for around 400 years before Elizabeth I revoked its privileges in 1597.
• Similarity: both groups depended on royal protection that could be withdrawn the moment the Crown saw more advantage in expulsion than in toleration.
• Similarity: both made an outsized economic contribution — Jewish moneylending kept Norman government solvent, Hanseatic trade supplied London with timber, wax and fur for centuries.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named institutions.
Secure: Two clear comparisons with relevant detail.
Developing: One developed comparison; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation about ‘both being migrants’.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which medieval Jewish migration to England was similar to or different from Italian Lombard banking migration after 1290.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Jews were brought in deliberately by William the Conqueror; Italians arrived as private operators chasing the gap left by the 1290 expulsion.
• Difference: Jews were the king’s personal property and could be taxed at will; Italian bankers operated as international firms (Bardi, Peruzzi) free to leave when royal debt collapsed in 1340.
• Similarity: both groups provided credit the Christian English economy could not generate internally because of the usury ban.
• Similarity: both left lasting marks on London geography — Old Jewry, Lombard Street and the symbol of the three golden balls.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named individuals or families.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1290 Edict of Expulsion for the development of finance in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: ended 220 years of Jewish presence in England and removed the main source of credit available to the Crown and to landholders.
• At the time: Italian bankers from Lucca, Florence and Genoa moved into the gap, settling around what became Lombard Street in London.
• At the time: financial techniques shifted — bills of exchange, partnerships and currency contracts replaced the simpler Jewish moneylending model.
• Over time: the expulsion became a model that other European rulers copied (France 1306, Spain 1492); England was first.
• Over time: there was no legal Jewish community in England until Cromwell’s readmission in 1656; the gap shaped the religious geography of British finance for centuries.
• Limitation: the immediate financial impact on royal credit was managed through the Italians; the deeper significance is in the precedent of expulsion by royal decree.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Hanseatic Steelyard for medieval and early modern London.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: connected London to a Baltic and North Sea trade network from the 1200s, supplying timber, wax, fur, pitch and grain.
• At the time: gave English merchants a direct competitor on their own riverbank and a model of long-distance corporate trade to imitate.
• At the time: Hanseatic privileges were a recurring grievance in late medieval Parliaments and one of the issues Elizabeth I had to manage in 1597.
• Over time: the eventual takeover of the Steelyard by English merchants prefigured the Elizabethan and Stuart trading companies (Muscovy, Levant, East India) that came next.
• Over time: the site was demolished in the nineteenth century to build Cannon Street station — a literal example of one trading network being built on top of another.
• Limitation: Hanseatic merchants stayed within the walled compound rather than integrating, so their cultural influence on London was limited.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Economic resources were the main factor shaping the position of foreign merchants and bankers in England between c1070 and 1600.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to economic resources and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic resources (in support): William the Conqueror brought Jewish lenders from Rouen in about 1070 because the Norman state needed credit it could not raise from Christians.
• Economic resources (in support): Hanseatic merchants were tolerated for Baltic timber, wax, fur and grain, and Italian bankers were used because they could finance Edward III’s war.
• Government: royal decisions decided who stayed — the 1290 Edict of Expulsion, and the revoking of Hanseatic privileges under Elizabeth I.
• Religion: the ban on Christian usury created the opening for Jewish lenders, and anti-Jewish preaching and the blood libel made their position unsafe.
• Role of individuals: Edward I chose expulsion once Jewish wealth was taxed out; the Bardi and Peruzzi gambled on royal credit and failed.
• Judgement: economic usefulness explains why each group was let in, but government decisions and religious hostility explain the timing of each expulsion.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which medieval Jewish moneylending in England was similar to or different from later Huguenot banking in the late 17th century.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Jews were the king’s personal property and could be expelled by royal decree; Huguenots were welcomed as Protestant refugees and could be naturalised under Parliament’s 1709 act for foreign Protestants.
• Difference: Jewish moneylending was tolerated to fill a gap left by the Christian usury ban; Huguenot banking joined an already-functioning English credit market and helped found the Bank of England in 1694.
• Similarity: both groups were valued primarily for their financial skill and the credit they brought.
• Similarity: both communities ended up shaping London geography — Old Jewry and Lombard Street for the Jews and Italians, Huguenot family banks in the City around the Bank of England.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named institutions.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) was similar to the Peasants' Revolt (1381).
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both involved face-to-face negotiations between the rebels and royal representatives, with the Crown offering pardons and promises — Richard II at Mile End in 1381, the Duke of Norfolk at Doncaster in 1536.
• Both ended in betrayal: Richard II revoked the charters within weeks; Henry VIII used Bigod's 1537 rising as an excuse to renege on the Doncaster pardon and execute around 200 ringleaders.
• Both were led by named individuals whose execution became a symbol — John Ball hanged July 1381, Robert Aske hanged in chains at York July 1537.
• Both drew religious legitimacy from sacred imagery — Ball's preaching from Genesis; the Five Wounds of Christ banner of 1536.

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points or one developed point.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Pilgrimage of Grace in the changing relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: largest peacetime rising in English history; around 30,000 under arms forced Henry VIII into negotiation he could not afford militarily.
• At the time: exposed the limits of Tudor royal authority — Henry had no army to match the marchers and had to play for time with the Doncaster pardon.
• At the time: led to swift reprisals — around 200 executions, Aske hanged at York 1537, dissolution accelerated through the larger monasteries 1538-40.
• Over time: strengthened the Council of the North as a permanent instrument of royal control over the region.
• Over time: shaped how later northern risings (Prayer Book 1549, Northern Earls 1569) framed themselves and how quickly they were crushed.
• Over time: a powerful precedent that religion could move tens of thousands — revisited under the Stuarts and in the Civil War era.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise dates and a clear judgement on what changed.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the rising without explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the changing shape of popular protest between 1381 and 1536.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the 1381 revolt was peasant-led, centred on serfdom and the poll tax, and won only verbal royal promises that were revoked within weeks.
• At the time: the 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace drew a cross-class coalition of peasants, gentry and clergy behind religious demands and put 30,000 armed men in the field.
• At the time: religion framed both risings — John Ball's preaching from Genesis in 1381, the Five Wounds of Christ banner in 1536.
• Over time: the Crown's method did not change. It bargained when outnumbered, then reneged and executed the leaders — Tyler and Ball, Aske and the Doncaster ringleaders.
• Over time: the scale of 1536 pushed the Tudor state into permanent watchfulness over the north through a strengthened Council of the North.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: ‘Religion was the main factor in causing popular uprisings against royal authority in the medieval and early modern periods.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh religion against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of religion as the main factor:
• 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace: dissolution of the monasteries, Five Wounds of Christ banner, demands for restoration of Catholic worship; 30,000 marchers.
• 1381 Peasants' Revolt: John Ball's preaching from Genesis (‘When Adam delved and Eve span...’) gave the rising religious legitimacy.
• Later: 1640s Civil War — Puritan radicals in the New Model Army drove constitutional change.

Weighed against the economy:
• 1381 trigger was the 1381 poll tax of 12d per adult, building on the long-term Statute of Labourers grievance.
• 1536: rumours of new taxes on baptisms, burials and marriages, plus bad harvests, fed alongside religious anger.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Aske's choice to frame the 1536 rising as a pilgrimage was decisive; without it the gentry might not have joined.
• Tyler and Ball gave the 1381 revolt leadership; Cromwell and Henry shaped the response in 1536.

Weighed against government:
• A weak boy-king regime in 1381 (Richard II under John of Gaunt) and Henry VIII's reliance on Cromwell's centralised administration in the 1530s both created political vulnerabilities.

Judgement: Top answers argue religion was the primary frame in 1536 and an important driver in 1381, but in both cases economic grievance, government weakness and individual leadership combined to make the rising large enough to matter. Religion shaped how revolt was justified; the economy made it likely.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing religion against at least two other factors with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Robert Aske in the Pilgrimage of Grace.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: as a Yorkshire lawyer he gave the rising legitimacy and discipline; coordinated the capture of York, Pontefract and Hull and drafted the rebels' articles.
• At the time: his choice to frame the movement as a ‘pilgrimage’ under the Five Wounds banner allowed gentry and clergy to join without open treason.
• At the time: his trust in Henry's pardon at Doncaster (December 1536) demobilised the marchers and exposed him to betrayal.
• Over time: his execution at York in 1537 became a Catholic memory of Tudor faithlessness, used during the Northern Earls' rising of 1569.
• Over time: the example of Aske showed later opposition movements that royal pardons could not be trusted — an attitude visible in seventeenth-century parliamentarians.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of who Aske was without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the actions of Henry VIII's government in 1536-37 were different from the actions of Richard II's government in 1381.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Henry VIII's reprisals were narrower and more targeted — around 200 named ringleaders executed under martial law in 1537, where the 1381 reprisals were far wider, with at least 1,500 rebels killed or executed.
• Difference: Henry used a manufactured excuse (Bigod's 1537 follow-up rising) to renege on the Doncaster pardon, where Richard II simply revoked the charters by royal will.
• Difference: Henry strengthened the Council of the North as a permanent instrument of control; Richard II made no comparable institutional change in 1381.
• Difference: Cromwell's role as a ‘low-born’ chief minister was a target of the rebels themselves in 1536, where the 1381 rebels targeted John of Gaunt as the king's uncle — a difference in the social politics of unpopular advisers.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, each with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Harrying of the North in the winter of 1069 to 1070.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was a deliberate winter campaign — William divided his army into mobile detachments based at York and sent them out across Yorkshire and beyond when food was scarcest and rebuilding hardest.
• Villages were burned, livestock slaughtered and grain stores and farming tools destroyed, leaving survivors to face famine through the winter and into the spring of 1070.
• Northern regions affected included Yorkshire (worst hit), Durham, Cheshire and the Tees valley — not a single concentrated battle but a months-long sweep across roughly two hundred miles.
• Chroniclers such as Orderic Vitalis described mass starvation in the months that followed, with people reduced to eating dogs, horses and worse.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Harrying of the North in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Harrying ended the 1069 northern revolt by destroying the regional resource base — villages, livestock and food stores — on which any future rising would have depended.
• It deterred further northern revolt under William I; the political effect is undisputed even when historians disagree about scale.
• Over time, it allowed wholesale redistribution of northern land to trusted Norman lords such as Alan Rufus at Richmond and the bishop of Durham, who garrisoned the North with new castles.
• It also matters morally and for historians: even Norman chroniclers like Orderic Vitalis condemned the campaign, and it has shaped William’s reputation among historians for nine centuries.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the chronicle evidence for the Harrying of the North.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Orderic Vitalis, a Norman monk at St Evroul writing his Ecclesiastical History around 1125 — more than fifty years after the events — condemned William and gave the figure of 100,000 dead in famine after the campaign.
• John of Worcester, an English monk writing earlier in the 12th century, gives a comparable picture of mass starvation and depopulation across northern England.
• Both writers worked decades after the Harrying using earlier sources and oral tradition, which explains why historians treat their numerical claims with caution.
• Both also show the unusual fact that even Norman-aligned writers were prepared to criticise William for this episode, suggesting the brutality was striking even by 11th-century standards.
• Why it matters: almost everything we know about the scale of the Harrying comes from these two writers, so how far they are trusted decides how the campaign is judged.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which landholding in Yorkshire and the North-east changed after the Harrying of the North.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Many Anglo-Saxon thegns who survived had no estates left to defend, accelerating the dispossession recorded later in Domesday Book where fewer than 10% of pre-conquest landholders still held land in 1086.
• Northern lands were granted to a small group of trusted Normans — Alan Rufus received the great honour of Richmond, the bishop of Durham was given vast estates — concentrating power in a few loyal hands.
• These new lords planted castles to hold the redistributed estates, weaving the network of motte-and-bailey strongpoints that anchored the North through the 12th century.
• Domesday’s 1086 entries of vasta est (waste) record a depressed taxable value across much of Yorkshire even sixteen years later — though historians caution that ‘waste’ can also reflect tenant flight or administrative reorganisation.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the disagreement between historians over the scale of the Harrying of the North.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the brutality was so striking that even Norman writers like Orderic Vitalis condemned William — the contemporary unease is itself historical evidence about how harsh the campaign was perceived to be.
• Modern historians such as Hugh Thomas (2003) read Orderic’s 100,000 figure as inflated by genre conventions and decades of distance, but agree the destruction was unprecedented in scale — the debate refines, rather than removes, the seriousness of the Harrying.
• Domesday ‘waste’ entries can be read as fiscal records of low taxable value as well as physical destruction, so the 1086 evidence requires careful handling rather than direct quotation.
• Importance later: how we judge the Harrying shapes how we judge Norman rule overall — whether the conquest was a measured takeover with continuity beneath (Hugh Thomas) or a violent rupture (Marc Morris).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of the Harrying.

‘The Harrying of the North was the turning point of the conquest. After that winter no part of England rose against William I again, and the North was handed to a new set of Norman lords.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the importance of the Harrying of the North? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: the Harrying was the decisive turning point in Norman control of England.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The Harrying ended the most dangerous revolt of William’s reign — the 1069 Danish-backed northern rising that had stormed York and threatened simultaneous risings in Devon, Cornwall and the Welsh Marches.
• It cleared the way for wholesale redistribution of northern land to a small group of Norman tenants-in-chief and the castle network that anchored their lordships.
• The political effect was permanent: large-scale revolt against William I did not happen again in the North after 1070, even when revolt flared in 1075 and 1088 elsewhere.
• It marked the end of William’s conciliatory phase; from 1070 onward Anglo-Saxon nobles were systematically dispossessed and the Norman aristocracy was consolidated.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• Hastings (1066) was the indispensable battlefield victory — without it there would have been no conquest to defend.
• The 1067–71 revolts as a whole, not just the northern revolt, drove the shift from conciliation to occupation; the Earls’ Revolt of 1075 and the 1088 rebellion against William II show consolidation continued long after the Harrying.
• Domesday Book (1086) and the redistribution it records represent a separate, longer process of administrative and tenurial settlement.
• Lanfranc’s Church reforms from 1070 transformed the Norman hold on personnel and ideology in ways the Harrying alone did not.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1925 League of Nations Council ruling on the Greek invasion of Bulgaria, published in the official League Gazette.
‘The Council, having considered the report of its commission, finds that Greek troops crossed the Bulgarian frontier without justification. It calls upon Greece to withdraw all forces immediately, and orders Greece to pay £45,000 in compensation to Bulgaria for damage caused. The Council reserves the right to apply economic sanctions if Greece does not comply.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons why the League’s response to the Bulgarian crisis was effective.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One point clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• It ruled clearly against the aggressor — finding Greek troops had crossed without justification.
• It set a specific compensation figure of £45,000 to make the ruling concrete.
• It threatened economic sanctions if Greece did not comply.
• The ruling came swiftly and was based on a commission’s report — lending legitimacy to the decision.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Corfu Crisis of 1923, from the murder of the Italian general to the Italian withdrawal from Corfu.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates; arrives at outcome through substantiated steps.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 27 August 1923: Italian General Tellini, working on the Greek-Albanian border commission, was murdered in Greek territory.
• Mussolini blamed Greece without evidence and demanded an apology and 50 million lire in compensation.
• When Greece refused, Mussolini ordered the bombardment and occupation of Corfu (31 August), killing several civilians.
• Greece appealed to the League; the Council was preparing to rule against Italy.
• Italy threatened to leave the League and the dispute was transferred to the Conference of Ambassadors, outside the League.
• The Conference compelled Greece to apologise and pay the 50 million lire.
• Italy withdrew from Corfu in late September 1923, having received what it demanded.
• Lesson: the League could be sidestepped by a great power willing to threaten withdrawal.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter by Lord Robert Cecil, British negotiator and former League of Nations Commission member, to a colleague in 1924.
‘The Vilna affair has done us a great deal of harm. We condemned Polish action, then we accepted Polish occupation. The League cannot afford to repeat this lesson too often. If our resolutions are not enforced, what authority do they carry?’

Source C: An extract from a 1924 article by an Italian journalist in the Milan newspaper Il Popolo d’Italia, the paper Mussolini had founded.
‘Corfu has demonstrated something useful. The League is a polite club for small nations. When a great power acts decisively, the League discovers it has no powers at all. Italy emerges from this episode with her dignity intact and a useful lesson learned.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the failures of the League of Nations in the 1920s. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a serious British insider view that the Vilna decision damaged the League’s authority. Provenance: a private letter from a leading British internationalist; likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: confirms historical record — Poland kept Vilna until 1939; the League’s climb-down weakened its credibility.
Source C — Content: a triumphant Italian framing of the League’s irrelevance to great powers. Provenance: a Mussolini-edited newspaper; designed to shape Italian and international opinion in favour of Italian assertiveness. Own knowledge: the dispute was indeed transferred to the Conference of Ambassadors; Mussolini did get the apology and 50 million lire he demanded.
Judgement: B is highly useful for measured British anxiety; C is useful as evidence of the political message Italian fascists drew, though one-sided in its framing.

practice_questions.text:
‘The League of Nations was more successful than not in the 1920s.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Aaland was a clear arbitration success accepted by both Sweden and Finland.
• Upper Silesia was partitioned and Bulgaria was settled in days, both without war.
• The specialist agencies (ILO, Health Committee, refugees) achieved durable humanitarian gains.
• Locarno (1925) and German League entry (1926) were major political wins for the wider system.
Challenging the statement:
• Vilna and Corfu were public failures, both involving a great power.
• The successes were small in scale; the failures involved much larger states.
• Structural weaknesses — no army, the unanimity rule, the missing USA — were visible from the start.
Judgement: successful between small states, already failing where great powers were involved, which is what mattered in the 1930s.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the Lithuanian government’s 1922 protest to the League of Nations on the seizure of Vilna.
‘The League has spoken; Poland has not listened. Our capital remains under foreign occupation. The principles of the Covenant are noble in Geneva and meaningless in Warsaw. If the League cannot defend the territorial integrity of its smaller members, what is its purpose?’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about the limitations of the League of Nations in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• The League condemned the seizure of Vilna but could not enforce its own decision.
• The Covenant’s principles are described as ‘noble in Geneva and meaningless in Warsaw’.
• Own knowledge: Poland kept Vilna throughout the inter-war period; France quietly backed Poland as an ally against Soviet Russia; the League had no army.
• Worth noting: an aggrieved government is likely to overstate its case for diplomatic effect.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the work of the League’s specialist agencies in the 1920s, focusing on the International Labour Organization, the High Commission for Refugees and the Health Committee.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more agency activities with their consequences; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked points with causal connectives.
Developing: Activities listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin coverage.

Indicative content:
• 1919: the International Labour Organization (ILO) was founded with the League, securing conventions on hours of work and child labour.
• 1921: Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen was appointed High Commissioner for Refugees, beginning the Nansen passport system that allowed stateless people to travel.
• Early 1920s: Nansen organised the repatriation of around 425,000 prisoners of war from Russia.
• 1922 onwards: the Health Committee containment of typhus epidemics in Poland and Russia, foundations for what later became the World Health Organization.
• 1926: the Slavery Convention banned the slave trade, with League oversight contributing to its end in Sierra Leone.
• Result: the League’s agencies achieved durable humanitarian gains that outlived the political League and shaped the post-1945 UN system.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Religious Settlement of 1559.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church of England and required officials to swear an oath of loyalty.
• The Act of Uniformity imposed an English Book of Common Prayer on every parish and required Sunday attendance, with a 12-pence fine for absence.
• The 39 Articles of 1563 set out Protestant doctrine, including salvation by faith and rejection of the Catholic mass as a sacrifice.
• Service appearance kept some Catholic features — vestments, altars, ambiguous communion wording — to allow outward conformity from the religiously cautious.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Puritan challenge to the Elizabethan Church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Puritans wanted to ‘purify’ the Church of remaining Catholic features such as vestments, altars and saints’ days, and demanded simpler services.
• They placed strong emphasis on preaching and Bible study, organising ‘prophesyings’ in the 1570s to improve clergy.
• A Presbyterian minority wanted bishops abolished and church government run by elected elders.
• A Separatist minority left the Church entirely to set up independent congregations.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the law treated English Catholics between 1568 and 1603.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A large group of ‘Church Papists’ outwardly conformed by attending Sunday services to avoid the 12-pence fine, while keeping Catholic belief in private.
• A smaller group of recusants refused attendance and faced rising fines — from 12 pence per Sunday to £20 per month from 1581.
• Catholic priests trained abroad were declared traitors under the 1585 Act, leading to around 130 executions by 1603.
• Catholic populations remained strongest in the north and west, where enforcement was patchier and old practices survived alongside formal conformity.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Elizabeth’s archbishops dealt with Puritan demands between 1566 and 1583.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Vestments Controversy of the 1560s led to around 37 London ministers being suspended by Archbishop Parker on Elizabeth’s orders.
• The prophesyings of the 1570s split the Church leadership: Archbishop Grindal refused to suppress them and was suspended in 1577.
• From 1583, Archbishop Whitgift enforced the ‘Three Articles’; around 200 Puritan ministers were suspended for refusing, though most later gave way.
• Puritan attacks on bishops were treated as attacks on royal authority over the Church, hardening Elizabeth’s view that they were a political threat.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the increase in recusancy fines in 1581.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It transformed the financial burden of refusing church attendance, raising fines from 12 pence per Sunday to £20 per month.
• It pushed many wealthy Catholic gentry to choose between bankruptcy and outward conformity, narrowing visible recusant communities.
• It hardened the political divide between ‘Church Papists’ and recusants, with the latter seen as politically suspect.
• Combined with the 1585 Act against priests, it set the framework for the executions of 130 priests by 1603.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Religion was the hardest problem Elizabeth’s government ever had to manage.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the challenges facing Elizabeth’s government between 1568 and 1603? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The 1559 Settlement had to balance Catholic, conformist and Puritan groups; failure would mean civil unrest as in France.
• Catholic threats — the Northern Rebellion, the missionaries, plots, the Armada — were all framed in religious terms.
• Managing the Puritans cost archbishops their careers (Grindal suspended, Whitgift mobilised) and split Parliament.
• Religious laws (Supremacy, Uniformity, recusancy, the 1585 Act) consumed parliamentary time across the reign.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Other challenges — war with Spain, the succession question, harvest failure, Irish rebellion — were equally serious in their own right.
• Patronage and faction were arguably more important to political stability than religious policy.
• The Settlement worked: most parishioners outwardly conformed and the regime survived four decades.
• Many religious crises were also political crises (e.g. Mary Queen of Scots), so isolating religion as ‘the most important’ oversimplifies.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a memorandum by General Lucius Clay, US Military Governor in Germany, sent to Washington on 28 June 1948, four days into the Berlin Blockade.
‘If we abandon Berlin we shall lose all of western Europe within months. Berlin is small and isolated, but the principle on which it stands is the principle on which our entire policy in Europe rests. We must supply the city by air for as long as the airlift lasts; if we cannot, we should consider an armed convoy and accept the risk of war.’

Source B: An extract from a Soviet Military Administration statement issued in East Berlin on 30 June 1948.
‘The technical disturbances on rail and road routes into Berlin are the consequence of the unilateral currency reform forced upon the city by the Western powers. The Soviet Union cannot accept being asked to accept Western banknotes in our zone. Once the currency question is settled, normal traffic will resume.’

How useful are Sources A and B to an historian studying the causes of the Berlin Blockade in 1948?

Explain your answer using Sources A and B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source A — Content: Clay argues that abandoning Berlin would cost the West the whole of Western Europe, and that supply by air is the first option. Provenance: a memorandum by the US Military Governor four days into the blockade, written for his own government and so likely to be frank. Own knowledge: the airlift began on 26 June 1948 and delivered about 2.3 million tonnes over nearly eleven months.
Source B — Content: presents the closures as technical problems caused by the Western currency reform, and promises normal traffic once the currency question is settled. Provenance: an official Soviet statement for public consumption, useful for the line Moscow wanted heard rather than for its real intentions. Own knowledge: the Deutsche Mark was introduced in the Western zones on 20 June and in Western Berlin on 23 June 1948; the blockade closed road, rail and canal routes from 24 June.
Judgement: both are useful but partial — A shows how seriously Washington took the risk of losing Berlin, B shows how Moscow justified the blockade; together they explain why neither side would back down.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Berlin Blockade led to the founding of NATO between June 1948 and April 1949.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the founding of NATO through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 20–23 June 1948: introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones and Western Berlin triggered the Soviet response.
• 24 June 1948: Stalin imposed a full blockade of West Berlin.
• 26 June 1948: the airlift began; over the following months it scaled up to a delivery every ninety seconds at peak.
• Autumn 1948: Western governments concluded that ad hoc coordination was inadequate and began negotiating a treaty.
• 4 April 1949: twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, before the blockade had even ended.
• 12 May 1949: Stalin lifted the blockade, leaving NATO in place as the lasting institutional consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C.

Source C: An extract from a speech by US Secretary of State Dean Acheson at the signing of the North Atlantic Treaty, Washington, 4 April 1949.
‘This treaty does not begin a war and does not seek one. It declares that twelve democratic nations stand together to deter aggression. The events of the past year have shown what an unwillingness to stand together can cost — the Berlin Blockade is the latest reminder. We have learned the lesson, and we mean to act on it.’

Source C suggests that NATO was created in answer to Soviet pressure in Europe. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source C and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Twelve democratic nations are standing together to deter aggression.
• The Berlin Blockade has shown the cost of not standing together.
• The treaty is defensive (it ‘does not seek’ war) and aimed at deterrence.
• The lesson of the past year is now driving institutional change.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949, while the airlift was still running.
• Article 5 committed every member to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Berlin Airlift was a greater victory for the West than the founding of NATO.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The airlift kept about 2.5 million West Berliners supplied for nearly eleven months.
• It beat the blockade without a shot being fired, so Stalin lifted it on 12 May 1949.
• It proved to Western Europe that the USA would stay and take risks for the continent.
• It handed the West a propaganda victory, with Soviet pressure seen to have failed in public.
Disagree:
• NATO was permanent while the airlift answered one crisis.
• Article 5 gave Western Europe a defence guarantee that lasted the whole Cold War.
• NATO brought American troops, air bases and, after 1951, an integrated command to Europe.
• The airlift did not stop Germany splitting into two states later in 1949.
Judgement: the airlift won the crisis, but NATO built the structure that kept Western Europe secure for forty years.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Berlin Airlift broke the Soviet Blockade between June 1948 and May 1949.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the lifting of the blockade through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 24 June 1948: the Soviet blockade closed road, rail and canal access into West Berlin, leaving roughly six weeks of stockpiled food.
• 26 June 1948: the airlift began as a temporary improvisation using Allied transport aircraft.
• Autumn 1948: the operation scaled up; Tegel airport was built in West Berlin in a few weeks to add a third runway.
• Winter 1948–49: coal was the largest cargo, sustaining heating and electricity through Berlin’s coldest months.
• Spring 1949: a transport landed every ninety seconds at peak; West Berliners were not starving and Soviet pressure was failing.
• 12 May 1949: Stalin lifted the blockade; the airlift continued until September to build stockpiles.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a private letter from Ernst Reuter, Mayor of West Berlin, to a friend abroad in December 1948.
‘The streets are cold and the lights flicker, but Berliners do not waver. They have understood that the airlift is more than coal and flour; it is a vote on whether free Europe still exists. Whatever happens in Washington, Moscow will not break us by hunger.’

Source E suggests that West Berliners saw the airlift as more than a supply operation. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source E and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Berliners see the airlift as a ‘vote on whether free Europe still exists’ — symbolic stake.
• They understand the airlift is ‘more than coal and flour’ — political meaning beyond physical supplies.
• Berliners do not waver despite cold and flickering lights — visible commitment.
• Reuter is confident Moscow ‘will not break us by hunger’.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The blockade began on 24 June 1948 and the airlift on 26 June.
• Over 277,000 flights carried about 2.3 million tonnes into the city, most of it coal.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Indian Removal Act on later US policy towards the Plains nations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through an explicit causal chain; precise factual support (1830 Act, Jackson, Trail of Tears 1838–39, Indian Territory, treaty-rewriting precedent).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about removal.

Indicative content:
• Legal precedent: removal showed that Congress could move Native peoples by statute, a tool reused on the Plains.
• Treaty-rewriting habit: existing treaties (e.g. Cherokee guarantees) were overridden, normalising broken promises.
• Indian Territory: the 1830s removals filled modern Oklahoma with displaced peoples, complicating later policy when the Plains nations were also pushed there.
• Cultural acceptance: the Trail of Tears trained the public to accept large-scale forced movement of Native peoples as normal.

practice_questions.text:
Has the discovery of gold been the main reason the Permanent Indian Frontier broke down?

• The 1848 California Gold Rush
• The doctrine of Manifest Destiny

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs gold against Manifest Destiny (and other factors); precise factual support across both bullets and additional material; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached.
Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative.

Indicative content:
• Gold: 1848 strike at Sutter’s Mill, 80,000 forty-niners in 1849, trails through Indian country, cholera, 1850 statehood for California.
• Manifest Destiny: O’Sullivan 1845, Polk’s 1844 election, religious and racial framing, justification for territorial gain.
• Other relevant material: Oregon Trail from 1841, 1846 Oregon Treaty, 1848 Mexican Cession, Bureau of Indian Affairs corruption.
• Judgement: top answers might argue that Manifest Destiny was the political enabler that allowed the gold rush to be tolerated, OR that gold was decisive because it created an unstoppable demographic surge. Either view, substantiated, can reach the top band.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Permanent Indian Frontier of 1834.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features.
Secure: Two valid features.
Developing: One developed; one undeveloped.
Emerging: Generalised description.

Indicative content:
• A geographic line: drawn from the Red River in the south to the Missouri River in the north, running through what is now Oklahoma, Kansas and Iowa.
• A legal exclusion: white settlers were barred and traders required federal licences, with the Indian Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834 providing the framework.
• A military element: the army built a chain of forts (Smith, Gibson, Leavenworth) to enforce the line.
• A purpose: it was meant to keep removed Eastern peoples and the Plains nations together west of the line, ‘in perpetuity’.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of US Indian policy.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a US history textbook, 1900.
“Federal policy in the early Republic balanced the rights of settlers with a sincere desire to protect Indian peoples through reservations and the Permanent Frontier.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a 2018 academic study.
“Federal policy was a sequence of broken promises. Each new line, treaty or reservation was a temporary holding pattern until settler pressure forced another retreat.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, supported differences.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support.
Developing: One difference; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 frames policy as a balanced and sincere effort; Interpretation 2 frames it as a sequence of broken promises.
• Interpretation 1 emphasises protection through reservations; Interpretation 2 emphasises retreat under settler pressure.
• Interpretation 1 portrays Washington positively; Interpretation 2 is critical of the federal record.
• Interpretation 1 stresses intentions; Interpretation 2 stresses outcomes.

practice_questions.text:
Why might the two interpretations of Indian policy above give different views?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise context.
Secure: Reason rooted in provenance or context with brief support.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’.
Emerging: Restates content of each interpretation.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: a 1900 textbook reflected the Frontier-Thesis era and a national mood that celebrated expansion; a 2018 study draws on a generation of revisionist scholarship.
• Purpose: a textbook aimed to build patriotic identity; an academic study aimed to weigh the federal record.
• Evidence: 1900 historians had limited access to Native sources; 2018 historians had treaty archives, reservation-era records and tribal histories.
• Audience: schoolchildren versus academic readers and policymakers.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Bureau of Indian Affairs on relations between Plains nations and the federal government.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (1824 founding, 1849 move to Interior, agents, annuity payments, corruption).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about the BIA.

Indicative content:
• Day-to-day management: agents distributed annuities and handled complaints, making the BIA the public face of US policy.
• Corruption: inflated costs and stolen annuities meant Plains nations received less than treaties promised, eroding trust.
• Distance from Washington: agents had wide local power but limited oversight, producing inconsistent policy and frequent abuses.
• Long-term consequence: by the 1860s the BIA’s record was so poor that even sympathetic federal officials were calling for reform — but the system remained until late in the century.

practice_questions.text:
‘The 1953 armistice was a victory for American containment policy.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• South Korea survived as a non-communist state, which was the original UN war aim under Resolutions 82 and 83.
• Communism was halted at roughly the line where the war had begun, the 38th parallel.
• The United States proved a limited war in Asia could be fought without nuclear escalation, and the US position in East Asia was consolidated.
Disagree:
• The armistice of 27 July 1953 was not a peace treaty, and no treaty has been signed since.
• Around two to three million Korean civilians died and most northern cities were flattened by bombing.
• Washington ended up accepting permanent partition, which it had never publicly endorsed.
• US relations with China froze for two decades, and Washington blocked the People’s Republic from the UN until 1971.
Judgement: Judged as strategy the armistice did vindicate containment; judged from Korea the cost was catastrophic and the outcome unfinished. The strongest answers hold both.

practice_questions.text:
‘The death of Stalin in March 1953 was the main reason the Korean War armistice was signed in July 1953.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Stalin died on 5 March 1953 and the new Soviet leadership wanted to ease East-West tensions.
• Without Soviet backing for a long war, Beijing and Pyongyang had far less reason to fight on.
• The pace of the talks changed within weeks of his death.
Disagree:
• Eisenhower took office in January 1953 promising to end the war and hinted that nuclear weapons might be used.
• The prisoner deadlock had to be solved separately: the June 1953 deal handed prisoners to a neutral commission.
• Both sides had accepted by mid-1951 that neither could win outright, so the pressure to settle predated Stalin’s death.
• Rhee’s release of 27,000 prisoners in June 1953 nearly wrecked the deal, showing other factors still mattered.
Judgement: Stalin’s death was necessary but not sufficient; it worked alongside Eisenhower’s pressure and the prisoner compromise.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Battle of the Imjin River in April 1951 was a defeat for UN forces.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The Gloucestershire Regiment lost 622 of about 850 men killed, wounded or captured.
• The position itself was lost and Eighth Army had to fall back.
• Chinese forces took the ground they had attacked.
Disagree:
• The delay imposed on the Chinese advance let the rest of UN forces withdraw in order.
• Chinese losses were very heavy and the spring offensive failed to break through to Seoul.
• Ridgway used the time bought to stabilise the line, which held for the rest of the war.
Judgement: At unit level Imjin was a British defeat; at operational level it helped stop the Chinese spring offensive. The strongest answers separate the two levels.

practice_questions.text:
‘Syngman Rhee was the main obstacle to ending the Korean War.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Rhee refused to sign the armistice and demanded that the war continue until Korea was reunified.
• On 18 June 1953 he released 27,000 anti-communist prisoners without permission, nearly wrecking the talks.
• Eisenhower had to buy his consent with a defence treaty, large economic aid and a modernised army.
Disagree:
• The two-year blockage was the prisoner-repatriation dispute, not Rhee: Beijing demanded that all prisoners be returned.
• Around half of the 132,000 communist prisoners held by the UN refused to go back, and Washington insisted on voluntary repatriation.
• Stalin’s death and Eisenhower’s pressure were the changes that actually moved both sides in 1953.
• Rhee acted only in the final weeks, once the deal was nearly done.
Judgement: Rhee complicated the ending rather than causing the delay; the prisoner dispute was the real obstacle.

practice_questions.text:
‘The long-term consequences of the Korean War shaped the wider Cold War in Asia.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• US-China relations froze for two decades and Washington blocked the People’s Republic from the UN until 1971.
• Korea convinced Washington that communism had to be contained in Asia, which fed the later commitment in Vietnam.
• NATO hardened and West Germany was rearmed by 1955 because Korea showed conventional invasion was a real risk.
• The peninsula stayed divided, with a heavily armed border and no peace treaty.
Disagree:
• The effects were uneven: Japan grew rich on US war procurement while China faced two decades of isolation.
• The war’s meaning is contested, and North and South Korea teach it in opposite ways.
• Some later Asian conflicts had their own local causes rather than Korean ones.
Judgement: Korea was a defining event for the Cold War in Asia, but its consequences were unevenly spread and are still argued over.

practice_questions.text:
‘Korea was the forgotten war.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• In the United States the name ‘the forgotten war’ became standard, and Vietnam soon absorbed public memory of Cold War fighting.
• American losses of about 36,000 dead were small beside Korean losses, so the war left a smaller mark on the US public.
• There was no victory parade and no peace treaty to remember.
Disagree:
• Two to three million Korean civilians died; nothing about that was forgotten in Korea.
• The bombing of the north shaped the North Korean state’s identity for decades afterwards.
• The armistice line still divides the peninsula and still shapes Korean politics.
Judgement: ‘Forgotten’ depends on whose memory is measured: largely true of Western publics, plainly false in Korea.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which medieval and 18th-century hospitals were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: medieval hospitals were attached to monasteries and focused on hospitality (the dying, lepers, pregnant women); 18th-century voluntary hospitals such as Guy’s (1724) and the London (1740) were funded by wealthy subscribers and treated patients with the aim of cure.
• Difference: medieval physicians used uroscopy and the four humours; 18th-century hospitals trained doctors at the bedside in a model influenced by Sydenham and Hunter.
• Similarity: both relied on charitable funding rather than fees from poor patients — the wealthy were treated at home in both periods.
• Similarity: both were limited by the medical theory of their time — humours in the Middle Ages, lingering humour ideas in the 18th century until germ theory.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Harvey for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: in 1628 his book De Motu Cordis proved the heart pumps blood in a continuous circulation, overturning Galen on a fundamental point.
• At the time: undermined the theoretical basis for bleeding as a treatment — though doctors continued bleeding for another 200 years.
• Over time: laid the foundation for the first human-to-human blood transfusion by Blundell at Guy’s in 1818.
• Over time: shifted the standard of medical proof from classical authority to anatomical observation and experiment, paving the way for Hunter and the 19th-century scientific revolution.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, including explicit acknowledgement of the gap between discovery and clinical application.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification of who Harvey was.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the separation of surgeons from barbers in 1745 for British medicine.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: surgeons left the barbers’ company and formed their own, ending the guild link that had kept surgery a trade.
• At the time: it fitted a wider professionalising trend — voluntary hospitals such as Westminster and Guy’s gave surgeons a teaching base.
• At the time: John Hunter’s insistence on dissection, observation and experiment gave the new profession a scientific claim.
• Over time: the Royal College of Surgeons followed in 1800 and surgical training became formal and examined.
• Over time: a trained, respected surgical profession was the group that took up anaesthetics and antisepsis in the 19th century.
• Limitation: status changed faster than results — without anaesthetics or antiseptics surgery stayed dangerous for another century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Has the role of the individual been the main factor in the modernisation of British medicine between 1600 and 1800? Explain your answer with reference to the role of the individual and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the role of the individual:
• Harvey’s individual experimentation produced the 1628 circulation discovery.
• Sydenham’s personal style of clinical observation broke with the textbook tradition.
• Hunter’s teaching shaped a generation of British surgeons including Jenner.
• Compare with later periods: Pasteur, Koch, Lister and Bevan all show individuals driving change in their fields.

Weighed against communication:
• Printed books carried Harvey’s and Sydenham’s ideas; without printing they would have stayed in their own circles.
• Newspapers in the 18th century spread quack remedies as well as legitimate ones — communication cut both ways.

Weighed against science and technology:
• Microscopes (Malpighi 1661) finally made Harvey’s capillaries visible; without instrument advances, theory could not be verified.
• Voluntary hospitals provided the institutional setting for surgical experiment.

Weighed against government:
• Government was largely absent — medicine was regulated by guilds and royal colleges, not the state.
• This contrasts sharply with the 19th and 20th centuries when government became dominant (Public Health Acts, NHS).

Judgement: Individuals dominated this period because the state stayed out, science was incomplete, and communication was slow. The 16-mark question rewards students who note that the same factors shift in weight across the sweep — the role of the individual was central in 1700 but had to share the stage with government and science by 1900.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes individuals only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of John Hunter for the development of British medicine.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: pushed surgery towards science by insisting on dissection, observation and experiment as the basis for surgical training.
• At the time: built up an enormous anatomical collection (now at the Royal College of Surgeons) and taught hundreds of students at St George’s.
• Over time: directly taught Edward Jenner, linking 18th-century scientific surgery to the breakthrough of vaccination in 1796.
• Over time: shaped the model of surgical training that 19th-century reformers (Lister included) would build on.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: a London newspaper advertisement for Dr James’s Powder, one of the best-known patent medicines of the eighteenth century. It promises the powder will cure fevers, gout and other complaints, names the shop where it can be bought and prints the testimony of satisfied customers.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying the treatment of disease in eighteenth-century Britain?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: the sweeping list of cures shows how little a paying customer could tell a real remedy from a useless one.
• Content: the printed testimony shows quackery using the new market in cheap newsprint to manufacture trust.
• Provenance: an advertisement written to sell, so it is worthless as evidence that the powder worked and excellent as evidence of how medicine was marketed.
• Contextual knowledge: there was no state regulation of medicine until the 19th century, while Sydenham’s clinical observation and the voluntary hospitals were changing elite practice.
• Limitations: it shows the commercial end of medicine, mostly in London, and nothing of hospital or rural care.
• Judgement: useful for quackery and for the communication factor, not for the effectiveness of 18th-century treatment.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the measures taken against the Great Plague of 1665.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Houses with infected residents were boarded up under guard for forty days, the door painted with a red cross and the words ‘Lord have mercy upon us’.
• The Lord Mayor ordered the killing of stray dogs and cats, blamed for spreading miasma; the order probably worsened the rat problem.
• Bonfires were lit in the streets and refuse was cleared, on the assumption that the disease was spread by foul air.
• Mass plague pits were dug at Aldgate, Finsbury and elsewhere when ordinary parish churchyards filled with bodies.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write a narrative account analysing how the Great Plague developed in London between April 1665 and February 1666.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• April–June 1665: outbreak reported in St Giles-in-the-Fields; weekly deaths begin to climb in the western suburbs and reach the City.
• July 1665: Charles II and his court leave for Salisbury, moving on to Oxford in September; wealthy Londoners flee to country estates while parish authorities order houses shut up and dogs and cats killed.
• August–September 1665: peak of the epidemic with over 7,000 weekly deaths recorded in the Bills of Mortality; mass plague pits dug at Aldgate and Finsbury.
• October 1665–February 1666: cold weather kills the fleas; deaths fall through the autumn; the king returns to Whitehall in February 1666 with around 100,000 Londoners dead.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Great Plague of 1665 for London society and government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It killed around 100,000 Londoners — perhaps a fifth or a quarter of the city — producing a labour shortage and disrupted trade for months.
• It exposed the social geography of the city: the rich fled to country estates while the poor were trapped in their parishes; this fed long-running resentment of court flight.
