• It strained parish administration to breaking point: searchers of the dead, parish clerks and constables were overwhelmed and the Bills of Mortality probably understated the toll.
• It softened later attitudes to Dissenters in London, because ejected ministers had returned to fill the gap left by fleeing Anglican clergy and preached plague sermons against the Five Mile Act.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how contemporary ideas about disease shaped the official response to the Plague.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, miasma theory shaped most measures: bonfires, refuse clearance and the closure of theatres and crowded gatherings all aimed at ‘cleansing’ the air.
• Belief in divine punishment fuelled days of fasting and prayer proclaimed by Charles II, and a wave of plague sermons in surviving pulpits.
• Significance over time: the absence of germ theory meant rats and fleas, the actual carriers, went untouched; this would only change with the work of Robert Koch and others over two centuries later.
• It also legitimised harsh measures such as shutting up of infected houses and killing of dogs and cats, which probably worsened conditions but seemed reasonable inside the framework of contemporary medicine.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Bills of Mortality as a record of the Plague.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were weekly printed lists of deaths in each London parish, broken down by reported cause; they had been printed since 1603.
• They depended on parish ‘searchers of the dead’ — usually older women from the poorhouse — who inspected bodies and judged cause of death for a few pence each.
• They probably underestimated plague deaths, because families paid searchers to record other causes to avoid the shutting-up order.
• They missed Dissenters and Jews who were buried outside the parish system, further reducing their reliability as a total death toll.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The worst thing about the Great Plague was not the number of dead but what it did to trust between London and its rulers.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the consequences of the Great Plague of 1665? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The flight of the court to Oxford and the rich to the country left the poor to face the plague alone, fuelling lasting resentment of royal absence and the visible inequality of the response.
• The shutting-up order, killing of dogs and cats, and digging of plague pits showed government acting hard but ineffectively; faith in central direction of public health was shaken.
• Dissenter ministers preaching in vacated pulpits softened London opinion towards Nonconformity and contributed to the political division between an Anglican country and a religiously plural capital.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The demographic shock was vast: around 100,000 deaths was the worst single mortality event of the century in London and reshaped the city’s labour market.
• The Plague accelerated the move of trades and population westwards and influenced the reconstruction priorities applied after the Fire of 1666.
• Some contemporaries gave the king credit for personal courage in returning to Whitehall in February 1666, and royal authority emerged largely intact.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Prohibition in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Prohibition was introduced by the 18th Amendment in January 1920 and enforced by the Volstead Act, banning the manufacture, sale and transport of alcohol.
• Illegal bars known as speakeasies opened across the country — New York alone had over 30,000 by 1929, more than its legal saloons before Prohibition.
• Bootlegging stretched from rum-runners off the coast to backyard stills inland; only around 1,500 federal agents were employed to police the entire country.
• Organised crime gangs, most famously Al Capone’s in Chicago, controlled the supply of illegal alcohol and used violence and bribery to protect their operations.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did Prohibition fail to achieve its aims?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Speakeasies multiplied rather than disappeared — New York had more illegal bars in the late 1920s than it had had legal saloons in 1919.
• Bootlegging and home-distilling were widespread; rum-runners brought alcohol from Canada and the Caribbean, while moonshine stills supplied rural areas.
• Organised crime grew rich and powerful: Al Capone’s Chicago operation took an estimated $60 million a year in 1927 from bootleg alcohol, gambling and protection rackets.
• Public officials were corrupted on a massive scale; police, prosecutors and politicians took bribes from gangs in many cities.
• Violence rose — gang wars over distribution culminated in the 1929 St Valentine’s Day Massacre.
• Federal Prohibition agents (around 1,500 nationally) were too few to police a country whose drinkers no longer accepted the law — even Hoover’s 1929 inquiry, the Wickersham Commission, would later admit Prohibition was unenforceable.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects showing how Prohibition produced the opposite of its aims, with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies a failure without explaining its cause.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Ku Klux Klan in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Klan was relaunched in Georgia in 1915 and grew rapidly across the South and Midwest, reaching perhaps 4–5 million members by 1925.
• It targeted African-Americans, Catholics, Jews and recent immigrants, defining itself by the WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) ideal.
• It dominated state politics in Indiana, Oregon and Colorado in the early 1920s, electing governors and members of Congress.
• Its activities included hooded marches, cross-burnings and lynchings, often unpunished by local courts and police.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did immigration policy change in the USA in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Before the First World War the USA had welcomed mass immigration — around 13 million Europeans arrived between 1900 and 1914.
• The 1921 Emergency Quota Act capped immigration at around 357,000 a year and tied national quotas to 3% of the foreign-born of each nationality in the 1910 census.
• The 1924 Immigration Act cut the overall total to 165,000 and pegged quotas to the 1890 census — before most southern and eastern Europeans had arrived — almost eliminating Italian, Polish and Russian arrivals.
• Asian immigration was banned outright by the 1924 Act, building on earlier exclusionary laws.
• The pattern of arrivals shifted decisively away from southern and eastern Europe and from Asia, in line with WASP campaigners’ preferences.
• The 1924 Act became the basis of US immigration policy for the next 41 years, until the Hart–Celler Act of 1965.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation tracing the legal change and its effects on the pattern of immigration with precise dates.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description of one Act.
Emerging: Names the Acts without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on dividing American society in the 1920s: Prohibition, or immigration restriction? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of Prohibition:
• It tried to remake everyday life for the entire country, dividing rural Protestant supporters from urban Catholic and immigrant opponents.
• It produced organised crime on a national scale, with Al Capone’s Chicago empire and the St Valentine’s Day Massacre.
• It corrupted police, courts and politicians, undermining trust in government.
• It lasted 13 years and was constantly contested in Congress.

In support of immigration restriction:
• The 1921 and 1924 Acts almost eliminated southern and eastern European arrivals and banned Asian immigration outright.
• The 1924 Act remained the basis of US immigration policy for 41 years, far longer than Prohibition.
• It was an explicit racial selection of who counted as American, with effects on community formation in cities for decades.
• It legalised the racial nationalism the Klan had been campaigning for, demonstrating how the cultural backlash captured federal policy.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that Prohibition was more visible at the time but immigration restriction had the deeper, longer-lasting effect on American society. The strongest answers also note that the two were connected — both had support from the same WASP rural-Protestant base.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparison with precise detail and a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the Sacco and Vanzetti case expose the divisions in 1920s America?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The case combined three of the decade’s defining tensions in a single trial: fear of communism (Red Scare), prejudice against Italian-Americans, and the move towards immigration restriction.
• The 1921 conviction rested on thin and contradictory evidence; the trial judge, Webster Thayer, openly described the defendants as ‘anarchist bastards’, suggesting bias rather than impartiality.
• Their six years of appeals and 1927 execution provoked international protests — rallies in Paris, London and Berlin showed how an American local trial had become a global symbol.
• Civil-liberties campaigners (including the new ACLU, founded 1920) used the case to argue that the Red Scare had eroded due process — an argument that long outlasted the trial.
• In 1977, fifty years after their execution, Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis issued a posthumous proclamation acknowledging the unfair trial.
• The case is named in the AQA spec because it concentrates the divisions of 1920s America in one event — a useful reference for any 8-mark or 12-mark question on the period.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance covering links to multiple 1920s themes and importance over time.
Secure: Clear explanation of why the case mattered.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to retelling the story.
Emerging: Describes the trial without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• On Black Thursday, 24 October 1929, nearly 13 million shares were sold on the New York Stock Exchange as prices began to collapse.
• On Black Tuesday, 29 October 1929, over 16 million shares were dumped and the market lost around $14 billion of value in a single day.
• Speculators who had bought on the margin were ruined — brokers’ loans (Lesson 2) had to be repaid in full even though the shares used as collateral were now worthless.
• A bankers’ consortium led by Richard Whitney briefly steadied the market on Black Thursday but could not prevent the collapse the following week.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the Wall Street Crash trigger the wider Great Depression?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Speculators who had bought on the margin were ruined; their broker loans, which had to be repaid in full, then collapsed banks that had lent the money.
• Banks had also invested customers’ deposits in the same shares; when prices fell, around 9,000 US banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out the savings of around nine million depositors who had never bought shares.
• Falling consumer demand turned the existing 1920s problem of over-production into mass lay-offs — industrial production fell by nearly half between 1929 and 1932.
• Unemployment rose from 1.6 million (3%) in 1929 to 12–13 million (25%) by 1932; without federal unemployment benefit, families relied on charity, soup kitchens and bread lines.
• Bank failures pulled small businesses down: around 25,000 American businesses collapsed in 1932 alone.
• The 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff (Lesson 7) added an external layer by triggering retaliation that strangled international trade and deepened the slump.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from financial panic through bank failures and unemployment to political collapse, with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation of effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description of the Crash itself.
Emerging: Identifies the Crash as a cause without explaining how it spread.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Dust Bowl in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Dust Bowl was a drought-stricken region of the southern Great Plains — Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas and Colorado — hit by enormous dust storms in the 1930s.
• Decades of intensive ploughing had stripped the topsoil’s natural cover; when drought arrived from 1931, the soil dried out and was carried away by wind.
• ‘Black Sunday’, 14 April 1935, saw a massive dust storm darken the sky from Texas to Chicago — one of around fourteen major storms that year.
• Around 2.5 million people fled the southern Plains, many heading to California, where they were derisively called ‘Okies’ whatever their home state.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the Great Depression affect ordinary Americans by 1932?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Unemployment reached 25% nationally and 80% in some industrial cities like Toledo; without federal unemployment benefit, families queued at soup kitchens and church bread lines.
• Evicted families built shanty towns of cardboard and packing crates — the ‘Hoovervilles’ named in bitter mockery of the president; the largest, in St Louis, housed thousands.
• Around 9,000 banks failed, wiping out the savings of nine million depositors who had no deposit insurance.
• Around 25,000 businesses collapsed in 1932 alone; suit-wearing former managers selling apples on street corners became a Depression image.
• In the southern Plains, the Dust Bowl forced 2.5 million people from their farms.
• In summer 1932 the Bonus Army of 17,000 First World War veterans was driven out of Washington by federal troops with bayonets and tear gas, after demanding early payment of a service bonus.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation across multiple groups with precise figures and named events.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one group.
Emerging: Identifies hardship without explaining its scale.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact in deepening the Great Depression: the failure of around 9,000 American banks, or the collapse of farm prices and the Dust Bowl? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of bank failures:
• Around 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out the savings of around nine million depositors, since deposit insurance did not yet exist.
• Bank failures destroyed credit for small businesses; around 25,000 collapsed in 1932 alone.
• Without functioning banks, mortgages and farm loans could not be rolled over — foreclosures rose sharply.
• The political crisis of bank panics by early 1933 forced Roosevelt’s ‘bank holiday’ in his first week (Lesson 7+).

In support of farm prices and the Dust Bowl:
• Crop prices had been falling since 1921 (Lesson 2); the Crash and 1930s drought halved them again, locking sharecroppers in debt.
• 2.5 million Americans fled the Plains as Black Sunday and similar storms made farming impossible.
• Migration to California overwhelmed local labour markets, suppressing wages and creating long-term communities of displaced families.
• The Dust Bowl made the Depression visible, reshaping American political appetite for federal intervention through the New Deal.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that bank failures had the wider economic impact (because they froze credit nationwide and wiped out savings) but the Dust Bowl had the deeper cultural and political impact (because it symbolised the collapse of American life and motivated specific New Deal programmes). The strongest answers note that both factors fed each other — bank failures foreclosed Plains farms; Plains foreclosures destroyed local banks.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of unemployment and homelessness on American society between 1929 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Unemployment rose from 1.6 million (3%) in 1929 to 12–13 million (25%) by 1932 — with peaks of 80% in some industrial cities.
• Without federal benefit, families relied on local charity, churches and soup kitchens; the Salvation Army ran bread lines in every major city.
• Hoovervilles — shanty towns of cardboard and packing crates — appeared in city parks and on waste ground; the largest in St Louis housed thousands.
• ‘Hoover blankets’ (newspapers) and ‘Hoover flags’ (empty pockets turned inside out) entered everyday speech, blaming the president for the slump.
• Confidence in the federal government collapsed: the 1932 Bonus Army episode showed unemployed war veterans being driven from Washington by their own army.
• The political effect was decisive: by November 1932 voters were ready for a fundamentally different presidency, opening the way for Roosevelt’s landslide (Lesson 7).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from individual hardship to political collapse with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies hardship without explaining its political effects.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a public speech by Aristide Briand, French Foreign Minister, at the Locarno signing ceremony, October 1925.
‘What we sign today is not merely a treaty of paper. It is a recognition that Germany and France, after fifty years of mutual fear, are partners in the rebuilding of Europe. Our western borders are now beyond dispute. Our quarrels will be resolved by arbitration, not by arms.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons why Briand presented the Locarno treaties as a turning point.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One point clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Germany and France are now ‘partners’ rather than rivals (after ‘fifty years of mutual fear’).
• The western borders are accepted as final (‘beyond dispute’).
• Disputes will be resolved by arbitration rather than war.
• It positions the treaty as a foundational shift after long Franco-German hostility.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Locarno treaties of 1925 led to Germany’s admission to the League of Nations in 1926.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 1923: Germany’s hyperinflation crisis; Stresemann becomes Chancellor and stabilises the currency.
• 1924: the Dawes Plan restructures reparations and brings American loans, calming Franco-German tensions.
• Early 1925: Stresemann and Briand begin negotiations on a security pact.
• October 1925: the Locarno treaties are signed; Germany voluntarily accepts its western borders.
• 1925-26: Austen Chamberlain won the Nobel Peace Prize for 1925; Stresemann and Briand won it for 1926.
• September 1926: Germany joins the League of Nations as a permanent Council member — rehabilitation complete and made possible by the goodwill generated by Locarno.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter by Gustav Stresemann to the German ambassador to London, December 1925.
‘Locarno gives us what bayonets could not: respectability and time. We have accepted the western frontiers because we cannot change them. We have left the eastern frontiers open because there our work is not finished. The Allies have what they want; we are positioned to work patiently for what we want.’

Source C: An extract from a 1925 article by Czechoslovak President Tomáš Masaryk in a Prague newspaper.
‘Germany has guaranteed her borders with France and Belgium. She has not guaranteed her borders with us, and we are told to be content with arbitration treaties. The peace settlements drew our frontiers; the Locarno spirit now hints they may yet be redrawn. The smaller states of Europe must remain on watch.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the 1925 Locarno treaties. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a candid private German calculation that Locarno is tactical, accepting the unchangeable in exchange for respectability and time. Provenance: a private letter from Stresemann to a senior diplomat; likely to express genuine policy thinking. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — Stresemann did not guarantee eastern frontiers and openly aimed to revise Versailles peacefully.
Source C — Content: a Czechoslovak warning that Locarno protects only the west and leaves successor states exposed. Provenance: a public article by the Czechoslovak president; aimed at domestic and international audiences; reflects the small-state view. Own knowledge: confirms Locarno’s asymmetry — arbitration treaties only with Poland and Czechoslovakia; the Sudetenland would later become Hitler’s lever.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German strategic thinking; C is highly useful for the small-state perspective; together they show the gap between the public ‘Locarno spirit’ and the underlying realities.

practice_questions.text:
‘Diplomacy outside the League made the inter-war world genuinely more peaceful.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Sixty-two states eventually renounced war as an instrument of national policy under the Kellogg-Briand Pact.
• Locarno brought Germany back into European diplomacy and led directly to its League entry in 1926.
• Reparations were eased by the Dawes Plan (1924) and the Young Plan (1929).
• The ‘Locarno spirit’ produced a genuine fall in tension for several years.
Challenging the statement:
• Kellogg-Briand had no enforcement mechanism — no penalties, no court, no army — and its signatories went on rearming.
• Locarno left the eastern frontiers open, and Stresemann treated it as a tactical move.
• The agreements depended on three foreign ministers; the structure collapsed once Stresemann died in 1929 and the Depression began.
Judgement: between roughly 1924 and 1929 the gains were real, but the structural flaws meant they evaporated as soon as conditions changed.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter by Sir Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, to his sister Hilda, just after the Locarno signing in October 1925.
‘There were tears at the table. Briand was visibly moved. Stresemann spoke as a man who had finally been given a chair at the table. I confess I felt that we had done a piece of work that may, with luck, end the wars of this century.’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about the diplomacy that produced the Locarno treaties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• A vivid eyewitness account of the emotional atmosphere at the Locarno signing.
• Stresemann is described as a man finally given a chair at the table, which captures Germany’s return to the great-power club.
• Own knowledge: Locarno was widely celebrated; Austen Chamberlain won the Nobel Peace Prize for 1925 and Stresemann and Briand won it for 1926.
• Worth noting: the optimism (‘end the wars of this century’) was not borne out, and a private letter captures spirit rather than calculation.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the negotiation and signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact between 1927 and 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• April 1927: Aristide Briand proposed a Franco-American treaty to outlaw war between the two countries, partly as insurance against German recovery.
• Late 1927: Frank B. Kellogg, US Secretary of State, suggested expanding the proposal to include all states, transforming a bilateral idea into a multilateral pact.
• Early 1928: negotiations widened, with European and American legal experts drafting the text.
• 27 August 1928: the pact was signed in Paris by 15 countries, including the USA, France, Britain, Germany, Italy and Japan.
• 1929 onwards: ratifications brought the total to 62 countries.
• The pact had no enforcement mechanism but provided a moral framework that would underpin the prosecution of aggressive war at the post-1945 Nuremberg trials.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following interpretation and use it to answer the question that follows.

Interpretation: An extract from a popular history of the West, 1955.
“The defeat of the Plains Indians was tragic but inevitable. From the moment the railroad and the rifle reached the Plains, the buffalo nations had no chance against the United States Army.”

How convincing is this interpretation about conflict on the Plains in the 1860s? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation that weighs convincing and unconvincing elements, anchored in named events of the 1860s; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation drawing on context with developed convincing/unconvincing points and a judgement.
Developing: Some evaluation but reliance on retelling the interpretation; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without using context.

Indicative content:
Convincing:
• Material differences were real: 25,000 US soldiers west of the Mississippi by 1869; railroads sped troop movement; modern rifles outranged bows.
• Sand Creek (1864) and the eventual reservation system show the long arc of US power.
Unconvincing:
• ‘Inevitable’ ignores Red Cloud’s War (1866–68): the Lakota fought the United States to a standstill and forced abandonment of the Bozeman Trail forts.
• Plains nations were not monolithic: the Crow scouted FOR the army, the Lakota fought it — outcomes depended on alliances.
• Specific US choices (Senate cuts to the annuity, the Bozeman Trail, Chivington’s decision at Sand Creek) created the conflict, not abstract inevitability.
Judgement: the interpretation captures the long-term direction but underplays Native agency and the role of specific decisions in the 1860s.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Sand Creek Massacre on relations between the United States and the Plains nations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (29 November 1864, Black Kettle, Chivington, ~150 dead, Congressional inquiry, frontier press).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about Sand Creek.

Indicative content:
• Collapse of trust: Black Kettle had been promised safety; the massacre proved that peaceful camps could be attacked, which discouraged future negotiation by the Cheyenne and Arapaho.
• Wider war: Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors retaliated against settlers and stagecoaches across the central Plains in early 1865, expanding the conflict.
• Eastern reaction: a Congressional inquiry condemned the massacre, splitting public opinion between East and West and weakening political support for hard-line Indian policy.
• Political consequence: Chivington escaped court martial because his commission had expired, but the massacre destroyed the political career of Colorado’s territorial governor and set a benchmark for atrocity that frontier officers would be judged against.

practice_questions.text:
Has Sand Creek (1864) had a greater impact on conflict on the Plains than Fetterman’s Trap (1866)?

• Sand Creek
• Fetterman’s Trap

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the two events against each other (and other factors); precise factual support across both bullets and additional material; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached.
Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative.

Indicative content:
• Sand Creek: 29 November 1864, Black Kettle, Chivington, ~150 dead, Congressional inquiry, collapse of Cheyenne trust, retaliation across the central Plains.
• Fetterman’s Trap: 21 December 1866, 81 US soldiers killed, Red Cloud’s War, abandonment of Bozeman Trail forts, second Fort Laramie Treaty 1868.
• Other factors: the 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty, the 1862 Dakota War, settler pressure from Pike’s Peak 1859, broken annuity payments.
• Judgement: top answers might argue Sand Creek had wider moral impact (East–West split) while Fetterman had direct strategic impact (forcing US retreat); or argue the events together produced the broken-trust environment that defined the rest of the period.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of Sand Creek.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a Denver newspaper editorial, December 1864.
“Colonel Chivington has won a great victory over the savages of the Plains. Colorado is safer tonight because of the courage of his men.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from the 1865 Congressional inquiry report.
“Colonel Chivington surprised and murdered, in cold blood, the unsuspecting men, women and children on Sand Creek, who had every reason to believe they were under the protection of the United States authorities.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, supported differences.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support.
Developing: One difference; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 calls the event a victory; Interpretation 2 calls it murder.
• Interpretation 1 praises Chivington’s men as courageous; Interpretation 2 frames the Cheyenne as unsuspecting victims under US protection.
• Interpretation 1 is celebratory; Interpretation 2 is condemnatory.
• Interpretation 1 frames Cheyenne as ‘savages’; Interpretation 2 frames them as a people with rights.

practice_questions.text:
Why might the two interpretations of Sand Creek above give different views?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise context.
Secure: Reason rooted in provenance or context with brief support.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’.
Emerging: Restates content of each interpretation.

Indicative content:
• Audience: a Denver newspaper wrote for white settlers fearful of Cheyenne raids; the Congressional inquiry wrote for federal lawmakers and a national audience.
• Purpose: the editorial wanted to celebrate a local hero and justify violence; the inquiry wanted to investigate misconduct and assign accountability.
• Time of writing: both were close in time but the inquiry had access to military testimony and survivor accounts the editorial did not.
• Provenance: a frontier paper reflecting settler interests versus a federal report reflecting eastern political pressure.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features.
Secure: Two valid features.
Developing: One developed; one undeveloped.
Emerging: Generalised description.

Indicative content:
• Defined territories: each major Plains nation (Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow, Shoshone) was assigned a recognised territory.
• Annuity payment: the United States promised $50,000 a year in goods (later cut by the Senate to ten years).
• Safe passage: Plains nations agreed to allow wagon trains to use the Oregon and California Trails without interference.
• Scale: around 10,000 people from many nations gathered at Horse Creek for the negotiations — the largest peace meeting yet held on the Plains.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Great Fire spread through London between 2 and 6 September 1666.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It began in the early hours of Sunday 2 September 1666 at Thomas Farriner’s bakery in Pudding Lane, near London Bridge.
• It burned for four days, fanned by an easterly wind and timber-framed houses, and destroyed about four-fifths of the walled City.
• Charles II and his brother James, Duke of York personally commanded firefighting and authorised the use of gunpowder to blow up houses and create firebreaks.
• It destroyed 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches, old St Paul’s Cathedral, the Royal Exchange, the Guildhall and the Custom House.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how London was rebuilt in the years after the Great Fire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It made around 70,000 of the City’s 80,000 inhabitants homeless, who camped at Moorfields, Tower Hill and Lincoln’s Inn Fields, requiring royal poor relief.
• It produced the Rebuilding Acts of 1667 and 1670, requiring all new houses to be built in brick or stone, with wider streets and standardised storey heights.
• It accelerated the westward expansion of fashionable London to Covent Garden, St James’s and the developing West End.
• It funded a generation of new churches: Sir Christopher Wren designed 51 City churches and the new St Paul’s Cathedral (1675–1710), paid for largely by a tax on coal entering the port.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the rumour that Catholics had started the Great Fire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Second Dutch War was in progress and Catholic France had joined the Dutch side, making foreign arson plausible to many Londoners.
• It produced the false confession and execution of Robert Hubert at Tyburn in October 1666, even though the Privy Council privately doubted his guilt.
• The Monument to the Fire (completed 1677) was given an inscription in 1681 blaming ‘the Popish faction’, fixing the rumour in stone.
• Significance over time: the rumour fed the Popish Plot panic of 1678 by reinforcing a national vocabulary of Catholic conspiracy, and the inscription was only re-cut after 1689.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Rebuilding Acts of 1667 and 1670.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They required all new houses in the City to be built in brick or stone rather than timber, ending the use of jettied timber-frame construction.
• They standardised four classes of dwelling by storey height and street type, regulating the appearance of the rebuilt City.
• They imposed wider streets and added pavements to ease traffic and reduce fire spread.
• They funded public buildings and the rebuilding of churches through a new tax on coal entering the port of London.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Sir Christopher Wren’s rebuilding programme for the City of London.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Wren designed 51 of the 87 lost City churches between 1670 and 1700, giving the rebuilt City a unique horizon of white-stone steeples.
• The new St Paul’s Cathedral (1675–1710), with its great dome over Ludgate Hill, became the visible symbol of Restoration London and one of the most admired buildings in Europe.
• Funded largely by the coal tax, the rebuilt churches gave Anglican worship the architectural confidence the Cavalier Parliament had legislated for.
• Wren’s rejection of the grand street plan but acceptance of the new building rules meant London kept its medieval street pattern but acquired a modern, fireproof fabric.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘In the long run the Great Fire did London more good than harm.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the effects of the Great Fire of 1666? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Reconstruction made the City fireproof: brick and stone replaced timber, and London never again suffered a fire on this scale.
• London’s last great plague was 1665 and nothing on that scale returned, though historians still argue about how much the rebuilding had to do with it.
• Wren’s 51 churches and St Paul’s Cathedral gave London a new architectural identity that became one of the most admired skylines in Europe.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Around 70,000 people were made homeless overnight; thousands lost everything they owned and many were never compensated.
• The City paid for reconstruction through the coal tax for forty years, putting financial weight on every Londoner.
• The Catholic arson rumour fed the Popish Plot panic of 1678 and contributed to the persecution of innocent Catholics over the next two decades.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which inoculation and vaccination were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: inoculation used material from a smallpox sore (variolation), risking a serious dose and able to spread the disease; vaccination used cowpox material, with much lower risk and no transmission of smallpox.
• Difference: inoculation was expensive (around £5 per child) and available only to the wealthy; vaccination was cheaper to produce, and after 1853 it was made compulsory for infants regardless of income.
• Similarity: both were preventive measures that aimed to give protection against smallpox by exposure to a mild form of disease.
• Similarity: both faced opposition from clergy and from those who feared introducing disease material into healthy bodies.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Edward Jenner for the prevention of disease in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: his 1796 experiment on James Phipps and 1798 Inquiry produced a safe alternative to inoculation, saving thousands of lives.
• At the time: triggered the first serious British government investment in public health (Parliamentary grants of £10,000 in 1802 and £20,000 in 1807).
• Over time: provided the template for Pasteur’s 1880s vaccines, which extended the principle to other diseases.
• Over time: vaccination programmes against polio, measles, rubella and many other diseases trace directly back to his work; smallpox was eradicated worldwide in 1980.
• Limitation worth noting: Jenner could not explain why vaccination worked, which delayed full acceptance until germ theory caught up.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with explicit recognition of the empirical-without-theory point.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: James Gillray’s cartoon ‘The Cow-Pock — or — the Wonderful Effects of the New Inoculation!’, published in London in 1802. It shows a crowded vaccination clinic where patients sprout small cows from their arms, faces and bodies.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying opposition to vaccination in Britain?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: the cows bursting from patients capture the fear that putting animal matter into a human body was unnatural.
• Content: the crowded room also shows that vaccination was already being done on a large scale by 1802.
• Provenance: a commercial satirical print made for a paying London public, so it exaggerates for effect but must have matched fears people already held.
• Contextual knowledge: opposition also came from inoculators losing their trade and from clergy calling it ‘beast matter’; Parliament nevertheless granted Jenner £10,000 in 1802.
• Limitations: satire is not evidence of how many people refused, and it says nothing about the poor outside London or about those who accepted vaccination.
• Judgement: very useful for the shape of the fear, much weaker as evidence of how widespread opposition was.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Has government been the main factor in the spread of vaccination in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh government against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of government:
• Parliamentary grants of £10,000 (1802) and £20,000 (1807) gave Jenner’s work official endorsement and resources.
• 1853 Vaccination Act made vaccination compulsory for infants; 1871 Act tightened enforcement.
• By the 1820s Britain ran the largest vaccination programme in the world — impossible without state organisation.
• Compare with later periods: government becomes ever more central in 1848/1875 Public Health Acts, 1911 National Insurance, 1948 NHS.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Without Jenner there is no vaccination — his curiosity, training under Hunter and willingness to experiment produced the breakthrough.
• Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had earlier brought inoculation to Britain through individual initiative.

Weighed against chance:
• The cowpox-smallpox link was Gloucestershire folk knowledge spotted by chance — without that observation, vaccination as we know it does not happen.

Weighed against religion:
• Religion appears here mainly as a brake (clergy opposition, ‘beast matter’ rhetoric) rather than a driver, but its weight in delaying acceptance is part of the story.

Judgement: Individuals discovered vaccination but only government action made it universal. The strongest answers note that the relative weight of factors changes across the period — in 1796 the individual is dominant, by 1853 government has overtaken — and that this trajectory continues across the whole sweep towards the 1948 NHS.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes government action only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1853 Vaccination Act for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: it made smallpox vaccination compulsory for infants — the first time the state ordered a medical treatment for everybody.
• At the time: compulsion provoked resistance and an organised anti-vaccination movement, strongest later in Leicester.
• At the time: smallpox deaths fell steeply across the rest of the century.
• Over time: the 1871 Act added vaccination officers to enforce it and the 1898 Act added a conscience clause — the first legal right to refuse.
• Over time: it set the pattern of state-run mass prevention that led to modern childhood vaccination and to eradication in 1980.
• Limitation: the Act spread a treatment that already worked; the discovery was Jenner’s, not the government’s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of inoculation (variolation) for medicine in 18th-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: provided the first effective preventive measure against smallpox in Britain after Lady Mary Wortley Montagu introduced it around 1721.
• At the time: showed that disease could be deliberately controlled rather than just endured — a major shift in how prevention was conceived.
• Over time: provided the model Jenner improved on with vaccination in 1796.
• Over time: although replaced by vaccination, the principle of deliberately exposing patients to a mild form of disease remained foundational for Pasteur’s 1880s vaccines.
• Limitation: it was risky (1 in 50 died), expensive and class-restricted, which is why a safer alternative was so urgently needed.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Richard Pipes (The Russian Revolution, 1990), arguing that the Provisional Government was destroyed mainly by Lenin’s ruthless determination to seize power. Interpretation B is from the American revisionist historian Sheila Fitzpatrick (The Russian Revolution, 4th edn 2017), arguing that the Provisional Government destroyed itself by failing to end the war or distribute land.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Pipes blames Lenin and the Bolsheviks; Fitzpatrick blames the Provisional Government’s own choices.
• Pipes presents the collapse as the work of a small fanatical party; Fitzpatrick presents it as the result of mass disillusionment.
• Pipes treats October as a hostile takeover; Fitzpatrick treats it as the end-stage of a wider process.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences with grounding in both.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of the Provisional Government’s collapse differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different traditions: Pipes draws on the totalitarian school; Fitzpatrick is a leading revisionist.
• Different evidence: Pipes uses Lenin’s writings and Bolshevik party records; Fitzpatrick uses social history of workers and peasants.
• Different purposes: Pipes is producing a moral indictment of Bolshevism; Fitzpatrick is producing a structural analysis aimed at undergraduates.
• Different time of writing: Pipes wrote at the end of the Cold War; Fitzpatrick has updated her account through several editions.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Order Number 1 destroyed the discipline of the Russian army and made any further continuation of the war impossible.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Order Number 1 (March 1917) gave soldiers’ committees control of weapons and made obedience to officers conditional.
• The June Offensive collapsed within ten days; whole units refused to attack.
• Mass desertion accelerated through the summer as soldiers heard that peasants were seizing land.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Discipline had already begun to break before Order Number 1, especially after the February mutinies in Petrograd.
• The Provisional Government’s own decision to continue the war, made independently of the Order, was equally responsible.
• Some units, especially Cossack and shock formations, retained discipline through the summer; total collapse came only after Kornilov.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation with relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Kornilov Affair of August 1917 on Russian politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Kerensky armed Bolshevik Red Guards from Soviet arsenals to defend Petrograd, equipping the very party that would overthrow him in October.
• The Bolsheviks emerged with prestige as the only force that had genuinely stood up to counter-revolution.
• By September they had majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets for the first time.
• Kerensky’s public denunciation of Kornilov alienated conservative officers, leaving him with no military reserve when the Bolsheviks acted in October.
• The Affair exposed Dual Power as unworkable — the Provisional Government had to call on its rival to save it.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking Kornilov’s march to October 1917.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General comments about Kornilov.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The Provisional Government failed because it continued the First World War.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the consequences of continuing the war
• consider other reasons for failure (such as land, Dual Power, the Kornilov Affair)
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for continuing the war being the most important factor:
• The June Offensive collapsed and accelerated mass desertion.
• Milyukov’s April note exposed the government’s commitment to Tsarist war aims, alienating the left.
• Soldiers’ refusal to fight underlay every other crisis — without their loyalty the government had no coercive power.

Arguments for other factors:
• Postponing land reform meant peasants seized land without authority and soldiers deserted to claim their share.
• Dual Power meant the government could not actually rule even when it wanted to.
• The Kornilov Affair handed the Bolsheviks the political opening they exploited in October.

Judgement should weigh the war against the structural and political failures.

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing all factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Dual Power on the authority of the Provisional Government between March and October 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The Provisional Government could pass laws, but the Petrograd Soviet controlled the loyalty of the workers and soldiers.
• Order Number 1 from the Soviet, not the government, set the rules of military discipline.
• On the issues that mattered most (war, land), the government had to negotiate with the Soviet rather than command.
• Coalition with socialists from May 1917 blurred the distinction without solving it.
• When the Kornilov Affair came, the government had to ask the Soviet for help, exposing Dual Power as unworkable.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking constitutional weakness to political collapse.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General comments about the Soviet.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1928 SPD pamphlet praising the Stresemann era as a genuine recovery and democratic success) and Interpretation B (a 1989 academic study by Detlev Peukert arguing Weimar in 1924–29 was ‘dancing on a volcano’) on the Stresemann era. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Stresemann era as a real success — stable currency, falling unemployment, diplomatic recognition through Locarno and League membership.
• Interpretation B presents it as fragile — rural depression, dependence on US loans, persistent political instability under an ageing right-wing President.
• Main difference: A emphasises measurable gains; B emphasises hidden structural weaknesses.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1928 SPD pamphlet on the Stresemann era) and Interpretation B (a 1989 academic study by Peukert) give different views about the ‘Golden Years’.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the 1928 SPD pamphlet aimed to win the next election by promoting the SPD's role in stabilising the Republic; Peukert's 1989 study aimed at scholarly analysis of long-term outcomes.
• They use different evidence — the SPD pamphlet emphasised industrial output and Locarno; Peukert integrates rural debt, US loan dependence and the rise of the Nazis after 1929.
• They were produced at different times — the 1928 source had no knowledge of the Wall Street Crash; Peukert benefits from sixty years of hindsight.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Stresemann's foreign policy of voluntary cooperation with the Allies was the most important achievement of the Weimar Republic, paving the way for German reintegration into Europe.' How convincing is Interpretation A about Stresemann's foreign policy?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because Locarno (October 1925) saw Germany voluntarily accept its western borders, easing French fears and earning international goodwill.
• Convincing because the League of Nations admitted Germany as a permanent Council member in 1926, restoring great-power status only seven years after Versailles.
• Less convincing because Locarno deliberately left the eastern borders open to revision, hinting that Stresemann's diplomacy was tactical rather than purely cooperative.
• Less convincing because the right rejected reintegration outright — the 1929 referendum against the Young Plan gave Hitler national exposure and previewed the Nazi threat.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing for Western diplomacy, but the eastern question and right-wing backlash limit the achievement.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of the recovery of the Weimar Republic between 1924 and 1929.
You may consider:
• economic developments including the new currency and the Dawes Plan
• diplomatic developments and Weimar culture.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Currency reform: the Rentenmark of November 1923 ended hyperinflation; the permanent Reichsmark followed in August 1924. • Dawes Plan (1924): restructured reparations; provided 800 million gold marks in US loans; roughly 25 billion marks of US capital flowed into Germany over five years; industrial output passed 1913 levels by 1928. • Diplomatic recovery: Locarno (1925) accepted western borders; League membership (1926); Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928); Young Plan (1929) reduced and stretched reparations. • Weimar culture: Bauhaus, Bertolt Brecht's plays, Berlin cabaret, Fritz Lang's Metropolis; but conservative backlash also growing. • Limits of recovery: unemployment never below 1.3 million; rural depression from 1927; six Chancellors between 1923 and 1929; Hindenburg replaced Ebert in 1925. • Conclusion: recovery was real but partial — economic and diplomatic gains rested on US loans and a fragile coalition; when Wall Street collapsed in October 1929 the foundations gave way. [Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1929 right-wing nationalist pamphlet attacking the Young Plan as a betrayal of Germany) and Interpretation B (a 1929 SPD newspaper editorial defending the Young Plan as a major reduction of reparations) on the Young Plan. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A condemns the Young Plan as betrayal — it accepted that reparations existed, locked Germany into payments until 1988 and confirmed the war-guilt clause.
• Interpretation B defends the Young Plan as success — it cut total reparations from 132 to 112 billion gold marks and gave Germany a clear path out of debt.
• Main difference: A frames the plan as moral defeat; B frames it as a pragmatic reduction.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The cultural energy of Weimar Germany — Bauhaus, Brecht, Berlin cabaret — was disconnected from the rest of the country, and its very brilliance fuelled conservative backlash.' How convincing is Interpretation A about Weimar culture?
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Convincing because the cultural revival was concentrated in Berlin and a few cities — Bauhaus headquarters, Brecht's theatre, jazz cabarets — while small towns and rural Germany had little exposure. • Convincing because conservatives, the churches and rural voters were genuinely alarmed by what they saw as moral collapse, providing rhetorical material the Nazis would later use to attack ‘cultural Bolshevism’. • Less convincing because Weimar culture had a wide reach in some areas — the German film industry exported globally; Metropolis (1927) and The Blue Angel (1930) were popular hits. • Less convincing because the conservative backlash had many sources, not just culture — agrarian depression, fear of communism and Versailles resentment all fed the right's growth. • Overall judgement: convincing for the urban-rural split and conservative backlash, but oversimplifies the cultural reach. [Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Norman feudal pyramid in England by 1086.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the top sat the king, who claimed all land in England by right of conquest and granted estates to his followers in return for service.
• Beneath the king sat around 180 tenants-in-chief recorded in Domesday Book, including Robert of Mortain (nearly 800 manors) and Odo of Bayeux.
• Tenants-in-chief sub-infeudated land to knights in return for military service of about forty days a year, the unit being called a knight’s fee.
• At the base were peasants — villeins, bordars, cottars, freemen and slaves — who worked the land for their Norman lord on similar terms to the Anglo-Saxon period.
• Why it mattered: because every estate was held in return for service, William could call up knights from the whole kingdom without paying wages for a standing army.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about sub-infeudation in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, sub-infeudation allowed a small Norman elite (perhaps 8,000 fighting men ruling two million Anglo-Saxons) to project knights into every shire by attaching military obligations to land.
• It tied tenants and sub-tenants to their lords by ownership rather than payment — far more durable than wages and far less dependent on cash income.
• It enabled rapid response to revolt: a tenant-in-chief could call up dozens or hundreds of knights for forty-day service from his sub-tenants, the system that produced the armies that crushed the 1067–71 risings.
• Importance later: sub-infeudation became the template for English landholding through the 12th and 13th centuries, recorded in feudal aids and survey records like the Cartae Baronum (1166).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the way William granted out the land of England to his tenants-in-chief after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They held estates directly from the king and owed him military service and counsel; Domesday records around 180 of them across England by 1086.
• The largest holdings went to William’s family and trusted supporters — Robert of Mortain held nearly 800 manors across twenty counties, Odo of Bayeux was lord of estates centred on Kent.
• They sub-infeudated portions of their estates to their own knights as knights’ fees, in return for forty days’ military service per year.
• They garrisoned castles, held private courts and were expected to bring their tenants to the king’s host when summoned.
• Sequence: William claimed all English land by right of conquest in 1066, granted the great estates to his family and commanders as revolt was crushed, and by 1086 Domesday recorded about 180 tenants-in-chief holding directly from him.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the Norman land settlement changed the Anglo-Saxon thegnage.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• By 1086 Domesday records that fewer than 10% of pre-conquest English landholders still held land; the thegnage as a class was effectively replaced within twenty years.
• Many thegns were killed in the campaigns of 1066–71 — from Hastings, the 1067–71 revolts, the Harrying of the North — or exiled abroad to Scotland and Scandinavia.
• Where they survived, English landholders typically held smaller estates as sub-tenants of incoming Normans — a sharp social demotion that marked the new shape of post-conquest society.
• Anglo-Saxon women landholders — widows of the killed and dispossessed — were sometimes married off to Norman incomers, transferring landed inheritance into Norman hands without further bloodshed.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about patronage in maintaining Norman royal authority between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, patronage created personal bonds of loyalty: tenants-in-chief held what they held because the king had granted it, and could lose it if they revolted.
• It allowed William to balance his coalition of Normans, Bretons, Flemings and French — rewarding Bretons like Alan Rufus with the honour of Richmond, settling Flemings in the south — without favouring any one group.
• When patronage broke down it produced revolt: the 1075 Earls’ Revolt and the 1088 rising against William II both involved tenants-in-chief who felt neglected or wronged.
• Importance later: the language of patronage, lordship and personal bond shaped English political culture far beyond 1100, framing later medieval kingship.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Norman success.

‘The Normans kept England because William gave it away. Land granted in return for service bought him an army in every shire and destroyed the class that could have led a national revolt.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for the success of Norman rule? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: the settlement of land was the key reason Norman rule succeeded.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• Concentrating land in around 180 tenants-in-chief, including the great holdings of Robert of Mortain and Odo of Bayeux, gave William military reach into every shire through their sub-tenants and knights.
• Sub-infeudation by knight’s fee turned land grants into a permanent supply of armed retainers, enabling rapid response to revolt and the garrisoning of castles across the country.
• The dispossession of Anglo-Saxon thegns recorded in Domesday Book (fewer than 10% surviving as landholders by 1086) removed the social class that could have led national resistance.
• Patronage allowed William to balance his Norman, Breton, Flemish and French followers without alienating any one bloc — though in 1075 and 1088 the system showed its strain.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• Castles and the network of c.500 of them by 1100 were the physical infrastructure of control alongside the legal pyramid; without them, the land settlement would have lacked the means of enforcement.
• Military victory at Hastings and the Harrying of the North destroyed the strongest opposition before the land settlement could be imposed.
• The Norman Church reform under Lanfranc transformed personnel and ideology in parallel with the land settlement; without it, Anglo-Saxon ecclesiastical authority might have remained a focus for resistance.
• Inherited Anglo-Saxon government structures — shires, sheriffs, hundred courts — provided the day-to-day machinery of rule that the new aristocracy used.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the trial and execution of Charles I in the changing relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: a reigning king tried by his own subjects in Westminster Hall and beheaded on 30 January 1649 — an unprecedented act in European history.
• At the time: established the Commonwealth republic (1649-60) under Cromwell and the Rump Parliament; Divine Right could no longer be defended in practice.
• Over time: parliamentary supremacy was permanently established — Charles II returned in 1660 only on Parliament's terms, James II was driven out in 1688.
• Over time: the trial set a constitutional precedent that a head of state could be held accountable; cited by 18th-century American revolutionaries and later democratic movements.
• Over time: Leveller ideas articulated during the war (Agreement of the People, Putney Debates) became foundational to later British radicalism, although the Putney text itself was lost until 1890.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the trial without explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of political radicalism in the New Model Army during the Civil War era.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the New Model Army of 1645 was paid, disciplined and promoted by merit, so ordinary soldiers gained a political voice no earlier army had.
• At the time: the Levellers under John Lilburne published the Agreement of the People in 1647, proposing manhood suffrage, regular elections and religious liberty.
• At the time: at Putney in October 1647 Rainsborough argued that the poorest man had a right to a vote; Ireton answered that only property gave a real stake in the country.
• At the time: Pride's Purge in December 1648 and the regicide of January 1649 were acts of the army, not of a free Parliament.
• Over time: Cromwell shot the Burford mutineers in May 1649, so radicalism was contained — but the Leveller programme was the most democratic yet written in England.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the demands of the Levellers were similar to the demands of the Chartists.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both demanded an extension of the franchise to ordinary men — the Agreement of the People (1647) proposed manhood suffrage (excluding servants); the People's Charter (1838) demanded universal manhood suffrage.
• Similarity: both proposed equal-sized constituencies, removing the unfair advantages of small or rotten boroughs.
• Similarity: both used the printing press to organise nationally — Leveller pamphlets in the 1640s, the Northern Star in the 1840s.
• Similarity: both were rejected in their own moment but their ideas eventually became law — manhood suffrage in 1918, equal constituencies and the secret ballot earlier.

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.
