practice_questions.text: ‘Ideas were the main factor in causing the English Revolution.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh ideas against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of ideas as the main factor:
• Charles I's commitment to Divine Right made compromise with Parliament constitutionally impossible.
• Parliament's claim that taxation required consent (Petition of Right 1628, Grand Remonstrance 1641) drew on long-running constitutional ideas going back to Magna Carta.
• Once war broke out, the New Model Army incubated more radical ideas — Leveller manhood suffrage, religious liberty — that pushed events further than most parliamentarians wanted.

Weighed against religion:
• Laudian reforms threatened Puritan worship and revived fears of Catholicism — the Scottish Covenanters' 1639-40 invasion was triggered by the prayer book.
• Religion supplied the language and motivation for many New Model Army soldiers; Cromwell's Puritan faith shaped the Commonwealth.

Weighed against money:
• Ship money and the eleven-year Personal Rule (1629-40) created the constitutional crisis; only Parliament could grant lawful taxation.
• The Long Parliament was summoned because Charles needed money for the Bishops' Wars; without that need there might have been no political confrontation.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Charles I's personal inflexibility — refusing to compromise, attempting to arrest the Five Members — made constitutional crisis into civil war.
• Cromwell's personal authority shaped the Protectorate and the limits of Leveller radicalism.

Cross-period weighing:
• Compare with 1381 (economic trigger) and 1536 (religious frame) — ideas of representation are most central in 1642 of the three.
• Long-term trajectory: ideas of consent and accountability seeded by the Civil War recur in 1776 (American Revolution) and 1832 (Reform Act).

Judgement: Top answers argue ideas about Divine Right vs parliamentary authority structured the conflict, but money (ship money), religion (Laudian reforms) and Charles's personal inflexibility were all needed to convert constitutional disagreement into civil war. Ideas were the frame; the other factors supplied the heat.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the New Model Army in the English Revolution.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: gave Parliament decisive military victory, especially at Naseby in June 1645 — ended the First Civil War.
• At the time: its discipline, regular pay and merit-based promotion broke the aristocratic model of military command.
• At the time: it became a political vehicle — Putney Debates 1647, the Agreement of the People, the December 1648 Pride's Purge that enabled the regicide.
• Over time: it suppressed the Levellers at Burford in 1649, showing the limits of its radicalism, but also kept Cromwell in power without Parliament — pioneering a politically powerful standing army.
• Over time: gave 19th-century radicals and Chartists a heritage of organised, principled British radicalism to draw on.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Levellers' demands were different from the demands of the Pilgrimage of Grace marchers.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in aim: the Levellers (1647 Agreement of the People) demanded manhood suffrage and a written constitution; the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) demanded restoration of the monasteries and the removal of Cromwell.
• Difference in religious orientation: the Levellers wanted religious liberty — freedom from any state-imposed church; the Pilgrimage demanded the protection of established Catholic practice.
• Difference in social base: the Levellers came from the New Model Army's soldiers and London craftsmen; the Pilgrimage drew on a cross-class coalition of peasants, town gentry and clergy.
• Difference in framing: the Levellers framed demands as universal rights; the Pilgrimage framed demands as the restoration of an older Catholic order.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a despatch by French general Joseph Joffre to the French government, dated 6 September 1914.
‘Soldiers of France: at the moment when the battle on which the salvation of the country depends is about to begin, no man may look behind. Every effort must be directed at attacking and driving the enemy back. A unit which can no longer advance must hold the ground it has won at any cost and die where it stands rather than retreat.’

Source A suggests that Joffre expected the Battle of the Marne to decide the fate of France. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The battle is one ‘on which the salvation of the country depends’.
• ‘No man may look behind’ - every effort must go into attacking.
• A unit that cannot advance must ‘die where it stands rather than retreat’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Joffre's counter-attack began on 5 September 1914, with German armies about 40 kilometres from Paris.
• The French government had already left Paris for Bordeaux.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the failure of the Schlieffen Plan between the German invasion of Belgium and the end of the Battle of the Marne.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Belgian resistance, Liège forts, BEF at Mons, German overextension, Joffre’s counter-attack, Moltke’s collapse); reaches the retreat to the Aisne through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 4 August 1914: Germany invaded Belgium; Liège forts held longer than planned, costing critical days.
• 23 August 1914: BEF held the German advance at Mons before retreating in good order.
• Late August 1914: Russian invasion of East Prussia forced Germany to divert troops east, weakening the right wing.
• Early September 1914: German armies neared Paris; the French government fled to Bordeaux.
• 5 September 1914: Joffre counter-attacked along the Marne; a gap opened between the German First and Second Armies.
• 6-9 September 1914: French and British troops drove into the gap, supported by Parisian taxis ferrying reinforcements.
• 12 September 1914: German army retreated to the Aisne; Moltke suffered nervous collapse and was sacked.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from the official war diary of British general Sir John French, commander of the BEF, dated 25 August 1914.
‘The men have done magnificently at Mons. The volume and accuracy of their rifle fire shocked the Germans into thinking they faced machine guns at every point of our line. We have inflicted heavy losses, but our left flank is now exposed. Retreat is the only choice.’

Source C: An extract from a memoir published in 1920 by German general Alexander von Kluck, commander of the German First Army in 1914, recalling the campaign.
‘The British Expeditionary Force, small as it was, fought with a discipline I had not expected from a colonial army. At Mons and the days that followed, our timetable suffered. We could not afford four days of attrition we had not budgeted for. Yet the strategic mistake was not at Mons — it was the gap that opened between the First and Second Armies in early September.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the BEF’s contribution to the Allied campaign of 1914. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Sir John French records professional BEF rifle fire shocking the Germans; flank exposed forced retreat. Provenance: an official war diary by the BEF commander, written contemporaneously — likely candid, though shaped by the commander’s wish to record his force’s success.
Source C — Content: Kluck acknowledges British discipline cost his army four critical days. Provenance: a German general’s post-war memoir — useful as enemy testimony but written six years later, with Kluck’s reputation invested in explaining the failure.
Own knowledge: The BEF was small (around 100,000) but professional; Mons (23 August) and Le Cateau (26 August) inflicted disproportionate casualties; the BEF rejoined the French line at the Marne where the gap Kluck mentions was exploited.
Judgement: B is highly useful as immediate British perspective; C is useful as German recognition but shaped by hindsight. Together they confirm the BEF’s contribution mattered out of proportion to its size.

practice_questions.text:
‘Moltke’s modifications to the Schlieffen Plan were the main reason for its failure in 1914.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Moltke weakened the right wing, the part of the plan that had to do the encircling.
• He strengthened the left wing in Alsace-Lorraine and sent troops east when Russia attacked, both at the right wing's expense.
• Schlieffen was said to have warned on his deathbed to keep the right wing strong, and Gerhard Ritter argued Moltke had undone the plan.

Disagree:
• Belgian forts at Liège held out longer than planned and cost the Germans critical days.
• The BEF slowed the advance at Mons on 23 August and again at Le Cateau on 26 August.
• Russia mobilised faster than the plan assumed, so some diversion east was forced on Germany.
• Supply lines and exhausted men had already broken down before the Marne; the timetable was unrealistic in any version.

Judgement: Moltke's changes made a difficult plan harder, but the plan rested on assumptions about Russia, Belgium and France that were never realistic.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British War Office assessment of the Battle of the Marne, written in October 1914.
‘The German advance has been halted at the Marne. Three factors combined to produce this outcome: stiffened French resistance under Joffre; the timely arrival of the BEF on the Allied left; and the over-extension of the German right wing, which permitted a gap to form between the First and Second Armies. The strategic significance of the battle is that the German plan to defeat France in six weeks has been definitively frustrated.’

Source F suggests that the Germans were stopped at the Marne by several causes at once. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• French resistance stiffened under Joffre.
• The BEF arrived in time on the Allied left.
• The German right wing over-extended, letting a gap open between the First and Second Armies.
• The plan to defeat France in six weeks has been ‘definitively frustrated’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Moltke suffered a breakdown and was replaced by Falkenhayn on 14 September 1914.
• The retreat to the Aisne led to the race to the sea and a trench line from the Channel to Switzerland.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the German invasion of Belgium and the BEF’s arrival in France in August 1914.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the BEF’s position at Mons through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 2 August 1914: Germany demanded free passage through Belgium; Belgium refused.
• 3 August 1914: Germany declared war on France.
• 4 August 1914: German troops crossed into Belgium; Britain declared war on Germany over Belgian neutrality.
• 5-16 August 1914: Liège forts resisted German siege guns longer than expected.
• Mid-August 1914: BEF began crossing the Channel — around 100,000 professional soldiers under Sir John French.
• 22 August 1914: BEF reached Mons in southern Belgium.
• 23 August 1914: At the Battle of Mons, the BEF inflicted heavy casualties on the German First Army before retreating in good order.
• 26 August 1914: Le Cateau saw a further BEF rearguard action, slowing the German advance still more.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Northern Rebellion of 1569.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was led by the Catholic earls of Northumberland (Thomas Percy) and Westmorland (Charles Neville).
• On 14 November 1569 the rebels seized Durham Cathedral, tore up the English Prayer Book, and held a Latin Catholic mass.
• It involved around 4,600 followers but stalled below 6,000 as southern Catholics failed to rise.
• It was suppressed by a royal army under the Earl of Sussex; around 450 rebels were hanged in their villages.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the papal bull of 1570 changed the treatment of English Catholics.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It declared Elizabeth a heretic and released Catholics from loyalty, recasting every recusant as a potential traitor in the regime’s eyes.
• The 1571 Treasons Act made it treason to import the bull or to call the queen a heretic.
• It accelerated the tightening of recusancy fines and church-attendance enforcement.
• It justified Walsingham’s expansion of intelligence work to track Catholic priests and plotters.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the missionary priests for Elizabeth’s religious policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, around 471 priests entered England from 1574, sustaining Catholic worship in private and challenging the policy of outward conformity.
• The arrival of the Jesuits in 1580, especially Campion and Persons, raised the political stakes; Campion was executed in 1581.
• The 1585 Act against priests trained abroad — producing roughly 130 executions — was a direct legislative response.
• Significance over time: the missionary effort kept Catholic communities alive into the seventeenth century but also fed Catholic anxieties that shaped the Babington Plot, Mary’s execution and the Armada.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Northern Rebellion of 1569 broke out and was defeated.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It exposed how quickly a regional Catholic faction could mobilise around Mary, Queen of Scots, prompting tighter watch on her household.
• It led to the public hangings of around 450 rebels, designed to deter future risings in the north.
• It accelerated the replacement of northern Catholic gentry with Crown-appointed administrators, weakening regional Catholic networks.
• It hardened the regime’s view that religion and political loyalty could not be separated, paving the way for the harsher post-1570 laws.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Elizabeth’s excommunication in 1570.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it gave Catholic plotters religious cover by formally releasing English Catholics from loyalty.
• It triggered immediate legal change — the 1571 Treasons Act — and reframed Catholic worship as a security issue.
• Significance over time: it shaped every later Catholic plot (Ridolfi, Throckmorton, Babington), the 1585 Act, and Spanish plans to depose Elizabeth.
• It illustrates how an event outside England could reshape English domestic policy for a generation.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Catholic threat to Elizabeth was real and growing. It was not a panic got up by her spymaster.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the Catholic threat to Elizabeth between 1568 and 1603? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The Northern Rebellion of 1569 was a genuine armed rising involving thousands of followers.
• The 1570 bull formally released Catholics from loyalty, making militant Catholicism a national-security issue.
• A succession of plots — Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586 — targeted the queen’s life.
• Around 471 missionary priests entered the country and roughly 130 were executed; the Spanish Armada of 1588 was the climax.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The Northern Rebellion stalled within seven weeks; ordinary Catholics did not rise.
• Most missionary priests focused on sacraments, not politics; many were not plotters.
• The regime survived every Catholic challenge, suggesting the threat was managed rather than overwhelming.
• Some historians argue Walsingham’s service had an interest in inflating the danger to justify resources.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: ‘Economic resources were the main factor shaping British involvement in the Atlantic slave trade between 1562 and 1833.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to economic resources and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic resources (in support): sugar, tobacco and cotton profits drove Liverpool, Bristol and Glasgow expansion; Royal African Company 1672; 1.5 million enslaved carried by Liverpool ships 1700-1807.
• Economic resources (in support): slave-trade money funded Lloyd’s of London, Barclays, the early steam engine and country houses such as Harewood House.
• Ideas: racial hierarchies and Christian-paternalist arguments justified slavery for centuries; Enlightenment and Quaker arguments helped end it.
• Role of individuals: Hawkins (1562-67), Wilberforce, Clarkson, Equiano, Cugoano — both sides of the abolition struggle had named figures whose actions mattered.
• Government: chartered the Royal African Company; passed the 1807 Slave Trade Act and 1833 Slavery Abolition Act; the £20 million compensation went to owners not the enslaved.
• War: the 1791 Haitian Revolution and the wars of the French Revolution undermined the Caribbean plantation system and created the strategic conditions for British abolition.
• Top-band judgement: economic resources were necessary but not sufficient. Sugar profits drove the trade; ideas changed how Britons judged it; individuals on both sides shaped the timing of abolition. The factors reinforced each other rather than acting alone.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of John Hawkins’s voyages of 1562-1567 for British involvement in the Atlantic slave trade.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Hawkins made the first English slave-trading voyages, attacking Portuguese ships and selling captives in the Spanish Caribbean.
• At the time: Elizabeth I knighted Hawkins and granted him a coat of arms showing a bound African; royal sanction made slaving a legitimate field for English shipping.
• Over time: Hawkins set the precedent that English involvement in the slave trade would combine piracy and commerce, a pattern continued by the Royal African Company in 1672.
• Over time: by the late 17th century slave trading had become a structured triangular system in which Liverpool, Bristol and London competed for shares.
• Limitation: Hawkins’s direct contribution was small in volume; significance lies in opening the door rather than running the trade himself.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act for Britain and its empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: ended slavery throughout most of the British Empire; around 800,000 enslaved people across the Caribbean were freed (subject to a transitional ‘apprenticeship’ period that ended in 1838).
• At the time: paid £20 million in compensation — equivalent to 40% of the government’s annual budget — to slave-owners, not to the formerly enslaved. The 2013 UCL Legacies database has named more than 46,000 recipients.
• Over time: created a vacuum in plantation labour that drew indentured Indian and Chinese workers to the Caribbean from the 1840s — a migration that connects to Lesson 11.
• Over time: Britain re-positioned itself rhetorically as the leader of global abolition while continuing to profit from cotton produced by slave labour in the United States until the 1860s.
• Over time: the £20 million compensation was not fully repaid by the Treasury until 2015 — meaning UK taxpayers were still paying the debt of slavery into the 21st century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the opening of the slave trade to private merchants in 1698.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the Royal African Company had held a chartered monopoly since 1672; Parliament opened the trade to any English merchant in 1698.
• At the time: Liverpool and Bristol grew fast on the trade and overtook London, and the volume of enslaved people carried rose sharply.
• At the time: slaving became an ordinary commercial investment rather than a royal enterprise, spreading the profits far more widely.
• Over time: Liverpool ships alone carried around 1.5 million enslaved Africans between 1700 and 1807, more than any other port in the world.
• Over time: that profit built docks, banks and insurance in British ports and reached country estates such as Harewood House.
• Limitation: demand from the sugar islands, not the 1698 Act alone, drove the growth; the Act removed a restriction rather than creating the trade.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the British settlement of Barbados in the 17th century was similar to or different from later British involvement in West Africa.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Barbados was a settler colony where English planters owned land directly; West African involvement was based on coastal trading forts run by chartered companies.
• Difference: Barbados depended on the forced labour of enslaved Africans transported across the Atlantic; West Africa supplied the labour rather than being colonised in the same form until the 19th century.
• Similarity: both fed the same triangular trade — British goods to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Caribbean, sugar back to Britain.
• Similarity: both were sustained by chartered monopoly companies (Royal African Company 1672; planter assemblies in Barbados) with state backing.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named institutions.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the abolitionist movement of the late 18th century for British public opinion on empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Clarkson’s research and the famous plan of the slave ship Brookes turned abstract numbers into images Parliament could not ignore.
• At the time: Equiano’s 1789 autobiography and the work of the Sons of Africa gave the movement Black voices that made British readers confront eyewitness testimony.
• At the time: sugar boycotts, with around 300,000 households participating, brought consumer politics into imperial debate for the first time.
• Over time: the model of pamphlets, petitions and parliamentary campaigning shaped later 19th-century reform movements (Anti-Corn Law League, Chartism).
• Over time: Britain’s self-image as ‘the nation that ended slavery’ became central to imperial propaganda for the next century, despite the contradiction with continued exploitation in India and Africa.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Cold War spread from Europe into Asia between 1949 and 1953.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the post-Korean War balance through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• August 1949: the USSR tested its first atomic bomb, ending the US monopoly.
• 1 October 1949: Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic of China; Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalists retreated to Taiwan.
• February 1950: the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance bound the two communist powers together.
• 25 June 1950: North Korean forces invaded the South across the 38th parallel.
• Late October 1950: Chinese forces entered the war when UN forces approached the Yalu River, throwing them back to the 38th parallel.
• 27 July 1953: the armistice at Panmunjom froze the conflict; the war confirmed the global reach of containment and tripled US defence spending.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Korean War unfolded between June 1950 and the Chinese intervention of October 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the Chinese intervention through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 25 June 1950: North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel; Seoul fell within three days.
• 27 June 1950: the UN Security Council passed Resolution 83 calling for armed assistance to South Korea, possible because the USSR was boycotting.
• 7 July 1950: Resolution 84 authorised a unified UN command under MacArthur.
• August 1950: UN and South Korean forces were pushed into the Pusan perimeter at the southern tip of the peninsula.
• 15 September 1950: MacArthur’s amphibious landing at Inchon collapsed the North Korean line.
• 19 October 1950: UN forces took Pyongyang and pushed toward the Chinese border, prompting Mao to send Chinese ‘volunteers’ into Korea later that month.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a US National Security Council paper, NSC-68, completed in April 1950 and presented to President Truman.
‘The Soviet Union, unlike previous aspirants to hegemony, is animated by a new fanatic faith antithetical to our own. The recent Chinese revolution and the Soviet atomic test have shifted the balance against us. We must build conventional and nuclear forces of unprecedented scale, and develop the capacity to wage limited war wherever Soviet pressure appears.’

Source A suggests that American planners believed events in 1949 had weakened the position of the USA. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The recent Chinese revolution has shifted the balance against the USA.
• The Soviet atomic test has ended the US monopoly and changed the strategic position.
• The USSR is ‘animated by a new fanatic faith antithetical to our own’ — ideological threat.
• The USA must build conventional and nuclear forces of unprecedented scale to wage limited war wherever Soviet pressure appears.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The USSR tested its first atomic bomb in August 1949 and Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.
• The Korean War from June 1950 turned NSC-68 into policy and US defence spending tripled.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a speech by Chairman Mao Tse-tung to the Central People’s Government, October 1950, explaining the decision to send Chinese forces into Korea.
‘If American imperialists were to occupy Korea, they would stand at our gate. Our country could not be at peace; our industry could not be rebuilt; our farmers could not work in safety. To save Korea is to defend China. To defend China is to defend the cause of socialism in Asia.’

Source C: An extract from US Secretary of State Dean Acheson’s testimony to a US Senate committee, February 1951, looking back on the previous autumn.
‘The Chinese intervention took us by surprise. We had assumed Mao would be too occupied with internal reconstruction to enter another war. We underestimated the political importance of a hostile force on his border, and overestimated the freedom we had to advance to the Yalu without consequence.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why China entered the Korean War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Mao frames the intervention as defensive, tying Chinese security to events in Korea. Provenance: a speech to the Chinese Central People’s Government — useful for the official Chinese justification, less useful for revealing private bargaining with Stalin. Own knowledge: roughly 250,000 Chinese ‘volunteers’ entered Korea in late October 1950 after MacArthur approached the Yalu; Mao had received Soviet pledges of equipment and air cover.
Source C — Content: admits an American miscalculation about Chinese willingness to act and the meaning of advancing to the Yalu. Provenance: Senate testimony four months later by the Secretary of State — useful for the genuine US explanation, partial because it is given in a hostile political context where Acheson is defending administration choices.
Own knowledge: the November 1950 Chinese counter-offensive recaptured Pyongyang and Seoul; the war then stalemated near the 38th parallel until 1953.
Judgement: Both sources are useful but partial — B reveals the official Chinese line, C reveals the post-event US assessment; together they show that border security and US misjudgement reinforced each other.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Korean War mattered more than Mao's victory in China for the development of the Cold War.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Korea was the first war in which communist and Western forces fought each other directly.
• It turned NSC-68 from a planning paper into policy and US defence spending tripled.
• It gave NATO a real integrated command and opened the argument for rearming West Germany.
• It produced a chain of US defence treaties in Asia during 1951, with Japan, the Philippines and the ANZUS states.
Disagree:
• Mao's victory on 1 October 1949 brought the largest population in Asia into the communist camp.
• The Sino-Soviet Treaty of February 1950 created the bloc that Washington then feared.
• Chinese intervention in late October 1950 is what made Korea dangerous, so China was the deeper cause.
• The Soviet atomic test of August 1949 had already ended the US monopoly before Korea began.
Judgement: China changed the map of the Cold War, but Korea changed what the West spent and built because of it.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the events in 1949 that convinced Western leaders the Cold War had become global.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the perception of a global Cold War through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• April 1949: NATO was founded by twelve countries, embedding the Western alliance in Europe.
• August 1949: the Soviet Union conducted its first successful atomic test, ending the US monopoly.
• October 1949: Mao Tse-tung proclaimed the People’s Republic of China; the Nationalists fled to Taiwan.
• Late 1949: the Truman administration was attacked at home for ‘losing China’, prompting a strategic review.
• February 1950: the Sino-Soviet Treaty linked the two communist powers in a public alliance.
• April 1950: NSC-68 set out a global containment strategy and called for tripled defence spending — turning a series of 1949 shocks into a coherent worldwide Cold War posture.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a French military report on the situation at Dien Bien Phu, written by an officer of the besieged garrison in late March 1954.
‘The Vietminh artillery has been brought up by means we did not believe possible. Bicycles, porters, and tracks cut through the jungle. Our airstrip is now under continuous fire and resupply is by parachute alone. The position is no longer a base of operations but an island.’

Source A suggests that the French position at Dien Bien Phu could no longer be held. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Vietminh artillery had been brought up ‘by means we did not believe possible’.
• The airstrip was under continuous fire, so resupply was by parachute alone.
• The base is described as ‘an island’ rather than a base of operations.
Contextual knowledge: Giap opened fire on 13 March 1954; the 13,000-strong garrison was cut off and surrendered on 7 May after a 56-day siege.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a public speech by Ho Chi Minh, broadcast on Vietminh radio in July 1954, days after the Geneva Accords were signed.
‘The Vietnamese people have driven out a great colonial power. The 17th parallel is a line on a map, not a border in our hearts. The struggle for independence is not yet complete; only when our country is whole and free of foreign interference will it be finished.’

Source B suggests that Ho Chi Minh did not regard the Geneva settlement as the end of the struggle. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He calls the 17th parallel ‘a line on a map, not a border in our hearts’.
• He says the struggle for independence ‘is not yet complete’.
• He sets the end point as a country that is whole and free of foreign interference.
Contextual knowledge: Geneva divided Vietnam only until reunification elections promised for July 1956; those elections were never held.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C.

Source C: An extract from a confidential US State Department briefing on the Geneva Accords, July 1954.
‘The proposed elections of July 1956 would, in current circumstances, hand the whole of Vietnam to the Vietminh. Free elections held in present conditions would return Ho Chi Minh as leader of the whole country. We cannot endorse a settlement that effectively concedes a country.’

Source C suggests that the United States could not accept the elections promised at Geneva. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source C and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The briefing says the 1956 elections would ‘hand the whole of Vietnam to the Vietminh’.
• Free elections in the conditions of 1954 would make Ho Chi Minh leader of the whole country.
• Washington will not endorse a settlement that ‘effectively concedes a country’.
Contextual knowledge: The United States and the State of Vietnam refused to sign the Accords, and Washington later backed Diem’s refusal to hold the 1956 vote.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a memoir by General Vo Nguyen Giap, written in the 1970s, recalling the planning of the Dien Bien Phu campaign.
‘The French believed our porters could not move heavy guns to the hills. We turned that belief into a trap. Tens of thousands carried artillery and shells along jungle paths for weeks, hauling guns up reverse slopes. When we opened fire, the French airstrip was finished within hours.’

Source D suggests that French assumptions about Vietminh logistics were the key to the Vietminh victory. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The French ‘believed our porters could not move heavy guns to the hills’.
• Tens of thousands of porters carried artillery and shells along jungle paths for weeks.
• Guns were hauled onto reverse slopes, out of sight of French air power.
Contextual knowledge: Giap opened fire on 13 March 1954 and the airstrip was unusable within hours, leaving the garrison dependent on parachute drops.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a contemporary report by the British correspondent at Geneva, published in The Times in late July 1954.
‘The Accords are presented as a temporary settlement. The 17th parallel is described as provisional and elections are promised by July 1956. Whether either side genuinely intends to hold those elections is doubtful. The Americans have refused to sign and the southern administration is unenthusiastic. A two-year settlement may quickly become a permanent partition.’

Source E suggests that the temporary division of Vietnam was likely to become permanent. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source E and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The Americans had refused to sign the Accords.
• The southern administration is described as ‘unenthusiastic’ about elections.
• The report doubts that either side genuinely intends to hold the 1956 vote.
Contextual knowledge: The 17th parallel was meant to last two years; in the event it divided Vietnam for twenty-one, until 1975.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter from a French officer at Dien Bien Phu, written shortly before the position fell in May 1954.
‘We are out of ammunition for the heavy guns and the resupply drops fall mostly behind enemy lines. The American refusal to bomb the besiegers has settled the matter. We will fight on, but the outcome is no longer a question of military skill.’

Source F suggests that the fall of Dien Bien Phu was no longer something French skill could prevent. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The heavy guns are out of ammunition.
• Resupply drops ‘fall mostly behind enemy lines’.
• The refusal of American air strikes ‘has settled the matter’.
Contextual knowledge: France had asked the United States for air strikes, and even atomic weapons, under Operation Vulture; Eisenhower refused without British support, which Churchill declined.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the arrival of the friars in thirteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They lived among ordinary people in towns rather than enclosed in monasteries, begging for their food.
• The Franciscans (Greyfriars) emphasised poverty and humility, while the Dominicans (Blackfriars) emphasised study and preaching.
• They settled deliberately in the rough, growing parts of cities — Newgate, Ludgate and university towns such as Oxford and Cambridge.
• They worked closely with the king, preaching the cause of the crusades and serving as royal ambassadors.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Roger Bacon for thirteenth-century learning.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, his Opus Majus (1267) for Pope Clement IV argued that Christian learning had to include languages, mathematics and experiment, not only theology.
• His emphasis on direct observation and the testing of claims went against the conventional dependence on authority alone in scholasticism.
• His proposals for magnifying lenses, gunpowder and calendar reform were unusual for his age and earned him a reputation as ‘Doctor Mirabilis’.
• Significance over time: his writings later became a foundation reference for the experimental tradition that flowered in the seventeenth-century scientific revolution.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which English higher education was changed by the rise of Oxford and Cambridge colleges.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Endowed colleges such as Merton (refounded 1274), Balliol (statutes 1282) and Peterhouse (1284) gave students a stable home with their own statutes, food and lodging.
• This caused the universities to settle into permanent institutions rather than loose communities of masters and pupils that could move from town to town.
• It caused the rise of the master-and-college tutorial structure that still shapes Oxford and Cambridge today.
• Wealthy patrons could direct study by writing the college statutes — for example, only certain numbers of fellows in particular subjects, sometimes in particular regions.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named colleges and dates and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which students were taught at Oxford or Cambridge in Edward I’s reign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Teaching was in Latin and almost all students were in minor orders — clerks of the Church.
• Students worked through the seven liberal arts (grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy) before moving to higher faculties.
• Lectures involved a master reading aloud from a set text such as Aristotle’s logic.
• Disputations required students to argue formal questions on either side of a problem before earning a degree.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the friars for the medieval Church and English society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the friars brought religious life out of the monastery and into the open streets, addressing the spiritual needs of the new towns.
• They became leading university scholars: Roger Bacon was a Franciscan; Duns Scotus joined the Franciscan order; Dominicans dominated the theology faculties at Oxford and Paris.
• They worked closely with the Crown, preaching the crusades and pressing for measures such as the 1290 expulsion of the Jews.
• Significance over time: friaries shaped the religious geography of English towns until the dissolution of the monasteries in the sixteenth century, and the educational influence of the Dominicans and Franciscans on European universities reached far beyond medieval England.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘The Church mattered more than the universities in shaping thirteenth-century English society.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Every parish in England was organised around a stone church and the sacraments; the Church kept the calendar, recorded births and deaths, and fed the poor.
• The friars (Franciscans and Dominicans) brought a new public religious life into every major English town in this single generation.
• Bishops sat in royal councils and parliaments and shaped major royal decisions.
• The Pope’s bull Clericis Laicos (1296) tested Edward’s authority directly and forced him to coerce the clergy.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Oxford and Cambridge produced the lawyers and clerks who staffed Edward’s administration, including future bishops and Lord Chancellors.
• Roger Bacon’s Opus Majus (1267) and Duns Scotus’s lectures shaped European intellectual life for two centuries.
• Endowed colleges (Merton, Balliol, Peterhouse) created a stable structure that would dominate English higher learning for centuries.
• In practice, friars, scholars and clergy operated through the universities, so the two institutions cannot be neatly separated.

A strong response weighs the parish-and-papal Church against the university world and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on multiple factors and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how al-Qaeda developed as a global network between 1988 and the eve of 9/11.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more turning points as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Peshawar 1988, break with Saudi Arabia 1990, 1996/1998 fatwas, 1998 embassy bombings, 2000 USS Cole); reaches the eve of 9/11 through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• August 1988: al-Qaeda founded in Peshawar by bin Laden and Abdullah Azzam at the end of the Soviet–Afghan war.
• August 1990: bin Laden’s offer to defend Saudi Arabia is rejected and US troops arrive on Saudi soil; this becomes the central grievance.
• 1994–96: bin Laden is stripped of Saudi citizenship and moves to Sudan, then to Afghanistan; the network gains a permanent base.
• 1996 and 1998 fatwas declare war on the United States and provide a rhetorical licence for civilian targeting.
• 7 August 1998: simultaneous embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam show the network can strike globally.
• October 2000: the USS Cole attack confirms operational capacity; planning for a US-soil strike, approved in 1999, is well advanced by summer 2001.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from a 1998 fatwa attributed to Osama bin Laden and the World Islamic Front, published in the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Quds al-Arabi, 23 February 1998.
‘The ruling to kill the Americans and their allies — civilians and military — is an individual duty for every Muslim who can do it in any country in which it is possible to do it, in order to liberate the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Holy Mosque from their grip.’

Study Source A. Source A suggests that by 1998 al-Qaeda had widened its targets to include civilians. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The fatwa’s explicit phrase ‘civilians and military’ implies al-Qaeda had moved beyond Cold War-style guerrilla tactics and now treated American non-combatants as legitimate targets, a step most Islamic scholars rejected.
• The reference to ‘the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Holy Mosque’ suggests al-Qaeda framed its aims around two specific places — Jerusalem and Mecca — turning Israeli–Palestinian and Saudi–American grievances into a single religious duty.
• The instruction that the duty falls on ‘every Muslim who can do it in any country’ suggests al-Qaeda already saw itself as a global franchise relying on independent action, not a single command structure.
• Publishing in Al-Quds al-Arabi suggests bin Laden wanted to reach an Arabic-speaking audience directly, bypassing both Western media and the religious authorities that would otherwise have rejected the ruling.

practice_questions.text: ‘The presence of American troops in Saudi Arabia after 1990 was the main reason al-Qaeda turned against the United States.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: the Saudi decision of August 1990 to accept American troops rather than bin Laden’s volunteer force turned a war hero into a dissident and drove him into exile.
• Agree: the 1996 fatwa was titled a declaration of war against the Americans occupying the land of the two holy places, naming the troop presence as the grievance.
• Agree: the grievance recruited a generation of Saudi nationals; fifteen of the nineteen 9/11 hijackers were Saudi citizens.
• Disagree: bin Laden’s ideology pre-dated 1990, shaped by the anti-Soviet jihad and the writings of Sayyid Qutb.
• Disagree: the 1998 fatwa put the al-Aqsa Mosque alongside the Holy Mosque, so Israeli–Palestinian grievances mattered too.
• Disagree: al-Qaeda also aimed to topple Arab governments it judged corrupt and to restore a caliphate, aims independent of any US deployment.
• Judgement: the troop presence was the grievance that gave the network its focus and its recruits, but the ideology was already in place before 1990.

practice_questions.text: ‘Al-Qaeda was a new kind of terrorist organisation.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: it was transnational rather than tied to one national grievance, drawing recruits from Saudi Arabia, Egypt and beyond.
• Agree: it deliberately killed civilians far from any war zone, as at Nairobi and Dar es Salaam in August 1998.
• Agree: it worked as a franchise, training thousands of fighters in Afghan camps who went home to form independent cells.
• Agree: it justified its methods through fatwas issued by a man with no standing as a cleric, which mainstream scholars rejected.
• Disagree: it grew directly out of the older mujahideen networks of the 1980s and used familiar tactics such as truck bombs.
• Disagree: earlier groups had also attacked civilians and operated across borders, so the difference was of scale rather than kind.
• Judgement: the combination of tight central planning with loose global reach was genuinely new, even though the parts were not.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from the fatwa issued by Osama bin Laden and the World Islamic Front, published in Al-Quds al-Arabi on 23 February 1998, declaring the killing of Americans a duty for every Muslim.
Source B: Extract from President Bill Clinton’s televised address of 20 August 1998, announcing cruise-missile strikes on al-Qaeda camps in Afghanistan and a factory in Sudan after the East African embassy bombings.

Study Sources A and B. How useful are Sources A and B to an historian studying al-Qaeda in the late 1990s? Explain your answer using Sources A and B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and own contextual knowledge for both sources to reach a substantiated judgement on usefulness.
Secure: Clear use of all three for both sources with some judgement.
Developing: Two of the three treated.
Emerging: Description of the sources without evaluation.

Indicative content:
• Content of Source A: it states al-Qaeda’s aims in the network’s own words and shows that civilians were now named as targets.
• Provenance of Source A: bin Laden was writing to recruit and to justify, not to describe, and he had no standing as a cleric, so it tells us what he wanted believed.
• Content of Source B: Clinton sets out how the United States understood the threat weeks after the embassy bombings, and what it thought military action could achieve.
• Provenance of Source B: a president speaking to a domestic audience during a political crisis will simplify and reassure; useful for official framing, less so for intelligence detail.
• Own knowledge: the August 1998 strikes missed bin Laden; the FBI later placed him on its Ten Most Wanted list; the USS Cole was attacked in October 2000.
• Judgement: read together the two sources give both sides of the confrontation, but neither shows the network’s internal organisation, for which the 9/11 Commission Report is far more useful.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how al-Qaeda’s methods changed between the 1996 fatwa and the attack on the USS Cole in October 2000.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence, with precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• The 1996 fatwa was rhetorical, aimed at the American troop presence in Saudi Arabia rather than at any particular operation.
• The February 1998 fatwa, issued with Ayman al-Zawahiri, widened the target list to civilians and gave followers a licence they used within six months.
• On 7 August 1998 simultaneous truck bombs at the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam embassies killed around 224 people, most of them African civilians.
• Clinton’s cruise-missile strikes of August 1998 failed to kill bin Laden, and the network learned that its Afghan sanctuary could absorb a punishment.
• In October 2000 suicide bombers in a small boat struck the USS Cole in Aden harbour, killing 17 sailors and proving the network could hit a warship.
• By then planning for the Planes Operation, approved by bin Laden in late 1999, was already well advanced.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Pasteur and Koch were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: Pasteur was a French chemist working originally on industry problems (wine, silk); Koch was a German country doctor working on patients and farm animals.
• Difference: Pasteur produced the general germ theory (1861) and developed vaccines; Koch identified specific bacteria for specific diseases and developed staining and culture techniques.
• Similarity: both used the microscope and rigorous experiment to overturn miasma theory; both worked in the 1860s-1880s.
• Similarity: both produced practical applications that reached Britain — Pasteur via vaccines and food preservation, Koch via bacteriological diagnosis.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Louis Pasteur for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: his 1861 germ theory replaced miasma as the basis of medical thinking, eventually changing British practice in surgery (Lister, 1867) and public health.
• At the time: his vaccines for chicken cholera (1879), anthrax (1881) and rabies (1885) extended Jenner’s principle to multiple diseases.
• Over time: provided the theoretical foundation for everything that followed — Koch’s bacteriology, Ehrlich’s magic bullets, Fleming’s penicillin.
• Over time: changed how Britain trained doctors, reorganised hospitals (sterilisation, antisepsis) and shaped public health policy across the late 19th and 20th centuries.
• Limitation: British acceptance was slow — many doctors clung to miasma into the 1880s, showing that discovery does not equal application.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and an awareness of the discovery-application gap.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: a photograph of anthrax bacteria taken by Robert Koch and published in 1877. Koch stained the bacteria so that they showed up under a microscope, then photographed them so that other scientists could see for themselves what he claimed to have found.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying how germ theory came to be accepted?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: it makes the invisible visible, which is exactly what the rivals of miasma theory had lacked.
• Content: publishing a photograph rather than a drawing invited other laboratories to check the claim, which is how bacteriology spread.
• Provenance: produced by Koch to prove his own case, so it is designed to persuade; but staining and photography could be repeated by others, which limited how far he could mislead.
• Contextual knowledge: Pasteur had published germ theory in 1861; Koch went on to identify tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883); many British doctors clung to miasma into the 1880s.
• Limitations: a photograph of one microbe proves nothing about how disease spread through a British city and nothing about why acceptance took so long.
• Judgement: strong evidence for the science and technology factor, weak evidence for the pace of change in Britain.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Has science and technology been the main factor in changing how disease was understood in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to science and technology and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh science and technology against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of science and technology as the main factor:
• The microscope was essential — without it, germs are invisible and miasma persists by default.
• Staining (Koch) and culture techniques (agar jelly) were technical advances that turned theory into specific identification.
• Across the wider sweep, science and technology grows in weight: Vesalius 1543, Harvey 1628, Jenner 1796, Pasteur 1861, Koch 1880s, Ehrlich 1909, Fleming 1928.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Pasteur, Koch and Ehrlich each pursued lines of work that competitors might have abandoned; persistence mattered.
• Compare with earlier periods — Vesalius and Harvey were essential individuals; Jenner’s 1796 experiment depended on personal initiative.

Weighed against communication:
• Scientific journals carried Pasteur’s and Koch’s findings across borders; without that communication network, science could not spread.
• Compare with medieval period when communication relied on Latin manuscripts and translation routes through Toledo.

Weighed against chance:
• Pasteur’s 1879 chicken-cholera vaccine came from a forgotten flask — chance triggered the discovery, but only because Pasteur was prepared to notice.

Judgement: In the germ theory revolution, science and technology was necessary but not sufficient — individuals decided who pursued which line, and communication carried the results. The strongest answers note that science and technology has greater weight in this period than in any earlier one, but that across the whole sweep the dominant factor varies (religion in 1348, government in 1948).

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes science only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Robert Koch for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: identified specific bacteria for anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883), giving doctors specific targets.
• At the time: developed staining and culture techniques that allowed others to repeat his work and extend it.
• Over time: founded modern bacteriology and the ‘one germ, one disease’ rule that underpins 20th-century medicine.
• Over time: his work paved the way for Ehrlich’s 1909 magic bullets, the BCG TB vaccine and the entire system of bacteriological diagnosis used in NHS laboratories.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Paul Ehrlich for the treatment of disease in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: he argued that if specific germs caused specific diseases, specific chemicals could destroy them without harming the patient — the ‘magic bullet’.
• At the time: the arsenic compound Salvarsan, announced in 1909, was the first chemical cure for an infectious disease.
• Over time: it opened the age of chemotherapy — Prontosil followed in 1932 and penicillin in the 1940s.
• Over time: the search for targeted drugs became the model for the pharmaceutical industry that now supplies the NHS.
• Limitation: Salvarsan was difficult and dangerous to administer, and the search for further magic bullets stalled for over twenty years.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Has slavery been the main cause of the American Civil War?

• Slavery and its expansion into new territories
• Other political and economic differences between North and South

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that distinguishes slavery’s existence from slavery’s expansion and weighs it against other factors; precise factual support across both bullets and additional material; substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached. Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit. Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative. Indicative content: • Slavery’s expansion: 1820 Missouri Compromise, 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act, 1856 Bleeding Kansas, 1857 Dred Scott, 1859 Harpers Ferry, Lincoln’s 1860 platform. • Other differences: industrial free-labour North versus plantation South; tariff disputes (e.g. nullification crisis legacy); states’ rights versus federal authority. • Other relevant material: Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin; Underground Railroad; Republican Party founded 1854; Democratic split in 1860. • Judgement: top answers argue that slavery’s expansion is the precise cause — not slavery in general or tariffs in isolation — because every flashpoint after 1820 turned on whether new western territories would be slave or free.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act on relations between North and South.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (Stephen Douglas, popular sovereignty, repeal of Missouri Compromise, Bleeding Kansas, Republican Party founded 1854, Pottawatomie Creek 1856, Lawrence sacked).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about the Act.

Indicative content:
• Repeal of the Missouri Compromise: by introducing popular sovereignty, the Act voided the 1820 line and made every new territory a potential slave or free state, raising the stakes nationwide.
• Bleeding Kansas: free-soil and pro-slavery settlers rushed in, producing rival governments and open political violence (Lawrence sacked, Pottawatomie Creek killings).
• Birth of the Republican Party: anti-extension northerners formed a new party in 1854, taking the place of the collapsing Whigs.
• Long-term consequence: the Act removed the framework that had managed the slavery question for thirty years and put a return to compromise out of reach by 1860.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of abolitionism in the United States before 1861.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features. Secure: Two valid features. Developing: One developed; one undeveloped. Emerging: Generalised description. Indicative content: • Cultural: Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852) sold 300,000 copies in the United States in its first year, shaping northern public opinion. • Practical: the Underground Railroad helped perhaps 100,000 enslaved people escape to free states or Canada, with conductors such as Harriet Tubman. • Militant: John Brown’s 1856 attack at Pottawatomie Creek and his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry made him a martyr in the North and a symbol of insurrection in the South. • Political: the Republican Party, founded 1854, gave anti-slavery-extension opinion a national electoral vehicle.

practice_questions.text:
Read this short interpretation and use it to answer the question that follows.

Interpretation: An extract from a Confederate veteran’s memoir, 1908.
“The war between the States was not about slavery. It was about the right of free states to govern themselves without dictation from a central government in Washington.”

How convincing is this interpretation about the causes of the Civil War? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation that weighs convincing and unconvincing elements; rooted in precise contextual knowledge of slavery’s expansion and states’ rights debates; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation drawing on context with developed convincing/unconvincing points and a judgement.
Developing: Some evaluation but reliance on retelling the interpretation; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without using context.

Indicative content:
Convincing:
• States’ rights language was used in southern political rhetoric.
• There were genuine economic and constitutional disagreements between North and South.
Unconvincing:
• Every flashpoint after 1820 turned on slavery in new territories: Missouri Compromise, Kansas-Nebraska, Dred Scott, Lincoln’s 1860 platform.
• The Confederate states’ own secession declarations (1860–61) named slavery as the central issue.
• ‘Free’ states in the memoir is an evasion: the states arguing for self-government were the ones whose economy depended on enslaved labour.
