Judgement: the interpretation is unconvincing as a description of cause; it is far more useful as evidence of how southern memory was reshaped after defeat.

practice_questions.text:
Why might historians now and historians in 1900 give different views of the causes of the Civil War?

Use your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on writers’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise context.
Secure: Reason rooted in provenance or context with brief support.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’.
Emerging: Restates content of each interpretation.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: in 1900 the ‘Lost Cause’ school dominated American history-writing, framing the war as a defence of self-government; from the 1960s onwards, civil-rights-era scholarship reframed it as a slavery war.
• Purpose: 1900 historians wrote in a culture seeking sectional reconciliation; modern historians weigh causes against archival evidence including secession declarations.
• Evidence: 1900 writers had limited access to enslaved peoples’ voices; modern writers use slave narratives, Confederate documents and demographic data.
• Audience: a reuniting white reading public versus an academic and general audience that includes Black perspectives.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the 1857 Dred Scott decision on the political crisis between North and South.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (Supreme Court, Roger Taney, Black citizenship denied, Missouri Compromise voided, northern outrage, Republican Party).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about the case.

Indicative content:
• Voided the Missouri Compromise: by ruling Congress had no power to ban slavery in any territory, the decision struck down the 1820 framework.
• Denied Black citizenship: the ruling that no Black person could be a US citizen radicalised abolitionist opinion in the North.
• Boosted the Republican Party: northern outrage helped Lincoln’s party win control of the House in 1858 and the presidency in 1860.
• Made compromise harder: with the Supreme Court itself out of step with northern opinion, future agreements over new territories looked impossible.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of the Jewry of 1275.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It banned Jews from lending money at interest, ending the only legal occupation many of them had.
• It ordered Jews into trade, farming or crafts, although Christian guilds excluded them from most of these.
• It required every Jew over the age of seven to wear a larger yellow felt badge in the shape of the Tablets of the Law.
• It imposed a poll tax of three pence on every Jew aged twelve and over.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the expulsion of the Jews in 1290.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the expulsion produced a parliamentary tax grant of around £116,000 — the largest single grant of Edward’s reign — plus the seized houses and debts of the expelled community.
• It marked a religious turning point: England became the first European kingdom to expel its Jews and was followed by France in 1306 and Spain in 1492.
• In the short term, around 2,000–3,000 people were forced abroad; some were robbed or drowned by ships’ captains in the Thames estuary.
• Over time, the expulsion lasted 366 years until Oliver Cromwell allowed Jews to return in 1656, shaping English religious culture for centuries.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise figures and named comparisons.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the position of England’s Jewish community was changed by the rise of Italian banking.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Riccardi of Lucca and other Italian houses could lend on a much larger scale than English Jews, financing the Welsh wars and royal building programmes.
• Once the king had a richer alternative source of credit, the practical value of Jewish moneylending to the Crown disappeared.
• The Statute of the Jewry (1275) banned Jewish usury altogether, which only made sense once Italian credit was available.
• Without their traditional protected role, the community lost the king’s self-interested protection — making the 1290 expulsion politically possible.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named bankers and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the persecution faced by Jews in England before 1290.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Blood libels, beginning at Norwich in 1144, falsely accused Jews of murdering Christian children for ritual purposes; the cult of Little Saint Hugh of Lincoln in 1255 saw nineteen Jews hanged.
• Violent pogroms targeted Jewish communities — in 1190 around 150 Jews were killed or driven to suicide at Clifford’s Tower in York.
• From 1218 Jews were forced to wear a yellow badge to mark them out from Christian neighbours.
• In 1278 around 269 Jews were hanged in London on charges of coin clipping.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of the Jewry of 1275 for the events of 1290.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 1275 Statute removed Jewish moneylending, the protected occupation that had given the community royal value — making them more expendable to the Crown.
• Forced into trades from which Christian guilds excluded them, many Jews fell into poverty and a few turned to coin clipping, leading to mass executions in 1278.
• The yellow badge made Jewish identity visible and easy to police, supporting later antisemitic propaganda.
• Significance over time: the Statute set the legal pattern (royal edict, public marker, restricted trade) that the 1290 expulsion completed.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘Financial gain, rather than religious belief, was the most important reason for the expulsion of the Jews in 1290.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The expulsion produced a parliamentary tax grant of around £116,000, the largest of the reign, which Edward needed for war and castle-building in Wales.
• The Crown also seized Jewish houses, synagogues and outstanding debts after 1290.
• Edward had already turned to the Riccardi of Lucca for credit, so the Jewish community had lost its financial usefulness.
• Earlier moves — the 1278 coin-clipping executions, repeated tallages — show the king extracting Jewish wealth before disposing of the community.

Arguments to weigh against:
• The blood libels at Norwich (1144) and Lincoln (1255) and the pogrom at York (1190) show centuries of religious hatred predating Edward.
• The 1275 Statute’s yellow badge and ban on usury were religious as much as economic measures, modelled on Church teaching.
• Edward’s mother Eleanor of Provence and the friars pressed him to act for religious reasons.
• Edward had already expelled Jews from Gascony in 1287, before the parliamentary tax bargain, suggesting a religious agenda was already in place.

A strong response weighs the financial bargain against centuries of religious antisemitism and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hoover's response to the Great Depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rugged individualism — Hoover insisted that Americans should overcome the slump through self-reliance, voluntary cooperation and local charity rather than federal welfare.
• The 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff raised US import duties on over 20,000 goods to record levels in an attempt to protect American factories and farms.
• The 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation made $2 billion of federal loans available to banks, railroads and large businesses to prevent further failures.
• Hoover authorised some public works such as the Hoover Dam (begun 1931) but refused direct federal aid to individuals.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did Hoover's policies fail to solve the Depression?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rugged individualism told Americans to rely on themselves and on charity, but private giving could not match the scale of the slump — soup kitchens were overwhelmed and Hoovervilles spread.
• The Hawley–Smoot Tariff (1930) was meant to protect US industry but provoked retaliation by 25 trading partners; world trade halved between 1929 and 1934, devastating American farm exports.
• The Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) lent to banks and large businesses but Hoover refused to extend it to families or municipalities — critics called it ‘a millionaires’ dole’.
• Hoover’s federal public works (Hoover Dam) were tiny relative to the 12–13 million unemployed and could not stem mass joblessness.
• The dispersal of the Bonus Army in July 1932 by federal troops destroyed what remained of his moral authority.
• The cumulative effect was that the slump deepened on his watch and the political appetite shifted decisively towards federal intervention — opening the way for Roosevelt’s landslide.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects across multiple policies with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one policy.
Emerging: Identifies a failure without explaining its cause.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Franklin D. Roosevelt's 1932 election campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Roosevelt promised ‘a new deal for the American people’ in his July 1932 Democratic Convention speech — the slogan that would define his presidency.
• He flew to Chicago to deliver his nomination acceptance in person, breaking the tradition that candidates stayed away from the convention — signalling activism.
• He campaigned in 38 states by train, an exhausting routine designed to show he was physically capable despite having had polio since 1921.
• His campaign attacked banks, big business and Hoover’s rugged individualism while promising explicit federal action; he avoided detailed plans, focusing on confidence and tone.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the dispersal of the Bonus Army in July 1932 damage Hoover's chances of re-election?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 17,000 unemployed First World War veterans had marched on Washington and camped near the Capitol demanding early payment of a service bonus due in 1945.
• On 28 July 1932 General Douglas MacArthur led federal troops with bayonets, tear gas and tanks to clear the camp — against orders to be cautious.
• Two veterans were shot dead and an infant died of tear-gas exposure; the camp was burned to the ground.
• Newsreel footage of US soldiers attacking US war veterans circulated in cinemas across the country.
• The episode confirmed Hoover’s public image as cold and out of touch — reinforcing the message of Hoovervilles and Hoover blankets.
• It came just four months before the November election; Roosevelt used the contrast to position himself as the candidate of compassion and action, helping deliver his 472–59 electoral landslide.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from a single event to the political verdict, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to retelling the event.
Emerging: Identifies the dispersal without explaining its political effect.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on Hoover's defeat in 1932: his economic policies, or his public image? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of his economic policies:
• The Hawley–Smoot Tariff (1930) cut world trade in half by 1934 and was condemned in advance by over 1,000 economists.
• The RFC (1932) lent to banks but refused individuals or local government, leaving most Americans untouched by federal aid.
• Rugged individualism rested on the belief that voluntary effort would suffice; with 12–13 million unemployed, voters had stopped believing it.
• His policies failed to halt 9,000 bank failures, 25,000 business collapses and 25% unemployment.

In support of his public image:
• Hoover refused to invite reporters into the White House and disliked public speaking, leaving him unable to defend his record on radio.
• Hoovervilles, Hoover blankets and Hoover flags personalised the Depression as his fault.
• His decision to dress for dinner in the White House every night while bread lines grew outside became a symbol of his detachment.
• The dispersal of the Bonus Army by federal troops in July 1932 confirmed an image of cold authority.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that the policies caused the slump to deepen, but it was Hoover’s public image — especially after the Bonus Army — that delivered the scale of his defeat. The strongest answers note that the two reinforced each other: had Hoover communicated like Roosevelt, he might have softened the political damage from his economic record; had his record been better, his cold manner might have been forgiven.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Roosevelt's victory in the 1932 presidential election on the federal government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Roosevelt won 472 electoral votes to Hoover’s 59 and 42 of the 48 states — one of the largest landslides of the twentieth century.
• The Democrats also won large majorities in both houses of Congress, ending the Republican federal dominance that had run since 1921.
• The mandate gave Roosevelt the political space to launch the New Deal at speed once he was inaugurated in March 1933 — the ‘Hundred Days’ (Lesson 8) saw 15 major laws passed.
• Confidence in federal government rose during the four-month inter-regnum, even as bank panics deepened, because voters expected change.
• Roosevelt’s fireside chats from 1933 onwards transformed the relationship between president and public — explaining policy directly through radio.
• The 1932 election also realigned American politics for a generation — the New Deal coalition (urban workers, southern Democrats, African-Americans, organised labour) would dominate elections until the late 1960s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from electoral landslide to long-term political realignment with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation of effects with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to the result itself.
Emerging: Identifies that Roosevelt won without explaining the consequences.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the Lytton Report on the Manchurian Crisis, presented to the League of Nations in October 1932.
‘The military operations of the Japanese troops on the night of 18-19 September 1931 cannot be regarded as measures of legitimate self-defence. The recently established Manchukuo regime cannot be regarded as having resulted from a genuine and spontaneous independence movement; it is an instrument of Japanese policy.’

Using Source A, identify two findings of the Lytton Report.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded points with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear points, briefly supported.
Developing: One point clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Japanese military action on 18-19 September 1931 was not legitimate self-defence.
• The new Manchukuo regime was not the result of a genuine independence movement.
• Manchukuo was an instrument of Japanese policy — a puppet state.
• Implicit finding: the Mukden Incident did not justify the invasion.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Manchurian Crisis from the Mukden Incident in September 1931 to Japan’s resignation from the League of Nations in 1933.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 18 September 1931: Mukden Incident — staged explosion on the South Manchurian Railway used as pretext.
• September 1931 onwards: Japanese forces advanced rapidly into Manchuria; China appealed to the League.
• December 1931: Lytton Commission established; the League sent investigators to Manchuria.
• February 1932: Manchuria fully under Japanese control; renamed Manchukuo with the deposed Chinese emperor as puppet ruler.
• October 1932: Lytton Report published, finding Japan in the wrong.
• February 1933: League Assembly voted 42-1 to adopt the Lytton Report.
• March 1933: Japan resigned from the League rather than accept the verdict; the League imposed no sanctions and took no further action.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a 1936 speech to the League Assembly by Emperor Haile Selassie of Abyssinia, after Italian forces had taken Addis Ababa.
‘I, Haile Selassie I, Emperor of Ethiopia, am here today to claim that justice which is due to my people. There is no precedent for a Head of State himself speaking in this Assembly. But there is no precedent for a people being victims of such injustice. We were the first nation to call upon the League. We have been told that the League can do nothing. It is us today. It will be you tomorrow.’

Source C: An extract from a private memorandum by British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare to the British Cabinet, December 1935.
‘We must avoid driving Mussolini into Hitler’s arms at all costs. The Italian dictator can still be bought back. The choice before us is not between principle and expediency, but between two evils — an aggrieved Italy joined to Germany, or a partial concession that may yet keep her with us.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Abyssinian Crisis. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a moral protest by the head of state of the victim country; warns the League that its weakness puts other countries at risk. Provenance: a famous public speech to the League Assembly by Haile Selassie in 1936; designed to shame the great powers and rally world opinion. Own knowledge: Italian forces did take Addis Ababa in May 1936; sanctions were lifted in July 1936; Haile Selassie went into exile.
Source C — Content: candid British strategic calculation that Mussolini must be appeased to keep him away from Hitler. Provenance: a private memorandum to the Cabinet; likely to express genuine policy thinking; not designed for public consumption. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935 offered Mussolini around two-thirds of Abyssinia; the leak forced Hoare’s resignation; the calculation about Hitler proved miscalculated when Mussolini joined the Rome-Berlin Axis anyway in October 1936.
Judgement: B is highly useful as a moral and political document but partial; C is highly useful for the strategic calculation behind British policy but reflects only one strand of British thinking.

practice_questions.text:
‘The League of Nations was killed by its members rather than by its structure.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Sanctions on Italy could have bitten but were deliberately weakened: oil, coal and steel were excluded and the Suez Canal stayed open.
• The Hoare-Laval Pact showed the League’s two leading members privately offering an aggressor most of what he wanted.
• Excluding oil was a political choice by Britain and France, not a structural fact.
Challenging the statement:
• The structural problems were genuine: no army, the unanimity rule, and the absent USA.
• The Manchurian failure owed as much to distance and to Japan’s permanent Council seat as to British and French choices.
• The Depression destroyed the cooperative economic conditions whatever members intended.
Judgement: members deserve heavy blame, above all over Abyssinia, but the structural defects made enforcement difficult from the start.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a 1933 speech by Yosuke Matsuoka, head of the Japanese delegation to the League of Nations, on Japan’s resignation from the League.
‘The Japanese government, which has consistently striven to follow the path of peace, finds itself unable to accept the report. Japan has done nothing in Manchuria that other great powers have not done elsewhere. We will not be lectured by those whose own colonies were taken by force. Japan therefore withdraws from the League.’

Using Source F, identify two things it shows about Japan’s response to the Manchurian Crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• Japan rejects the Lytton Report and justifies withdrawal from the League.
• The ‘great-power hypocrisy’ argument: Japan has done nothing other empires did not do.
• Own knowledge: the Assembly adopted the report 42-1 in February 1933, Japan resigned in March 1933 and kept Manchukuo.
• Worth noting: an official justification that says nothing about the Mukden Incident being staged.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Abyssinian Crisis from the Wal Wal incident in December 1934 to the lifting of League sanctions in July 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• December 1934: the Wal Wal incident on the Italian Somaliland-Abyssinian border gave Mussolini a pretext.
• October 1935: Italian forces invaded Abyssinia from Eritrea and Italian Somaliland.
• November 1935: the League declared Italy the aggressor and imposed economic sanctions, but excluded oil, coal and steel; the Suez Canal stayed open.
• December 1935: the Hoare-Laval Pact was secretly negotiated, offering Mussolini around two-thirds of Abyssinia; the plan was leaked and Hoare was forced to resign.
• Spring 1936: Italian forces, using tanks, aircraft and mustard gas, advanced steadily.
• May 1936: Italian forces took Addis Ababa; Haile Selassie went into exile; Italy declared the conquest complete.
• June 1936: Haile Selassie’s speech to the League Assembly in Geneva.
• July 1936: League sanctions lifted; the League’s authority effectively destroyed.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Babington Plot of 1586.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the plot gave Walsingham the written evidence (Mary’s ciphered reply) needed to put Mary on trial — something earlier plots had not produced.
• It allowed Parliament to demand and obtain Mary’s execution after almost two decades of pressure.
• It demonstrated the value of the intelligence service: Phelippes’s code-breaking became the template for later Elizabethan counter-espionage.
• Significance over time: Mary’s removal cleared the political path for the 1603 Stuart succession; it also pushed Philip II from supporting plots to launching the Armada in 1588.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Mary’s execution in 1587 led to war with Spain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It removed Philip II’s preferred political solution (a Mary-led coup) and committed him to a full invasion of England.
• Spanish preparations for the Armada accelerated through 1587 — Drake’s raid on Cadiz in April 1587 was a direct response to those preparations.
• It allowed the Pope to renew the call for a Catholic crusade against England, with Philip II as its leader.
• It hardened the English regime: the 1593 Act against Popish Recusants would not have had the same support without Mary’s removal as a focus.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Mary’s arrival in England in 1568 changed Elizabeth’s religious policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Within 18 months, Mary’s presence helped trigger the Northern Rebellion of 1569 — the earls planned to marry her to Norfolk and force her recognition as heir.
• It contributed to the Pope’s 1570 bull Regnans in Excelsis, which excommunicated Elizabeth and made every recusant a potential traitor.
• It pushed the regime towards harsher recusancy laws — the 1571 Treasons Act and rising fines.
• It justified the expansion of Walsingham’s intelligence service to track Catholic plotters around Mary.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Ridolfi and Throckmorton plots for the treatment of Mary, Queen of Scots.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, each plot intensified Parliament’s demands for Mary’s execution — demands Elizabeth resisted.
• Ridolfi (1571) led to the execution of the Duke of Norfolk in 1572 but spared Mary; it also showed Spain was willing to back Catholic invasion.
• Throckmorton (1583) revealed French involvement and led to the expulsion of the Spanish ambassador, hardening foreign policy.
• Significance over time: each plot tightened the rules around Mary’s captivity and built the political pressure that made the Babington trap politically possible in 1586.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the way Walsingham trapped Mary in 1586.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was a Catholic conspiracy led by Anthony Babington to assassinate Elizabeth and free Mary, Queen of Scots.
• Letters between Mary and the plotters were smuggled in and out of Chartley Hall hidden inside a beer barrel.
• Walsingham’s agents intercepted every letter; Thomas Phelippes deciphered them, including Mary’s reply approving the plot.
• Babington and the conspirators were tried and executed in September 1586; Mary was tried at Fotheringhay in October.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Keeping Mary, Queen of Scots, alive in England made Elizabeth safer rather than weaker.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the effect of Mary, Queen of Scots, on Elizabeth’s security? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• While Mary lived, Catholic plotters focused on a clear figurehead and could be tracked by Walsingham — her household at Chartley produced the evidence used to convict her.
• Plot interceptions (Ridolfi, Throckmorton, Babington) gave Parliament the political cover to harden recusancy law against the wider Catholic community.
• Philip II preferred a Mary-led coup to a full invasion; while she lived, large-scale war with Spain could be deferred.
• Foreign Catholic powers were divided over Mary’s fate, weakening their ability to act in concert.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Mary’s existence triggered the Northern Rebellion of 1569 within eighteen months of her arrival.
• The 1570 papal excommunication was issued partly because of her claim and made every English Catholic a potential traitor.
• The repeated plots required an ever-larger and more expensive intelligence operation.
• It was only after her execution that Spain launched the Armada — arguably the most direct threat the regime ever faced.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Popish Plot of 1678.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was a fabricated conspiracy in which Titus Oates and Israel Tonge swore that Jesuits were planning to assassinate Charles II and replace him with his Catholic brother James.
• It was given credibility by the unsolved murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey, the magistrate who had taken Oates’s deposition, on Primrose Hill in October 1678.
• It led to the Second Test Act of 1678, which barred Catholics from sitting in Parliament, though the Lords forced through a proviso that let James, Duke of York keep his seat.
• It produced a wave of executions: at least 22 Catholics, including Archbishop Oliver Plunkett in 1681, were hanged on the basis of Oates’s perjury.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write a narrative account analysing how the Popish Plot caused a national crisis between 1678 and 1681.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Autumn 1678: Oates and Tonge swear depositions accusing Jesuits of planning to murder Charles II; their stories appear far-fetched but fit existing fears of France and Catholicism.
• 17 October 1678: Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey is found dead on Primrose Hill; the unsolved murder turns Oates’s claims into a credible threat in Protestant eyes.
• Late 1678: Letters from Edward Coleman, James’s secretary, are seized and seem to corroborate the plot; he is executed in December 1678 and the Second Test Act bars Catholics from Parliament.
• 1679–1681: At least 22 Catholics, including Archbishop Plunkett, are executed; Shaftesbury seizes the moment to launch Exclusion Bills against James.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Second Test Act and the executions that followed the Popish Plot.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It triggered the Second Test Act of 1678, which excluded Catholics from Parliament, although a proviso let James keep his seat in the Lords.
• It produced a wave of trials and executions of Catholic priests and laymen — at least 22 in all — including Archbishop Oliver Plunkett in 1681.
• It created the political opening Shaftesbury needed to launch the Exclusion Bill campaign against James as heir.
• It hardened popular anti-Catholicism in pamphlet, sermon and pope-burning processions, leaving an enduring legacy of suspicion.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Rye House Plot of 1683 and how it was discovered.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was a Whig conspiracy to ambush and kill Charles II and James, Duke of York, at Rye House in Hertfordshire as they returned from the Newmarket races.
• It was abandoned when a fire at Newmarket forced the royal brothers to leave early, and was betrayed by the informer Josiah Keeling in June 1683.
• It led to the executions of Lord William Russell in July 1683 and Algernon Sidney in December 1683, while the Earl of Essex died in the Tower.
• Its discovery caused the Duke of Monmouth, Charles’s illegitimate Protestant son, to flee to the Continent.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Rye House Plot for Charles II’s authority after 1683.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the plot allowed Charles to portray the Whigs as violent republicans and to govern with renewed Tory support.
• It justified the purge of corporations through quo warranto writs, replacing Whig officeholders with loyal Tories and remaking borough charters.
• Significance over time: it secured Charles’s personal rule from 1681 to 1685 without summoning Parliament and laid the foundation for the smooth Tory accession of James II in 1685.
• It also contributed to longer-term resentment that would resurface in Monmouth’s rebellion of 1685 and ultimately the Glorious Revolution of 1688.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Fear of Catholicism, not the ambition of politicians, shaped the last years of Charles II’s reign.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the politics of Charles II’s later reign? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Anti-Catholic fear made Oates’s fabricated Popish Plot believable in 1678 and produced the Second Test Act and a wave of executions.
• It was fear of a Catholic king, not personal hatred of James, that powered the Exclusion Bills of 1679–81 and the formation of the Whig party.
• Even the Rye House conspirators justified violence by pointing to a Catholic succession, showing how religion drove radical action.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Political ambition, especially Shaftesbury’s, exploited fear rather than created it; the Whig and Tory split was a struggle for power as much as theology.
• Chance events — the Newmarket fire, Godfrey’s murder, Keeling’s betrayal — tipped the balance in directions no one planned.
• Charles II’s skilful use of dissolution, French subsidies and the corporations gave the monarchy options that fear alone could not have produced.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from the 9/11 Commission Report, presented to the United States Congress and President in July 2004.
‘The most important failure was one of imagination. We do not believe leaders understood the gravity of the threat… The attacks of September 11, 2001, were a shock, but they should not have come as a surprise. Islamist extremists had given plenty of warning that they meant to kill Americans indiscriminately and in large numbers.’
Source B: Extract from President George W. Bush’s address to a joint session of Congress, 20 September 2001, announcing the War on Terror and setting out demands to the Taliban.

Study Sources A and B. How useful are Sources A and B to an historian studying the impact of the 9/11 attacks on the United States? Explain your answer using Sources A and B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and own contextual knowledge for both sources to reach a substantiated judgement on usefulness.
Secure: Clear use of all three for both sources with some judgement.
Developing: Two of the three treated.
Emerging: Description of the sources without evaluation.

Indicative content:
• Content of Source A: three years after the event the official American verdict located part of the impact in a recognised intelligence failure, which is what justified the new surveillance powers and the Department of Homeland Security.
• Provenance of Source A: a bipartisan commission reporting to Congress carries unusual authority, but it was written for a domestic audience and for the body that had funded the response.
• Content of Source B: Bush’s address shows the immediate political impact — a declared War on Terror, an ultimatum to the Taliban, and the demand that other states choose a side.
• Provenance of Source B: a speech made nine days after the attacks is making a case and raising the cost of later restraint, so it shows intent rather than outcome.
• Own knowledge: NATO invoked Article 5 on 12 September; the USA Patriot Act was signed on 26 October; Operation Enduring Freedom began on 7 October 2001.
• Judgement: together they cover the political and institutional impact well, but neither shows the impact on ordinary Americans, including the rise in harassment of Muslim and Sikh communities.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the four-flight attack of 11 September 2001 unfolded between 8.46am and 10.28am Eastern time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking the four flights as a chain with precise timings (8.46am Flight 11, 9.03 Flight 175, 9.37 Flight 77, 9.59 South Tower collapse, 10.03 Flight 93, 10.28 North Tower collapse); reaches the moment the towers fell with clear cause and consequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with timings.
Developing: Events listed; some links missing.
Emerging: Thin chronology, vague on timings.

Indicative content:
• 8.46am: American 11 hits the North Tower of the World Trade Center.
• 9.03am: United 175 hits the South Tower; live television confirms a coordinated attack.
• 9.37am: American 77 hits the Pentagon; New York airspace and the FAA close.
• 9.59am: South Tower collapses, killing those still in stairwells and large numbers of firefighters.
• 10.03am: United 93 crashes near Shanksville after passengers retake the cockpit; the fourth target (probably the Capitol or White House) is denied.
• 10.28am: North Tower collapses, ending the immediate sequence; the death toll reaches 2,977.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Photograph of New York firefighters and rescue workers on the rubble of the World Trade Center, published in international news media on 12 September 2001.

Study Source B. Source B suggests that the immediate response to the attacks fell on New York’s own emergency services. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the photograph without inference.

Indicative content:
• The photograph, taken on the same afternoon, suggests the speed at which civilians and emergency services moved into the wreckage despite the dust, smoke and risk of secondary collapse.
• The presence of firefighters in numbers implies the response was led by the city’s emergency services rather than the military, supporting the picture of 9/11 as an attack first absorbed at municipal level.
• The fact that an Associated Press photographer reached the scene that afternoon suggests media access was rapid, helping make 9/11 the most-photographed event of its kind.
• The crowded scene supports the casualty figure of 2,977 — the rescue effort was outsized because the loss of life among civilians and first responders was outsized.

practice_questions.text: ‘NATO’s invocation of Article 5 on 12 September 2001 was the most important international consequence of the 9/11 attacks.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: the unanimous invocation by all nineteen members was the first in NATO’s history and treated the attack as an attack on the whole alliance.
• Agree: it underwrote European participation in the 2001 Afghanistan campaign and in the International Security Assistance Force from December 2001.
• Agree: it redefined a Cold War alliance built against the Soviet Union as a counter-terrorism alliance fighting in Asia.
• Disagree: UN Security Council Resolution 1368, passed the same day, gave the wider legal recognition of a right of self-defence.
• Disagree: the deeper international consequence was the War on Terror declared on 20 September, which reached far beyond NATO members.
• Disagree: the political mood created by 9/11 also gave the Bush administration the licence it later used to argue for war in Iraq.
• Judgement: Article 5 mattered most for NATO itself; the wider international consequence was the open-ended War on Terror.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how security inside the United States was changed in the year after the 9/11 attacks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence, with precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• Within weeks cockpit doors were reinforced and pilots were told not to open them during a hijacking, reversing the previous policy of cooperation.
• The USA Patriot Act, signed on 26 October 2001, expanded telephone surveillance, financial monitoring and the detention of non-citizens.
• The Aviation and Transportation Security Act of November 2001 created the Transportation Security Administration and federalised airport screening.
• Through 2002 private airport screeners were replaced, and the screening regime most travellers still recognise took shape.
• The Homeland Security Act of November 2002 created the Department of Homeland Security, merging 22 federal agencies in the largest reorganisation of the US government since the Second World War.

practice_questions.text: ‘The 9/11 attacks changed life inside the United States more than they changed American policy abroad.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: air travel changed permanently, with reinforced cockpit doors, universal screening and a new federal screening agency.
• Agree: the Patriot Act gave the FBI and NSA powers over telephone records and electronic communications that had not existed before September 2001.
• Agree: Muslim and Sikh communities reported sharp rises in harassment, with the FBI recording a large jump in anti-Muslim incidents in the following year.
• Disagree: abroad the change was greater still — Operation Enduring Freedom began on 7 October 2001 and NATO went to war outside Europe for the first time.
• Disagree: the pre-emption doctrine and the 2002 National Security Strategy rewrote the rules under which America used force.
• Disagree: the political mood created by the attacks made the 2003 invasion of Iraq possible.
• Judgement: domestic change was deep and lasting, but the reach of the change abroad, including two wars, was greater.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a press conference by US President Dwight D. Eisenhower, Washington, 7 April 1954, replying to a question on the strategic importance of Indochina.
‘You have a row of dominoes set up. You knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly. So you could have a beginning of a disintegration that would have the most profound influences. The loss of Indochina would lead to the fall of Burma, Thailand, the peninsula and Indonesia. Now you are talking really about millions and millions of people.’

Source A suggests that Eisenhower believed the loss of Indochina would spread far beyond Vietnam. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• If one domino falls, the next will follow with ‘certainty’.
• The loss of Indochina would lead specifically to the fall of Burma, Thailand, the peninsula and Indonesia.
• ‘Millions and millions of people’ would be affected by the chain reaction.
• The disintegration would have ‘most profound influences’ beyond Indochina.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Eisenhower spoke on 7 April 1954, a month before the French surrender at Dien Bien Phu.
• By 1954 the USA was paying around 80 per cent of French military costs in Indochina.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a despatch by British war correspondent Brian Crozier, filed from Hanoi in mid-April 1954, three weeks before the surrender at Dien Bien Phu.
‘The garrison’s position is no longer defensible. Vietminh artillery commands every square metre of the plateau, and the runway is closed by mortar fire. Resupply by parachute is increasingly intercepted by anti-aircraft batteries. Without American intervention, which appears unlikely, the surrender is now a matter of weeks rather than months.’

Source B suggests that the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu could no longer be saved. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Vietminh artillery commands every square metre of the plateau.
• The runway is closed by mortar fire, blocking air resupply.
• Parachute resupply is increasingly intercepted by anti-aircraft batteries.
• American intervention ‘appears unlikely’, removing the only realistic external lifeline.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The siege began on 13 March 1954 and the garrison surrendered on 7 May.
• Britain and the US Congress both refused to back American air strikes to relieve the base.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C and Source D.

Source C: An extract from a memorandum by John Foster Dulles, US Secretary of State, written for President Eisenhower in March 1954.
‘A French defeat in Indochina without our intervention would invite further communist aggression in Asia. Yet to commit American forces in support of an unpopular colonial war is politically impossible. The path forward must be to convert Indochina into a national struggle by Asians against communism, with American material but not American troops.’

Source D: An extract from a Vietminh declaration issued from Hanoi after the Dien Bien Phu surrender, May 1954.
‘The fall of Dien Bien Phu is the funeral of French colonialism in Indochina. The Vietnamese people have shown that a determined nation can defeat a foreign army. We will not now exchange French rule for American supervision; we will accept only true independence.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources C and D to a historian studying how the First Indochina War became a Cold War problem in 1954. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source C — Content: shows the US dilemma — defeat would ‘invite further communist aggression’ but US troops would be politically impossible. Provenance: an internal US State Department memo by the Secretary of State; useful for the genuine US calculation, less useful as evidence of public US framing.
Own knowledge: by 1954 the USA was paying around 80 per cent of French military costs; Eisenhower’s domino theory speech of 7 April 1954 expressed the same logic publicly.
Source D — Content: defines the Vietminh’s position as opposition to any foreign supervision, including American. Provenance: a Vietminh public declaration immediately after victory — useful for the official line directed at international audiences, partial because it is propaganda.
Own knowledge: Soviet and Chinese pressure on the Vietminh at Geneva produced the 17th-parallel compromise; the US refusal to sign the final declaration shows how Cold War logic overrode the local settlement.
Judgement: Both sources are useful but partial — C reveals the private US bargain (material aid, not troops), D reveals the Vietminh’s post-victory framing; together they show why the war did not end at Dien Bien Phu but became a long Cold War problem.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how French involvement in Vietnam ended between 1950 and the Geneva agreement of 1954.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the Geneva agreement through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1950: the USA began funding the French war effort following Mao’s 1949 victory in China.
• 1953: the French chose Dien Bien Phu as the location for a set-piece battle, expecting a tactical advantage.
• 13 March 1954: the siege of Dien Bien Phu began with surprise Vietminh artillery in the surrounding hills.
• 7 April 1954: Eisenhower set out the domino theory at his press conference; Britain and Congress refused to back US intervention.
• 7 May 1954: the French garrison surrendered, ending French Indochina.
• 21 July 1954: the Geneva agreement divided Vietnam temporarily at the 17th parallel pending elections in 1956.

practice_questions.text:
‘Cold War thinking, rather than Vietnamese nationalism, explains why the fighting in Vietnam continued after 1954.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• By 1954 the USA was paying around 80 per cent of French military costs because of the domino theory.
• Eisenhower set out that theory publicly on 7 April 1954, treating Indochina as the first domino.
• The USA refused to sign the Geneva declaration because it expected Ho Chi Minh to win the 1956 elections.
• Moscow and Beijing pressed Ho to accept division at the 17th parallel to avoid a wider war.
Disagree:
• Ho declared Vietnamese independence on 2 September 1945, before the Cold War reached Asia.
• The Vietminh had fought the Japanese and then the French for national independence, not for Moscow.
• Diem's repression of suspected Vietminh in the South created a home-grown insurgency from 1959.
• The National Liberation Front of December 1960 grew out of southern grievances against Diem.
Judgement: nationalism supplied the fighters and the cause, but Cold War thinking supplied the money and the reason the war did not end in 1954.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Geneva agreement of July 1954 led directly to the founding of the Vietcong in December 1960.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the founding of the Vietcong through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 21 July 1954: the Geneva agreement divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel and called for elections in 1956.
• Late 1954: the USA refused to sign the final declaration; Diem’s government in Saigon refused on the same grounds, anticipating a Vietminh victory in any nationwide vote.
• 1955: Diem consolidated power in the South and began a campaign of repression against suspected Vietminh.
• 1956: the scheduled reunification elections were not held, removing the political path to unification.
• 1959: armed insurgency by southern communists began, with weapons and direction increasingly coming from the North along the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
• 20 December 1960: the National Liberation Front — the Vietcong — was formally founded, turning Cold War-era frustration with the failed Geneva settlement into a long armed conflict.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1915 British recruitment poster, distributed across London by the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee.
‘At the Front your comrades stand in mud, holding the line for England. They ask you only this: come and stand beside us. Your country needs you. Will you wait until the trenches reach Dover before you answer?’

Source A suggests that recruiting appeals in 1915 used both duty and fear to persuade men to enlist. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Men are told comrades are ‘holding the line for England’ in the mud and need them.
• ‘Your country needs you’ - a direct appeal to patriotic duty.
• ‘Will you wait until the trenches reach Dover’ raises the threat of invasion.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Britain relied on volunteers until conscription began in January 1916.
• Kitchener's recruitment drive of 1914-15 raised the Pals battalions that fought on the Somme.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Western Front developed from movement to stalemate between September 1914 and the spring of 1915.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Marne, race to the sea, First Ypres, trench systems, first gas attack); reaches the trench deadlock through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 5-12 September 1914: Battle of the Marne ended the Schlieffen timetable; German army retreated to the Aisne.
• Mid-September 1914: Both sides began the ‘race to the sea’ — outflanking attempts northwards.
• October-November 1914: First Battle of Ypres — both sides reached the Channel coast; no flanks remained to turn.
• Late 1914: Continuous trench line ran from the Channel to the Swiss border; cavalry became obsolete.
• Early 1915: Both sides developed elaborate trench systems with support and reserve lines.
• April 1915: Germany released chlorine gas at Ypres in the first large-scale chemical attack — an early sign that breakthrough now required new weapons.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private letter by British infantryman Private Ernest Cooper to his mother, dated October 1916.
‘Mother, do not believe what the papers say about the Front. The mud is up to our knees. Every man has trench foot and lice. The shelling is constant. We have been told tomorrow will be a great push. The men are not afraid; they are tired. Tired beyond what you can imagine at home.’

Source C: An extract from the private diary of Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, written in November 1916 at the close of the Battle of the Somme.
‘The Somme was a strategic necessity. The relief of Verdun, the holding of the German army to the Western Front, and the building of an experienced British army for 1917 — all required us to attack and to hold the line in attack. Casualties were grievous, but the alternative was worse.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the experience and strategy of the Battle of the Somme. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: A frontline soldier’s testimony — mud, trench foot, lice, exhaustion. Provenance: a private letter from son to mother, written contemporaneously — likely candid but limited to one section of front, and may have been written to reassure rather than fully describe.
Source C — Content: Haig defends attrition as strategically necessary. Provenance: the commander-in-chief’s own diary, written as the battle closed — useful for his strategic reasoning, but he had a personal stake in justifying the losses.
Own knowledge: 1 July 1916 produced 57,470 British casualties; the Somme did relieve Verdun and inflicted heavy German losses; the BEF that fought on the Somme was largely Kitchener volunteers without prior battle experience.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the soldier’s experience but not for strategy; C is useful for strategic intent but partial in its framing. Used together they capture both ends of the chain.

practice_questions.text:
‘The development of new tactics and technology was the main reason the deadlock of trench warfare was finally broken in 1918.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• German stormtroop infiltration tactics produced the largest advances since 1914 in March 1918.
• The Allies combined creeping barrages, counter-battery fire, tanks and aircraft; Cambrai in 1917 and Amiens in 1918 showed what that could do.
• Predicted artillery fire removed the warning that a long bombardment used to give the defenders.

Disagree:
• American manpower - around two million troops in France by the armistice - gave the Allies weight Germany could not match.
• Germany had burned out its best divisions in the Spring Offensive and could not replace them.
• The naval blockade and the collapse of the German home front thinned German resistance.
• Foch's appointment as Allied commander in March 1918 co-ordinated the attacks as earlier years had not.

Judgement: New tactics and technology broke the line, but American manpower, German exhaustion and unified Allied command are what made the breakthrough count.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential British medical report on trench casualties, dated November 1916.
‘Of the casualties this month, 60 per cent were caused by artillery fire, 25 per cent by machine gun and rifle fire, and 2 per cent by gas. The remaining 13 per cent reflected miscellaneous causes including disease, trench foot, and accident. The dominance of artillery confirms that the modern Western Front is principally a battle of guns.’

Source F suggests that artillery, not rifles or machine guns, dominated the Western Front. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Sixty per cent of that month's casualties came from artillery fire.
• Machine-gun and rifle fire caused a quarter of them.
• The report concludes that the front is ‘principally a battle of guns’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• By 1916 most front-line casualties on the Western Front came from shells rather than bullets.
• Counter-battery fire and sound-ranging became central to attack planning for that reason.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how new weapons and tactics developed on the Western Front between 1915 and 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the 1917 tank deployment through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• April 1915: Germany released chlorine gas at the Second Battle of Ypres — first large-scale chemical attack.
• 1915 onwards: Both sides developed gas masks; phosgene and later mustard gas (1917) followed.
• July 1916: The Battle of the Somme demonstrated the limits of mass infantry assault against entrenched defence.
• September 1916: Tanks (the British Mark I) made their debut at Flers-Courcelette on the Somme.
• 1916-17: Creeping artillery barrages and accurate counter-battery fire became standard tactics.
• November 1917: The Battle of Cambrai used nearly 400 tanks together for the first time, demonstrating the potential of combined arms.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Ngo Dinh Diem alienated rural South Vietnam between 1955 and 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (1956 elections refused, return of land to landlords, Catholic favouritism, Strategic Hamlets, Buddhist crisis); reaches Diem’s 1963 collapse through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1955: Diem took power after a referendum widely seen as rigged.
• 1956: he refused to hold the Geneva-promised reunification elections, which he and the Americans knew Ho would win.
• Late 1950s: land reforms were reversed; landlords reclaimed estates and demanded back-rents to 1945.
• 1962: the Strategic Hamlets programme forcibly moved peasants into fortified villages, breaking ancestral ties to land.
• Catholic favouritism and family rule (Nhu, Madame Nhu) alienated the Buddhist majority.
• May–June 1963: the Buddhist crisis, including Thich Quang Duc’s self-immolation, destroyed remaining legitimacy.
• November 1963: Diem and Nhu were murdered in a US-tolerated military coup, leaving political chaos.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Vietcong was formed and grew between 1954 and 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with precise detail (post-Geneva regroupment of southern Vietminh, Diem’s policies, NLF founding 1960, Ho Chi Minh Trail, peasant recruitment, growth into insurgency); arrives at the situation in late 1963 through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1954: Geneva Accords required southern Vietminh to regroup north, but many activists stayed underground in the south.
• 1955–1959: Diem’s land policies, sectarian appointments and refusal of elections angered rural peasants.
• December 1960: the National Liberation Front (NLF) was formed; Diem dismissed it as the ‘Vietcong’.
• 1960–62: Hanoi sent troops, weapons and cadres south along the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia.
• 1962–63: the Strategic Hamlets programme drove fresh recruits into Vietcong ranks.
• June–November 1963: the Buddhist crisis and Diem’s overthrow created political chaos in which the Vietcong expanded operations.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Buddhist crisis of May–June 1963 destroyed Diem’s legitimacy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise detail (flag ban Hue, troops firing on protesters, Thich Quang Duc 11 June, Madame Nhu ‘barbecue’ remark, US press reaction, generals plotting); reaches the November coup through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• May 1963: Diem’s government banned Buddhist flags in Hue on Buddha’s birthday while allowing Catholic flags.
• Buddhist protests followed; troops fired into the crowd, killing nine.
• 11 June 1963: monk Thich Quang Duc burned himself to death in a Saigon street; photographs went around the world.
• Madame Nhu publicly described the protests as ‘barbecues’, deepening the scandal.
• Through summer 1963: more self-immolations and brutal raids on Buddhist temples destroyed Diem’s standing.
• The US administration, faced with mounting domestic and international pressure, signalled it would not block a coup.
• November 1963: Diem and Nhu were murdered in a military coup.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Vietcong guerrilla tactics let the insurgency operate against a much stronger opponent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more aspects of guerrilla strategy with concrete examples (peasant integration, Ho Chi Minh Trail, ambushes, tunnel systems, traps, political pressure); arrives at the strategic effect through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked points with causation.
Developing: Points listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin reasoning.

Indicative content:
• Vietcong fighters lived among villagers and worked in rice paddies by day, ambushing patrols by night.
• Recruitment grew from peasant grievances over the Strategic Hamlets programme and Diem’s land policy.
• Tunnel networks (e.g. Cu Chi) allowed fighters to disappear underground when conventional forces arrived.
• Booby-trapped paths and punji stakes neutralised the firepower advantage of foot patrols.
• Hanoi supplied northern weapons, advisers and cadres along the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia.
• Political assassination of Saigon-appointed officials weakened government authority in rural areas.
• Cumulatively, these tactics imposed a steady political and military cost that conventional firepower could not eliminate.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the United States moved from limited support of Diem to encouragement of his overthrow between 1955 and 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (Eisenhower’s domino-theory backing, Kennedy’s expansion of advisers, Strategic Hamlets backed, Buddhist crisis turning point, signalled non-block of coup); arrives at Diem’s 1963 fall through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1955: Eisenhower committed to backing Diem to prevent the dominoes falling in Asia.
• 1956: Washington supported Diem’s refusal of the Geneva-promised elections.
• 1961–63: Kennedy increased US ‘military advisers’ from around 800 to over 16,000 to shore up the southern army.
• 1962–63: the US backed the Strategic Hamlets programme as a counter-insurgency tool.
• May–June 1963: the Buddhist crisis turned American press and political opinion against Diem.
• Autumn 1963: the Kennedy administration signalled to the South Vietnamese generals it would not block a coup.
• 1–2 November 1963: generals seized Saigon, Diem and Nhu were murdered — ending eight years of US client rule under one strongman.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how political instability in South Vietnam between November 1963 and 1964 helped the Vietcong grow.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with precise detail (coup against Diem, seven 1964 governments, ARVN morale, Vietcong territorial gains, Hanoi supply, Tonkin precipitating US escalation); reaches the eve of US escalation through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1–2 November 1963: military coup; Diem and Nhu were murdered.
• 22 November 1963: Kennedy assassinated; LBJ took over US policy mid-crisis.
• 1964: seven different South Vietnamese governments held office in twelve months.
• ARVN morale and command suffered; rural districts increasingly fell under Vietcong control.
• Hanoi accelerated infiltration of cadres and weapons along the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
• August 1964: the Gulf of Tonkin incident gave Johnson the political authority for direct US escalation.
• By early 1965 the question for Washington had shifted from supporting an ally to whether to take over the war.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the idea of representation in Britain and America between 1215 and 1783.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Magna Carta in 1215 tied new taxes to the consent of a council, and the 1265 Parliament brought knights and burgesses into that council.
• At the time: the Civil War and the trial of Charles I in 1649 established that a king could not tax or rule without Parliament.
• At the time: from 1765 the American colonists argued that a Parliament in which they had no members could not lawfully tax them.
• Over time: the Declaration of Independence in 1776 turned the principle into a written constitution that British radicals could quote.
• Over time: 'no taxation without representation' became a founding argument of British reform, from Wyvill's Yorkshire Association to the Chartists.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the American Revolution for the citizen-state relationship in Britain.
