practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • At the time: loss of the thirteen colonies discredited Lord North's government; reform movements at home (Wyvill's Yorkshire Association 1779-83) revived demands for parliamentary reform. • At the time: the Declaration of Independence translated English constitutional ideas (consent, natural rights) into a written constitution that British radicals could quote. • Over time: provided the central reference point for British reformers from Tom Paine's Rights of Man (1791-92) to the Chartists in the 1830s and 1840s, who explicitly cited American precedent. • Over time: the slogan ‘no taxation without representation’ became one of the founding arguments of British democratic reform; it shaped the language of every later franchise extension. • Over time: established that a Parliament that misrepresents people could itself be removed — a precedent that sat behind 19th-century reform agitation. [8 marks] Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail. Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods. Developing: Significance weighted to one period only. Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the American Revolution and the English Revolution were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both were triggered by disputes over taxation without proper consent — ship money in the 1630s, the Stamp Act and Townshend Duties in the 1760s.
• Similarity: both produced written political statements rooted in Lockean ideas of consent — the Agreement of the People (1647) and the Declaration of Independence (1776).
• Similarity: both ended with a king's authority destroyed by his own subjects — Charles I executed in 1649, George III's authority rejected over the colonies in 1776.
• Similarity: both seeded a long tradition of British democratic reform — the Civil War feeding into the Levellers and Chartists, the American Revolution into the Yorkshire Association and Paine.

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: ‘Ideas were the main factor in causing the American Revolution.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Students should weigh ideas against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course. In support of ideas as the main factor: • ‘No taxation without representation’ was a constitutional principle inherited from Magna Carta (1215) and the English Civil War (1642-49) — ideas already familiar to colonists. • Lockean concepts of natural rights and government by consent shaped the Declaration of Independence in 1776 and Tom Paine's Common Sense (1776). • The Patriot leadership were lawyers and merchants steeped in English political theory; their resistance was framed in legal-constitutional language, not just material grievance. Weighed against the economy: • The Seven Years War (1756-63) left Britain with massive debt; the Stamp Act 1765 and Townshend Duties 1767 were attempts to make the colonies pay. • Without the British need for revenue, the constitutional argument might have remained academic. Weighed against war: • The Seven Years War created the imperial situation that made the dispute necessary; without French expulsion from Canada in 1763, the colonies would have continued to depend on British protection. • French intervention from 1778 was decisive in the American victory at Yorktown. Weighed against government: • Lord North's hard-line response to the Boston Tea Party (Coercive Acts 1774) closed Boston harbour and removed Massachusetts self-government — turning a tax dispute into an existential conflict. • George III's intransigence prevented a constitutional compromise that earlier ministries might have brokered. Cross-period weighing: • Compare with 1381 (economy as trigger) and 1649 (ideas as frame) — the American Revolution most resembles 1649 in privileging ideas over immediate economic distress. • Significance over time: ideas are decisive in the long run; the language of 1776 outlived its specific context and reshaped 19th-century British politics. Judgement: Top answers argue ideas of representation and consent supplied the frame, but the economic burden of war debt, government miscalculation (Coercive Acts) and French military intervention all converted constitutional argument into successful revolution. Ideas were necessary but not sufficient. [16 marks plus 4 SPaG] Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing ideas against at least two other factors with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement. Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them. Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Declaration of Independence (1776) for ideas about representation.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • At the time: translated English constitutional principles — consent of the governed, natural rights — into a written constitution for the first time. • At the time: justified rebellion not as an exceptional act but as a duty when government broke its compact with the people; a stronger claim than the Civil War tradition. • Over time: provided British radicals with a working model of representative government on the other side of the Atlantic. • Over time: shaped Tom Paine's Rights of Man (1791-92), the language of the Yorkshire Association, and the People's Charter (1838) — British reformers pointed to the American example. • Over time: its formula ‘life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness’ became a transatlantic shorthand for democratic government, used in human-rights argument well into the twentieth century. [8 marks] Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail. Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods. Developing: Significance weighted to one period only. Emerging: Description of the Declaration without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the colonists' grievances in 1763-75 were different from the grievances of the Pilgrimage of Grace marchers in 1536.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in cause: the colonists' main grievances were taxes imposed without colonial representation (Stamp Act 1765, Townshend Duties 1767); the Pilgrimage of Grace marchers protested the dissolution of the monasteries and the religious break with Rome.
• Difference in framing: the colonists framed grievances in constitutional and Lockean language — rights, consent, representation — while the Pilgrimage framed grievances in defence of an older Catholic religious order.
• Difference in goal: the colonists eventually demanded full independence and a written constitution; the Pilgrimage demanded a free Parliament at York and the restoration of the monasteries within the existing kingdom.
• Difference in scale: the American grievances built into a thirteen-colony coordinated movement over a decade; the Pilgrimage was a single mass rising contained within a single autumn-winter campaign.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Robert Service (Lenin: A Biography, 2000), arguing that the October Revolution succeeded mainly because of Lenin’s own ruthless determination to seize power against his colleagues’ caution. Interpretation B is from the British historian Orlando Figes (A People’s Tragedy, 1996), arguing that October succeeded because the Provisional Government had already destroyed itself.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of October 1917 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Service emphasises Lenin’s personal will; Figes emphasises the structural collapse of the Provisional Government.
• Service treats October as a Bolshevik achievement; Figes treats it as a default outcome.
• Service focuses on intra-party debate (Lenin vs Kamenev/Zinoviev); Figes focuses on the wider political context.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences with grounding in both.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of October 1917 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different evidence: Service uses Lenin’s letters and central committee minutes; Figes uses social history of soldiers, peasants and workers.
• Different purposes: Service is writing a biography of Lenin and naturally foregrounds the man; Figes is writing a panoramic narrative of the revolution.
• Different perspectives: Service focuses on agency; Figes focuses on context.
• Different time of writing: both are post-Soviet, but Figes’s panoramic approach reflects the new social-history wave of the 1990s.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘the October Revolution was a tightly planned coup by a few thousand armed men, not a mass popular rising.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee coordinated the seizure of stations, bridges and government buildings using a few thousand Red Guards, sailors and soldiers.
• Casualties at the Winter Palace were light; defenders were a few hundred cadets and the Women’s Battalion.
• Most Petrograd citizens slept through the night and woke up to find a new government.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• The Bolsheviks held a majority in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets by September, suggesting genuine mass support among workers and soldiers.
• The Second Congress of Soviets ratified the takeover the next morning, giving it a degree of popular legitimacy.
• A coup cannot succeed without an underlying political climate ready to accept it — mass disillusionment with the Provisional Government was real.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation with relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Lenin’s April Theses on Bolshevik strategy in 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• They reversed the Bolshevik leadership’s previous willingness to cooperate with the Provisional Government; Stalin and Kamenev had been arguing for conditional support before April.
• They produced the slogan ‘Peace, Land, Bread’, which separated the Bolsheviks from every other socialist group.
• They committed the party to ending the war, gaining soldier support that culminated in the September soviet majorities.
• They argued for ‘all power to the soviets’, providing the institutional cover under which October would be presented.
• They set the framework for the eventual rejection of the Constituent Assembly in January 1918.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking the April Theses to October.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General comments about Lenin.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The Bolsheviks won power in October 1917 mainly because of the strength of their party organisation.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the strengths of Bolshevik organisation
• consider other factors (such as the failures of the Provisional Government and the Kornilov Affair)
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for organisation being the most important factor:
• Lenin’s 1903 model produced a disciplined party able to act decisively on 24–25 October.
• Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee was a precise instrument other socialist groups could not match.
• Membership grew from 24,000 in February to 350,000 by October — the apparatus could mobilise.

Arguments for other factors:
• The Provisional Government’s refusal to end the war or distribute land created the political conditions for Bolshevik growth.
• The Kornilov Affair handed the Bolsheviks weapons, prestige and Soviet majorities.
• Lenin’s personal insistence on immediate insurrection was decisive against Kamenev and Zinoviev.

Judgement should weigh agency (party, leader) against context (war, land, Kornilov).

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the seizure of power on the night of 24–25 October 1917 on Russian government.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The Provisional Government was overthrown; ministers were arrested in the Winter Palace.
• The Council of People’s Commissars (Sovnarkom) was created the next morning, with Lenin as chairman.
• The Decree on Peace called for an immediate armistice, leading to the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918.
• The Decree on Land legalised the peasant seizures of summer 1917 and abolished private ownership of land.
• The walkout of Mensheviks and right-wing Socialist Revolutionaries from the Second Congress isolated the Bolsheviks but allowed them to govern unopposed in the new institutions.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking the seizure to the new government and its first decrees.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about the takeover.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the founding of Jamestown in 1607.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the Virginia Company landed 105 men on the James River and two-thirds were dead within a year from dysentery, malaria and starvation.
• At the time: survival depended on John Smith’s leadership and on corn supplied by the Powhatan Confederacy under Wahunsenacawh.
• At the time: John Rolfe’s tobacco from about 1614 gave the colony an export crop and turned a military outpost into a plantation society.
• Over time: Jamestown was the first permanent English settlement in North America, the base from which the thirteen colonies grew.
• Over time: the labour demand it created pulled in indentured servants and then enslaved Africans, the first arriving at Point Comfort in 1619.
• Limitation: the colony almost failed several times; its significance rests on what followed rather than on its early strength.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Government was the main factor in the loss of the thirteen American colonies.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Government (in support): after 1763 London taxed the colonies to cover war debt — the Stamp Act of 1765, the Townshend duties of 1767 and the Tea Act of 1773.
• Government (in support): the Coercive Acts of 1774 closed Boston port and hardened colonial opinion; a century of light-touch rule had set very different expectations.
• War: the Seven Years’ War created both the debt and the need for troops in America, and fighting from 1775 turned protest into revolution.
• War: French intervention from 1778 turned a colonial revolt into an Atlantic war Britain could not win, ending at Yorktown in 1781.
• Ideas: ‘no taxation without representation’ gave colonists a principle, not just a grievance, and the Declaration of Independence of 4 July 1776 stated it.
• Economic resources: colonial trade was valuable enough that Britain fought for it, and trade resumed quickly after 1783.
• Judgement: government decisions supplied the grievance, but war supplied the means; without French naval power the colonists could not have made the break stick.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Pilgrim Fathers’ voyage of 1620 for British colonisation of North America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 102 passengers crossed the Atlantic; the Mayflower Compact established self-government by consent before they landed.
• At the time: half the settlers died in the first winter; survival depended on Wampanoag food supplies.
• Over time: triggered the 1630 Puritan ‘Great Migration’ of around 20,000 settlers to Massachusetts under John Winthrop.
• Over time: established New England as a colony defined by religion, education (Harvard 1636) and town-meeting government — very different from plantation Virginia.
• Over time: the Mayflower story has been adopted into United States foundation mythology, shaping modern Anglo-American memory of the colonial period.
• Limitation: in numerical terms the Pilgrim Fathers were a tiny group; their long-term significance is symbolic and political rather than demographic.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1783 Treaty of Paris for the British Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: recognised the independence of the thirteen American colonies; Britain lost around two million colonists and most of its mainland North American empire.
• At the time: produced the Black Loyalist resettlement in Nova Scotia and (from 1787) Sierra Leone — a small but important migration of formerly enslaved people who had fought for the British.
• Over time: pushed British attention east, towards India and the East India Company (Plassey 1757 had already shown the route); Australia was claimed in 1788 partly to replace the lost American convict destinations.
• Over time: the ‘second British Empire’ of the 19th century took a different shape: military rule over non-white populations rather than white settler colonies.
• Limitation: trade with the United States resumed quickly; British exports to America were higher in 1800 than in 1775. The political loss did not break the economic relationship.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which colonisation of Virginia in the 17th century was similar to or different from colonisation of New England in the same period.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Virginia was driven by economic resources — tobacco profits, indentured servants and (from 1619) enslaved Africans; New England was driven by religion — Puritan and Separatist migration.
• Difference: Virginia developed a plantation economy with concentrated landholding; New England developed dispersed town settlements with strong local government and education (Harvard 1636).
• Similarity: both depended on Indigenous food supplies in their early years — the Powhatan in Virginia, the Wampanoag in New England.
• Similarity: both saw catastrophic Indigenous population collapse from European disease, with around 90% of the Atlantic seaboard Indigenous population dying by 1700.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named groups.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of indentured servitude for the early British colonies in North America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: indentured servitude was the main form of migrant labour for 17th-century Virginia, providing tobacco labour for around four to seven years per servant.
• At the time: around 200,000 indentured servants crossed the Atlantic in the 17th century; about four in ten died before completing their term.
• At the time: indentures gave poor English, Scottish and Irish migrants a route to the colonies they could not have afforded otherwise.
• Over time: as tobacco profits rose and the African slave trade scaled up, planters preferred enslaved labour, which had no end-date and no ‘freedom dues’; by 1700 indentures were in decline.
• Over time: the shift from indentured servants to chattel slavery hardened racial categories in the colonies and shaped the legal codes (e.g. Virginia Slave Codes 1705) that defined African slavery as inheritable and lifelong.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the way the Normans built motte-and-bailey castles across England after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The motte was a raised earth mound, sometimes shaped from a natural rise and sometimes built up from scratch using forced English labour, with a wooden tower on top serving as the lord’s residence and final stronghold.
• The bailey was a flat enclosed courtyard beside the motte, surrounded by a ditch and timber palisade, holding the hall, chapel, stables and quarters for the Norman garrison.
• Motte-and-baileys could be built in a fortnight or less using local timber and conscripted labour, which made them the Normans’ tool of choice for rapid colonisation.
• They were sited at strategic points such as river crossings, road junctions and town entrances rather than purely defensive positions.
• Sequence: a castle at Hastings within days of the landing, then castles in the towns that submitted in 1066, then a wave of new building in every district that revolted between 1067 and 1071.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the stone castles built in England between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They had massive walls, sometimes over four metres thick at the base, as at the White Tower of London begun in the 1070s.
• They were built at major royal and urban centres — the White Tower at London, Colchester reusing Roman stonework, and Rochester under Bishop Gundulf — rather than at every minor lordship.
• Construction was slow and expensive, so only the king and the wealthiest tenants-in-chief could afford to build in stone; most castles by 1100 were still timber on earth.
• Stone keeps doubled as administrative centres and royal residences, projecting permanence and Norman authority over the city below.
• Why it mattered: stone said the conquest was permanent. A timber castle could be burned; a keep like the White Tower told Londoners the Normans were never leaving.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which castle-building changed Anglo-Saxon towns and villages between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Whole streets of English houses were demolished to clear ground for castles — at Lincoln, 166 houses were pulled down to make room for the new motte and bailey.
• Local English peasants were forced to dig ditches, raise mottes and cut timber under the labour duty of castle-work, draining the agricultural workforce during building seasons.
• Castle garrisons of Norman knights gave lords a permanent base from which to ride out, collect rents, hold private courts and intimidate the surrounding population.
• The visibility of a motte over a market square stamped Norman authority on every shire town — an effect that the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records as bitter resentment among the English.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about motte-and-bailey castles for the Norman Conquest of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, motte-and-baileys allowed William’s small army (perhaps 8,000 fighting men) to plant a network of strongholds across a kingdom of two million people, beginning within hours of landing at Hastings.
• The speed of construction (a fortnight or less) meant the Normans could respond to revolt by flooding disturbed areas with new castles — the response to the 1067–71 rebellions and the Harrying of the North.
• Importance later: by 1100 there were roughly 500 castles, and the network they formed underpinned tenant-in-chief lordship throughout the twelfth century.
• They reshaped English geography: market towns, road junctions and county centres reorganised around the new fortresses, a pattern still visible in cities such as York, Lincoln and Cambridge.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about where the Normans chose to site their castles.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Castles built at river crossings (Wallingford, Cambridge) and road junctions (Berkhamsted) gave the Crown control over movement, trade routes and the ability to track armed bands.
• Two castles in towns such as York and Lincoln — on opposite banks of the river — ensured no rebel force could occupy a city without facing armed Norman garrisons from both sides.
• The Welsh Marches were anchored by lordships at Hereford, Shrewsbury and Chester, creating a fortified frontier that stabilised the western borderlands.
• Castles in former rebel zones such as Yorkshire after the Harrying gave the Crown a permanent armed presence and discouraged further revolt.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Norman control.

‘Castles are the reason the Normans kept England. A few thousand knights could not have held two million people without a fortified base in every shire.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons why the Normans held on to England? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: castles were the most important reason the Normans held England.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The number of castles rose from c.50 to c.500 between 1066 and 1100 — a permanent armed Norman garrison in every shire which made revolt physically harder.
• Castles such as the White Tower of London projected royal authority over the capital and the kingdom’s economic centre.
• During the rebellions of 1067–71 and the Harrying of the North, new castle-building was William’s direct response to revolt and the means of preventing future ones.
• By 1100 castles structured tenant-in-chief lordship across the country — the basis of Norman political control.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The Battle of Hastings itself was won by cavalry and archery, not castles — without that military victory there would have been no conquest to consolidate.
• The Harrying of the North (1069–70) terrorised resistance into submission through deliberate destruction, not through castle garrisons alone.
• The redistribution of land to c.180 tenants-in-chief (recorded in Domesday) tied the new aristocracy to the Crown by reward, with castles being only one part of that bond.
• Norman government structures — the inherited shires, sheriffs and writs — allowed routine taxation and justice to function alongside military control.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1932 Nazi Party leaflet claiming Hitler offered the only solution to mass unemployment) and Interpretation B (a 1932 SPD newspaper editorial blaming Bruning's austerity for the depth of the Depression) on the cause of the political crisis of 1930–32. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the crisis as solvable only by Hitler — mass unemployment, dependency on US loans and political stalemate required a strong leader.
• Interpretation B presents the crisis as worsened by Bruning's deflationary policies — cuts to wages and benefits when six million were unemployed deepened the slump.
• Main difference: A frames the crisis as a leadership vacuum requiring Hitler; B frames it as policy failure that created political space for extremism.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1932 Nazi leaflet) and Interpretation B (a 1932 SPD newspaper editorial) give different views about the cause of the 1930–32 political crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the Nazi leaflet aimed to recruit voters frightened by unemployment; the SPD editorial aimed to defend the elected government against authoritarianism.
• They use different evidence — the leaflet cites unemployment figures and Hitler's leadership claims; the editorial cites Bruning's emergency decrees and Article 48 abuse.
• They were produced from different political positions — both written in 1932 but with opposing interests in how the crisis was interpreted.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The 1929 Wall Street Crash and the Depression that followed were the single most important cause of Hitler's rise to power.' How convincing is Interpretation A about the rise of the Nazi Party between 1928 and 1932?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (12 seats) in 1928 to 37.4% (230 seats) in July 1932 — a rise that tracked unemployment reaching six million.
• Convincing because Nazi policy did not change in this period — the surge was driven by external economic catastrophe, not by ideological conversion.
• Less convincing because Bruning's austerity worsened the Depression and made the political system uniquely vulnerable — a different Chancellor might have contained the Nazi rise.
• Less convincing because Nazi propaganda, SA street violence and fear of Communism all contributed; the Depression was the trigger but not the only cause.
• Less convincing because Nazi support actually fell from 37% to 33% by November 1932, suggesting the Depression alone was not driving an unstoppable rise.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing as the trigger but understates the role of Bruning, propaganda and political miscalculation by Hindenburg's circle.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Triggered withdrawal of US loans — the 25 billion marks of capital that had funded German industry under the Dawes Plan was recalled, causing factories and banks to fail.
• Caused mass unemployment — industrial output fell by 40% between 1929 and 1932; six million Germans were jobless by 1932, about a third of the workforce.
• Destroyed political stability — the SPD-led grand coalition collapsed in March 1930 and Hindenburg appointed Bruning, who governed by Article 48 emergency decree.
• Drove voters to extremes — the Nazi vote rose from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932; the Communist KPD also grew, from 10.6% to 16.9%, squeezing the political centre.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the Nazi Party grew rapidly in support between 1928 and 1932.
You may consider:
• the impact of the Depression and unemployment
• the role of Nazi propaganda, the SA and Hitler's appeal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Depression as trigger: industrial output fell 40% (1929–32); six million unemployed by 1932; banks failed; soup queues stretched through major cities.
• Bruning's austerity worsened conditions: wage and benefit cuts deepened the slump; government by Article 48 alienated Reichstag voters; he was nicknamed the ‘Hunger Chancellor’.
• Nazi vote surge: 12 seats (1928) to 107 (1930) to 230 (July 1932) — biggest party in Reichstag.
• SA growth: from 100,000 in 1930 to 400,000 by July 1932; offered welfare and uniforms to unemployed young men; provided street muscle and the appearance of order.
• Propaganda and Hitler's appeal: Goebbels's modern campaigns; Hitler's aircraft tour of twenty cities; targeted messages to unemployed (jobs), middle class (anti-Communism), farmers (subsidies), industrialists (rearmament), nationalists (Versailles revision); unifying concept of Volksgemeinschaft.
• Limits: November 1932 vote fell to 196 seats; party finances collapsing.
• Conclusion: the Depression and Bruning's response provided the opportunity; Nazi propaganda, SA muscle and Hitler's targeted appeal converted that opportunity into votes — but the surge had peaked by November 1932 and only Hindenburg's appointment of Hitler in January 1933 prevented its decline.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1933 conservative writer arguing middle-class fear of Communism drove voters to Hitler) and Interpretation B (a modern academic study arguing Goebbels's propaganda and Hitler's personal appeal were decisive) on why ordinary Germans voted Nazi between 1930 and 1932. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A emphasises negative motivation — voters were repelled by KPD growth and the threat of Bolshevik revolution.
• Interpretation B emphasises positive attraction — Goebbels's modern propaganda machine, Hitler's aircraft tours and his oratory created loyalty.
• Main difference: A frames Nazi voters as reluctant defenders against Communism; B frames them as actively persuaded by Nazi messaging.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about the early Soviet government? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A treats Lenin’s early decrees as popular, practical responses to peasant land hunger and war weariness; B treats them as cynical promises designed to neutralise opponents until the Cheka could be built.
• A presents the dispersal of the Constituent Assembly as a regrettable necessity; B presents it as proof the Bolsheviks never intended to share power.
• Reference must be made to specific content of both interpretations rather than just paraphrase.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual evidence from both interpretations. Secure: comparison made with some textual reference. Developing: paraphrase of each rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the role of the Cheka under Lenin?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: A may be a Soviet-era textbook defending the Cheka as a wartime necessity; B may be a Western academic study highlighting Red Terror victims.
• Different time of writing: post-1991 access to Cheka archives changed what historians could say.
• Different perspectives or schools: orthodox Soviet versus liberal/Western (e.g. Pipes) framings of Bolshevik violence.
• Different evidence base — memoirs, party records, victim testimony.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons the Bolsheviks won the Civil War? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test what the interpretation claims (e.g. that Trotsky’s leadership was decisive) against named contextual evidence: Trotsky’s armoured train, use of ex-Tsarist officers under commissars, Red Army growth from c.300,000 to c.5 million.
• Weigh against alternative factors: White disunity (Denikin and Kolchak never coordinating), Red interior lines around Moscow and Petrograd, peasant fear of landlord restoration.
• Note historiographical position — totalitarian-school readings emphasise Bolshevik organisation; revisionists stress structural advantages.
• Reach a substantiated judgement on how convincing the interpretation is overall.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge applied with a clear judgement. Developing: knowledge used but unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on Russia in 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Territorial: loss of Ukraine, Poland, Finland, the Baltic provinces — about a third of the population and half of industry.
• Economic: loss of coal and grain regions worsened food shortages and contributed to War Communism.
• Political: the treaty split the Bolsheviks from the Left SRs, prompting the SR uprising and the August 1918 attempt on Lenin’s life.
• Military: White generals used the treaty to recruit support, accelerating the Civil War.
• Effects must be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with some development. Developing: effects identified but undeveloped. Emerging: simple description of the treaty.]

practice_questions.text: ‘Trotsky’s leadership of the Red Army was the most important reason the Bolsheviks won the Civil War.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Trotsky’s leadership, White disunity and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for Trotsky’s leadership being most important:
• Built Red Army from c.300,000 to c.5 million using ex-Tsarist officers under political commissars.
• Personally directed front-line operations from his armoured train; held Petrograd against Yudenich.
• Imposed iron discipline including the death penalty for desertion.

Arguments for other factors:
• Geography: Reds held the centre with the railway network; could move troops on interior lines.
• White disunity: Denikin, Kolchak, Yudenich and Wrangel never coordinated; political aims clashed.
• Peasant attitudes: fear that a White victory would reverse the 1917 land seizures.
• Foreign intervention was small in scale and gave the Bolsheviks a propaganda gift.
• Cheka and Red Terror suppressed internal opposition.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. Trotsky was decisive in turning a militia into an army, but his work was only possible because the Reds had geographical advantages and divided enemies.

[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment of factors with some judgement. Developing: factors covered but limited weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing without judgement.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the establishment of the Cheka on Russia between 1917 and 1922.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Suppression of opposition: arrests of Mensheviks, SRs and anarchists; closure of opposition newspapers.
• Red Terror after August 1918: mass executions, hostage-taking, an estimated 140,000 deaths by 1922.
• Created an institutional model of secret-police violence inherited by later bodies (GPU, OGPU, NKVD).
• Enabled grain requisitioning during War Communism by terrorising rural resistance.
• Reinforced the Bolshevik monopoly on power and made multi-party Soviets impossible.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with some development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: description of the Cheka without effects.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1933 editorial in a Republican-leaning newspaper attacking the alphabet agencies as wasteful federal overreach) and Interpretation B (a 1934 article by a Tennessee Valley farmer praising the TVA for bringing electricity and flood control). What is the main difference between these views about the First New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the alphabet agencies as a wasteful expansion of federal power that bypassed Congress and undermined private enterprise.
• Interpretation B presents the TVA as a transformation that brought tangible improvements — electricity, flood control, jobs — to one of the poorest regions in America.
• Main difference: A frames the New Deal as overreach by Washington; B frames it as targeted help that local communities welcomed.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1933 Republican editorial) and Interpretation B (a 1934 article by a Tennessee Valley farmer) give different views about the First New Deal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the editorial spoke to readers worried about federal power and big government; the farmer’s article spoke to neighbours who had benefited directly from TVA dams.
• They use different evidence — the editorial cites federal spending and constitutional concerns; the farmer cites electricity reaching his farm and flood damage prevented.
• They were produced from different positions — an urban Republican commentator opposed to Roosevelt versus a rural beneficiary in a poor region transformed by the TVA.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Roosevelt’s first hundred days saved American capitalism from collapse.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the impact of the First New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Emergency Banking Act of 9 March 1933 stopped a banking collapse: $1 billion of deposits flooded back within a fortnight after the four-day bank holiday and Treasury inspections.
• Convincing because Glass-Steagall and the FDIC restored confidence that personal savings up to $5,000 were safe.
• Convincing because the alphabet agencies (CCC, FERA, AAA, NRA, PWA, TVA) employed millions and lifted farm income by around 50% in two years.
• Less convincing because unemployment remained high — around 11 million still out of work in 1934 — and full recovery only came with war production from 1941.
• Less convincing because the Supreme Court later struck down the NRA (1935) and AAA (1936) as unconstitutional, exposing structural weaknesses.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing in stopping the collapse and rebuilding confidence; less convincing as an explanation of full economic recovery.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Emergency Banking Act of March 1933 on the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stopped the banking panic — the four-day bank holiday closed every bank for inspection; only those judged solvent reopened on 13 March, and around $1 billion of cash flooded back into deposits within a fortnight.
• Restored confidence through Roosevelt’s first fireside chat on 12 March, which explained the rescue in plain language to millions of radio homes — reframing the federal government as protector rather than spectator.
• Created the foundation for further reform — the June 1933 Glass-Steagall Act built on the success by establishing the FDIC, which insured deposits up to $5,000 and separated commercial from investment banking.
• Saved roughly 5,000 sound banks by allowing supervised reopening, and permanently reduced the rate of bank failures — the lifeblood without which alphabet-agency spending could not have circulated through the economy.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Roosevelt’s First New Deal had a major impact on the United States in 1933–34.
You may consider:
• the banking and farm rescue measures
• the alphabet agencies and federal employment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Banking rescue: the Emergency Banking Act (9 March 1933) closed banks for inspection; reopening triggered $1 billion of redeposits; Glass-Steagall (June 1933) created the FDIC insuring savings up to $5,000.
• Farm rescue: the AAA (May 1933) paid farmers to cut production; six million pigs slaughtered; farm income rose around 50% within two years.
• Mass relief: FERA distributed $500 million through Harry Hopkins; CCC employed 2.5 million young men by 1942 at $30/month; CCC built 800 state parks and planted three billion trees.
• Industrial recovery: NRA codes on wages, hours and prices; blue eagle symbol; 2.5 million employers signed up. PWA $3.3 billion built the Grand Coulee Dam, the Lincoln Tunnel and the Triborough Bridge.
• Regional reform: TVA built 20 dams in seven southern states, brought electricity to over half the valley by 1940 and controlled flooding.
• Communication: fireside chats turned the presidency into a daily presence in millions of radio homes.
• Limits: 11 million still unemployed in 1934; the New Deal cushioned but did not end the Depression; the Supreme Court later struck down NRA (1935) and AAA (1936).
• Conclusion: the First New Deal’s major impact was political and psychological as well as economic — it stopped the collapse, rebuilt confidence and redrew the role of the federal government in American life, even though full recovery would have to wait for the war.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The CCC enrolled young unmarried men aged 18–25 in conservation work in national forests, parks and on flood-control schemes. Around 2.5 million young men passed through it by 1942.
• Recruits were paid $30 a month, of which $25 was sent home to their families — combining direct relief for young men with cash transfers to households still suffering from unemployment.
• The CCC planted roughly three billion trees, built 800 state parks and constructed thousands of miles of trails — visible improvements to the American landscape that built support for the New Deal.
• It was administered jointly by the Departments of Labor, Interior and Agriculture and the Army, which ran the camps in military style — controversial to some but giving recruits structure and skills.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which surgery before 1846 and surgery after 1900 were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: pre-1846 surgery relied on speed because patients were conscious; post-1900 surgery used anaesthetics so operations could last hours.
• Difference: pre-1846 theatres were dirty and infection killed up to half of patients; post-1900 aseptic theatres used sterilised instruments, gowns and rubber gloves.
• Similarity: in both periods surgeons worked on amputations, tumours and trauma — the procedures continued, but the survival rates were transformed.
• Similarity: in both periods individual surgeons (Liston, Lister, Halsted) drove change through personal example.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Joseph Lister for the development of surgery in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Lister’s 1865 use of carbolic acid on a compound fracture, published in The Lancet in 1867, cut amputation mortality from around 46% to 15% in his Glasgow ward.
• At the time: he applied Pasteur’s germ theory directly to surgery, providing the first practical antiseptic system.
• Over time: his work was the foundation of aseptic surgery (sterile theatres, gloves, autoclaves) that became standard by 1900.
• Over time: Lister’s methods made invasive surgery on the chest and abdomen possible, opening the door to 20th-century operations.
• Limitation: many British surgeons resisted his system into the 1880s, showing that significance is shaped as much by acceptance as by discovery.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and an awareness of the resistance.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Joseph Lister’s article in The Lancet, March 1867. Writing as professor of surgery at Glasgow, he describes dressing compound fractures with carbolic acid, explains that he is applying Pasteur’s germ theory to wounds, and gives the numbers of his patients who lived and died.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying the development of antiseptic surgery?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: it links a scientific theory to a bedside method, which is what makes 1867 a turning point rather than a lucky remedy.
• Content: the mortality figures let other surgeons test the claim — Lister reported amputation deaths falling from about 46% to 15%.
• Provenance: written by Lister to persuade a sceptical profession through the leading British medical journal, so the results are presented as favourably as he honestly could.
• Contextual knowledge: many British surgeons rejected the carbolic spray into the 1880s because it was unpleasant, results varied in untrained hands and germs were invisible.
• Limitations: it reports one surgeon’s own ward and his own figures, so it cannot show how far practice changed elsewhere.
• Judgement: excellent for the moment of change and for the communication factor, limited as evidence of national practice.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Has science and technology been the main factor in the development of surgery in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to science and technology and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh science and technology against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of science and technology as the main factor:
• Pasteur’s 1861 germ theory was the scientific precondition for Lister’s antisepsis.
• Chemistry produced chloroform and carbolic acid; engineering produced steam autoclaves; Landsteiner’s 1901 blood-group science enabled transfusion.
• X-rays (Röntgen 1895) gave surgeons their first view inside a living body.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Simpson personally tested chloroform; Lister personally pushed antisepsis against resistance; Halsted personally introduced rubber gloves.
• Compare to Vesalius (1543) and Harvey (1628), where individuals were also decisive but science took longer to translate into practice.

Weighed against religion:
• Religion slowed change — clergy quoted Genesis 3:16 against chloroform in childbirth; only Queen Victoria’s use of chloroform in 1853 broke the resistance.

Weighed against war:
• The First World War (1914–18) accelerated the spread of transfusion, X-rays, antisepsis and plastic surgery (Gillies at Sidcup) far faster than peacetime would have allowed.

Judgement: in 19th-century surgery, science and technology was necessary but not sufficient. Without Pasteur there is no Lister; without Lister’s personal advocacy, science alone would not have entered British operating theatres for another generation. Across the longer sweep, the dominant factor varies (religion in 1348, government in 1948).

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes science only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of James Simpson for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Simpson’s 1847 introduction of chloroform in Edinburgh gave British surgery a fast-acting anaesthetic that worked better than ether.
• At the time: chloroform spread quickly into childbirth and surgery, made respectable by Queen Victoria’s use in 1853.
• Over time: his work made longer, deeper operations technically possible, even though the ‘Black Period’ followed because infection had not yet been solved.
• Over time: chloroform remained a standard anaesthetic into the 20th century before safer alternatives replaced it.
• Limitation: anaesthesia without antisepsis raised mortality before Lister; Simpson’s significance is partly defined by what came after him.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of aseptic surgery for British hospitals by 1900.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: instead of killing germs during an operation, aseptic surgery kept them away from the wound altogether.
• At the time: steam autoclaves from the 1880s, gowns, masks, scrubbed hands and rubber gloves changed how a theatre was run.
• At the time: by 1900 most British operating theatres were aseptic and infection rates had fallen sharply.
• Over time: it made long operations inside the chest and abdomen survivable, opening the way to 20th-century surgery.
• Over time: the routines it created — sterile fields and theatre discipline — are still the basis of hospital infection control.
• Limitation: asepsis solved infection in theatre, not on the ward; hospital-acquired infection returned with MRSA from the 1960s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which a castle was attacked in the late thirteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Mining tunnelled under a castle wall, propping the tunnel with timber that was then burned to collapse the masonry above.
• Sapping picked away at masonry under cover of wooden screens, gradually weakening the stonework.
• Bombardment used stone-throwing engines such as the counterweight trebuchet (e.g. Edward’s ‘Warwolf’ at Stirling 1304) and the smaller torsion-powered mangonel.
• Scaling used ladders and movable wooden towers to attack the walls directly.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the different parts of an Edwardian army on campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Heavy cavalry of knights and men-at-arms, riding warhorses and equipped with mail or partial plate, lance and sword — the prestigious arm of any army.
• Longbow archers, mainly drawn from south Wales and Cheshire, capable of shooting around ten arrows a minute at 200 yards.
• Genoese and Gascon crossbowmen, slower-firing but powerful, often shielded behind a wooden pavise during sieges.
• Mass infantry raised by commissions of array, armed with spears, short swords and axes.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which English battlefield tactics were changed by the longbow by 1307.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At Falkirk in 1298, massed Welsh and English longbow volleys broke Wallace’s schiltrons after cavalry alone had failed, showing archery could decide a pitched battle.
• Commanders began to combine archers with cavalry as a deliberate tactic — archers softening enemy formations, cavalry charging the gaps.
• A trained archer could shoot ten arrows a minute compared with two crossbow bolts, raising the rate of fire any commander could deliver.
• The model would dominate the Hundred Years War a generation later (Crécy 1346, Agincourt 1415), making 1298 a turning point.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named battles and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about siege warfare in Edward I’s campaigns.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Most medieval campaigns were sieges, not battles — a single castle could deny an enemy a whole region until it was taken.
• Sieges were extremely expensive: Edward’s ‘Warwolf’ trebuchet at Stirling in 1304 took weeks to build and cost large sums in timber, ropes and skilled labour.
• Significance over time: rather than fight repeated sieges, Edward built ring after ring of stone castles in Wales to make Welsh resistance impossible — the Iron Ring programme.
• The skills Edward’s army learned in Wales (mining, sapping, bombardment) were carried into Scotland after 1296 and into the Hundred Years War.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise figures and named campaigns.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the changes in armour between 1272 and 1307.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Knights gradually reinforced mail hauberks with the ‘coat of plates’, plus separate metal plates over shins, knees and elbows, increasing weight and protection.
• The growing cost of armour pushed up the cost of equipping a knight, widening the gap between knights and ordinary infantry.
• A heavily armoured knight was harder to kill but slower in close fighting, encouraging the use of longer weapons and more disciplined infantry.
• Over time, the changes laid the ground for the full plate armour of the fourteenth century — affecting not just England but warfare across Europe.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with specific examples and consequences.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘Infantry, rather than cavalry, was the most important arm in Edward I’s armies.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• At Falkirk in 1298 it was massed Welsh and English longbow archers who broke Wallace’s schiltrons; the cavalry could only finish off a beaten enemy.
• Most campaigns were sieges, where infantry, archers and crossbowmen mattered far more than mounted knights.
• Welsh longbowmen and Genoese crossbowmen were among Edward’s most reliable troops; their numbers grew through the reign.
• The shift to combined-arms tactics in the 1290s raised the long-term importance of infantry across European warfare.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Cavalry remained the prestigious arm: a charge of knights and men-at-arms could decide a battle on open ground.
• At Stirling Bridge in 1297 the destruction of the English cavalry decided the campaign, suggesting it was still the decisive force.
• Edward’s status as a warrior-king depended on commanding mounted knights, not foot-soldiers.
• Heavy cavalry remained essential to break a defeated infantry formation in pursuit.

A strong response weighs infantry against cavalry across Welsh and Scottish campaigns and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Union naval blockade on civilians in the Confederate states between 1861 and 1865.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed effects, each supported by precise factual detail (specific shortages, prices, riots) and linked back to the question of civilian experience.
Secure: Two relevant effects with some supporting detail; clear focus on civilians.
Developing: One effect developed and one weak, or two effects covered superficially.
Emerging: Generalised description of the blockade with little focus on civilian impact.

Indicative content:
• Severe shortages of food, salt, medicine and imported goods, leading to malnutrition in Southern cities.
• Hyperinflation: Confederate dollars collapsed, with a barrel of flour reaching $1,000 by 1865.
• The Richmond Bread Riots of April 1863, in which mostly women looted shops in the Confederate capital.
• Disruption of cotton exports, undercutting plantation revenue and forcing planters to borrow heavily.
• Damage to civilian morale that contributed to desertion rates rising in the Confederate army from late 1863 onwards.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 on civilians in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise detail and clear distinction between civilian groups (Black, white, Northern, Southern).
Secure: Two clear effects with some supporting detail.
Developing: One developed effect and one weak, or both partially covered.
Emerging: Vague comment on slavery without specific Proclamation effects.

Indicative content:
• Around 200,000 Black men joined the Union Army and Navy after January 1863, transforming the demographics of the Union forces.
• Hundreds of thousands of enslaved people fled to Union lines as ‘contraband’, weakening Southern plantation labour.
• Deepened opposition among some Northern Democrats, who saw the war shifting from Union preservation to abolition.
• Reframed the war internationally — Britain and France, both of which had abolished slavery, found it harder to recognise the Confederacy diplomatically.
• Did not free enslaved people in the loyal border states, leaving a legal gap that the 13th Amendment (1865) closed.

practice_questions.text:
Which had the greater impact on civilians during the American Civil War?

• The economic impact
• The social and racial impact

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that weighs economic impact against social, racial or political impact and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout; specialist vocabulary (Greenback, conscription, contraband, hyperinflation).
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets, with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of economic and other impacts, but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Description of the war’s effects with no comparison of the two bullets.

Indicative content:
The economic impact:
• Confederate hyperinflation and collapse of currency.
• Northern industrial boom and the introduction of Greenbacks, income tax and national banks.
• Sherman’s March to the Sea destroyed an estimated $100 million of Southern economic infrastructure.
• Long-term: Southern agriculture took decades to recover; the North accelerated its industrial lead.
The social and racial impact:
• Social impact: more than 20,000 women volunteered as hospital nurses and many more took factory and clerical jobs; gender roles shifted.
• Racial impact: emancipation, Black military service and the eventual 13th Amendment transformed the lives of around 4 million enslaved people.
• Political impact: vast expansion of federal power and a permanent shift in the federal-state balance.
• Human cost: 620,000 dead, ~2 per cent of the US population, leaving widows, orphans and disabled veterans across both sections.
Judgement: economic impact was profound but inseparable from racial and political change; a top-band answer reaches an explicit overall verdict and justifies it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the New York Draft Riots of July 1863 on civilian society in the North.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual support; clearly distinguishes immediate from longer-term consequences.
Secure: Two clear effects with some development.
Developing: One effect developed; one weak or general.
Emerging: Description of the riots without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Exposed deep class tensions in Northern society — the $300 commutation fee was attacked as ‘a rich man’s war and a poor man’s fight’.
• At least 119 people killed; Black New Yorkers were targeted, with the Colored Orphan Asylum on Fifth Avenue burned down.
• Federal troops were diverted from Gettysburg battle aftermath to restore order, showing the war’s reach into Northern cities.
• Damaged Lincoln administration support among Irish-American communities.
• Forced the federal government to refine conscription, including buying out poorer draftees and prioritising volunteer recruitment for the rest of the war.

practice_questions.text:
Which group of civilians suffered more during the American Civil War?

• Civilians in the South
• Civilians in the North

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; precise detail on both sections; deploys specialist vocabulary.
Secure: Clear comparison of Northern and Southern experience with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both sections but weighing limited; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of one section more than the other; little comparison.

Indicative content:
Civilians in the South:
• Naval blockade caused chronic shortages and starvation; bread riots in Richmond 1863.
• Hyperinflation made Confederate currency worthless by 1865.
• Sherman’s March physically destroyed Georgia and the Carolinas; cities such as Atlanta and Columbia burned.
• Around 25 per cent of military-age Southern white men died in the war; widows, orphans and disabled veterans concentrated in the South.
Civilians in the North:
• Northern conscription riots (NYC 1863) caused at least 119 deaths and exposed bitter class divisions.
• Northern food prices rose sharply, eroding wages.
• Around 360,000 Union soldiers died; their families were Northern civilians.
• Around 4 million enslaved people, mostly in the South, gained freedom — their wartime experience was suffering AND liberation, complicating any simple suffering league table.
Judgement: in absolute terms the South’s civilian collapse was deeper, but a top answer recognises that Black Southern civilians experienced something the North did not — emancipation — and weighs that into the judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Sherman’s March to the Sea (November–December 1864) on the civilian economy of the South.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise detail; engages with both physical and psychological dimensions.
Secure: Two clear effects, supported.
Developing: One developed effect and one general.
Emerging: Description of the march itself with little focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Direct destruction of an estimated $100 million of property — railroads (‘Sherman’s neckties’), mills, plantations, livestock.
• Disabled the Confederate transport network — supplies could no longer move from Georgia to Lee’s army in Virginia.
• Spread civilian fear: Sherman’s explicit aim to make Southerners ‘feel the hard hand of war’ broke confidence in Confederate ability to protect civilians.
• Accelerated desertion in the Confederate army as soldiers received letters describing destruction at home.
• Long-term: Georgia’s recovery into the 1880s was hampered by the loss of rail and agricultural infrastructure.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the three Exclusion Bills were defeated between 1679 and 1681.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were proposed laws that would have barred James, Duke of York from the throne because of his Catholicism, introduced in three separate Parliaments between 1679 and 1681.
• The first Bill of May 1679 passed its second reading in the Commons by 207 to 128 before Charles II dissolved Parliament to stop it.
• The second Bill, late in 1680, passed the Commons but was thrown out by the House of Lords after a speech by the Earl of Halifax.
• The third Bill was reintroduced at the Oxford Parliament in March 1681, which Charles dissolved after just one week.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Exclusion Crisis for English political life by 1685.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It produced the first English party division between Whigs (favouring exclusion and parliamentary right) and Tories (defending hereditary right and the Anglican Church).
• It led Charles II to dissolve the Oxford Parliament in 1681 and rule without Parliament for the rest of his reign, financed by French subsidies and customs revenue.
• It triggered the purge of Whigs from borough corporations after the Rye House Plot, leaving James II to inherit a strongly Tory political landscape in 1685.
• It politicised printed pamphlets, sermons and loyal addresses to an unprecedented degree, leaving a lasting culture of partisan publication.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Earl of Shaftesbury during the Exclusion Crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Shaftesbury organised the Whig campaign in Parliament and outside it, drafting Exclusion Bills and coordinating petitions and Green Ribbon Club activity.
• He used the Popish Plot panic to push the case for excluding James, making the Catholic succession the central political question of the late 1670s.
• Significance over time: his trial for treason in 1681 and acquittal demonstrated the political muscle of the City of London; his flight to Holland and death in 1682 marked the collapse of organised Whig politics until 1688.
• His arguments fed into the political theory of John Locke (his secretary), whose ‘Two Treatises of Government’ were drafted during the Crisis and shaped post-1688 thinking.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
