Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the emergence of the Tories in 1679–1681.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Tories defended hereditary right, arguing that the Crown descended to the next heir by birth and that Parliament had no power to alter the succession.
• They drew their core support from country squires, cathedral clergy and the universities, and were closely tied to the Anglican Church.
• They organised loyal addresses to the king after the Oxford Parliament, especially from corporations, which flooded into Whitehall in 1681–82.
• The label ‘Tory’ began as an insult, originally meaning an Irish Catholic outlaw, but was adopted by the king’s defenders.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of what followed Charles II’s dissolution of the Oxford Parliament in March 1681.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Exclusion Bill was killed: it could not be reintroduced because Charles never summoned another Parliament during his reign.
• Charles published a printed declaration justifying his action that was read in churches, swinging public opinion behind the Crown.
• Tory loyal addresses flooded in from corporations, accelerating the political reaction that culminated in the Rye House Plot purges.
• The Crown lost access to parliamentary taxation but compensated through Louis XIV’s subsidies of around £385,000 between 1681 and 1685.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Exclusion Crisis was a religious quarrel. Fear of a Catholic king, not political ambition, drove it.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the causes of the Exclusion Crisis? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The Popish Plot of 1678 unleashed religious panic that gave the Exclusion campaign its energy and political legitimacy.
• James’s open Catholicism after 1673 made the succession a religious question first; without it, Whigs would have had no case.
• Tories defended hereditary right partly to defend the Anglican Church — the religious settlement of 1662 was at stake on both sides.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Shaftesbury’s ambition to dominate government drove the timing and tactics of the Bills; he had been a Cabal minister before he became a Whig leader.
• The contest was also constitutional: who decides the succession — God, descent, or Parliament? — which is a question about power, not creed.
• Charles II’s decision to take French subsidies in order to dissolve Parliament was a political calculation, not a religious one.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1933 speech by Adolf Hitler to the Reichstag, shortly before Germany’s withdrawal from the League of Nations.
‘Germany has fulfilled the disarmament terms of Versailles. We have no army worthy of the name, no air force, no navy. Other powers have not disarmed in turn. Germany cannot remain at a conference where she is treated as an inferior. We must therefore leave both the Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons given by Hitler for leaving the League of Nations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded reasons with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear reasons, briefly supported.
Developing: One reason clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Germany had disarmed under Versailles but other powers had not disarmed in return.
• Germany was being treated as an inferior at the conference.
• Other powers had broken the spirit of the disarmament agreement.
• Implicit reason: continued League membership without equality of treatment was unacceptable to the Nazi regime.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of Hitler’s foreign-policy actions from his appointment as Chancellor in January 1933 to the Dollfuss Affair of July 1934.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1933: Hitler appointed Chancellor; began to plan rearmament and treaty revision.
• Spring 1933: Hitler used the Geneva Disarmament Conference to demand equality with the Allies.
• October 1933: Germany withdrew from both the Disarmament Conference and the League; the Allied response was silence, encouraging further moves.
• January 1934: Hitler signed a ten-year Non-Aggression Pact with Poland to break the French alliance system in eastern Europe and buy time for rearmament.
• July 1934: Austrian Nazis, encouraged from Berlin, attempted a coup in Vienna; they assassinated Chancellor Dollfuss but failed to seize power.
• Mussolini moved Italian troops to the Brenner Pass and threatened intervention; Hitler publicly disowned the rebels.
• The episode taught Hitler that the Allies and the League would not act, but a determined great power could still stop him — for now.

practice_questions.text:
‘Lebensraum was the most important of Hitler’s foreign-policy aims in the years 1933 to 1939.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached. Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial. Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question. Indicative content: Supporting the statement: • Lebensraum — living space carved out of Poland, Ukraine and European Russia — was the long-term goal set out in Mein Kampf and the one that shaped the eventual war in the east. • It was openly anti-Slav and anti-communist, which is why the eastern frontier mattered to Hitler far more than the western one. Challenging the statement: • Treaty revision came first in practice: leaving the Disarmament Conference and the League in October 1933, conscription and the Luftwaffe in 1935, the Rhineland in 1936. • Pan-Germanism produced the actual crises of 1938: Anschluss with Austria and the demand for the Sudetenland. • The three aims overlapped — tearing up Versailles cleared the path for pan-German union, which pushed Germany’s borders eastward toward Lebensraum. Judgement: Lebensraum was the deepest aim, but treaty revision and pan-Germanism drove the moves Hitler actually made in the 1930s.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources B and C.

Source B: An extract from a 1934 private memorandum by the British Foreign Office on Hitler’s German-Polish Non-Aggression Pact.
‘The German-Polish agreement does not represent a change of heart in Berlin. It is a tactical move calculated to weaken the French alliance system in eastern Europe and to give the Reich time to rearm without the threat of a Polish counter-stroke. We should not mistake calculation for moderation.’

Source C: A 1934 newspaper editorial in the Manchester Guardian, after the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss.
‘The murder of Dr Dollfuss in Vienna is a German act, however much Berlin protests. The hand was Austrian, the inspiration was Nazi. Signor Mussolini’s prompt movement of troops to the Brenner Pass has shown what the League could not: that bold action by a great power, and not paper protest, is what now restrains Berlin.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying Hitler’s early foreign policy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: argues the Polish Pact was tactical, not a sign of moderation. Provenance: a private Foreign Office memorandum, not designed for public consumption; likely to express genuine analytical thinking. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — the pact gave Hitler time to rearm and broke the French alliance system; it was torn up in 1939.
Source C — Content: argues only great-power action, not League protest, restrained Hitler. Provenance: a contemporary editorial in a liberal British paper, designed to influence British public opinion in mid-1934. Own knowledge: confirms historical record — Mussolini did move troops to the Brenner; the League made no response; Hitler did publicly disown the Austrian Nazi rebels.
Judgement: B is highly useful for British official thinking but reflects only one strand of analysis; C is useful for contemporary press reaction and for the lesson Hitler drew, but as an editorial it makes a polemical case rather than a balanced judgement.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Hitler used diplomacy between 1933 and 1934 to disguise the long-term aims of Nazi foreign policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail. Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage. Indicative content: • October 1933: Hitler walked out of the Geneva Disarmament Conference and the League, framing withdrawal as a fair response to the Allied refusal to disarm and presenting the Reich as a victim rather than a regime preparing to rearm. • January 1934: the ten-year Non-Aggression Pact with Poland disguised Nazi hostility to Slavs, broke the French alliance system in eastern Europe and bought time for rearmament. • July 1934: after Austrian Nazis murdered Dollfuss, Hitler publicly disowned the rebels, distancing Berlin from a coup it had encouraged and preserving the option of a later Anschluss. • Each step was tactical: the underlying aims of treaty revision, pan-German union and Lebensraum did not change.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Dollfuss Affair from the rise of Austrian Nazi agitation in early 1934 to Mussolini’s response at the Brenner Pass.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives. Developing: Events listed; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage. Indicative content: • Early 1934: Austrian Nazi agitation increased, encouraged by Berlin and aimed at union with Germany. • 25 July 1934: Austrian Nazis stormed the Vienna Chancellery and shot Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss. • The rebels proclaimed Anschluss with Germany but failed to seize the rest of the government. • Austrian government forces crushed the coup within hours; the rebels surrendered or fled. • Mussolini, whose family was hosting the Dollfuss family in Italy at the time, was personally outraged and moved Italian divisions to the Brenner Pass on the Austrian border. • Mussolini threatened to intervene if Hitler attempted to march on Vienna. • Hitler, not yet ready for a confrontation with Italy, publicly disowned the Austrian Nazi rebels and pulled back.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the diary of British infantryman Private Cyril Tyler of the Sherwood Foresters, written in his trench notebook on the night of 1 July 1916.
‘We went over at half past seven. The wire was not cut where we crossed and the men piled up against it. The Hun guns started before we had gone twenty yards and we could see they were not in the least shaken by our shells. We lost the company commander and most of the officers in the first minute.’

Source A suggests that the first day of the Somme failed because the bombardment had not done its job. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• ‘The wire was not cut where we crossed and the men piled up against it.’
• German guns opened fire ‘before we had gone twenty yards’.
• The defenders were ‘not in the least shaken by our shells’.
• Officers were lost in the first minute, so the attack lost its leaders on the spot.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• A seven-day bombardment fired about 1.5 million shells, but many were duds and the German dugouts ran up to 12 metres deep.
• The British Army suffered 57,470 casualties on 1 July 1916, including 19,240 dead.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum written by German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn to Kaiser Wilhelm II in December 1915, as printed in his post-war memoirs; no copy of the memorandum survives in the archives.
‘France has reached the limit of what she can endure. If we choose a sector she must defend at all costs, the French army will bleed itself to death within range of our guns whether or not we take the position. Verdun, with its forts and history, is such a sector.’

Source C: An extract from a despatch by French general Robert Nivelle in October 1916, sent to the French High Command after the recapture of Fort Douaumont.
‘Eight months of attack have cost the enemy as dearly as they have cost us. Our losses are heavy, but our soldiers are not broken. The German army has spent itself before our guns no less than we have spent ourselves before theirs. They shall not pass.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Battle of Verdun. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: shows Falkenhayn’s explicit reasoning that Verdun was chosen because France would have to defend it. Provenance: a memorandum Falkenhayn says he sent to the Kaiser, known only from his own post-war account; intended to justify a plan, so likely to overstate confidence. Own knowledge: French final losses (~377,000) and German (~337,000) made the bleeding plan a near-even exchange, undermining the strategy.
Source C — Content: a French claim that Verdun has cost Germany as much as France. Provenance: an official despatch after the recapture of Douaumont, intended to boost morale; may exaggerate German exhaustion. Own knowledge: the rotation of divisions through the noria and the Voie Sacrée supply road kept France in the fight; the Somme also drew German troops away.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German strategic thinking but partial; C is useful as contemporary French reaction but reflects propaganda value. Together they show the gap between Falkenhayn’s plan and its actual outcome.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Somme campaign developed between the start of the bombardment in late June 1916 and the end of the offensive in November 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (1.5 million shells, 1 July, Flers-Courcelette, 15 September, mid-November); reaches the close of the campaign through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 24 June 1916: a seven-day British bombardment fired 1.5 million shells; many were duds, the wire was largely uncut, and German dugouts survived.
• 1 July 1916: at 7.30am infantry advanced in extended lines; ~57,470 casualties on the first day, including 19,240 dead.
• July–August: smaller-scale attacks (Mametz Wood, High Wood, Pozières) ground forward at heavy cost.
• 15 September 1916: tanks deployed for the first time at Flers-Courcelette; mechanically unreliable but pointed towards combined-arms tactics.
• October–November: rain turned the battlefield to mud; the offensive halted in mid-November after a six-mile advance.
• Outcome: ~420,000 British, 200,000 French and 465,000 German casualties; Germany withdrew in early 1917 to the Hindenburg Line.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Battle of the Somme was a costly failure that achieved very little.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• 57,470 British casualties fell on the first day and about 420,000 by November, for an advance of roughly six miles.
• The bombardment did not cut the wire or destroy the deep German dugouts, and the infantry walked into prepared machine-gun fire.
• No breakthrough was made and the German line in the west held for another two years.

Disagree:
• The offensive drew German divisions away from Verdun, which was one of its stated aims.
• German losses of about 465,000 fell on an army that could not replace them, and Falkenhayn was sacked in August 1916.
• The British learned about creeping barrages, counter-battery fire and tank co-operation, and used those lessons in 1917 and 1918.
• Germany pulled back to the Hindenburg Line in early 1917, which shows the pressure had told.

Judgement: The Somme failed as a breakthrough and the cost was enormous, but ‘achieved very little’ is too strong: it relieved Verdun, wore down the German army and taught the BEF how to fight.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the war diary of German staff officer Lieutenant-Colonel Friedrich von Lossberg, chief of staff of the German Second Army, recording observations after touring the Somme front line in late September 1916.
‘The English artillery is no longer the chaotic curtain of last year. Their barrage now moves with the infantry as one body. Our forward dugouts give less protection than before. The men in the line speak of the new motor-vehicles — the tanks — with a fear we have not yet learned to answer.’

Source F suggests that British tactics on the Somme had improved since the previous year. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The British barrage ‘now moves with the infantry as one body’, unlike the year before.
• German forward dugouts ‘give less protection than before’.
• German soldiers speak of the new tanks ‘with a fear we have not yet learned to answer’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Tanks were first used at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916.
• Germany withdrew to the Hindenburg Line in early 1917 and developed defence in depth in reply.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Battle of Verdun developed between February 1916 and December 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the close of the battle through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 21 February 1916: German bombardment opened with around one million shells in ten hours along an eight-mile front.
• 25 February 1916: Fort Douaumont fell within four days of the opening assault.
• Pétain took command of French defence; the noria rotation system kept fresh divisions in the line and the Voie Sacrée road kept up to 6,000 lorries a day moving supplies.
• 1 July 1916: the British and French opened the Somme offensive, forcing Germany to thin out attacking divisions at Verdun.
• August 1916: Falkenhayn was sacked and replaced by Hindenburg and Ludendorff after the bleeding plan failed to break France.
• October–November 1916: French counter-attacks under Nivelle retook Fort Douaumont on 24 October and Fort Vaux on 2 November; the battle wound down in December with combined casualties around 700,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the experience of Huguenot migrants in the late 17th century was similar to or different from the experience of evictees during the Highland Clearances.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Huguenots fled religious persecution by a foreign king (Louis XIV); Highland evictees were forced out by their own clan chiefs in the pursuit of profit from sheep farming.
• Difference: Huguenots were welcomed and naturalised by Charles II and James II because their skills were valued; Highland evictees received no government protection and were often turned out without warning.
• Similarity: both groups produced lasting communities far from their place of origin — Huguenot silk weavers in Spitalfields, Highland diaspora in North America and Australia.
• Similarity: both migrations were shaped by economic resources — Huguenot skills attracted them to British towns, Cheviot sheep displaced Highlanders from the glens.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Ulster Plantation and the Highland Clearances were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: the Ulster Plantation was a government-directed migration in which James I confiscated Catholic Irish land for Protestant settlers; the Highland Clearances were private, driven by individual landlords seeking profit from sheep.
• Difference: Ulster settlers were given land they had not previously held; Highland tenants were removed from land their families had farmed for generations.
• Similarity: both involved displacement of an existing population — Catholic Irish in Ulster, Gaelic Highlanders in the glens.
• Similarity: both produced large overseas diasporas — Scots-Irish migration to America from Ulster, Highland migration to Cape Breton, North Carolina and Australia.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Huguenot migration for Britain in the late 17th and 18th centuries.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: around 50,000 refugees arrived in a kingdom of around 5 million — one of the largest single migrations in early modern Britain.
• At the time: Spitalfields silk weaving, Canterbury and Norwich textile trades were transformed; Huguenot bankers were founder members of the Bank of England in 1694.
• Over time: the word ‘refugee’ entered English from French; later refugee movements (Jewish 1881, Ugandan Asian 1972) were measured against Huguenot success as a precedent.
• Over time: Huguenot family names (Garrick, Olivier, Bosanquet, Courtauld) became woven into the British establishment, showing how integration could happen across generations.
• Limitation: assimilation took 100+ years; French churches in London survived into the 19th century, showing that integration was gradual rather than immediate.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Government was the main factor shaping migration to, from and within Britain between 1600 and 1850.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Government (in support): James I directed the Ulster Plantation from 1609, confiscating land in six counties and setting the terms on which settlers held it.
• Government (in support): Charles II and James II issued proclamations welcoming Huguenots, and Parliament passed a naturalisation act for foreign Protestants in 1709.
• Government (against): the state neither directed nor stopped the Highland Clearances; landlords acted for themselves and tenants had no protection.
• Religion: Louis XIV’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 pushed around 200,000 Huguenots out of France, and shared Protestantism made Britain the obvious refuge.
• Economic resources: Huguenot silk and banking skills made them welcome, while Cheviot sheep made Highland tenants worth less to their chiefs than pasture.
• Judgement: government decided where migration was engineered, but religion and profit decided where people moved on their own. The clearances show the state at its most passive, the plantation at its most active.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Huguenot migration to Britain after 1685 was similar to or different from the Ulster Plantation of 1609.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: religion drove both. Huguenots fled Louis XIV’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685; the Ulster Plantation moved Protestants into Catholic Ireland to secure the kingdom.
• Difference: Huguenots chose to come and were received by royal proclamation; Ulster settlers were planted deliberately by James I on land the Crown had confiscated.
• Difference: Huguenots arrived where their skills were wanted and integrated into English towns; Ulster settlers were imposed on a hostile population and stayed separate from it.
• Similarity: both left communities that lasted for centuries — Spitalfields silk weaving and Huguenot family banks, Scots-Irish Ulster and its later migration to America.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named examples.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Highland Clearances for Scotland and the wider British world.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: tens of thousands of Gaelic-speaking tenants were evicted between c1750 and 1860, ending the traditional clan-tenancy system that had survived the 1745 Jacobite rising.
• At the time: the population of the Highlands fell sharply; coastal crofting townships, Lowland slums and emigrant ships absorbed the displaced.
• Over time: Highland diasporas in Cape Breton (Canada), North Carolina, Australia and New Zealand carried Gaelic language, ballads and clan identity overseas.
• Over time: the clearances became a defining episode in modern Scottish national memory and a touchstone for debates on land ownership and the Crofters’ Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886.
• Limitation: economic migration from rural Scotland would have happened to some extent without the clearances, given the pull of industrial Glasgow.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Chartism in the development of British democracy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Chartism mobilised millions of working people for the first time, with petitions of 1.3m (1839), 3.3m (1842) and several million (1848).
• At the time: it created the techniques of mass political organisation — the Northern Star newspaper, mass meetings on Kersal Moor and Kennington Common, and a permanent national leadership.
• Over time: five of the six points eventually became law — secret ballot 1872, working-class male suffrage 1867 and 1884, paid MPs 1911, universal manhood suffrage 1918.
• Over time: every later mass movement — trade unions, suffragettes, the Labour Party — used methods Chartism pioneered, even when it lost in its own moment.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise dates and examples and a clear judgement about why Chartism mattered despite failing.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples covering both at the time and over time.
Developing: Some explanation of significance, mostly weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Simple description of what Chartism was, with little explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Peterloo Massacre of 1819 for the campaign for parliamentary reform.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: around 60,000 people gathered peacefully at St Peter's Field on 16 August 1819, and the cavalry charge killed at least 18 and injured several hundred.
• At the time: the government answered with repression, not concession — the Six Acts of late 1819 restricted meetings and taxed the radical press.
• At the time: mass open-air meetings in the industrial towns became dangerous to organise for the next decade.
• Over time: Peterloo became the symbol reformers used to argue that the unreformed system governed by force, feeding the pressure behind the 1832 Reform Act.
• Over time: Chartists and later trade unionists invoked Peterloo as proof that the state would use violence against unarmed protest.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Peterloo Massacre and the Newport Rising were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both involved unarmed or lightly armed working people gathering for political reform — the vote at Peterloo, the release of Chartist leaders at Newport.
• Similarity: both ended with the state using military force, killing protesters — at least 18 at Peterloo, at least 22 at Newport.
• Similarity: both were used by the government to justify further repression rather than reform — the Six Acts after Peterloo, transportation of Chartist leaders after Newport.
• Similarity: both became powerful symbols of state violence used by later reform movements to argue for change.

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: ‘The economy was the main factor in the demand for parliamentary reform between 1819 and 1848.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the economy against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the economy as the main factor:
• Post-Napoleonic distress, the 1815 Corn Laws and high bread prices fuelled the Peterloo gathering of 1819.
• Industrial wages and unemployment built the Chartist constituency — the petitions were strongest in industrial towns hit by trade slumps in 1839 and 1842.
• The Anti-Corn Law League of the same period showed how directly economic grievance shaped political pressure.

Weighed against ideas (democracy, representation):
• The People’s Charter set out a fully democratic programme — universal manhood suffrage, secret ballot — not just economic demands.
• Chartism drew on radical traditions stretching back to the Levellers and Tom Paine; ideas about representation gave the discontent its shape.

Weighed against communication:
• The Northern Star, mass petitioning and the new railway network turned local economic anger into national political movements.
• Government repression of the press through the Six Acts was an admission that communication, not poverty alone, was the threat.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Henry ‘Orator’ Hunt, Feargus O’Connor and William Lovett gave the movement leadership, focus and a public voice.

Judgement: Top answers argue that the economy created the conditions but ideas, communication and individuals gave the movement its political form. Without ideas of representation, hungry workers might have rioted; with them, they petitioned and organised.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others, with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples comparing the economy with other factors; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them; judgement asserted rather than substantiated.
Emerging: Lists factors without comparison or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Great Reform Act 1832 for the relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: redistributed 56 rotten-borough seats to industrial cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds for the first time.
• At the time: standardised the franchise at the £10 householder level, adding around 217,000 voters and raising the electorate to roughly one in seven adult men.
• Over time: it set the precedent that the franchise could be widened by Act of Parliament, paving the way for the 1867, 1884, 1918 and 1928 Acts.
• Over time: by excluding working men it directly fuelled Chartism and the longer struggle for democracy that ran into the twentieth century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation covering both at the time and over time with precise detail and a clear judgement on what changed.
Secure: Clear explanation with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of what the Act did with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the methods of the Chartists were different from the methods of the reformers at Peterloo in 1819.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in organisation: Peterloo was a single mass open-air meeting called to hear Henry 'Orator' Hunt; Chartism ran a permanent national movement with local committees, a written charter and a national convention.
• Difference in communication: the Peterloo reformers depended on word of mouth and a radical press the Six Acts then taxed out of reach; the Chartists had the Northern Star reaching around 50,000 readers a week, the railways and mass petitioning.
• Difference in tactics: Peterloo was a demonstration for the vote; Chartism combined petitions of 1.3 million (1839) and 3.3 million (1842) signatures with a physical-force wing that marched on Newport in 1839.
• Difference in programme: the Peterloo crowd asked broadly for parliamentary reform; the Chartists set out six specific constitutional demands in the People's Charter of 1838.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct ways, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two ways with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Anglo-Saxon system of local government that the Normans inherited.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• England was divided into shires (counties), each supervised by a royal officer called the sheriff or shire-reeve who collected royal revenues and presided over the shire court.
• Below the shire sat the hundred — smaller units that met monthly in their own courts to handle local justice, theft, debt and minor violence.
• The king communicated with sheriffs and shire courts through writs — short sealed documents in Old English or Latin sent across the kingdom on royal business.
• A national land tax called the geld was assessed on shires and hundreds in ‘hides’ and collected as cash, originally to pay off Viking raiders.
• Why it mattered: because shires, sheriffs and the geld already worked, William could tax and judge England from the first year without building a system of his own.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Anglo-Saxon government continued under the Normans after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both used the shire as the basic unit of local government, with a royal officer (sheriff or shire-reeve) collecting revenues and presiding over the shire court.
• Both relied on the writ — short sealed royal documents — to communicate the king’s instructions to his officers across the kingdom.
• Both raised cash through the geld land tax, assessed in hides on shires and hundreds and collected by sheriffs.
• Both used trial by ordeal in serious criminal cases, with the courts reading physical outcomes as God’s judgement on innocence or guilt.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the Normans changed English government after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Anglo-Saxon great earls held lands in their own right and were semi-independent regional powers, while Norman tenants-in-chief held land formally from the king on knight-service.
• The Normans added forest law — royal hunting reserves with savage penalties for poaching — which had no Anglo-Saxon equivalent.
• The Normans introduced the murdrum fine, a collective penalty on the hundred where a Norman was killed, designed to protect the new ruling class.
• Norman inheritance favoured primogeniture (eldest son takes the lot), in contrast to the partible inheritance often used in Anglo-Saxon families.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about forest law in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, forest law placed vast tracts of countryside under royal control, restricting English access to timber, game and grazing — the New Forest was created by clearing villages of their inhabitants in Hampshire.
• Penalties for poaching and clearing land were extreme — blinding, mutilation, sometimes execution — an unprecedented intrusion of royal power into ordinary peasant life.
• It generated significant royal income through fines collected by foresters in their own courts, separate from the ordinary common law system.
• Importance later: forest law remained one of the bitterest English grievances against royal authority for over a century and was only rolled back by Magna Carta and the Charter of the Forest in 1217.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the murdrum fine for Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the murdrum fine made every English hundred collectively responsible for the safety of Norman incomers, deterring revenge attacks on isolated knights, sheriffs and lords.
• It generated steady royal revenue from communities that could not produce a killer or prove the dead man was English (the ‘presentment of Englishry’).
• It marked a sharp legal divide between Norman and English subjects of the same king, reinforcing the ethnic dimension of post-conquest rule.
• Importance later: the fine long outlived the conquest generation. By about 1179 the Dialogue of the Exchequer said English and Normans had intermarried so much that nobody could tell them apart, yet the fine was profitable and was not abolished until 1340.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Norman government.

‘Norman government was Anglo-Saxon government with French names on it. Shires, sheriffs, hundred courts, writs and the geld all carried on; only the men at the top changed.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about government in England after 1066? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: the conquest brought more continuity than change to English government.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The framework of shires, hundreds and sheriffs continued largely intact — the local machinery of revenue collection and justice was Anglo-Saxon in origin and Norman in personnel.
• The writ as the standard royal instruction continued; sealed royal letters in Old English (and increasingly Latin) carried Norman commands through inherited channels.
• The geld land tax, in ‘hides’ assessed on shires and hundreds, was kept and indeed re-used by William to fund campaigns and military service obligations.
• Most ordinary justice still happened in hundred and shire courts using ordeals; trial by combat was a Norman addition but the bulk of dispute resolution went on as before.
• Hugh Thomas’s ‘continuity beneath rupture’ thesis emphasises that beneath new Norman lords, English peasants ploughed the same fields and used the same courts.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The personnel of government changed almost completely — thegns dispossessed by 1086 (fewer than 10% surviving as landholders), Norman tenants-in-chief and bishops in their place.
• Forest law and the murdrum fine were genuinely new, creating royal hunting reserves and ethnic distinctions in justice unknown before 1066.
• Norman castles, sub-infeudation and knight-service reorganised the relationship between landholding and military obligation in ways inconsistent with the ‘continuity’ reading.
• Lanfranc’s Church reforms, the Domesday survey itself and the central concentration of power in c.180 tenants-in-chief all suggest a sharper political change than the institutional continuity alone.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1933 article by Franz von Papen claiming the new cabinet would ‘tame’ Hitler within months) and Interpretation B (a 1948 memoir by an SPD politician arguing that Papen's deal made Nazi dictatorship inevitable) on Hitler's appointment as Chancellor. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the appointment as a controlled conservative manoeuvre — Hitler was outnumbered eight-to-three in cabinet and would be boxed in by Papen as Vice-Chancellor.
• Interpretation B presents the appointment as the moment Weimar democracy was lost — Papen had handed dictatorial machinery to a man with no respect for it.
• Main difference: A frames the deal as containment; B frames it as catastrophic miscalculation.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1933 Papen article) and Interpretation B (a 1948 SPD memoir) give different views about Hitler's appointment as Chancellor.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written at different times — Papen in 1933 had to defend his role to a conservative readership; the SPD writer in 1948 had seen the consequences of Nazi rule and the Holocaust.
• They had different purposes — Papen aimed to reassure conservative elites that the Nazis were under control; the SPD memoir aimed to apportion historical blame.
• They had access to different evidence — the 1948 writer knew about the Enabling Act, the camps and the war; Papen at the time of writing did not.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in January 1933 was the inevitable result of the Nazi Party's electoral success during the Depression.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about how Hitler became Chancellor?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Nazis were the largest Reichstag party from July 1932 with 230 seats — no government could be formed without acknowledging them.
• Convincing because Hindenburg's circle saw harnessing the Nazi vote as the only way to govern without the SPD.
• Less convincing because the Nazi vote fell from 37.4% to 33.1% between July and November 1932 — the surge was already ebbing.
• Less convincing because the appointment was the product of personal deals, not electoral logic — the Cologne meeting of 4 January 1933 between Papen and Hitler was decisive.
• Less convincing because Hindenburg had refused Hitler the chancellorship as recently as 13 August 1932; only Papen's intervention changed that.
• Overall judgement: the Depression and Nazi vote share created the conditions, but the specific appointment was the product of elite miscalculation rather than electoral inevitability. Historiographically, Sonderweg arguments stress structural inevitability while contingency-focused historians stress the avoidable choices of January 1933.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Papen's chancellorship (June–December 1932) on the political crisis that led to Hitler's appointment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Preussenschlag of 20 July 1932 dismissed the elected SPD-led Prussian government and removed the largest democratic stronghold in Germany — a major step in the breakdown of Weimar self-defence.
• Papen's lack of Reichstag support (he lost a confidence vote 512 to 42 in September 1932) entrenched government by Article 48 decree and discredited parliamentary politics still further.
• The November 1932 election he called produced a Nazi loss — but also showed no stable majority was available to anyone, deepening the appearance that only authoritarian rule could work.
• After his dismissal in December, Papen's resentment of Schleicher led to the Cologne meeting of 4 January 1933 with Hitler, the deal that put Hitler in the Chancellery on 30 January 1933.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933.
You may consider:
• the role of the Depression and the Nazi vote share
• the role of Papen, Hindenburg and Schleicher.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Depression and Nazi growth: industrial output fell 40% (1929–32); six million unemployed; Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37.4% (July 1932), making them the largest Reichstag party.
• Hindenburg's reluctance: refused Hitler the chancellorship on 13 August 1932; called him ‘the Bohemian corporal’; appointed Bruning, Papen, Schleicher in turn.
• Papen's role: Cabinet of Barons (June 1932); Preussenschlag dismissing Prussian SPD government (July 1932); Cologne meeting with Hitler (4 January 1933); served as Vice-Chancellor in cabinet of three Nazis and eight conservatives.
• Schleicher's failure: cross-front strategy collapsed in four weeks; resigned 28 January 1933; murdered in Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) for his earlier role.
• Limits of inevitability: Nazi vote had fallen by November 1932 to 196 seats; party finances near bankruptcy; without Papen's intervention Hitler might never have been appointed.
• Conclusion: the Depression and Nazi vote share created the political space; structural collapse of Weimar parliamentary government under Article 48 deepened it; but the specific appointment was driven by Papen's vendetta against Schleicher and Hindenburg's catastrophic acceptance of the ‘hired’ Hitler argument.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1990s biographer arguing Hindenburg's age and conservative advisers were decisive in Hitler's appointment) and Interpretation B (a 2000s structural historian arguing Weimar democracy was already dead before January 1933) on the failure of Weimar democracy. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A focuses on personal agency — Hindenburg, Papen and Schleicher made avoidable choices that put Hitler in office.
• Interpretation B focuses on structural collapse — rule by Article 48, four chancellors in a year and the destruction of Prussia in July 1932 had already ended democratic government.
• Main difference: A sees Hitler's appointment as a contingent personal failure; B sees it as the formal recognition of a regime that had already ceased to function.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a US National Security Council briefing paper prepared for President Eisenhower, October 1957.
‘The launching of Sputnik has produced a wave of public concern. The satellite itself is a small object, but the rocket that placed it in orbit demonstrates a Soviet capability to deliver a nuclear warhead at intercontinental range. We must expect a corresponding loss of confidence among our European allies in the protection offered by the United States.’

Source A suggests that Sputnik mattered as a military warning and not only as a scientific success. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The rocket that launched Sputnik proves a Soviet ability to deliver a nuclear warhead between continents.
• Sputnik has produced a wave of public concern within the United States.
• European allies may lose confidence in American protection.
• The shock undermines the assumption that the USA holds a clear technological lead.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Sputnik 1 was launched on 4 October 1957 and Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika a month later.
• Congress answered by founding NASA in 1958 and pouring money into science education.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a televised address by Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, broadcast on 14 April 1961, two days after Yuri Gagarin’s flight.
‘Comrade Gagarin has shown the world what the workers’ state can achieve. Where the capitalists boast of profit, we have placed a man among the stars. Let our friends abroad see in this a guarantee — the cause of socialism marches faster than the cause of imperialism.’

Source C: An extract from a memorandum by US Vice-President Lyndon B. Johnson to President Kennedy, 28 April 1961.
‘Failure to be first in this race carries a heavy price in international standing. The American people will accept a costly programme provided it offers a clear chance of overtaking the Soviet Union in a dramatic and visible way. A manned lunar landing within the decade would, in my judgement, achieve that aim.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying superpower attitudes to the early space race in 1961. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Khrushchev frames Gagarin’s flight as proof that socialism outpaces capitalism. Provenance: a public Soviet broadcast two days after the flight, designed for both domestic and foreign audiences. Own knowledge: Gagarin orbited the Earth on 12 April 1961 in Vostok 1; the USSR also held the firsts of Sputnik (1957) and Sputnik 2 (with Laika).
Source C — Content: Johnson advises that catching up in a dramatic, visible way is politically essential and proposes a moon landing as the goal. Provenance: a private memorandum from the Vice-President to the President, two weeks after Gagarin, before Kennedy’s May 1961 lunar pledge. Own knowledge: Apollo 11 finally landed on the Moon in July 1969, achieving the goal Johnson recommended.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding Soviet propaganda use of space achievements but partial; C is useful as confidential US strategic thinking but reflects one adviser’s emphasis on prestige.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how military rivalry between the superpowers developed from the founding of NATO in 1949 to the launch of Sputnik in 1957.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, weapons, alliance membership); reaches Sputnik through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• April 1949: NATO founded by twelve Western states, committing them to collective defence.
• August 1949: Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb, ending the US monopoly and prompting fears of a missile gap.
• November 1952: USA tested the first hydrogen bomb; USSR tested its own thermonuclear device in August 1953, narrowing the gap further.
• May 1955: West Germany joined NATO, prompting the Soviet creation of the Warsaw Pact five days later.
• Mid-1950s: both sides invested heavily in long-range bombers and began work on intercontinental missiles.
• October 1957: Sputnik 1 was launched, demonstrating Soviet ability to deliver a warhead at intercontinental range and triggering the space race.

practice_questions.text:
‘The space race mattered more as Cold War propaganda than as part of the arms race.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Kennedy sold Apollo in May 1961 as a project impressive to mankind, not as a weapons programme.
• Sputnik in 1957 and Gagarin in 1961 were used by Khrushchev to claim that socialism was outpacing capitalism.
• Apollo 11 in July 1969 was watched live by an estimated 600 million people and reclaimed the symbolic lead.
• Astronauts and cosmonauts became national heroes rather than military figures.
Disagree:
• The rocket that launched Sputnik was built as an intercontinental missile and could carry a warhead.
• ICBMs and, from 1960, the Polaris submarine missile came out of the same technology.
• Spy satellites gave both sides real intelligence on each other's missile numbers from 1960.
• Early-warning and reconnaissance satellites later made arms-control agreements possible to verify.
Judgement: prestige was the public purpose, but the same rockets carried the warheads, so the two functions cannot be separated.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential report to the Soviet Politburo by the head of the Soviet missile programme, Sergei Korolev, dated November 1957.
‘The successful launch of Sputnik should be welcomed but not overestimated. The same engines that placed our satellite in orbit must now be developed into reliable intercontinental missiles. Without that step, the satellite is a feat of engineering, but not a guarantee of our national security.’

Source F suggests that Soviet planners treated the space programme and the missile programme as one project. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: Korolev links the satellite engines directly to the development of intercontinental missiles — useful evidence that Soviet planners saw space and arms races as one technical project.
• Provenance: a confidential Politburo report from the head of the missile programme — likely to give a frank assessment unavailable in public propaganda.
• Own knowledge: the R-7 rocket that launched Sputnik was the same booster developed for ICBM use.
• Useful context: the report’s caution warns that propaganda success had not yet been matched by deployable warheads — a different picture from Khrushchev’s public boasts.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the steps in the space race between the launch of Sputnik in 1957 and the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at Apollo 11 through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• October 1957: Sputnik 1 launched, demonstrating Soviet rocket capability and triggering an American crisis of confidence.
• 1958: NASA founded; the United States passed the National Defense Education Act to channel funds into science and engineering.
• April 1961: Yuri Gagarin became the first person to orbit the Earth, deepening the Soviet lead.
• May 1961: Kennedy committed the United States to a manned lunar landing before the decade ended.
• March 1965: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk; the Gemini programme answered later that year.
• December 1968: Apollo 8 became the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon.
• July 1969: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, completing the goal Kennedy set and reclaiming the symbolic lead for the United States.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a press conference given by President Dwight D. Eisenhower, Washington DC, 7 April 1954.
‘Finally, you have broader considerations that might follow what you would call the falling domino principle. You have a row of dominoes set up. You knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly. So you could have a beginning of a disintegration that would have the most profound influences.’

Source A suggests that Eisenhower saw the loss of one country in the region as a threat to all of it. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He uses the image of ‘a row of dominoes’ in which the first knocked over brings down the last.
• He says the last domino will fall ‘very quickly’, so the danger is fast as well as wide.
• He describes the result as ‘a disintegration that would have the most profound influences’.
Contextual knowledge: Eisenhower spoke on 7 April 1954, weeks before Dien Bien Phu fell; by then the United States was paying about 80 per cent of France’s war costs in Indochina.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Robert McNamara, US Secretary of Defense, to President Kennedy, dated November 1961.
‘The loss of South Vietnam to communism would not only destroy SEATO but would undermine the credibility of American commitments elsewhere. The struggle there is hard, but it is winnable through advisers, training and the resettlement of the rural population away from Vietcong influence.’

Source C: An extract from an interview given by Buddhist monk Thich Tri Quang to a Western journalist in Hue, July 1963, published in a French magazine.
‘Diem treats Buddhists as foreigners in our own country. His Catholic family rules; his soldiers fired on our people in May. Strategic Hamlets are prisons. We do not want communism, but neither will we accept this.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying US involvement in South Vietnam under Kennedy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: McNamara frames Vietnam as a test of US credibility and presents adviser policy as winnable. Provenance: a private memo from Defense Secretary to President, intended to shape policy not public opinion — useful for showing how Domino-Theory thinking dominated decisions. Own knowledge: adviser numbers rose from around 800 to over 16,000 between 1960 and late 1963; Strategic Hamlets launched 1962.
Source C — Content: shows the religious and political grievances that Strategic Hamlets and Diem’s rule provoked. Provenance: a Buddhist monk to a French journalist, July 1963 — first-hand and contemporary, but partial to the protest movement. Own knowledge: the May 1963 Hue shootings, Thich Quang Duc’s self-immolation in June, and Madame Nhu’s ‘barbecues’ remark all confirm the picture.
Judgement: B is highly useful for elite policy thinking but optimistic; C is highly useful for showing the political reality on the ground that Washington was missing.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the United States moved from supporting France in Indochina in 1954 to backing the overthrow of Diem in November 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Geneva, MAAG, Strategic Hamlets, Buddhist crisis); arrives at the November 1963 coup through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin or muddled chronology with little linking.

Indicative content:
• 1954: Geneva split Vietnam at the 17th parallel; the US replaced France as the South’s patron.
• 1955: Diem became president of South Vietnam with US backing and refused 1956 elections.
• Late 1950s: MAAG advisers trained the ARVN; aid flowed in.
• 1960: Vietcong (NLF) formed in the South.
• 1961–1963: Kennedy raised advisers from c.800 to over 16,000.
• 1962: Strategic Hamlets launched; alienated the rural population.
• May–June 1963: Hue shootings and Thich Quang Duc’s self-immolation discredited Diem internationally.
• 1–2 November 1963: South Vietnamese generals overthrew Diem with US tacit consent.

practice_questions.text:
‘The failure of the Strategic Hamlets programme was the main reason US policy in Vietnam was in crisis by November 1963.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The hamlets, launched in 1962, forced peasants off ancestral land and were widely resented.
• Many were badly built, officials stole the construction money, and the Vietcong infiltrated them.
• A programme meant to cut the Vietcong off from the villages ended up recruiting for them.
Disagree:
• Diem’s political failures ran deeper: he refused the 1956 elections, ruled through his family and favoured Catholics in a mostly Buddhist country.
• The Buddhist crisis of May–June 1963, and Thich Quang Duc’s self-immolation on 11 June, destroyed Diem’s international standing on their own.
• Land policy had already alienated the countryside in the late 1950s, before the hamlets existed.
• Domino-theory thinking in Washington turned every local setback into a strategic crisis.
Judgement: The hamlets were a symptom of a deeper problem: Diem’s regime could not generate legitimacy with or without them.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a cable sent by US Ambassador to South Vietnam Henry Cabot Lodge to Washington, late August 1963.
‘We are launched on a course from which there is no respectable turning back: the overthrow of the Diem government. There is no possibility of any further effective collaboration with him. Our task is to manage the transition so that the war effort is not weakened.’

Source F suggests that by August 1963 the United States had decided that Diem could not be saved. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Lodge says the United States is ‘launched on a course from which there is no respectable turning back’.
• He states there is ‘no possibility of any further effective collaboration’ with Diem.
• The task is now to manage the transition without weakening the war effort.
Contextual knowledge: The generals struck on 1–2 November 1963 and Diem and Nhu were murdered; Washington had signalled it would not stand in the way.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Buddhist crisis of 1963 transformed US attitudes towards Diem between May and November of that year.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details (Hue, Thich Quang Duc, Madame Nhu, Lodge cable, the November coup).
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 8 May 1963: South Vietnamese troops fired on Buddhists marking the Buddha’s birthday in Hue, killing several.
• 11 June 1963: monk Thich Quang Duc self-immolated in Saigon; the photograph appeared worldwide.
• Summer 1963: Madame Nhu publicly mocked the protests as ‘barbecues’, deepening the international outrage.
• August 1963: US Ambassador Lodge cabled that there could be ‘no further effective collaboration’ with Diem.
• Autumn 1963: Washington signalled it would not stand in the way of a coup.
• 1–2 November 1963: South Vietnamese generals seized power; Diem and Nhu were assassinated.
• 22 November 1963: Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, leaving the Vietnam decision to Johnson.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Photograph taken in Kabul, October 1996. The image shows two women in pale blue burqas walking past a wall on which a Taliban poster has been pasted. The poster lists banned activities, including music, television and unaccompanied movement of women.

Study Source A. Source A suggests that the Taliban imposed their rules on Kabul very quickly. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences, each rooted in a specific detail of the source (the burqas, the poster of banned activities, the date so soon after the Kabul takeover).
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference; some detail.
Emerging: Description of the source without inference.

Indicative content:
• The image shows that the regime imposed strict dress rules on women very rapidly — the burqas are seen on a Kabul street within a month of the Taliban capture of the capital.
• The poster listing banned activities suggests the regime governed by public prohibition rather than persuasion, with rules pinned up in public spaces for citizens to read.
• The combination of women walking unaccompanied past a poster forbidding that very thing implies that early enforcement may have been uneven, or that the photograph was taken before the male-relative rule was tightened.
• The presence of a foreign journalist with a camera in 1996 suggests Western media still had some access to Kabul before later restrictions on photography of living things.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: A passage written in 2002 by a British journalist who had reported from Kabul during Taliban rule.
‘What people forget is that for the women in the bazaar in 1996 the Taliban had a single, terrible attraction: they ended the rocketing. Mujahideen warlords had been firing on the city for four years. The Taliban took Kabul in three days and the rockets stopped. Within months the women were locked in their homes — but the rockets had stopped.’

Study Source B. Source B suggests that some Afghans welcomed the Taliban in 1996. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The journalist suggests that personal safety mattered more than political freedom for some Kabul civilians (‘the rockets stopped’), implying the Taliban’s appeal was an end to civil-war violence rather than support for its ideology.
• The passage implies that the warlord period was so destructive that some women weighed enforced seclusion against the certainty of being shelled, a calculation hidden from later Western coverage.
• The phrase ‘within months’ suggests early acceptance turned to resentment quickly, but that the regime won initial legitimacy through restoring order rather than through genuine consent.
• Writing in 2002, after the regime had fallen, the journalist’s reflective tone suggests a corrective to a simpler post-9/11 view of the Taliban as universally hated.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Taliban came to control most of Afghanistan between 1994 and 1996.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Kandahar 1994, Mullah Omar, ISI backing, fall of Kabul September 1996, execution of Najibullah); arrives at the establishment of Taliban rule through a substantiated chain.
