Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 1992–94: warlord civil war shattered Kabul and discredited the mujahideen leadership.
• 1994: Mullah Omar and a small group of madrasa students confronted a local warlord in Kandahar, and the story attracted thousands of recruits from refugee camps.
• Pakistan’s ISI intelligence service quietly funded weapons, fuel and trucks to the new movement.
• 1995: the Taliban captured Herat in the west, opening the way north and east.
• September 1996: the Taliban entered Kabul as the Northern Alliance retreated; they executed former president Najibullah and hanged his body publicly.
• By the end of 1996, around two-thirds of the country was under Taliban control, and the Northern Alliance was confined to the north-east.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Taliban policy turned international opinion against the regime between 1996 and March 2001.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (women policy 1996, sheltering bin Laden 1996, Mazar-i-Sharif massacre 1998, UN Resolution 1267 1999, Bamiyan Buddhas March 2001); reaches the eve of 9/11 through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• September 1996: the Taliban entered Kabul and imposed bans on female employment and education that drew immediate Western condemnation.
• From late 1996 the regime hosted Osama bin Laden, who used Afghan camps to plan the 1998 East African embassy bombings.
• August 1998: the Mazar-i-Sharif massacre of Hazara civilians turned Iran and parts of the Muslim world against the regime.
• October 1999: UN Security Council Resolution 1267 imposed sanctions for the failure to extradite bin Laden.
• 2000: the USS Cole bombing further linked the regime to international terrorism.
• March 2001: the destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas drew condemnation from UNESCO and most Muslim states, leaving only three governments still recognising the Taliban on the eve of 9/11.

practice_questions.text: ‘The Taliban’s treatment of women was the most important reason it became internationally isolated by 2001.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: the exclusion of women from work and from school beyond the age of eight was visible from 1996 and drew immediate Western condemnation.
• Agree: campaigns such as the Feminist Majority Foundation’s, chaired by Mavis Leno from 1997, kept the issue in front of Western governments for years.
• Disagree: the sheltering of Osama bin Laden was the reason for UN sanctions under Resolution 1267 in 1999, the formal basis of the regime’s isolation.
• Disagree: the massacre of around 2,000 Hazara civilians at Mazar-i-Sharif in August 1998 turned Iran and much of the Muslim world against the regime.
• Disagree: the destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas in March 2001 drew condemnation from UNESCO, the Egyptian Grand Mufti and even Saudi Arabia.
• Judgement: women’s policy was the most consistent grievance from 1996, but isolation was cumulative, and the al-Qaeda sanctuary was what put the regime outside the law.

practice_questions.text: ‘Mullah Mohammed Omar was the most important reason for both the rise and the fall of the Taliban regime.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: the story of his confronting a warlord in Kandahar in 1994 turned a group of madrasa students into a national movement.
• Agree: his religious authority, sealed by the donning of the Cloak of the Prophet in 1996, gave the Taliban a legitimacy other warlords could not claim.
• Agree: his personal protection of bin Laden under Pashtunwali, and his order to destroy the Bamiyan Buddhas, brought the regime down.
• Disagree: the movement grew out of conditions he did not create — the 1992–96 warlord civil war, the refugee camps and the madrasas of the Pakistan border.
• Disagree: Pakistan’s ISI supplied the weapons, fuel and political cover that turned recruits into an army.
• Disagree: the regime fell to American and British air power working with Northern Alliance ground forces after 9/11.
• Judgement: he was the decisive individual, but the conditions that produced the Taliban and the coalition that destroyed it were both beyond his control.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of what followed the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It became a propaganda triumph: the Armada Portrait of Elizabeth and the ‘Gloriana’ image were promoted across the country to fix the victory in popular memory.
• It boosted Protestant morale across Europe and weakened the prestige of Spain as the leading Catholic power.
• It gave English naval commanders confidence that fed into expanded exploration in the 1590s and the continued Anglo-Spanish war until 1604.
• It hardened anti-Catholic feeling at home, giving Parliament cover to pass the 1593 Act against Popish Recusants.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the fireship attack at Calais on 28 July 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it was the moment that broke the Armada’s tight crescent formation, scattering ships north along the Flemish coast and exposing them to attack at Gravelines the next day.
• It ended any chance of the Armada meeting the Duke of Parma’s invasion army — the rendezvous Philip II’s plan depended on.
• It demonstrated the value of close-quarter tactics and naval initiative, traits that would shape later English campaigns.
• Significance over time: the fireships became a defining symbol of the victory, embedded in Elizabethan propaganda and English naval tradition.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Drake’s raid on Cadiz in 1587 and its effect on the Armada.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 30 Spanish ships were burnt at Cadiz, reducing the strength of the fleet that would sail in 1588.
• The destruction of seasoned barrel staves spoiled food and water on the Armada and contributed to disease and supply problems.
• The launch of the Armada was delayed by a year — from 1587 to 1588 — giving England more time to prepare.
• The raid damaged Philip II’s prestige across Europe and gave Drake personal celebrity status as the man who ‘singed the King of Spain’s beard’.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Sir John Hawkins’s work as Treasurer of the Navy before 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, his redesign of warships into longer, lower, faster race-built galleons gave English captains a tactical edge over the larger Spanish ships.
• The new ships carried more long-range bronze cannon, making stand-off broadsides possible — the tactic that won the Channel battles.
• His reforms to dockyards and pay reduced corruption and improved fleet readiness in the years before the Armada.
• Significance over time: the race-built design became the model for English warships into the seventeenth century, shaping later voyages and naval doctrine.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the way the Spanish Armada was built and commanded.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It consisted of around 130 ships carrying roughly 19,000 soldiers and 8,000 sailors.
• It sailed in a tight crescent formation designed to protect transports from English ships trying to break through.
• Its commander after the death of his predecessor was the Duke of Medina Sidonia, an inexperienced choice.
• Its mission was to escort the Duke of Parma’s 30,000-strong veteran army from the Netherlands to invade Kent.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Armada was beaten by English skill. The weather only finished off a fleet that was already defeated.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Hawkins’s race-built galleons were faster and better armed than the Spanish ships and gave the English a clear technological edge.
• English commanders chose stand-off broadside tactics rather than boarding, exploiting their long-range guns.
• Drake’s 1587 Cadiz raid weakened Spanish supply and delayed the launch by a year.
• The fireship attack at Calais was a deliberate English decision that scattered the crescent formation before the storms arrived.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Without Atlantic storms on the voyage home, far more Spanish ships would have returned to Spain — the weather caused the bulk of total losses.
• Spanish strategic overreach (no deep-water port for Parma) was as important as English skill.
• Medina Sidonia’s inexperience and Philip II’s rigid orders helped the English as much as English action did.
• Disease, hunger and Spanish supply failure played independent roles.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a leaflet distributed by Hungarian students in Budapest, 22 October 1956.
‘We demand the immediate withdrawal of all Soviet troops from Hungarian soil, the holding of free elections by secret ballot, the return of Imre Nagy to the leadership and the right of Hungarian workers to manage their own enterprises. We are not the enemies of socialism. We are the enemies of foreign occupation.’

Source A suggests that the Hungarian students wanted change without leaving communism. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Withdrawal of Soviet troops from Hungarian soil.
• Free elections by secret ballot.
• Return of Imre Nagy to the leadership.
• Right of Hungarian workers to manage their own enterprises.
• The students frame themselves as anti-occupation, not anti-socialist.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Students marched in Budapest on 23 October 1956 and pulled down a giant statue of Stalin.
• Imre Nagy returned as Prime Minister and ended one-party rule before announcing neutrality on 1 November.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a confidential telegram from the British ambassador in Moscow, Sir William Hayter, to the Foreign Office, 4 November 1956.
‘Soviet patience with Hungary has reached its limit. The decision to intervene was sealed when Nagy announced neutrality and departure from the Warsaw Pact. Moscow could not allow this precedent without risking the unravelling of its position in Eastern Europe.’

Source C: An extract from a 1957 article in the Soviet government newspaper Pravda explaining the intervention.
‘The events in Hungary were no spontaneous protest by workers. Reactionary elements, encouraged by Western broadcasts, sought to drag the country out of the socialist family. Soviet help was requested by loyal Hungarian comrades to defend socialism against counter-revolution.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying Soviet motives for the November 1956 invasion of Hungary. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: identifies Nagy’s neutrality announcement as the trigger and the ‘precedent’ risk for Moscow. Provenance: confidential telegram from a senior diplomat to his own government — likely to give a frank, well-informed assessment. Own knowledge: Nagy made the neutrality announcement on 1 November; the Soviet invasion began on 4 November.
Source C — Content: blames ‘reactionary elements’ and Western broadcasts; presents the invasion as defending socialism on Hungarian request. Provenance: Soviet state newspaper writing one year after the event — designed to justify Soviet action to domestic and foreign Communists. Own knowledge: the Janos Kadar government was installed by Moscow; the ‘invitation’ was not credible.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding Soviet decision-making but reflects one Western diplomat’s view; C is useful as evidence of Soviet justification but cannot be taken at face value as motivation.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Hungarian Uprising developed from Khrushchev’s Secret Speech in February 1956 to the Soviet invasion of Budapest on 4 November 1956.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, names, places); reaches the invasion through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• February 1956: Khrushchev delivered the Secret Speech denouncing Stalin, raising hopes of reform across the Eastern Bloc.
• June 1956: Polish workers struck in Poznan; Gomulka came to power in October and reached a compromise with Moscow.
• July 1956: Khrushchev removed Matyas Rakosi as Hungarian leader; replacement Erno Gero proved equally unpopular.
• 23 October 1956: Hungarian students marched in Budapest demanding reforms; security forces opened fire.
• 24 October to 28 October: Imre Nagy returned as Prime Minister; Soviet troops in Budapest pulled back.
• 1 November 1956: Nagy announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and become neutral.
• 4 November 1956: Around 200,000 Soviet troops and 2,500 tanks invaded Budapest, crushing the uprising and installing Janos Kadar.

practice_questions.text:
‘The West could have done nothing to save the Hungarian Uprising in 1956.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Hungary sat inside the Soviet sphere agreed at Yalta and had no NATO neighbour.
• Any military move risked direct war with a Soviet Union that already had nuclear weapons.
• The Suez Crisis split Britain and France from the USA at the decisive moment.
• The Soviet Union committed around 200,000 troops and 2,500 tanks, far more than any relief force could face.
Disagree:
• Radio Free Europe broadcasts told Hungarians to hold firm and raised hopes of help that never existed.
• American talk of rolling back communism had promised far more than Washington would deliver.
• The USA had privately ruled out intervention from the start, so the rhetoric was misleading rather than mistaken.
• Stronger diplomatic pressure, or a UN force, was never seriously attempted.
Judgement: military help was never realistic, but Western words encouraged the Hungarians to expect it, so the West could at least have been honest.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of a Budapest schoolteacher, kept during November 1956 and translated for publication in 1996.
‘4 November. The tanks came in the night. We hear shooting from across the river all morning. The radio that called us heroes yesterday is silent today. My students have hidden their textbooks. People say Nagy has gone to the Yugoslav embassy. We thought the world was watching, but the world has other work today.’

Source F suggests that Hungarians felt abandoned by the outside world. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: captures the suddenness of the invasion (‘tanks came in the night’) and the silence of supportive radio broadcasts — useful evidence of how Hungarians experienced the crackdown.
• Provenance: a contemporaneous diary by an ordinary Hungarian, not a politician — offers the civilian perspective that official sources usually miss.
• Own knowledge: the Soviet invasion began on 4 November; Nagy did take refuge in the Yugoslav embassy; the Kadar regime moved quickly to silence opposition.
• Useful contrast: the diary’s closing observation — that ‘the world has other work today’ — reflects the impact of Suez on Western attention.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Soviet response to Imre Nagy’s reforms between 23 October and Nagy’s execution in June 1958.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at Nagy’s execution through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 23 October 1956: Hungarian students marched; security forces opened fire; Soviet leadership initially undecided.
• 24 October 1956: Imre Nagy returned as Prime Minister; Khrushchev briefly considered a Polish-style compromise.
• 1 November 1956: Nagy announced neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact — a step Khrushchev decided he could not accept.
• 4 November 1956: Soviet invasion using around 200,000 troops and 2,500 tanks; Janos Kadar installed as new leader.
• November 1956: Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy; was lured out under safe-conduct and arrested.
• 1957: Nagy held in custody in Romania; tried in secret in Hungary in 1958.
• June 1958: Nagy executed by the Kadar regime, sending a Cold War signal that no Eastern Bloc leader could leave the alliance and survive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Anti-Slavery movement and the Anti-Corn Law League were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both organised mass petitioning of Parliament — anti-slavery petitions of the 1780s and 1790s, the League’s petitions of the 1840s — to apply pressure on MPs from outside the electorate.
• Similarity: both used charismatic individuals (Wilberforce, Cobden, Bright) as a parliamentary face for a much wider organisation built on local groups.
• Similarity: both targeted a specific Act of Parliament rather than the whole political system, and both succeeded — the 1807 Slave Trade Act and the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act for one; the 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws for the other.
• Similarity: both used pamphlets, public lectures and moral arguments to change public opinion before changing the law.

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Olaudah Equiano for the anti-slavery movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: his autobiography (1789) was a bestseller, going through nine editions in his lifetime and reaching readers across Britain who had no other contact with the realities of slavery.
• At the time: his lecture tours of Britain put a Black voice and a human face on a system most British people experienced only through sugar and cotton.
• Over time: he provided one of the founding texts of African and African-American autobiographical writing, used by historians and abolitionists worldwide for the next two centuries.
• Over time: his work corrects the modern misconception that abolition was a gift from white reformers — Equiano shows enslaved and formerly enslaved people were central to ending the trade.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of who Equiano was without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of organised pressure groups in Britain between 1780 and 1846.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade (1787) built the first national campaign, using petitions, lecture tours and the sugar boycott of 1791.
• At the time: those methods delivered real law — the Slave Trade Act 1807 and the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.
• At the time: the Anti-Corn Law League from 1838 added paid staff, the penny post of 1840, the railways and election screening, and won repeal in 1846.
• Over time: a recognisable model of the modern pressure group existed by 1846 — organised, national, well funded, and able to force change without holding office.
• Over time: suffragists, trade unions and modern campaigners all worked inside that model, which is why these campaigns matter beyond their own causes.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: ‘The role of individuals was the main factor in the success of the anti-slavery and Anti-Corn Law campaigns.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of individuals as the main factor:
• Wilberforce gave anti-slavery its parliamentary voice and persistence over twenty years; without him the cause might have lacked a Commons advocate.
• Cobden and Bright built the Anti-Corn Law League into a national operation; their lecture tours and parliamentary speeches were central to repeal in 1846.
• Equiano, Lord Shaftesbury and Hannah More each shaped specific aspects of the moral case.

Weighed against communication:
• The penny post (1840) and the railways were what allowed the League to operate nationally; without them, individuals could not have reached a mass audience.
• Pamphlets, petitions and the radical press carried both campaigns far beyond their leaders.

Weighed against religion:
• Quaker networks built anti-slavery long before Wilberforce joined Parliament; without that organisation, no individual could have started the movement.
• Shaftesbury’s evangelical Christianity gave factory reform its moral framework.

Weighed against ideas (rights, free trade):
• Anti-slavery drew on Enlightenment ideas about natural rights and Christian equality.
• The League drew on classical economics and free-trade theory; ideas gave each cause its public legitimacy.

Judgement: Top answers argue that individuals matter only inside the conditions that make them effective. The Quaker network, the penny post and free-trade ideas turned Wilberforce, Cobden and Shaftesbury into national figures. Without those wider factors, the same individuals would have been minor MPs.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others, with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples comparing individuals to other factors; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists factors without comparison or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Anti-Corn Law League for British politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: forced repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, lowering bread prices and ending agricultural protection at a moment of Irish Famine.
• At the time: split the Conservative Party (Peel against most of his MPs), reshaping party politics for a generation.
• Over time: created the model of the professional pressure group — paid staff, national reach, election screening — used by trade unions, suffragists and modern campaigners.
• Over time: the symbolic victory of the unrepresented middle class over the landed interest reinforced the trajectory of further parliamentary reform.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of what the League did with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the methods of the anti-slavery movement and the Chartists were different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: anti-slavery focused on a single targeted Act of Parliament; Chartism demanded six wide-ranging constitutional changes at once.
• Difference: anti-slavery used a national consumer boycott (sugar 1791) as a key tactic; Chartism used mass meetings and the threat of physical force.
• Difference: anti-slavery had cross-class support including aristocrats and Quaker merchants; Chartism was a working-class movement that explicitly contrasted itself with the middle class after 1832.
• Difference: anti-slavery succeeded with the political class largely on its side; Chartism was rejected by Parliament three times.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the diary of an Australian sergeant serving near Broodseinde, written in October 1917.
‘The shell fire turned the Flanders fields into a swamp. Men slid into shell holes filled to the brim and could not be pulled out. Yet our guns kept walking forward in front of us at the proper pace, and where the mud allowed, we walked behind them as we had been trained.’

Source A suggests that the ground at Passchendaele was ruinous but British artillery tactics had improved. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Shellfire had turned the Flanders fields into ‘a swamp’.
• Men ‘slid into shell holes filled to the brim and could not be pulled out’.
• ‘Our guns kept walking forward in front of us at the proper pace’ - a creeping barrage.
• The infantry ‘walked behind them as we had been trained’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Allied bombardment destroyed the Flanders drainage system, and August 1917 was the wettest in thirty years.
• Plumer's ‘bite and hold’ attacks at Menin Road, Polygon Wood and Broodseinde depended on that artillery accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the British Expeditionary Force’s tactics evolved between the first day of the Somme on 1 July 1916 and the Battle of Cambrai on 20 November 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more developments as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Somme errors, Messines mines, Plumer’s bite and hold, sound-ranging, Cambrai); reaches Cambrai through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked developments with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant developments listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between developments.

Indicative content:
• 1 July 1916: catastrophic first-day Somme losses revealed that walking-pace advance into uncut wire and surviving German dugouts was unworkable.
• Late 1916: tanks deployed at Flers-Courcelette (15 September) showed potential despite mechanical failure.
• Early 1917: Germany withdrew to the Hindenburg Line; the BEF reorganised infantry into platoons of riflemen, bombers, Lewis-gunners and rifle-grenadiers.
• 7 June 1917: 19 mines detonated under the Messines Ridge, capturing the position cleanly with low losses — the explosion was heard in London.
• Summer 1917: General Plumer’s ‘bite and hold’ method took Menin Road, Polygon Wood and Broodseinde with overwhelming artillery support.
• 20 November 1917: 476 tanks broke the Hindenburg Line on a six-mile front at Cambrai, demonstrating mass-tank surprise attack as a tactical answer to trench warfare.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by General Sir Hubert Gough to GHQ in late August 1917.
‘The terrain is no longer practicable for the rapid breakthrough that was originally planned. The drainage of the Flanders plain is destroyed, the rains continue, and our tanks cannot move. To press on now in the same form would be to send men into a marsh.’

Source C: An extract from a War Cabinet memorandum by Field Marshal Haig, dated October 1917, recording the strategic case for continuing the offensive.
‘The French army is recovering from severe disturbance and cannot lead a major offensive this year. Russia is a broken reed; the Eastern Front will release fresh German divisions. We must keep the German forces fixed in Flanders. To break off our attack would invite catastrophe in 1918.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the decision to continue the Passchendaele offensive. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Gough acknowledges the terrain is no longer suitable for breakthrough. Provenance: a frontline army commander writing internally to GHQ; likely to give a candid operational picture, though he may also be defending his early lack of progress. Own knowledge: Haig replaced Gough with the more methodical Plumer in late August/September 1917, suggesting agreement with the operational picture.
Source C — Content: Haig argues continued attack is needed because of French mutiny recovery and the looming German reinforcement from Russia. Provenance: a senior commander writing to government; intended to justify continued offensive, so likely to overstate strategic necessity. Own knowledge: General Nivelle’s April offensive had triggered widespread French army mutinies; the Bolshevik seizure of power on 7 November 1917 confirmed that German troops would soon move west.
Judgement: B is useful for the operational reality; C is useful for strategic reasoning but partial — a defence of an unpopular decision. Together they show the gap between local conditions and high-command priorities.

practice_questions.text:
‘British generals were incompetent and the soldiers paid the price.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• 57,470 casualties fell on the first day of the Somme and about 275,000 at Passchendaele.
• Haig kept attacking at Passchendaele after the rain had made the ground impassable.
• Gough was left pushing for rapid breakthrough for weeks before Plumer's methods replaced his.

Disagree:
• The BEF learned: sound-ranging, predicted fire, platoon organisation and accurate creeping barrages did not exist in 1916.
• Messines in June 1917 and Cambrai in November 1917 were carefully planned successes.
• The Hundred Days of 1918 produced the fastest advance of the war on the Western Front.
• No army had a template for breaking trench deadlock, and Haig was under pressure to keep Germany busy while the French army recovered from mutinies.

Judgement: ‘Incompetent’ is too strong. British generalship was uneven and made costly mistakes, but it also led a real tactical transformation that won the war in 1918.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter by General Sir Herbert Plumer to his wife, dated 8 October 1917.
‘Bite and hold has gained us Menin Road, Polygon Wood, and now Broodseinde. The barrage moves at the proper rate; the men keep behind it; we take the ground we can hold and stop. We do not chase glory across mud we cannot move guns over. The men deserve nothing less.’

Source F suggests that Plumer deliberately limited each attack to what his guns could support. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• ‘Bite and hold’ has taken Menin Road, Polygon Wood and now Broodseinde.
• ‘The barrage moves at the proper rate; the men keep behind it.’
• ‘We take the ground we can hold and stop’ - no chasing distant objectives.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Plumer's methods replaced Gough's push for rapid breakthrough after the setbacks of early August 1917.
• The same careful artillery and infantry co-operation shaped the Hundred Days in 1918.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the events of the Third Battle of Ypres between the opening bombardment in mid-July 1917 and the capture of Passchendaele village in November 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Messines, opening 31 July, Plumer takeover, capture of village 6/10 November); reaches the close of the battle through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 7 June 1917: Messines Ridge captured cleanly when 19 mines were detonated under the German line — the explosion heard in London.
• Mid-July 1917: a 14-day Allied bombardment fired over four million shells, destroying the Flanders drainage system.
• 31 July 1917: Third Ypres opened under Gough; rapid breakthrough was meant to drive towards Belgian U-boat ports but stalled in worsening rain.
• Late August 1917: Haig replaced Gough with Plumer, who introduced ‘bite and hold’.
• Sept–Oct 1917: Plumer’s carefully prepared advances took Menin Road (20 Sept), Polygon Wood (26 Sept) and Broodseinde (4 Oct).
• 6 November 1917: Canadian troops captured Passchendaele village; the offensive was halted by 10 November after roughly five miles of advance for around 275,000 British and Empire casualties.

practice_questions.text: ‘Economic resources were the most important factor in British expansion in India between 1757 and 1857.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh economic resources against at least two other factors (war, ideas, role of individuals, government) with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of economic resources as the main factor:
• The East India Company was a trading company; its drive into India followed cotton, opium and tea profits.
• The 1765 Bengal *diwani* gave the Company tax revenue that funded its armies; one province paid for the conquest of others.
• British industrial demand for cotton and Indian markets for British manufactures made empire commercially self-sustaining.

Weighed against war:
• Plassey 1757, the Mysore wars (1767-99), the Maratha wars and the Sikh wars repeatedly turned trading posts into provinces.
• The 1857 reprisals showed that without superior military force the Company could not hold India.

Weighed against the role of individuals:
• Clive’s personal generalship at Plassey, Hastings’ political consolidation, Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse and the Rani of Jhansi’s resistance all shaped events that economic forces alone do not explain.

Weighed against ideas:
• Macaulay’s 1835 Minute on Education and evangelical missionary activity provided ideological justification; Indian responses to evangelism helped trigger 1857.

Judgement: Economic resources drove expansion but war secured it — the two reinforced each other. Individuals decided pace; ideas decided how empire was administered. The strongest answers reach across the period to compare 1757 (private corporation profit) with 1858 (state-led empire).

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes economic causes only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Battle of Plassey (1757) for the development of British rule in India.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Clive’s victory installed a puppet Nawab (Mir Jafar) and gave the East India Company effective control of Bengal.
• At the time: the 1765 grant of *diwani* turned military victory into permanent tax revenue from one of India’s richest provinces.
• Over time: Bengali tax revenue funded the Company army that conquered the rest of India over the following century.
• Over time: Plassey is conventionally treated as the start of British India — the moment a trading company became a territorial empire.
• Limitation: the Company would still have needed Hastings’ later consolidation to turn military victory into a workable government.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which East India Company rule in India was different from Crown rule after 1858.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: before 1858 a chartered trading company ruled, with its own army, courts, currency and tax system; after 1858 the Crown ruled directly through a Viceroy and the India Office in London.
• Difference: Company government answered to shareholders, with Parliament supervising through the Board of Control created in 1784; after 1858 ministers answered to Parliament for India directly.
• Difference: the Company annexed states through the Doctrine of Lapse and, in Oudh in 1856, for alleged misgovernment; after 1858 princely adoptions were respected and annexation stopped.
• Similarity: both rested on the Indian army and on Indian tax revenue, and in both periods almost no Indians held senior political power.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named examples.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1857 Indian Rebellion for British rule in India.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the rising spread from Meerut across northern and central India and took the British fourteen months to suppress, with savage reprisals.
• At the time: the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the East India Company and transferred rule to the Crown, with a Viceroy in India and the India Office in London.
• At the time: Bahadur Shah II was tried and exiled to Burma, ending the Mughal line.
• Over time: British policy avoided open interference with religion and custom, restricted missionary activity and respected princely adoptions.
• Over time: in 1877 Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India, making the empire a formal part of British monarchy.
• Over time: Indian nationalists later called the rising the ‘First War of Independence’, so it shaped how both countries remembered empire.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Warren Hastings for the East India Company.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: as first Governor-General from 1772, Hastings centralised Company government and standardised tax collection.
• At the time: he expanded and reorganised the sepoy army that would later conquer the rest of India.
• At the time: he commissioned scholarly translation of Indian texts (Bhagavad Gita) and respected local elites — an early orientalist style of empire.
• Over time: Pitt’s India Act of 1784 had already given Parliament a Board of Control, and his impeachment trial of 1788-95 hardened that oversight.
• Over time: his governorship became the model the Company built on for the next 70 years.
• Limitation: his methods were ruthless — corruption charges were not entirely without basis.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the impact of empire on India was different from its impact on Britain.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference (economic): Britain gained tea, cotton and indigo for its consumer revolution and wealth for country houses and banks, while India saw cash crops replace subsistence farming and its textile industry restricted to protect Lancashire.
• Difference (human cost): the Bengal famines of 1770 and 1943 each killed millions in India; Britain had no comparable cost.
• Difference (political): Britain gained an empire and a route to wealth for younger sons of the gentry; India lost control of its own government until 1947.
• Similarity: both societies were changed culturally — English-language schooling and railways in India, and Indian words such as bungalow, pyjamas and shampoo in English.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named examples.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the 1848 Public Health Act and the 1875 Public Health Act were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: the 1848 Act was adoptive (towns could choose to opt in); the 1875 Act was compulsory across all local authorities.
• Difference: the 1848 Act focused on a General Board of Health; the 1875 Act covered sewers, water, refuse, food, housing and notifiable disease in one statute.
• Similarity: both were responses to cholera epidemics that exposed urban sanitary failure.
• Similarity: both were shaped by individual reformers (Chadwick in 1848, Disraeli’s government and earlier figures in 1875) and by communication of scientific evidence.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of John Snow for the development of public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Snow’s 1854 Broad Street pump map proved cholera was waterborne seven years before Pasteur’s germ theory.
• At the time: removing the pump handle stopped new cases and convinced local officials that water, not bad air, was the route of infection.
• Over time: Snow’s methods (mapping, statistical comparison) became foundational for epidemiology.
• Over time: his findings helped justify Bazalgette’s sewer system and the 1875 Public Health Act once germ theory caught up.
• Limitation: the General Board of Health rejected his findings; he was not vindicated until the 1860s — significance is shaped by acceptance over time.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and the timeline of acceptance.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1875 Public Health Act for public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: it made action compulsory for every local authority, unlike the adoptive 1848 Act that many towns had ignored.
• At the time: it put sewers, water, refuse, food inspection, slaughterhouses, building standards and notifiable disease into one statute.
• At the time: the same government passed the Artisans’ Dwellings Act for slum clearance and laws on food and river pollution.
• Over time: it ended laissez-faire in public health and made the local medical officer of health a permanent part of British government.
• Over time: it set the direction that led to the Liberal reforms of 1906-11 and to the NHS in 1948.
• Limitation: enforcement depended on local money and local will, so improvement stayed uneven for decades.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Has government been the main factor in improving public health in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh government against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of government as the main factor:
• The 1848 and 1875 Public Health Acts could only be delivered by Parliament — the 1875 Act ended laissez-faire and made action compulsory.
• Liberal welfare reforms 1906–11 and the 1948 NHS continued the pattern of government-led public health.
• Compare medieval period: in 1348 there was almost no central government action on the Black Death; in 1948 the NHS was a state monopoly.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Chadwick built the case for 1848; Snow proved waterborne cholera; Bazalgette engineered London’s sewers; Bevan delivered the NHS.
• Without these individuals, government would have acted later or weaker.

Weighed against communication:
• Chadwick’s 1842 report, Mayhew’s journalism, Punch cartoons during the Great Stink, the 300,000 copies of the 1942 Beveridge Report — communication built the political pressure on government.

Weighed against science and technology:
• Pasteur’s germ theory (1861) and Koch’s bacteriology (1876–83) changed what government could justify; without science, public health spending could be argued away.

Judgement: government was the lever that delivered change, but the lever was pulled by individuals, communication and science. Across the sweep, government becomes more important after democratic reform (1867) and again after the world wars. The strongest answers note the change in government’s role from absent (1348) to compulsory (1875) to universal (1948).

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes government action only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Edwin Chadwick for the development of public health in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Chadwick’s 1842 report assembled the statistical case that bad housing caused poverty and disease, not the reverse.
• At the time: it directly shaped the 1848 Public Health Act and the General Board of Health.
• Over time: established the principle that public health was a fit subject for national legislation, paving the way for 1875 and beyond.
• Over time: his statistical method — comparing mortality across districts — became standard in modern epidemiology.
• Limitation: his authoritarian style provoked backlash; the General Board was abolished in 1858. Significance is shaped by both contribution and reaction.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and an awareness of the backlash.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: John Snow’s map of the Soho cholera outbreak, published in 1855. Each death is marked as a black bar against the house where it happened, and the bars cluster tightly around the water pump in Broad Street.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying the causes of cholera in Victorian London?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: the clustering is the argument — it puts a water pump, not bad air, at the centre of the deaths.
• Content: it also lets a historian see the exceptions Snow tested, such as nearby workers who drank beer and stayed well.
• Provenance: made by a doctor investigating an outbreak he had walked himself and published to persuade officials, so it is evidence gathered on purpose and organised around his case.
• Contextual knowledge: Snow proved this seven years before germ theory and could not show what was in the water; the General Board of Health rejected his findings and stayed with miasma.
• Limitations: it maps one outbreak in one district, cannot explain how cholera reached the pump and cannot show why officials refused to act.
• Judgement: outstanding for method and for the water-borne case, limited for explaining why change took so long.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1962 history of the American West written for a general American readership):
‘The Mountain Meadows Massacre was the desperate act of a frontier community under siege. With Buchanan’s army marching towards them, the southern Utah Mormons believed any wagon train might carry hostile spies. The killings were a tragedy, but they were the work of frightened men in extraordinary circumstances, not a planned atrocity.’

Interpretation B (from a 2002 study by historians using newly released Latter-day Saint Church archives):
‘Mountain Meadows was not a panicked overreaction but a co-ordinated militia operation. Local leaders gave specific orders, the truce flag was a deliberate trap, and the cover-up that blamed the Paiute alone lasted twenty years. The massacre exposes the closed authority of the early Utah theocracy.’

How convincing is Interpretation B? Use Interpretations A and B and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s argument; engages directly with the specific claims (co-ordinated, truce as trap, twenty-year cover-up, closed theocracy); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation of B with reference to A; some own knowledge applied; judgement reached.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to summarise rather than weigh; one or two pieces of own knowledge.
Emerging: Describes the interpretations or the topic without evaluating B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Truce flag tactic and direct involvement of John D. Lee — planning, not panic.
• The cover-up blaming the Paiute alone held for almost two decades.
• Lee’s 1876 trial revealed militia structure and chain of command.
• Federal investigators were obstructed for years by Mormon authorities.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• The Utah War of 1857–58 created genuine fears of federal invasion.
• Local rumours linked the Arkansas party to the murder of the apostle Parley P. Pratt in Arkansas in May 1857.
• Most modern Mormon scholarship rejects the ‘direct order from Brigham Young’ thesis.

Judgement: B is the stronger explanation of how the killings happened, but a top-band answer notes that A captures the war-hysteria context that made militia action thinkable in the first place.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B again.

Interpretation A: 1962 history of the American West written for a general American readership.
Interpretation B: 2002 study by historians using newly released Latter-day Saint Church archives.

Why might Interpretations A and B have different views of the Mountain Meadows Massacre? Use both interpretations and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in author purpose, evidence available, time of writing or audience — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons; some clarity.
Developing: One reason developed and one weak; or both partially explained.
Emerging: Reasons describe what each interpretation says, missing the question.

Indicative content:
• Different evidence available: B uses Latter-day Saint Church archives released in the late 20th century, which the 1962 author of A could not see.
• Different time of writing: A was written in 1962, when American historiography was less revisionist; B in 2002, after the rise of revisionist Western history (Limerick, White) reframed frontier violence.
• Different purpose: A’s general-reader survey aimed for a digestible ‘tragedy’ framing; B’s academic study aimed to test responsibility precisely.
• Different audiences: A was written for a wide American readership in the early 1960s; B for an academic and Mormon-history audience post-millennium.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 2010 study of US religious freedom):
‘Federal anti-polygamy laws between 1862 and 1890 were necessary defences of the rule of law. The Constitution could not tolerate a single religious group claiming the right to ignore federal statutes. The 1890 Manifesto was not a tragedy — it was the price of citizenship, and the Mormons paid it because they wanted to be Americans.’

How convincing is Interpretation C? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s argument; weighs the ‘necessary defence of law’ framing against alternative readings; supports judgement with precise own knowledge of the three federal laws and the 1890 Manifesto.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial use of own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the laws without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• The Constitution required equal application of federal law in all territories.
• Plural marriage was widely judged exploitative of women in 19th-century debate.
• Mormons themselves accepted the 1890 Manifesto as the route to statehood — a form of consent.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• The 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act dissolved the Church and seized property — a level of state action against a religion unique in US history.
• Polygamy continued unofficially in some communities for years after 1890.
• An alternative reading sees the laws as religious coercion rather than constitutional defence.

Judgement: C captures one valid framing — constitutional defence — but a top-band response notes the laws went well beyond preventing polygamous unions to dismantling the Church itself.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C again.

Interpretation C: a 2010 study of US religious freedom.
Interpretation D (from a 1998 social history written by a Latter-day Saint historian):
‘The Edmunds-Tucker Act of 1887 was an act of religious persecution. The dissolution of the Church and the confiscation of its property went far beyond punishing polygamy. The 1890 Manifesto was a forced surrender, made under economic and legal duress, by a community whose alternative was destruction.’

Why might Interpretations C and D have different views of the federal anti-polygamy laws? Use both interpretations and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons focused on author identity/purpose, audience, evidence emphasis or framing — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed reason and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons summarise the interpretations rather than explaining difference.

Indicative content:
• Different author standpoints: C is written from a constitutional/legal-history perspective; D by a Mormon historian using community sources and oral memory.
• Different evidence emphasis: C focuses on statutes and federal-court reasoning; D on the lived experience of Mormon families under prosecution.
• Different purpose: C aims to defend a constitutional principle; D aims to recover a community story of suffering.
• Different audiences: C addresses a legal-academic readership; D writes within and for a Latter-day Saint scholarly community.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1995 academic study of US territorial expansion):
‘The fundamental obstacle to Utah statehood was not polygamy at all but theocracy. Washington could not accept a community where civic and religious authority were the same person. The 1890 Manifesto only became a route to statehood because it implied the separation of church and state Brigham Young had refused.’

How convincing is Interpretation E? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s ‘theocracy not polygamy’ thesis; substantiates judgement with precise own knowledge of Mormon-federal relations 1857–1896.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial use of own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with E’s specific argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• Buchanan sent the 1857 army against Mormon political control, not solely against polygamy.
• The Edmunds Act stripped Mormons of voting rights in Utah — an attack on theocratic governance.
• Federally appointed governors and judges were specifically designed to break Mormon civic dominance.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• Public Eastern outrage was framed primarily around polygamy, not theocracy.
• The 1882 and 1887 Acts targeted plural marriage by name.
• The 1890 Manifesto explicitly addressed marriage practice, not church-state separation.

Judgement: E offers a sharp insight — theocratic authority WAS as alarming to Washington as plural marriage — but a top-band answer recognises both targets shaped federal action.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E again.

Interpretation E: a 1995 academic study of US territorial expansion.
Interpretation F (from a popular history of the American West, published 2018):
‘The Mormon question was settled by money. The 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act seized Church property and pushed the Latter-day Saints towards bankruptcy. Once survival was at stake, plural marriage became negotiable in a way it had never been when only principle was on the table.’

Why might Interpretations E and F have different views of how the Mormon question was settled? Use both interpretations and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in audience, purpose, evidence and time of writing — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons describe interpretations rather than explaining difference.

Indicative content:
• Different audiences and purposes: E is an academic territorial-expansion study foregrounding constitutional theory; F is a popular history foregrounding pragmatic and economic causes that engage general readers.
• Different evidence emphasis: E focuses on the apparatus of governance (governors, voting rights); F on Church finances and the property seizure.
• Different historiographical framing: E sits in 1990s political history; F in 2010s revisionist popular history with a more cynical view of religious-political compromise.
• Different time of writing: F (2018) follows decades of work emphasising material and economic factors in religious history.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the new houses the gentry built under Elizabeth.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They often had ground plans shaped like the letter E or H, in honour of Elizabeth.
• They used large windows of small leaded panes — Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire was said to have ‘more glass than wall’.
• They featured decorative chimneys, multiple fireplaces, and a long gallery for display.
• They were built or remodelled in brick or stone with two storeys, replacing earlier timber buildings.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the gentry came to run county government under Elizabeth.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The gentry filled most of the offices of justice of the peace, sheriff and militia captain — the people who ran county government day to day.
• They came to dominate the House of Commons, increasing its confidence in dealing with the Crown.
• Their wealth gave them the leisure to take on unpaid public office, embedding the regime in county society without paid bureaucracy.
• Their growing power helped fund Elizabeth’s government — gentry contributions to militia, charity and parish work were significant.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about dress and the rules on apparel in Elizabethan society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Men wore padded doublets, breeches, and starched white ruffs that grew increasingly large by the 1580s.
• Women wore farthingales (hooped skirts) over tight bodices, with elaborate sleeves and decorative trims.
• Wealthy clothing used purple, red, black with silver, pearls and embroidery as status markers.
• Sumptuary laws such as the 1574 statute restricted purple silk and cloth-of-gold to the royal family and the highest nobility.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how rising food prices affected different groups in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Landowning gentry and yeoman farmers benefited — the same harvest sold at higher prices increased their income.
• Wage labourers and the urban poor were squeezed because wages did not keep up with prices, especially in years of harvest failure (1586, 1594, 1596–97).
• Merchants and middlemen profited from handling and trading the more valuable produce.
• Government action was needed: rising poverty drove the Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598 to manage the visible distress.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the sale of monastic land for the rise of the gentry.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Vast amounts of former monastic land were thrown onto the market in the 1530s; gentry families bought it cheap and held it through Elizabeth’s reign.
• Returns from this land rose with food prices in the 1570s and 1580s, expanding gentry wealth.
• Newly enriched gentry were able to fund larger houses, more education, and entry into Parliament.
• It tied the gentry to the Protestant settlement — restoring monastic land to the Catholic Church would have meant losing their estates.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Elizabethan age was a golden age only for those who already owned land.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about living standards in Elizabethan England? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The gentry grew in wealth, houses and political power; theatre and music flourished; long-distance trade and exploration expanded.
• Diet, dress and housing improved noticeably for the middling sort — the ‘Great Rebuilding’ produced larger, brighter homes.
• Yet harvest failures in 1586, 1594 and 1596–97 brought real hunger; vagrancy rose sharply; the 1572 Vagabonds Act classed jobless beggars as criminals.
• Catholic recusants faced rising fines, missionary executions and the constant threat of treason charges.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Cultural achievements (Shakespeare, the Armada, the spread of print) were genuinely shared with townspeople through theatre, ballads and pamphlets.
• Some Poor Law provision (1598) was real and locally administered — it cushioned at least the most vulnerable.
• Higher real wages for skilled craftsmen in some regions complicate the ‘poor got poorer’ story.
• The wider European context made even modest English stability look golden by comparison.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1935 speech by Senator Huey Long arguing the New Deal had failed to help working people enough) and Interpretation B (a 1936 Democratic Party campaign leaflet praising Social Security and the Wagner Act). What is the main difference between these views about the New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the New Deal as inadequate — the rich kept their fortunes and ordinary Americans had not been lifted out of hardship.
• Interpretation B presents the New Deal as a transformation — pensions, unemployment insurance and union rights for the first time in American history.
• Main difference: A frames the New Deal as a missed chance for radical redistribution; B frames it as a historic achievement that helped working Americans.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1935 Huey Long speech) and Interpretation B (a 1936 Democratic Party campaign leaflet) give different views about the New Deal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — Long’s speech aimed to recruit support for his Share Our Wealth movement and a possible 1936 presidential challenge; the campaign leaflet aimed to re-elect Roosevelt.
• They use different evidence — Long cites the persistence of great private fortunes; the leaflet cites the Wagner Act and Social Security as concrete reforms.
• They were produced from different political positions — a populist senator to the left of Roosevelt versus the official Democratic campaign defending the President’s record.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘The New Deal failed African-Americans more than it helped them.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the experience of African-Americans under the New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because AAA payments to landowners encouraged the eviction of black sharecroppers and tenant farmers across the South.
• Convincing because NRA codes set lower wages for southern workers, where most black Americans lived; CCC camps were segregated; and Roosevelt refused to back a federal anti-lynching bill to keep southern Democratic votes.
• Convincing because domestic and agricultural workers, the bulk of black female employment, were excluded from Social Security.
• Less convincing because around 200,000 black Americans found CCC work; Roosevelt’s informal ‘Black Cabinet’ (including Mary McLeod Bethune) gave the federal government a moral language on race that earlier presidents had refused.
• Less convincing because federal relief and WPA employment did reach urban black communities, especially in northern cities — the 1936 black vote shifted decisively to the Democrats.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on rural and structural failures; partially overstated on the symbolic and federal-employment gains.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Supreme Court rulings against the New Deal between 1935 and 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Schechter v. United States (May 1935) struck down the NRA as unconstitutional, ending the system of industry codes on wages, hours and prices, and forcing Roosevelt to find new constitutional foundations for federal action.
• United States v. Butler (January 1936) struck down the original AAA — the federal payment system to farmers had to be rebuilt under different legal authority via the 1938 second AAA.
• The rulings provoked Roosevelt’s 1937 court-packing plan to add up to six new justices, which was rejected by Congress and damaged his political authority during his second term.
• In response to the rulings, Roosevelt and Congress designed the 1935 Wagner Act and Social Security Act with stronger constitutional foundations — making the Second New Deal more focused on workers’ rights and federal taxation than direct industry regulation.
