[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Roosevelt launched a Second New Deal in 1935.
You may consider:
• Supreme Court strikes against the First New Deal
• pressure from radical critics such as Huey Long, Father Coughlin and Dr Townsend.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Court strikes: Schechter (May 1935) struck down the NRA; the AAA was vulnerable; Roosevelt needed reforms with safer constitutional foundations.
• Persistent unemployment: around 11 million still out of work in 1934; the First New Deal had stopped collapse but not delivered full recovery.
• Huey Long: Senator from Louisiana, ‘Share Our Wealth’ movement, $5,000 per family promise; threatened a 1936 third-party run before his assassination in September 1935.
• Father Coughlin: weekly radio broadcasts to 40 million listeners demanding bank nationalisation and silver-backed currency.
• Dr Townsend: $200-a-month pension proposal for the over-60s, with strong support among the elderly.
• 1936 election approaching: Roosevelt needed a sharper offer to working-class voters and the elderly.
• Result: Wagner Act (union rights); Social Security Act (pensions, unemployment insurance, aid to dependent children); WPA (8.5 million workers employed); wealth tax raising top rates to 75%.
• Outcome: Roosevelt won 46 of 48 states in 1936.
• Conclusion: the Second New Deal was Roosevelt’s response to a pincer of judicial blockage and populist pressure — the Court forced a constitutional rebuild and the radicals forced a redistributive turn.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Social Security Act of 1935.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It established federal pensions for retired Americans aged over 65, funded by payroll taxes on workers and employers — the first national old-age pension system in American history.
• It introduced unemployment insurance jointly run by the federal government and the states, providing a temporary income to workers who lost their jobs.
• It included aid to dependent children for poor families, particularly widows and abandoned mothers raising children alone.
• It excluded domestic and agricultural workers — meaning many African-American and Mexican-American women, and farm labourers, were not covered.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It divided conquered Gwynedd into the new English-style counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth.
• Each new county was given a sheriff, an exchequer and a system of writs based on English common law.
• The Marcher lordships of eastern Wales kept their semi-independent status under the statute.
• Some Welsh customs, such as partible inheritance, were tolerated alongside English law.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Wales was changed by the second Welsh war of 1282–83.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed at Cilmeri on 11 December 1282 and his head paraded in London — ending the line of native Welsh princes.
• His brother Dafydd was executed in 1283 by hanging, drawing and quartering — the first English nobleman ever sentenced to that punishment, designed to deter further rebellion.
• The Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) imposed English shire administration on Gwynedd, dividing it into Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth.
• Edward began the Iron Ring castle programme — Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and (after 1295) Beaumaris — under Master James of St George.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Edward I built and settled his castles in Wales after 1283.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The castles were placed where a fleet from England could resupply them by sea, so a Welsh rising could not starve the garrison.
• Each castle was paired with a planted English borough, a walled town settled with English merchants and craftsmen who paid rents directly to the king.
• They used concentric design — a lower outer wall ringing a higher inner wall — with polygonal towers and gatehouses that were small fortresses in their own right.
• They were designed by the Savoyard mason Master James of St George at a total cost of roughly £80,000.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Iron Ring of castles for Edward I’s control of Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the castles deterred rebellion: when Madog ap Llywelyn rose in 1294–95, the existing fortresses held out long enough for Edward to bring an army back from his French preparations.
• The paired planted boroughs spread English settlement, trade and taxation into the conquered north-west, embedding royal control beyond simple military presence.
• The total cost of around £80,000 forced new taxation, including the wool tax of 1294, with knock-on effects on the whole reign.
• Significance over time: the buildings still dominate the north Welsh landscape; the political settlement they enforced lasted into the union with England under the Tudors.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise figures and named campaigns.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Treaty of Aberconwy (1277) for Llywelyn ap Gruffudd’s position.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Llywelyn lost most of his territory east of the Conwy River, reduced to a small principality of Gwynedd.
• He kept the title Prince of Wales for his lifetime, but the title now had limited political reach.
• He was forced to perform homage to Edward at Westminster at Christmas 1277, accepting the king’s overlordship in person.
• The first ring of castles (Flint, Rhuddlan, Builth and Aberystwyth) was begun on his borders, leaving him surrounded by royal garrisons that helped trigger the second war of 1282.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with specific examples and consequences.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘The conquest of Wales was driven more by Llywelyn’s defiance than by Edward I’s ambition.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Llywelyn refused homage to Edward five times between 1274 and 1276, breaking the conditions of the 1267 Treaty of Montgomery.
• His shelter of his rebel brother Dafydd and his planned marriage to Eleanor de Montfort were direct provocations.
• The 1282 rising was opened by Dafydd’s attack on Hawarden Castle, not by an English invasion.
• Edward’s 1277 war was preceded by repeated diplomatic warnings, suggesting the king tried to avoid full conquest.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Edward’s 1277 campaign was vastly larger than any previous English expedition into Wales, indicating long-term ambition.
• The Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) showed a determination to remake Welsh government wholesale, far beyond what Llywelyn’s defiance required.
• The Iron Ring of castles — Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech, Beaumaris — was disproportionate to mere policing and pointed to a settled colonial project.
• The creation of the Prince of Wales as an English title in 1301 fits a deliberate policy of erasing native rulership.

A strong response weighs Llywelyn’s actions against Edward’s wider strategy and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from President George W. Bush’s address to a joint session of Congress, 20 September 2001.
‘Tonight, the United States of America makes the following demands on the Taliban: deliver to United States authorities all the leaders of al-Qaeda who hide in your land. Close every terrorist training camp in Afghanistan. The Taliban must act, and act immediately. They will hand over the terrorists, or they will share in their fate. Every nation in every region now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.’

Study Source A. Source A suggests that Bush was prepared to treat the Taliban regime itself as a target. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The phrase ‘or they will share in their fate’ suggests Bush regarded the Taliban regime itself as a legitimate military target, not just al-Qaeda; this is a doctrine of state responsibility for harbouring terrorists.
• The list of demands — deliver leaders, close every camp — suggests Bush was framing public, unconditional terms that the Taliban could not accept without losing power.
• The line ‘either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists’ implies a global doctrine: third states would be judged by their attitude to the United States, leaving little neutral ground.
• The address’s tone, given to Congress nine days after 9/11, suggests Bush was deliberately raising the political cost of any later restraint.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Photograph published in Western media in late 2001. The image shows US Special Forces soldiers on horseback alongside Northern Alliance fighters in turbans and woollen pakol caps in northern Afghanistan. A B-52 contrail crosses the sky above them. Western newspapers captioned the image ‘The 21st-Century Cavalry’.

Study Source B. Source B suggests that the United States relied on Afghan fighters and air power rather than large American ground forces. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source (horsemen, B-52 contrail, Northern Alliance fighters, Western caption).
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference; some detail.
Emerging: Description without inference.

Indicative content:
• The pairing of Special Forces with Northern Alliance fighters shows that the US relied on Afghan ground proxies rather than large American formations — the ‘light footprint’ model.
• The B-52 contrail above suggests how the war was actually being won — precision air power directed by small ground teams — rather than by horseback charges.
• The Western press caption ‘The 21st-Century Cavalry’ suggests how American media framed the campaign as fast, romantic and heroic, helping to sustain domestic political support in the early phase.
• The image’s composition, showing American and Afghan fighters together, suggests an effort to portray the campaign as a partnership rather than a Western occupation.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was overthrown between 7 October and 7 December 2001.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence, with precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• 7 October 2001: US and UK air strikes opened against Taliban command and air-defence sites; Taliban air defences collapsed within days.
• Late October: US Special Forces deployed alongside Northern Alliance commanders, calling in air strikes onto Taliban front lines.
• 9 November: Mazar-i-Sharif fell, opening the road north and east; CIA cash payments encouraged local commanders to switch sides.
• 13 November: Kabul fell as the Taliban withdrew rather than face urban bombing; the Northern Alliance entered without a major fight.
• Late November: cornered Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters retreated to Tora Bora and Kandahar.
• Early December: US air strikes pounded Tora Bora; bin Laden slipped over the border into Pakistan.
• 7 December: Kandahar fell, ending Taliban government in Afghanistan just 61 days after the opening air strikes.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Tony Blair’s government committed Britain to the 2001 Afghanistan campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (‘shoulder to shoulder’ speech 11 September, Article 5 invocation 12 September, Cabinet decisions, opening cruise-missile strikes from Royal Navy submarines, SAS deployment); reaches the British role in the fall of Kabul through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 11 September 2001 (afternoon): Blair told reporters in Brighton that Britain would stand ‘shoulder to shoulder’ with the United States.
• 12 September: NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time, giving Blair a multilateral framework for British action.
• Mid-September: emergency Cabinet meetings authorised contingency planning by the Ministry of Defence.
• Late September: Royal Navy submarines were repositioned within cruise-missile range of Afghanistan; SAS reconnaissance teams were deployed.
• 7 October: British cruise missiles were among the first strikes, alongside US weapons.
• October–December: SAS detachments worked with Northern Alliance commanders; British refuelling tankers supported US air operations.
• By 7 December the British contribution had helped enable the air campaign that broke the regime, locking in a partnership Blair would later extend to Iraq.

practice_questions.text: ‘American air power was the main reason the Taliban regime collapsed so quickly in 2001.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: the Taliban’s air force and air defences were destroyed within ten days, leaving no answer to precision bombing.
• Agree: air strikes called in by small Special Forces teams broke the Taliban front line in November and turned a stalemate into a rout.
• Disagree: air power alone had not moved the front line during three weeks of bombing; it was the Northern Alliance that took the ground.
• Disagree: CIA officers paid local commanders large sums in cash, and whole districts changed hands without a fight.
• Disagree: the Northern Alliance had spent five years preparing and pushed forward with conviction once the front line broke.
• Disagree: the Taliban chose to withdraw from Kabul rather than be bombed in a city, so political calculation mattered too.
• Judgement: air power was the enabler, but the speed of the collapse depended on the combination of bombing, Afghan ground forces and cash.

practice_questions.text: ‘The escape of Osama bin Laden at Tora Bora was the most important outcome of the 2001 Afghanistan campaign.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: capturing or killing bin Laden was a stated aim of the campaign, and his escape left it unachieved until the Abbottabad raid of 2011.
• Agree: a 2009 US Senate Foreign Relations Committee report judged the decision to rely on Afghan militias rather than US troops the moment the chance was lost.
• Agree: al-Qaeda’s survival in Pakistan’s tribal areas underwrote the long war that Western forces were still fighting a decade later.
• Disagree: the overthrow of the Taliban regime itself was the larger outcome, ending the sanctuary that had produced 9/11.
• Disagree: the Bonn Agreement and the ISAF mandate created a new Afghan state, shaping the country for twenty years.
• Disagree: the light-footprint model, praised in 2001, left warlords in control of the provinces and allowed the Taliban to regroup.
• Judgement: Tora Bora was the clearest failure, but the decisions taken at Bonn and about ISAF shaped Afghanistan more deeply.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Domesday survey of 1085 to 1086.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William ordered it at his Christmas court at Gloucester in 1085, and the survey was complete by August 1086 — less than nine months of fieldwork across 31 shires.
• Royal commissioners (typically a bishop, baron and clerk) travelled in circuits to each shire and questioned juries from the hundreds under oath, working from a fixed list of questions.
• For each manor the commissioners recorded the holder in 1066 and 1086, the value ‘then’ and ‘now’, the geld assessment in hides, ploughs, peasants and resources such as mills, fisheries and woodlands.
• The results were written up in Latin in two volumes — Great Domesday for most of England and Little Domesday for Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex — and stored in the royal treasury at Winchester.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Domesday Book in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Domesday gave William the data he needed to raise the geld accurately at a moment of military emergency — the threatened Danish invasion of 1085 had brought a mercenary army to England that had to be paid.
• It locked down the shape of the post-conquest aristocracy by recording around 180 tenants-in-chief and confirming who held what, by what right, from whom — the legal record of the Norman land settlement.
• It demonstrated royal authority by showing William knew, in writing, what every manor in his kingdom was worth — the 12th-century commentator Richard FitzNigel later said its findings could not be appealed.
• Importance later: Domesday entries became the working baseline for every later royal taxation and legal claim throughout the medieval period, and the volume survives at the National Archives today.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the procedure the Domesday commissioners used in 1086.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Commissioners worked from a fixed list of questions covering the holder in 1066 and 1086, the geld assessment in hides, ploughs, peasants and resources, and the value ‘then’ and ‘now’.
• Each circuit of commissioners was made up of a bishop, a baron and a clerk — men of high status whose seniority underwrote the authority of the survey.
• In each shire they sat in the shire court and questioned juries from the hundreds — panels of named English and Norman freemen sworn to give evidence on oath.
• Returns were written up in Latin and sent to royal clerks at Winchester, who compressed them into the per-shire entries of Great Domesday.
• Why it mattered: sworn juries of English and Norman freemen made the returns hard to argue with, which is why Domesday entries were still being used as proof of ownership centuries later.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Christmas council at Gloucester in December 1085.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the council took place in the middle of an invasion crisis — Cnut IV of Denmark was preparing a fleet to claim the English throne, and William had brought a large mercenary army to England that had to be paid.
• William’s decision to commission a kingdom-wide survey at this moment shows that royal administration responded to military pressure with sharper data, not simply more troops.
• The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records William’s ‘deep speech’ with his council about how the country was occupied; the council marks the conversion of vague royal knowledge into systematic record.
• Importance later: the decision produced Domesday Book itself, the working baseline of English royal administration for centuries to come.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the Domesday survey affected the English population.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The survey confirmed in writing the dispossession of the Anglo-Saxon thegnage; fewer than 10% of pre-conquest English landholders still held land in 1086, with most lost to death, exile or demotion.
• Domesday recorded English peasants — villeins, bordars, cottars, freemen and slaves — with their numbers and obligations on each manor, fixing the working population in fiscal records under their new Norman lords.
• The geld assessments enabled more accurate royal taxation that drew cash from the rural population, intensifying the financial demands on Anglo-Saxon villages.
• In Yorkshire and Cheshire many villages were recorded as ‘waste’ (vasta est) — a fiscal label that captured the after-effects of the Harrying as well as later tenurial reorganisation, depressing the recorded value of the region for decades.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

Note on careful evidence handling: high-band answers acknowledge that ‘waste’ in Domesday is fiscal data and not always a direct headcount of destruction.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Domesday Book.

‘Domesday Book is the greatest thing Norman government did. No other ruler in Europe could have counted a kingdom in a year, and no other record shaped English administration for so long.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the achievement of Norman government? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: Domesday Book was the most striking achievement of Norman government.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• In less than nine months, royal commissioners surveyed 31 shires, 13,000 settlements and over 268,000 named individuals — a feat of administrative reach unequalled in medieval Europe.
• The book locked down the post-conquest land settlement by recording around 180 tenants-in-chief and confirming who held what from the king — the legal record of the Norman aristocracy.
• Its tax data underpinned the royal finances during the 1085 invasion crisis and for decades afterwards, providing the geld base that paid armies and built castles.
• Significance over time: Domesday entries became the working baseline of medieval English administration, and the book survives at the National Archives today as one of the most cited documents in English history.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The Battle of Hastings (1066) was the indispensable military victory; without it there would have been no kingdom to survey.
• The network of c.500 castles by 1100 was the physical infrastructure of Norman control alongside the documentary infrastructure of Domesday.
• Lanfranc’s Church reforms transformed Norman authority over personnel and ideology in ways the survey alone did not achieve.
• Inherited Anglo-Saxon administrative machinery — shires, sheriffs, the geld assessment in hides — made Domesday possible; the achievement is shared, not purely Norman.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the reopening of the London theatres after 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Only two licensed companies could perform new spoken drama: the King’s Company under Thomas Killigrew and the Duke’s Company under William Davenant, both holding royal patents from 1660.
• Female roles were played by professional actresses for the first time in English history; Margaret Hughes is recorded playing Desdemona on 8 December 1660.
• Restoration comedy — including plays by Etherege, Wycherley, Behn and Congreve — mixed witty dialogue, sexual intrigue and satire of London elite society.
• Theatres used candlelit interiors, raked seating and movable scenery, and audiences included the king himself; performances normally began at 3:30 p.m.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how women came to work as professional actresses in England after 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It created a new paid profession for women, with star actresses such as Nell Gwyn and Elizabeth Barry becoming celebrities at court and in the City.
• It opened the way for female playwrights such as Aphra Behn, who became the first English woman to make a living from writing.
• It widened the visible role of women in public life even though their legal position under coverture did not change.
• It made theatre a politically charged space, with mistresses, courtiers and partisans visible side by side in the boxes.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about women appearing on the public stage from 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the appearance of professional actresses such as Margaret Hughes and Nell Gwyn ended the tradition of boys playing women and was given royal backing in Charles II’s 1662 letter.
• It produced a generation of stars and the first female playwright to earn a living, Aphra Behn, with hits including ‘The Rover’ in 1677.
• Significance over time: it established women as a permanent presence on the English stage and in print, opening a slow path towards wider public participation.
• It also shifted the meaning of theatre — plays could now use sexual relationships in ways that boys’ performances could not, helping to define Restoration comedy as a genre.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about London’s coffee houses by 1675.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A coffee house was open to any man who paid a penny entry, which is why they were nicknamed ‘penny universities’.
• They provided free newspapers and pamphlets, making them the main centre of news and political conversation in London.
• Particular trades clustered at particular houses: Edward Lloyd’s, opened in 1686, grew into the centre of marine insurance and Jonathan’s, opened around 1680, into the home of stock-jobbing.
• They were almost exclusively male spaces, with women appearing chiefly as servers or as the wives running the business.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how coffee houses changed public life in London under Charles II.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They created an open public space for political and business news, accessible for the price of a penny and open to anyone who could pay.
• They became hubs of trade and finance, with Lloyd’s and Jonathan’s coffee houses developing into the institutional ancestors of the insurance and stock markets.
• They gave anti-court opinion a place to circulate, which is why Charles II tried to suppress them by proclamation in December 1675.
• Their successful resistance to closure demonstrated the limits of royal control over public opinion in Restoration London.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Restoration gave women a bigger public role in name only. The law that held them down did not move.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the position of women in Restoration England? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Coverture remained intact: married women could not own property or sign contracts, leaving most legal disadvantages of women in place.
• Coffee houses, the new engine of news and business, were almost wholly male spaces, signalled by the satirical ‘Women’s Petition Against Coffee’ of 1674.
• Royal mistresses had political influence but no formal authority and depended entirely on the king’s favour.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Professional actresses including Nell Gwyn, Elizabeth Barry and Anne Bracegirdle became national celebrities and built careers and incomes of their own.
• Aphra Behn became the first English woman to live by her pen, with successful plays and the novel ‘Oroonoko’ in 1688.
• Women published on religion (Margaret Fell), poetry (Katherine Philips) and politics, expanding the female voice in print.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about Lenin’s decision to introduce the NEP? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat the NEP as a pragmatic, life-saving rescue from War Communism; B may treat it as a betrayal of socialist principles or a tactical move to buy time.
• A may emphasise Lenin’s flexibility; B may emphasise the dictatorship reinforced through the ban on factions.
• Specific textual reference required for both.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison with precise evidence from both interpretations. Secure: comparison with some textual reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the Kronstadt Rising of 1921?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: an early Soviet account aiming to discredit the sailors as White-led versus a Western account presenting them as betrayed revolutionaries.
• Different evidence: post-1991 archive access changed the documentary base.
• Different schools of thought: orthodox Soviet versus liberal/Western or revisionist readings.
• Different time of writing — closer to or further from the events.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the impact of War Communism on the Soviet economy? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test specific claims of the interpretation against named context: industrial output collapsing to a fifth of 1913 levels, Volga famine 1921-22 killing roughly five million, sown area shrinking under requisitioning.
• Weigh competing causes: civil-war disruption and territorial loss under Brest-Litovsk also damaged output.
• Note historiography — orthodox Soviet, totalitarian and revisionist readings differ on whether failure was inherent or imposed by circumstances.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge applied with a clear judgement. Developing: knowledge used unevenly. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Kronstadt Rising on Bolshevik policy in 1921.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Triggered the abandonment of War Communism: the Tenth Party Congress voted for the NEP days after the rising.
• Confirmed the regime’s willingness to use the Red Army against its own former supporters.
• Justified the ban on factions inside the party — presented as essential discipline in a time of crisis.
• Reinforced the use of the Cheka to track Bolsheviks suspected of sympathy with the sailors.
• Long term, fed the totalitarian-school reading that Bolshevism could only survive by repression of any internal alternative.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with some development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the rising.]

practice_questions.text: ‘The introduction of the NEP did more to save the Soviet regime in 1921 than any other policy.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider the NEP, the suppression of Kronstadt and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for the NEP being most important:
• Replaced grain requisitioning with a tax in kind, restoring peasant incentive to plant.
• Allowed small trade and the Nepmen to revive city consumption.
• By 1926 output recovered roughly to 1913 levels — gave the regime time to consolidate.

Arguments for other factors:
• Suppression of Kronstadt removed an internal challenge from former Bolshevik supporters.
• Tambov Rising and other peasant revolts were crushed by the Red Army with chemical weapons.
• Famine relief from the American Relief Administration kept millions alive in the Volga region.
• The ban on factions ensured no internal Bolshevik challenge to Lenin’s line.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. the NEP secured the economic base, but the regime survived because economic relaxation was bought with political repression.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of grain requisitioning on Russian society between 1918 and 1921.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Drop in sown area as peasants refused to grow surplus grain.
• Volga famine of 1921-22 killed approximately five million.
• Peasant uprisings, including the Tambov Rising, requiring military reconquest of the countryside.
• Worsened relations between the Bolshevik regime and the peasant majority.
• Acceptance of foreign aid (American Relief Administration) despite the ban on private charity.
• Triggered the policy reversal of the NEP at the Tenth Party Congress.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with some development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of requisitioning.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Lyndon B. Johnson to the American people, 4 August 1964.
‘Repeated acts of violence against the armed forces of the United States must be met not only with alert defence, but with positive reply. That reply is being given as I speak to you tonight. We seek no wider war.’

Source A suggests that Johnson wanted to look firm without committing to a wider war. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He says repeated acts of violence must be met ‘with positive reply’, not defence alone.
• He tells viewers that the reply is already being given as he speaks.
• He closes with ‘we seek no wider war’, framing the action as limited.
Contextual knowledge: The broadcast followed the reported second Gulf of Tonkin attack of 4 August 1964; three days later Congress passed the Tonkin Resolution 88-2 in the Senate.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964 led to the launch of Operation Rolling Thunder in March 1965.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Maddox, Tonkin Resolution, Pleiku, Rolling Thunder, Da Nang); arrives at the bombing campaign through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin or muddled chronology.

Indicative content:
• 2 August 1964: USS Maddox engaged North Vietnamese torpedo boats in the Gulf of Tonkin.
• 4 August 1964: a second alleged attack — later judged to have been false sonar — was reported.
• 7 August 1964: Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution 88-2, authorising ‘all necessary measures’.
• Late 1964: instability in Saigon and Vietcong gains increased pressure for escalation.
• 7 February 1965: Vietcong attack on the US base at Pleiku killed several Americans.
• 2 March 1965: Operation Rolling Thunder began as the bombing response.
• 8 March 1965: 3,500 US marines landed at Da Nang to protect the airbase — the first official ground combat troops.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Robert McNamara, US Secretary of Defense, to President Johnson, dated November 1965.
‘The bombing has not significantly damaged Hanoi’s capacity to support the war in the South. Infiltration on the Ho Chi Minh Trail has if anything increased. We must consider whether continuation of Rolling Thunder serves our political objectives.’

Source C: An extract from an interview with a North Vietnamese road-repair brigade leader, given to a sympathetic French journalist in 1967 and later published in Hanoi.
‘The bombs come; we hide. The bombs go; we rebuild. A bridge takes one night to mend. Half a million of our women work the roads. The Americans cannot stop us by air alone — they would need to invade, and they will not.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of Operation Rolling Thunder. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: McNamara concedes Rolling Thunder has not damaged Hanoi’s war effort. Provenance: a private memo from Defense Secretary to President in 1965, intended for policy not public — useful for showing internal doubt at the highest level. Own knowledge: 864,000 tonnes of bombs dropped 1965–68; the Pentagon’s own analysts later judged it a strategic failure.
Source C — Content: shows the North’s capacity to absorb bombing through dispersal and rapid repair. Provenance: a brigade leader interviewed by a sympathetic French journalist for Hanoi publication — partial but with first-hand experience. Own knowledge: an estimated 500,000 mainly women worked road repair; the Ho Chi Minh Trail was never cut by air power alone.
Judgement: B is highly useful for elite policy doubt; C is highly useful for ground-level explanation of why bombing did not work, but its propaganda framing must be acknowledged.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason US ground forces could not defeat the Vietcong was the failure of the search-and-destroy strategy.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Search-and-destroy aimed at casualties rather than ground, so cleared areas were reoccupied as soon as US units left.
• The Vietcong chose when and where to fight; an estimated 80 per cent of engagements were started by them.
• The body-count metric corrupted reporting: civilians in free-fire zones were counted as enemy dead, so commanders misread their own progress.
Disagree:
• Air power was constrained: Johnson would not bomb Hanoi’s centre or Haiphong for fear of Soviet or Chinese intervention.
• The Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through Laos and Cambodia, beyond the reach of US ground operations.
• Soviet and Chinese aid replaced North Vietnamese losses faster than the United States could inflict them.
• Political instability in Saigon meant there was no legitimate southern government for the war to defend.
Judgement: Search-and-destroy failed, but the deeper mismatch was between conventional firepower and a political war fought among the population.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a 1965 BBC television documentary on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, presented by a British journalist who had travelled along it.
‘The trail is not a road. It is a thousand paths through forest and mountain, by truck, by bicycle, by porter. American bombs crater it; men with shovels fill in the craters. Each month the trail carries more rifles, more rice, more men south than the month before.’

Source F suggests that US bombing could not cut the supply route to the south. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The trail is ‘not a road’ but ‘a thousand paths through forest and mountain’.
• Craters made by American bombs are filled in by men with shovels.
• Each month the trail carries more rifles, rice and men south than the month before.
Contextual knowledge: The trail ran through Laos and Cambodia, outside the area US ground forces were allowed to enter; Nixon’s secret bombing of Cambodia from 1969 was a later attempt at the same problem.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how US ground troop numbers in Vietnam grew from 16,000 advisers under Kennedy to over 500,000 combat troops under Johnson.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and figures.
Secure: Three or more linked events; causal connectives; accurate.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Late 1963: Kennedy left around 16,000 US advisers in South Vietnam.
• August 1964: Tonkin Resolution gave Johnson legal authority for force.
• February–March 1965: Pleiku attack triggered Rolling Thunder.
• 8 March 1965: First combat troops — 3,500 marines — landed at Da Nang.
• End of 1965: 184,000 US troops in country.
• End of 1966: 385,000 troops.
• 1967: over 485,000 troops; Westmoreland’s attrition strategy at full scale.
• 1968: peak of 540,000 troops — despite which the Vietcong launched the Tet Offensive that January.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1934 Goebbels speech presenting the Night of the Long Knives as Hitler's defence of the German people from a treacherous SA conspiracy) and Interpretation B (a post-war study arguing the purge was a calculated bargain with the army to secure Hitler's succession to Hindenburg) on the Night of the Long Knives. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the killings as a defensive emergency — Hitler acted as ‘supreme judge’ against an SA plot to overthrow the state.
• Interpretation B presents the killings as a deliberate political deal — Hitler removed the SA in exchange for army loyalty after Hindenburg's death.
• Main difference: A frames the purge as defensive crisis-management; B frames it as a calculated transaction.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1934 Goebbels speech) and Interpretation B (a post-war academic study) give different views about the Night of the Long Knives.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — Goebbels in 1934 needed to justify state murder to a German public; the post-war historian aimed to explain the consolidation of dictatorship.
• They had access to different evidence — the historian could use the Hitler Oath of 2 August 1934 and Reichswehr archives; Goebbels could not refer to the army's deal openly.
• They were written in different political conditions — Goebbels under regime censorship; the historian after free access to documents.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Enabling Act of March 1933 was the moment Weimar democracy ended.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the establishment of Hitler's dictatorship?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Enabling Act gave the cabinet power to pass laws without the Reichstag or the President for four years — the legal foundation of dictatorship.
• Convincing because within four months it was used to ban trade unions (2 May), the SPD (22 June) and all other parties (14 July).
• Less convincing because the Decree for the Protection of the People and State (28 February 1933) had already suspended civil liberties — democracy was effectively over before 23 March.
• Less convincing because the Hitler Oath and Fuhrer title only came on 2 August 1934 — the army's independence as an institution was not subordinated until then.
• Less convincing because Weimar democracy had been governed by Article 48 since March 1930 — some structural historians argue parliamentary government had ended even before Hitler's appointment.
• Overall judgement: the Enabling Act was the decisive legal step but the breakdown was a process running from March 1930 to August 1934, not a single moment.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Reichstag Fire of 27 February 1933 on Hitler's establishment of his dictatorship.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It triggered the Decree for the Protection of the People and State on 28 February 1933 — suspending civil liberties and allowing detention without trial; never repealed.
• Around 4,000 KPD activists were arrested, neutralising the largest opposition party before the 5 March election.
• It contributed to the Nazi vote of 43.9% in March 1933 — with the DNVP's 8.0%, gave Hitler a working coalition for the Enabling Act.
• It enabled the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 — with the KPD removed and the Centre Party bargained over Catholic schools, the two-thirds majority for constitutional amendment was achievable.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how Hitler turned the Chancellorship into a personal dictatorship between January 1933 and August 1934.
You may consider:
• the use of legal instruments (Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung)
• the use of state violence (Night of the Long Knives) and the death of Hindenburg.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Legal route: Reichstag Fire Decree (28 Feb 1933) suspended civil liberties; Enabling Act (23 Mar 1933) let cabinet legislate alone; banning of trade unions (2 May), SPD (22 Jun), all parties (14 Jul); civil service purge under April 1933 law.
• Gleichschaltung: federal states placed under Reich Commissioners; DAF replaced unions; one-party state declared 14 July 1933.
• State violence: Night of the Long Knives, 30 June 1934 — Rohm and at least 85 SA leaders murdered; Schleicher, Klausener and Strasser also killed; SA neutralised.
• Army deal: Blomberg's spring 1934 agreement — remove the SA threat in exchange for army support as Hindenburg's successor; Hitler Oath of 2 August 1934 sworn to Hitler personally.
• Contingency: Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934 allowed merger of Chancellor and President; 19 August plebiscite endorsed it with 88%.
• Conclusion: legal instruments built the framework, the Night of the Long Knives bought the army's loyalty, and Hindenburg's death allowed the consolidation. None alone would have been enough — together they took eighteen months to turn a coalition Chancellor into Fuhrer.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1980s functionalist historian arguing that Nazi consolidation was an improvised process driven by events such as the Reichstag Fire) and Interpretation B (a 1990s intentionalist historian arguing that Hitler followed a clear plan to dismantle democracy from January 1933) on the establishment of Hitler's dictatorship. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A frames consolidation as opportunistic — the Reichstag Fire and Hindenburg's death were exploited rather than planned.
• Interpretation B frames consolidation as the execution of a long-held plan — the Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung and the SA purge were all foreseeable steps.
• Main difference: A emphasises improvisation and contingency; B emphasises planning and intent.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1935 communiqué issued at the close of the Stresa Conference, signed by representatives of Britain, France and Italy.
‘The three Powers find themselves in complete agreement in opposing, by all practicable means, any unilateral repudiation of treaties which may endanger the peace of Europe, and will act in close and cordial collaboration to this end. The independence of Austria, in particular, must be maintained.’

Using Source A, identify two aims of the Stresa Front.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded aims with brief embedded support. Secure: Two clear aims, briefly supported. Developing: One aim clear; second weak or repeats first. Emerging: General comment without specific aims. Indicative content: • Opposition to any unilateral repudiation of treaties — aimed at German rearmament announced in March 1935. • Maintenance of Austrian independence — aimed at preventing Anschluss. • Close and cordial collaboration between Britain, France and Italy — a great-power coalition against German revisionism. • Implicit aim: to deter further German treaty-breaking by collective action.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources A and B.

Source A: An extract from a 1935 communiqué issued at the close of the Stresa Conference, signed by representatives of Britain, France and Italy.
‘The three Powers find themselves in complete agreement in opposing, by all practicable means, any unilateral repudiation of treaties which may endanger the peace of Europe, and will act in close and cordial collaboration to this end. The independence of Austria, in particular, must be maintained.’

Source B: An extract from a 1935 private memorandum by British Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare to the Cabinet, on the proposed Anglo-German Naval Agreement.
‘German rearmament is a fact and cannot be undone. The choice before us is not whether the Reich will build a navy but whether that navy will be limited by treaty or by nothing at all. A 35% ratio caps Germany at a level the Royal Navy can comfortably overmatch. Refusing the agreement would not stop construction; it would simply leave us without restraint.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources A and B to a historian studying Allied responses to German rearmament in 1935. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source A — Content: a public statement of three-power unity against German treaty-breaking and any threat to Austria. Provenance: a formal Stresa communiqué designed to deter Hitler and reassure domestic publics. Own knowledge: confirms the scope of the Front (Britain, France, Italy) but conceals its fragility — Italy was already preparing to invade Abyssinia and Britain was already in talks with Berlin on naval limits.
Source B — Content: a candid British rationale for accepting a naval deal with Germany; framed as damage limitation. Provenance: a private memorandum to the Cabinet, expressing genuine policy thinking; not designed for public consumption. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — the agreement was signed in June 1935, allowed Germany 35% of Royal Navy tonnage and a submarine fleet, was not coordinated with France or Italy, and undermined Stresa within weeks.
Judgement: A is useful as a public statement of unity but misleading on Allied solidity; B is highly useful for British strategic calculation but reflects only one strand of British and Allied thinking.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of Hitler’s major foreign-policy moves in 1935, from the Saar plebiscite in January to the Anglo-German Naval Agreement in June.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1935: the Saar plebiscite under League supervision; about 90% voted to return to Germany; Hitler used the result for propaganda.
• March 1935: Hitler announced open conscription, set the army at 36 divisions and admitted the existence of the Luftwaffe; Versailles military clauses openly broken.
• Allied protest but no military or economic response; France did not mobilise.
• April 1935: Britain, France and Italy met at Stresa and condemned German rearmament; pledged to defend Austrian independence.
• June 1935: Britain signed the Anglo-German Naval Agreement allowing Germany 35% of Royal Navy tonnage and a submarine fleet; France and Italy were not consulted.
• The bilateral deal undermined the Stresa Front within weeks; Hitler had handed clear evidence of Allied disunity.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Saar plebiscite of January 1935 and how Hitler turned its result to his advantage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 1919: Versailles placed the Saar under League administration for fifteen years and promised the inhabitants a vote at the end of that period.
• January 1935: the plebiscite was held under League supervision; about 90% voted to return to Germany, about 9% for continued League rule and only a tiny fraction for France.
• Hitler had played no part in rigging the vote, so he could present the result as proof that pan-German feeling was real rather than Nazi-invented.
• The territory and its coal returned to German control without Allied resistance, strengthening Germany economically.
• March 1935: with that political cover, Hitler announced conscription and the existence of the Luftwaffe two months later.
• The Saar was a special case, since Versailles itself had promised the vote, so it was a propaganda gain rather than a treaty breach.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935 destroyed the Stresa Front.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Stresa was a three-power agreement to defend the treaties; within weeks Britain dealt with Berlin alone and consulted neither France nor Italy.
• The agreement legalised a major Versailles violation, allowing Germany a navy 35% the size of the Royal Navy, including submarines.
• It showed Hitler that British policy was not tied to French security concerns.
Challenging the statement:
• Mussolini’s invasion of Abyssinia in October 1935, and the League sanctions that followed, split Italy from Britain and France for good.
• The front was fragile from the start: Italy was already preparing the Abyssinian invasion when it signed at Stresa in April.
• The Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935 did more than the naval deal to discredit Anglo-French policy.
Judgement: the naval agreement holed the Stresa Front within weeks, but Abyssinia sank it.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the collapse of the Stresa Front, from its formation in April 1935 to the lifting of League sanctions on Italy in July 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• April 1935: Stresa Front formed by Britain, France and Italy to oppose German treaty-breaking and protect Austrian independence.
• June 1935: Britain signed a bilateral Anglo-German Naval Agreement without consulting France or Italy; the political basis of the front was weakened.
• October 1935: Mussolini invaded Abyssinia; Britain and France imposed League sanctions on Italy.
• December 1935: the Hoare-Laval Pact secretly offered Mussolini around two-thirds of Abyssinia; the leak forced Hoare’s resignation but the damage was done.
• Spring 1936: Mussolini drifted away from Britain and France toward Germany; the Stresa Front was effectively dead.
• July 1936: League sanctions on Italy lifted; Mussolini moved closer to Hitler, leading to the Rome-Berlin Axis in October 1936.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Second Boer War (1899-1902) for Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: secured British control of the gold-producing Transvaal and Orange Free State, completing southern African empire.
• At the time: cost 22,000 British dead, £200 million and exposed weaknesses in army recruitment and organisation.
• At the time: concentration camps killed around 28,000 Boer civilians and at least 20,000 Africans — reported in Britain by Emily Hobhouse.
• Over time: cracked the moral case for empire and prompted reform — the 1904 Inter-Departmental Committee on Physical Deterioration and Liberal welfare reforms 1906-11.
• Over time: Boer political memory shaped 20th-century South African nationalism and the route to apartheid in 1948.
• Limitation: the Treaty of Vereeniging’s settlement was generous to the Boers, suggesting Britain learned to integrate former enemies after costly conflicts.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Cecil Rhodes for British expansion in southern Africa.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: founded De Beers (1888); his control of Kimberley diamond mines and Cape politics gave him the resources to push British rule north.
• At the time: as Cape Colony Prime Minister from 1890, he chartered the British South Africa Company and seized the territories that became Rhodesia.
• At the time: the 1895 Jameson Raid — an attempt to overthrow the Transvaal government — was a Rhodes-backed disaster that helped trigger the Boer War.
• Over time: his ‘Cape to Cairo’ ambition shaped British grand strategy in Africa for a generation.
• Over time: his Rhodes Scholarships still bring international students to Oxford; his statues have been the focus of the Rhodes Must Fall campaigns since 2015, marking him as one of the most contested individuals in modern British memory.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Ideas were the main factor in British expansion in Africa between 1800 and 1914.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to ideas and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ideas (in support): the ‘civilising mission’, missionary activity and the anti-slavery cause gave Britain a moral self-image that justified taking territory.
• Ideas (in support): social Darwinism and imperial propaganda — cigarette cards, music hall songs, school textbooks, Kipling’s 1899 ‘The White Man’s Burden’ — kept the public behind expansion.
• Economic resources: palm oil replaced the slave trade in West Africa, and diamonds at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand from 1886 drew British capital south.
• Government and war: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect the Suez route to India, crushed Mahdist resistance at Omdurman in 1898 and fought the Boer War of 1899-1902.
• Role of individuals: Rhodes and the British South Africa Company, Kitchener in Sudan, Livingstone as missionary-explorer.
• Judgement: ideas justified what economic resources made profitable and what military force made possible. The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 shows all three working together.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Scramble for Africa and earlier British expansion in India were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: India was acquired piecemeal by a chartered company over 100 years; Africa was partitioned in less than 30 years through diplomatic conferences.
• Difference: in India a single company (East India Company) drove expansion until 1858; in Africa expansion mixed state action (Egypt, Sudan), chartered companies (British South Africa Company) and individual settlers.
• Similarity: both were justified by ideas of civilising mission and (later) social Darwinism.
• Similarity: both depended on superior military force at key moments — Plassey 1757, Omdurman 1898, the Boer War.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of social Darwinism for British attitudes to empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: misapplied Darwin’s 1859 theory to argue that ‘fitter’ races would inevitably rule ‘weaker’ ones — bad biology, but politically convenient.
• At the time: gave intellectual cover to the Scramble for Africa, the partition of Asia and the assumption that empire was natural rather than political.
• At the time: shaped propaganda — Kipling’s 1899 ‘White Man’s Burden’, school textbooks, music hall songs.
• Over time: discredited by 20th-century scientific consensus and by the racism it justified; its legacy reshaped post-1945 thinking on race and empire.
• Limitation: empire would have happened without social Darwinism — economic resources and strategic competition were already in motion before 1884.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Berlin Conference of 1884-85 for the partition of Africa.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: set the rules for European partition — the ‘effective occupation’ principle required colonisers to plant flags and sign treaties to claim territory.
• At the time: regularised competition between European powers and prevented (some) wars between them over African boundaries.
• At the time: no African leaders were present; African states had no voice in the partition of their own continent.
• Over time: the borders drawn at and after Berlin became the borders of independent African states from the 1950s, dividing communities and grouping rivals together.
• Over time: a foundational moment in the global colour line that shaped 20th-century race relations.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: Nightingale led an officially sanctioned nursing party at Scutari; Seacole was refused by the War Office and funded her own passage.
• Difference: Nightingale shaped national policy through statistics, training and books; Seacole’s influence was more personal, focused on soldiers near the front.
• Similarity: both nursed British soldiers in the Crimean War, with significant impact on the men they treated.
• Similarity: both faced obstacles — gender for Nightingale, race and class for Seacole — and built recognition partly through writing (Notes on Nursing 1859; Wonderful Adventures 1857).

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Florence Nightingale for the development of nursing and hospitals in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Scutari mortality fell from around 42% to 2% after the 1855 Sanitary Commission and her cleanliness regime in six months in 1854–55.
• At the time: gave evidence to the 1857 Royal Commission using statistical rose diagrams that proved disease killed more soldiers than bullets.
• Over time: Notes on Nursing and Notes on Hospitals (1859) shaped Victorian and Edwardian hospital design (pavilion plan).
• Over time: the 1860 Nightingale Training School at St Thomas’ spread professional nursing across Britain and the empire.
• Limitation: religious nursing orders preceded her; her achievement was professionalising secular nursing in Britain rather than inventing nursing itself.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and an awareness of context.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1858 Medical Act for medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: it created the General Medical Council and a national register of qualified doctors.
• At the time: it drew a legal line between trained practitioners and the quacks who had traded freely for a century.
• At the time: it ended the old separation of physicians, surgeons and apothecaries into rival legal orders.
• Over time: registration made a shared standard of training possible, which mattered once germ theory changed what a doctor had to know.
• Over time: nursing followed the same path towards a trained profession after the Nightingale School opened in 1860.
• Limitation: registration did not by itself make treatment better, and it left nursing and midwifery unregulated for decades.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Has the role of the individual been the main factor in the reform of nursing and hospitals in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to the role of the individual and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the role of the individual:
• Nightingale, Seacole, Lister, Bazalgette and Chadwick all personally shaped 19th-century health reform.
• Nightingale’s statistics, books and Training School were each driven by personal initiative.

Weighed against war:
• Without the Crimean War there is no Scutari mission and no Royal Commission.
• The First World War later accelerated transfusion, X-rays and plastic surgery in Britain.

Weighed against communication:
• Times war reporting created the political pressure that sent Nightingale to Crimea.
• Notes on Nursing 1859 and Notes on Hospitals 1859 spread her ideas across Britain.

Weighed against government:
• The 1858 Medical Act and the 1875 Public Health Act regulated the framework in which individuals worked.
• The 1857 Royal Commission gave Nightingale’s statistics a political route into policy.

Judgement: in 19th-century hospital reform individuals were necessary — their personal commitment carried reform across decades — but they relied on war, communication and government to deliver impact. Across the wider sweep, the dominant factor varies (religion in 1348, government in 1948).

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes individuals only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Mary Seacole for the development of nursing in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: provided nursing care to British soldiers near the Crimean front despite being refused by the War Office.
