• At the time: published Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands (1857), one of the earliest autobiographies by a Black British woman.
• Over time: her example became central to discussions of race, class and recognition in British nursing history; statue installed outside St Thomas’ Hospital in 2016.
• Over time: her belated recognition shows how racial barriers shaped which 19th-century reformers entered the public memory.
• Limitation: her direct policy impact in her own time was limited compared with Nightingale’s; significance is partly measured by later recognition.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise examples and historical context.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Florence Nightingale’s diagram of the causes of death in the British army in the east, published in 1858. Each wedge stands for one month of the Crimean War, and the area shaded for deaths from preventable disease dwarfs the area for deaths from wounds.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying why British army medical care was reformed after the Crimean War?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: it shows that disease, not fighting, killed most soldiers — the single fact that made reform unanswerable.
• Content: the monthly wedges show the death rate falling after the sanitary work of spring 1855, which points to the cause.
• Provenance: produced by Nightingale for ministers and the Royal Commission on the Health of the Army, so it is built to win an argument, though it rests on official army returns.
• Contextual knowledge: she took 38 nurses to Scutari in 1854; the government’s Sanitary Commission flushed the sewers there in March 1855; she published Notes on Nursing and Notes on Hospitals in 1859.
• Limitations: it counts deaths, not care, and says nothing about nursing on the ward or about Mary Seacole’s work near the front.
• Judgement: very useful for how reform was argued for and won, less useful for what nursing was actually like.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about Stalin’s rise to power between 1924 and 1929? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat Stalin’s victory as the result of bureaucratic skill and luck; B may treat it as the inevitable triumph of a ruthless personality.
• A may emphasise rivals’ mistakes; B may emphasise Stalin’s manipulation.
• Specific textual reference required for both interpretations.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual reference. Secure: comparison with some reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the role of Lenin’s Testament in Stalin’s rise?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: a Soviet account written under Stalin downplaying the Testament versus a later Western academic account treating it as decisive.
• Different time of writing: post-1956 (Khrushchev) and post-1991 access to suppressed documents.
• Different perspective — émigré Trotskyist authors versus orthodox Soviet writers.
• Different evidence used.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what each interpretation says rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about why Stalin defeated Trotsky? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test what the interpretation claims (e.g. Stalin’s bureaucratic control was decisive) against named context: General Secretary post from 1922, Lenin Enrolment 1924, control of congress delegates.
• Weigh other factors: Trotsky’s tactical mistakes, Permanent Revolution vs Socialism in One Country, his Jewish background and late conversion to Bolshevism.
• Cite historiography — totalitarian school (Conquest) versus revisionist accounts.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge applied with a clear judgement. Developing: knowledge unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Stalin’s appointment as General Secretary in 1922 on the power struggle to succeed Lenin.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gave Stalin control of all major party appointments — gorkom secretaries, congress delegate selections, factory committee chairs.
• Allowed the Lenin Enrolment of 1924 to fill the party with members loyal to Stalin’s machine.
• Meant the votes against Trotsky and later Zinoviev and Kamenev were already in place before policy debates began.
• Enabled the suppression of Lenin’s Testament at the Thirteenth Party Congress in 1924.
• Underpinned the eventual expulsion of the United Opposition (1927) and the defeat of the Right (1929).
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the role.]

practice_questions.text: ‘Stalin won the power struggle of 1924-1929 mainly because his rivals underestimated him.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Stalin’s position as General Secretary, the rivals’ mistakes and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for the rivals’ mistakes:
• Trotsky failed to fight for Lenin’s Testament in 1924.
• Zinoviev and Kamenev backed Stalin against Trotsky in 1924, then panicked and joined Trotsky in the United Opposition in 1926 — too late.
• Trotsky’s arrogance alienated potential allies; he was absent from Lenin’s funeral.
• Bukharin was loyal to the NEP when Stalin abandoned it — isolated him on the Right.

Arguments for other factors:
• Stalin’s position as General Secretary gave him decisive control of appointments and congress votes.
• Socialism in One Country fitted the post-revolutionary mood better than Permanent Revolution.
• Tactical sequence: Stalin allied with each rival before destroying them in turn.
• Soviet party culture rewarded bureaucratic loyalty over revolutionary glamour after 1921.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. rivals’ mistakes mattered, but Stalin’s control of the party machine ensured every mistake was punished.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the suppression of Lenin’s Testament on the Soviet leadership in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Saved Stalin from removal as General Secretary, despite Lenin’s explicit recommendation.
• Demonstrated that Zinoviev and Kamenev preferred Stalin to Trotsky in 1924 — a decision they would later regret.
• Allowed Stalin to keep control of the party apparatus.
• Set a precedent for hiding inconvenient documents inside the party — a habit that would expand under Stalin’s rule.
• Helped sustain the public image of party unity that Stalin used to attack rivals as ‘factionalists’.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the suppression.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1944 newspaper article praising Roosevelt’s leadership for delivering economic recovery) and Interpretation B (a 1945 economist’s study arguing only the war ended the Depression). What is the main difference between these views about the recovery?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents recovery as the achievement of Roosevelt’s leadership, his fireside chats, Lend Lease and the war effort.
• Interpretation B presents recovery as the structural effect of vast war spending and conscription rather than political leadership.
• Main difference: A frames recovery as Roosevelt’s personal success; B frames it as the economic consequence of the war regardless of who was president.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1944 newspaper article praising Roosevelt) and Interpretation B (a 1945 economist’s study) give different views about American recovery.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the wartime newspaper aimed to support morale and a fourth Roosevelt term; the economist’s study aimed to analyse the structural drivers of recovery in retrospect.
• They use different evidence — the article cites Roosevelt’s speeches and political decisions; the economist cites federal spending figures and unemployment data.
• They were produced at different points — one in the middle of the war when patriotic framing dominated, one after victory when more sober analysis was possible.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘The Second World War transformed the position of African-Americans in the United States more than the New Deal had ever done.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the wartime experience of African-Americans?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because Executive Order 8802 (June 1941) banned discrimination in defence industries and created the Fair Employment Practices Committee — the first federal civil-rights action since Reconstruction.
• Convincing because around 1.5 million African-Americans moved north and west in the second Great Migration, taking industrial jobs that the New Deal had not delivered.
• Convincing because the Tuskegee Airmen and the Double V Campaign undermined segregationist arguments and laid foundations for post-war civil-rights demands.
• Less convincing because the armed forces remained segregated and the Detroit race riot of June 1943 (34 dead, mostly black) showed home-front racism intensifying.
• Less convincing because the New Deal had already begun the political shift — the ‘Black Cabinet’, federal employment, and the 1936 black vote moving to the Democrats.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on economic mobility and federal action; less convincing as a claim of full transformation given continued segregation and violence.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Second World War on women in American society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Mass entry into industrial work — around 6 million women joined the workforce between 1941 and 1944, many welding ships, riveting aircraft and assembling tanks; female employment rose from around 14 million to 19 million.
• Cultural shift symbolised by Rosie the Riveter — the 1943 Norman Rockwell cover and J. Howard Miller’s ‘We Can Do It’ poster reframed female industrial work as patriotic and competent.
• Federal action on childcare — the 1942 Lanham Act funded around 3,000 day-care centres, a small but unprecedented federal presence in family life.
• Partial and reversed gains — female wages in heavy industry averaged around 60% of men’s; around 4 million women were dismissed in 1945–46 to make way for returning servicemen, although the experience of earning skilled wages reshaped expectations that would resurface in the 1960s.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the Second World War ended the Great Depression in the United States.
You may consider:
• Lend Lease and federal war spending
• mobilisation of the workforce, including women and African-Americans.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lend Lease (March 1941) sent around $50 billion of supplies to Britain and the USSR; American factories started filling with war orders before Pearl Harbor.
• Federal spending rose from $9 billion (1939) to $98 billion (1944) — about twenty times the New Deal’s peak.
• War production figures: 297,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks, 8,800 warships; the Ford Willow Run plant built a B-24 every 63 minutes at peak.
• Conscription removed 12 million men from the unemployment count; the federal government directly employed around 4 million.
• Women joined the workforce in millions; female employment rose from 14 million to 19 million.
• 1.5 million African-Americans moved to northern and western cities for war work; Executive Order 8802 banned discrimination in defence industries.
• Wages rose around 65%; tax extended to most workers; new industries developed in California, Tennessee and the Gulf coast.
• Limits: rationing, segregated armed forces, Japanese-American internment of 120,000.
• Conclusion: the war ended the Depression because it combined deficit spending, conscription and political consensus that the New Deal had never achieved — structural rather than just political transformation.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Lend-Lease Act of March 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lend Lease allowed the United States to lend or lease war supplies — weapons, food, oil — to Britain, the Soviet Union and other Allies, without immediate payment.
• It effectively ended American neutrality before Pearl Harbor by tying the US economy to the Allied war effort.
• Around $50 billion of supplies were shipped under Lend Lease by 1945, with about $32 billion to Britain and around $11 billion to the USSR.
• Roosevelt described the policy as lending a neighbour your hose if their house was on fire, framing it as common-sense self-defence rather than entry into the war.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the way an Anglo-Saxon village worked in the years before 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Villages were typically 20 to 60 households clustered around a parish church and the lord’s hall, with houses of timber and thatch.
• Arable land was farmed in the open-field system — long thin strips spread across two or three great fields, with each peasant holding strips in each so good and poor land were shared.
• Crops rotated between winter wheat, spring barley and fallow on a two- or three-field system, alongside common pasture, hay meadow and woodland.
• Most peasants ate coarse bread of barley, rye or maslin, pottage of dried peas and beans, and occasional cheese or meat at festivals.
• Why it mattered: the open-field village was the unit the Normans taxed and ruled, so keeping it working mattered more to a new lord than changing it.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which daily life in England stayed the same after the Norman Conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both societies organised arable farming through the open-field system, with peasants holding strips of land in two or three great fields around their village.
• Both relied on the agricultural calendar of ploughing, sowing, haymaking, harvest and slaughter, with the same crops of wheat, rye, barley and oats.
• Both used markets and towns — London, York, Winchester, Norwich, Lincoln continued as major commercial centres after 1066.
• In both periods most peasants attended their parish church for Sunday worship and for baptisms, marriages and funerals, with the parish system continuing intact.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Norman rule changed daily life in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Norman forest law placed vast tracts of countryside under royal hunting reserves, with savage penalties for poaching, taking firewood or grazing pigs — restrictions unknown before 1066.
• Major towns such as Norwich and Nottingham now had French quarters — new boroughs around the castle settled by Norman merchants and craftsmen, distinct from the existing English population.
• The Normans introduced lordly deer parks attached to manor houses, separating elite hunting leisure from peasant working land in a way Anglo-Saxon halls had not.
• Castles such as Lincoln were built by demolishing rows of English houses (166 at Lincoln), reshaping the urban landscape under Norman lordship.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about forest law for the lives of ordinary English people between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Forest law placed huge tracts of countryside under royal hunting privilege, with peasants on the edges losing customary rights to gather firewood, snare rabbits, take fallen timber or graze pigs in the woodland.
• Penalties were savage by the standards of common law — blinding, mutilation, sometimes execution — and policing was carried out by separate royal foresters whose courts cut across ordinary local justice.
• At the New Forest in Hampshire, William cleared villages of their inhabitants to create the reserve — a stark act of rural displacement remembered bitterly by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
• Forest law generated significant royal income from fines on those who breached it, intensifying the financial pressure on peasant communities adjacent to royal forests.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the new French quarters in major English towns after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, French quarters at Norwich, Nottingham, Northampton and Southampton gave Norman merchants, craftsmen and clergy their own boroughs alongside the Anglo-Saxon old towns — physical separation of the two communities within walking distance.
• They concentrated incoming Norman skills (stonemasonry, leatherwork, fine cloth) and money in distinct urban quarters, accelerating the growth of late 11th-century English towns.
• Domesday records the new boroughs (novus burgus) at several towns, suggesting royal interest in registering and taxing the new settlements separately from the older English ones.
• Importance later: many of these French quarters became the dominant commercial centres of their towns — Norwich’s new market eclipsed the older Tombland and is still the main market square today.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of life after 1066.

‘For the ordinary English family the conquest changed very little. The same strips were ploughed, the same church was attended and the same dues were paid; only the name of the lord was different.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about daily life in England after the Norman Conquest? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: the conquest brought little real change to the daily life of ordinary English people.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The open-field system, two- or three-field crop rotation and parish church framework continued largely intact — peasants ploughed the same strips and worshipped in the same churches.
• The agricultural calendar of ploughing, haymaking, harvest, threshing and slaughter was unchanged; food remained coarse bread, pottage and occasional meat for most.
• Old English remained the everyday language of the village; Latin and French ran the courts and great houses but did not penetrate the cottage.
• Domesday confirms most peasants still lived as villeins, bordars or cottars on the same manors, simply with a Norman name at the top of the entry rather than an English one.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• Norman forest law restricted peasant access to woodland, game and grazing across huge tracts of countryside — a sharp legal innovation with savage penalties (blinding, mutilation, execution).
• Castles such as Lincoln were built by demolishing rows of English houses (166 at Lincoln), changing the look and feel of major towns immediately.
• French quarters at Norwich, Nottingham and elsewhere imposed new urban centres on existing towns, separating Norman from English populations and shifting commercial gravity.
• Lordly deer parks, the murdrum fine and the new dominance of stone castles and cathedrals reshaped the landscape and legal life of England by 1100.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Extract from a UN Office on Drugs and Crime country report on Afghan opium production, published 2007.
‘In 2001 Afghan opium poppy cultivation stood at around 8,000 hectares following the Taliban ban; by 2007 it has reached 193,000 hectares. Production is concentrated in Helmand province, where the insurgency has secured the cooperation of farmers and traders. The opium economy now exceeds the legal export earnings of the Afghan state.’

Study Source A. Source A suggests that Karzai’s government had lost control of the opium economy. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise figure or phrase from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one supporting detail.
Developing: One inference; some detail.
Emerging: Description without inference.

Indicative content:
• The 24-fold increase in cultivation suggests Karzai’s government had no effective drug-control policy in the south — a policy area in which the Taliban regime had demonstrably succeeded.
• The phrase ‘the insurgency has secured the cooperation of farmers’ suggests opium was binding villagers to the Taliban, not the government, in the very provinces where Karzai needed legitimacy.
• That the opium economy ‘exceeds legal export earnings’ suggests the formal Afghan economy was being dwarfed by an illegal one Karzai could not tax or regulate.
• The concentration in Helmand suggests the insurgency had a stable revenue base in the British zone of operations — a point of obvious concern to a UN agency.

practice_questions.text:
Source B: Extract from a 2006 BBC report on the British deployment to Helmand province.
‘The Defence Secretary said it would be a peacekeeping mission and we hoped not to fire a shot. Six weeks in, our company has been in firefights almost every day. We are at platoon houses scattered across the province, dug in behind sandbags, fighting Taliban units that nobody told us would still be here.’

Study Source B. Source B suggests that the Taliban had recovered strongly by 2006. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise quotation from the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one quotation.
Developing: One inference with limited evidence.
Emerging: Paraphrase without inference.

Indicative content:
• The phrase ‘we hoped not to fire a shot’ suggests British political leaders had badly misread the security situation in southern Afghanistan in 2006.
• The line ‘Taliban units that nobody told us would still be here’ suggests intelligence and policy briefings underestimated the regrowth of the movement; the resurgence had outpaced the government’s assessment of it.
• The reference to ‘platoon houses scattered across the province’ suggests British forces were spread thinly, holding ground rather than dominating it — a sign of how serious the resurgence already was.
• The contrast between ‘peacekeeping’ rhetoric and ‘firefights almost every day’ suggests British forces faced organised insurgent units, not isolated terrorists, by mid-2006.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Hamid Karzai’s government was established between November 2001 and October 2004.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Bonn conference December 2001, ISAF authorisation, emergency Loya Jirga 2002, constitutional Loya Jirga December 2003, January 2004 constitution, October 2004 election); reaches the elected presidency through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• November 2001: with Kandahar still falling, the UN convened four Afghan delegations in Bonn under Lakhdar Brahimi.
• 5 December 2001: the Bonn Agreement made Karzai chairman of an Afghan Interim Administration; he was inaugurated in Kabul on 22 December.
• 20 December 2001: UN Security Council Resolution 1386 authorised ISAF to maintain security in Kabul.
• June 2002: an emergency Loya Jirga elected Karzai head of state for the transitional period.
• December 2003: a constitutional Loya Jirga drafted the new constitution.
• January 2004: the constitution was promulgated, declaring Afghanistan an Islamic republic with elected institutions.
• October 2004: Karzai was elected president with 55% of the vote in the country’s first direct presidential election.
• The Bonn roadmap had been delivered procedurally even as the country’s underlying problems went unsolved.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Taliban regrouped and returned to fighting between 2002 and 2006.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical chain linking three or more events with precise detail (flight to Pakistan tribal areas, ISI sympathies, opium revenue, low-level violence 2002–05, NATO expansion 2006, Helmand deployment); reaches the full insurgency through clear causation.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causation.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Late 2001–early 2002: Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters fled south and east into Pakistan’s tribal areas where parts of the ISI continued to give quiet support.
• 2002–04: small Taliban units began re-entering Afghanistan to attack district centres and government officials.
• By 2005 the opium harvest in Helmand was funding fighters, weapons and motorcycles; shadow courts began operating in Pashtun villages.
• August 2003: NATO took over ISAF, but the force was still concentrated in Kabul.
• 2006: NATO expanded ISAF nationwide; British forces deployed to Helmand from May 2006 expecting peacekeeping and meeting heavy combat.
• By the end of 2006 a full insurgency was under way across the south and east, with Operation Mountain Thrust and Operation Medusa testing the new NATO posture.

practice_questions.text: ‘The light Western footprint after 2001 was the most important reason the Karzai government failed to control Afghanistan.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: ISAF was authorised under Resolution 1386 for Kabul only, around 4,500 troops from 18 countries, and Donald Rumsfeld refused requests to expand it.
• Agree: outside Kabul security was left to warlords such as Dostum, Ismail Khan and Gul Agha Sherzai, who kept their militias and their revenues.
• Agree: with no state presence in the southern districts, the Taliban were able to return from 2002 and to run shadow courts by 2005.
• Disagree: the opium economy grew from around 185 tonnes in 2001 to 8,200 tonnes in 2007, a structural problem no troop level alone could solve.
• Disagree: the Taliban sanctuary in Pakistan’s tribal areas lay beyond the reach of any force deployed inside Afghanistan.
• Disagree: corruption inside the Karzai government, from unpaid police to contracts awarded to relatives, cost it legitimacy on its own account.
• Judgement: the light footprint was the decision that allowed warlordism, opium and the Pakistan sanctuary to consolidate, but those problems would have been hard to fix even with more troops.

practice_questions.text: ‘The Bonn Conference of December 2001 shaped the problems Afghanistan faced for the next decade.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: excluding the Taliban turned a defeated movement into a permanent opposition that later attempts at negotiation could never undo.
• Agree: Bonn chose Hamid Karzai, a Pashtun with little independent power base, and gave him authority that barely reached beyond Kabul.
• Agree: authorising ISAF for Kabul alone fixed the light footprint that left the provinces to warlords.
• Disagree: Bonn also delivered its roadmap — an emergency Loya Jirga in 2002, a constitution in January 2004 and an elected president in October 2004.
• Disagree: the deeper problems, above all opium and the Pakistan sanctuary, pre-dated Bonn and were outside its remit.
• Disagree: later choices, especially Rumsfeld’s refusal to expand ISAF and the 2006 NATO deployment to Helmand, mattered as much.
• Judgement: Bonn set the framework for both the achievements and the failures, but later decisions determined which of the two prevailed.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a newspaper report by the American journalist Seymour Hersh, published on 13 November 1969 after his investigation into the events at My Lai.
‘On 16 March 1968 Charlie Company entered a Vietnamese hamlet known as My Lai 4. They found no enemy. They killed, by their own subsequent admissions, hundreds of civilians: women, children, the very old. The army called it a battle. The army called the dead enemy. It was a massacre.’

Source A suggests that Hersh believed the army had misdescribed what happened at My Lai. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He states that Charlie Company ‘found no enemy’ in the hamlet.
• He names the dead as civilians — women, children and the very old.
• He contrasts the army’s label of a battle with his own word, ‘a massacre’.
Contextual knowledge: The army had reported a four-hour action with 128 Vietcong killed; between 350 and 504 unarmed civilians died, and only Lieutenant Calley was ever convicted.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a US Army press release describing the My Lai operation, dated 17 March 1968.
‘American Division forces engaged a strong enemy unit at My Lai 4 yesterday morning, killing 128 Vietcong in a sharp four-hour action. Light US casualties. The hamlet was a long-suspected Vietcong stronghold.’

Source C: An extract from the testimony of warrant officer Hugh Thompson Jr to a US army inquiry, given in late 1969.
‘I saw soldiers shooting civilians who were trying to surrender. I landed my helicopter between them and ordered my crew to fire on our own troops if the killing did not stop. The dead were old men, women and small children. There were no enemy fighters in that hamlet.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the events at My Lai. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: claims a four-hour engagement and 128 Vietcong dead. Provenance: an army press release issued the day after the events — primary evidence of how the army initially framed the massacre. Own knowledge: the operation was concealed for over a year; the body-count metric encouraged officers to classify civilians as enemy dead.
Source C — Content: directly contradicts B with eyewitness detail of unarmed civilians and an absence of enemy fighters. Provenance: sworn testimony to an army inquiry by a witness whose helicopter intervention saved lives — high credibility, given under oath. Own knowledge: between 350 and 504 civilians were killed; Hersh broke the cover-up in November 1969; only Calley was convicted.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding the cover-up itself; C is highly useful for the events. Read together they show how systematically the army misreported the massacre.

practice_questions.text:
‘The My Lai massacre was the main reason American public opinion turned against the Vietnam War.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The killings, revealed in November 1969, gave the anti-war movement undeniable evidence of what the war had become.
• Ronald Haeberle’s photographs reached front pages around the world.
• Calley’s conviction and Nixon’s intervention on his behalf deepened public distrust of official accounts.
Disagree:
• Opinion had already turned: a Gallup poll of October 1967 was the first in which more Americans said sending troops was a mistake than said it was not.
• The Tet Offensive of January 1968 and Walter Cronkite’s ‘stalemate’ broadcast of 27 February 1968 came a year and more before My Lai was known.
• The draft fell hardest on working-class and African American families, which fed opposition from the mid-1960s.
• Martin Luther King Jr had denounced the war publicly in April 1967.
Judgement: My Lai crystallised and hardened opposition that was already strong; Tet, the draft and televised reporting were earlier and arguably deeper causes.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a memoir by a US infantry sergeant who served in Vietnam in 1967, published in 1985.
‘Body count was everything. The captain wanted twenty before he wrote his report. We learned to count anyone we found in a free-fire zone, fighter or farmer. After a while you stopped asking who they were. The numbers went up. The war went on. We knew we were not winning anything that could be measured.’

Source F suggests that the body-count metric distorted how the war was being measured. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The captain ‘wanted twenty before he wrote his report’, so the number came before the facts.
• Anyone found in a free-fire zone was counted, ‘fighter or farmer’.
• The soldiers themselves knew they ‘were not winning anything that could be measured’.
Contextual knowledge: Pentagon analysts later concluded that a large share of recorded enemy dead were uninvolved civilians, and Westmoreland’s ‘crossover point’ claims collapsed at Tet in January 1968.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the My Lai massacre came to be exposed and prosecuted between March 1968 and 1971.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 16 March 1968: Charlie Company killed between 350 and 504 unarmed civilians at My Lai.
• 17 March 1968: army press release described it as a battle with 128 Vietcong dead.
• March 1969: soldier Ronald Ridenhour sent letters to congressmen describing what he had heard.
• Late 1969: army inquiry began; Hugh Thompson testified.
• November 1969: journalist Seymour Hersh broke the story in syndicated newspapers.
• December 1969: Haeberle’s colour photographs appeared in Life magazine.
• March 1971: Lieutenant William Calley convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment.
• 1971–1974: Nixon intervened; Calley released from house arrest after roughly three and a half years.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source G.

Source G: An extract from a published interview with a member of Vietnam Veterans Against the War, given in April 1971 during the Capitol Hill medal-throwing protest.
‘I was 19 in the Mekong. I came home and the war was still on the television. The men I served with are dying again, and the men dying now are the brothers of the men we already killed. We did not earn these medals; the country did not earn this war.’

Source G suggests that veterans opposed the war because of what they had seen themselves. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source G and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The speaker served at nineteen and came home to find the war still running.
• He says the men now dying are ‘the brothers of the men we already killed’.
• He rejects the decorations: ‘we did not earn these medals’.
Contextual knowledge: Vietnam Veterans Against the War was founded in 1967; in April 1971 hundreds of members threw their medals onto the steps of the Capitol.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the official war diary of an Australian battalion at Anzac Cove, written on the night of 25 April 1915.
‘We have been ashore since dawn. The cliffs above the beach are held in strength and our advance has not reached its objectives. The cove was not the beach we were directed towards. Casualties heavy and no clear position from which to organise the next attempt.’

Source A suggests that the Anzac Cove landing went wrong from the first day. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The battalion is ashore but ‘our advance has not reached its objectives’.
• ‘The cove was not the beach we were directed towards’ - they landed in the wrong place.
• ‘The cliffs above the beach are held in strength.’
• Casualties were heavy, with ‘no clear position from which to organise the next attempt’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The ANZACs came ashore about a mile north of the intended beach on 25 April 1915.
• The five-week gap after the failed naval attack of 18 March let Liman von Sanders and Mustafa Kemal prepare the defence.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum written by Winston Churchill to the British War Council in January 1915.
‘Are we to admit that there is no other way of winning the war than by sending fresh armies to slaughter on the Western Front? The Dardanelles offers the only short cut. Force the straits, and Constantinople falls. The Black Sea opens to Russia, the Balkan states join us, and the German alliance crumbles.’

Source C: An extract from a despatch by Sir Ian Hamilton, the British commander at Gallipoli, sent to Lord Kitchener in August 1915 from the peninsula.
‘The terrain is more terrible than any of our advisers anticipated. The Turk fights with skill and courage on his own ground. Disease takes as many men as the rifle. We need fresh divisions, fresh water, and a clearer plan, or we cannot break out of the beachhead.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Gallipoli campaign. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: lays out Churchill’s strategic case for the Dardanelles. Provenance: a memorandum by the operation’s leading champion to the body that would approve it; clearly intended to persuade and likely to overstate prospects. Own knowledge: the failed naval attack on 18 March 1915 stopped the strategic vision in its tracks; only four neutral states ever joined the Allies and not because of the Dardanelles.
Source C — Content: gives a frontline assessment of why the campaign was failing — terrain, Ottoman skill, disease. Provenance: a despatch from the British commander to the Secretary of State for War; well-placed to assess operational reality but also defending his own conduct. Own knowledge: Ottoman defence under Liman von Sanders and Mustafa Kemal exploited the high ground; Suvla Bay landings in August failed to break out; evacuation completed January 1916 with ~250,000 Allied casualties.
Judgement: B is highly useful for the strategic vision but partial; C is useful for operational realities but written by a commander defending his record. Together they show why the side-attack idea collapsed.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Gallipoli campaign developed from the naval attack in February 1915 to the final evacuation in January 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (19 Feb naval bombardment, 18 March, 25 April, Suvla Bay, evacuation Dec 1915–Jan 1916); reaches the close of the campaign through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 19 February 1915: opening Anglo-French naval bombardment of the Dardanelles forts.
• 18 March 1915: full naval assault halted by Turkish mines; three Allied battleships sank.
• Five-week pause allowed Liman von Sanders and Mustafa Kemal to organise the Ottoman defence.
• 25 April 1915: land landings at Cape Helles (British/French) and Anzac Cove (ANZACs); steep cliffs and prepared defenders pinned the attack to the beaches.
• August 1915: Suvla Bay landings sought to break out but were blocked by Ottoman positions on the high ground; disease (dysentery, typhoid) crippled the force.
• December 1915–January 1916: cleanly executed evacuation removed troops with low casualties; total Allied casualties reached around 250,000.

practice_questions.text:
‘Gallipoli was a strategically sound plan ruined by poor execution.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Knocking the Ottoman Empire out of the war and opening a supply route to Russia would have been a real prize.
• The naval attack of 18 March 1915 threw away surprise and gave the defenders five weeks to prepare.
• The ANZACs landed at the wrong beach, and the August landings at Suvla Bay were not exploited.

Disagree:
• The premise was untested: taking Constantinople might not have made the Ottoman Empire surrender.
• The terrain - steep cliffs, no fresh water, narrow beaches - favoured the defenders whatever the plan.
• Dysentery, typhoid and the August heat took men out of the line as fast as wounds did.
• Ottoman troops under Liman von Sanders and Mustafa Kemal were far better than Allied planners assumed.

Judgement: Execution was poor, but the strategy also rested on guesses about Ottoman collapse that were never tested. Both halves of the campaign were weak.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a memoir by Russian general Aleksei Brusilov, written in the 1920s and published in English translation as A Soldier’s Notebook.
‘In June 1916 my four armies broke the Austrian line on a 350-kilometre front. We took prisoners by the hundreds of thousands. Yet the Tsar’s government failed to send the reserves required to exploit the breach, and within weeks German divisions arrived from France to stiffen the line. Our victory dissolved into bleeding.’

Source F suggests that the Brusilov Offensive succeeded at first but could not be exploited. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Four Russian armies broke the Austrian line on a 350-kilometre front in June 1916.
• Prisoners were taken ‘by the hundreds of thousands’.
• The government ‘failed to send the reserves required to exploit the breach’.
• German divisions arrived from France and the victory ‘dissolved into bleeding’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• About 400,000 Austrian prisoners were taken and Russian casualties reached roughly a million.
• The strain fed the food shortages and discontent that broke the Tsarist regime in 1917.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the major events on the Eastern Front between Russia’s mobilisation in August 1914 and the Brusilov Offensive of summer 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Tannenberg, Masurian Lakes, Brusilov Offensive); reaches summer 1916 through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• August 1914: Russia mobilised faster than Germany expected and invaded East Prussia, drawing German troops from the Western Front.
• 26–30 August 1914: Battle of Tannenberg destroyed the Russian Second Army; Hindenburg and Ludendorff emerged as German national heroes.
• September 1914: Battle of the Masurian Lakes drove Russia out of East Prussia; combined Tannenberg and Masurian Lakes losses ~250,000.
• 1915: German and Austro-Hungarian advance pushed Russia out of Poland; Tsar Nicholas II personally took command of the army, tying him directly to the war’s reverses.
• Summer 1916: General Brusilov’s offensive broke the Austro-Hungarian line on a 350-km front; 400,000 Austrian prisoners taken; Germany forced to send divisions east, easing pressure on Verdun and the Somme.
• Cost: roughly one million Russian casualties; the strain accelerated revolutionary pressures that broke the Tsarist regime in 1917.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1936 speech by Adolf Hitler to the Reichstag, on the day of the Rhineland reoccupation.
‘In this historic hour, when in the Reich’s western provinces German troops are at this minute marching into their future peacetime garrisons, we all unite in two sacred vows. First, we swear to yield to no force whatever in the restoration of the honour of our people. Second, we pledge that we have no territorial demands to make in Europe. Germany will never break the peace.’

Using Source A, identify two claims Hitler made on 7 March 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded claims with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear claims, briefly supported.
Developing: One claim clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific claims.

Indicative content:
• German troops were marching into peacetime garrisons in the western provinces.
• Germany would yield to no force in restoring national honour.
• Germany had no territorial demands in Europe.
• Implicit claim: the reoccupation was a defensive act, not a step toward war.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the events of 1936, from the Rhineland reoccupation in March to the formation of the Anti-Comintern Pact in November.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 7 March 1936: three German battalions entered the demilitarised Rhineland in defiance of Versailles and Locarno; commanders had orders to retreat if challenged.
• France was in mid-election and did not act; Britain treated the move as Germany ‘going into its own back garden’.
• The reoccupation removed the buffer protecting France and undermined French alliances with Czechoslovakia and Poland.
• July-October 1936: the Spanish Civil War began; German and Italian intervention on Franco’s side brought the dictators into practical cooperation.
• October 1936: agreements between Italy and Germany formalised the Rome-Berlin Axis; Mussolini’s 1 November speech in Milan named it publicly.
• 25 November 1936: the Anti-Comintern Pact between Germany and Japan committed both powers to cooperate against the Communist International.
• By the end of 1936, Hitler had moved from diplomatic isolation in early 1935 to leadership of a fascist bloc spanning Berlin, Rome and Tokyo.

practice_questions.text: Study Sources B and C. Source B: An extract from a 1936 private Cabinet memorandum by Stanley Baldwin, British Prime Minister, in the days after the Rhineland reoccupation. ‘The German action is a clear breach of Locarno. But our public has no stomach for war over German territory occupied by Germans. We must support the French in protest, but we cannot support military action that the British people would not back.’ Source C: An extract from a 1936 article by the French journalist Geneviève Tabouis in L’Œuvre, written shortly after the Rhineland reoccupation. ‘Today we have lost the war which we never began. The buffer that protected our eastern frontier is gone. Our allies in Warsaw and Prague will draw the obvious conclusion. France stood alone for an hour and chose not to act; Britain has chosen for us.’ Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Rhineland Crisis. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a candid British Cabinet view that the breach was clear but military response was politically impossible. Provenance: a private memorandum to the Cabinet by the Prime Minister, expressing genuine policy thinking; not designed for public consumption. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — British public opinion in 1936 leaned toward a settlement, and Britain refused to back French military action.
Source C — Content: a French journalist arguing the strategic loss for France and its eastern allies; blames Britain for paralysing France. Provenance: a contemporary newspaper article designed to influence French opinion and government action. Own knowledge: confirms historical record — the demilitarised zone protected France’s eastern alliance system, which weakened after 1936 and contributed to the abandonment of Czechoslovakia at Munich in 1938.
Judgement: B is useful as British official thinking but reveals only one strand; C is useful for French strategic perception but is polemical and overstates Britain’s sole responsibility — France did have the option to act alone.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Rome-Berlin Axis was formed in 1936 and what it gave Hitler.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail. Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage. Indicative content: • April 1935: Italy stood with Britain and France at Stresa against German treaty-breaking. • October 1935 onwards: Mussolini invaded Abyssinia and League sanctions pushed Italy away from its Stresa partners. • Summer 1936: German and Italian forces intervened together for Franco in the Spanish Civil War, building practical cooperation. • October 1936: agreements between Rome and Berlin covered Austria, the Balkans, Spain and economic cooperation; Mussolini named the Axis in a Milan speech on 1 November. • Effect: German diplomatic isolation was broken, and Italy was removed as the obstacle to Anschluss that it had been in 1934. • Limit: the Axis was not yet a military alliance — that came with the Pact of Steel in 1939 — and Mussolini still pursued his own interests.

practice_questions.text:
‘The remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936 was the most serious of Hitler’s treaty violations before 1938.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• It broke the 1925 Locarno Treaty, which Germany had signed freely, as well as Versailles.
• It removed the demilitarised buffer that protected France and underpinned the French alliance system in eastern Europe.
• German forces could now fortify the western frontier, so France could no longer credibly march east to defend Poland or Czechoslovakia.
• German commanders had orders to retreat if challenged, so the Allied failure to act transformed Hitler’s confidence.
Challenging the statement:
• Conscription and the Luftwaffe in March 1935 rebuilt German military power itself, without which the Rhineland move was impossible.
• Leaving the League and the Disarmament Conference in October 1933 was the first test of Allied resolve, and it too went unanswered.
• The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 was a violation Britain actually legalised by treaty.
Judgement: the Rhineland was the most consequential breach because of what it did to French strategy, but it rested on the rearmament of 1935.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the formation of the fascist bloc in 1936-37, from the Rhineland reoccupation to Italy’s accession to the Anti-Comintern Pact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 7 March 1936: Rhineland reoccupation; Britain and France did not act, signalling Allied weakness.
• Summer 1936: Spanish Civil War began; German and Italian forces intervened on Franco’s side, drawing the two dictators together.
• October 1936: bilateral agreements between Italy and Germany formalised the Rome-Berlin Axis on Austria, the Balkans and Spain.
• 1 November 1936: Mussolini’s Milan speech publicly named the Axis.
• 25 November 1936: Anti-Comintern Pact signed between Germany and Japan, committing both to cooperate against the Comintern.
• November 1937: Italy joined the Anti-Comintern Pact, completing the three-power alignment of Berlin, Rome and Tokyo.
• By the end of 1937, Hitler had moved from diplomatic isolation in 1935 to leadership of a fascist bloc with global reach.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised speech by Nikita Khrushchev to the Supreme Soviet, 7 May 1960.
‘The American imperialists wished to keep their criminal activity secret. We held the news of the captured pilot, and they walked into the trap. Now the world can see the value of their words about peace. We invited them to talk; they sent spy planes. We must judge them by their deeds.’

Source A suggests that Khrushchev wanted to expose American dishonesty in public. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Khrushchev accuses the Americans of trying to keep ‘criminal activity secret’ through a cover story.
• He claims the pilot’s capture exposes the gap between American ‘words about peace’ and their actions.
• He frames the overflights as an answer to a Soviet invitation to talk — a betrayal of diplomacy.
• He invites the audience to judge the United States by deeds rather than words.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Powers's U2 was shot down over Sverdlovsk on 1 May 1960 and he was captured alive.
• Khrushchev held back the news of the pilot until the Americans had issued a weather-plane cover story.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a press statement by President Eisenhower, 11 May 1960.
‘Information collection by aerial reconnaissance has been a vital and disagreeable necessity for the United States. We live in a world that has not yet escaped the shadow of surprise attack. The flights have been authorised by me. They will be suspended in the interest of the talks at Paris, but I shall not apologise for measures necessary to our defence.’

Source C: An extract from a confidential British Cabinet briefing prepared by the Foreign Office for Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, 13 May 1960.
‘The American refusal to apologise will probably end the summit before it begins. Khrushchev needs a public concession to manage hardline opinion in Moscow; the President cannot offer one without surrendering control of US intelligence policy. The Prime Minister should expect the talks to collapse on the opening day.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why the Paris Summit collapsed in May 1960. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Eisenhower defends overflights as ‘vital and disagreeable’, suspends them but refuses to apologise. Provenance: a public presidential statement five days before the summit, designed for both domestic and foreign audiences. Own knowledge: Eisenhower had personally authorised the U2 flights since 1956; the cover story collapsed when Khrushchev produced Powers alive.
Source C — Content: identifies the apology gap as the breaking point and predicts collapse on opening day. Provenance: a confidential briefing for the British Prime Minister, written between informed allies — likely to give a frank assessment. Own knowledge: Khrushchev did walk out on 16 May after Eisenhower refused to apologise.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding the American public position but reflects political need to project firmness; C is useful as informed insider analysis predicting the actual outcome — both together capture the dynamic that ended the summit.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the U2 Crisis developed from the launch of Powers’s mission on 1 May 1960 to the collapse of the Paris Summit on 16 May 1960.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, places, names); reaches the summit collapse through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1 May 1960: Powers took off from Peshawar; his U2 was shot down by a Soviet S-75 missile near Sverdlovsk.
• 3-4 May 1960: Khrushchev held the news while NASA prepared a cover story about a lost weather plane.
• 5 May 1960: Khrushchev announced the shoot-down to the Supreme Soviet, drawing the American cover story into the open.
• 7 May 1960: Khrushchev produced Powers alive and the recovered wreckage, exposing the deception.
• 11 May 1960: Eisenhower took personal responsibility but refused to apologise, defending overflights as a defensive necessity.
• 16 May 1960: Khrushchev opened the Paris Summit with a denunciation, demanded an apology, and walked out when none came — ending the Thaw.

practice_questions.text:
‘The U2 Crisis was the most serious setback to East-West relations before 1962.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The Paris Summit collapsed on the day it opened and Khrushchev withdrew his invitation to Eisenhower.
• Test-ban talks stalled and no treaty was signed until 1963.
• Khrushchev came under pressure from Soviet hardliners and hardened his line on Berlin.
• The Camp David talks of 1959 had been the warmest superpower contact since 1945, and the affair erased them.
Disagree:
• The Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956 had already shown how little the Thaw was worth.
• The Berlin Wall of August 1961 was a sharper crisis at the time and lasted twenty-eight years.
• The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 carried a far greater risk of nuclear war.
• Arms spending on both sides kept rising throughout the Thaw, so there may have been little substance to lose.
Judgement: the U2 affair ended a promising initiative, but Berlin and Cuba brought the two sides closer to war.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential briefing by the head of Soviet air-defence forces to Khrushchev, dated 5 May 1960.
‘The American aircraft has been brought down by a Dvina missile near Sverdlovsk at an altitude of 20,700 metres. The pilot was captured alive with maps and identity documents. Recommendation: hold this information for two days while the Americans construct a cover story, then expose them publicly. The political effect will be greater than the military.’

Source F suggests that the Soviet leadership planned the political trap in advance. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: confirms that the Soviets deliberately delayed the announcement to trap the Americans into a cover story — useful evidence that the political effect was the goal, not just the military shoot-down.
• Provenance: a confidential military briefing to the Soviet leader — likely to give an honest internal account.
• Own knowledge: the U2 was indeed brought down by an S-75 (NATO code SA-2) Dvina missile near Sverdlovsk on 1 May; Powers was captured alive.
• Useful interpretation: the source explicitly frames the affair as a political operation, supporting the view that Khrushchev planned the trap from the start.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the immediate consequences of the U2 Crisis for superpower relations from May 1960 through to the construction of the Berlin Wall in August 1961.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the Berlin Wall through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 16 May 1960: the Paris Summit collapsed; the test-ban initiative stalled.
• August 1960: Powers was tried in Moscow and sentenced to ten years.
• Late 1960: the US Corona satellite reconnaissance programme produced its first usable images, replacing manned overflights.
• January 1961: Kennedy took office; the CIA assessed renewed Berlin crisis as highly likely.
• June 1961: Kennedy and Khrushchev met at the Vienna Summit, where Khrushchev pressed hard on Berlin and Kennedy left rattled.
• August 1961: facing a continued exodus through Berlin, Khrushchev authorised the building of the Berlin Wall — the harder Soviet line forecast since the U2 affair was now visible in concrete and barbed wire.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the harvest failures of the 1590s affected the poor.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They drove food prices to record levels — the ‘four wet years’ of 1594–97 caused real famine in the north and Cumbria.
• They forced more landless labourers and small tenants on to the road as vagrants, increasing the visible poor.
• They triggered minor unrest such as the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596, raising fears of wider disorder.
• They created the political pressure that produced the 1598 Poor Law and its compulsory parish poor rate.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it consolidated earlier laws and gave the parish a clear, workable framework for relief during the famine years.
• It made the poor rate compulsory and required every parish to have Overseers of the Poor, embedding welfare in local government.
• It distinguished between the impotent poor (relief), the able-bodied (work) and vagrants (punishment), which became the basis of welfare thinking for two centuries.
• Significance over time: it formed the foundation of the 1601 Poor Law, which was not replaced until the New Poor Law of 1834.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how enclosure added to poverty in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Common land was fenced off for private sheep farming, depriving poor families of grazing, fuel and gleaning rights.
• Sheep farming required far fewer labourers than arable farming, so rural jobs disappeared in enclosed parishes.
• Evicted tenants drifted to towns or became wandering vagrants, swelling the visible poor and triggering local fear.
• It contributed to the political pressure for both vagrancy laws (1572) and Poor Relief Acts (1576, 1598).

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the distinction between the impotent poor and sturdy beggars.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it shaped who received relief: the elderly, disabled and orphaned were given parish pensions, while jobless wanderers were whipped or punished.
• It allowed Parliament to pass harsh laws like the 1572 Vagabonds Act without seeming heartless to the disabled and elderly.
• It assumed that able-bodied beggars chose not to work — an assumption that ignored unemployment caused by enclosure and harvest failure.
• Significance over time: the deserving/undeserving framework persisted in English welfare thinking up to the 1834 New Poor Law and beyond.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the loss of monastic charity for the Elizabethan poor.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It removed the largest source of charity for the rural poor — almshouses, food doles and accommodation that abbeys had provided.
• It transferred former church land to gentry buyers, who increasingly farmed for profit and enclosed common fields.
• It increased the visibility of poverty as church-run charity disappeared and was replaced unevenly by parish provision.
• It contributed to the political pressure for a state-organised welfare system — the path that led to 1572, 1576 and 1598.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘Elizabeth’s government acted on poverty because it was frightened of disorder, not because it felt pity.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for the Elizabethan Poor Laws? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
