• The 1572 Vagabonds Act used whipping, ear boring and even the death penalty to deter sturdy beggars — punitive, not charitable.
• The Privy Council was alarmed by reports of riots and disturbances around grain prices in the 1580s and 1590s.
• The Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 produced an immediate upgrade in vagrancy enforcement.
• Maimed soldiers were singled out for relief partly because their unrest threatened the regime, not just out of sympathy.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• The 1576 Act required materials for the able-bodied to work, recognising poverty as a structural problem.
• The 1598 Act funded pensions for the impotent poor through a compulsory rate — a genuine welfare commitment.
• Christian charity, expressed through the parish, was central to relief in practice; many gentry left endowments for almshouses.
• London institutions like Christ’s Hospital for orphans show real compassion alongside fear of disorder.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the early Royal Society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It grew out of a Gresham College meeting in November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren and was granted its first Royal Charter by Charles II in July 1662.
• It was a private subscription society funded by fellows’ weekly dues, not by the Treasury, despite the king’s patronage and the silver mace he presented.
• It met weekly at Gresham College, with Robert Hooke as Curator of Experiments demonstrating air-pump, microscope and astronomical effects.
• Its secretary Henry Oldenburg edited ‘Philosophical Transactions’ from 1665, the first English-language scientific journal still in publication.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Charles II built up royal patronage of the arts and sciences.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He chartered the Royal Society in 1662, gave it a silver mace and made the king its formal patron, but provided no Treasury funding.
• He founded the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in 1675, with John Flamsteed as the first Astronomer Royal, to produce accurate star charts for navigation.
• He founded the Royal Mathematical School at Christ’s Hospital in 1673 to train navigators for the navy and merchant fleet.
• He commissioned Sir Peter Lely as court painter from 1661 and supported the composer Henry Purcell at the Chapel Royal.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Royal Society developed between 1660 and 1687.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It gave the loose Gresham College meeting a corporate identity, allowing it to hold property, choose officers and admit fellows formally.
• Its ‘Nullius in verba’ motto and the practice of repeating each other’s experiments embedded the principle of reproducibility at the heart of English natural philosophy.
• Its journal ‘Philosophical Transactions’ (1665) created a permanent printed record of experimental work, accessible to scientists across Europe.
• It allowed the Society to give the imprimatur in 1687 to Isaac Newton’s ‘Principia Mathematica’, the foundational text of modern physics.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about royal patronage for the development of the Royal Society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, royal patronage gave the new Society prestige, legal personality and the king’s mace; it allowed fellows to claim authority for their experimental method against rivals.
• The Royal Charter let the Society admit fellows from across Europe, building an international scientific reputation that would otherwise have been impossible.
• Royal patronage came without Treasury funding, so the Society had to live on subscriptions; this kept it independent of changing royal policy and protected it through later political storms.
• Significance over time: the Society outlasted the dynasty that founded it; it continuously published ‘Philosophical Transactions’ from 1665 and gave the imprimatur to Newton’s ‘Principia’ in 1687, helping to make English science world-leading by 1700.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Samuel Pepys’s presidency of the Royal Society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It tied the Society to the practical needs of naval administration: Pepys had reformed Royal Navy victualling and shipbuilding and used Society contacts on technical questions.
• It gave the Society a President with court access at exactly the moment Newton’s ‘Principia’ needed institutional backing to be printed.
• Pepys gave the imprimatur to the ‘Principia Mathematica’ in 1687, signing his name on the title page as President and giving the book the Society’s formal endorsement.
• It demonstrated that the Society could survive the death of its royal patron Charles II in 1685 and the political crisis around James II without losing its scientific role.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Royal Society succeeded because it never depended on the Crown for money.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the success of the Royal Society? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The Society was funded by fellows’ subscriptions, not by the Treasury, so it could choose its own experiments and admit foreign fellows without political interference.
• Independence allowed it to publish ‘Philosophical Transactions’ freely from 1665 and to give the imprimatur to Newton’s ‘Principia’ in 1687, even as the political climate shifted under James II.
• Membership reached far beyond court: Boyle was a wealthy private patron, Hooke a salaried curator, and many fellows were merchants, ship’s captains and physicians outside the royal household.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Royal patronage gave the Society its prestige, its mace and its legal corporate status, without which it could not have admitted fellows or held property.
• Charles II personally founded the Royal Observatory in 1675 and the Royal Mathematical School in 1673, both of which fed practical work back into the Society.
• Without the king’s 1662 Charter, the Gresham College group would have been one Oxford–London circle among many and might never have outlasted its founders.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Great Cause of 1291–92.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Thirteen candidates put forward claims to the Scottish throne after the Maid of Norway’s death.
• Edward I acted as arbitrator on condition that the candidates first acknowledged him as ‘Lord Paramount’ of Scotland at Norham in May 1291.
• Hearings took place over eighteen months, with English and Scottish lawyers reviewing each claim.
• On 17 November 1292 Edward gave judgement at Berwick in favour of John Balliol, descended through the elder line of Earl David of Huntingdon.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the relationship between England and Scotland changed because of the Great Cause.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Edward’s acceptance as ‘Lord Paramount’ in 1291 caused a permanent shift: every Scottish king from then on held his crown subject to an English overlord’s judgement.
• It caused John Balliol to be repeatedly humiliated — Scottish appellants brought lawsuits against him in the English court at Westminster.
• The 1294 demand for Scottish troops to fight in France caused the appointment of a council of twelve and the auld alliance of 1295, the first Scottish–French treaty.
• The deteriorating relationship caused Edward’s invasion in 1296, the sack of Berwick and the deposition of Balliol — ending the kingdom of Scotland in Edward’s eyes.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple causal links developed with precise figures and named places.
Secure: Two or more effects clearly explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but explanation is largely descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements about the Great Cause with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Treaty of Birgham (1290) for relations between England and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the treaty agreed that the Maid of Norway would marry Edward I’s heir while Scotland remained ‘separate and divided’ from England.
• It set out an early model of dynastic union: two kingdoms joined only in the persons of the future king and queen, with separate laws and courts.
• Its collapse with the Maid’s death later in 1290 left the throne empty, opening the way to the Great Cause.
• Significance over time: a peaceful Birgham-style merger of the crowns is roughly what eventually happened in 1603 under James VI and I — only after three centuries of war.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Edward I’s invasion of Scotland in 1296.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Edward stormed Berwick-upon-Tweed on 30 March 1296 and sacked the town in a two-day massacre.
• His cavalry crushed a Scottish relieving army at the Battle of Dunbar on 27 April 1296.
• At Montrose on 8 July 1296 he stripped John Balliol of his royal regalia in person, earning him the nickname ‘Toom Tabard’.
• The great seal of Scotland was broken into four pieces and the Stone of Scone was carried south to Westminster Abbey.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the sack of Berwick (March 1296) for the war between England and Scotland.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Berwick was Scotland’s richest port and a major centre of Flemish trade; its destruction wiped out a key economic base of the Scottish crown.
• The two-day massacre with up to 7,000 dead, including the Flemish merchants of the Red Hall, made the war unmistakeably one of conquest and not mere arbitration.
• It cleared the way for Dunbar (April) and the deposition of Balliol at Montrose (July), allowing Edward to claim Scotland as a conquered territory by August 1296.
• Significance over time: Berwick never again recovered its position as the trading capital of Scotland, and the memory of the sack hardened Scottish resistance through the rest of Edward’s reign.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples and figures.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘John Balliol’s humiliation was the main reason for the war between England and Scotland.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Edward repeatedly allowed Scottish appellants to bring lawsuits against Balliol in the English court at Westminster, treating the king of Scots as a vassal.
• The 1294 feudal demand that Balliol provide troops for the French war was deliberately humiliating and impossible to obey.
• Scottish nobles set up a council of twelve in 1295 to govern in Balliol’s name precisely because they thought he could no longer act as a free king.
• The auld alliance of 1295 was the direct response to that humiliation and provoked Edward’s 1296 invasion.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Edward’s overlordship had been built into the Great Cause from 1291 — the legal trap was set before Balliol was chosen.
• The dynastic accident of Alexander III’s 1286 death and the Maid of Norway’s 1290 death created the vacuum into which Edward stepped.
• Edward’s wider strategy of pressing English overlordship across the British Isles — already shown in Wales — would have produced conflict with Scotland eventually whoever was king.
• The economic strain of war with France in 1294 — the maltolt, the Riccardi collapse — made conquest of Scotland the cheapest source of additional revenue.

A strong response weighs Balliol’s personal humiliation against the deeper structural pressures and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on multiple factors and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1937 Nazi propaganda film celebrating the autobahns and KdF holidays as proof of national renewal) and Interpretation B (a modern study of German real wages arguing that workers funded the rearmament boom through stagnant pay and longer hours) on the Nazi economy. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the recovery as broadly shared — autobahns, full employment and subsidised leisure.
• Interpretation B presents the recovery as paid for by workers — flat real wages, a longer working week and consumer shortages.
• Main difference: A frames the economy as a national success story; B frames it as a hidden transfer from workers to the rearmament programme.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1937 Nazi propaganda film) and Interpretation B (a modern study of German real wages) give different views about the Nazi economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They had different purposes — the 1937 film aimed to mobilise public consent for rearmament; the modern study aimed to measure economic outcomes against pre-Nazi benchmarks.
• They drew on different evidence — the film used selected sites and individuals; the modern study used wage indices, working-hours data and household budgets.
• They were produced under different conditions — the 1937 film under regime censorship and propaganda direction; the modern study with full archival access.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Nazi recovery between 1933 and 1939 made ordinary Germans materially better off.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the impact of Nazi economic policy on workers and consumers?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because unemployment fell from six million in 1933 to under 200,000 in 1939 — jobs were a real material gain.
• Convincing because KdF gave 10 million Germans a holiday by 1938; Beauty of Labour improved canteens and washrooms.
• Less convincing because real wages did not match 1928 levels until 1938; the working week rose to over 49 hours by 1939.
• Less convincing because consumer goods (meat, butter, textiles) were rationed in all but name as resources went to rearmament.
• Less convincing because workers lost trade unions and the right to strike; workbooks from 1935 restricted job movement; women and Jews were redefined out of work.
• Overall judgement: jobs were a real gain, but pay, hours, choice and freedom were lost — the answer depends on which group of workers and which year you choose.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Four Year Plan of 1936 on the German economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Investment poured into synthetic substitutes — new plants for synthetic oil and Buna rubber at Leuna and Schkopau; reduced but did not eliminate import dependence.
• Steel was forced into new plants like the Hermann Goring Werke at Salzgitter; private firms (Krupp, IG Farben) saw mass orders.
• Military spending rose from around 10% of GDP in 1936 to roughly 18% by 1938; aircraft production reached around 8,000 per year by 1939.
• Consumer goods squeezed — meat, butter and textile shortages by 1939; foreign-exchange crisis deepened, prompting Schacht's resignation as Economics Minister in November 1937.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how Nazi economic policy between 1933 and 1939 affected different groups in German society.
You may consider:
• the impact on industrialists and the unemployed
• the impact on workers and consumers.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Industrialists: Krupp, Thyssen, IG Farben and the Hermann Goring Werke benefited from rearmament orders; cartels protected from foreign competition; trade-union threat removed.
• Unemployed: official unemployment fell from six million (1933) to under 200,000 (1939); RAD and conscription absorbed young men; autobahn programme employed roughly 125,000.
• Workers: jobs and KdF leisure programmes (10m holidays by 1938); but no unions, no strikes, real wages flat until 1938, working week up to 49 hours, workbooks from 1935.
• Consumers: shortages of meat, butter and textiles by 1939; Volkswagen savings scheme paid in by 336,000 with no civilian cars delivered before 1945.
• Excluded groups: Jews dismissed from civil service (April 1933); women squeezed out of professions; conscripts removed from civilian work.
• Conclusion: industrialists and the previously unemployed gained substantially; workers gained jobs but lost wage freedom; consumers funded the rearmament boom through shortages and inflation suppressed by price controls. The recovery was real but unevenly shared, and depended on a permanent expansion of military spending.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1980s economic historian arguing the Nazi recovery was a genuine economic miracle that pre-dated rearmament) and Interpretation B (a 2000s historian of armaments arguing the recovery was overwhelmingly driven by military spending) on the German economy 1933–39. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A frames the recovery as productive — civil public works, autobahns and demand stimulus generated growth even before rearmament took off.
• Interpretation B frames the recovery as militarised — conscription, the Four Year Plan and arms orders were the main driver of falling unemployment from 1935.
• Main difference: A stresses civil work creation; B stresses rearmament as the engine of growth.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the growth of trade unionism between 1834 and 1889.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Owen's GNCTU of 1834 claimed half a million members and collapsed within a year, showing both the appetite for national organisation and its limits.
• At the time: the transportation of the Tolpuddle Martyrs in 1834 showed the law could still be turned against workers, and the 800,000-signature petition showed public pressure could overturn it.
• At the time: the New Model Unions from 1851 won respectability, and with it the TUC (1868), the Trade Union Act 1871 and the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act 1875.
• At the time: new unionism brought unskilled workers in through the matchgirls' strike of 1888 and the London Dock Strike of 1889.
• Over time: union membership doubled in the three years after 1889, and the Labour Representation Committee of 1900 became the Labour Party with 29 MPs in 1906.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Tolpuddle Martyrs for the development of trade unionism in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the 800,000-signature petition and London demonstrations of up to 100,000 forced the government to pardon the men by 1836 — proving public pressure could overturn an unjust verdict.
• At the time: it warned trade unionists that obscure laws (the 1797 oath-taking statute) could be used against them, encouraging caution and respectability in the New Model Union generation.
• Over time: the case became a founding myth of the British labour movement — the Tolpuddle Festival is still held annually, and Loveless is invoked alongside the Levellers and Chartists in trade union speeches today.
• Over time: it set a precedent that mass petitioning of central government could check legal injustice, a tactic later used by Chartists, anti-slavery campaigners and the suffragettes.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of what happened to the Martyrs without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the New Model Unions of the 1850s and the new unionism of the 1880s were different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: New Model Unions covered skilled craftsmen (engineers, carpenters) on high subscriptions; new unionism organised unskilled workers (matchgirls, dockers) on low fees.
• Difference: New Model Unions emphasised benefits and bargaining and avoided strikes where possible; new unionism used mass strikes (1888 matchgirls, 1889 dockers) as a primary weapon.
• Difference: New Model Unions sought respectability and legal recognition (Trade Union Act 1871); new unionism deliberately mobilised public sympathy through the press to defeat employers directly.
• Difference: New Model Unions were politically cautious; new unionism led directly to the Labour Representation Committee 1900 and the Labour Party 1906.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: ‘The role of the individual was the main factor in the rise of trade unionism between 1834 and 1900.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of individuals as the main factor:
• George Loveless turned a Dorset wage dispute into a national symbol; without his oath, Tolpuddle would not have happened.
• Robert Owen built the GNCTU from scratch with a vision of cooperative society.
• Annie Besant’s journalism and Ben Tillett, Tom Mann and John Burns’s leadership of the dockers turned local disputes into national victories.

Weighed against the economy:
• Industrial wages, lockouts and the cost of bread were the constant pressure that forced workers to organise — without economic distress, individuals had nothing to mobilise.

Weighed against government:
• The Combination Acts (1799-1800) repealed in 1824-25, the Trade Union Act 1871, and the 1875 Conspiracy Act each shaped what unions could legally do; the legal framework set the limits inside which individuals operated.

Weighed against communication:
• The Tolpuddle petition, the Northern Star tradition continued in the trade union press, and the international solidarity that brought Australian dockers’ donations to London in 1889 turned local actions into national events.

Weighed against ideas (rights, free association):
• The right to combine, the dignity of labour and (later) socialist ideas of class solidarity gave the movement its moral framework.

Judgement: Top answers argue that individuals matter, but only as the leaders of forces already in motion. Loveless without the Dorset wage cuts is just a farm worker; Tillett without the dockers’ existing grievances is just an organiser without followers.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples comparing individuals to other factors; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Lists factors without comparison or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the London Dock Strike of 1889 for the trade union movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 100,000 dockers paralysed the world’s largest port for five weeks, winning the ‘dockers’ tanner’ (sixpence an hour), union recognition and overtime rates.
• At the time: international solidarity (Australian unions sent £30,000) showed strikers could win even against the wealthiest employers.
• Over time: total trade union membership doubled in three years, bringing unskilled workers permanently inside the movement.
• Over time: the alliance of unions, the ILP and socialist groups in the 1900 Labour Representation Committee — and the 1906 Labour Party — built directly on the political confidence of the dockers’ victory.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the strike with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the legal position of trade unions in 1875 was different from their position in 1799.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in legality: the Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800 made it a crime for workers to organise for better pay or hours; by 1875 unions were lawful bodies whose funds were protected by the Trade Union Act 1871.
• Difference in the right to act: in 1799 collective bargaining itself was criminal, and as late as 1834 the Tolpuddle men were transported under the oath-taking law of 1797; the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act 1875 made peaceful picketing lawful.
• Difference in the state's stance: in 1799 Parliament legislated to suppress combination; by 1875 it legislated to protect it, and unions had a national voice through the TUC founded in 1868.
• Difference in security: early unions had no protection for their money and could be broken by a single prosecution; after 1871 they had a stable financial base that made long disputes possible.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct ways, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two ways with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1929 US history textbook):
‘Reconstruction was a tragic era. Carpetbaggers and ignorant freedmen, propped up by federal bayonets, plundered the prostrate South. The white people of the South suffered as no Americans had ever suffered before, until at last decent citizens reasserted control in 1877.’

Interpretation B (from a 1988 academic study of Reconstruction):
‘Reconstruction was an unfinished revolution. Around 2,000 Black men held public office, the first state-funded schools were built across the South, and three constitutional amendments redefined American citizenship. The tragedy was not Black participation but its violent overthrow.’

How convincing is Interpretation B? Use Interpretations A and B and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s ‘unfinished revolution’ thesis; engages directly with its specific claims (2,000 Black officials, schools, amendments, violent overthrow); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation of B with reference to A; relevant own knowledge; judgement reached.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to summarise; one or two pieces of own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without evaluating B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Hiram Revels (Mississippi, 1870) and around 16 Black Congressmen show genuine political participation.
• The Freedmen’s Bureau founded around 4,000 schools and distributed 21 million rations.
• The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments rewrote constitutional citizenship.
• Reconstruction state governments funded the South’s first public-education systems.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• ‘Forty acres and a mule’ was rescinded; freedpeople did not gain economic independence.
• Sharecropping replaced slavery as a coercive labour system.
• Some state legislatures did experience corruption (Louisiana, South Carolina).
• Reconstruction was overthrown by violence rather than collapsing of its own weight.

Judgement: B is the stronger interpretation in light of modern evidence; a top-band answer notes that A captures the post-1877 narrative deliberately built to discredit Reconstruction.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 1965 popular history of post-war America):
‘The 13th Amendment ended slavery in name but the Black Codes recreated it in substance. Mississippi led the way: vagrancy laws criminalised unemployment, apprenticeship laws bound Black children to white employers, and contracts forced workers to sign for a year or face arrest. Without the 14th Amendment and the 1866 Civil Rights Act, freedom would have meant nothing.’

How convincing is Interpretation C? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s argument; engages with the specific claims about Black Codes recreating slavery and the role of federal action; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• Mississippi’s 1865 Black Code did include vagrancy, apprenticeship and contract clauses functioning as a substitute for slavery.
• Northern outrage at the Codes drove the 1866 Civil Rights Act and the 14th Amendment.
• Without federal intervention the codes would have remained on the books.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• ‘Recreated it in substance’ overstates — freedpeople could marry legally, hold property and could not be sold.
• The Freedmen’s Bureau provided real legal protection that slaves had never had.
• Black political participation under Radical Reconstruction goes beyond the framework C implies.

Judgement: C captures the threat the Codes posed and the necessity of federal action, but a top-band answer recognises that the new federal protections produced rights distinctly different from those available under slavery.

practice_questions.text:
Was Reconstruction a success between 1865 and 1877?

• What Reconstruction achieved
• What Reconstruction failed to change

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs achievements against limits and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout; deploys specialist vocabulary (freedman, Black Code, sharecropping, Radical Republican, Reconstruction Amendment).
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides; limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of Reconstruction with little engagement with the question of success.

Indicative content:
What Reconstruction achieved:
• 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments redefined US citizenship.
• Around 2,000 Black officials elected, including Hiram Revels as first Black US Senator (1870).
• Around 4,000 schools founded by the Freedmen’s Bureau.
• 1866 Civil Rights Act — first federal civil rights law in US history.
• State-funded education systems established in many Southern states for the first time.

What Reconstruction failed to change:
• ‘Forty acres and a mule’ rescinded; sharecropping trapped freedpeople in debt.
• Black Codes reasserted control until federal intervention; even then, voter intimidation rose.
• Reconstruction was overthrown by 1877; rights granted on paper were violated in daily life.
• Andrew Johnson’s obstruction slowed reform; even Radical Reconstruction relied on federal troops who would soon withdraw.

Judgement: Reconstruction achieved more than the ‘tragic era’ framing allowed but less than its constitutional ambitions promised; a top-band answer reaches an explicit verdict and substantiates it.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation D.

Interpretation D (from a 1990 study of US constitutional history):
‘The 14th Amendment was the most important law passed in 19th-century America. It made citizenship national rather than state, guaranteed due process and equal protection, and gave the federal government the authority to defend individual rights against the states. Every later civil rights victory rested on it.’

How convincing is Interpretation D? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of D’s ‘most important law’ claim; weighs against alternatives (13th Amendment, 1866 Civil Rights Act, 15th Amendment); supports judgement with own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the 14th Amendment without engagement with D’s claim.

Indicative content (supporting D):
• Defined citizenship by birth on US soil — settling decades of debate.
• Created the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses still central to US law.
• Provided the constitutional basis for later civil rights legislation.
• Federalised individual rights against state interference.

Indicative content (qualifying D):
• The 13th Amendment ended slavery itself — arguably more transformative.
• The 1866 Civil Rights Act preceded the 14th and provided its template.
• Practical enforcement of the 14th was weak in the 19th century — Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) hollowed out equal protection.
• Impact only became central in the 20th-century civil rights movement, decades after the Reconstruction era.

Judgement: D’s claim is defensible for long-term significance, but a top-band answer notes that the 14th’s 19th-century reach was limited by judicial retreat — the ‘most important law’ framing is a long-view verdict, not an 1868 one.

practice_questions.text:
Which was the more important in transforming the lives of formerly enslaved people?

• The 13th Amendment
• The Civil Rights Act of 1866

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; deploys specialist vocabulary; precise on both measures.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of one or both with little comparison.

Indicative content:
The 13th Amendment:
• Abolished slavery itself — the foundational change without which nothing else mattered.
• Constitutional, not statutory — harder to repeal.
• Applied uniformly across all states, including the loyal border states the Emancipation Proclamation had not reached.

The Civil Rights Act of 1866:
• Defined citizenship and equal rights to make contracts, sue, give evidence and own property.
• Gave federal courts jurisdiction over violations of these rights, providing a real remedy.
• Without it, Black Codes would have left freedom theoretical.
• Provided the legal template that became the 14th Amendment.

Judgement: the 13th was the more transformative single change in legal status; the 1866 Act made that change practically meaningful in daily Southern life. A top answer reaches a clear verdict on the comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1995 social history of the post-war South):
‘The Freedmen’s Bureau was the most important federal agency of Reconstruction. Its schools educated a generation of Black children. Its courts protected freedpeople against fraudulent labour contracts. Its rations kept people alive in a war-shattered region. When it was wound down in 1872, much of the support structure for emancipation went with it.’

How convincing is Interpretation E? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s claim about the Bureau’s importance; weighs against alternatives (Constitutional Amendments, Civil Rights Act, military Reconstruction); supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the Bureau without engaging with E’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• Around 4,000 schools founded; many of the South’s historically Black colleges began under Bureau auspices.
• 21 million rations distributed in the famine-stricken war zone.
• Bureau courts adjudicated thousands of labour-contract disputes in favour of freedpeople.
• Wind-down in 1872 coincided with the visible weakening of Reconstruction.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• The Bureau was always under-funded and under-staffed for the size of the South.
• Constitutional Amendments and the 1866 Civil Rights Act provided the deeper legal framework.
• Radical Reconstruction’s federal troops mattered as much as Bureau staff for protection.
• Bureau wind-down was a symptom rather than the cause of federal retreat.

Judgement: E captures the everyday significance of the Bureau but overstates its position in the wider architecture of Reconstruction; a top answer balances on-the-ground reach against constitutional reform.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Drake’s voyage around the world.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Drake brought back roughly £400,000 in Spanish gold and silver, allowing Elizabeth to clear most of her foreign debts and reward her investors at £47 to the £1.
• At the time, the voyage was a propaganda blow against Spain — Drake raided unprotected Spanish ports and captured the treasure ship Cacafuego, then was knighted publicly on the Golden Hind in 1581.
• Over time, it established an English claim to a Pacific shore (‘New Albion’) and a route around the world that later companies could follow.
• Over time, it became a model for English long-distance voyaging, feeding into the trading companies (Levant 1581, East India 1600) and into the longer story of English overseas expansion.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of John Hawkins’s slaving voyages between 1562 and 1568.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Triangular route: Hawkins sailed from England to West Africa, where he seized or bought captive Africans, then crossed the Atlantic to sell them in the Spanish Caribbean in exchange for sugar, hides and pearls.
• Royal investment: Elizabeth herself was a financial investor and lent Hawkins ships such as the Jesus of Lubeck, making the voyages a Crown-backed enterprise rather than a private adventure.
• Conflict with Spain: the third voyage ended at the Spanish ambush at San Juan de Ulua in 1568, in which most of Hawkins’s men were killed and the young Drake barely escaped.
• Scale: the three voyages trafficked an estimated 1,200–1,400 Africans, breaking the Spanish-Portuguese trade monopoly.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Roanoke colony for English exploration.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Raleigh’s 1585 and 1587 colonies were the first English attempts to settle North America, planting the idea of an English Atlantic empire.
• At the time, the colony produced the first English child born in the Americas, Virginia Dare, in 1587 — a propaganda image of English presence on the continent.
• Significance over time: the failure of the colony — the lost colonists and the ‘CROATOAN’ carving — showed that under-funded private enterprise could not sustain a colony, lessons later applied at Jamestown in 1607.
• Significance over time: the patent system Raleigh used became the legal model for the Virginia Company and other later English colonies in the Americas.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Drake’s voyage around the world between 1577 and 1580.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Royal commission: Drake left Plymouth in December 1577 with a secret commission from Elizabeth to raid Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America.
• Capture of the Cacafuego: in 1579 Drake’s ship the Golden Hind seized the Spanish treasure ship Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion off the coast of Peru, taking gold, silver and jewels worth a fortune.
• Claim to New Albion: Drake landed on the Californian coast in 1579 and claimed it for Elizabeth as ‘New Albion’.
• Knighthood: on his return in 1580 Drake was knighted by Elizabeth on board the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Hawkins’s redesign of the English navy after 1577.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Hawkins as Treasurer of the Navy from 1577 introduced lighter, lower, more manoeuvrable race-built galleons with longer-range guns.
• At the time, the new ship design allowed English captains to outrun and outshoot the heavier Spanish galleons in 1588 without closing for boarding.
• Significance over time: race-built galleons set the pattern for English warship design for the next century, including the ships that fought the Anglo-Dutch wars.
• Significance over time: the navy that defeated the Armada was institutionally as well as technologically prepared, enabling later expansion of English naval power into the 1600s.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The voyages of Hawkins, Drake and Raleigh did more for Elizabeth at home than they did to begin an empire.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the importance of the Elizabethan voyages? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• Drake’s 1580 plunder cleared Elizabeth’s foreign debts and rewarded her investors — an immediate boost to royal finances.
• Hawkins’s race-built galleons defeated the Armada in 1588, securing the regime against invasion.
• Sea Dogs propaganda — Drake’s knighthood, the ‘singeing of the King of Spain’s beard’ at Cadiz in 1587 — gave Elizabeth a Protestant heroic narrative at home.
• Roanoke failed twice; no English colony survived in North America during Elizabeth’s reign.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Drake’s circumnavigation gave England an institutional model and an Atlantic claim later companies built on.
• The trading companies founded under Elizabeth (Muscovy 1555, Levant 1581, East India 1600) were the seed of later British global trade.
• Raleigh’s patent and the lessons of Roanoke directly shaped the Virginia Company and Jamestown in 1607, only four years after Elizabeth’s death.
• Hawkins’s slaving voyages, while small, opened a sea route and a commercial logic that the British state would later industrialise after 1660.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a private letter by Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty to his wife, written aboard HMS Lion on the night of 31 May 1916.
‘There is something wrong with our bloody ships today. Three battlecruisers gone in an afternoon — magazines unprotected, signalling slow, the German gunnery sharper than I had supposed. Yet we have driven Scheer back to his base and there he will stay.’

Source A suggests that British battlecruisers had a serious design weakness at Jutland. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• ‘Three battlecruisers gone in an afternoon.’
• Their magazines were unprotected and signalling was slow.
• German gunnery was ‘sharper than I had supposed’.
• Even so, ‘we have driven Scheer back to his base’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• HMS Indefatigable, Queen Mary and Invincible all blew up, killing more than 3,000 men.
• Britain lost 14 ships and 6,094 men and Germany 11 ships and 2,551 men, but the High Seas Fleet rarely put to sea again.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the German U-boat campaign developed from the first declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1915 to the introduction of the convoy system in May 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Feb 1915 declaration, Lusitania 7 May 1915, 1 Feb 1917 resumption, April 1917 tonnage, first convoy May 1917); reaches the convoy system through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• February 1915: Germany declared the first unrestricted submarine warfare campaign in the waters around Britain.
• 7 May 1915: U-20 sank the RMS Lusitania off Ireland, killing 1,198 including 128 Americans; US protests forced Germany to suspend unrestricted attacks in late 1915.
• 1 February 1917: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, calculating six months of attacks could starve Britain into peace before the USA could intervene.
• March 1917: Zimmermann Telegram became public, contributing to US declaration of war on 6 April 1917.
• April 1917: 881,000 tons of British merchant shipping sunk — Britain estimated to have around six weeks of food remaining.
• May 1917: experimental convoy from Gibraltar to Britain lost no ships, prompting a system-wide shift to convoying that halved monthly losses by the end of 1917.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum written for the British War Cabinet in April 1917 by a staff officer in the Admiralty’s Anti-Submarine Division.
‘The losses in merchant shipping have reached a level beyond what our island can sustain. Without an immediate change in tactics — the gathering of merchantmen into convoys under naval escort — we shall be defeated by starvation before the year is out. The Admiralty’s reluctance to proceed must yield to necessity.’

Source C: An extract from a German Admiralty staff paper of August 1917.
‘The British system of convoying has reduced our targets to a needle in a vastly enlarged haystack. To attack we must first find a convoy and then survive the escort. Monthly tonnage destroyed has fallen by more than a third since May. The promise of a six-month decision has not been kept.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the convoy system in 1917. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: an Admiralty staff officer urging the Cabinet to back convoying. Provenance: a memorandum from inside the Admiralty’s own anti-submarine staff, well-placed to know the shipping figures but written to overcome senior resistance to convoying. Own knowledge: April 1917 losses of 881,000 tons; first experimental convoy from Gibraltar in May 1917 lost no ships.
Source C — Content: confirms the convoy system was working from the German side. Provenance: a German Admiralty staff paper, well-placed to assess U-boat performance, written in August 1917 within Germany’s own naval bureaucracy and unlikely to overstate British success. Own knowledge: total Allied losses ultimately around 5,000 ships across the war, but monthly figures halved by late 1917; the U-boats were no longer a strategic threat by 1918.
Judgement: B is useful for the British policy debate; C is highly useful as independent confirmation that convoying defeated the campaign. Together they illuminate both why the system was adopted and how it worked.

practice_questions.text:
‘The British naval blockade was the most important factor in defeating Germany.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The blockade cut Germany off from food and raw materials year after year; the ‘Turnip Winter’ of 1916-17 broke civilian morale.
• A German government inquiry after the war put civilian deaths from blockade-related hunger and disease at around 750,000.
• The sailors who mutinied in November 1918 were hungry men refusing a last sortie, and the mutiny brought the Kaiser down.
• Jutland kept the High Seas Fleet in port, so the blockade could not be broken.

Disagree:
• American entry in April 1917 and the arrival of about two million US troops changed the balance of manpower.
• The German Spring Offensive of March 1918 showed Germany could still attack in strength, so the blockade had not beaten it.
• The Hundred Days from 8 August 1918 defeated the German army in the field.
• It was the convoy system, not the blockade, that stopped Britain being starved out first.

Judgement: The blockade was the slowest-acting cause and it broke the German home front, but the army was beaten in the field in 1918. The blockade made defeat certain; the Hundred Days made it happen.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of US Ambassador to Britain Walter Hines Page, written on 3 February 1917.
‘The Germans have today declared their submarines will sink without warning every ship found in the war zone. The President called me from Washington this morning — the long American patience is at an end. American honour, American shipping and American lives can be threatened no longer.’

Source F suggests that unrestricted submarine warfare ended American patience with Germany. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Germany has declared it will sink ‘without warning every ship found in the war zone’.
• The President telephoned that morning: ‘the long American patience is at an end’.
• The threat is put in three terms - American honour, American shipping and American lives.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917 and the USA broke off relations on 3 February.
• Congress declared war on 6 April 1917, after the Zimmermann Telegram was published on 1 March.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the events of the Battle of Jutland from the German departure from harbour on 30 May 1916 to the German return to harbour on 1 June 1916.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Hipper bait, Beatty pursuit, magazine losses, Scheer turn-aways, night escape); reaches the German return through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 30 May 1916: Scheer ordered the High Seas Fleet to sea, planning to lure part of the British fleet into a trap with Hipper’s battlecruisers.
• 31 May afternoon: Beatty pursued Hipper south but ran into Scheer’s battleships; British battlecruisers Indefatigable and Queen Mary blew up when shells reached their magazines.
• Late afternoon: Jellicoe’s Grand Fleet arrived from the north; Scheer found himself trapped against the larger British force.
• Twice during the engagement Scheer used the ‘battle turn-away’ under cover of destroyer torpedo runs and smoke to escape the British line.
• HMS Invincible blew up while crossing Scheer’s ‘T’; total British losses 14 ships and ~6,094 men, German 11 ships and ~2,551 men.
• Night of 31 May: Jellicoe declined risky night action; Scheer slipped through the British line and reached harbour by morning of 1 June, after which the High Seas Fleet rarely left port.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about Stalin’s collectivisation? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat collectivisation as a heroic modernisation programme that fed Soviet industrial growth; B may treat it as a brutal assault on the peasantry that produced famine.
• A may emphasise mechanisation and grain delivery; B may emphasise dekulakisation and the Holodomor.
• Specific textual reference required for both.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual reference. Secure: comparison with some reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the Ukrainian famine of 1932-33?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: a Soviet-era account denying or minimising the famine versus a post-1991 Ukrainian or Western account treating it as the Holodomor or genocide.
• Different time of writing: closed Soviet archives until 1991 limited what earlier historians could prove.
• Different perspective — Russian, Ukrainian, émigré or Western academic.
• Different evidence: state grain procurement records versus survivor testimony.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the targeting of kulaks during collectivisation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test specific claims of the interpretation against named context: Stalin’s call to ‘liquidate the kulaks as a class’ (Dec 1929), quota-driven local denunciations, around five million people affected, a fifth executed or worked to death.
• Weigh the ‘rich peasant’ framing against the political nature of the label — many were ordinary peasants targeted for resistance.
• Note historiographical positions — totalitarian school stresses Stalin’s personal will; revisionists stress local activists and quota culture.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge applied with clear judgement. Developing: knowledge unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of forced collectivisation on the Soviet countryside between 1929 and 1933.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Mass dekulakisation: roughly five million people targeted; deportations to Siberia, executions and forced-labour colonies.
• Livestock slaughter: cattle stocks halved between 1929 and 1933.
• Famine in Ukraine, the North Caucasus and Kazakhstan: roughly four million Ukrainians and 1.5 million Kazakhs died.
• Internal passports (December 1932) tied peasants to villages, creating a second-class status.
• State control: the kolkhoz system gave Moscow direct extraction power; political control was achieved.
• Productivity: grain and livestock outputs took decades to recover to 1928 levels.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of collectivisation.]

practice_questions.text: ‘Stalin pursued collectivisation mainly to fund the Five Year Plans.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider economic needs, political motivations and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for funding the Plans:
• The Plans needed grain to feed industrial cities and grain exports to fund foreign machinery.
• The 1927 procurement crisis convinced Stalin the NEP could not deliver enough.
• Industrial workers needed cheap food — collectivised agriculture provided it through forced extraction.

Arguments for political and ideological motives:
• Crushing kulaks eliminated the rural class Stalin saw as a threat to socialism.
• Collectivisation reasserted state control over the countryside that Lenin’s NEP had relaxed.
• Stalin could use anti-kulak campaigns to defeat Bukharin and the Right.
• Marxism-Leninism treated peasant smallholding as a relic to be abolished.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. the economic logic was real, but collectivisation also extended Stalin’s political power, defeating Bukharin and giving the regime control of the countryside that the Tsars had never achieved.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of dekulakisation on Soviet society between 1929 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Roughly five million people deported, executed or forced into labour colonies.
• Loss of the most productive farmers undermined long-term agricultural output.
• Created a forced-labour pool that fed early gulag construction projects.
• Quota-driven denunciations damaged village communities and trust.
• Strengthened the regime’s grip on the countryside by removing potential leaders of resistance.
• Reinforced fear — peasants entered kolkhozes to avoid being labelled kulak.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of dekulakisation.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised speech by Walter Ulbricht, leader of East Germany, broadcast on 13 August 1961, the day the sector boundary was sealed.
‘The criminal trafficking in human beings that takes place at our open border with West Berlin must end. Hostile elements use the city as a gateway to weaken the workers’ state. The protection of our socialist achievements requires us to act. Steps will be taken in agreement with our Warsaw Pact allies.’

Source A suggests that the East German government blamed the West for the loss of its people. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• ‘Trafficking in human beings’ through the open border must be stopped.
• ‘Hostile elements’ use Berlin as a gateway to weaken the East German state.
• Protection of ‘socialist achievements’ requires action.
• The action is presented as agreed with Warsaw Pact allies, framing it as legitimate.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• More than 16,000 East Germans left through Berlin in the first eleven days of August 1961.
• The sector boundary was sealed with barbed wire in the early hours of 13 August 1961.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a confidential cable from the British military mission in West Berlin to the Foreign Office, 14 August 1961.
‘The barbed wire was strung along the sector boundary overnight by East German police and construction units, with Soviet troops in reserve at safe distance. Western patrols were not interfered with. Our assessment is that the operation aims to stop the refugee outflow rather than to challenge Western access. The danger now is that hot heads on either side will start shooting.’

Source C: An extract from a radio address by Walter Ulbricht to East German workers, 18 August 1961.
‘The protective wall against the West will safeguard our economy and our peace. Productive labour can no longer be lured away by the dollar. Comrades, this measure does not divide; it secures.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the building of the Berlin Wall in August 1961. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: gives a calm assessment of the operation, identifies the goal as stopping refugees rather than challenging Western access, flags the risk of accidental shooting. Provenance: a confidential British military cable from the field to the Foreign Office — likely to give a frank, professional assessment. Own knowledge: barbed wire was indeed strung overnight on 13 August by East German forces with Soviet troops held back; Western patrols were not blocked.
Source C — Content: presents the Wall as a ‘protective’ measure to safeguard the economy from Western lures. Provenance: a public Ulbricht broadcast aimed at East German workers — designed to legitimise the action domestically. Own knowledge: the refugee outflow had reached over 16,000 in the first eleven days of August; the Wall did stabilise the East German workforce.
Judgement: B is highly useful as informed contemporary observation; C is useful as evidence of what the East German regime wanted its workers to believe, less useful as straightforward fact — both together capture military reality and political framing.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Berlin crisis developed from Khrushchev’s November 1958 ultimatum to the building of the Wall on 13 August 1961.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, refugee figures, named meetings); reaches the Wall through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• November 1958: Khrushchev demanded the Western powers leave Berlin within six months; the deadline passed without action.
• 1959-1960: refugee numbers continued to rise; the Eisenhower-Khrushchev Camp David talks produced no settlement.
• May 1960: the U2 affair ended the Paris Summit, hardening Soviet policy.
• June 1961: Khrushchev pressed Kennedy at the Vienna Summit, threatening a separate East German treaty by December; Kennedy returned shaken.
• July 1961: 30,000 East Germans fled west; Ulbricht pressed for a closed border.
• 1-11 August 1961: more than 16,000 fled in eleven days, raising the political emergency.
• 13 August 1961: East German forces sealed the sector boundary overnight, beginning the Berlin Wall.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Berlin Wall was a defeat for the Soviet Union rather than a victory.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The Wall handed the West a propaganda gift: a state that had to build a barrier to keep its own people in.
• Around 140 people died trying to cross between 1961 and 1989.
• Border guards defected, among them Conrad Schumann, who jumped the wire at Bernauer Strasse on 15 August 1961.
• Kennedy's visit in June 1963 drew huge crowds and made West Berlin a symbol of Western resolve.
Disagree:
• The Wall did what it was built to do: it stopped the loss of skilled workers and stabilised the East German economy.
• Khrushchev avoided forcing a Western retreat from West Berlin, which would have risked war.
• Kennedy accepted the Wall rather than reversing it, judging that a wall was better than a war.
• Berlin stopped being a first-rank flashpoint after 1961, which suited Moscow.
Judgement: a propaganda defeat in the long run, but in 1961 it solved the problem Khrushchev actually had.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter by US General Lucius Clay to President Kennedy, written from West Berlin on 28 October 1961.
‘The standoff at Checkpoint Charlie has lasted sixteen hours. Soviet armour faces our M48s. I have ordered our tanks to hold their ground. The Soviets must understand that the United States cannot be pushed by salami tactics. I expect them to back down by morning.’

Source F suggests that the United States was determined not to be pushed out of Berlin. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: confirms US tanks confronted Soviet armour at Checkpoint Charlie for sixteen hours — useful evidence of how serious the standoff became.
• Provenance: a private letter from the senior US general in Berlin to the President — likely to give a frank assessment unavailable in public statements.
• Own knowledge: the standoff ended on 28 October 1961 when both sides withdrew tanks — Clay’s prediction was largely correct.
• Useful interpretation: the source frames Berlin policy as resisting ‘salami tactics’, supporting the view that Kennedy chose firmness without escalation.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the construction of the Berlin Wall from the closure of the sector boundary on 13 August 1961 through to Kennedy’s ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’ speech in June 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the speech through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 13 August 1961: East German forces sealed the sector boundary overnight with barbed wire.
• 15 August 1961: border guard Conrad Schumann defected at Bernauer Strasse.
• 19 August 1961: Vice-President Johnson and General Clay arrived in West Berlin; a US battle group drove up the autobahn from West Germany.
• Late August - September 1961: the wire was replaced with concrete; watchtowers and a death strip were added.
• 27-28 October 1961: the Checkpoint Charlie standoff lasted sixteen hours before both sides withdrew tanks.
• 1962-1963: the Wall hardened into a permanent installation; an estimated 140 people died trying to cross over time.
• 26 June 1963: Kennedy delivered his ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’ speech in West Berlin, framing the Wall as an offence against humanity but the city as proof of Western resolve.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Navigation Acts of the 1660s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Act of 1660 required goods carried to or from English colonies to travel in ships built and owned in England or its colonies, with English masters and three-quarters English crews.
• The Act of 1660 listed ‘enumerated’ goods such as sugar, tobacco and cotton that could only be sent to England, even if their final market was elsewhere in Europe.
• The Staple Act of 1663 required European goods bound for the colonies to first be landed in an English port and pay duties before being re-exported.
• Their main target was Dutch shipping, which by 1660 carried more freight than every other European nation combined.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Dutch raid on the Medway in June 1667.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Admiral Michiel de Ruyter led the Dutch fleet up the river Medway, broke the protective chain across the river at Chatham and burned much of the English fleet at anchor.
