• The English flagship ‘Royal Charles’ was captured and towed back to the Netherlands as a trophy.
• It was the worst defeat in English naval history and ended the Second Dutch War with a heavy English humiliation.
• It led to the impeachment and exile of Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, who was made the public scapegoat for the disaster.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Navigation Acts changed English trade and shipping.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They captured colonial freight business from Dutch shippers, forcing it into English bottoms and accelerating the growth of the English merchant fleet through the 1670s and 1680s.
• They concentrated re-export trade in London and other English ports, where European goods bound for the colonies had to be landed and pay duties.
• They produced strong customs revenues from sugar, tobacco and cotton landed at English ports, which helped finance the Crown after the Restoration.
• Their enforcement also strained relations with the colonies, especially New England, and produced ongoing smuggling that the Crown would crack down on with new admiralty courts in the 1680s.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Medway raid for Charles II’s government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it ended the Second Dutch War in humiliation, forced the unfavourable Treaty of Breda in July 1667, and destroyed faith in the existing naval administration.
• It led directly to the impeachment of Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, who fled to France in November 1667 — clearing the way for the Cabal ministry.
• It empowered Samuel Pepys to push through reforms of victualling, pay and shipbuilding from 1668 onwards, building the first generation of English ships of the line.
• Significance over time: it ended Dutch dominance of shipping by exposing both navies as evenly matched, and the long-term outcome was a rising English fleet by the 1680s.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Third Dutch War for Charles II’s relationship with Parliament.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Cavalier Parliament refused to vote war taxes unless Charles withdrew the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence; he did so in March 1673.
• Parliament passed the First Test Act in 1673, forcing Sir Thomas Clifford and James, Duke of York from public office and breaking the Cabal.
• Parliament forced Charles to make a separate peace at the Second Treaty of Westminster in 1674, four years before France finished its own war.
• The episode showed that Parliament could use control of taxation to override royal foreign policy — a precedent that would shape the Exclusion Crisis and the 1689 settlement.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘English sea power grew under Charles II because of the law, not because of the navy.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the rise of English sea power between 1660 and 1685? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The Navigation Acts of 1660, 1663 and 1673 captured colonial freight business from the Dutch and gave English shippers a guaranteed market in colonial trade.
• Booming customs revenue from sugar, tobacco and cotton funded the Crown and the Royal Navy without recourse to parliamentary supply, especially after 1681.
• Mercantilist support for chartered companies (East India, Royal African, Hudson’s Bay) extended English maritime reach across three oceans.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Pepys’s reforms of victualling, pay and shipbuilding from 1668 onwards built the first generation of English ships of the line that gave the Royal Navy its later edge.
• The Anglo-Dutch wars themselves — even when lost, as at the Medway — pushed the navy to professionalise tactics, gunnery and dockyard organisation.
• Charles II’s alliance with France in the Third Dutch War, although unpopular, gave England a strategic free hand against the Dutch fleet.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised commentary by CBS Evening News anchor Walter Cronkite, broadcast 27 February 1968.
‘To say that we are mired in stalemate seems the only realistic, yet unsatisfactory, conclusion. To say that we are closer to victory today is to believe, in the face of the evidence, the optimists who have been wrong in the past. It is increasingly clear to this reporter that the only rational way out then will be to negotiate.’

Source A suggests that Cronkite no longer believed official claims that the war was being won. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He calls stalemate ‘the only realistic, yet unsatisfactory, conclusion’.
• He says believing in victory means believing ‘the optimists who have been wrong in the past’.
• He concludes that ‘the only rational way out’ is to negotiate.
Contextual knowledge: Cronkite broadcast this on 27 February 1968, a month after Tet; on 31 March Johnson announced a partial bombing halt, peace talks and his own withdrawal from the race.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a Military Assistance Command Vietnam (MACV) press briefing in Saigon, 1 February 1968.
‘The enemy attacks of last night will turn out to be his last desperate effort. He has thrown his reserves against well-defended targets. ARVN units have responded vigorously. We expect to see significant Vietcong losses in the coming hours.’

Source C: An extract from a North Vietnamese Army officer’s after-action report on the Tet Offensive, written in March 1968 and released to historians by Hanoi in the 1990s.
‘Our forces in many provinces took heavy losses and could not be replaced. The expected popular uprising did not occur. Yet the political effect in the United States has been greater than we hoped. The Americans no longer believe their own generals.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of the Tet Offensive. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: predicts a desperate enemy effort and significant Vietcong losses. Provenance: an MACV briefing on the day of the offensive itself, intended to reassure the press — useful for showing how the US military framed Tet at the moment, but written without knowing the strategic outcome. Own knowledge: 84,000 enemy troops attacked more than 100 targets; the Vietcong did indeed take catastrophic losses (40,000–50,000) but the strategic effect was the opposite of what MACV expected.
Source C — Content: concedes military disaster but identifies the political victory in the US. Provenance: a Hanoi after-action report by an NVA officer, intended for internal use, only released decades later — credible on losses, because an internal report had to be honest to be of any use. Own knowledge: Cronkite’s 27 February report, Johnson’s 31 March withdrawal and Westmoreland’s reassignment all confirm the political effect.
Judgement: B is useful for the immediate American framing but unreliable on outcome; C is highly useful as a candid assessment of why a tactical defeat became a strategic victory.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a press dispatch by an Associated Press correspondent reporting from Saigon, 1 February 1968.
‘Vietcong commandos blasted into the US Embassy compound this morning and held part of the grounds for six hours before being killed. The flag of the United States flew over a battlefield inside the supposedly secure South Vietnamese capital. Millions of Americans watched the footage on the evening news.’

Source D suggests that Tet shook American confidence because it struck places assumed to be safe. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Vietcong commandos ‘blasted into the US Embassy compound’ in the capital itself.
• They held part of the grounds for six hours before being killed.
• The footage reached millions of Americans on the evening news.
Contextual knowledge: The embassy attack was one of more than 100 targets hit on 30–31 January 1968, weeks after Westmoreland had told Congress the enemy was broken.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Tet Offensive was the turning point of the Vietnam War.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• On 31 March 1968 Johnson announced a partial bombing halt, peace talks and his decision not to seek re-election.
• Westmoreland’s request for 200,000 more troops was refused and he was reassigned in June 1968.
• The gap between official optimism and televised reality opened the credibility gap; Cronkite called the war a stalemate on 27 February 1968.
• The Democratic Party split and Nixon won the November 1968 election on a promise to end the war.
Disagree:
• Militarily Tet was a heavy defeat for the communists: 40,000 to 50,000 dead and the southern insurgency crippled.
• The hoped-for popular uprising in the South never happened.
• Opposition at home was already growing from 1965, and polls had turned by October 1967.
• The war ran for seven more years, so Tet decided nothing on the ground.
Judgement: Tet was decisive politically rather than militarily: it ended the Johnson presidency and made eventual US withdrawal the only viable policy.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Tet Offensive developed from the start of the attacks on 30 January 1968 to Johnson’s announcement on 31 March 1968.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details.
Secure: Three or more linked events; causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 30–31 January 1968: 84,000 Vietcong and NVA troops attacked more than 100 cities and bases during the Tet ceasefire.
• 31 January 1968: Vietcong commandos breached the US Embassy compound in Saigon, broadcast on US television.
• 31 January – 24 February 1968: battle of Hue saw 25 days of urban combat and the discovery of mass graves of Vietnamese civilians.
• Late February 1968: Vietcong driven back across South Vietnam at a cost of 40,000–50,000 dead.
• 27 February 1968: Walter Cronkite told CBS viewers the war was ‘mired in stalemate’.
• March 1968: Westmoreland requested 200,000 more troops; Johnson rejected the request.
• 31 March 1968: Johnson announced a partial bombing halt, peace talks and his decision not to seek re-election.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source G.

Source G: An extract from a New York Times editorial, 5 February 1968.
‘For three years the Administration has assured us that the Vietcong were broken, that the war was being won, that the end was in sight. Last week, in the streets of Saigon and Hue, those assurances were burned along with the cities. The American public deserves an honest accounting.’

Source G suggests that the newspaper no longer trusted official statements about the war. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source G and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• It says the administration has given assurances ‘for three years’ that the Vietcong were broken.
• Those assurances ‘were burned along with the cities’ of Saigon and Hue.
• It demands ‘an honest accounting’ for the American public.
Contextual knowledge: The editorial appeared five days after Tet began; the gap between official claims and televised reality became known as the credibility gap.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William Wallace and Andrew Murray waited until roughly half the English army had crossed the narrow wooden bridge before charging.
• The English vanguard was cut off when the bridge collapsed under the panicked retreat.
• As many as 5,000 English soldiers were killed or drowned in the Forth.
• The victory led to Wallace being knighted and named ‘Guardian of Scotland’ in March 1298.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Battle of Falkirk (1298) for the Anglo-Scottish war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The destruction of the schiltrons by massed Welsh and Cheshire longbowmen caused the longbow to emerge as Edward’s decisive battlefield weapon.
• Wallace’s defeat caused him to resign the Guardianship and turn to a guerrilla campaign and diplomatic work in France.
• Falkirk caused a tactical lesson that shaped English warfare for 150 years — armoured cavalry combined with massed archers, used at Crécy and Agincourt.
• The battle did not end Scottish resistance — instead it caused a longer war of small engagements and changing leadership, leaving Scotland unconquered when Edward died.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Multiple effects developed with precise figures and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about William Wallace for the First War of Scottish Independence.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, his victory at Stirling Bridge in September 1297 humiliated Surrey’s army and broke Edward’s claim to a finished conquest.
• His public title of ‘Guardian of Scotland’ gave Scottish resistance a legitimate political voice between 1297 and 1298.
• His brutal execution in August 1305 — tried with a laurel crown, hanged, drawn and quartered — turned him into a Scottish national martyr at the moment Edward intended to erase him.
• Significance over time: Wallace became a long-term symbol of Scottish resistance, celebrated for centuries afterwards in poetry, history and (in the modern period) film.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Edward I’s response to Robert Bruce’s coronation in 1306.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Three of Bruce’s brothers were captured, tried and executed by hanging, drawing and quartering.
• Bruce’s sister Mary and the Countess of Buchan, who had crowned him, were hung in iron cages outside Roxburgh and Berwick castles.
• Aymer de Valence was sent north as commander and defeated Bruce at the Battle of Methven on 19 June 1306.
• Edward had himself carried north on a litter despite his serious illness, intending to crush the rebellion in person.

[8 marks]
Mastering: A clear sequence of developments, each step linked to the next, with precise detail.
Secure: An ordered account of two or three developments with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described but the order or the links between them are unclear.
Emerging: Simple statements with little order or supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Edward I’s death at Burgh-by-Sands (1307) for the Anglo-Scottish war.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Edward had been carried north on a litter to lead the renewed war in person; his death on 7 July 1307 left the campaign without its most committed leader.
• His son and heir, Edward II, abandoned the march and turned south — giving Robert Bruce the breathing room he needed to rebuild a Scottish army.
• The 1296 conquest was now visibly unfinished: an anointed king of Scots in arms, no decisive English presence north of the Forth.
• Significance over time: within seven years of Edward’s death the Scots crushed Edward II’s army at Bannockburn (1314), and the ‘Hammer of the Scots’ tomb inscription was added long afterwards as the verdict it had failed to earn in life.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: ‘Edward I deserved the title “Hammer of the Scots”.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support of the title:
• Edward stormed and sacked Berwick in 1296 with thousands of dead and crushed the Scottish army at Dunbar within a month, deposing John Balliol the same year.
• At Falkirk in 1298 he destroyed Wallace’s schiltrons with massed longbow fire, breaking organised Scottish resistance for years.
• His commander Aymer de Valence defeated Robert Bruce at Methven (1306), forcing Bruce into hiding.
• His punishments — hanging Bruce’s brothers, caging the women who crowned him, executing Wallace as a traitor — were brutal expressions of royal power.

Arguments against the title:
• The label is a tomb inscription added long after Edward’s death, possibly in the sixteenth century, not a contemporary verdict.
• At his death in July 1307 Robert Bruce was an anointed king of Scots raising armies in the Highlands.
• The brutality at Berwick, Wallace’s execution and the caging of Bruce’s female allies created the very martyrs that fuelled the Scottish cause.
• Within seven years of Edward’s death his son was crushed at Bannockburn (1314); the ‘hammering’ clearly did not stick.

A strong response weighs the genuine victories against the unfinished nature of the conquest and reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that Edward earned the title in his own court but not from history.

[16 marks]
Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides and a supported judgement.
Developing: Description of more than one factor with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described with no real judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Statement to the United Nations Security Council by Hans Blix, Executive Chairman of UNMOVIC, on 27 January 2003.
‘Iraq appears not to have come to a genuine acceptance — not even today — of the disarmament that was demanded of it… However, the inspections have not found such weapons.’
Source B: Foreword by the Prime Minister Tony Blair to the British government dossier ‘Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction’, September 2002.
‘What I believe the assessed intelligence has established beyond doubt is that Saddam has continued to produce chemical and biological weapons, that he continues in his efforts to develop nuclear weapons, and that he has been able to extend the range of his ballistic missile programme.’

Study Sources A and B. How useful are Sources A and B to an historian studying the case made for war against Iraq in 2002–03? Explain your answer using Sources A and B and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Integrates content, provenance and own contextual knowledge for both sources to reach a substantiated judgement on usefulness.
Secure: Clear use of all three for both sources with some judgement.
Developing: Two of the three treated.
Emerging: Description of the sources without evaluation.

Indicative content:
• Content of Source A: an inspector with direct access reports both limited Iraqi cooperation and, crucially, that no weapons had been found.
• Provenance of Source A: Blix was reporting formally to the Security Council in January 2003, so he had to be precise; but inspections were incomplete, and he could not say that nothing existed.
• Content of Source B: Blair states the British case at its strongest, claiming continued production of chemical and biological weapons and an extended missile range.
• Provenance of Source B: a foreword to a public dossier is a case-making document by a leader seeking support, which is why the Chilcot Inquiry judged the threat presented with a certainty that was not justified.
• Own knowledge: UNMOVIC carried out around 700 inspections at over 500 sites; ElBaradei told the Council in March 2003 that the Niger documents were forgeries; the Iraq Survey Group later found the programmes had ended in the 1990s.
• Judgement: both are useful because they are opposite kinds of evidence — an operational report and a political case — and the gap between them is itself the historian’s finding.

practice_questions.text:
Source C: Photograph of around one million people at a Stop the War Coalition rally in central London on 15 February 2003, on the eve of the Iraq War. Banners read ‘Not in My Name’ and ‘Listen to the Inspectors’.

Study Source C. Source C suggests that opposition to the war in Britain was broad and mainstream. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source C and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the photograph without inference.

Indicative content:
• The scale of the crowd — described as around one million on Hyde Park Corner alone — implies that opposition to the war was not confined to the political left or to traditional protest groups; it was a mainstream public position.
• The slogan ‘Listen to the Inspectors’ implies that the protesters did not reject the disarmament process itself, but believed the UN inspections under Blix should be allowed to run their course before military action was authorised.
• ‘Not in My Name’ implies a sense of personal political identity being tied to opposition: protesters are distinguishing themselves from a government acting on their behalf rather than rejecting government authority altogether.
• The choice of Hyde Park as a venue, on a single coordinated day with rallies in 600 cities worldwide, suggests a globally networked protest movement using the internet and mass media — features absent in earlier anti-war movements.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how United Nations diplomacy on Iraq developed between November 2002 and March 2003.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence, with precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• 8 November 2002: UN Resolution 1441 passed unanimously, giving Iraq a final opportunity to comply and bringing UNMOVIC inspectors back under Hans Blix.
• November–December 2002: inspectors returned; Iraq submitted a 12,000-page declaration that the United States said was incomplete.
• 27 January 2003: Blix reported limited cooperation but no weapons found, language harder than American officials had hoped for.
• 5 February 2003: Colin Powell put the American intelligence case to the Security Council.
• 7 March 2003: Blix reported tangible progress and asked for more time, while ElBaradei told the Council that the documents behind the Niger uranium claim were forgeries.
• Mid-March 2003: with France signalling a veto, the United States and United Kingdom abandoned the second resolution; the invasion began on 20 March.

practice_questions.text: ‘United Nations Resolution 1441 made the invasion of Iraq more likely rather than less.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: by setting a test of a final opportunity to comply, 1441 created a deadline that the United States could declare Iraq had failed.
• Agree: the 12,000-page Iraqi declaration was immediately called incomplete, which was treated as the material breach the resolution warned of.
• Agree: unanimous passage let Washington and London argue that authority for force already existed, so no second resolution was strictly needed.
• Disagree: 1441 brought inspectors back after four years, and by March 2003 Blix was reporting tangible progress and asking for more time.
• Disagree: France, Russia and China read the resolution as requiring a further decision by the Council, so it constrained rather than licensed force.
• Disagree: the decision for war rested on the Bush administration’s judgement, made before 1441, that containment had failed.
• Judgement: 1441 gave the invasion its legal argument, but the political decision had already been taken; the resolution supplied the ground, not the reason.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the British government made its public case for war against Iraq between September 2002 and March 2003.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence, with precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• September 2002: the government published the dossier ‘Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction’, with a foreword by Blair claiming the programme was active, detailed and growing.
• The dossier repeated four times the claim that Iraqi forces could deploy chemical or biological weapons within 45 minutes of an order.
• Late 2002: ministers argued that British support depended on Iraqi non-cooperation, and backed the UN route through Resolution 1441.
• January–February 2003: a second briefing, later called the ‘dodgy dossier’, was published; part of it had been copied from a postgraduate thesis available online.
• 15 February 2003: around a million people marched in London, and ministers answered that the UN process had been exhausted.
• 18 March 2003: the Commons voted 412 to 149 for military action, with 139 Labour MPs rebelling.

practice_questions.text: ‘The international response to Iraq in 2002–03 was very different from the response in 1990–91.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: in 1990 Resolution 678 authorised force; in 2003 no second resolution was secured and the coalition assembled outside UN authorisation.
• Agree: in 1990 Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Syria joined the coalition; in 2003 most Arab states refused to host the operation and Turkey’s parliament refused the use of its territory.
• Agree: in 1991 European opinion broadly accepted the war; on 15 February 2003 between six and ten million people marched in over 600 cities.
• Disagree: both crises began with unanimous Security Council resolutions condemning Iraqi behaviour, in 1990 and again in November 2002.
• Disagree: in both, a US-led coalition with strong British support did the fighting, and the two wars had many of the same commanders and weapons.
• Disagree: in both, Arab governments were more supportive than their populations.
• Judgement: the legal basis and the breadth of support were very different, because in 1990 Iraq had invaded a neighbour while in 2003 the case rested on contested claims about weapons.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Liberal reforms 1906–11 and the post-1948 welfare state were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: the Liberal reforms were contributory and means-tested (worker, employer and state pay in); the 1948 NHS was universal and tax-funded.
• Difference: the 1911 National Insurance Act covered only the worker; the post-1948 system covered the whole family.
• Similarity: both expanded the role of the state in health and welfare and were responses to social investigation (Booth, Rowntree, Beveridge).
• Similarity: both reforms followed major wars (Boer War, World War Two) that exposed the link between poverty and national fitness.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Booth and Rowntree for the development of public health and welfare in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Booth’s 1889–1903 survey found 30.7% of Londoners below the poverty line; Rowntree’s 1901 York study found 28%.
• At the time: Rowntree’s ‘primary’ vs ‘secondary’ poverty distinction undermined moral explanations of poverty.
• Over time: their evidence directly informed Liberal reforms 1906–11 and was cited by Beveridge in 1942.
• Over time: their methods (statistical surveys, line-by-line investigation) became the template for modern social research.
• Limitation: their findings were not enough on their own — the Boer War shock and the 1906 Liberal landslide were also needed for legislation.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and statistics.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Seebohm Rowntree’s Poverty: A Study of Town Life, published in 1901. His investigators visited almost every working-class household in York. He worked out the smallest income a family needed for food, rent and clothing, and found that 28% of the city lived below that line.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying poverty in Britain around 1900?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: the figure of 28% turned poverty from an opinion into a measurement.
• Content: his split between ‘primary’ poverty and ‘secondary’ poverty destroyed the argument that the poor were simply feckless.
• Provenance: a Quaker manufacturer paying for a house-to-house survey of his own city; he had a reforming purpose, but his method was set out so that others could check it.
• Contextual knowledge: Booth had found 30.7% below the line in London (1889-1903), and Boer War recruiting rejected about 40% of volunteers as unfit.
• Limitations: one city in one year, and York was not an industrial giant like Manchester; where the poverty line is drawn is itself a judgement.
• Judgement: strong evidence of the scale of poverty and of the new statistical method, weaker as a picture of Britain as a whole.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Has war been the main factor in driving change in British public health? Explain your answer with reference to war and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh war against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of war as the main factor:
• Boer War recruit rejections (40% unfit) directly fed Liberal reforms 1906–11 and the school meals/medical inspections agenda.
• First World War accelerated antiseptic surgery, transfusion (Landsteiner 1901), X-rays (Röntgen 1895), plastic surgery (Gillies, Sidcup).
• Second World War: evacuation exposed urban poverty to rural Britain, the Emergency Medical Service nationalised hospitals temporarily, and rationing improved working-class diet — all paving the way for the 1948 NHS.

Weighed against communication:
• Booth, Rowntree, the 1942 Beveridge Report and Mayhew’s journalism each translated war and poverty into political pressure.

Weighed against government:
• The 1911 National Insurance Act, the 1948 NHS and the 1875 Public Health Act could only be delivered by Parliament.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Lloyd George, Churchill, Beveridge, Bevan, Nightingale, Lister and Bazalgette each shaped specific reforms.

Judgement: war repeatedly forced action by exposing the gap between Britain’s aspirations and its workforce’s health, but war alone did not legislate — communication built the case and government delivered the law. Across the medieval and early modern periods war did much less for public health, suggesting war becomes a stronger factor only when combined with mass democracy and statistical thinking.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes wars only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of David Lloyd George for the development of welfare in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: as Chancellor he introduced the Old Age Pensions Act 1908 (5 shillings a week for single people over 70).
• At the time: designed and led the National Insurance Act 1911, the first nationwide health and unemployment insurance.
• At the time: his 1909 People’s Budget triggered the Lords crisis and the 1911 Parliament Act, reshaping the British constitution.
• Over time: National Insurance contributions remained a feature of the British welfare system through Beveridge and beyond.
• Limitation: his scheme covered the worker, not the family, and excluded most women and the elderly — significance is partial.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and acts.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Boer War for public health policy in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: recruiting officers rejected about 40% of volunteers as unfit, and over 60% in Manchester.
• At the time: the 1903 Inter-Departmental Committee on Physical Deterioration tied that unfitness to undernourishment in childhood.
• At the time: it turned welfare from a moral question into a security question — Britain needed a fit population to hold an empire.
• Over time: it pushed the Liberals towards child-focused reform, with free school meals in 1906 and school medical inspections in 1907.
• Over time: it set the pattern repeated after both world wars, where war exposed the health of the population and forced government to act.
• Limitation: Booth and Rowntree’s evidence and the 1906 landslide were needed as well; war on its own legislated nothing.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Irish migration to Britain in the 1840s and Jewish migration to Britain after 1881 were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Irish migration was pushed by economic collapse and famine; Jewish migration was pushed by religious persecution and pogroms in the Russian Empire.
• Difference: there was no legal restriction on Irish entry to Britain (it was internal Union movement); the Jewish arrivals provoked the 1905 Aliens Act, the first peacetime British immigration restriction.
• Similarity: both groups concentrated in industrial cities — Liverpool and Manchester for the Irish, the East End of London and Leeds for the Jewish migrants.
• Similarity: both faced hostile stereotyping in the British press — the Punch ‘Paddy and the pig’ cartoons for the Irish, the British Brothers League agitation for the Jewish arrivals.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named institutions.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which transportation of British convicts to Australia and Indian indentured migration to East Africa were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: transportation was a judicial punishment imposed by British courts on around 162,000 convicts (1788-1868); Indian indenture was a contract system used to recruit around 1.5 million workers across the empire (1834-1920).
• Difference: transportees had no legal right of return; indentured workers had a contract that in theory entitled them to a passage home after three to five years.
• Similarity: both moved labour around the empire under conditions of physical control — convict ships, indentured ships and plantation barracks shared many features.
• Similarity: both produced lasting communities at the destination: around 20% of modern Australians descend from convicts; East African Asian communities trace back to the Uganda Railway and indentured plantation labour.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and numbers.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Irish migration to Britain in the 19th century.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: around one million people left Ireland during and after the 1845-49 Great Famine; those who stayed in Britain transformed Liverpool, Manchester, Glasgow, London and Cardiff.
• At the time: by 1851 around 23% of Liverpool’s population was Irish-born; the 1850 restoration of the Catholic hierarchy in England responded to this presence.
• Over time: Irish migration shaped Liberal politics throughout the 19th century, with Gladstone’s Home Rule campaigns of 1886 and 1893 a direct response to the Irish vote in Britain.
• Over time: Irish-Catholic communities created lasting institutions — parishes, GAA clubs, Catholic schools — that defined British urban culture into the 20th century.
• Over time: the famine memory shaped Anglo-Irish relations through partition (1921), the Troubles and the modern republic.
• Limitation: integration over generations means present-day Irish-British identity is hard to track; the demographic story is clearer than the cultural one.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1905 Aliens Act for British attitudes towards immigration.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: first peacetime restriction on immigration to Britain; targeted ‘undesirable’ aliens, primarily the Jewish refugees from the Russian Empire arriving since 1881.
• At the time: created an immigration officer system at the ports and an appeals process for those refused entry.
• At the time: gave political legitimacy to anti-immigration arguments, with figures like William Evans-Gordon and the British Brothers League shaping the debate.
• Over time: established the principle that the British state could choose whom to admit — a precedent for the 1914 Aliens Restriction Act, the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act and modern immigration law.
• Over time: Jewish refugees from the 1930s, especially those fleeing Nazi Germany, faced barriers shaped in part by 1905 procedures and culture.
• Limitation: the 1905 Act admitted only around 1,000 refusals a year initially; its symbolic and legal importance was greater than its immediate numerical impact.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Economic resources were the main factor in migration to, from and within the British Empire between 1788 and 1914.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to economic resources and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic resources (in support): the end of slavery in 1833 created a plantation labour crisis that indenture filled, moving around 1.5 million Indians and 200,000 Chinese between 1834 and 1920.
• Economic resources (in support): famine and poverty pushed the Irish to Liverpool, Manchester and Glasgow, and industry pulled British workers from countryside to city.
• Government: transportation was state punishment, sending around 162,000 convicts to Australia between 1788 and 1868, and the 1905 Aliens Act was the first peacetime restriction on entry to Britain.
• Religion: pogroms in the Russian Empire after 1881 drove around 150,000 Jewish refugees to Britain — a push that had nothing to do with wages.
• Ideas: imperial confidence made settlement in Canada, Australia and Africa look like a duty as well as an opportunity.
• Judgement: economic resources moved the largest numbers, but government decided who was forced to move and who was allowed in, and religion explains the refugee flows economics cannot.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the experience of Jewish migrants to Britain after 1881 was similar to or different from the earlier Huguenot experience after 1685.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Huguenots were welcomed, and Parliament’s 1709 act for foreign Protestants opened a route to naturalisation; Jewish migrants were eventually restricted by the 1905 Aliens Act.
• Difference: Huguenots were Protestant, sharing the religion of the English political class; Jewish migrants faced a popular and political antisemitism that overlapped with anti-foreign feeling.
• Similarity: both were religious refugees from continental persecution — Huguenots from Louis XIV’s Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685), Jews from the Russian pogroms after 1881.
• Similarity: both built lasting communities and institutions in specific neighbourhoods — Huguenot Spitalfields silk weaving, Jewish East End sweated trades, synagogues and the Jewish Chronicle (1841).

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named institutions.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1915 popular history written by a Southern Democrat):
‘The carpetbaggers were the great evil of the post-war South. They came down with empty pockets and left with full ones, leaving behind crushing taxes, broken state finances and the secret society of the Klan, which honourable Southerners formed in self-defence.’

Interpretation B (from a 1989 academic study of Reconstruction):
‘The carpetbagger stereotype is myth. Most Northerners who moved South were teachers, ministers, professionals and Union veterans. The Ku Klux Klan was founded in 1866 by Confederate veterans, not by carpetbaggers, and existed to attack the very people the Southern Democrat label sought to discredit.’

How convincing is Interpretation B? Use Interpretations A and B and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s argument; engages with the specific claims (myth, professional carpetbaggers, Klan founded by Confederate veterans); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with reference to A; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the labels without engaging with B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Foner and Powell’s research shows around 50,000 Northerners moved South; many were teachers, lawyers and Union veterans.
• The Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, by six Confederate veterans in 1866; Nathan Bedford Forrest, a Confederate general, became its first Grand Wizard.
• Klan violence targeted carpetbaggers, scalawags and Black Republicans — the Klan attacked carpetbaggers, it did not include them.
• A minority of carpetbaggers were corrupt, but corruption existed across all post-war state governments, North and South.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• Some Reconstruction state governments did experience high taxes and corruption (Louisiana, South Carolina).
• A few high-profile carpetbagger administrators became personally wealthy — the stereotype had a kernel of evidence.
• The pre-1960s historiography that A reflects was the dominant US view for half a century.

Judgement: B is the stronger interpretation in light of modern evidence; a top-band answer notes A reflects the post-1877 narrative built to discredit Reconstruction.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B again.

Interpretation A: 1915 popular history written by a Southern Democrat.
Interpretation B: 1989 academic study of Reconstruction.

Why might Interpretations A and B have different views of carpetbaggers? Use both interpretations and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in author purpose, evidence available, time of writing or audience — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons describe what each interpretation says.

Indicative content:
• Different author standpoints: A is written by a Southern Democrat in 1915 with a partisan stake in the Reconstruction story; B is by an academic in 1989 with no comparable political loyalty.
• Different time of writing: A sits inside the ‘Lost Cause’ tradition dominant in early-20th-century Southern history; B follows the post-1960s revisionist turn led by Foner.
• Different evidence available: B can draw on local archives, military records and Bureau correspondence opened up later; A relies heavily on contemporary Southern Democrat polemic.
• Different audiences: A addresses a popular Southern readership comfortable with the ‘tragic era’ framing; B writes for an academic readership expecting evidence-led scholarship.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 2003 study of US violence and law):
‘The Ku Klux Klan was destroyed by federal action between 1870 and 1872. The Enforcement Acts gave Grant the tools, the South Carolina prosecutions of 1871 used them, and within two years the original Klan had ceased to exist as a coherent national organisation. The story of how white-supremacist violence then continued belongs to the White Leagues, the Red Shirts and the Klan’s second incarnation in 1915.’

How convincing is Interpretation C? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s ‘destroyed by federal action’ thesis; engages with specific claims (Enforcement Acts, South Carolina prosecutions, successor groups); supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the Klan without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• The 1870 and 1871 Enforcement Acts criminalised interference with Black voting rights and authorised federal troops.
• Grant used the Klan Act in nine South Carolina counties in 1871; hundreds of Klansmen were prosecuted.
• The original Klan was effectively dispersed by 1872.
• White-supremacist violence reorganised under different names — White Leagues, Red Shirts — rather than continuing as the Klan.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• ‘Destroyed’ overstates — the rituals, hoods and ideology survived locally.
• Federal effort was uneven by region; rural Mississippi saw fewer prosecutions.
• White-supremacist violence in real continuity with the Klan continued throughout the 1870s under the new labels.
• The Klan’s 1915 revival drew on uninterrupted Southern memory.

Judgement: C captures a real federal achievement — the original Klan was broken — but a top-band answer notes that the underlying violence was not destroyed, only relabelled.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C again.

Interpretation C: a 2003 study of US violence and law.
Interpretation D (from a 1992 social history of African Americans in the South):
‘The Klan was never really destroyed in 1872. The men, the methods and the message all reappeared in the White Leagues and the Red Shirts within months. To call this a victory for federal law is to mistake a name change for a defeat.’

Why might Interpretations C and D have different views of how the Klan ended? Use both interpretations and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in author standpoint, evidence emphasis, audience or time of writing.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons describe interpretations.

Indicative content:
• Different evidence emphasis: C focuses on federal-law records and prosecutions; D on Black community memory and oral histories of continued terror.
• Different author standpoints: C is institutional/legal history; D is bottom-up social history of African American experience.
• Different audiences: C writes for a legal-history readership; D for a community-history readership.
• Different framings of success: C measures by organisational defeat of the Klan as a label; D by lived experience of ongoing white-supremacist violence.

practice_questions.text:
Which was the more important reason Reconstruction ended?

• The Compromise of 1877
• Northern political retreat after 1873

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Compromise against other factors and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (carpetbagger, scalawag, Redeemer, Enforcement Acts, Slaughter-House Cases).
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of multiple causes with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of 1877 without comparing it with the other bullet.

Indicative content:
The Compromise of 1877:
• The Compromise withdrew the last federal troops from the South in 1877.
• Without federal protection, Reconstruction state governments could not survive against organised intimidation.
• Hayes ratified what was already being negotiated locally between Northern and Southern Republicans.

Northern political retreat after 1873:
• 1873 economic depression turned Northern voters against further Southern intervention.
• Slaughter-House Cases (1873) narrowed the 14th Amendment’s reach.
• White-supremacist violence (Klan, White Leagues, Red Shirts) had already retaken most of the South before 1877.
• Internal Republican fatigue with Southern questions; Grant’s administration was distracted by scandal.
• Most Southern states had been ‘redeemed’ before the Compromise; 1877 ratified an existing reality.

Judgement: the Compromise of 1877 was the formal endpoint, but the deeper causes — depression, Court rulings, violence and political fatigue — had hollowed out Reconstruction first; a top-band answer reaches a clear verdict on cause vs symptom.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1996 study of US federalism):
‘The end of Reconstruction was not really about troops or terror at all. It was about the federal-state balance. The Slaughter-House Cases of 1873 narrowed the 14th Amendment, the United States v. Cruikshank decision in 1876 stripped its enforcement powers, and by 1877 the constitutional retreat was already complete. The withdrawal of soldiers was the symptom, not the cause.’

How convincing is Interpretation E? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s ‘federal-state balance’ thesis; engages with specific claims (Slaughter-House, Cruikshank, retreat already complete); supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with E’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• Slaughter-House Cases (1873) narrowed the 14th Amendment’s Privileges and Immunities Clause.
• United States v. Cruikshank (1876) ruled that the federal government could not prosecute private actors for civil-rights violations.
• These rulings limited federal enforcement BEFORE the 1877 troop withdrawal.
• Most Southern states were ‘redeemed’ by 1875 — legal retreat preceded military retreat.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• Federal troops had still been doing real protective work in South Carolina and Louisiana up to 1877.
• Klan violence required physical, not just legal, federal response.
• The Compromise of 1877 was followed by a sharp deterioration in Black voting rights, suggesting troops had mattered.
• Violence and law worked together; separating them gives a partial picture.

Judgement: E correctly draws attention to the constitutional retreat, but a top-band answer notes that the troop withdrawal mattered as a guarantee in its own right.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1957 magazine feature celebrating Levittown as the model of American family life) and Interpretation B (a 1962 study by sociologist Michael Harrington on poverty hidden by suburban prosperity). What is the main difference between these views about post-war America?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents post-war America as a uniformly prosperous society of homeowners, consumer goods and family life in new suburbs.
• Interpretation B presents post-war America as a divided society in which around 40 million people lived in poverty hidden by middle-class affluence.
• Main difference: A frames the era as universal prosperity; B frames it as selective prosperity that left a third of the country behind.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1957 magazine feature celebrating Levittown) and Interpretation B (a 1962 study by Michael Harrington on hidden poverty) give different views about post-war America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the magazine aimed to sell suburban lifestyles to middle-class advertisers; the study aimed to push the federal government towards anti-poverty action.
• They use different evidence — the feature focuses on white suburban families with new washing machines; the study focuses on Appalachian miners, rural black tenants, the urban poor and elderly Americans.
• They were produced at different points and with different concerns — one at the height of the Eisenhower consensus, one as the Kennedy and Johnson administrations were preparing the War on Poverty.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘The 1944 GI Bill was the most important cause of post-war prosperity.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the causes of post-war American prosperity?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the GI Bill funded around 7.8 million veterans through college or training and 4.3 million home purchases — building a mass middle class with federal money.
• Convincing because GI mortgages with no down payment underwrote the suburban housing boom: 13 million new homes built between 1948 and 1958.
• Less convincing because mass car ownership (60 million cars by 1960), the 1956 Interstate Highways Act and consumer credit (Diners Club 1950, BankAmericard 1958) also drove the boom.
• Less convincing because federal mortgage insurance through the FHA was as decisive as the GI Bill itself, and structurally older.
• Less convincing because cheap oil, post-war global American economic dominance and pent-up consumer demand from the rationing years also mattered.
• Less convincing because the GI Bill’s benefits were largely denied to black veterans in practice through redlining and segregated colleges — so it built prosperity for white families more than ‘American’ prosperity.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing as a contributory cause of the white middle-class boom; overstated as the single most important cause.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the growth of the suburbs on American society between 1945 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Created a mass middle class — 13 million new homes were built between 1948 and 1958 and around a third of Americans lived in suburbs by 1960; the GI Bill and FHA mortgages underwrote the move.
• Reshaped urban geography — cities lost middle-class taxpayers and inner-city neighbourhoods decayed; the 1956 Interstate Highways Act made commuting from suburbs into work feasible.
• Defined a domestic ideal that pushed women back into the home — magazines and television sitcoms presented suburbs as places of stay-at-home mothers and breadwinner fathers, even as around 19 million women were now in paid work.
• Hardened racial segregation — redlining by the FHA and restrictive covenants by builders like William Levitt kept black families out of subsidised suburbs; Levittown had no African-American residents in 1953.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the United States enjoyed such rapid prosperity between 1945 and 1960.
You may consider:
• federal action including the GI Bill and the Interstate Highways Act
• consumer goods, suburbs and television.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• GI Bill (1944): 7.8 million educational beneficiaries; 4.3 million home loans; underwrote a mass middle class.
• Interstate Highways Act (1956): 41,000 miles of motorway, $25 billion budget; tied suburbs to jobs and made shopping malls and drive-ins viable.
• Federal mortgage insurance through the FHA expanded from war to peace and kept down payments low.
• Levittown (1947 onwards): assembly-line housebuilding; $7,990 a home; 17,000 houses by 1951; emulated nationwide; 13 million new homes 1948–58.
• Mass car ownership: 26 million cars (1945) to 60 million (1960); cheap oil at around 25 cents a gallon.
• Consumer credit: Diners Club (1950), BankAmericard (1958), hire purchase for white goods.
• Television: 90% household ownership by 1960; advertising tripled; created a national consumer market.
• Cold War: defence spending sustained employment in Los Angeles, Seattle, Texas and Florida.
• Limits: 22% in poverty by 1960; redlining excluded black families; rural America and inner cities largely missed out.
• Conclusion: prosperity was driven by federal policy as much as private enterprise — the GI Bill and the highways laid the foundations, while consumer goods and suburbs filled them. But the boom was racially structured and geographically uneven, which shaped the politics of the 1960s.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1944 GI Bill.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It gave returning veterans federal money for college tuition or vocational training; around 7.8 million veterans took up the educational benefit.
• It offered low-interest home loans with no down payment for veterans; around 4.3 million homes were bought on GI loans, fuelling the suburban boom.
• It included one year of unemployment pay for returning veterans, easing the transition from military to civilian life.
• It largely failed to deliver these benefits to black veterans in practice because FHA redlining and segregated colleges kept them out of the subsidised suburbs and best universities.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a 1938 private diary entry by Lord Halifax, British Foreign Secretary, on the Anschluss with Austria.
‘The thing was bound to happen sooner or later. We deplore the method. We cannot pretend that the union of seventy million Germans is in itself a thing we should oppose, when the alternative is force we are not prepared to use. The Cabinet is agreed: protest, yes; war, no.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons given by Halifax for Britain’s response to Anschluss.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded reasons with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear reasons, briefly supported.
Developing: One reason clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• German-Austrian union was ‘bound to happen sooner or later’.
• Britain could not justifiably oppose the union of seventy million Germans on principle.
• Britain was not prepared to use force to prevent it.
• Implicit reason: Cabinet judgement that protest, but not war, was the appropriate response.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Anschluss crisis from the Berchtesgaden meeting in February 1938 to the Wehrmacht entry into Austria on 12 March.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 12 February 1938: Schuschnigg summoned to Berchtesgaden; bullied into accepting Seyss-Inquart as Interior Minister with police control, an amnesty for jailed Nazis, and a German veto over Austrian foreign policy.
• 20 February 1938: Anthony Eden resigned as British Foreign Secretary, partly over Chamberlain’s policy toward the dictators.
• 9 March 1938: Schuschnigg announced a plebiscite on Austrian independence within four days.
• 11 March 1938: Hitler demanded cancellation of the plebiscite and Schuschnigg’s resignation; Schuschnigg gave way; Seyss-Inquart took over and invited German troops in.
• 12 March 1938: Wehrmacht crossed into Austria without resistance.
• 14 March 1938: Hitler made a triumphal entry into Vienna; Mussolini accepted the move; Britain and France protested but did not act.
• April 1938: a Nazi-conducted plebiscite recorded an official 99% in favour of union.

practice_questions.text:
‘British appeasement in the 1930s was a rational policy, not a moral failure.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Britain could not fight Germany, Italy and Japan at once, and the Dominions had said they would not back a war over central Europe.
• Rearmament began in earnest only in 1936-37; radar, fighter aircraft and anti-aircraft defences were not ready in 1938, and the Chiefs of Staff warned that war that year risked defeat.
• The USA was isolationist after the 1935 Neutrality Acts and Stalin’s USSR was distrusted across the political class.
• Public memory of 1914-18 left little appetite for another European war.
Challenging the statement:
• The wartime ‘Guilty Men’ case argued that a generation of leaders failed to see the dictators for what they were and failed to arm in time.
• Chamberlain’s confidence in his own dealings with Hitler was a serious misjudgement.
• Czechoslovakia, a treaty ally of France, was abandoned at Munich without being consulted.
• Each concession strengthened Hitler’s position for the next demand.
Judgement: appeasement was a rational response to severe constraints, but the personal misjudgement of Hitler and the abandonment of Czechoslovakia cannot be defended by that case alone.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Mussolini’s position on Austria changed between July 1934 and March 1938.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail. Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage. Indicative content: • July 1934: after Austrian Nazis murdered Dollfuss, Mussolini moved Italian divisions to the Brenner Pass and threatened to intervene; Hitler backed down and disowned the rebels. • April 1935: Italy joined Britain and France at Stresa and pledged to defend Austrian independence. • October 1935 to July 1936: the invasion of Abyssinia and the League sanctions that followed broke Italy away from Britain and France. • October 1936: the Rome-Berlin Axis aligned Mussolini with Hitler. • 1936-38: German and Italian cooperation for Franco in Spain turned that alignment into a working partnership. • March 1938: Mussolini accepted Anschluss without resistance, and Hitler sent his thanks at once, declaring ‘I shall never forget this’.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a 1938 private memorandum by Neville Chamberlain to the Cabinet, on policy toward Germany.
‘We cannot fight Germany, Italy and Japan at the same time. The Empire is overstretched. The Dominions will not back a war over central Europe. Time is on our side if we use it; rearmament is now the priority. War must be the last resort, not the first.’

Using Source B, identify two things Source B shows about British appeasement in 1938.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points drawn precisely from the source, each supported by a short embedded reference and by own knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source, with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; the second vague or a repeat of the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific points.

Indicative content:
• Britain could not fight Germany, Italy and Japan at the same time, and the Empire was overstretched.
• The Dominions would not back a war over central Europe.
• Rearmament was the priority and time was thought to be on Britain’s side.
• Own knowledge: rearmament was the Treasury priority from 1936; the Neutrality Acts limited US support; Stalin’s USSR was distrusted.

practice_questions.text:
‘British appeasement in 1938 was caused above all by military weakness.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Rearmament had begun in earnest only in 1936-37; radar, fighter aircraft and anti-aircraft defences were not yet operational in 1938.
• The Chiefs of Staff warned the Cabinet repeatedly that war in 1938 carried a serious risk of defeat.
• The Royal Navy could not meet threats from Germany in the North Sea, Italy in the Mediterranean and Japan in the Far East at the same time.
Challenging the statement:
• Public memory of 1914-18 left little appetite for war; the Oxford Union had voted in 1933 not to fight for King and Country.
• Allies were thin: the USA was isolationist after the 1935 Neutrality Acts and Stalin’s USSR was distrusted.
• Canada, Australia and South Africa had told London they would not back a European war that looked unjustified.
• Chamberlain sincerely believed Hitler had real grievances that could be settled by negotiation.
Judgement: military weakness set the limits, but the policy also rested on political judgement about what Hitler wanted.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1939 BDM publication celebrating young women's loyalty to the Volksgemeinschaft) and Interpretation B (a 1980s oral history of women born in the 1920s arguing the regime's traditional rhetoric collided with wartime factory work) on Nazi policy towards women. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents Nazi women's policy as a unified ideology — motherhood, sport and racial pride.
• Interpretation B presents the policy as contradictory in practice — women were honoured at home and conscripted into factories.
• Main difference: A frames the policy as ideologically coherent; B frames it as practically contradictory.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1939 BDM publication) and Interpretation B (a 1980s oral history) give different views about Nazi policy towards women.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They had different purposes — the 1939 publication aimed to mobilise consent for Nazi gender ideology; the oral history aimed to collect lived experience.
• They drew on different evidence — the publication used model BDM members; the oral history used elderly women's memories of marriage, factory work and rationing.
• They were produced under different conditions — the 1939 source was censored Nazi propaganda; the oral history had post-war freedom to disagree with regime ideology.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Hitler Youth and BDM successfully turned a generation of Germans into committed Nazis by 1939.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the impact of Nazi youth policy?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because membership rose from 100,000 in 1933 to 8.5 million by 1939; the 1936 Hitler Youth Law and 1939 Youth Service Law made membership effectively universal.
• Convincing because schools were brought into line under Rust, with racial hygiene compulsory and elite Napola/Adolf Hitler Schools trained the future cadre.
• Less convincing because alternative youth groups — Edelweiss Pirates, Swing Youth — existed in working-class and middle-class areas precisely because the HJ was unpopular with some young people.
• Less convincing because oral histories show older boys often resented the HJ as bullying and repetitive; younger children absorbed propaganda more deeply than teenagers.
