• Less convincing because Catholic and Confessional Church families maintained alternative loyalties through Sunday school and family practice.
• Overall judgement: Nazi youth policy reached almost every German child by 1939 but its depth varied with age, region, family background and date — reach was high, conversion uneven.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Nazi religious policy on the German churches between 1933 and 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Concordat of 20 July 1933 bought Catholic neutrality and removed the Centre Party from politics — but its terms were broken within months as Catholic youth groups were attacked.
• The Reich Church was created in 1933 under Ludwig Muller to absorb Protestant churches — but failed to capture all pastors, prompting the breakaway Confessional Church (Barmen Declaration, 1934).
• Resistance grew — Niemoller was imprisoned in 1937; Pope Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (March 1937) condemned Nazi racial ideology and was read from Catholic pulpits.
• Sunday attendance largely held up — the regime infiltrated leadership but did not capture lay believers, demonstrating the limits of Nazi totalitarian reach.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of Nazi social policy and its impact on Germans.
You may consider:
• policies aimed at women and young people
• policies aimed at the Christian churches.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Women: Three Ks slogan; Marriage Loans 1933; Mother's Cross 1938; Lebensborn 1936; exclusion from professions early on; from 1937 push back into factories; RAD extended to women in 1939; 14 million working by 1944.
• Young people: Hitler Youth Law 1936; Youth Service Law 1939; HJ membership 100,000 (1933) to 8.5 million (1939); Napola and Adolf Hitler Schools; rewritten curriculum under Rust; PE up to around 15 per cent of school time; racial hygiene compulsory.
• Churches: Concordat July 1933; Reich Church under Muller; Confessional Church 1934 with Barmen Declaration; Niemoller imprisoned 1937; Bonhoeffer executed 1945; Mit brennender Sorge encyclical 1937.
• Limits: women contradiction between motherhood and factory work; Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth as alternatives; church resistance from Confessional and Catholic clergy.
• Conclusion: Nazi social policy reached every major institution — family, school and pulpit — but its depth was uneven. Indoctrination was strongest with younger children; weakest with older boys, professional women and committed Christians. The regime infiltrated leadership but rarely captured private conviction.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1937 Nazi propaganda film celebrating the Hitler Youth as the future of Germany) and Interpretation B (a Confessional Church sermon arguing the regime was capturing children from their parents) on Nazi youth policy. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the HJ as a national triumph — comradeship, sport and loyalty to Hitler.
• Interpretation B presents the HJ as a threat to family and faith — an attempt to displace Christian upbringing.
• Main difference: A celebrates state youth policy; B sees it as competition with family and church.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Lanfranc’s reform of the English Church between 1070 and 1089.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He replaced almost all Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans or Norman-trained clergy by 1080, leaving Wulfstan of Worcester as the leading English exception kept on for his reputation.
• At the 1075 council of London he tightened Church discipline — banning simony, regulating clerical marriage, reviving synods — and ordered several rural sees to move into towns (Sherborne to Salisbury, Selsey to Chichester, Dorchester to Lincoln).
• He drove a great cathedral-building programme in the Romanesque style imported from Normandy: Canterbury, Lincoln, Old Sarum, St Albans, Worcester and Durham among others were all begun or rebuilt under his archiepiscopate.
• In 1072 at Windsor he secured a written profession from Thomas of Bayeux acknowledging Canterbury’s primacy over York, settling the long-running dispute in Canterbury’s favour.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the deposition of Stigand in 1070 for Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Stigand’s removal at the Easter council at Winchester in 1070 cleared the way for Lanfranc’s appointment, which gave William a loyal reformer in the senior English see.
• It also justified retrospectively William’s 1066 invasion: Stigand’s pluralism (holding Canterbury and Winchester at once) and uncanonical pallium from antipope Benedict X had been used by Pope Alexander II to bless the Norman invasion.
• It opened the door to a wider purge: by 1080 almost all English bishops had been replaced with Normans, transforming the institutional voice of the English Church.
• Importance later: Stigand’s deposition marked the start of a programme of Norman ecclesiastical control that survived through Lanfranc’s death in 1089 and shaped Church appointments for the rest of William’s and his sons’ reigns.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the cathedral building programme in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cathedrals were rebuilt at unprecedented scale — Canterbury (begun 1070), Lincoln (1072), St Albans (1077), Old Sarum (1075), Durham (1093) — far larger than the Anglo-Saxon churches they replaced.
• They used the round-arched Romanesque style imported from Normandy, with thick walls, massive piers and small windows giving the buildings a heavy, fortress-like feel.
• Several cathedrals were relocated from rural sites into nearby towns at the 1075 council of London — Sherborne to Old Sarum, Selsey to Chichester, Dorchester to Lincoln — tying ecclesiastical centres to Norman urban and military networks.
• The buildings doubled as visible symbols of Norman authority — like castles, but for the spiritual rather than the military hierarchy.
• Why it mattered: a Norman bishop in a huge Norman cathedral made the new order visible from miles away, doing for the Church what castles did for the lay lords.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the 1075 council of London for the Norman reform of the English Church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the council revived the practice of regular synods and established a forum for ongoing reform of Church discipline; it banned simony, regulated clerical marriage and tightened canon law.
• It moved several rural Anglo-Saxon sees into towns (Sherborne to Salisbury, Selsey to Chichester, Dorchester to Lincoln) — aligning ecclesiastical centres with Norman urban networks of castles, courts and markets.
• It strengthened the office of archdeacon and clarified the separation of Church courts from secular courts, deepening the Church’s institutional autonomy.
• Importance later: the disciplinary measures of 1075 became the template for English ecclesiastical councils through the 12th century, and the urban relocations are still visible in the modern map of English cathedral cities.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which the leadership of the English Church changed after Lanfranc’s appointment in 1070.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Within a decade almost every English diocese had a Norman or Norman-trained bishop — Lanfranc himself at Canterbury, Thomas of Bayeux at York, Walkelin at Winchester, Remigius at Lincoln — transforming the personnel of the English Church.
• The exceptions are striking: Wulfstan of Worcester was kept on for his reputation, becoming the only Anglo-Saxon bishop still in office at William’s death in 1087 — a deliberate gesture of continuity in an otherwise wholesale replacement.
• Lanfranc and the new Norman bishops drove the cathedral building programme, the 1075 council of London and the Canterbury-vs-York primacy dispute — the institutional Church now spoke with a Norman voice on every major issue.
• Lanfranc also acted as William’s effective regent during the Earls’ Revolt of 1075 while the king was in Normandy — showing how thoroughly the new ecclesiastical leadership was tied into royal politics.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of the Norman Church.

‘Lanfranc’s reform of the Church mattered as much as the land settlement. Bishops sat in the king’s council and in the shire courts, and by 1080 almost all of them were Norman.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the importance of Church reform in establishing Norman rule? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: Church reform mattered as much as the land settlement in establishing Norman rule.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• By 1080 almost every English diocese had a Norman bishop, transforming the institutional voice of the English Church alongside the transformation of the lay landholding class.
• The cathedral building programme — Canterbury, Lincoln, Old Sarum, St Albans, Durham, Worcester — visibly stamped Norman authority on the English landscape, just as castles did.
• The 1075 council of London tightened Church discipline and reorganised dioceses to align with Norman urban centres, paralleling the way the land settlement aligned political power with new tenants-in-chief.
• Lanfranc acted as effective regent during the 1075 Earls’ Revolt, showing that the Church reform underpinned royal authority at moments of crisis as well as in routine government.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The redistribution of land to around 180 tenants-in-chief recorded in Domesday transformed the social structure of England in ways no Church reform alone could match.
• The network of c.500 castles by 1100 was the physical infrastructure of military control — without castles, neither the lay nor the ecclesiastical settlement could have been enforced.
• The Harrying of the North and the wider crushing of revolt 1067–71 broke organised Anglo-Saxon resistance before either reform programme could take effect.
• Inherited Anglo-Saxon government — shires, sheriffs, the geld — provided the day-to-day administrative machinery that the Norman elite, lay and ecclesiastical, used.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: ‘The actions of individuals were the main factor in the achievement of votes for women in 1918.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement. In support of individuals as the main factor: • Millicent Fawcett built the NUWSS into a 50,000-strong organisation that maintained constitutional pressure for two decades. • Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst founded the WSPU in 1903 and kept the cause in the news through arson, window-smashing and hunger strikes. • Emily Davison’s death at the 1913 Derby provided a national martyr that no parliamentary bill could. Weighed against war: • Around 1.7 million women were employed in war work by 1917, undermining the ‘separate spheres’ argument. • The need to redraw the male franchise so that returning soldiers kept the vote forced Parliament to legislate, opening a window for women’s suffrage. Weighed against ideas (equality, democracy): • The trajectory of franchise extension since 1832 made female exclusion increasingly hard to defend in principle. • The arguments of John Stuart Mill (1869) and decades of suffragist pamphleteering had shifted educated opinion long before 1914. Weighed against government: • Asquith’s personal hostility blocked progress before 1914; Lloyd George’s coalition government was needed to pass the 1918 Act. • Force-feeding and the ‘Cat and Mouse Act’ were also acts of government — repression that backfired by generating sympathy. Weighed against communication: • Votes for Women, public lectures, mass meetings and early newsreels carried the cause far beyond active members. Judgement: Top answers argue that the Pankhursts and Fawcett mattered, but militancy had stalled by 1913 and the breakthrough required war work, the franchise problem and a new government to combine. Individuals supplied leadership; the wider factors supplied the opportunity. [16 marks plus 4 SPaG] Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear analysis with examples comparing individuals to other factors; reaches a judgement. Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them. Emerging: Lists factors without comparison or judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the suffragists and the suffragettes were different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in methods: suffragists (NUWSS) used peaceful, constitutional methods such as petitions, lobbying MPs, public meetings and parliamentary bills; suffragettes (WSPU) used militant direct action including window-smashing, arson, and hunger strikes.
• Difference in size: by 1914 the NUWSS had around 50,000 members; the WSPU had around 5,000 active members.
• Difference in leadership: the NUWSS was led by Millicent Fawcett, who maintained a broad coalition; the WSPU was tightly controlled by Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst.
• Difference in attitude to publicity: suffragists sought respectability and cross-bench support; suffragettes deliberately courted controversy to keep the cause in the press.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Pankhursts for the women’s suffrage campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst founded the WSPU in 1903 and gave the campaign a militant strategy that the constitutional NUWSS would not.
• At the time: their willingness to break the law and undergo imprisonment, hunger strike and force-feeding kept the cause in newspapers and Parliament for over a decade.
• Over time: they became national symbols of organised female protest, used by later movements as proof that direct action could shift politics.
• Over time: historians now debate whether their militancy actually slowed the cause after 1912 — a debate they would not be having if the Pankhursts had not made the choices they did.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of who the Pankhursts were without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the NUWSS suffragist campaign for the achievement of votes for women.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Millicent Fawcett brought regional societies together in 1897 and built the NUWSS to around 50,000 members by 1914, roughly ten times the size of the WSPU.
• At the time: the suffragists used petitions, lobbying and parliamentary bills, and built a body of sympathetic MPs in the Commons long before 1914.
• At the time: the NUWSS kept campaigning during the war while the WSPU suspended militancy, so the constitutional case was still being made when the franchise was redrawn.
• Over time: most historians now argue the 1918 Act owed more to that patient pressure, to women's war work and to the need to re-enfranchise returning soldiers than to militancy, which had stalled by 1913.
• Over time: the suffragist model of respectable national organisation shaped the campaign for equal franchise in 1928 and for equality law after 1970.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the First World War for the achievement of votes for women.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: around 1.7 million women in munitions, transport and the auxiliary services by 1917 made the ‘separate spheres’ argument hard to sustain.
• At the time: the practical need to redraw the male franchise so that returning soldiers kept the vote forced Parliament to legislate, opening a political window.
• Over time: the 1918 Act set the precedent of female enfranchisement that the 1928 Act extended to equal terms; later equality legislation (1970, 1975, 2010) built on this foundation.
• Over time: the example of British women’s war work and enfranchisement was used in suffrage campaigns across the British Empire and beyond.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of war work without explanation of why it mattered for the vote.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the suffragists and the Anti-Corn Law League were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both organised outside Parliament because their members lacked the vote; both used petitions, lobbying and public meetings to pressure MPs.
• Similarity: both built large national organisations with paid staff, regional branches and a network of lecturers — the suffragists with around 50,000 members by 1914.
• Similarity: both were patient and law-abiding, contrasting themselves with more militant rivals (Chartists for the League, suffragettes for the suffragists).
• Similarity: both ultimately succeeded by changing public opinion to the point that Parliament could not resist (1846 Corn Laws repeal, 1918 Act).

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from President Kennedy’s televised address to the American people, 22 October 1962.
‘Within the past week, unmistakable evidence has established the fact that a series of offensive missile sites is now in preparation on that imprisoned island. The purpose of these bases can be none other than to provide a nuclear strike capability against the Western Hemisphere. To halt this build-up, a strict quarantine on all offensive military equipment under shipment to Cuba is being initiated.’

Source A suggests that Kennedy saw the missiles in Cuba as a direct threat to the United States. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• ‘Unmistakable evidence’ of offensive missile sites being prepared in Cuba.
• The purpose of the bases ‘can be none other than’ nuclear strike capability against the Western Hemisphere.
• The quarantine is needed to halt the further build-up of offensive military equipment.
• Kennedy frames Cuba as ‘imprisoned’, suggesting the missiles are imposed by an outside power.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• A U2 photographed the missile sites on 14 October 1962 and Kennedy was briefed on 16 October.
• The quarantine came into force on 24 October and Soviet ships turned back rather than test it.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a confidential cable from Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin to Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko, 27 October 1962.
‘The Attorney General [Robert Kennedy] called me to the Justice Department this evening. He spoke with the President’s authority. He said the Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed within a few months but that any public mention of this would make agreement impossible. The President needed an answer within twenty-four hours.’

Source C: A summary of the argument Robert Kennedy set out in his memoir Thirteen Days, published in 1969 after his death.
‘The President had no intention of going to war over obsolete missiles in Turkey that we had already decided to remove. But he could not say so publicly — the alliance would have suffered and the appearance of weakness would have invited further Soviet pressure. The private assurance to Dobrynin was the only practicable path.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the resolution of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: confirms the secret Jupiter-for-Cuba deal, the requirement of secrecy and the twenty-four hour deadline. Provenance: a confidential Soviet ambassador’s cable to Moscow at the moment of resolution — likely to give a frank account of what was actually said. Own knowledge: Robert Kennedy did meet Dobrynin on the evening of 27 October; the Jupiters were withdrawn by April 1963 as promised.
Source C — Content: explains why the deal had to remain secret — alliance management and the appearance of weakness. Provenance: a posthumous memoir written for publication, giving a self-justifying account of one participant. Own knowledge: matches what later declassification revealed; Robert Kennedy’s account is broadly consistent with archive evidence.
Judgement: B is highly useful as contemporaneous diplomatic record; C is useful as participant analysis but partial as memoir — both together explain why the orthodox ‘clean Kennedy victory’ story took hold.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Cuban Missile Crisis developed from the discovery of the missiles on 14 October 1962 to Khrushchev’s announcement of withdrawal on 28 October 1962.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, names, decisions); reaches the resolution through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 14 October 1962: a US U2 reconnaissance flight photographed Soviet medium-range missile sites under construction in Cuba.
• 16 October 1962: Kennedy was briefed and convened ExComm to consider options in secret.
• 22 October 1962: Kennedy addressed the nation on television, announcing the missiles and imposing a naval quarantine.
• 24 October 1962: the quarantine line came into effect; Soviet ships approached, then turned back or were boarded peacefully.
• 26 October 1962: Khrushchev sent a private letter offering withdrawal in return for a US no-invasion pledge.
• 27 October 1962 (Black Saturday): a US U2 was shot down over Cuba; a second harder Khrushchev letter demanded the Jupiters; Robert Kennedy met Dobrynin to offer a secret Jupiter deal.
• 28 October 1962: Khrushchev announced the dismantling of the missiles; the crisis ended.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Cuban Missile Crisis was the moment the Cold War came closest to nuclear war.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Soviet nuclear missiles were being made ready ninety miles from Florida and could reach most American cities.
• On 27 October a Soviet missile shot down a US U2 over Cuba and killed its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson.
• Soviet submarine officers off Cuba came within one vote of firing a nuclear torpedo at US destroyers.
• An air strike could not have destroyed every missile, and the Joint Chiefs were pressing for invasion.
Disagree:
• Berlin in 1948-49 and again in 1961 also put Soviet and American forces face to face.
• Atomic weapons were considered during the Korean War without being used.
• Both leaders worked hard to avoid escalation, which suggests the crisis was under control throughout.
• Some historians argue the Able Archer exercise of 1983 was a comparable danger.
Judgement: Cuba is the closest moment for which there is firm evidence, because several separate paths to nuclear use were open at the same time.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a confidential note by US Defence Secretary Robert McNamara, written for President Kennedy on 27 October 1962.
‘If we attack Cuba tomorrow morning, my best estimate is that we shall lose between five and ten thousand men in the first three days. The Soviets may use tactical nuclear weapons against the invasion. The risk that this becomes a general nuclear exchange is, in my judgement, real and substantial.’

Source F suggests that an American invasion of Cuba could have ended in nuclear war. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: gives concrete casualty estimates and identifies the risk of Soviet tactical nuclear use — useful evidence of how senior US officials assessed the danger.
• Provenance: a confidential note from the Defence Secretary to the President at the moment of decision — likely to express an honest judgement.
• Own knowledge: declassified Soviet sources confirm tactical nuclear weapons were on Cuba; Soviet submarine commanders nearly used a nuclear torpedo on Black Saturday.
• Useful interpretation: McNamara’s framing of the risk as ‘real and substantial’ supports the view that the Cuban Missile Crisis was the closest moment to nuclear war.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the relations between Cuba, the USSR and the United States from Castro’s revolution in January 1959 to the discovery of the Soviet missiles in October 1962.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the missile discovery through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• January 1959: Castro overthrew Batista; began nationalising US-owned property.
• 1960: Castro signed trade agreements with the USSR; Eisenhower imposed an economic embargo.
• April 1961: CIA-backed Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs and were defeated within three days; Castro openly aligned Cuba with the USSR.
• Spring 1962: Khrushchev decided to deploy nuclear missiles to Cuba to deter another invasion and answer US Jupiter missiles in Turkey.
• Summer 1962: Soviet ships secretly delivered missiles, equipment and around 40,000 troops to Cuba.
• 14 October 1962: a US U2 photographed missile sites under construction at San Cristóbal, triggering the crisis.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from Woodrow Wilson’s war message to the US Congress, delivered on 2 April 1917, drawn from official Congressional records.
‘The recent course of the Imperial German government is in fact nothing less than war against the government and people of the United States. Vessels of every kind, of every sort and every flag, have been ruthlessly sent to the bottom without warning. There can be no choice. The world must be made safe for democracy.’

Source A suggests that Wilson believed Germany had already made war on the United States. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• German policy is ‘nothing less than war against the government and people of the United States’.
• Ships ‘of every kind, of every sort and every flag’ have been sunk without warning.
• ‘There can be no choice’ - Wilson presents war as forced on America.
• He adds a wider aim: ‘the world must be made safe for democracy’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917.
• The Zimmermann Telegram was published on 1 March 1917 and Congress declared war on 6 April.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Admiral Henning von Holtzendorff, Chief of the German Admiralty Staff, sent to the Kaiser on 22 December 1916, urging the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare.
‘I do not hesitate to assert that, as the situation now stands, we can force England to make peace within five months by means of an unrestricted submarine campaign. The risk of an American declaration of war is one that we must accept; even if America enters the war, our submarines will starve England out before the new enemy can effectively fight.’

Source C: An extract from a confidential British Cabinet briefing on US opinion, January 1918.
‘The Zimmermann Telegram of January 1917, made public in our papers in March, transformed American sentiment more decisively than two years of submarine outrages. The proposal to dismember the United States in alliance with Mexico spoke directly to ordinary Americans about the German threat to the homeland.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why the United States entered the war in 1917. Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: lays out the German calculation that the U-boat campaign could starve Britain out before America could effectively intervene. Provenance: a memorandum from the Chief of the Admiralty Staff to the Kaiser, written to persuade and likely to overstate certainty. Own knowledge: unrestricted submarine warfare resumed 1 February 1917; Wilson broke relations 3 February; Congress voted to declare war 6 April 1917; April 1917 was the worst month for British shipping (881,000 tons sunk).
Source C — Content: argues that the Zimmermann Telegram, not just submarine warfare, transformed American sentiment. Provenance: a British Cabinet briefing in January 1918, written by officials with access to the British intelligence which had decoded the telegram; well-placed but partial — Britain had a strong interest in framing US entry as a moral response to German conduct. Own knowledge: telegram intercepted mid-January 1917, published 1 March 1917; combined with the resumption of submarine warfare to push Wilson to war.
Judgement: B is highly useful for German thinking but partial as it overstated success and dismissed US weight; C is useful for understanding American public opinion but written from a self-interested British perspective. Together they show why both German decisions were needed to bring the USA in.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the events that led the United States from neutrality at the start of 1917 to a declaration of war in April 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (1 Feb resumption of U-boat war, 3 Feb diplomatic break, mid-Jan interception of Zimmermann Telegram, 1 March publication, 2 April Wilson speech, 6 April vote); reaches the declaration through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 1 February 1917: Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare, calculating Britain could be starved out in six months.
• 3 February 1917: Wilson broke off diplomatic relations with Germany.
• Mid-January 1917: British naval intelligence intercepted and decoded the Zimmermann Telegram proposing a German–Mexican alliance against the USA.
• 1 March 1917: Britain made the Zimmermann Telegram public, swinging American opinion sharply.
• March–April 1917: U-boats sank several US-flagged vessels including the Vigilancia and Healdton.
• 2 April 1917: Wilson asked Congress to declare war (‘the world must be made safe for democracy’).
• 6 April 1917: Congress voted to declare war on Germany; first American Expeditionary Force units reached France in June 1917.

practice_questions.text:
‘US entry in April 1917 was the most important turning point of the war.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• About two million American troops were in France by the armistice, and 4.7 million Americans served in all.
• American money, food and shipping steadied the Allied war effort from 1917.
• US entry set Germany a deadline, which is what forced the gamble of the Spring Offensive.

Disagree:
• Russia's collapse and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk freed about 50 German divisions and gave Germany its only real chance of victory.
• American troops were not present in strength until the summer of 1918, so the entry carried little immediate military weight.
• The failure of the Spring Offensive, the Hundred Days and the naval blockade are all strong rival candidates.
• The convoy system from May 1917 was what actually saved Britain from starvation.

Judgement: US entry mattered most in the long run because it set a deadline Germany could not meet, but it only decided the war alongside the Russian collapse that created the chance in the first place.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a despatch by British ambassador to Russia Sir George Buchanan to the Foreign Office, dated 16 March 1917.
‘The Tsar abdicated yesterday. The army is no longer reliable; the Petrograd garrison sided with the rioters. A Provisional Government has been formed which intends to continue the war. I would advise that this intention rests on a fragile base of public support.’

Source F suggests that the Provisional Government's decision to stay in the war rested on weak support. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• ‘The Tsar abdicated yesterday’ - dating the abdication to 15 March 1917.
• ‘The army is no longer reliable; the Petrograd garrison sided with the rioters.’
• The new Provisional Government ‘intends to continue the war’.
• Buchanan warns that this intention ‘rests on a fragile base of public support’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Provisional Government's summer offensive collapsed within weeks and desertion spread.
• Lenin returned in April 1917 promising peace, and the Bolsheviks took power on 7 November 1917.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Russia moved from continued participation in the war in March 1917 to the signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Tsar abdication, Lenin’s sealed train, summer offensive collapse, October Revolution, Brest-Litovsk); reaches the treaty through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 15 March 1917: Tsar Nicholas II abdicated after Petrograd bread riots; a Provisional Government took power and chose to continue the war.
• April 1917: Germany allowed Lenin a sealed train back to Petrograd, calculating that Bolshevik agitation would weaken Russian war commitment.
• Summer 1917: Provisional Government’s ‘Kerensky Offensive’ collapsed within weeks; tens of thousands of soldiers deserted.
• 7 November 1917: Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd (October by Russian calendar); immediate offer of peace talks to Germany.
• December 1917: armistice on the Eastern Front opened the way to formal negotiations.
• 3 March 1918: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk signed; Russia surrendered Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Ukraine and other territories — about a third of its population. Around 50 German divisions began transferring west for the Spring Offensive.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Richard Nixon, 3 November 1969.
‘The defence of freedom is everybody’s business — not just America’s business. Under our new policy, we shall provide assistance to those Asian nations capable of and willing to participate in their own defence. The South Vietnamese have continued to gain in strength. As a result they have been able to take over combat responsibilities from our American troops.’

Source A suggests that Nixon presented Vietnamisation as a policy that shared the burden rather than an American retreat. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He says the defence of freedom is ‘everybody’s business — not just America’s business’.
• Assistance will go to Asian nations ‘capable of and willing to participate in their own defence’.
• He claims the South Vietnamese have grown strong enough to take over combat duties.
Contextual knowledge: Nixon announced Vietnamisation on 3 November 1969; US troop numbers fell from a peak of 540,000 to under 50,000 by mid-1972 while the ARVN grew to over a million men.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Nixon’s decision to invade Cambodia in April 1970 led to the largest student strike in US history.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise dates and details (Cambodia announcement, Kent State, Jackson State, the campus strike, Congress’s response).
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin or muddled chronology.

Indicative content:
• March 1969: Nixon began secret B-52 bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu), concealed from Congress.
• 30 April 1970: Nixon announced the Cambodia incursion in a televised address.
• 1–4 May 1970: campus protests erupted across the United States.
• 4 May 1970: Ohio National Guardsmen shot four unarmed students dead at Kent State University.
• 5–15 May 1970: nationwide student strike spread to around more than 450 campuses; over four million students walked out.
• 14–15 May 1970: police killed two students at Jackson State College in Mississippi.
• June 1970: the Senate voted to repeal the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and passed the Cooper-Church Amendment to limit operations in Cambodia; the repeal took effect in January 1971.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a 1972 New York Times news analysis of Nixon’s February 1972 visit to Beijing.
‘The visit changes the shape of the Cold War. Hanoi can no longer assume Chinese support is unconditional. Moscow must now compete for American friendship rather than count on it. The Vietnam War, while continuing, is no longer the central event of American foreign policy.’

Source C: An extract from a Vietnamese diplomat’s memoir, published in Hanoi in the 1990s, recalling Politburo discussions in spring 1972.
‘Comrade Mao’s reception of the American president disturbed us. We were told the Chinese would maintain their aid — but we were also told to prepare for the possibility that Beijing’s priorities had shifted. We knew the war must now be ended on terms we could secure quickly.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of Nixon’s opening to China on the Vietnam War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: argues the Beijing visit reshaped Cold War alignments and pressured Hanoi. Provenance: a New York Times news analysis written immediately after the visit, for a US public audience — useful for showing how the move was understood at the time, but reflects American framing. Own knowledge: Kissinger had visited Beijing secretly in July 1971; the Sino-Soviet split made the opening possible; Linebacker II in December 1972 followed within ten months.
Source C — Content: shows Hanoi acknowledging the disturbance the visit caused. Provenance: a Politburo-level memoir published in the 1990s, written with hindsight and likely smoothed for publication — useful as the Vietnamese view, but not contemporary documentary evidence. Own knowledge: the Paris Peace Accords were signed January 1973; Hanoi did indeed feel the urgency of a settlement.
Judgement: B is highly useful for immediate US understanding; C is highly useful for the Vietnamese response, with the caveat that hindsight may shape its emphasis. Together they show the opening worked diplomatically even as the war continued.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a televised report on the Kent State shootings, broadcast on NBC News, 4 May 1970.
‘Today four students at Kent State University in Ohio were shot dead by Ohio National Guardsmen during a protest against the war in Cambodia. Nine others were wounded. Witnesses describe the soldiers turning and firing into a crowd that included students walking to class. The university is closed indefinitely.’

Source D suggests that the Cambodian incursion turned protest at home into violence. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• Four students were shot dead by National Guardsmen during a protest against the war in Cambodia.
• Nine others were wounded, and witnesses describe soldiers firing into a crowd that included students walking to class.
• The university closed indefinitely.
Contextual knowledge: Nixon had announced the incursion on 30 April 1970; over four million students walked out afterwards, and two more students were killed at Jackson State on 14–15 May.

practice_questions.text:
‘The decision to invade Cambodia was the most damaging moment of Nixon’s Vietnam policy.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The incursion, announced on 30 April 1970, reignited a campus movement that Vietnamisation had been quietening.
• Four students were killed at Kent State on 4 May and two at Jackson State on 14–15 May.
• Over four million students walked out, the largest student strike in American history.
• Congress moved against presidential war power: the Senate voted to repeal the Tonkin Resolution and passed the Cooper-Church Amendment.
Disagree:
• Watergate did more lasting harm: it forced Nixon’s resignation in August 1974 and destroyed the political capacity to enforce the 1973 Accords.
• The Christmas bombings of December 1972 caused comparable international outrage.
• Vietnamisation had already conceded that the United States would not win the ground war.
• The secret bombing of Cambodia from March 1969 had begun the widening before 1970.
Judgement: Cambodia was the most damaging moment for the home front; Watergate was more damaging for the outcome of the war.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the diplomatic and military steps Nixon took between 1969 and 1972 to extract the United States from Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details (Vietnamisation announcement, secret bombing of Cambodia, Kissinger’s 1971 Beijing visit, Easter Offensive, Linebacker II).
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• March 1969: Nixon authorised secret B-52 bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu).
• 3 November 1969: Nixon announced the Vietnamisation policy on television.
• April 1970: Cambodian incursion by US ground troops.
• July 1971: Kissinger visited Beijing secretly.
• February 1972: Nixon visited China; opened relations with Mao.
• Spring 1972: North Vietnamese Easter Offensive.
• April–October 1972: Linebacker I bombing of North Vietnam.
• December 1972: Linebacker II ‘Christmas Bombings’ of Hanoi and Haiphong forced Hanoi back to the negotiating table.
• Through this period US troop numbers fell from 540,000 to under 50,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1926 General Strike in the changing relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: around 1.7 million workers came out across transport, print and heavy industry; the strike was the largest coordinated industrial action in British history.
• At the time: the TUC General Council called it off unconditionally on day nine, exposing the limits of sympathy striking as a political tool; the miners stayed out and were starved back to work by November.
• At the time: the Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Act 1927 outlawed sympathy strikes, banned civil-service unions from affiliating to the TUC and cut Labour Party funding through ‘contracting in’.
• Over time: union membership halved from 8.3m (1920) to 4.4m (1933); industrial relations remained shaped by the 1927 framework until partial repeal in 1946.
• Over time: a permanent warning about the limits of confrontation that shaped union thinking through the post-war consensus and into the Thatcher era; the 1980-84 reforms explicitly built on the 1927 model.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the strike without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the changing power of trade unions between 1926 and 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the defeat of the General Strike in May 1926 and the Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Act 1927 outlawed sympathy strikes and cut Labour Party funding; membership fell from 8.3 million in 1920 to 4.4 million by 1933.
• At the time: wartime and post-war full employment rebuilt union strength, Attlee repealed the 1927 Act in 1946, and by the 1960s the TUC met ministers monthly.
• At the time: In Place of Strife failed in 1969, and the Winter of Discontent of 1978-79 turned public opinion against the unions.
• Over time: the Acts of 1980, 1982 and 1984 and the defeat of the Miners' Strike in March 1985 ended the post-war assumption that unions would be partners in government.
• Over time: membership fell from about 13 million in 1979 to under 7 million by 2000, and individual employment law replaced union strength as the main protection of workers' rights.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the 1926 General Strike and the 1984-85 Miners' Strike were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Similarity: both were triggered by attempts to cut miners' jobs or wages and centred on the coal industry as a flashpoint of wider economic change. • Similarity: both produced sustained government preparation in advance — Baldwin's OMS in 1926, Thatcher's coal stockpiling and police mobilisation from 1981-84. • Similarity: both ended in defeat for the workers, with consequent legislation strengthening employer and government powers (1927 Act, 1980-84 Acts). • Similarity: both lost the communications battle — the BBC tilt and British Gazette in 1926, television framing of Orgreave in 1984. [8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail] Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise detail. Secure: Two similarities with some support. Developing: Two simple points. Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: ‘Government action was the main factor in the decline of trade union power in the twentieth century.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh government against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of government as the main factor:
• 1927 Trade Disputes Act outlawed sympathy strikes and cut Labour funding after the General Strike.
• Thatcher's incremental legislation: 1980 Employment Act on picketing, 1982 Act ending the closed shop, 1984 Trade Union Act requiring ballots before strike action.
• Government preparation in 1926 (OMS) and 1984-85 (coal stockpiling, police) shaped both decisive defeats.

Weighed against the economy:
• Mass unemployment in the early 1930s eroded membership from 8.3m to 4.4m faster than legislation could.
• Deindustrialisation from the 1970s shrank the coal, steel, shipbuilding and dock industries that were the heart of organised labour.
• Globalisation from the 1980s shifted manufacturing abroad, reducing the strategic leverage of national strikes.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Baldwin's strategic patience in 1926 and Thatcher's confrontational approach in 1984-85 shaped both critical contests.
• Arthur Scargill's refusal to ballot before the 1984 strike fatally weakened the NUM's legal and political position.

Weighed against ideas:
• Public belief in the right to strike weakened after the Winter of Discontent of 1978-79; new free-market thinking gained ground in the 1980s.
• The post-war social-democratic settlement that legitimised tripartite consultation lost ideological hold from the late 1970s.

Cross-period weighing:
• Compare with the rise of unions in 1834-1889 (Tolpuddle, GNCTU, dockers' strike) where economic conditions and individual leadership outweighed government action.
• The pattern is one of waves rather than steady decline — legislation rolls back what economy and ideas have already softened.

Judgement: Top answers argue government legislation accelerated and locked in changes that economic restructuring and shifts in public opinion had begun. Government action was the most direct cause of decline, but the underlying conditions of deindustrialisation and changing ideas about labour made it possible.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing government against at least two other factors with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Margaret Thatcher's trade union reforms of 1980-84.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the 1980 Employment Act narrowed lawful picketing; the 1982 Act allowed employers to sue unions and ended the closed shop; the 1984 Trade Union Act required secret ballots before strike action.
• At the time: provided the legal framework that defeated the Miners' Strike of 1984-85; courts could fine the NUM for unlawful action.
• At the time: ended the post-war assumption that unions would be partners in government economic management.
• Over time: union membership fell from 13m (1979) to 6.7m (2000); collective bargaining coverage shrank decisively.
• Over time: shifted the balance of workplace protection from collective union strength to individual employment law (minimum wage, working time, equal pay) by the 1990s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the reforms without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the role of the BBC in 1926 was different from the role of the press in supporting the Chartists in the 1830s and 1840s.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Difference in stance: the BBC in 1926 broadcast government bulletins and refused TUC airtime; the Northern Star from 1837 was an explicitly Chartist newspaper edited by Feargus O'Connor with around 50,000 weekly readers. • Difference in technology: the BBC reached homes nationally through wireless broadcasting; the Chartist press depended on print, the penny post and the railway network. • Difference in ownership: the BBC was a state-influenced public broadcaster supplemented by Churchill's British Gazette; the Chartist press was independent commercial publishing serving a specific movement. • Difference in effect: the BBC tilt towards the government helped contain the General Strike; the Northern Star built mass Chartist organisation but did not deliver the franchise in its own moment. [8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail] Mastering: Two distinct differences, each with precise detail. Secure: Two differences with some support. Developing: Two simple points. Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text:
Which was the more important reason the Great Plains were settled between 1862 and 1890?

• The 1862 Homestead Act
• The railroads and new farming technology

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Homestead Act against other factors and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (sod-buster, dry farming, transcontinental railroad, open range).
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of multiple causes with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of the Homestead Act with no comparison of the two bullets.

Indicative content:
The 1862 Homestead Act:
• Around 1.6 million homestead claims completed between 1862 and 1934 — the largest single redistribution of public land in US history.
• 160-acre quarter sections shaped the geography of Plains farming for generations.
• Federal land was free at a moment when Eastern land was scarce and expensive.

The railroads and new farming technology:
• Pacific Railroad Act 1862 and the 1869 transcontinental railroad opened the Plains physically and advertised them.
• Around 175 million acres of railroad land grants — railroads were larger landowners than the Homestead Act’s claimants.
• New technologies (steel plough, windmills, dry farming, drought-resistant wheat, barbed wire) were what made the Plains farmable.
• Push factors: post-Civil War unemployment, European famine and persecution drove emigration.
• High failure rate: more than half of homestead claims were abandoned, suggesting the Act alone was not enough.

Judgement: the Homestead Act was the legal framework, but it would not have settled the Plains alone — the railroads, technology and immigration were equally indispensable; a top-band answer reaches an explicit verdict on this combination.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the completion of the transcontinental railroad in 1869 on the Great Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed effects with precise factual detail and clear distinction between strands of impact.
Secure: Two relevant effects with some support.
Developing: One effect developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of the railroad without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Cut journey time across the continent from around six months to about a week, transforming migration costs.
• Allowed Texas longhorn cattle to be moved by rail from cowtowns like Abilene to Eastern markets, creating the cattle boom of the 1870s.
• Accelerated the destruction of the buffalo herds — railroad construction crews and tourist hunters killed millions, with herds fragmented by the line itself.
• Made the Plains nations militarily isolatable — the US Army could move troops along the line in days rather than months.
• Drew European immigrants to the Plains via railroad-marketing offices in Sweden, Germany and Britain.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of barbed wire (patented by Joseph Glidden in 1874) on the Great Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual detail; engages with both farmer and rancher perspectives.
Secure: Two relevant effects with some support.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of barbed wire without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Allowed homesteaders to fence 160-acre claims cheaply for the first time, protecting crops from drifting cattle.
• Closed the open range, ending the era of long cattle drives north from Texas.
• Triggered the ‘fence-cutting wars’ in Texas and elsewhere as ranchers attacked homesteader fences in the late 1870s.
• Concentrated cattle ranching on smaller, fed and fenced operations — investment shifted from herd size to ranch infrastructure.
• Disrupted Plains nations’ remaining hunting routes by carving up grassland with new fences.

practice_questions.text:
Which was the more important in changing the Great Plains?

• The railroads
• The 1862 Homestead Act

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; deploys specialist vocabulary; precise on both factors.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of one or both with little comparison.

Indicative content:
The railroads:
• Without rail, settlers could not move bulk crops to market — making 160-acre farms commercially viable.
• Railroad-funded immigration agents recruited the European settlers who took up much of the homestead land.
• Railroad land sales (175 million acres of grants) accounted for a vast share of Plains settlement, often alongside homestead claims.
• Railroads supplied the timber, machinery and barbed wire that made the Plains farmable.

The 1862 Homestead Act:
• The Homestead Act provided the legal mechanism for land transfer that no railroad could replicate.
• Around 1.6 million homestead claims testify to the Act’s independent reach.
• Many homesteaders settled on land miles from any rail line, surviving by older means.
• Push factors (Civil War dislocation, European persecution) operated independently of either factor.

Judgement: the railroads and the Homestead Act worked as a system; isolating one is artificial. A top-band answer concludes that they were complementary, with railroads more important for commercial viability and the Act more important for legal access.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the winter of 1886-87 (the ‘Big Die-Up’) on the cattle industry of the Great Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual detail; engages with both immediate and structural consequences.
Secure: Two relevant effects.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of the winter without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Killed up to nine-tenths of cattle in some northern ranges, wiping out years of accumulated wealth in months.
• Bankrupted many British and Eastern ranching syndicates, ending the boom in absentee ownership.
• Forced surviving ranchers onto smaller, fenced operations with stored winter feed.
• Combined with barbed wire to end the open-range era; Texas-to-Kansas long drives ceased.
• Concentrated ranching on more capital-intensive, smaller-herd operations that survived into the 20th century.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of new technology (steel plough, windmill, dry farming) on Plains agriculture between 1860 and 1890.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual detail; clearly distinguishes specific technologies.
Secure: Two relevant effects.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of technology without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• John Deere’s steel plough cut through Plains sod that had broken Eastern iron ploughs — making fields cultivatable for the first time.
• Windmill-pumped wells reached deep aquifers, providing reliable water for stock and households where surface water was scarce.
• Dry farming techniques (breaking up soil after rain, leaving fallow alternate years) raised yields in low-rainfall areas like the Dakotas.
• Drought-resistant Russian wheat, brought by Mennonite immigrants, made wheat farming reliable in Kansas.
• Together these technologies extended the ‘line of farms’ west of the 100th meridian, into land that had been unfarmable a generation earlier.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which surgery in the First World War and surgery today were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: WWI surgery relied on antiseptic carbolic acid and emergency amputation, whereas modern surgery uses keyhole techniques, lasers and robotics.
• Difference: WWI blood transfusion was experimental, with limited storage; today the National Blood Transfusion Service supplies routine, screened blood.
• Similarity: both rely on X-rays (Röntgen 1895) to locate fractures and foreign bodies.
• Similarity: both are pushed forward by war — WWI by shrapnel injuries, today’s techniques refined in conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Alexander Fleming for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Fleming’s 1928 observation of Penicillium notatum killing staphylococcus on a contaminated plate at St Mary’s Hospital was the first identification of a natural antibiotic.
• At the time: he published his findings in 1929 but could not purify penicillin and moved on.
• Over time: his discovery was the foundation Florey and Chain developed into a usable drug from 1939 onwards.
• Over time: penicillin became the prototype antibiotic; further antibiotics (streptomycin 1944, cephalosporins) followed the same model.
• Limitation: Fleming alone did not produce a medicine — without Florey, Chain and wartime mass production his observation might have stayed in the journals.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named individuals.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Alexander Fleming’s paper in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology, 1929. He describes how a mould that had contaminated a culture plate at St Mary’s Hospital stopped staphylococcus growing around it, names the substance penicillin, and notes that he could not produce it in useful amounts.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying the discovery of penicillin?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: it is the first record of the effect, so it fixes the discovery to 1928-29 and to Fleming.
• Content: his own admission that he could not purify it explains why nothing happened for ten years.
• Provenance: a research paper written for other scientists soon after the event, so it is close to the discovery and open to checking, though it is Fleming’s account of his own work.
• Contextual knowledge: Florey and Chain took up the paper at Oxford in 1939, proved the drug on mice in 1940 and on a patient in 1941, and US industry then scaled production for D-Day in 1944.
• Limitations: it captures the chance observation only, and nothing of the war, money and industry that turned it into a medicine.
• Judgement: essential for the chance factor and for the discovery, useless on its own for the development of the drug.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Has chance been the main factor in medical breakthroughs in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to chance and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh chance against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of chance as the main factor:
• Fleming 1928: contaminated mould plate produced penicillin.
• Pasteur 1879: a forgotten chicken-cholera culture weakened to give him the principle of attenuated vaccines.
• Paré 1530s: running out of cauterising oil forced him to use a soothing salve which worked better.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Fleming’s plate produced nothing usable; Florey and Chain made it a drug. Jenner deliberately tested cowpox in 1796.

Weighed against war:
• WWII funding and demand turned penicillin into a battlefield drug. WWI accelerated transfusion, X-rays and plastic surgery (Gillies).

Weighed against science and technology:
• Deep-tank fermentation and electron microscopy were what scaled and explained the breakthrough. Without germ theory, Lister’s 1867 antiseptic surgery had no scientific footing.

Judgement: chance opens doors but explains nothing. Across the medieval, early modern and modern periods accidental discoveries only became medicines when prepared minds, organised science, war and government converted them. The named factor is real but secondary — chance plus an individual willing to chase it down is the irreducible combination.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes accidents only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Second World War for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: WWII drove the mass production of penicillin in the United States from 1941, supplying the Allies by D-Day 1944.
• At the time: Archibald McIndoe’s Guinea Pig Club at East Grinstead pioneered burns reconstruction for RAF aircrew.
• At the time: nationalisation of hospitals through the Emergency Medical Service set a precedent used in 1948 for the NHS.
• Over time: penicillin became the model for further antibiotics (streptomycin, cephalosporins) into the 1970s.
• Over time: the Beveridge Report (1942) and the postwar welfare state directly built on wartime experience of state-organised healthcare.
• Limitation: many WWII innovations built on WWI work (transfusion, plastic surgery, X-rays) so the war accelerated rather than originated.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named individuals.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of antibiotic resistance for healthcare in Britain since 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: penicillin and the antibiotics that followed made bacterial infection routinely curable for the first time in history.
• Over time: heavy prescribing in general practice and routine use in farming gave bacteria constant pressure to adapt.
• Over time: MRSA appeared in the 1960s and spread through hospital wards, and by the 1990s ‘superbugs’ were a national news story.
• Over time: it changed how hospitals are run, with infection-control teams, hand-hygiene campaigns and rules limiting prescribing.
• Judgement worth making: resistance shows that medical progress can create new problems, which is why change and progress are not the same thing.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the design and prices of the public playhouses.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Open-air structure: playhouses were polygonal wooden buildings, around three storeys high, with a central yard open to the sky and covered galleries around the sides.
• Mixed audience pricing: groundlings paid one penny to stand in the yard, two pennies bought a gallery seat, and a cushion cost one penny extra.
• Performance times: plays were performed in the afternoon because there was no artificial lighting strong enough for evening performances.
• Boy actors: women were not allowed on the public stage, so boy apprentices played all female roles in companies like the Lord Chamberlain’s Men.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
