Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how noble patronage protected Elizabethan acting companies.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Legal cover: the 1572 Vagabonds Act classed unattached actors as vagrants, but actors with a noble patron were exempt — patronage was the difference between a respectable career and being whipped.
• Stable companies: companies named after their patron (Lord Chamberlain’s Men, Lord Admiral’s Men, the Queen’s Men from 1583) developed long-term casts and shared business stakes among their sharers.
• Court access: patronage opened the door to court performances at Whitehall and Greenwich, which paid more than public performances and reinforced the company’s status.
• Protection from the City: a play licensed by the Master of the Revels under noble patronage could not easily be banned by the City of London Corporation.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Puritan opposition to the theatre.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Moral attack on plays: Puritan writers such as Philip Stubbes in Anatomy of Abuses (1583) condemned the playhouses as a training ground for vanity, violence and idleness. • Objection to boys playing women: Puritans argued that boys dressing as women on stage was scandalous and broke biblical commandments. • Plague theology: London Puritan preachers argued that plague outbreaks were God’s judgement on the playhouses and demanded their closure. • Long-term goal: Puritans pushed for outright abolition of the theatre — which they achieved in 1642 once Parliament took power, closing the theatres for eighteen years. [8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.] Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail. Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail. Developing: Points identified with limited explanation. Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how opposition from the City of London shaped where playhouses were built.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The City of London Corporation banned playhouses from operating inside the City walls from 1574, citing plague, crime and disorder.
• As a direct effect, purpose-built playhouses such as The Theatre (1576) and the Curtain were built in Shoreditch, just north of the City limits.
• The Rose and the Swan were built in Southwark, on the south bank of the Thames, outside the City’s jurisdiction; further playhouses followed there in the late 1590s.
• The result was a permanent geography of theatre on the edges of the City — clustered with bear-baiting rings, taverns and brothels — that defined Elizabethan and Jacobean playgoing.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the way an Elizabethan acting company was organised.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Sharer system: the Lord Chamberlain’s Men was made up of around a dozen sharers who jointly owned the business; Shakespeare and Richard Burbage were both sharers.
• Boy apprentices: female roles were performed by boy apprentices, since women were not allowed on the public stage.
• Repertory performance: companies performed a different play each afternoon, six days a week, with new plays added constantly.
• Noble patron: every successful company was legally tied to a patron (the Lord Chamberlain, the Lord Admiral, the Queen herself), which protected the actors from the 1572 Vagabonds Act.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The Elizabethan theatre survived because the queen protected it, not because audiences loved it.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the Elizabethan theatre? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The 1572 Vagabonds Act would have shut down acting altogether if the Crown had not allowed noble patrons to exempt their companies.
• Elizabeth set up the Queen’s Men in 1583 specifically to perform at court, signalling royal endorsement.
• The Master of the Revels system from 1581 licensed plays under royal authority, blocking the City of London from banning licensed work.
• When the Puritans took political power in 1642, public popularity was no protection — the theatres were closed for eighteen years, showing royal backing was the missing ingredient.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• A penny entry brought audiences of two to three thousand several afternoons a week — the business model was self-sustaining.
• The geographic spread of playhouses (The Theatre 1576, the Curtain, the Rose, the Swan, and further Southwark playhouses by the late 1590s) shows commercial demand drove construction, not court order.
• The mixed audience — apprentices, gentry, courtiers, foreigners — meant the theatre had a constituency the Crown could not have manufactured.
• Playwrights like Marlowe and Shakespeare wrote in part for a paying public and shaped their work to it; the cultural achievement is not a court-only product.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the three main features of the battlefield site at Stirling Bridge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The wooden bridge: so narrow that only two horsemen could cross abreast, it fed the English army across the Forth at a trickle and could not pass reinforcements once the fighting began.
• The carse: soft, wet meadow inside a tight loop of the river, crossed by a single causeway — ground on which armoured cavalry could not charge or manoeuvre.
• Abbey Craig: the steep crag a mile north of the crossing from which Wallace and Moray observed the crossing and timed their attack.
• The river loop: the Forth curled round the low ground on three sides, leaving troops caught there no way out except the bridge.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the make-up of the English army that fought at Stirling Bridge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Its core was armoured knights on warhorses — the arm that had won at Dunbar in 1296 but was cancelled by the soft carse.
• It was commanded by John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, elderly and reluctant, with the treasurer Hugh de Cressingham pressing for speed and economy.
• It substantially outnumbered the Scots and included thousands of infantry, including Welsh spearmen — but only the portion across the bridge could fight.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the site of Stirling Bridge for the outcome of the battle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The bridge as bottleneck: only part of the army could cross before the attack, so the Scots fought half the English force with all of their own.
• The bridgehead seizure: once the Scots held the northern end, the remaining English strength was irrelevant — the width of the bridge stopped any rescue.
• The carse and loop: soft ground cancelled the English advantage in heavy cavalry and the river cut off retreat, turning defeat into destruction.
• Comparison strengthens the point: at Falkirk in 1298, on firm open ground, the same Scots army was destroyed — the site was the difference.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Battle of Stirling Bridge, 11 September 1297.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The approach: Wallace and Moray positioned on Abbey Craig; the English under Warenne and Cressingham at the bridge; Lundie's warning about a ford ignored on grounds of cost.
• The crossing: the army files over two abreast through the morning; the Scots wait until roughly half — vanguard, knights, Cressingham — is inside the river loop.
• The attack: spearmen charge from the crag and seize the bridgehead; knights flounder on the carse; some drown in the Forth; Cressingham is killed.
• The end: Warenne, unable to reinforce across the bottleneck, destroys the bridge and retreats to Berwick; thousands of English dead including around a hundred knights.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the ways in which Edward I’s rule of Scotland was affected by the Battle of Stirling Bridge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• English administration collapsed: the hated treasurer Cressingham was dead, Warenne retreated to Berwick, and Scotland north of the border was effectively lost for a season.
• Wallace's rise: the victory made him Guardian of Scotland and gave the revolt a leader with proven success, followed by raids into northern England.
• Edward's response: the defeat brought the king back to take personal command, leading to Falkirk in 1298 and the far longer, costlier wars that followed.
• Military lesson: the battle punctured the assumption that mounted knights automatically beat infantry — though Falkirk showed the lesson was about ground, not spearmen alone.

practice_questions.text: 'The English lost at Stirling Bridge because of their commanders' mistakes rather than the strength of the Scots' position.' How far does a study of the site of the Battle of Stirling Bridge support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the site and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The English council knew the ground: Lundie warned that the bridge was a trap and offered a flanking crossing by the ford; Cressingham's concern for cost and Warenne's lethargy sent the army over anyway.
• The shambolic crossing — started, recalled, restarted, with Warenne reportedly oversleeping — handed the Scots their timing.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• The position would have punished even competent handling: any force beyond the bridge stood on carse inside a river loop, and no commander could widen a two-horse bridge under attack.
• Wallace and Moray used the site with real skill — waiting on Abbey Craig, letting half the army cross, then striking the bridgehead rather than the vanguard.
• Context: Stirling was the unavoidable gateway crossing, so the English had limited strategic choice about meeting the enemy there.
A developed judgement weighing commander error against the inherent strength of the site is required for the top level.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the growth of monasticism in England between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A wave of new abbeys was founded by Norman lords — Battle Abbey on the field of Hastings (begun about 1070), Selby (1069), Shrewsbury (1083), Lewes Cluniac priory (1078) — raising the total of English monasteries from around 60 in 1066 to roughly 250 by 1100.
• Most followed the Rule of St Benedict, organising monks’ days around the eight services of the Divine Office, periods of manual work and periods of reading and study.
• Some, such as Lewes, followed the Cluniac reform — an elaborate liturgy of prayer, independence of secular lords, and direct loyalty to the Pope — tying English monasticism to the wider European reform movement.
• Patronage worked both ways: lords gave land to abbeys in exchange for prayers for their souls, which is how the new monasteries became substantial economic landholders.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Norman monastic foundations such as Battle Abbey for the consolidation of Norman rule.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, abbey foundations such as Battle Abbey on the Hastings battlefield framed the conquest in religious terms — the high altar marking where Harold fell was a public penance and a public claim that William’s victory had been God’s judgement.
• Norman lords used abbey foundations to embed their authority on their estates — an abbey would clear and drain land, pray for the founder’s soul, and serve as a stable cultural and economic centre.
• Cluniac priories such as Lewes (1078) tied English monasticism to a wider European reform network that gave the new Norman elite cultural prestige and connected them to the papacy.
• Importance later: by 1100 there were around 250 monasteries in England, and these foundations remained centres of Latin learning, Anglo-Norman power and economic activity through the medieval period.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about education and learning in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cathedral and monastic schools at Canterbury, Lincoln and Durham trained boys in Latin grammar, rhetoric, music and basic arithmetic, with more advanced schools teaching the seven liberal arts.
• Lanfranc himself had run a school of European reputation as prior of Bec in Normandy, where his pupils included Anselm — a model he carried into his English archiepiscopate.
• Latin remained the language of royal writs, Church liturgy and the Domesday Book itself, while Anglo-Norman was used in royal courts and lordly households.
• Old English continued as the everyday language of the village, with vernacular records such as the Peterborough version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle still being written in some monasteries into the 12th century.
• Why it mattered: the schools trained the clerks who wrote the writs, ran the courts and compiled Domesday, so Latin learning was part of the machinery of Norman government.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about William I’s refusal to do homage to Pope Gregory VII in 1080.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Gregory VII was pressing kings across Europe to acknowledge papal supremacy through homage; William’s refusal kept English royal authority over the Church distinct from the papacy.
• William continued to pay Peter’s Pence as a customary annual tribute but kept the right to appoint English bishops — a working compromise that preserved his alliance with Lanfranc.
• Lanfranc supported William’s position, framing it as protection of the English Church against outside meddling rather than open defiance of Rome — a position the wider Investiture Controversy would soon make harder to maintain.
• Importance later: the 1080 refusal set the Norman pattern of Church-state relations that survived under William II, prompted the Anselm clash from 1093, and shaped how Henry I and Stephen handled papal authority through the 12th century.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the quarrel between William II and Anselm over the English Church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, William II had left Canterbury vacant for four years (1089–93) and pocketed its revenues; Anselm’s appointment in 1093 immediately set up a confrontation when Anselm refused to pay royal demands or accept full royal control.
• Anselm’s recognition of Pope Urban II against William’s preferred candidate, and his insistence that bishops owed obedience to Rome on disputed matters, drew England into the European Investiture Controversy that William I had previously kept at arm’s length.
• Anselm went into exile rather than accept what he saw as royal interference — an extraordinary step for an Archbishop of Canterbury and a sign of how serious the issue had become.
• Significance over time: the dispute did not end with Rufus’s death in 1100. It continued under Henry I until a compromise was reached in 1107 and shaped the entire 12th-century pattern of English Church-state relations, including the later Becket crisis under Henry II.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Church reform.

‘Norman reform of the Church was about power, not religion. William and Lanfranc changed the men, the buildings and the map of the dioceses, and left the beliefs of ordinary people alone.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the Norman reform of the English Church? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: Norman Church reform was driven more by political control than by religious renewal.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The replacement of almost all Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans by 1080 transformed the institutional voice of the English Church — political control of personnel, not new doctrine, was the most striking change.
• The cathedral building programme — Canterbury, Lincoln, Old Sarum, Durham — visibly stamped Norman authority on the landscape; the buildings doubled as instruments of conquest like castles.
• The 1075 council of London moved sees into Norman urban centres, aligning Church geography with the new political map.
• William I’s refusal to do homage to Pope Gregory VII in 1080, and his control over papal access to England, show that royal authority over the Church mattered more than full integration with Rome.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• Stigand’s deposition for pluralism and uncanonical appointment was a genuine reform measure aligned with the wider European reform movement under Pope Alexander II and Pope Gregory VII.
• The Cluniac influence at Lewes (1078) and the wider monastic reform tradition that shaped Norman foundations were religious rather than political in origin.
• Wulfstan of Worcester was kept on for his religious reputation, suggesting the Norman regime did value English sanctity where it found it.
• Anselm’s clash with William II from 1093, and his willingness to go into exile rather than accept royal interference, shows that Norman Church reform produced churchmen who would defy royal authority on principle.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (an intentionalist historian arguing Hitler planned the Holocaust from at least the 1920s) and Interpretation B (a functionalist historian arguing the genocide emerged from improvised decisions taken between 1939 and 1942) on the origins of the Final Solution. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Holocaust as the execution of a long-held plan — antisemitism in Mein Kampf and the consistency of Nazi rhetoric.
• Interpretation B presents the Holocaust as a product of stepped radicalisation — ghettoisation, Einsatzgruppen and Wannsee emerging under wartime conditions.
• Main difference: A emphasises a single decision from above; B emphasises a process radicalising under war and occupation.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why an intentionalist historian (Interpretation A) and a functionalist historian (Interpretation B) give different views about the origins of the Final Solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They draw on different evidence — intentionalists weight Hitler's speeches and Mein Kampf; functionalists weight the bureaucratic record of mid-level officials and the chronology of policy.
• They start from different historical questions — intentionalists ask ‘what did Hitler decide?’; functionalists ask ‘how did the system radicalise?’
• They were writing in different decades — the intentionalist tradition was strongest in the 1960s–70s; the functionalist tradition gained ground from the 1980s with new archival access in occupied Eastern Europe.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 marked the start of the persecution of Jews in Nazi Germany.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the development of Nazi racial policy?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Nuremberg Laws were the first comprehensive legal framework: stripping citizenship, banning intermarriage, defining Mischling categories.
• Convincing because the laws gave bureaucratic structure to subsequent persecution and emigration policy.
• Less convincing because persecution began in spring 1933 — the SA-led boycott of 1 April and the Civil Service Law of 7 April dismissed Jewish judges, teachers and academics.
• Less convincing because Jewish students and patients had been quotaed out of universities and hospitals before September 1935.
• Less convincing because non-Jewish victims (Sinti and Roma, disabled Germans through T4, gay men) faced persecution from 1933–39 in parallel.
• Overall judgement: 1935 was a decisive legal escalation but not the start — persecution of Jews and other targeted groups began with the regime's first weeks in power.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942 on Nazi racial policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Coordinated the Final Solution — Heydrich, Eichmann and senior officials from across the Nazi state agreed responsibilities for the deportation and murder of all 11 million European Jews.
• Aligned policy across occupied Europe — deportations from Western Europe, including France, the Netherlands and Italy, were channelled towards the death camps in occupied Poland.
• Industrialised the killing — from 1942 the dedicated death camps at Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek murdered Jews on arrival; transports rather than mass shootings became the main method.
• Removed bureaucratic friction — the Justice Ministry, Foreign Office and railway authorities were enrolled in the killing programme rather than left as obstacles.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how Nazi racial policy radicalised between 1933 and 1942.
You may consider:
• stages of legal and social persecution before 1939
• stages of mass killing during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1933 stage: 1 April boycott of Jewish businesses; Civil Service Law of 7 April dismissing Jewish professionals; Dachau opened.
• 1935 stage: Nuremberg Laws strip citizenship and ban intermarriage; introduce Mischling categories; Sinti and Roma soon brought under same provisions.
• 1938 stage: Kristallnacht (9–10 November) destroys 267 synagogues, 7,500 businesses; 91 murdered, 30,000 sent to camps; community fined one billion marks.
• 1939 stage: T4 euthanasia programme against disabled Germans (around 70,000 deaths); ghettoisation in occupied Poland.
• 1941 stage: Einsatzgruppen mass shootings from June 1941 in occupied Soviet territory (around 1.3–1.5 million victims, including Babi Yar 29–30 September 1941).
• 1942 stage: Wannsee Conference (20 January) coordinates the Final Solution; death camps at Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno, Majdanek receive deportations from across occupied Europe.
• Conclusion: the radicalisation was stepped, not single-step. War and occupation transformed legal exclusion into mass shooting and industrial murder. The functionalist consensus is that the move to industrial killing emerged from the conditions of 1941–42, even though Nazi ideology and Hitler's antisemitism were constants from 1933.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a textbook arguing the Holocaust was solely the murder of European Jews) and Interpretation B (a Holocaust Educational Trust resource arguing it should be remembered alongside the persecution of Sinti and Roma, disabled Germans and other targeted groups) on the victims of Nazi racial policy. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A focuses exclusively on Jewish victims as the defining target of Nazi racial policy.
• Interpretation B sets Jewish victims at the centre but extends the historical record to include Sinti and Roma, T4 victims, gay men and Soviet POWs.
• Main difference: A treats Holocaust history as singular; B treats it as centrally about Jewish victims but historically inseparable from the persecution of other groups.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about the Five Year Plans? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat the Plans as a triumph of socialist modernisation; B may treat them as a brutal forced-labour project that disguised quality failures.
• A may emphasise Magnitogorsk and tonnage gains; B may emphasise the White Sea Canal’s death toll.
• Specific textual reference required for both.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual reference. Secure: comparison with some reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about Stakhanovism in the 1930s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: a Soviet-era source celebrating Stakhanov to motivate workers versus a Western academic study analysing the propaganda.
• Different time of writing: 1930s contemporary versus post-1991 archive-based.
• Different perspective — orthodox Soviet versus revisionist (Fitzpatrick on workers’ daily life).
• Different evidence: official records versus worker memoirs.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the success of the Five Year Plans? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test specific claims of the interpretation against named context: coal output 35 to 64 million tonnes (1928-32), Magnitogorsk and the Dnieper Dam, USSR third-largest industrial economy by 1940.
• Weigh against quality failures, gulag labour disguised in totals, consumer goods scarcity, and accidents on crash construction sites.
• Cite historiographical positions — orthodox Soviet versus totalitarian and revisionist readings.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement, naming the metric.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge with clear judgement. Developing: knowledge unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Five Year Plans on Soviet workers in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Long hours and harsh discipline: lateness over 20 minutes a criminal offence by 1940.
• Internal passports controlling where workers could live; kolkhoz peasants tied to villages.
• Stakhanovite pressure to exceed norms; rewards for high producers, penalties for laggards.
• Crash construction caused accidents and shoddy quality, with frequent industrial injuries.
• Female employment rose from 3 to 13 million; women carried the ‘double burden’ at home.
• Wrecking trials scapegoated engineers for project failures.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description.]

practice_questions.text: ‘The Five Year Plans were primarily a programme of war preparation rather than economic modernisation.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Stalin’s aims, the showcase projects and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for war preparation:
• Stalin’s 1931 speech: ‘close this gap in ten years or they crush us.’
• Heavy industry priority — coal, steel, oil — the foundation of armaments.
• Third Plan (1938-41) explicitly turned to armaments; military spending hit nearly a third of expenditure by 1940.
• Industrial base survived Barbarossa — the test the Plans had been designed for.

Arguments for economic modernisation:
• Magnitogorsk, Dnieper Dam and the Moscow Metro were showcased as socialism, not weapons.
• Female employment, education and welfare gains had no military rationale.
• Stakhanovism celebrated production as a virtue in itself.
• Autarky aimed at long-term economic self-sufficiency, not just war readiness.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. modernisation and war preparation overlapped, but war was the deadline that drove every decision.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Stakhanovism on Soviet workers in the mid-1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Pressure to exceed output norms across factories and mines, with norms repeatedly raised.
• Rewards for top producers (housing, holidays, bonuses) created a privileged tier of workers.
• Peer hostility against Stakhanovites — some were physically attacked by colleagues whose norms they had raised.
• Reinforced Stalin’s message that production was a moral duty.
• Provided propaganda heroes that masked the use of forced labour and accident rates.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of Stakhanovism.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1953 conservative magazine article praising McCarthy for exposing real Communist subversion) and Interpretation B (a 1955 study by a civil-liberties lawyer condemning McCarthyism for destroying careers without evidence). What is the main difference between these views about McCarthyism?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents McCarthy as a defender of national security who uncovered real Communist activity inside the federal government.
• Interpretation B presents McCarthyism as a wave of unsubstantiated smears that destroyed innocent careers and narrowed American freedom of speech.
• Main difference: A frames McCarthy’s investigations as necessary national security work; B frames them as a civil-liberties disaster regardless of any genuine espionage.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1953 conservative magazine article praising McCarthy) and Interpretation B (a 1955 civil-liberties study condemning him) give different views about McCarthyism.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the magazine aimed to support the Republican Party at the height of the Cold War; the study aimed to defend civil liberties against future political smears.
• They use different evidence — the magazine cites the Hiss conviction and the Rosenbergs; the study cites the Hollywood blacklist and innocents fired without due process.
• They were written at different points — the 1953 article was published before the Army-McCarthy hearings exposed McCarthy’s methods; the 1955 study was written after his Senate censure made his methods publicly toxic.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Senator Joseph McCarthy alone caused the climate of fear in 1950s America.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the Red Scare in the United States?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because McCarthy’s February 1950 Wheeling speech, his Senate committee from 1953 and his Army-McCarthy hearings (1954) defined the public face of the Red Scare and gave it his name.
• Convincing because his unsubstantiated accusations made it electorally dangerous for senators, journalists and presidents (including Eisenhower) to challenge him.
• Less convincing because the climate of fear pre-dated McCarthy — HUAC began Hollywood hearings in October 1947, Truman’s federal loyalty programme began in March 1947, and the Hollywood blacklist was in place by November 1947.
• Less convincing because real Cold War events — the Soviet bomb (1949), the Communist victory in China (1949) and the Korean War (1950) — created the anxiety McCarthy exploited; the Hiss conviction (January 1950) and Rosenberg arrest (July 1950) appeared to confirm subversion regardless of McCarthy’s claims.
• Less convincing because by 1953 around 4.7 million federal workers had been investigated under Truman’s order, before McCarthy’s power was at its peak.
• Overall judgement: substantially overstated — McCarthy was a national symbol but the machinery of fear was wider, older and more institutional than one senator.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of HUAC’s 1947 hearings on Hollywood.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Created the Hollywood Ten case — ten writers and directors refused to answer the question on Communist Party membership and were jailed for contempt of Congress between 1947 and 1948.
• Triggered the Hollywood blacklist — the Waldorf Statement (November 1947) announced studios would not employ Communists; around 320 entertainment workers eventually lost their jobs.
• Drove leading figures abroad or into silence — Charlie Chaplin lost his US re-entry permit in 1952; composer Hanns Eisler was deported; many writers worked anonymously under pseudonyms for years.
• Reshaped American film — studios avoided controversial themes about race, poverty or trade unions for years; political conformity in mass culture became the norm and persisted into the early 1960s.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why McCarthyism became such a powerful political force in the United States between 1950 and 1954.
You may consider:
• Cold War setbacks abroad and espionage cases at home
• HUAC, federal loyalty programmes and Senator McCarthy himself.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• External shocks: Soviet atomic bomb (August 1949); Communist victory in China (October 1949); Korean War from June 1950.
• Espionage cases: Alger Hiss convicted of perjury (January 1950); Julius and Ethel Rosenberg arrested (July and August 1950), convicted (1951) and executed (1953).
• HUAC: October 1947 Hollywood hearings; Hollywood Ten jailed; Waldorf Statement; blacklist of around 320 entertainment workers.
• Truman’s Federal Loyalty Programme (Executive Order 9835, March 1947): around 4.7 million federal workers investigated by 1953; around 560 dismissed.
• McCarran Act 1950: required Communist organisations to register; vetoed by Truman, override by Congress.
• McCarthy’s rise: 9 February 1950 Wheeling speech; chairmanship of Senate Committee on Government Operations 1953–54; investigations of State Department, Voice of America, US Army.
• Press amplification: McCarthy’s charges repeated without checking; few senators willing to confront him.
• Limits: Army-McCarthy hearings (April–June 1954) and Welch’s ‘sense of decency’ rebuke; approval fell from 50% to 35%; Senate censure 67–22 in December 1954.
• Conclusion: McCarthyism was powerful because real Cold War events made fear plausible, federal and corporate machinery turned that fear into action, and McCarthy supplied a name and face to the campaign — but his exposure on television proved that the same media power could break him as quickly as it had built him.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Hollywood Ten case of 1947.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ten Hollywood screenwriters and directors refused on First Amendment grounds to answer HUAC’s question on Communist Party membership in October 1947.
• They were charged with contempt of Congress and jailed for between six and twelve months.
• Their refusal triggered the Waldorf Statement of November 1947, in which the major Hollywood studios announced they would not employ Communists.
• They became the first names on a blacklist that eventually reached around 320 entertainment-industry workers; many never worked under their own names again.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text: ‘War was the main factor in the end of the British Empire after 1945.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to war and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• War (in support): the Second World War left Britain with debts of more than twice its yearly national income and dependent on an American loan; rationing continued at home until 1954.
• War (in support): the 1942 fall of Singapore to Japan shattered the myth of European racial superiority in Asia, fuelling post-war independence movements.
• War (in support): the 1956 Suez Crisis showed Britain could not act militarily without US consent; decolonisation accelerated immediately afterwards.
• Ideas: anti-colonial nationalism — Gandhi’s satyagraha, Nkrumah’s positive action, Pan-Africanism — gave colonised people a programme and an identity.
• Role of individuals: Gandhi (1947 Indian independence), Nkrumah (1957 Ghana), Kenyatta (1963 Kenya), Macmillan (1960 Wind of Change) — key figures shaped the timing and form of decolonisation.
• Government: the 1945 Labour government’s welfare-state priorities and 1947 Indian independence Act; the 1957 Macmillan government’s acceptance of African independence.
• Economic resources: the post-war dollar gap and the financial crisis at Suez 1956 made empire unaffordable.
• Top-band judgement: war was decisive in creating the conditions (1945 bankruptcy, 1956 humiliation), but ideas and individuals shaped what filled the vacuum. The factors reinforced each other — nationalism existed before 1939, but the wars made imperial defence economically and politically impossible.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: ‘The role of individuals was the main factor in the end of the British Empire.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to the role of individuals and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Individuals (in support): Gandhi’s 1930 Salt March and 1942 Quit India campaign turned Indian National Congress into a mass movement that British rule could not contain.
• Individuals (in support): Nkrumah’s 1949 Convention People’s Party and his ‘positive action’ tactic produced Ghana’s 1957 independence — Britain’s first African retreat.
• Individuals (in support): Kenyatta’s leadership of KANU and his 1963 election as Kenyan Prime Minister; Macmillan’s 1960 Wind of Change speech accepting decolonisation.
• War: the World Wars left Britain economically incapable of imperial defence.
• Ideas: anti-colonial nationalism, Pan-Africanism and the discrediting of imperial racism after the Second World War.
• Suez 1956: a structural moment in which the US replaced Britain as the Western great power.
• Limitation: individuals worked within structures — Gandhi could not have produced 1947 without 1942 wartime destruction; Nkrumah could not have produced 1957 without Britain’s post-Suez economic weakness.
• Top-band judgement: individuals shaped the timing and the political form of independence, but the conditions that made it possible were created by war and economic exhaustion. Strongest answer: structural factors created a window; individuals decided who walked through it and on what terms.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1956 Suez Crisis for the end of the British Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: revealed Britain’s inability to defend the canal without US consent; Eisenhower’s pressure on the pound forced withdrawal in November 1956.
• At the time: Anthony Eden resigned in January 1957; Conservative politics turned decisively away from imperial confrontation.
• At the time: emboldened anti-colonial movements across the empire — Nasser’s defiance was celebrated from Cairo to Accra to Delhi.
• Over time: accelerated African decolonisation; within seven years Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Tanganyika, Uganda and Kenya had all become independent.
• Over time: confirmed the special relationship with the United States as the central feature of post-imperial British foreign policy.
• Limitation: decolonisation was already happening before Suez (India 1947, Sudan 1956); the crisis sped it up rather than starting it.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Mahatma Gandhi for the end of British rule in India.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: developed satyagraha (non-violent resistance) into a mass political technique through the 1920-22 non-cooperation movement, the 1930 Salt March and the 1942 Quit India campaign.
• At the time: turned Indian National Congress from an elite organisation into a movement British rule could not contain by force.
• At the time: gave Indian nationalism a moral authority that resonated globally, including with American public opinion that mattered to British post-war calculations.
• Over time: Gandhi’s methods were copied by Martin Luther King in the US Civil Rights movement and by Nkrumah’s Convention People’s Party in Ghana.
• Over time: his assassination in January 1948 by a Hindu nationalist exposed the limits of his vision and the human cost of partition.
• Limitation: Gandhi opposed partition and could not prevent it; structural factors (war, economic exhaustion) shaped the timing more than he did.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Indian and Pakistani independence in 1947 for the British Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Attlee sent Mountbatten as the last Viceroy and independence came on 14-15 August 1947, with boundaries drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in five weeks.
• At the time: partition displaced around 12 million people and killed at least one million; Gandhi opposed it and was assassinated in January 1948.
• At the time: Britain lost the ‘jewel in the crown’, the colony around which imperial strategy had been built since 1857.
• Over time: without the Indian Army and Indian revenue, holding the rest of the empire by force became far harder; Burma and Ceylon followed in 1948.
• Over time: independence gave a model to African nationalists, and Nkrumah’s ‘positive action’ was modelled on Gandhi’s methods.
• Limitation: Britain kept its African and Middle Eastern possessions for another decade, so 1947 began decolonisation rather than completing it.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Indian independence in 1947 was similar to or different from Ghanaian independence in 1957.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Indian independence was accompanied by partition into India and Pakistan, displacing around 12 million and killing at least one million; Ghanaian independence was a relatively peaceful transition under Nkrumah.
• Difference: India had a long-established nationalist movement (Congress founded 1885); Ghana’s Convention People’s Party was only founded in 1949.
• Similarity: both were led by individuals (Gandhi/Nehru in India, Nkrumah in Ghana) trained in mass non-violent campaigning.
• Similarity: both reflected post-war British incapacity to maintain empire by force, with economic exhaustion and US pressure shaping the timing.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named individuals.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the East India Company under Charles II.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It received the port of Bombay from Charles II in 1668 in return for an annual rent of £10, giving it a fortified harbour directly under its control.
• It was granted near-sovereign powers in its Indian territories, including the right to fortify, mint money, hold courts and raise its own troops.
• It maintained around 700 European soldiers in India by 1685 and the beginnings of an Indian sepoy army.
• It already operated factories at Surat and Madras and along the coasts of Java and Sumatra, dealing in cotton, spices, silks and indigo.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Royal African Company.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was first chartered in 1660 as the ‘Company of Royal Adventurers’ and refounded in 1672 with James, Duke of York as its governor and Charles II as a major shareholder.
• It held a monopoly on English trade with West Africa, including the transatlantic slave trade, until its monopoly was eroded after 1689.
• By the 1680s it was shipping about 5,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic every year.
• Enslaved people purchased by the Company were branded with the initials ‘DY’ for the Duke of York on the chest.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the English state came to run the slave trade under Charles II.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It made the Royal African Company one of the most profitable chartered companies of the period, shipping about 5,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic every year by the 1680s.
• It tied the English state directly into the trade through the king’s shareholding and James’s governorship, normalising state-backed slaving for the next century.
• It supplied the labour force for the sugar plantations of Jamaica and Barbados, generating customs revenue that helped finance Charles II’s rule without Parliament after 1681.
• It established the slave-trading network of forts on the West African coast (Cape Coast Castle and others) which would underwrite English commercial dominance in the eighteenth century.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Hudson’s Bay Company charter of 1670.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it gave England a chartered claim to the entire Hudson Bay watershed — an area named ‘Rupert’s Land’ after Prince Rupert, the Company’s first governor and the king’s cousin.
• It established a fur-trading network with Cree and other First Nations peoples, bringing beaver pelts into the English economy and challenging French dominance in Canada.
• Significance over time: the Hudson’s Bay Company is the oldest continuously operating commercial company in North America and its 1670 charter underpinned English claims to most of modern Canada.
• It established the model of a chartered company governing vast non-European territory with quasi-governmental powers, a model copied for the East India Company and Royal African Company.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how Catherine of Braganza’s 1662 dowry extended England’s overseas reach.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It brought Bombay (modern Mumbai) to the English Crown, which Charles II handed to the East India Company in 1668 as the foundation of English Indian power.
• It brought Tangier on the North African coast, which guarded the entrance to the Mediterranean; the cost of holding it ran to roughly £1.5 million across the reign before evacuation in 1684.
• It gave English merchants trading rights in Brazil and the Portuguese East Indies, opening new commercial opportunities.
• It allied England with Portugal against Spain, supporting Portuguese independence and English Atlantic and Indian Ocean trade.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A (written for practice): ‘The chartered trading companies were the most lasting thing Charles II’s reign produced.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the legacy of Charles II’s reign for England’s place in the world? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Reasons the interpretation is convincing:
• The East India Company, granted Bombay in 1668 and near-sovereign powers in its Indian territories, became the institutional vehicle of British rule in India for the next two centuries.
• The Royal African Company under James, Duke of York normalised state-backed slaving and built the West African fort network that anchored English commerce in the eighteenth century.
• The Hudson’s Bay Company chartered in 1670 created an English claim to most of modern Canada and is still operating, the longest-lived such company in North American history.

Reasons it is less convincing:
• Pepys’s naval reforms after 1668 created the first generation of English ships of the line, without which the chartered companies could not have been protected.
• Royal patronage of the arts and sciences (Royal Society 1662, Royal Observatory 1675) gave English science and architecture an enduring world-leading reputation.
• The Tory reaction after 1681 and the strong financial position Charles II left to James II shaped the political landscape that the Glorious Revolution would then reorder.

[8 marks — judge how convincing the interpretation is, using its own wording and your own knowledge.]

Mastering: Detail from the interpretation weighed against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement.
Secure: Points for and against, supported with relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Emerging: Simple comment on the interpretation.

practice_questions.text: ‘Iraq was stable by the end of George W. Bush’s presidency in January 2009.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: the 2007 surge under Petraeus and the Sunni Awakening in Anbar cut civilian deaths sharply through 2008.
• Agree: elections had been held under the January 2004 constitution, and Saddam had been tried and executed in December 2006.
• Agree: the Status of Forces Agreement of November 2008 set a credible timetable for US combat troops to leave by the end of 2011.
• Disagree: around four million Iraqis were displaced, and more than 100,000 documented civilian deaths had been recorded since 2003.
• Disagree: Maliki’s government was Shia-dominated, leaned on Iranian backing and excluded Sunni political participation.
• Disagree: the surge reduced violence without settling the sectarian question, and ISIS emerged from the same Sunni areas within five years.
• Judgement: Iraq was far less violent in January 2009 than in 2006–07, but stability needs a political settlement, and that had not been reached.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: Photograph published in international news media in 2004 showing a hooded prisoner standing on a box with wires attached to his hands, taken by US military police at the Abu Ghraib prison, Iraq.

Study Source A. Source A suggests that the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib was treated as routine by some of those guarding them. How do you know? Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two supported inferences each rooted in a precise detail of the source.
Secure: Two inferences with at least one detail.
Developing: One inference with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the photograph without inference.

Indicative content:
• The fact that US military police took the photograph themselves implies abuse was treated by some service personnel as routine or even celebratory rather than concealed, suggesting weak supervision and a culture failure within the prison’s chain of command.
• The choice of imagery — hooded, posed, with mock electrical wires — implies that humiliation was a tool of interrogation rather than an unintended by-product, raising questions about the wider detention regime authorised in 2003–04.
• The publication of the image in international media in May 2004 implies that strategic damage was severe: the image circulated in al-Qaeda recruitment material and stripped the war of its human-rights framing.
• The fact that only enlisted soldiers, not their commanders, were court-martialled implies that institutional accountability was limited, deepening the legitimacy crisis the photograph caused.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the war in Iraq developed between the fall of Baghdad in April 2003 and the al-Askari shrine bombing in February 2006.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more turning points (Baghdad falls April 2003; CPA Orders 1 and 2 May 2003; ‘Mission Accomplished’ 1 May 2003; insurgency from late 2003; Saddam captured December 2003; Abu Ghraib April 2004; transitional government June 2004; elections December 2005; Samarra February 2006) as a chain of cause and consequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; some links missing.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 9 April 2003: Baghdad falls; the regime collapses but no plan exists for the transition.
• May 2003: CPA Orders 1 and 2 dissolve the Iraqi army and exclude Ba’ath-party members from public life, creating a pool of armed unemployed Sunni Arabs.
• Late 2003: insurgent attacks against coalition forces escalate; IEDs become the signature weapon.
• 13 December 2003: Saddam is captured near Tikrit but the war does not abate.
• April 2004: the publication of the Abu Ghraib photographs damages the war’s legitimacy at home and abroad.
• June 2004: a transitional government takes office; al-Qaeda in Iraq emerges as a foreign-fighter network.
• December 2005: parliamentary elections produce a Shia-dominated government with weak Sunni participation.
• 22 February 2006: the al-Askari Shia shrine in Samarra is bombed; sectarian civil war begins.

practice_questions.text: ‘Dissolving the Iraqi army and excluding Ba’ath-party members from public office were the most damaging Western decisions of the Iraq War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: CPA Order 2 sent around 400,000 soldiers home unpaid and armed, handing the insurgency a pool of trained recruits.
• Agree: CPA Order 1 removed a generation of Sunni Arab teachers, doctors, engineers and officials from public life in a single stroke.
• Agree: the Chilcot Inquiry and the US Army’s own histories judged these the most damaging Western policy decisions of the war.
• Disagree: the decision to invade with no plan for the occupation was the prior failure that made everything after it harder.
• Disagree: the Abu Ghraib photographs of 2004 stripped the occupation of its moral standing and gave al-Qaeda in Iraq its recruiting imagery.
• Disagree: unsecured ammunition dumps supplied the artillery shells used in roadside bombs, a separate and avoidable failure.
• Judgement: the two CPA orders did the deepest structural damage, because they built the Sunni alienation that outlasted the occupation itself.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how violence in Iraq was reduced between the announcement of the surge in January 2007 and the end of the Bush presidency in January 2009.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence, with precise factual detail.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology without causal links.

Indicative content:
• January 2007: Bush announced an additional 30,000 US troops, mostly for Baghdad, under General David Petraeus.
• The new counter-insurgency doctrine put troops among the population to protect civilians rather than hunting fighters from large bases.
• Through 2007 Sunni tribes in Anbar province turned against al-Qaeda in Iraq and accepted American support, the Sunni Awakening.
• Together these cut the flow of foreign fighters and the sectarian killing that had peaked after the Samarra bombing of February 2006.
• Civilian deaths fell sharply in 2008, and in November 2008 the Status of Forces Agreement set a withdrawal timetable running to the end of 2011.
• Violence fell without a political settlement, and Maliki continued to exclude Sunni participation.

practice_questions.text: ‘The wars of 1991 and 2003 both ended without solving Iraq’s problems.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides argued with precise evidence and a sustained line of reasoning.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides and a judgement.
Developing: Some argument with limited evidence.
Emerging: Description with little judgement.
Note: the 4 SPaG marks on this paper are attached to this question.

Indicative content:
• Agree: in 1991 Saddam survived, the Shia and Kurdish uprisings were crushed, and twelve years of sanctions and no-fly zones followed.
• Agree: by 2009 Iraq had elections and a constitution but also four million displaced people and a government with no Sunni reach.
• Agree: in both cases the military verdict came far faster than any political settlement, and in both the settlement never arrived.
• Disagree: 1991 achieved its stated aim, the liberation of Kuwait, and upheld the principle that borders cannot be changed by force.
• Disagree: 2003 removed a regime responsible for Halabja and the 1991 massacres, and Saddam was tried and executed.
• Disagree: the two end-states were very different — a stable if brutal dictatorship in 1991, a fragile sectarian state in 2009.
• Judgement: both wars ended with the central political question unresolved, which is why ISIS could seize Mosul five years after 2009.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the Munich Agreement, signed on 30 September 1938 by Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler and Mussolini.
‘Germany, the United Kingdom, France and Italy, taking into consideration the agreement which has already been reached in principle for the cession to Germany of the Sudeten German territory, have agreed on the following terms and conditions governing the said cession. The evacuation will begin on 1 October. It will be completed by 10 October.’

Using Source A, identify two terms of the Munich Agreement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded terms with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear terms, briefly supported.
Developing: One term clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific terms.

Indicative content:
• The Sudeten German territory would be ceded to Germany.
• Evacuation by Czechoslovak forces would begin on 1 October 1938.
• Evacuation would be completed by 10 October 1938.
• Implicit term: the agreement was made by the four powers, not Czechoslovakia.

practice_questions.text:
Study Sources B and C.

Source B: An extract from a 1938 newspaper report on Chamberlain’s return to 10 Downing Street, holding the Anglo-German declaration signed at Munich.
‘The Prime Minister waved the famous piece of paper before a delighted London crowd. “My good friends,” he said, “this is the second time in our history that there has come back from Germany to Downing Street peace with honour. I believe it is peace for our time.”’

Source C: An extract from a 1938 private memorandum by President Edvard Beneš of Czechoslovakia, written shortly after the Munich Conference.
‘We have been betrayed by friends to whom we owed loyalty. France was bound to us by treaty since 1924; she has not honoured it. Britain spoke of self-determination but applied it only on the German side. We were not at the table where our country was divided. We have lost the fortifications, the industry, the strategic depth. The state will not survive.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Munich Agreement. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each.
Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description or accusations of bias.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: a celebratory British public scene as Chamberlain announces ‘peace for our time’. Provenance: a contemporary newspaper report designed for British readers, capturing public mood at a single moment. Own knowledge: confirms the historical record — Chamberlain genuinely believed he had bought lasting peace; British and French opinion was overwhelmingly relieved; Churchill’s ‘defeat without a war’ verdict was a minority view.
Source C — Content: the bitter Czech presidential view that Britain and France had abandoned a treaty ally and divided the country in its absence. Provenance: a private memorandum by the Czechoslovak President; not designed for public consumption; reflects the perspective of the country most directly harmed. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — France had a treaty obligation to Czechoslovakia from 1924; Czechoslovakia was not at the conference; the Sudetenland contained the country’s mountain fortifications and a third of its industry; Beneš resigned shortly afterwards.
Judgement: B is useful as a snapshot of British public reaction but partial — it reflects relief, not strategic judgement; C is highly useful for the Czech perspective and for the practical consequences, but reflects a national grievance and not the wider picture of British constraints.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the Sudeten Crisis from the May 1938 Czech mobilisation to the signing of the Munich Agreement on 30 September.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• May 1938: Czech partial mobilisation in response to false rumours of German troop movements; the ‘May Crisis’ showed the Czechs would resist.
• Spring-summer 1938: Henlein’s Sudeten German Party raised demands the Czech government could not meet, on Berlin’s instructions.
• 12 September 1938: Hitler’s Nuremberg speech demanded self-determination for the Sudeten Germans; riots followed; the Czech government declared martial law.
• 15 September 1938: Chamberlain flew to Berchtesgaden; accepted the principle of cession.
• 22 September 1938: Bad Godesberg meeting; Hitler raised demands to immediate military occupation; Chamberlain refused; war preparations began.
• 28 September 1938: Mussolini proposed a four-power conference.
• 29-30 September 1938: Munich Conference; Britain, France, Germany and Italy agreed terms; Czechoslovakia was not present.
• 1-10 October 1938: German occupation of the Sudetenland; Poland seized Teschen; Hungary took further border areas.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Munich Agreement left Czechoslovakia defenceless between October 1938 and March 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 1-10 October 1938: the Sudetenland was transferred to Germany, taking with it the mountain fortifications that formed the country’s western defence.
• October 1938: Poland seized the Teschen district and Hungary took further border areas; Slovakia and Ruthenia gained autonomy.
• The rump state lost around a third of its industrial capacity and most of its strategic depth, and the German border now ran close to Prague.
• Beneš resigned and went into exile; Emil Hácha became President.
• 14-15 March 1939: Slovakia declared independence under German encouragement and Hácha was pressured in Berlin into accepting a German protectorate.
• 15 March 1939: German troops entered Prague, and the state that Munich had left standing ceased to exist.

practice_questions.text:
‘Munich was a greater surrender to Hitler than the Anschluss.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• At Munich Britain and France negotiated and signed away the territory of a state that was not in the room; Beneš was kept in an antechamber.
• Czechoslovakia lost its mountain fortifications, around a third of its industry and its strategic depth, leaving the rump state indefensible.
• France had been bound to Czechoslovakia by treaty since 1924 and did not honour it, which told every small state what French treaties were worth.
Challenging the statement:
• Anschluss annexed a whole sovereign state, while Munich transferred only the Sudetenland.
• Anschluss was a unilateral act that Britain and France met with protest alone, so no one signed anything away.
• Munich could be presented as self-determination for three million Germans, which made it far easier to defend at the time.
Judgement: Anschluss took more territory, but Munich was the greater surrender because Britain and France put their names to it.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of Chamberlain’s shuttle diplomacy across September 1938, from his Berchtesgaden meeting on 15 September to his return to Downing Street on 30 September.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 15 September 1938: Chamberlain flew to Berchtesgaden; agreed to the principle that the Sudetenland should be transferred to Germany.
• 19 September 1938: Anglo-French note urged the Czech government to accept transfer; Beneš gave way.
• 22 September 1938: Chamberlain met Hitler at Bad Godesberg; Hitler raised demands to immediate military occupation; Chamberlain refused.
• 24-27 September 1938: war preparations — Royal Navy mobilised, gas masks distributed in Britain, French reservists called up.
• 28 September 1938: Mussolini, alarmed at war, proposed a four-power conference.
• 29-30 September 1938: Munich Conference; agreement signed in the early hours of 30 September.
• 30 September 1938: Chamberlain met Hitler privately and signed the Anglo-German declaration; flew back to London and announced ‘peace for our time’.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the design of Acton Burnell Castle.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A compact rectangular red sandstone block with a tower at each corner and battlements licensed in 1284 — castle costume on a house.
• Large, elegant windows set low in the walls, where a real fortress would have arrow slits.
• A first-floor great hall with private chambers, designed for administration, entertaining and comfort.
• No moat, strong curtain wall, gatehouse or garrison accommodation.
• The great barn nearby, whose surviving gable ends mark the traditional meeting place of the 1283 parliament.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Robert Burnell’s career for the house he built.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Chancellor of England from 1274 until his death in 1292 — head of Edward's administration for nearly the whole working reign.
• Bishop of Bath and Wells from 1275 — church office and income stacked on state office.
• Enormous landed wealth accumulated through royal service, funding building at his birthplace village.
