• A professional administrator rather than a warrior baron — the new kind of power the house embodies.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of why it mattered, with precise detail and clear links to wider events.
Secure: Two developed reasons, each supported with relevant detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but the answer stays descriptive.
Emerging: Simple statements with no real explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the licence to crenellate granted for Acton Burnell in 1284.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It shows fortification as status: by the 1280s a licence advertised royal favour more than military need, and Burnell's battlements were ornament on a domestic house.
• It shows royal control: even the appearance of fortification in England required the king's permission — a contrast with the anarchy of private castles in earlier reigns.
• Its timing shows the reward culture around Edward's servants: granted at the height of Burnell's indispensability, alongside the parliament held at his manor.
• It supports the site's biggest argument: England at peace, where defence had become display.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the parliament held at Acton Burnell in 1283 and what came of it.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Context: autumn 1283, Edward in the Welsh Marches following the second Welsh war and the fall of Dafydd; government travelling with the king.
• The setting: parliament summoned to the Shropshire manor of the Chancellor, Robert Burnell; tradition places the sessions in the great barn whose gable ends survive.
• The outcome: the Statute of Acton Burnell, letting merchants register debts before mayors and recover them quickly, strengthened by the Statute of Merchants at Westminster in 1285.
• The meaning: royal law reaching into commercial life, credit protected because Edward's wars ran on it, and a private house hosting national government.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Acton Burnell as evidence about government in Edward I’s England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The rise of the administrator: the house was built not by birth or conquest but by office — Burnell's chancellorship turned service into stone.
• Government on the move: a parliament at a minister's rural manor shows royal government operating wherever the king stood.
• Law for commerce: the 1283 statute connects the site to wool, credit and the Italian bankers financing Edward's wars.
• Peace as the precondition: a chief minister could build for comfort in the Midlands because royal justice, not private war, ruled England.

practice_questions.text: 'Acton Burnell shows that castles were no longer needed in Edward I's England.' How far does a study of Acton Burnell support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Acton Burnell and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The building itself: great windows, first-floor hall, no serious defences — a house in castle costume, safe in a governed shire.
• The licence to crenellate as honour rather than necessity shows fortification reduced to heraldry in England.
• The barn parliament and debt statute show a realm ruled by law, parliaments and credit — the tools that had replaced garrisons.
Against the statement (contextual knowledge):
• The same regime was simultaneously building Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech — where rule was contested, true castles were still indispensable.
• Within twenty years, Scottish war would show fortresses deciding campaigns (Lessons 10-11).
• So the accurate judgement is geographical: castles were no longer needed in the pacified English heartland, and precisely because royal power there rested on the law and finance the site itself commemorates.
A developed judgement distinguishing England from the reign's frontiers is required for the top level.

practice_questions.text: ‘The anchorage at Calais was the main reason the Armada failed.’ How far does a study of the Armada campaign support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the campaign and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Calais was an open roadstead, not a harbour: the fleet lay exposed to wind and to attack, with no shelter, no repairs and no resupply.
• Ships anchored close together in the open were the perfect target for fireships; the crescent that a week of gunfire had failed to break was scattered in a single night.
• Cutting the cables to escape left the fleet without its best anchors, which is why so many ships were driven ashore on the Scottish and Irish coasts weeks later.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• The fleet was only at Calais because Spain held no deep-water port on the invasion coast — the flaw was on the map before the anchorage was ever used.
• Parma’s army could not come out while Dutch flyboats watched the shallow ports of Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort, so the rendezvous would have failed anyway.
• Race-built galleons, culverins and English home ports won the running fight up the Channel and the close action at Gravelines on 29 July.
• Autumn storms on the north-about route home destroyed more ships than any single moment of the campaign.

[16 marks — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the English fleet’s ships and home ports in 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Race-built galleons — longer, lower and faster than the Spanish ships, designed for gunnery rather than boarding.
• Long-range culverins, allowing the English to bombard from distances at which Spanish soldiers could not grapple and board.
• Home ports along the Channel (Plymouth and the anchorages up-Channel), giving resupply of powder, shot and food that the Armada, far from any friendly harbour, could not match.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Spain’s lack of a deep-water port for the outcome of the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It broke the rendezvous: the Armada could not wait safely anywhere near Parma's army, while Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort were too shallow for the galleons and blockaded by Dutch flyboats.
• It forced the fleet into the exposed Calais roadstead — the precondition for the fireship attack that broke the crescent without a battle.
• It denied repair and resupply: every English ship fought a day's sail from a friendly port; the Armada fought at the end of a supply line stretching to Spain.
• Ultimately it made the whole plan depend on perfect timing between a fleet and an army that could not communicate — a flaw visible on the map before a shot was fired.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the fireship attack at Calais changed the course of the Armada campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The situation on 27 July: the Armada anchored in the open roadstead, ammunition low, Parma needing days he did not have, the English fleet anchored to windward.
• The attack: eight fireships, loaded with pitch and powder, sent down the wind in darkness into the packed anchorage.
• The immediate result: captains cut their cables; the crescent formation that a week of gunnery had failed to break was scattered in one night.
• The consequences: the scattered fleet was caught at Gravelines short of shot; the abandoned anchors doomed ships on the storm coasts of the north-about route home.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the weather in the defeat of the Spanish Armada.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The weather gauge: holding the upwind position let the English choose the range and timing of every engagement in the Channel.
• The double shift after Gravelines: wind first drove the Armada towards the Zeeland sandbanks, then backed just in time to spare it — but pushed it into the North Sea, making the north-about route the only way home.
• The autumn gales: storms on the Scottish and Irish coasts destroyed more ships than English gunfire, finishing a fleet that could no longer anchor.
• Balance: weather alone does not explain the defeat — the plan's geographical flaw and English gunnery created the situation the storms completed; 'God blew and they were scattered' was propaganda as well as piety.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: 'The Spanish Armada was defeated by geography rather than by the English navy.' How far does a study of the Armada campaign support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the campaign and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The missing deep-water port made the rendezvous with Parma close to impossible before the fleets ever met.
• The Calais roadstead's exposure enabled the fireships; the Zeeland banks nearly wrecked the fleet; the north-about route and Atlantic storms destroyed perhaps half of it — far more than battle did.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• English choices exploited the geography: refusing to board, holding the weather gauge, striking with fireships at the one moment the anchorage made them decisive.
• Race-built ships and culverins won Gravelines on gunnery, breaking ships and morale before the storms took over.
• The Dutch flyboat blockade — allied action, not geography — pinned Parma in port.
A developed judgement weighing environmental causes against human agency is required for the top level.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a German army diary entry by Captain Rudolf Binding, written near the Somme on 28 March 1918.
‘We have advanced further in seven days than the Allies advanced in the whole of 1916. The British defences crumbled before our barrage and our infantry. Yet our supplies cannot keep pace with our men, and the men themselves are tired beyond what fresh divisions can fix. The advance has begun to outrun what we can hold.’

Source A suggests that the Spring Offensive advanced fast but could not sustain itself. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• The Germans advanced further in seven days than the Allies had in the whole of 1916.
• ‘The British defences crumbled before our barrage and our infantry.’
• ‘Our supplies cannot keep pace with our men.’
• The men are ‘tired beyond what fresh divisions can fix’.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Operation Michael opened on 21 March 1918 with 6,600 guns and stormtroop infiltration tactics.
• Germany lost about a million men between March and July 1918, including elite divisions it could not replace.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the German Spring Offensive developed between its opening on 21 March 1918 and the Allied counter-attack on the Marne on 18 July 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Operation Michael 21 March, Foch as Generalissimo 26 March, Haig ‘backs to the wall’, the five offensives, Marne 18 July); reaches the close through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 21 March 1918: Operation Michael opened with 6,600 guns firing over a million shells in five hours; stormtrooper tactics broke the British Fifth Army.
• 26 March 1918: Marshal Foch appointed Allied Generalissimo, coordinating all Allied forces — a direct response to the breakthrough.
• 11 April 1918: Haig issued his ‘backs to the wall’ order during Operation Georgette.
• April–June 1918: further offensives (Blücher, Gneisenau) reached the Marne and were within 50 miles of Paris but missed strategic objectives.
• Through July: stormtrooper logistics broke down; about a million German casualties from March to July, including elite divisions Ludendorff could not replace.
• 18 July 1918: French and American counter-attack at the Marne (the Friedensturm offensive) ended the German initiative for good.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by General Erich Ludendorff to Field Marshal von Hindenburg, dated 9 August 1918.
‘Yesterday — the eighth of August — was the black day of the German army. The morale of certain divisions on the Amiens front broke under the combined assault of tanks, aircraft and an artillery barrage we had not anticipated. We can no longer count on victory. Defensive war has become our only option.’

Source C: An extract from the British official despatch on the Battle of Amiens, written by Field Marshal Haig and forwarded to the War Cabinet on 12 August 1918.
‘On 8 August our Fourth Army, supported by 552 tanks and 800 aircraft, attacked along an eleven-mile front. The advance reached eight miles by nightfall. Some 13,000 prisoners and 200 guns were taken. The German army did not stand and fight in the manner we had grown to expect.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Battle of Amiens (8 August 1918). Use the sources and your own knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Ludendorff’s blunt admission that 8 August broke the German army. Provenance: an internal memo to his superior; written candidly to alert command, not to perform. Own knowledge: Amiens combined 552 tanks, 800 aircraft, predicted fire and combined-arms infantry — the BEF’s mature toolkit.
Source C — Content: Haig’s detailed numbers (552 tanks, 800 aircraft, 13,000 prisoners, 200 guns, eight miles in a day) confirm the scale and method. Provenance: an official despatch by the British commander to the War Cabinet, well-placed but partly intended to defend his command’s record. Own knowledge: 8 August opened the Hundred Days; ~188,000 German prisoners were taken by British and Empire troops between August and November 1918.
Judgement: Both highly useful. B is unusually candid for a senior German commander, providing rare insight into German morale; C is detailed and procedural, with the limit that Haig had reasons to highlight British achievement. Together they build a strong picture of the battle’s tactical and psychological impact.

practice_questions.text:
‘Germany lost the war because of internal collapse on the home front, not military defeat.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• The blockade killed around 750,000 German civilians and left the cities close to starvation.
• Sailors mutinied at Kiel on 3 November 1918 rather than sail, and workers' councils took over in Munich and other cities.
• The Kaiser abdicated on 9 November and the new republican government asked for terms.
• Germany's allies gave way first: Bulgaria on 29 September, the Ottoman Empire on 30 October and Austria-Hungary on 3 November.

Disagree:
• The German army was beaten in the field: Amiens on 8 August was Ludendorff's ‘black day’ and the Hindenburg Line fell in late September.
• British and Empire troops took about 188,000 German prisoners between August and November 1918.
• The Spring Offensive had already destroyed Germany's best divisions, with about a million casualties from March to July.
• The collapse at home followed the defeats: the mutiny began when sailors were ordered out on a hopeless sortie.

Judgement: The home front did collapse, but it collapsed because the army had been beaten. Military defeat came first and brought the rest on.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the diary of British civil servant Sir Maurice Hankey, secretary to the British War Cabinet, recording events in early November 1918.
‘News from Kiel: sailors mutinied rather than put to sea against the Royal Navy. Workers’ councils now reported in Munich. The Kaiser’s position is untenable. A republican government will form within days, and we shall meet German envoys in Foch’s railway carriage at Compiègne. The eleventh hour approaches.’

Source F suggests that the German collapse in November 1918 was happening at both the naval and the civilian level. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Sailors at Kiel ‘mutinied rather than put to sea against the Royal Navy’.
• Workers' councils are ‘now reported in Munich’.
• ‘The Kaiser's position is untenable’ and a republican government is expected within days.
• German envoys are about to meet Foch at Compiègne.

Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Kiel mutiny began on 3 November 1918, after orders for a final sortie in late October.
• The Kaiser abdicated on 9 November and the armistice was signed at 5am on 11 November.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Hundred Days campaign drove Germany from the Battle of Amiens on 8 August 1918 to the armistice on 11 November 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events with causation; precise dates and details (Amiens, Hindenburg Line breakthrough, allied collapses, Kiel mutiny, abdication, Compiègne); reaches the armistice through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 8 August 1918: Battle of Amiens; combined-arms attack with 552 tanks, 800 aircraft, predicted fire and infantry took eight miles in a day. Ludendorff called it ‘the black day of the German army’.
• Late September 1918: Allied breakthrough of the Hindenburg Line at the Canal du Nord (27 Sept) and St Quentin Canal (29 Sept); ~188,000 German prisoners taken by BEF over the Hundred Days.
• 29 September 1918: Bulgaria signed armistice; 30 October Ottoman Empire; 3 November Austria-Hungary.
• 3 November 1918: sailors at Kiel mutinied after orders for a final sortie in late October; the mutiny spread inland.
• 9 November 1918: Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated; a German republic was declared.
• 5am, 11 November 1918: armistice signed in Foch’s railway carriage at Compiègne; ceasefire took effect at 11am, ending the war.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the arrival of HMT Empire Windrush in 1948 for post-war Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 492 Caribbean migrants arrived weeks before the 1948 British Nationality Act became law, and it made every Commonwealth citizen a UK and Colonies citizen from January 1949.
• At the time: filled labour shortages in the new NHS, London Transport, British Rail and northern textile mills; around 250,000 Caribbean migrants followed by 1962.
• Over time: triggered the 1958 Notting Hill attacks and the racist murder of Kelso Cochrane in 1959, generating Claudia Jones’s West Indian Gazette and the indoor Caribbean Carnival.
• Over time: led to the 1962 and 1971 Commonwealth Immigrants Acts which restricted the rights the 1948 Act had created.
• Over time: produced the 2018 Windrush scandal, in which descendants of the original arrivals were wrongly detained, denied services and deported — a live political legacy 70 years later.
• Limitation: Black presence in Britain pre-dates Windrush by centuries; the symbolic significance is greater than the demographic novelty.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Claudia Jones for post-war Black British political and cultural life.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: founded the West Indian Gazette in March 1958, Britain’s first major Black newspaper, four months before the Notting Hill attacks.
• At the time: organised the 1959 indoor Caribbean Carnival at St Pancras Town Hall — a public statement of Caribbean cultural pride after the 1958 violence.
• At the time: campaigned against the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act and helped build the community organising that matured in the 1970s.
• Over time: her carnival became today’s Notting Hill Carnival — the largest street festival in Europe and the most visible cultural product of post-1948 migration.
• Over time: Jones is increasingly central to British school curricula on Black British history, with a Royal Mail stamp issued in 2008 and her 100th birthday commemorated in 2015.
• Limitation: she died young (1964); her organisations did not survive long after her, but the carnival did.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1972 Ugandan Asian arrival in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Idi Amin’s August 1972 expulsion order gave around 80,000 Ugandan Asians 90 days to leave; around 27,200 came to Britain.
• At the time: one of the largest single refugee arrivals in modern British history; the Heath government’s Uganda Resettlement Board ran reception camps.
• At the time: domestic opposition was strong — Enoch Powell campaigned against admission — but the government accepted Britain’s responsibility to British passport-holders.
• Over time: many Ugandan Asians became business owners and professionals in Leicester, the East Midlands and London; Leicester became Britain’s most diverse city by the 2011 census.
• Over time: the resettlement is now used as a positive case study of refugee integration in policy debates.
• Limitation: the 27,200 admitted were British passport-holders; without that legal status the response might have been very different.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Government was the main factor shaping Commonwealth migration to Britain between 1948 and 1981.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Government (in support): the 1948 British Nationality Act made every Commonwealth citizen a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies, opening the door.
• Government (in support): the 1962 and 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Acts and the 1971 Immigration Act closed it again, the last using ‘patriality’ to favour those with a British-born parent or grandparent.
• Economic resources: post-war labour shortages pulled migrants into the NHS, London Transport, British Rail and the northern mills, and the Caribbean had high unemployment.
• Ideas: racism shaped both the reception migrants met and the law, from ‘No Irish, No Blacks, No Dogs’ signs to the patriality rule.
• Role of individuals: Enoch Powell recruited Caribbean nurses as Minister of Health and later campaigned against admission; Claudia Jones built Black political and cultural organisation; Heath admitted 27,200 Ugandan Asians in 1972.
• Judgement: government set the legal frame at every stage, but it was responding to labour demand and to public opinion, so its decisions were as much effect as cause.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Caribbean migration to Britain after 1948 was similar to or different from Ugandan Asian arrival in 1972.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Caribbean migration was a continuous economic flow over 14 years (1948-62); Ugandan Asian arrival was a one-off refugee crisis compressed into 90 days in 1972.
• Difference: Caribbean migrants came to fill labour shortages in low-wage sectors; Ugandan Asians arrived as established professionals and traders dispossessed of their businesses by Amin.
• Similarity: both were British subjects exercising rights established by post-1948 nationality law — that legal status shaped the British government’s ability to admit them.
• Similarity: both faced significant domestic opposition (Notting Hill 1958, Powell’s 1972 campaign), but became central to the cities they settled in (London for Caribbean migrants, Leicester for Ugandan Asians).

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named events.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1982 Falklands War for British post-imperial identity.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 255 British and 649 Argentinian servicemen died; Argentina surrendered on 14 June 1982 after a 74-day campaign.
• At the time: revived a patriotic sentiment that the post-Suez generation had thought impossible; Thatcher’s government won a landslide in the 1983 general election partly on the back of the war.
• At the time: confirmed the principle that the remaining British Overseas Territories were defended by their inhabitants’ choice rather than imperial possession.
• Over time: shaped Argentine politics for a generation — the defeat brought down the military junta and helped restore democracy.
• Over time: the war complicated the British post-imperial story: a state that had spent 30 years dismantling empire was willing to fight for the last fragments.
• Limitation: the Falklands were tiny in scale (around 2,000 inhabitants); the symbolic significance is far greater than the geopolitical.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1939 foreign-press article impressed by the orderly, modern image of Nazi Germany at the 1936 Berlin Olympics) and Interpretation B (a post-war social history arguing the same Olympics functioned as a temporary propaganda mask) on Nazi propaganda. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Olympics at face value — orderly, modern, internationally engaged.
• Interpretation B presents the Olympics as a managed performance — antisemitic posters temporarily removed, foreign visitors carefully steered.
• Main difference: A reads the regime through its propaganda; B reads through what propaganda was hiding.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1939 foreign-press article on the 1936 Olympics) and Interpretation B (a post-war social history) give different views about Nazi propaganda.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They had access to different evidence — the 1939 article saw only what foreign visitors were allowed to see; the post-war historian had archival access to ministerial directives.
• They had different purposes — the 1939 article aimed at a foreign audience interested in international sport; the historian aimed to assess Nazi public-relations strategy.
• They were written in different times — 1939 was before the war exposed Nazi violence; post-war work after Nuremberg trial evidence had accumulated.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Nazi propaganda created total support for the regime among the German population.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about Nazi control over German society?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because Goebbels controlled press, radio, film and culture from March 1933 — around 70% of households had a Volksempfanger by 1939.
• Convincing because mass rallies, Triumph of the Will and the 1936 Olympics produced unparalleled spectacle and projected national unity.
• Less convincing because resistance persisted — the Confessional Church, Bonhoeffer, Niemoller; Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth among the young; Catholic mass attendance largely held up.
• Less convincing because the Gestapo had only around 32,000 officers and depended on civilian denunciation — suggesting tacit acceptance and self-policing rather than positive belief.
• Less convincing because oral histories show older Germans often saw through the propaganda; younger children absorbed it more thoroughly.
• Overall judgement: Nazi propaganda achieved unprecedented reach but conviction was uneven; consent and coercion blurred together; total support is too strong a claim.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Goebbels's control of radio and film on Nazi Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Radio reached around 70% of homes by 1939 through the cheap Volksempfanger; loudspeaker pillars in workplaces and squares amplified Hitler's speeches.
• The deliberately limited tuning range of the Volksempfanger neutralised foreign broadcasting (BBC German service) for most ordinary Germans.
• Film, including Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will (1935) and Olympia (1938), set a new standard for political cinema and shaped international perceptions of the regime.
• Wochenschau newsreels framed every cinema visit with Nazi-approved coverage of the war, rallies and Hitler — meaning even non-political audiences were exposed to regime messaging.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how the Nazi regime maintained control over the German population.
You may consider:
• the role of propaganda and culture (Goebbels, Volksempfanger, rallies)
• the role of the police state (SS, Gestapo, concentration camps, civilian informers).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Propaganda: Reich Ministry from March 1933; Reich Chamber of Culture controlling press, radio, film, art; Volksempfanger reaching 70% of homes by 1939.
• Spectacle: Nuremberg rallies from 1933; Triumph of the Will (1935); Olympia (1938); 1936 Berlin Olympics.
• Censorship and culture: 1933 book burnings; 1937 Degenerate Art exhibition; blood-and-soil realism; Speer's monumental architecture.
• Police state: SS expanding from around 200 to 240,000 by 1939; Himmler unifying Reich police from 1936; concentration camps holding around 25,000 by 1939; Volksgerichtshof for political offences.
• Gestapo and informers: only around 32,000 officers but roughly 80% of investigations from civilian tips; block wardens; self-policing as the dominant mechanism.
• Limits: Confessional Church resistance; Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth; foreign radio listening; private jokes; oral history evidence of uneven conviction.
• Conclusion: Nazi control combined unprecedented propaganda reach with a smaller-than-imagined police force whose effect was multiplied by civilian denunciation. Both were essential; neither alone was sufficient. Hollywood images of an omnipresent secret police understate the role of consent and self-policing in maintaining the regime.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1980s historian arguing the Gestapo was an omnipresent and ruthlessly efficient instrument of total control) and Interpretation B (a 2000s social historian arguing the Gestapo was small in number and depended on civilian denunciation) on the Nazi police state. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Gestapo as an unaided machine of state surveillance.
• Interpretation B presents the Gestapo as a small force amplified by civilian informers and self-policing.
• Main difference: A locates the cause of fear in the Gestapo itself; B locates it in the social fabric of denunciation.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Richard Nixon, 23 January 1973.
‘At 12:30 Paris time today, the agreement on ending the war and restoring peace in Vietnam was initialled by Dr Henry Kissinger on behalf of the United States, and Special Adviser Le Duc Tho on behalf of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. We have achieved a peace with honour. The South Vietnamese people have the right to determine their own future, without outside interference.’

Source A suggests that Nixon wanted the Accords understood as an honourable end rather than a defeat. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• He calls the outcome ‘a peace with honour’.
• He says the South Vietnamese have the right to determine their own future.
• That right is to be exercised ‘without outside interference’.
Contextual knowledge: The Accords, signed on 27 January 1973, required US withdrawal within sixty days but left around 150,000 North Vietnamese troops inside the South.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private memorandum by Henry Kissinger to President Nixon, October 1972.
‘The North will not withdraw its troops from the South. We cannot get them to. The best we can secure is a decent interval — a period during which a southern government can survive on its own. After that, the political question must work itself out by Vietnamese means.’

Source C: An extract from an interview with President Nguyen Van Thieu of South Vietnam, given to a Western journalist in spring 1975, shortly before his resignation.
‘The Americans signed a treaty that left their enemy’s army on our soil. They promised us in 1973 they would return if Hanoi broke the agreement. They did not return. Saigon will fall because the United States allowed it to fall.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why Saigon fell in 1975. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: shows Kissinger admitted privately that the deal would not save the South in the long run, only buy a ‘decent interval’. Provenance: a private memo from the National Security Adviser to the President in October 1972, never intended for publication — high credibility for understanding US elite calculation. Own knowledge: the Accords left around 150,000 NVA troops in the South, confirming the structural concession.
Source C — Content: shows Thieu blaming the United States for breaking its 1973 commitments. Provenance: an interview given by the resigning South Vietnamese president to a Western journalist — partial, intended to shape his historical reputation. Own knowledge: Watergate destroyed Nixon’s authority; the Case-Church Amendment of 1973 banned further US military action; military aid was cut from 2.27 billion in 1973 to 700 million in 1975.
Judgement: B is highly useful for elite US calculation; C is highly useful for the South Vietnamese view, with the caveat that it is partly self-justifying. Read together they support an explanation centring on US political collapse rather than purely on North Vietnamese strength.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the steps from the Paris Peace Accords in January 1973 to the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise dates and details (Accords, Case-Church, Nixon resignation, aid cuts, Spring Offensive, Frequent Wind).
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 27 January 1973: Paris Peace Accords signed; NVA troops remained in the South.
• 29 March 1973: last US combat troops left; 591 POWs returned in Operation Homecoming.
• June 1973: Case-Church Amendment banned further US military operations in Indochina.
• November 1973: War Powers Resolution passed over Nixon’s veto.
• August 1974: Nixon resigned over Watergate; Ford took office without political authority for renewed bombing.
• 1973–75: US military aid to Saigon cut from 2.27 billion to 700 million.
• March 1975: Hanoi launched its spring offensive; Buon Ma Thuot fell 10 March, Hue 25 March, Da Nang 30 March.
• 21 April 1975: Thieu resigned, blaming US betrayal.
• 29–30 April 1975: Operation Frequent Wind evacuated 7,000 people; Saigon fell as North Vietnamese tanks smashed through the Independence Palace gates.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a CBS Evening News broadcast by Walter Cronkite, 30 April 1975.
‘Saigon fell to communist forces today. The last Americans were lifted from the embassy roof by helicopter as North Vietnamese tanks rolled through the streets. After more than a decade, more than 58,000 American dead and 150 billion dollars, the war that defined a generation has ended in defeat.’

Source D suggests that the fall of Saigon was reported at home as an American defeat. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source D and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• The broadcast says the last Americans were lifted from the embassy roof as North Vietnamese tanks entered the city.
• It gives the cost as more than 58,000 American dead and 150 billion dollars.
• It states plainly that the war ‘has ended in defeat’.
Contextual knowledge: Operation Frequent Wind lifted about 7,000 people out on 29–30 April 1975; Vietnamese losses were far higher than American ones, at roughly three million dead.

practice_questions.text:
‘The fall of Saigon in 1975 was caused more by the collapse of South Vietnam than by the strength of North Vietnam.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: A sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• South Vietnam had been propped up by the United States since 1955 and never built a government with broad legitimacy.
• The ARVN in 1975 had no fuel, no spare parts and no American air cover; Thieu’s ordered withdrawal turned into a rout.
• Watergate and the Case-Church Amendment of June 1973 removed any American power to enforce the Accords.
• Congress cut military aid to Saigon from 2.27 billion dollars in 1973 to 700 million in 1975.
Disagree:
• Hanoi’s 1975 offensive was a disciplined conventional campaign that took the South in seven weeks.
• The Accords of January 1973 had already left around 150,000 North Vietnamese troops inside the South.
• Soviet and Chinese aid to the North continued at high levels while American aid to Saigon was being cut.
• Years of Vietcong and NVA pressure, including Tet in 1968, had built the ground for 1975.
Judgement: Both were necessary: southern weakness was fatal only once the American guarantee was withdrawn, and Hanoi had the patience and the conventional strength to exploit it.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source G.

Source G: An extract from the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund’s dedication ceremony speech in Washington DC, November 1982.
‘On this wall are the names of 57,939 men and women. Each name is a son or daughter, a husband or wife, a brother or sister. We do not say here whether the war was right or wrong. We say only that these Americans went where their country sent them, and they did not come home.’

Source G suggests that the memorial was designed to remember the dead without judging the war. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source G and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct points taken from the source, each supported by a short quotation and developed with accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: Two relevant points from the source with brief support; some contextual knowledge used.
Developing: One clear point from the source; the second vague or a repeat; little context.
Emerging: A general comment about the source with no specific support.

Indicative content:
• It says the wall carries the names of 57,939 men and women.
• Each name is presented as a family member, not a statistic.
• It states ‘we do not say here whether the war was right or wrong’.
Contextual knowledge: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial was dedicated in November 1982 with 57,939 names; more have been added since as later deaths were attributed to the war.

practice_questions.text: ‘The winding, shallow channel of the Medway should have stopped the Dutch on its own.’ How far does a study of the site of the Medway raid support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the site and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The Medway is narrow, shoal-banked and mud-lined, navigable for great ships only on the tide and only with pilots who knew it.
• The river ran a dozen miles inland from Sheerness to Chatham, so an attacker had to hold the passage behind him as well as force it.
• Three man-made layers backed the channel up: the fort at Sheerness, the iron chain at Gillingham with its batteries and guardships, and Upnor Castle above the moorings.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• The Dutch had pilots who knew the channel — among them English seamen who had deserted after years of pay in worthless tickets — so the river’s natural defence was handed to the enemy.
• A channel only defends what is defended: Sheerness was unfinished, the chain’s batteries lacked platforms and gunners, and the guardships were skeleton crews.
• The fleet was laid up unmanned because Plague, Fire and two years of war had emptied the treasury — the target existed because of money, not geography.
• De Ruyter’s use of the tides, fireships and boarding parties on 10–14 June 1667 shows the channel could be beaten by seamanship.

[16 marks — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the condition of the English fleet at Chatham in 1667.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The great ships were laid up — moored without full crews, stores or rigging — as a deliberate economy by a bankrupt government.
• Skeleton crews and unpaid men: sailors held tickets instead of wages, morale had collapsed, and some English seamen actually served the Dutch as pilots.
• The flagship Royal Charles lay at her moorings so lightly manned that a Dutch boarding party took her almost without a fight.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Crown’s financial problems for the success of the Dutch raid on the Medway.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Money explains the target existing at all: the battle fleet was laid up because Plague, Fire and two years of war had emptied the treasury.
• Money explains each defensive failure: Sheerness unfinished, the chain's batteries without platforms or gunners, guardships undermanned.
• Money explains the pilots: seamen paid in worthless tickets deserted, and some guided the Dutch through the shoals — the river's natural defence sold off by neglect.
• The raid then deepened the crisis it exposed, forcing peace at Breda on Dutch terms.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Dutch raid on the Medway, 10–14 June 1667.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 10 June: De Ruyter's fleet, with Cornelis de Witt aboard, lands at Sheerness; the unfinished fort falls and the river mouth is lost.
• 12 June: working upriver on the tide with expert pilots, the Dutch break the chain at Gillingham, burn the guardships and capture the Royal Charles.
• 13 June: under fire from Upnor Castle and shore batteries, fireships burn the Royal Oak, Loyal London and Royal James at their moorings.
• 14 June and after: the Dutch withdraw with the tide, towing the Royal Charles, and blockade the Thames for weeks; roughly a dozen warships have been lost, some scuttled by the defenders themselves.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the Medway raid for Restoration England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Immediate panic: invasion rumours in London, runs on the goldsmiths, Pepys sending his wife and gold to safety — a collapse of confidence in the government.
• Political consequences: Peter Pett scapegoated and sent to the Tower; Clarendon driven from office into exile by the autumn.
• Diplomatic consequences: the Treaty of Breda signed in July 1667 on terms England could no longer contest.
• Naval consequences: root-and-branch rebuilding of the Medway defences (including a proper fort at Sheerness) and reform of naval administration, in which Pepys's office was central.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: ‘The Dutch succeeded on the Medway because of English neglect rather than Dutch skill.’ How far does a study of the site of the Medway raid support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the site and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Every layer of the site's defences failed through neglect: Sheerness unfinished, the chain's batteries unmanned, guardships skeleton-crewed, the fleet itself laid up unpaid.
• The scuttling of ships by the defenders and the desertion of pilots to the enemy show a system collapsing from within.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• Navigating great ships up a winding, shoal-banked, tidal river under fire was seamanship of the highest order, and De Ruyter's disciplined use of tides, fireships and boarding parties exploited each weakness precisely.
• The Dutch plan — seizing Sheerness first, forcing the chain, striking the moorings, withdrawing intact with a prize — shows judgement, not luck.
• Context: the raid was a calculated stroke to force better terms at Breda, timed for when England could not respond.

[16 marks — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text:
Which had the greater impact on the Plains nations?

• The 1887 Dawes Act
• The Battle of the Little Bighorn

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (allotment, annuity, reservation, Ghost Dance).
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of one or both with little comparison.

Indicative content:
The 1887 Dawes Act:
• Dawes Act reduced tribal landholding from around 138 million acres to 48 million between 1887 and 1934 — a two-thirds loss.
• Forced cultural assimilation: removal of children to boarding schools where Indigenous languages were forbidden.
• Allotment broke up communal landholding traditions; ‘surplus’ land went to white settlement.
• Long-term: shaped tribal poverty and land tenure for the entire 20th century.

The Battle of the Little Bighorn:
• Symbolic power of the most spectacular Native victory of the Plains wars.
• Provoked the federal response that broke Lakota military independence by 1881.
• Led directly to the surrender of Crazy Horse and the exile of Sitting Bull.
• Triggered the campaign of cultural and territorial reduction that the Dawes Act later codified.

Judgement: Little Bighorn was decisive militarily but Dawes was the deeper, longer-lasting blow; a top-band answer reaches an explicit verdict and substantiates it. A nuanced answer notes the two are connected: Dawes only became politically possible because the Plains nations had been militarily defeated.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1900 popular American history written for a general readership):
‘The closing of the frontier in 1890 was the climax of the American story. Brave pioneers had crossed a continent, civilisation had triumphed over wilderness, and the United States stood ready to take its place among the great powers of the earth.’

Interpretation B (from a 1991 study of the American West):
‘The closing of the frontier in 1890 was the climax of a long process of conquest. The Plains nations were not a wilderness to be civilised but communities to be dispossessed. The Dawes Act, Wounded Knee and the 1890 Census report belong together as the formal end of that conquest.’

How convincing is Interpretation B? Use Interpretations A and B and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s ‘long process of conquest’ thesis; engages with specific claims (Plains nations as communities, Dawes Act, Wounded Knee, 1890 Census); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with reference to A; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Dawes Act 1887: reduction of tribal land from 138m to 48m acres.
• Wounded Knee Massacre, 29 December 1890: at least 250 Lakota killed.
• Buffalo destruction reducing herds from 30m to fewer than 1,000 by 1885 — deliberate federal weapon.
• Plains nations had complex political and economic life pre-1840 — not a ‘wilderness’.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• Settler experience was hard and many homesteaders died — the ‘triumphal’ framing reflects real human achievement.
• A speaks for the dominant late-19th-century American self-understanding (Turner Thesis).
• A’s framing is not factually wrong, just morally selective — a difference of emphasis.

Judgement: B is the stronger interpretation in light of modern evidence; a top-band answer notes A reflects the dominant national narrative of its own moment.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 2005 study of US Indian policy):
‘The Dawes Act of 1887 was sold to the public as humanitarian reform. Senator Dawes himself believed allotment would lift Indigenous families out of poverty by giving them private property. The reality was the destruction of communal land tenure and the loss of two-thirds of remaining tribal land in fifty years. Good intentions did not change devastating outcomes.’

How convincing is Interpretation C? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s ‘humanitarian intentions, devastating outcomes’ thesis; engages with specific claims; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the Dawes Act without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• Henry Dawes and his allies described the Act in humanitarian terms; the ‘Friends of the Indian’ lobby supported it.
• Tribal landholding fell from 138m acres to 48m between 1887 and 1934.
• Allotments often went to land too dry for family farming.
• Forced boarding-school removal devastated language and culture independent of land loss.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• Some allotments were genuinely productive and family-supporting.
• Not all reformers were sincere; the Act had clear settler-colonial beneficiaries who expected ‘surplus’ land.
• Cultural impact was as devastating as economic impact — C focuses on land loss but boarding schools also need weighting.

Judgement: C captures the gap between framing and outcome accurately; a top-band answer notes that the cultural assault (boarding schools, language ban) was as important as the land loss the interpretation foregrounds.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation D.

Interpretation D (from a 1996 study of the Plains nations after 1850):
‘Wounded Knee was not the end of resistance — it was the moment outside observers stopped noticing it. Lakota communities continued to refuse allotment, hide ceremonies, and assert rights to the Black Hills throughout the 20th century. To call 1890 a closing is to use a settler calendar.’

How convincing is Interpretation D? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of D’s ‘continuing resistance’ thesis; engages with specific claims; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of Wounded Knee without engaging with D’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting D):
• Lakota legal action over the Black Hills continued; the Supreme Court ruled in 1980 that the seizure had been unlawful.
• Continued resistance to allotment and language suppression in many tribal communities.
• ‘Closing of the frontier’ was a US Census definition with no equivalent meaning to the Plains nations.

Indicative content (qualifying D):
• Wounded Knee did mark the end of large-scale armed resistance.
• Federal control of reservations was effective from 1890.
• The 1890 framing is useful for understanding US policy even if not for understanding Lakota experience.

Judgement: D’s point is well-taken — resistance continued under different forms — but a top-band answer notes the closing of armed resistance was a real change, even if cultural and legal resistance continued.

practice_questions.text:
Was the closing of the frontier in 1890 an achievement or a tragedy?

• The case for achievement
• The case for tragedy

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that takes an explicit position on achievement vs tragedy and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (Manifest Destiny, allotment, Ghost Dance, Frontier Thesis).
Secure: Clear argument addressing both sides; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both sides with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of the closing of the frontier with no clear comparison of the two bullets.

Indicative content:
The case for achievement:
• Continental nation united by transcontinental rail since 1869.
• Around 1.6 million homestead claims completed by 1934; the Plains transformed into a major agricultural region.
• Sectional civil war wounds beginning to heal under shared westward expansion.
• Industrial economy on track to overtake Britain’s by 1890.

The case for tragedy:
• Plains nations dispossessed, buffalo destroyed (30m to fewer than 1,000), Wounded Knee Massacre (December 1890).
• Dawes Act reduced tribal land by two-thirds.
• Closing came at the cost of around 4 million people enslaved emancipated but trapped in sharecropping; Reconstruction overthrown by 1877.
• ‘Closing’ framing was a settler-perspective summary; Plains nations did not regard 1890 as a closure but as a moment of catastrophe.

Judgement: a defensible verdict can argue achievement OR tragedy OR both. The 12-mark band rewards an explicit, substantiated position. A top-band answer recognises the closing was both achievement (for one set of Americans) and catastrophe (for another), and weighs the two.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1993 study of post-Civil War America):
‘Federal policy toward the Plains nations between 1867 and 1890 was strikingly consistent: confine, contain, and assimilate. Whether under Republican or Democratic administrations, the small reservations policy, the destruction of the buffalo, and the Dawes Act all served the same long aim.’

How convincing is Interpretation E? Use the interpretation and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s ‘consistent policy’ thesis; engages with specific claims; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of policy without engaging with E’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• 1867 Medicine Lodge and 1868 Fort Laramie Treaties established small reservations.
• Buffalo destruction was tolerated and encouraged across multiple administrations.
• 1887 Dawes Act under Republican Congress shared assumptions with the 1881 Helen Hunt Jackson’s ‘reform’ lobby.
• Bipartisan support for assimilationist boarding schools throughout the era.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• Grant’s ‘Peace Policy’ (1869) attempted a more conciliatory approach via Quaker reservation agents — not identical to military containment.
• The Great Sioux War (1876-77) was a sharper military rupture than the ‘consistent’ framing implies.
• Some reformers (the ‘Friends of the Indian’) genuinely opposed harsher Western politicians.

Judgement: E captures real consistency in long-term aims but flattens significant differences in method and tone; a top-band answer concedes the underlying continuity while noting genuine variation in how it was pursued.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the ground Harold chose for the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The ridge: the English position ran along a crest roughly seven hundred metres wide, forcing any attacker to advance uphill, which slowed cavalry and reduced the effect of archery.
• The marshy flanks: small stream valleys with soft ground on either side of the ridge prevented the Normans outflanking the shield wall.
• The London road: the site sat astride the main route out of the Hastings peninsula, which is why Harold chose it to block William's advance.
• The Weald: forest behind the ridge offered the English cover for retreat and later hid the Malfosse ditch.
• Why it mattered: the ridge, the marshy flanks and the London road together forced William into frontal uphill attacks, which is why an all-infantry army held out until dusk.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of the English defeat.

‘Harold picked the strongest position in England and his shield wall was unbeatable on it. The English lost Hastings only because their own men would not stay on the ridge.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for the English defeat at Hastings? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: the position was so strong that only English indiscipline can explain the defeat.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The shield wall held the crest against archers, infantry and cavalry from morning until late afternoon, which was extraordinary for a medieval battle.
• Marshy stream valleys on both flanks stopped William outflanking the line, so every attack had to come uphill.
• Part of the English right left the crest to chase the fleeing Bretons and was cut down on the low ground; the feigned retreats then repeated the trick.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The wall was already thinning through attrition, and the fyrd was standing where housecarls had fallen; discipline was not the only pressure on it.
• Harold’s army was worn down by Stamford Bridge and a fast march, and he chose to fight before all his men had arrived.
• William’s handling of the crisis — riding bare-headed to rally the line, then using the retreats deliberately — was skill, not English error alone.
• Harold’s death, and those of Gyrth and Leofwine, removed the leadership that held the line together.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Harold’s choice of ground at the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the crest, slopes and marshy flanks made the all-infantry English army as strong as it could be, forcing frontal uphill attacks that failed from morning to late afternoon.
• Strategically: by planting his army on the London road, Harold turned a battle into the decisive engagement — William had to win here or starve in his peninsula.
• Limits of the choice: the position could hold but not manoeuvre; once discipline slipped and men followed the fleeing Bretons downhill, the same slopes became a killing ground, showing the choice of ground only worked while the wall held it.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the way the battlefield environment shaped the fighting at Hastings on 14 October 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Morning: Normans form up on the low ground and attack uphill; arrows shot uphill are wasted against shields; charges arrive winded and the wall holds.
• The crisis: the Bretons on the softest ground near the marsh break and flee; the rumour that William is dead; William lifts his helmet to rally his men; English pursuers are destroyed on the low ground.
• Afternoon: feigned retreats repeatedly tempt men off the crest; attrition thins the wall through a battle of exceptional length.
• Dusk: the wall finally breaks, Harold is killed, and even the pursuit is shaped by the ground at the Malfosse ditch.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the death of King Harold at the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the shield wall had held all day while he lived; his death (with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine already dead) removed all leadership and the army broke.
• Politically: there was no adult, crowned rival left with comparable legitimacy — the battle became a conquest of the whole kingdom rather than one lost battle.
• For the site: tradition places the high altar of Battle Abbey on the spot where he fell, showing how the Normans themselves marked his death as the decisive moment.
• The debated manner of death (the Bayeux Tapestry arrow tradition) shows how quickly the event passed into propaganda and legend.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: 'William won the Battle of Hastings because of his enemies' mistakes rather than his own skill.' How far does a study of the battlefield at Hastings support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the battlefield and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• English troops abandoned the crest to pursue the Bretons and were destroyed on the low ground — the site shows discipline failing, since the position was only strong while held.
• Harold offered battle before his army was complete, fresh from the Stamford Bridge campaign, when waiting would have strengthened him and starved William.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• William's combined-arms coordination on unfavourable ground — rotating archers, infantry and cavalry against a hilltop wall for a whole day — was skill, not luck.
• The rally after the Breton collapse (the helmet moment) and the disciplined use of feigned retreats turned the terrain's one weakness for the defenders into a weapon.
• The campaign context: harrying Harold's family lands to force battle at a time of William's choosing was calculated generalship.
A developed judgement weighing site evidence against contextual knowledge is required for the top level.

[16 marks]
Mastering: A sustained judgement, built from named features of the site and tested against wider knowledge of the period.
Secure: Clear argument using site features and relevant contextual knowledge.
Developing: Some use of the site, with limited wider knowledge.
Emerging: Describes the site without answering the statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the 1911 National Insurance Act and the 1948 National Health Service were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: 1911 was contributory and means-tested for workers; 1948 was universal and tax-funded for every resident.
• Difference: 1911 covered the worker only; 1948 covered the whole family including wives and children.
• Similarity: both were responses to social investigation (Booth/Rowntree, Beveridge) and major wars (Boer, WWII).
• Similarity: both expanded the role of the state in healthcare and faced opposition from the British Medical Association.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Beveridge for the development of the welfare state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Beveridge designed the 1909 Labour Exchanges as a young Liberal civil servant.
• At the time: his December 1942 Social Insurance and Allied Services report named the five giants (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness) and proposed cradle-to-grave social insurance.
• At the time: 300,000 copies were sold; the report shaped wartime public opinion and became Labour’s 1945 manifesto template.
• Over time: family allowances (1945), the National Insurance Act 1946, the National Health Service Act 1946 and the National Assistance Act 1948 all built directly on Beveridge’s blueprint.
• Over time: the contributory model he designed is still used in 21st-century National Insurance.
• Limitation: Beveridge wrote the plan but did not legislate it — a Labour landslide and Bevan’s political skill were also necessary.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named acts.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the National Health Service Act 1946 for healthcare in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: it brought hospitals, GPs and community services into one state-funded system, free at the point of use for every resident.
• At the time: it nationalised the voluntary and local-authority hospitals that had grown up piecemeal since the 18th century.
• At the time: it forced a two-year negotiation with the BMA before the service could open on 5 July 1948.
• Over time: demand ran far beyond Treasury forecasts, and charges for spectacles and dentures in 1951 drove Bevan out of the Cabinet.
• Over time: the structure it created is still the framework of British healthcare, and free at the point of use has stayed politically untouchable.
• Limitation: the Act settled how care was paid for, not how much of it the country could afford — that argument has run ever since.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Has war been the main factor in creating the welfare state and the NHS in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to war and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh war against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of war as the main factor:
• WWII evacuation made urban poverty visible to rural Britain; the EMS nationalised hospitals from 1939; rationing established universal entitlement.
• The 1942 Beveridge Report was a wartime commission building on military Keynesianism and the recognition that healthy citizens were a national-security asset.
• The Boer War (1899–1902) had already pushed Liberal reforms 1906–11 by exposing recruit unfitness.

Weighed against communication:
• Booth and Rowntree turned anecdote into evidence by 1901; the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies turned policy into popular politics.

Weighed against government:
• The 1945 Labour landslide, with a majority of 146, delivered the National Health Service Act 1946; without parliamentary numbers, Beveridge’s plan would have stayed a paper.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
