• Bevan’s deal with the BMA was the make-or-break political move; without his compromise of January-May 1948 the launch would have failed.

Judgement: war repeatedly created the conditions for welfare leaps (1906–11, 1948) by exposing the gap between Britain’s aspirations and its citizens’ health, but war alone did not legislate. The Boer War without Booth/Rowntree, or WWII without Beveridge and Bevan, would not have produced the same leap. War is the necessary trigger, not the sufficient cause.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes wars only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Aneurin Bevan for the development of healthcare in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Bevan as Labour Minister of Health from 1945 designed and steered the National Health Service Act 1946.
• At the time: his compromise with the BMA in early 1948 (consultants kept private pay-beds; GPs remained self-employed contractors) prevented a doctors’ boycott and let the NHS open on 5 July 1948.
• At the time: he resigned in 1951 over the introduction of charges for spectacles and dentures, defending the principle of free at point of use.
• Over time: the NHS structure he created — tripartite (hospitals, GPs, community services), tax-funded, universal — remains the framework of British healthcare today.
• Over time: his model influenced post-war health systems across Europe and the Commonwealth.
• Limitation: significance is partly a product of war and the Beveridge Report — without those preconditions Bevan’s plan would have had no political opening.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named acts.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: the British Medical Association’s statement to its members in January 1948, six months before the National Health Service opened. It told doctors that the government’s scheme was so far from the essential principles of their profession that they should reject it completely.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying opposition to the NHS?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: the language shows the objection being framed as professional principle rather than as money.
• Content: it is an instruction to members, so it shows the BMA organising a boycott that could have stopped the launch.
• Provenance: an official statement by the doctors’ own body at the height of the dispute, so it is authoritative for the BMA’s public position — but it is a negotiating position as much as a belief.
• Contextual knowledge: doctors feared becoming salaried civil servants; Bevan let consultants keep private pay-beds and GPs stay self-employed, and the BMA voted to accept about five weeks before 5 July 1948.
• Limitations: it speaks for the BMA leadership rather than every doctor, and not at all for patients, who were strongly in favour.
• Judgement: strong for the shape and language of medical opposition, weak for how deep or how lasting it was.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the Czechoslovak Communist Party’s Action Programme, published 5 April 1968.
‘The leading role of the Communist Party shall be sustained, but it must rest on persuasion not coercion. Censorship shall be ended; rehabilitation of those wrongly imprisoned shall continue; managers of enterprises shall be given new freedoms within socialist planning. We shall remain a loyal member of the Warsaw Pact.’

Source A suggests that Dubcek wanted to reform communism rather than abandon it. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Censorship to be ended.
• Rehabilitation of those wrongly imprisoned to continue.
• Managers of enterprises to gain new freedoms within socialist planning.
• The Communist Party’s leading role retained but based on ‘persuasion not coercion’.
• Czechoslovakia to remain a loyal member of the Warsaw Pact.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• The Action Programme was published on 5 April 1968 and kept one-party rule and Warsaw Pact membership.
• Warsaw Pact troops invaded anyway on the night of 20-21 August 1968.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a confidential letter from East German leader Walter Ulbricht to Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev, 15 July 1968.
‘Comrade Brezhnev, the situation in Czechoslovakia threatens our common achievements. Once one party loses its leading role, the question will be asked in Berlin and Warsaw. Words are not enough. Decisive action is required and must come from the Warsaw Pact as a whole.’

Source C: An extract from a confidential CIA assessment for President Johnson, 1 September 1968.
‘The Soviet decision to invade was driven by fear of contagion in the bloc, particularly in East Germany and Poland. The action was supported by the GDR and Polish leaderships. Romania’s refusal to participate has weakened Warsaw Pact unity, but Moscow has secured short-term control of Czechoslovakia.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying Soviet motives for the August 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Ulbricht presents the Czech situation as a threat to East Germany and Poland and demands Warsaw Pact action. Provenance: a confidential letter between communist leaders, written six weeks before the invasion — likely to give frank pressure rather than public posturing. Own knowledge: Ulbricht and Gomulka did press Brezhnev to act; East Germany feared its own people would demand similar reforms.
Source C — Content: identifies fear of contagion as the main Soviet motive and notes Romanian refusal as a weakening factor. Provenance: a confidential CIA assessment for the President shortly after the invasion — likely to give a cautious, well-sourced judgement. Own knowledge: Romania did refuse troops; Yugoslavia condemned the action; Western Communist parties broke with Moscow.
Judgement: B is highly useful as evidence of pressure on Brezhnev from within the bloc; C is useful as informed Western analysis of Soviet calculation — together they capture both the inputs and the outputs of the Soviet decision.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Prague Spring developed from Dubcek’s appointment in January 1968 to the Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, names, places); reaches the invasion through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• January 1968: Alexander Dubcek replaced Antonin Novotny as First Secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party.
• March 1968: censorship effectively ended; an open public sphere emerged.
• 5 April 1968: the Action Programme set out ‘socialism with a human face’, retaining one-party rule and Warsaw Pact membership.
• Late July 1968: Cierna nad Tisou negotiations — Dubcek reassured Brezhnev but did not satisfy Moscow.
• July-August 1968: Ulbricht and Gomulka pressed Brezhnev for intervention; the Politburo decided in mid-August.
• 20-21 August 1968: around 250,000 Warsaw Pact troops invaded; Dubcek and the leadership were arrested and flown to Moscow.
• August-September 1968: Dubcek was forced to sign the Moscow Protocols accepting Soviet demands; the reforms were rolled back.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 was a defensive response to a real threat to socialism.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• Moscow's public case, carried by TASS, was that loyal Czechoslovak comrades had asked for help against counter-revolution.
• Ulbricht and Gomulka genuinely feared that reform in Prague would spread to East Germany and Poland.
• Some hardline Czechoslovak officials did write the letter of invitation that Moscow used to justify the action.
• An open press and free debate could in time have carried Czechoslovakia toward multi-party politics.
Disagree:
• Dubcek's Action Programme of April 1968 kept one-party rule and Warsaw Pact membership.
• Dubcek reassured Brezhnev at Cierna nad Tisou in late July that neither was in question.
• The Brezhnev Doctrine of November 1968 was framed as a general rule, which points to fear of reform rather than of rebellion.
• Romania refused to take part and Yugoslavia condemned the invasion, so the bloc itself did not accept the defensive case.
Judgement: the invasion defended Soviet control rather than socialism; the counter-revolution Moscow described did not exist.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from the memoir of Zdenek Mlynar, a Czechoslovak party leader taken to Moscow with Dubcek in August 1968, published in the West in 1980.
‘In the Kremlin Brezhnev told Dubcek with tears in his eyes that the issue had not been counter-revolution but the obligations of the bloc. The Soviet Union, he said, had paid for these countries with the blood of its soldiers in 1945. They could never be allowed to drift away. We had no answer to this.’

Source F suggests that Brezhnev acted to hold the bloc together rather than to stop a counter-revolution. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: records Brezhnev framing the invasion as an obligation of the bloc, not as a response to counter-revolution — useful evidence that the public TASS justification was for show.
• Provenance: a memoir by a Czechoslovak leader who was in the room — close to the conversation, though written years afterwards for publication.
• Own knowledge: matches the Brezhnev Doctrine declared in November 1968 — the principle that no member could leave the bloc.
• Useful interpretation: supports the view that the invasion was about Soviet imperial control rather than ideology.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the consequences of the Czechoslovak invasion from August 1968 to the declaration of the Brezhnev Doctrine in November 1968.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the doctrine through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 21 August 1968: Soviet aircraft seized Prague airport; tanks rolled into the city; Dubcek and the leadership arrested.
• Late August 1968: Dubcek forced to sign the Moscow Protocols accepting Soviet demands.
• August-September 1968: symbolic resistance in Czechoslovakia — turned signs, underground radio — but no armed conflict; around 70,000 fled west.
• September-October 1968: Western Communist parties (Italy, France) condemned the invasion; Yugoslavia and Romania denounced it.
• November 1968: Brezhnev declared the Brezhnev Doctrine in a speech in Warsaw, formalising the right of the Warsaw Pact to defend socialism in any member state.
• January 1969: student Jan Palach’s self-immolation captured the loss of hope and became a long-term symbol of resistance.
• April 1969: Gustav Husak replaced Dubcek as First Secretary, beginning twenty years of ‘normalisation’.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about Stalin’s role in the Great Terror? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat Stalin as the central architect personally directing every stage of the Terror; B may treat the violence as a chain reaction shaped by local quotas and denunciations.
• A may emphasise show trials and the murder of Kirov; B may emphasise NKVD quotas and bureaucratic chaos.
• Specific textual reference required for both.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual reference. Secure: comparison with some reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the show trials of the Old Bolsheviks?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different schools of thought: totalitarian (Conquest) versus revisionist (Fitzpatrick, Getty).
• Different time of writing: pre-1991 (limited archive access) versus post-1991 (NKVD records released).
• Different purposes: a Soviet-era textbook versus a Western academic study.
• Different evidence: trial transcripts versus survivor memoirs and Politburo papers.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the causes of the Great Terror? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test specific claims of the interpretation against named context: Kirov’s murder December 1934, three Moscow show trials, NKVD quotas under Yezhov, around 750,000 executions in 1936-38.
• Weigh totalitarian readings (Stalin’s personal will) against revisionist accounts (denunciations from below, bureaucratic chaos).
• Cite Conquest or Fitzpatrick and Getty as schools of thought.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. Stalin set the political climate that made the violence possible, but the quota system and local denunciations shaped its scale.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge with clear judgement. Developing: knowledge unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the purge of the Red Army officer corps in 1937 on the Soviet Union by 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Loss of experienced leadership: 3 of the 5 marshals shot, around 35,000 officers removed.
• Surviving officers afraid to take initiative or report bad news, weakening tactical decision-making.
• Stalin promoted political loyalty over military skill in replacements.
• Contributed to the catastrophic early defeats of Operation Barbarossa in summer 1941.
• Forced rapid emergency promotions during the war (Zhukov, Konev, Rokossovsky) once skilled officers were missing.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the purge.]

practice_questions.text: ‘The Great Terror was driven mainly by Stalin’s personal will to eliminate rivals.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Stalin’s personal role, the work of the NKVD and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for Stalin’s personal will (Conquest):
• Personally signed death lists; demanded confessions from Bukharin and others.
• Exploited Kirov’s murder to launch the Terror.
• Used trials to destroy the Old Bolsheviks who had known Lenin.
• Removed and shot Yagoda, then Yezhov, when each had served his purpose.

Arguments for other factors (revisionist):
• Quota culture in the NKVD drove arrests beyond the centre’s explicit list.
• Denunciations from below targeted neighbours, rivals and class enemies.
• Local activists rewarded for finding ‘enemies’; central control was patchy.
• The 1932-33 famine and the strain of collectivisation produced political fear that Stalin could exploit.
• Beria’s appointment in late 1938 wound the worst of the violence down — suggesting it was not pure central control.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. Stalin set the political climate and signed the key death lists, but the scale was driven by quotas and local denunciations.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the cult of personality on Soviet society in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stalin’s portraits in classrooms, factories and kolkhozes shaped daily public life.
• Socialist Realism in art, novels and film made the cult inescapable culturally.
• Photographs and textbooks rewrote history to remove disgraced figures and place Stalin alongside Lenin.
• Many Soviets genuinely believed Stalin was being deceived by NKVD officials acting alone, sustaining loyalty to him through the Terror.
• Made dissent psychologically as well as politically dangerous — criticism of Stalin felt like criticism of socialism itself.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the cult.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1964 essay by Martin Luther King defending non-violent protest as the moral path to civil rights) and Interpretation B (a 1964 speech by Malcolm X attacking integration and arguing for self-defence). What is the main difference between these views about the civil-rights movement?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents non-violent protest as morally and tactically right — only love can drive out hate, and federal action will follow disciplined suffering.
• Interpretation B presents integration as inadequate and self-defence as legitimate — black Americans should not turn the other cheek to racist violence.
• Main difference: A frames the struggle as a moral campaign for inclusion; B frames it as a fight for survival in which non-violence is a luxury black Americans cannot afford.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1964 essay by Martin Luther King) and Interpretation B (a 1964 speech by Malcolm X) give different views about the civil-rights movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written from different ideological positions — King drew on Gandhi and Christian theology; Malcolm X drew on the Nation of Islam and an analysis of white American violence as the central problem.
• They were addressing different audiences — King aimed to win white liberal support and federal action; Malcolm X aimed to mobilise black urban communities outside the South.
• They reflected different lived experiences — King grew up in a southern middle-class clerical family; Malcolm X grew up in northern poverty after his father’s suspected lynching by white supremacists.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘The civil-rights movement’s legal victories were the work of mass struggle, not key leaders alone.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the civil-rights movement between 1954 and 1968?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because around 40,000 black residents walked for 381 days in the Montgomery Bus Boycott; around 70,000 students took part in sit-ins; tens of thousands faced state violence in Mississippi voter-registration drives.
• Convincing because the 1964 and 1965 Acts followed mass televised confrontations — Birmingham’s fire hoses and Selma’s ‘Bloody Sunday’ — not negotiations between leaders and presidents.
• Convincing because the Black Power Movement, the Black Panthers and the 1965–68 urban riots also pressured federal action without King-style leadership.
• Less convincing because King’s leadership of the SCLC, the ‘Letter from Birmingham Jail’ and the ‘I have a dream’ speech mattered as moral focal points.
• Less convincing because Thurgood Marshall’s legal strategy at the NAACP produced Brown v Board; lawyers and judges drove some victories that mass action could not have produced alone.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing — mass struggle was decisive in pushing federal action, but leaders’ strategic choices shaped which struggles became national breakthroughs.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56) on the civil-rights movement in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Made Martin Luther King a national figure — the 26-year-old Baptist minister became the public spokesman for the boycott and went on to found the SCLC in 1957.
• Demonstrated that economic boycotts could force change — for 381 days around 40,000 black residents of Montgomery refused to ride the buses, bankrupting the bus company and ending bus segregation when the Supreme Court ruled in November 1956.
• Established the model of non-violent direct action that drove the sit-ins (1960), Freedom Rides (1961) and the Birmingham campaign (1963).
• Inspired the wider movement — ordinary participants gained confidence that mass action worked, and Rosa Parks’s arrest became a symbol of dignified refusal that organised resistance could build on.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was passed.
You may consider:
• mass protest from Montgomery to Birmingham
• the role of leaders such as Martin Luther King and Presidents Kennedy and Johnson.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Brown v Board (1954) and Little Rock (1957) established federal supremacy on segregation; resistance forced federal action when needed.
• Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56) ended bus segregation and made King a national figure.
• Greensboro sit-ins (February 1960) and the Freedom Rides (May 1961) tested existing federal rulings; Kennedy administration sent marshals after attacks.
• Birmingham campaign (April–May 1963): Bull Connor’s use of dogs and fire hoses on television shocked the nation.
• Letter from Birmingham Jail (April 1963) defended non-violent direct action.
• March on Washington (28 August 1963): around 250,000 people; King’s ‘I have a dream’ speech.
• Kennedy proposed the legislation in June 1963; assassinated November 1963.
• Lyndon Johnson made the bill a memorial to Kennedy and used his Senate experience to push it through despite an 83-day southern filibuster.
• Malcolm X and rising Black Power gave moderates an incentive to settle with King.
• Result: Civil Rights Act of 1964 (signed 2 July 1964) banned segregation in public places and discrimination in employment.
• Conclusion: the Act passed because televised mass protest converted legal arguments into political pressure that two presidents and Congress could no longer ignore — leaders mattered, but only because mass struggle made their leadership consequential.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1965 Selma to Montgomery campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was a campaign for the right to vote — black residents of Selma, Alabama, marched to demand the federal government enforce voter registration in the Deep South, where literacy tests and intimidation kept most black citizens off the rolls.
• On 7 March 1965 (‘Bloody Sunday’), state troopers attacked marchers at Edmund Pettus Bridge with clubs and tear gas; television footage was broadcast nationally and forced federal action.
• A second attempt led by Martin Luther King turned back at the bridge; a third march, protected by federalised National Guard, completed the journey to Montgomery (21–25 March 1965) with 25,000 participants.
• The campaign produced the Voting Rights Act of August 1965, which outlawed literacy tests and dramatically increased black voter registration: in Mississippi from around 7% in 1964 to around 67% by 1969.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Brixton Riots of 1981 for the changing relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: three days of unrest in April 1981 with around 300 police and 65 civilians injured and 28 buildings burned, but no fatalities; spread to Toxteth, Moss Side and Handsworth through the summer.
• At the time: forced government attention to police-community relations; the sus law's role in Operation Swamp 81 was directly linked to the trigger.
• At the time: Lord Scarman's inquiry (November 1981) identified ‘racial disadvantage’ in housing, employment and policing.
• Over time: led directly to the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, codifying stop-and-search.
• Over time: shaped the road to the Macpherson Report 1999, which finally adopted the term ‘institutional racism’ that Scarman had rejected.
• Over time: a benchmark moment for race-relations policy that returns whenever urban policing failures recur.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the riots without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the growth of minority-rights law in Britain between 1948 and 2010.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the British Nationality Act 1948 confirmed the right of Commonwealth citizens to settle in Britain, but said nothing about discrimination in housing or work.
• At the time: the Bristol Bus Boycott of 1963 and the Race Relations Acts of 1965, 1968 and 1976 outlawed discrimination in public places, then in housing and employment, then indirect discrimination.
• At the time: the Brixton Riots of 1981 and the Scarman Report led to the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, which codified stop and search.
• Over time: the Macpherson Report of 1999 put institutional racism into policy language and shaped two decades of police reform.
• Over time: the Equality Act 2010 pulled the protections into one framework, but the Windrush scandal of 2017-18 showed that rights on paper do not guarantee fair treatment.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both timeframes.
Developing: Significance weighted to one timeframe only.
Emerging: Description without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Bristol Bus Boycott (1963) and the suffragists' campaign were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both used non-violent constitutional pressure rather than direct action — the boycott as a form of organised peaceful protest, the suffragists with petitions and lobbying MPs.
• Similarity: both succeeded by changing public opinion and forcing institutional change — the bus company climbed down in 1963; the 1918 Representation of the People Act followed decades of suffragist pressure.
• Similarity: both contrasted themselves with more militant rivals — the boycott avoided the confrontation of US protest at the time; the suffragists distinguished themselves from the suffragettes.
• Similarity: both shaped subsequent legislation — the boycott influenced the 1965 Race Relations Act; suffragist pressure shaped the 1918 and 1928 Acts.

[8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: ‘Government legislation has been the main factor in advancing minority rights in Britain since 1948.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh government against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of government as the main factor:
• 1948 British Nationality Act, 1965/1968/1976 Race Relations Acts, 1975 Sex Discrimination Act, 2010 Equality Act — legislation provided enforceable rights.
• Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 reformed stop and search after Scarman.
• Macpherson Report 1999 — a government-commissioned inquiry that institutionalised the language of racism in policy.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Paul Stephenson organised the Bristol Bus Boycott in 1963.
• Doreen Lawrence's four-year campaign after the 1993 murder forced the Macpherson inquiry into existence in 1997; the report would not have happened without her.
• Lord Scarman and Sir William Macpherson translated public events into binding policy recommendations.

Weighed against ideas:
• The shift from ‘separate but equal’ assumptions in the 1950s to a positive ideal of multi-racial citizenship by 2000 changed what legislation was possible.
• The concept of ‘institutional racism’ itself shifted political possibility.

Weighed against communication:
• Television coverage of Brixton in 1981 forced government action; social media was central to the BLM organisation in 2020.
• The Lawrence family used the press systematically to keep the case visible during the 1990s.

Cross-period weighing:
• Compare with women's suffrage: legislation followed but did not lead the campaigning — the 1918 Act came after decades of pressure.
• Compare with Chartism: ideas and pressure preceded legal reform by decades; the same is true of minority rights.

Judgement: Top answers argue legislation locked in changes that individual leadership and shifting public ideas had begun. Government action has been decisive but reactive; the underlying movement of public opinion and the persistence of campaigners have been the deeper drivers.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing government against at least two other factors with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Macpherson Report (1999) for British policing and minority rights.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: a public inquiry into the murder of Stephen Lawrence and the failed Metropolitan Police investigation; concluded the Met was institutionally racist.
• At the time: defined ‘institutional racism’ and brought the term into routine British policy language for the first time.
• At the time: led to immediate reforms in police recruitment, training and complaint procedures.
• Over time: enabled the eventual conviction of two of Stephen Lawrence's killers in 2012 after the double jeopardy rule was changed.
• Over time: shaped two decades of policing policy; revisited and challenged in subsequent reviews of the Met (Casey Review 2023) but never displaced.
• Over time: the language of ‘institutional’ discrimination became standard in debates about other organisations and other minorities.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the report without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Brixton Riots of 1981 were different from the Peterloo Massacre of 1819.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in casualties: at Peterloo the cavalry charged unarmed protesters and killed at least 18; at Brixton there were no fatalities despite the unrest, with 300 police and 65 civilians injured.
• Difference in trigger: Peterloo was a planned mass meeting at St Peter's Field for parliamentary reform; Brixton ignited spontaneously after a specific incident during Operation Swamp 81.
• Difference in state response: after Peterloo the government tightened repression with the Six Acts; after Brixton the government commissioned the Scarman Report and reformed police powers in the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984.
• Difference in aim: Peterloo demanded the vote; Brixton was a protest against discriminatory policing rather than a campaign for a specific legal reform.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from Neville Chamberlain’s speech in Birmingham on 17 March 1939, two days after the German occupation of Prague.
‘Is this in fact a step in the direction of an attempt to dominate the world by force? While we shall not stand in the way of any reasonable efforts on the part of Germany to expand her exports, we are resolved that no nation shall imagine it can with impunity rend the structure of international order. There is hardly anything I would not sacrifice for peace, but there is one thing I must except — the liberty which we have enjoyed for hundreds of years and which we will never surrender.’

Using Source A, identify two changes in Chamberlain’s position on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded changes with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear changes, briefly supported.
Developing: One change clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific changes.

Indicative content:
• A new acceptance that Germany may be aiming for European domination by force.
• A pledge that Britain will resist further German aggression.
• A pledge that Britain will not surrender its liberty for peace.
• Implicit change: a public turn from negotiation to deterrence.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the events of March 1939, from the German occupation of Prague on 15 March to the British guarantee to Poland on 31 March.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 14-15 March 1939: Hácha summoned to Berlin and pressured into signing acceptance of a German ‘protectorate’; Slovakia declared independence under German encouragement.
• 15 March 1939: Wehrmacht entered Prague at 6 a.m.; Hitler personally visited Prague Castle that night.
• 17 March 1939: Chamberlain’s Birmingham speech publicly turned British policy.
• 21 March 1939: Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and a corridor across Polish territory; Poland refused.
• 23 March 1939: Lithuania ceded Memel to Germany under pressure.
• 31 March 1939: Chamberlain announced the British guarantee to Poland in the House of Commons; France joined within days.
• April 1939: peacetime conscription introduced in Britain; Mussolini invaded Albania on 7 April; Greece and Romania received similar guarantees later in April.

practice_questions.text: Study Sources B and C. Source B: An extract from a 1939 private memorandum by Lord Halifax, British Foreign Secretary, to the Cabinet. ‘The argument for further negotiation has run out. Czechoslovakia was not a German-speaking population; the principle of self-determination cannot be invoked. Public opinion has changed and so must our policy. We must move from concession to deterrence; the Polish guarantee is the means.’ Source C: An extract from a 1939 leading article in The Times, written shortly after the German occupation of Prague. ‘Six months ago this newspaper supported the Munich Agreement on its merits. We do not regret that judgement, given the case as it then stood. But the German action of 15 March is a different matter. The seizure of a Slav population destroys the foundation of appeasement. Trust has not been broken; it never existed.’ Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the end of British appeasement. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and own knowledge; substantiated judgement on each. Secure: Clear evaluation using all three elements; judgement made. Developing: Some evaluation, two of three handled; judgement implicit. Emerging: Description or accusations of bias. Indicative content: Source B — Content: a candid Cabinet rationale for moving from negotiation to deterrence; identifies self-determination as the failed argument. Provenance: a private memorandum to the Cabinet by the Foreign Secretary; reflects genuine policy thinking; not for public consumption. Own knowledge: matches the historical record — Halifax did push the policy turn after Prague; the Polish guarantee followed on 31 March. Source C — Content: a major British newspaper turning against the policy it had previously supported; treats Prague as the watershed. Provenance: a contemporary newspaper editorial designed to influence public and political opinion. Own knowledge: The Times had been a leading supporter of appeasement under Geoffrey Dawson; its turn was a significant signal in British political culture. Judgement: B is useful for the high-level Cabinet calculation; C is useful for the public mood and the role of the press in shaping it. Together they capture the joint shift in elite and public opinion that ended appeasement.

practice_questions.text:
‘The occupation of Prague in March 1939 mattered more than Munich in bringing Britain to war.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Prague took a Slav population, so self-determination — Hitler’s pretext since 1933 — could no longer be used.
• It broke the Munich understanding within six months and destroyed the premise on which Chamberlain’s policy rested.
• Within two weeks Chamberlain made his Birmingham speech and Britain guaranteed Poland; peacetime conscription followed in April.
Challenging the statement:
• Munich created the conditions: it stripped Czechoslovakia of its fortifications and made the March 1939 seizure almost costless.
• British rearmament, which made resistance possible by 1939, was well under way before Prague.
• The decision for war came over Poland in September 1939, not over Prague.
Judgement: Prague was the hinge for British opinion and policy, but it only mattered because Munich had already given Hitler the ground.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how Britain moved from the guarantee to Poland on 31 March 1939 to the introduction of peacetime conscription in April.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 21 March 1939: Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and an extraterritorial corridor across Polish territory; Poland refused.
• 31 March 1939: Chamberlain told the House of Commons that Britain would lend Poland all support in its power; France joined within days.
• Effect: the guarantee committed Britain in advance and reversed the policy of avoiding eastern European commitments, so Hitler could no longer assume Britain would stay out.
• 7 April 1939: Mussolini invaded Albania, and Britain guaranteed Greece and Romania later that month.
• April 1939: Britain introduced peacetime conscription for the first time outside a major war, signalling that rearmament had entered a new phase.
• Limit: the guarantee could deter but not defend — Britain and France had no way of relieving German pressure on Poland, as September 1939 proved.

practice_questions.text:
‘The occupation of Prague ended appeasement because it destroyed British trust in Hitler’s word.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached. Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial. Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question. Indicative content: Supporting the statement: • Munich had committed Hitler to take no further European territory; Prague broke that within six months. • Chamberlain’s authority rested on Hitler honouring agreements, so once trust went the policy could not continue. Challenging the statement — other reasons mattered too: • The seized population was Slav, so the moral case built on self-determination collapsed at the same moment. • British public opinion turned: The Times, which had backed Munich, changed its line and Conservative MPs demanded a new policy. • Strategic logic shifted: the loss of the rump Czech state exposed Poland as the next target, so deterrence replaced negotiation. Judgement: the collapse of trust was the trigger, but the moral, political and strategic cases for appeasement failed together.

practice_questions.text: ‘Leicester rebuilt Kenilworth to win the queen, not to display his own greatness.’ How far does a study of Kenilworth support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Kenilworth and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Leicester’s Building was a four-storey block of state apartments raised so the queen and her ladies could be lodged in modern comfort beside the medieval hall.
• The privy garden below the walls — terraces, obelisks, aviary and fountain — was laid out for royal eyes, and was rebuilt by English Heritage from an eyewitness description.
• The 1575 entertainments argued in allegory for the queen’s hand, and one entertainment pressing the theme was never performed.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• The new gatehouse and the great windows cut into the Norman keep advertised Leicester’s own wealth and taste to every visitor, whether or not the queen came.
• Kenilworth was a royal gift of 1563; keeping it magnificent protected his standing at court and showed what favour was worth.
• A progress served purposes beyond courtship — royal visibility, hospitality to the whole travelling court, and the display of an orderly realm.

[16 marks — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the entertainments staged at Kenilworth in July 1575.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Lady of the Lake pageant welcoming Elizabeth across the mere on her arrival.
• A swimming pageant with a performer as Arion riding a mechanical dolphin on the lake.
• Fireworks reportedly heard many miles away, masques by night and hunting by day.
• The sheer duration and cost — nineteen days, with gossip claiming a thousand pounds a day.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about royal progresses for Elizabeth’s style of rule, using Kenilworth as your example.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Visibility: progresses displayed the queen to her subjects across the country — monarchy performed in person, with Kenilworth 1575 its most spectacular stage.
• Economy: courtiers bore the crushing cost of hosting, so the crown bought magnificence with favour instead of money.
• Control of the elite: the hope and expense of a visit kept nobles competing to demonstrate loyalty — Leicester rebuilt a castle for the privilege.
• Propaganda reach: printed accounts like Gascoigne's carried the spectacle far beyond those present.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of Elizabeth's visit to Kenilworth in July 1575.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arrival, 9 July: greeted by pageantry including the Lady of the Lake welcoming her to the castle across the mere.
• The stay: nineteen days of hunting, bear-baiting, masques, fireworks heard at great distance, and the Arion water pageant on the lake.
• The subtext: entertainments of courtship and marriage, with one pressing entertainment never performed — read by most historians as Leicester's final bid for her hand.
• Departure, 27 July: the queen left unmarried; the visit passed into legend through the Langham letter and Gascoigne's Princely Pleasures.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about what the 1575 visit cost Leicester.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It measures what royal favour was worth pursuing: contemporaries spoke of a thousand pounds a day, on top of years of building — spending aimed at one listener.
• It shows the court economy: Elizabeth's gift of the castle in 1563 flowed back to her as hospitality — favour converted to loyalty and display.
• It shows the risk side of the system: Leicester died in 1588 heavily in debt; competitive magnificence could ruin even the greatest favourite.
• It strengthens the courtship reading: expenditure this extreme fits a suit for the queen's hand, not routine hospitality.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: 'Kenilworth in 1575 shows that entertainment was really politics at Elizabeth's court.' How far does a study of Kenilworth support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Kenilworth and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The pageants argued in allegory — the Lady of the Lake and marriage masques staged Leicester's suit; the unperformed entertainment suggests a message the queen declined to hear.
• The buildings themselves were political instruments: Leicester's Building and the garden existed to honour and persuade one guest.
• The scale of spending only makes sense as investment in favour — the currency of Elizabethan politics.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• Much of the programme was straightforward pleasure — hunting, fireworks, acrobats — the shared culture of the court rather than coded argument.
• The politics had limits: the spectacular suit failed; Elizabeth kept the marriage question unanswered here as everywhere, suggesting entertainment could ask but never decide.
• Progresses served purposes beyond courtship — royal visibility and the display of a loyal, orderly realm.
A developed judgement on how far pleasure and politics can be separated at this court is required for the top level.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1944 Nazi People's Court verdict denouncing the July 1944 plotters as a small clique of cowards) and Interpretation B (a 1960s West German memorial study presenting the plotters as patriotic martyrs whose action preserved an alternative Germany) on the July 1944 bomb plot. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the plotters as treasonous — isolated, self-interested and contemptible.
• Interpretation B presents the plotters as patriotic — representative of an alternative Germany willing to risk death to end the war.
• Main difference: A frames the plot as criminal failure; B frames it as morally and politically significant resistance.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1944 People's Court verdict) and Interpretation B (a 1960s West German memorial study) give different views about the July 1944 bomb plot.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the People's Court verdict aimed to legitimise mass executions; the memorial study aimed to construct a usable post-war German identity.
• They drew on different evidence — the verdict used selective interrogation transcripts; the memorial study used surviving conspirators' testimony, family papers and archival access.
• They were written under different political conditions — the verdict under regime control with no possibility of dissent; the memorial study under the Federal Republic, which adopted the Bendlerblock as official memorial.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'German opposition to the Nazi regime was insignificant because it failed to remove Hitler.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about resistance under the Third Reich?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because no internal opposition toppled the regime — Stauffenberg's bomb on 20 July 1944 failed; Hitler survived; around 5,000 conspirators were eventually arrested.
• Convincing because youth groups (Swing Youth, Edelweiss Pirates) and the White Rose were small in number and easily crushed.
• Less convincing because Galen's August 1941 sermon halted the official T4 programme — opposition could change policy.
• Less convincing because the White Rose's sixth leaflet was smuggled to Britain and dropped over Germany by Allied aircraft — it reached a mass audience.
• Less convincing because significance is not the same as effectiveness — Niemoller, Bonhoeffer, Stauffenberg and the Scholls preserved an alternative Germany that shaped post-war identity.
• Overall judgement: opposition did not topple the regime but it changed specific policies (T4) and preserved a moral alternative that was decisive in shaping the post-1945 Federal Republic. To dismiss it as ‘insignificant’ conflates effectiveness with significance.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the war on the German civilian population between 1939 and 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Total-war mobilisation from February 1943 closed cinemas, restaurants and luxury shops; women aged 17 to 45 were required to register for war work; rationing tightened (bread, meat, fat).
• Allied bombing killed around 600,000 German civilians by 1945 and made 7.5 million homeless — Hamburg's firestorm (July 1943) killed around 37,000 in a week; Dresden's destruction (February 1945) killed around 25,000 in two nights.
• Forced labour from across occupied Europe — around 7.5 million foreign workers in German factories by 1944, a quarter of the workforce, often housed in barracks under starvation rations.
• Refugee crisis — around 12 million ethnic Germans fled westward from the eastern provinces in winter 1944–45; the sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff in January 1945 cost around 9,000 lives.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of opposition to Nazi rule in Germany between 1933 and 1945.
You may consider:
• youth, religious and student opposition
• conservative and military resistance, including the July 1944 bomb plot.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Youth subcultures: Swing Youth (mostly middle-class, Hamburg/Berlin, jazz from 1939); Edelweiss Pirates (working-class, Ruhr/Cologne, attacking HJ patrols, 12 hanged in Cologne 1944).
• Religious resistance: Niemoller imprisoned 1937–45; Bonhoeffer hanged at Flossenburg 9 April 1945; Galen's August 1941 sermon halting the official T4 programme; Catholic encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (1937).
• Student resistance: White Rose, Munich, 1942–43; six leaflets; Hans, Sophie Scholl and Probst executed by guillotine 22 February 1943; Huber and others followed.
• Conservative-military resistance: Beck, Goerdeler, Stauffenberg; Operation Valkyrie; bomb at Wolf's Lair 12:42pm on 20 July 1944; conspirators shot the same night; around 5,000 arrested.
• Limits and significance: no opposition removed Hitler; significance lies in preserving alternative Germany; Galen's sermon changed T4 policy; the Bendlerblock became post-war memorial; effectiveness vs significance is the key historiographical move.
• Conclusion: youth, religious, student and conservative resistance never combined into a single movement and never threatened the regime militarily. They were significant rather than effective — preserving moral and political alternatives that became foundational for the Federal Republic after 1945.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1990s historian arguing wartime opposition was driven mainly by revulsion at Nazi crimes against Jews and the disabled) and Interpretation B (a 2000s historian arguing wartime opposition was driven mainly by recognition that the war could not be won) on the motives of the July 1944 conspirators. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A frames the conspirators as morally driven — Holocaust knowledge, T4, Kristallnacht as the trigger.
• Interpretation B frames the conspirators as strategically driven — military defeat after Stalingrad, the bombing campaign, the prospect of Soviet occupation.
• Main difference: A sees moral revulsion as the engine; B sees calculation about war's outcome as the engine.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Richard Nixon to the American people, 1 June 1972, on his return from Moscow.
‘In Moscow we have signed agreements that will reduce the danger of nuclear war and slow the costly arms race. We have not ended our differences with the Soviet Union. What we have done is establish that even the most powerful adversaries can sit at a table and limit the risks of their rivalry. The road from confrontation to negotiation is long, but the first turn has been taken.’

Source A suggests that Nixon saw the Moscow agreements as a beginning rather than an ending. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
From the source:
• Reducing the danger of nuclear war.
• Slowing the costly arms race.
• Establishing that even ‘most powerful adversaries’ can sit at a table and limit the risks of their rivalry.
• Taking the ‘first turn’ from confrontation to negotiation.
• Nixon explicitly notes that differences have not been ended — useful balance.
Contextual knowledge to credit:
• Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1 in Moscow on 26 May 1972.
• SALT 1 capped missile numbers but not multiple warheads, so arsenals kept growing.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a confidential briefing by US National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger to President Nixon, 12 May 1972.
‘The Soviets need this agreement more than we do. Their economy cannot match continued arms spending; their split with China leaves them encircled; the East European bloc requires constant policing. They want SALT to free resources for these problems. We can therefore demand a tight agreement on land-based missiles where they have an advantage.’

Source C: An extract from a confidential memorandum from Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko to General Secretary Brezhnev, 8 May 1972.
‘An agreement at Moscow will give us breathing space and recognise our parity with the United States. The American interest in this is real but limited — their domestic politics, particularly Vietnam, force them toward concessions. We should hold firm on missile defence limits and accept the freeze on offensive numbers.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying superpower motives for SALT 1. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Kissinger argues the Soviets are the more eager party because of economy, China and Eastern Europe. Provenance: a confidential briefing for the President, two weeks before the summit — likely to give frank strategic analysis. Own knowledge: the Sino-Soviet split was real; Soviet defence spending was rising as a share of GNP; the bloc did require constant management.
Source C — Content: Gromyko argues American domestic politics, especially Vietnam, push the United States toward concessions. Provenance: a confidential memorandum between top Soviet officials — likely to give frank assessment of bargaining position. Own knowledge: Vietnam was indeed a major drag on Nixon’s domestic position; opposition to the war was rising.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding US assumptions and their inflation of Soviet weakness; C is useful for understanding Soviet assumptions and their inflation of US weakness — together they show how each side believed the other needed the deal more, which is itself a feature of détente bargaining.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how superpower relations developed from the end of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962 to the signing of SALT 1 in May 1972.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (dates, treaties, leaders); reaches SALT 1 through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• June 1963: Washington-Moscow hotline opened to prevent dangerous misunderstandings.
• August 1963: Partial Test Ban Treaty banned nuclear testing in the atmosphere, in space and underwater.
• 1964: Khrushchev removed; Brezhnev took power and stabilised the Soviet leadership.
• August 1968: Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia; the Brezhnev Doctrine declared in November.
• Late 1960s: nuclear arsenals reached mutually assured destruction; Vietnam drained American resources.
• November 1969: SALT talks opened in Helsinki.
• February 1972: Nixon visited China and met Mao Tse-tung, splitting the communist powers.
• 26 May 1972: Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1 in Moscow, including the ABM Treaty and the Interim Agreement on offensive missiles.

practice_questions.text:
‘Détente had brought real change to the Cold War by 1972.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
This question also carries four extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

Mastering: Sustained argument that answers the statement directly; precise and accurate knowledge on both sides; a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting knowledge on both sides; a judgement is reached and supported.
Developing: Some relevant knowledge, mostly on one side; the judgement is asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: General comments with little accurate detail and no real judgement.

Indicative content:
Agree:
• SALT 1, signed in Moscow on 26 May 1972, was the first arms-control treaty between the superpowers.
• The ABM Treaty limited each side to two missile-defence systems, accepting that neither could win a first strike.
• The Basic Principles Agreement committed both sides to settle their disputes peacefully.
• Nixon's visit to Beijing in February 1972 broke the assumption of a single communist bloc.
• Brandt's Ostpolitik had already settled West Germany's relations with Moscow and Warsaw.
Disagree:
• SALT 1 did not cap multiple warheads, so the number of warheads kept rising after 1972.
• Eastern Europe stayed under Soviet control and the Brezhnev Doctrine of 1968 still applied.
• Both systems still treated the other as fundamentally hostile.
• The USA was still fighting in Vietnam and both sides went on backing opposite sides elsewhere.
• The Berlin Wall still stood and Germany was still divided.
Judgement: the way the rivalry was managed changed a great deal by 1972; the rivalry itself changed very little.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F. (Helsinki falls just after the period you are examined on; it is used here to show where détente led.)

Source F: An extract from a confidential briefing by the East German Foreign Ministry to the Politburo, dated September 1975.
‘The Helsinki Final Act consolidates our western border and recognises the GDR’s sovereignty. The price is the human-rights basket, which Western broadcasters will exploit. On balance, the gains exceed the costs — provided we manage the citizens’ expectations of new freedoms with care.’

Source F suggests that the East German government believed it had gained more than it lost at Helsinki. How do you know?

Explain your answer using Source F and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear inference that answers the question, supported by precise detail from the source and by accurate contextual knowledge.
Secure: A supported inference using detail from the source, with some contextual knowledge.
Developing: A valid point taken from the source, but the support is thin or the contextual knowledge is missing.
Emerging: Copies or paraphrases the source without making an inference.

Indicative content:
• Content: identifies the recognition of the GDR’s sovereignty and border as a major Soviet bloc gain — useful evidence of why the bloc agreed to the human-rights clauses.
• Provenance: a confidential briefing for the East German Politburo — likely to give a frank cost-benefit calculation.
• Own knowledge: the Helsinki Final Act recognised existing European borders, including the inner German border, while requiring the signatories to respect human rights.
• Useful interpretation: confirms that the Eastern Bloc itself anticipated the propaganda problem the human-rights clauses would create — supporting the view that détente had real consequences inside the bloc.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the superpowers moved toward détente between Nixon taking office in January 1969 and the signing of SALT 1 in May 1972.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; reaches the end point through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• January 1969: Nixon took office with Henry Kissinger as his National Security Adviser, both wanting to manage the rivalry rather than win it.
• November 1969: the SALT talks opened in Helsinki, the first sustained arms-control negotiation between the superpowers.
• August 1970: West Germany's Ostpolitik produced the Moscow Treaty, accepting Europe's post-war borders and easing tension in the centre of the continent.
• September 1971: the Four Power Agreement on Berlin settled Western access rights, removing the sharpest flashpoint of the previous decade.
• February 1972: Nixon visited Beijing and met Mao Tse-tung, giving Moscow a reason to keep Washington close.
• 26 May 1972: Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT 1 in Moscow - the ABM Treaty limiting missile defences and the Interim Agreement freezing missile numbers for five years.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1972 NOW campaign leaflet calling the Equal Rights Amendment essential to ending sex discrimination) and Interpretation B (a 1973 STOP ERA pamphlet by Phyllis Schlafly arguing the amendment would harm American families). What is the main difference between these views about the women’s movement?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the ERA as the constitutional foundation of equal pay, equal employment and the next stage of women’s legal rights.
• Interpretation B presents the ERA as a threat to family security, alimony, single-sex bathrooms and the existing legal protections that benefited married women.
• Main difference: A frames the women’s movement as the completion of unfinished civil-rights work; B frames it as an attack on the family that ordinary women would lose by.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1972 NOW campaign leaflet) and Interpretation B (a 1973 STOP ERA pamphlet by Phyllis Schlafly) give different views about the women’s movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the NOW leaflet aimed to mobilise career women and progressive activists; Schlafly’s pamphlet aimed to mobilise religious housewives in the South and Midwest.
• They use different evidence — NOW cited employment-discrimination cases and the Equal Pay Act; Schlafly cited the threat of military conscription, ending alimony and mixed-sex facilities.
• They were produced from different ideological positions — a feminist organisation pushing constitutional amendment versus a Catholic conservative defending traditional family roles.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society was the most successful reform programme since the New Deal.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about Johnson’s domestic reforms?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the 1964 Civil Rights Act, the 1965 Voting Rights Act and the 1968 Fair Housing Act ended legal segregation and dramatically increased black voter registration.
• Convincing because Medicare and Medicaid (1965) gave around 19 million elderly and 10 million poor Americans federal health insurance, an achievement the New Deal had not managed.
• Convincing because the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965) was the first major federal aid to education in American history, sending over $1 billion to schools serving poor children.
• Convincing because the poverty rate fell from around 22% in 1959 to around 11% by 1973 — the largest reduction in American history.
• Less convincing because Vietnam War spending rose to around $20 billion a year by 1968 and undermined the War on Poverty financially and politically.
• Less convincing because urban riots in Watts (1965), Detroit (1967) and after King’s death (1968) showed that the underlying inequalities the Great Society addressed were not solved.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on legislative breadth and impact — comparable to the New Deal in scope and arguably greater in lasting reach — but undercut politically by Vietnam.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963) on American women.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Gave a vocabulary to widespread female dissatisfaction with the post-war suburban ideal — ‘the problem that has no name’ named the gap between expectation and lived experience for educated white women.
• Sold around 3 million copies in three years, reaching a mass middle-class audience and prompting consciousness-raising groups across the country.
• Helped inspire the founding of the National Organization for Women in June 1966, with Friedan as its first president; NOW grew from 300 to around 40,000 members by 1974.
• Reframed feminism as a programme for educated women in employment as well as a civil-rights project — setting the agenda for Title VII enforcement, Title IX (1972) and the push for the Equal Rights Amendment.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the women’s movement won major legal victories between 1963 and 1973.
You may consider:
• new women’s organisations and writers, such as Friedan and NOW
• reform-minded presidents and Congresses.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963): around 3 million copies sold; named ‘the problem that has no name’.
• Equal Pay Act (June 1963), signed by Kennedy: banned wage discrimination on grounds of sex.
• Title VII of Civil Rights Act (1964): banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex; word ‘sex’ added by Howard W. Smith.
• Founding of NOW (June 1966): Friedan, Pauli Murray, Aileen Hernandez and 24 others; lobbied for equal pay, anti-discrimination enforcement, childcare and reproductive rights.
• Younger women’s liberation groups (Redstockings, the Furies) pushed harder on cultural and personal politics.
• Title IX (1972): banned sex discrimination in any federally funded education programme; transformative for women’s sport, science and graduate study.
• Reed v Reed (1971): Supreme Court extended equal-protection guarantees to women.
• Roe v Wade (January 1973): legalised abortion across the United States.
• Reform-minded presidents: Kennedy (Equal Pay Act), Johnson (Title VII), Nixon (signed Title IX).
• Conclusion: the legal victories combined writers and organisations naming the problem (Friedan, NOW), allies in the federal government during a reform decade, and Supreme Court rulings extending civil-rights logic from race to sex.
