The defeat of the ERA and the lasting controversy over Roe show the limits of the same period.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Great Society programme launched by Lyndon Johnson from 1964.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It included a ‘War on Poverty’ created by the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act, with Job Corps for vocational training, Head Start pre-school for poor children and Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA).
• It established Medicare in 1965 to provide federal health insurance for Americans over 65 and Medicaid in 1965 for the very poor; together the programmes covered around 29 million Americans by 1969.
• The Elementary and Secondary Education Act (April 1965) was the first major federal aid to education, sending over $1 billion to schools serving poor children.
• The 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act abolished the 1924 quota system that had favoured northern Europeans, opening the door to immigration from Asia, Africa and Latin America.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

practice_questions.text: ‘The role of the individual has been the main factor in changing the relationship between citizen and state in Britain.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of individuals as the main factor:
• Simon de Montfort summoned commoners to Parliament in 1265 — without his political need for support against royalist holdouts, the precedent of representation might not have emerged.
• Emmeline Pankhurst founded the WSPU in 1903 and kept the suffrage cause in the news through arson, hunger strikes and force-feeding.
• Doreen Lawrence campaigned for four years after the 1993 murder to force the 1997 inquiry, whose 1999 report put the language of institutional racism into British policy.

Weighed against war:
• 1914-18 reshaped what was politically possible for women's suffrage; the practical need to redraw the male franchise opened a window for the 1918 Act.
• The English Civil War (1642-51) created the New Model Army, the institutional vehicle for Leveller radicalism.

Weighed against ideas:
• Lockean concepts of natural rights and government by consent shaped the 1776 Declaration of Independence and indirectly the 1832 Reform Act.
• Egalitarian preaching by John Ball in 1381 provided ideological cover that no individual leader could replicate.

Weighed against the economy:
• The 1381 poll tax, the 1815 Corn Laws and 1981 unemployment all created conditions in which protest became likely — with or without specific leaders.
• Industrial decline and the gold standard set the stage for the 1926 General Strike that no individual could have caused alone.

Cross-period weighing:
• Compare 1381 (Tyler and Ball mattered, but the conditions made revolt likely with or without them) with 1903 (Pankhursts mattered, but war work was decisive in 1918).
• Pattern: individuals shape HOW change happens; the wider factors determine WHEN it happens.

Judgement: Top answers argue individuals are necessary but not sufficient. They give campaigns leadership and visibility; the underlying conditions of war, economy, religion and ideas determine whether their efforts succeed.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples comparing individuals to other factors; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: ‘Communication has been the main factor in shaping mass movements in Britain since 1500.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Students should weigh communication against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course. In support of communication: • Sermons and pamphlets carried Leveller ideas through the New Model Army in the 1640s and the Putney Debates of 1647. • The penny post, mass petitioning and the Northern Star made Chartism a national movement in the 1830s and 1840s. • The BBC's coverage of the 1926 General Strike and the suffragette paper Votes for Women shaped how those campaigns were understood. • Television footage of Brixton in 1981 and social media's role in BLM in 2020 organised mass response in a way earlier movements could not. Weighed against the economy: • 1381 poll tax, 1815 Corn Laws, 1926 mining wages, 1981 unemployment — economic distress was always the underlying spark. • Without economic grievance, the best communication networks could not have built mass movements. Weighed against ideas: • Lockean rights, Levellers' Agreement of the People, ‘no taxation without representation’, the suffragette motto ‘Deeds not words’ — ideas gave movements their language. • Communication carried these ideas, but the ideas themselves were what made people act. Weighed against government: • Government repression of communication (Six Acts 1819, 1927 Act) shows the state took it seriously. • Government concession (1832 Act, 1918 Act) is what mass communication ultimately aimed at. Cross-period weighing: • Compare 1381 (sermon-based, slow spread) with 2020 (social media, instant). The form of communication has changed; the role — turning local grievance into national pressure — has been constant. Judgement: Top answers argue communication is the multiplier — it turns grievance into movement and movement into political pressure. But the underlying grievance comes from elsewhere (economy, ideas, religion); communication amplifies but does not create. [16 marks plus 4 SPaG] Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement. Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them. Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1918 Representation of the People Act in the long history of franchise extension since 1832.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: gave the vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 with a property qualification; the electorate almost tripled, from about 7.7 million to over 21 million.
• At the time: ended a century of exclusion of working-class men begun by the 1832 Reform Act, finally delivering universal manhood suffrage.
• At the time: enfranchised around 8.4 million women for the first time in a parliamentary election.
• Over time: set the precedent for the Equal Franchise Act 1928 and the lowering of the voting age to 18 in 1969.
• Over time: completed the long arc of franchise extension begun by Chartism's six points in 1838 — five of which were now law.
• Over time: shifted the basis of British politics from a property-based franchise to a citizenship-based one, the modern foundation of British democracy.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the Act without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the relationship between citizen and state in Britain in 1215 was different from that relationship in 2010.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference in political voice: in 1215 there was no Parliament and Magna Carta protected only free men, a minority; by 2010 every adult citizen could vote, stand for election and petition Parliament.
• Difference in legal status: in 1215 most people were unfree villeins tied to a lord's land; by 2010 the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Equality Act 2010 gave rights enforceable in British courts.
• Difference in how the state answers challenge: in 1215 the king had the charter annulled within ten weeks and went back to war; by 2010 challenge ran through elections, the courts, a free press and public inquiry.
• Difference in who counts as the political nation: in 1215 it was the barons and the Church; by 2010 citizenship was defined by law rather than by land, birth or religion.

[8 marks — 4 marks per difference: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail]

Mastering: Two distinct ways, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two ways with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Levellers and the Chartists were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Similarity: both demanded an extension of the franchise to ordinary men — the Agreement of the People (1647) proposed manhood suffrage; the People's Charter (1838) demanded universal manhood suffrage. • Similarity: both used the printing press to spread ideas across the country — Leveller pamphlets in the 1640s, the Northern Star in the 1830s and 1840s. • Similarity: both were rejected in their own moment but their core demands eventually became law — manhood suffrage in 1918, secret ballot in 1872. • Similarity: both faced state repression — the Levellers suppressed at Burford in 1649; Newport Rising Chartists transported in 1840. [8 marks — 4 marks per similarity: a clear point developed with specific supporting detail] Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise detail. Secure: Two similarities with some support. Developing: Two simple points. Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the seven AQA factors framework for understanding the changing relationship between citizen and state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time of study: provides a structure for thinking about cause and consequence across an 850-year sweep that would otherwise feel like disconnected events.
• At the time of study: directly maps to the 16-mark factors essay, which asks students to weigh the named factor against others.
• At the time of study: forces students to recognise that no single cause explains major change — 1381, 1536, 1649, 1832, 1918 and 1981 all required combinations of factors.
• Over time: reflects mainstream historiography on British political change, in which structural conditions interact with individual leadership rather than either dominating alone.
• Over time: equips students with a vocabulary for analysing causation that transfers to other periods and topics.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both immediate and long-term significance with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of the framework's significance with examples.
Developing: Some explanation but limited to immediate significance.
Emerging: Description of the factors without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which government action on public health in 1348 and 1948 were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Note: the exam sets either the similarity version or the difference version of this question, never both. Answer two ways, each dealing with both sides.
• Difference: in 1348 royal government had almost no public health machinery and relied on prayer and street-cleaning orders; in 1948 it created a universal, tax-funded NHS.
• Difference: in 1348 disease was framed as divine punishment; in 1948 it was framed as a public-policy problem to be solved with science and law.
• Similarity: both moments involved central authority responding to mass health crises (Black Death, postwar reconstruction).
• Similarity: both periods relied on individuals to act locally — medieval town councils, modern GPs — because the centre alone could not deliver care.

[8 marks — 4 marks for each way: 1–2 marks for a supported point, 3–4 marks for a developed point that deals with both sides]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Beveridge Report (1942) for medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Beveridge named the five giants (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness) and proposed cradle-to-grave social insurance plus a free national health service.
• At the time: 300,000 copies sold, building public expectation that any postwar government must legislate welfare.
• Over time: directly shaped the 1945 Family Allowances Act, the 1946 National Insurance Act, the 1946 NHS Act and the 1948 National Assistance Act.
• Over time: the contributory model and universal entitlement remain features of 21st-century British welfare.
• Limitation: Beveridge wrote a plan but did not legislate it — a Labour majority and Bevan’s political skill were necessary to deliver the NHS.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named acts.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: the Beveridge Report, Social Insurance and Allied Services, published by the government in December 1942. It named five giants — want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness — and proposed insurance for everyone from cradle to grave. About 300,000 copies were sold to the public.

How useful is Source A to a historian studying why Britain built a welfare state after 1945?
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Useful Is the Source
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Content: naming the giants gave the public a simple map of what reform had to defeat, with disease among them.
• Content: the proposal for a free health service is the direct line to the NHS Act of 1946.
• Provenance: an official report by a civil servant published while the war was still being fought, so it was read as a promise about the peace.
• Contextual knowledge: evacuation and the Emergency Medical Service had already made state action normal; Labour won a landslide in 1945 and legislated the plan.
• Limitations: a plan is not an outcome — it cannot show whether the reforms worked, and the sales figure shows interest rather than agreement.
• Judgement: very useful for the communication factor and for wartime expectations, limited as evidence of what the welfare state delivered.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of content and provenance tested against contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on usefulness for the stated enquiry.
Secure: Clear evaluation of content and provenance supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Comments on content or provenance with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the source without judging its usefulness.

practice_questions.text: Has the role of the individual been the main factor in the development of British medicine? Explain your answer with reference to the role of the individual and other factors. Use a range of examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the individual as the main factor:
• Vesalius (1543), Paré (1530s–90s) and Harvey (1628) corrected Galen on anatomy, surgery and circulation.
• Jenner (1796) developed vaccination through deliberate experiment.
• Lister (1867) applied germ theory to surgery; Bevan (1948) created the NHS through political compromise.

Weighed against science and technology:
• Vesalius needed printing and improved drawing techniques; Lister needed Pasteur’s germ theory (1860s) and Koch’s microbe identification (1876, 1882). Without these tools the individual’s insight could not have been applied.

Weighed against war:
• Nightingale’s reforms required the Crimean platform; penicillin’s mass production required WWII; the NHS required wartime nationalisation of hospitals through the EMS.

Weighed against government:
• The 1875 Public Health Act, the 1911 National Insurance Act and the 1946 NHS Act were delivered by parliamentary majorities, not individual genius.

Judgement: individuals open doors that no committee opens, but their work only becomes systemic medicine when science gives it tools, war creates pressure, communication spreads it and government legislates it. The individual is necessary but not sufficient — in earlier periods (1348, 1665) individuals existed but the supporting factors did not, so change was limited. The right answer is that the individual is the strongest factor in moments of breakthrough, while government dominates the modern era of system-wide change.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes individuals only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the printing press for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: from c1500 the printing press allowed Vesalius’s De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543), with its detailed anatomical drawings, to circulate across Europe within years rather than centuries.
• At the time: Paré’s surgical writings and Harvey’s De Motu Cordis (1628) reached university libraries and practising physicians at a pace impossible under manuscript copying.
• At the time: it weakened the Church’s monopoly over medical learning by allowing lay readers and Protestant universities to access medical texts.
• Over time: the model of printed peer-reviewed publication carried into journals like The Lancet (1823); Lister’s 1867 antiseptic surgery results spread the same way.
• Over time: mass-circulation paperbacks (e.g. the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies in 1942) extended the same logic to public policy.
• Limitation: print only mattered because individuals had something to say — without Vesalius, Harvey or Lister, the press would have spread no medicine.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of science and technology for medicine in nineteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Pasteur’s germ theory (1861) replaced miasma as the explanation of disease.
• At the time: microscopes, staining and culture on agar let Koch tie specific bacteria to anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883).
• At the time: chemistry gave surgery chloroform (1847) and carbolic acid (1865), and engineering gave London Bazalgette’s sewers.
• Over time: it made prevention and cure specific rather than general, leading to Ehrlich’s Salvarsan (1909) and to antibiotics.
• Over time: it gave government the evidence it needed to justify compulsory public health in 1875.
• Limitation: science explained and enabled, but individuals had to apply it and government had to fund it; British doctors clung to miasma into the 1880s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time, with precise examples and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Some significance, weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Identification only, with little explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about Stalin’s leadership during the Great Patriotic War? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat Stalin as a strategic mastermind whose State Defence Committee directed Soviet victory; B may treat him as a leader whose paranoia caused early disasters and whose orders cost Soviet lives.
• A may emphasise Stalingrad and Kursk; B may emphasise Order 227 and Barbarossa paralysis.
• Specific textual reference required for both.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual reference. Secure: comparison with some reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about why the USSR won the Great Patriotic War?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: a Soviet-era account stressing the genius of Stalin and the heroism of the people versus a Western academic account stressing Lend-Lease and German strategic errors.
• Different time of writing: post-1991 archival access changed what historians could prove about Lend-Lease numbers and Soviet losses.
• Different perspective — orthodox Soviet, Western, post-Soviet Russian, German.
• Different evidence: official records, memoirs, captured Wehrmacht documents.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the impact of Operation Barbarossa on the Soviet Union? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test specific claims of the interpretation against named context: 22 June 1941 launch, three million Axis troops, three million Soviet casualties by December, Luftwaffe destroying most of the Soviet air force on the ground.
• Weigh against the Soviet response: factory evacuation east of the Urals, T-34 production, women in industry.
• Cite Stalin’s personal failure to act on intelligence and the impact of the 1937 officer purge.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge with clear judgement. Developing: knowledge unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the eastward evacuation of Soviet industry between July and December 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 1,500 factories dismantled and moved beyond the Urals, out of German bomber range.
• Production of tanks, aircraft and shells restarted within months on new sites in the Urals and Siberia.
• By 1942 Soviet weapons output exceeded German output — reversing the early disaster.
• Created the industrial base for the Stalingrad and Kursk counter-offensives.
• Concentrated industry in the east laid the foundations of the post-war Soviet economy.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the evacuation.]

practice_questions.text: ‘Stalin’s personal leadership was the most important reason the USSR won the Great Patriotic War.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Stalin’s decisions, the contribution of the Red Army and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for Stalin’s leadership:
• Chaired the State Defence Committee that ran the war effort.
• Approved the eastward factory evacuation that saved Soviet production.
• Tactical relaxation of repression and revival of Orthodox Church mobilised patriotic feeling.
• Eventually delegated military strategy to Zhukov and other professionals.

Arguments for other factors:
• Generals such as Zhukov and Konev directed the operational victories.
• Soviet manpower — including 500,000 women in the Red Army — absorbed German offensives.
• Industrial output (T-34 tanks) and Lend-Lease (400,000 trucks, 14,000 aircraft) supplied the army.
• German strategic errors: failing to take Moscow in 1941, dividing Army Group South in 1942.
• Stalin’s mistakes — ignoring Barbarossa warnings, paralysis in June 1941, Order 227 — nearly lost the war.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. Stalin’s decisions on factory evacuation and his eventual delegation mattered, but victory rested on the Red Army, the home front and German strategic errors.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Great Patriotic War on Soviet society between 1941 and 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 27 million dead, with two-thirds civilians; 1,700 cities and 70,000 villages destroyed.
• Half a million women served in the Red Army; female factory employment surged again.
• Tactical relaxation: Orthodox Church reopened, Comintern dissolved, ‘Motherland’ replacing ‘socialism’ in propaganda.
• Continuing repression: Order 270, deportation of Chechens, Crimean Tatars and Volga Germans, SMERSH screening returning soldiers.
• Reinforced Stalin’s personal authority and the legitimacy of the regime through victory.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the war.]

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the design of the White Tower.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A colossal stone keep roughly ninety feet tall with walls up to fifteen feet thick at the base, corner turrets and small high windows.
• Caen limestone dressings imported by sea from Normandy, over Kentish ragstone walling — Norman identity built into the fabric.
• A first-floor entrance reached by a removable external stair, leaving attackers facing blank wall.
• The Chapel of St John the Evangelist built into the keep — a complete Norman church inside the fortress.
• Its position in the angle of the Roman city walls, commanding the Thames approach to London.
• Why it mattered: height, thickness and a first-floor door told Londoners that a small Norman garrison could hold the city against them, and would.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Norman London.

‘London was never really conquered in 1066. It bargained, and the castles William planted in it show that he knew a city that submits by choice can change its mind.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about Norman control of London after 1066? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: London submitted by negotiation rather than conquest, and the Norman castles there were built against that risk.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The city was not taken by assault: William circled it, ravaged the surrounding shires, and its leaders came out to submit at Berkhamsted.
• Fortifications went up in the city’s south-east corner immediately after the coronation, before any revolt had begun.
• Baynard’s Castle and Montfichet’s Tower were planted at the western end, so garrisons bracketed the city from both sides.
• The keep faced inwards as much as outwards: a first-floor entrance up a removable stair and walls fifteen feet thick assume a hostile population close by.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The Roman wall corner and the command of the Thames show the site was also chosen against attack from outside, including a Danish fleet.
• The keep was a palace and treasury as well as a fortress, so it was built for government, not only for fear.
• Two castles in one town was the standard Norman pattern at York and Lincoln too; London was not a special case of distrust.
• The building took a generation and was finished around 1100, long after the danger of a London rising had passed.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the building materials used in the White Tower.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stone itself was the message: against England's timber castles and houses, a ninety-foot stone keep declared permanence — the conquest was not a raid.
• Caen limestone, shipped at great expense from Normandy, made the building visibly Norman — identity and reach displayed in the fabric.
• The cost and the generation-long build show the resources the Norman state could command, including English labour and taxation.
• Durability had practical significance too: the keep resisted fire and assault in ways timber could not, and it still stands — evidence of intent fulfilled.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Normans took control of London after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Late 1066: London submits by negotiation after William's army circles and devastates the surrounding counties; coronation at Westminster on Christmas Day.
• Immediately after: William orders fortifications in the city's south-east corner while he withdraws to Barking — castles inside the city from the start.
• Around the mid-1070s: work begins on the great stone keep under Gundulf of Rochester, protected by the Roman wall angle, commanding the Thames.
• The finished system: the White Tower in the east with Baynard's Castle and Montfichet's Tower in the west, garrisons bracketing England's greatest city.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the White Tower for Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Control of London: the keep overawed the kingdom's largest, richest and most independent-minded city and commanded its river.
• Symbolically: scale, stone and Caen dressings made Norman permanence visible to every Londoner — psychological control alongside military.
• For government: fortress, palace, treasury and prison in one — royal government concentrated in a defensible point.
• Wider pattern: the Tower is the maximum case of the urban castle policy applied at York, Lincoln, Norwich and elsewhere — one building standing for a national system.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: 'The White Tower was built to impress rather than to defend.' How far does a study of the White Tower support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the White Tower and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The expense of Caen stone and the sheer scale exceed any defensive need — a plain keep would defend as well; this one was designed to be seen and understood.
• The chapel, hall and royal chambers show a palace of lordship and ceremony, not a pure fortress.
• By the time the keep was substantially complete (c.1100), the era of great revolts was over — its finished role was statement more than shield.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• Fifteen-foot walls, the first-floor entrance with removable stair, small high windows and the Roman-wall corner are serious defensive engineering, designed while rebellion was live (1067-71).
• A garrison inside a hostile city genuinely needed a secure base — the Tower was to control London, and control needed both fear and physical security.
• The two functions were one Norman idea: a building that could not be taken WAS the impression.
A developed judgement weighing display against defence, tied to named features, is required for the top level.

[16 marks]
Mastering: A sustained judgement, built from named features of the site and tested against wider knowledge of the period.
Secure: Clear argument using site features and relevant contextual knowledge.
Developing: Some use of the site, with limited wider knowledge.
Emerging: Describes the site without answering the statement.

practice_questions.text: ‘Economic resources were the main factor in Britain’s changing relationship with Europe between 1945 and 2020.’ To what extent do you agree? Explain your answer with reference to economic resources and other factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic resources (in support): Marshall aid of $2.7 billion in 1948 tied reconstruction to European cooperation, and by 1961 the EEC was plainly outgrowing Britain.
• Economic resources (in support): the 1973 application was driven by trade and growth once the Commonwealth alternative had faded.
• Government: Heath negotiated entry, Wilson held the 1975 referendum, Cameron called the 2016 referendum to settle a party split.
• War and the Cold War: the EEC began as a Cold War project with NATO as its shield; the end of the Cold War brought the 1992 Maastricht Treaty and eastward enlargement in 2004.
• Ideas: sovereignty was the reason most Leave voters gave in 2016, ahead of immigration.
• Role of individuals: de Gaulle vetoed British entry twice, in 1963 and 1967.
• Judgement: economic weakness pushed Britain towards Europe and economic strain shaped every stage, but the decisions to enter and to leave were political, taken by governments and, twice, by referendum.

[16 marks + 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the named factor against at least two others across the period, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear argument addressing the named factor and at least one other, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Single factor described without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the end of free movement in 2020 for migration to Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: free movement ended on 31 December 2020, eleven months after Britain formally left the EU.
• At the time: a points-based system replaced it, treating EU and non-EU migrants alike on salary and skills.
• At the time: agriculture, hospitality, construction, transport and food processing lost the East European labour they had come to depend on since 2004.
• Over time: net migration rose rather than fell, reaching a record 906,000 in the year to mid-2023, as recruitment shifted to India, Nigeria and the Philippines.
• Over time: new routes carried their own migrations — over 192,000 Hong Kong BN(O) arrivals by 2024, and visas for Ukrainians from 2022.
• Limitation: the change was about who sets the rules rather than about numbers; the political significance is clearer than the demographic one.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 2004 EU enlargement for migration to Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: ten new EU members (eight from Eastern Europe) were granted free movement of workers; Britain, Ireland and Sweden chose not to apply transitional restrictions.
• At the time: actual flows vastly outstripped the Blair government’s 13,000-a-year estimate; Polish, Lithuanian and Slovakian workers settled across Britain.
• At the time: by the 2011 census Polish was the second most-spoken language in England, and Poland was the second most common country of birth after India.
• Over time: structurally embedded East European labour in agriculture, hospitality, construction, transport and food processing.
• Over time: shaped the 2016 referendum — migration was the second most common reason Leave voters gave, after taking decisions in the UK.
• Over time: end of free movement on 31 December 2020 created acute labour shortages in those exact sectors, which the post-Brexit points-based system has only partly resolved.
• Limitation: the British state had legal authority to apply transitional restrictions but chose not to — the ‘significance’ here is partly a story of British political choices.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 2016 Brexit referendum for British migration policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 52%-48% Leave vote on 23 June 2016 mandated the end of free movement.
• At the time: politically toxic for the major parties — Cameron resigned, Labour split, the Conservative Party committed to delivery.
• Over time: 31 January 2020 formal withdrawal; 31 December 2020 end of free movement.
• Over time: post-Brexit points-based system treats EU and non-EU migrants alike on salary and skills criteria; the government chose to use it to recruit globally for the NHS and care sectors.
• Over time: net migration reached 906,000 in the year to mid-2023, nearly three times the peak under free movement — the political settlement turned out to be about who controls migration, not its scale.
• Over time: the Leave vote reshaped the structure of the United Kingdom itself — reviving Scottish independence debate and complicating the Northern Ireland Protocol.
• Limitation: the long-term economic significance is still being assessed; the political significance is already evident.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which migration from the European Union after 2004 was similar to or different from earlier Commonwealth migration after 1948.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Commonwealth migration was based on shared British subjecthood under the 1948 Nationality Act; EU migration was based on free movement under EEC and EU treaties.
• Difference: Commonwealth migrants came from countries with deep British connections through empire; EU migrants from 2004 came from Eastern European countries with no shared imperial history.
• Similarity: both were direct results of British government decisions (1948 Nationality Act; 2004 decision not to apply transitional restrictions) and exceeded official forecasts.
• Similarity: both became politically contested when their scale produced a backlash — the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act after Caribbean arrivals, the 2016 Brexit vote after Eastern European arrivals.

[8 marks — 4 marks per comparison: name the way, then develop it with precise detail]
Mastering: Two developed comparisons with precise dates and named events.
Secure: Two clear comparisons.
Developing: One developed; second basic.
Emerging: Vague generalisation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the end of the Cold War for Britain’s relationship with Europe.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall and 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union ended the security logic that had bound Western Europe together since 1957.
• At the time: the 1992 Maastricht Treaty turned the EEC into the European Union, with deeper political integration; Britain opted out of the single currency.
• Over time: the 2004 EU enlargement absorbed eight post-Communist Eastern European countries, reshaping intra-EU migration.
• Over time: shaped the political environment for the 2016 Brexit referendum — migration debate was inseparable from EU enlargement debate.
• Over time: post-Cold-War European integration eventually became the issue Britain left the EU to escape.
• Limitation: the immediate post-1990 effect was modest — the major migration changes followed the 2004 enlargement, fifteen years later.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and examples.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: ‘The rebuilding of St Paul’s was Christopher Wren’s achievement rather than Charles II’s.’ How far does a study of St Paul’s support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to St Paul’s and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Wren surveyed the old cathedral in 1666 and proposed the dome before the Fire; the design that rose after 1675 was his.
• The Great Model of 1673–4 and the transformed Warrant Design show one architect holding a single vision across a generation.
• Wren brought the new science to the site: geometry and experiment, worked out with Robert Hooke, solved the structural problems of the dome.
Against the statement (site evidence and context):
• Wren built nothing without the royal warrant of 1675, and it was Charles II who added the clause allowing ‘variations, rather ornamental than essential’ that let him change the design.
• The clergy, not Wren, settled the plan: they rejected the Great Model and insisted on a long nave and choir.
• The money came from Parliament’s coal duty under the Rebuilding Acts, not from Wren or the Crown — London paid for its own cathedral by heating itself.
• By 1685 only the choir walls stood; the achievement was still a promise, and the dome belongs to 1710.

[16 marks — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the design finally approved for the new St Paul’s in 1675.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Warrant Design: a traditional long-plan cathedral with nave and choir, approved by royal warrant after the clergy rejected the domed Great Model.
• The royal clause permitting 'variations, rather ornamental than essential', which Wren used to transform the design during construction.
• Classical construction in Portland stone, replacing the Gothic of the old cathedral.
• Its funding framework — the coal tax under the Rebuilding Acts.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the argument over the design of the new St Paul’s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It shows tradition against innovation: clergy defending the English long-plan cathedral against a scientist-architect's centralised classical dome.
• It shows how Charles II governed: rather than impose a side he approved the traditional design and quietly armed Wren with the variations clause.
• It shows the prestige of the new science: the Royal Society's geometry and experiment reshaping the nation's chief church.
• The outcome — a warrant on paper, a dome in the sky — shows where cultural authority was actually moving in Restoration England.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of what happened to St Paul's between 1666 and 1685.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• September 1666: the Great Fire guts the old cathedral; the booksellers' stock stored in the crypt burns; the shell proves unstable.
• Late 1660s: patching attempts fail and demolition is accepted; Wren emerges as the architect of the rebuilding.
• 1670-75: the design battle — First Model, the rejected Great Model of 1673-4, and the 1675 Warrant Design with the royal variations clause.
• 1675-85: the foundation stone laid in June 1675, coal-tax funding flowing, and the choir walls well advanced in Portland stone by the end of Charles II's reign.

[8 marks — a linked narrative: what happened, what that caused, and where it led.]

Mastering: Three linked stages in sequence, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: A clear sequence of events with relevant detail.
Developing: Events described with limited linkage.
Emerging: Simple description; little sequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the coal tax for the rebuilding of London’s churches.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It solved the central problem — a Crown that could not pay (the same poverty exposed on the Medway in 1667) — with a steady parliamentary duty collected at the port.
• It spread the cost in pennies across everyone who burned coal in London: the city rebuilt its own cathedral by heating itself.
• It funded a programme, not just a building: dozens of Wren parish churches rose with St Paul's as a co-ordinated new skyline.
• Its reliability made a thirty-five-year project financeable — long-term public works from long-term public revenue.

[8 marks — two or three developed points, each explaining why this mattered at the time and afterwards.]

Mastering: Two or three points fully developed, each showing why it mattered, with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two points explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Points identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; importance not explained.

practice_questions.text: 'The rebuilding of St Paul's shows the confidence of Restoration England more than its problems.' How far does a study of St Paul's support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to St Paul's and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The decision itself: after plague, fire and the Medway humiliation in three years, England chose to build Europe's grandest new cathedral — recovery declared in Portland stone.
• The Royal Society connection: Wren and Hooke rebuilding with geometry and experiment shows a culture confident in its new science.
• Steady coal-tax finance and walls rising by 1685 show institutions capable of sustaining a generation-long project.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• The site records the problems first: a cathedral ruined by neglect, civil war stabling and fire — the Restoration inherited and suffered catastrophe before it built.
• The design battle shows a divided culture, and the Crown's inability to fund the work itself echoes the bankruptcy behind the Medway disaster.
• Completion lay far beyond the period — in 1685 confidence was a promissory note, not a finished dome.

[16 marks — reach a judgement on the statement using the site and your contextual knowledge.]

Mastering: Site features linked to wider events, both sides weighed, sustained judgement.
Secure: Site features used with relevant contextual knowledge and a judgement.
Developing: Some site detail with limited wider context.
Emerging: Simple description of the site.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from the public text of the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939 by Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov.
‘The two Contracting Parties undertake to refrain from any act of force, any aggressive action and any attack against one another, whether individually or jointly with other Powers. In the event of either Party becoming the object of warlike action by a third Power, the other Party shall in no manner lend its support to this third Power.’

Using Source A, identify two terms of the Nazi-Soviet Pact.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, source-grounded terms with brief embedded support.
Secure: Two clear terms, briefly supported.
Developing: One term clear; second weak or repeats first.
Emerging: General comment without specific terms.

Indicative content:
• Both parties undertook to refrain from any act of force or aggressive action against one another.
• Both parties undertook not to support any third power that attacked the other.
• The agreement applied whether the action was individual or jointly with other powers.
• Implicit term: the public text contained no reference to the secret protocol dividing eastern Europe.

practice_questions.text:
‘Hitler bore overwhelming responsibility for the outbreak of war in September 1939.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout.
Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial.
Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim.
Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Every territorial action between 1933 and 1939 was German: leaving the League, rearmament, the Rhineland, Anschluss, the Sudetenland, Prague and the Danzig demand.
• The invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 was a deliberate German choice, and Hitler ignored the Anglo-French ultimatum.
Challenging or qualifying the statement:
• The Nazi-Soviet Pact removed the eastern obstacle and made the September invasion possible in the form it took.
• A.J.P. Taylor argued in 1961 that Hitler was an opportunist whom other powers enabled rather than a master planner.
• Western failures shaped the conditions: Manchuria, Abyssinia, the Rhineland, Anschluss, Munich and the slow Moscow talks of 1939.
Judgement: the active aggression was always German, so responsibility is overwhelming but not exclusive.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the path to war from the failure of the Anglo-French-Soviet talks in summer 1939 to the British and French declarations of war on 3 September.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as causal chain; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives. Developing: Events listed; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage. Indicative content: • April-August 1939: Anglo-French-Soviet talks dragged; Britain sent a junior delegation by slow ship; Poland refused Red Army transit. • Mid-August 1939: talks broke down; Stalin concluded the West was not serious. • 23 August 1939: Ribbentrop and Molotov signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact in Moscow; secret protocol divided eastern Europe. • 25 August 1939: Britain formalised its alliance with Poland; Hitler postponed the invasion briefly. • 1 September 1939: Germany invaded Poland at 4:45 a.m.; Wehrmacht used Blitzkrieg tactics. • 1-2 September 1939: Britain and France issued ultimatums demanding immediate withdrawal. • 3 September 1939: ultimatums expired; Britain (11 a.m.) and France (5 p.m.) declared war on Germany. • 17 September 1939: Soviet forces entered eastern Poland in line with the secret protocol; Poland ceased to exist by the end of the month.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 cleared the way for the German invasion of Poland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates. Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail. Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial. Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage. Indicative content: • April to August 1939: Anglo-French-Soviet talks dragged; Britain sent a junior delegation by slow ship and would not press Poland to allow Red Army transit. • 23 August 1939: Ribbentrop and Molotov signed the pact in Moscow, and a secret protocol divided eastern Europe into spheres of influence. • Effect: Germany’s eastern flank was secure, so Hitler no longer risked the two-front war that had crippled Germany in 1914-18. • 25 August 1939: Britain formalised its alliance with Poland; Hitler postponed the attack briefly, then went ahead. • 1 September 1939: German forces invaded Poland at 4:45 a.m. using Blitzkrieg tactics. • 17 September 1939: Soviet forces entered eastern Poland under the secret protocol, so German troops did not have to occupy the whole country.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the part the Soviet Union played in the outbreak of war between April and September 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail and dates.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology with weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• April 1939: Britain and France opened talks with Moscow on a tripartite alliance against further German aggression.
• Summer 1939: the talks dragged; Poland refused Red Army transit and Stalin concluded the Western powers were not serious.
• August 1939: Berlin offered a non-aggression pact, territory and time — terms the Western powers would not match.
• 23 August 1939: the pact was signed; the secret protocol assigned eastern Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere.
• 1 September 1939: Germany invaded Poland with its eastern flank secure.
• 17 September 1939: Soviet forces entered eastern Poland, and by the end of the month Poland had ceased to exist as a state.
• Stalin did not start the war, but the pact removed the obstacle that might have deterred Hitler.

practice_questions.text:
‘Hitler was an opportunist rather than a planner in the years 1933 to 1939.’

How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — How Far Do You Agree
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that engages the exact claim, weighs both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout. Secure: Clear argument covering both sides with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached. Developing: Some discussion of both sides but limited weighing; judgement partial. Emerging: Describes events without engaging the claim. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry a further 4 marks on this question. Indicative content: Supporting the statement: • A.J.P. Taylor argued in The Origins of the Second World War (1961) that Hitler had no master plan and exploited the openings other powers gave him. • The timing of the crises was set by circumstance: French elections in March 1936, Mussolini’s realignment by 1938, the failure of the Moscow talks in August 1939. • Hitler backed down over Austria in 1934 when Mussolini resisted, and took it in 1938 when he did not. Challenging the statement: • The broad goals — treaty revision, pan-Germanism and Lebensraum — were set out in Mein Kampf and never changed. • Rearmament from 1933 to 1935 was deliberate preparation, not improvisation. • The invasion of Poland went ahead after the Anglo-Polish alliance was signed, so it was not simply taking an open door. Judgement: most historians now treat Hitler as both — consistent in aims, opportunist in timing.
